versioning_note: Two version fields. `version` tracks crop content (planting dates, sources, biological data) and bumps when data inside `crops` changes. `schema_version` tracks the shape of the dataset (rule structure, sub-object schemas, top-level fields) and bumps when structure changes. They are independent: a content-only edit bumps `version` alone; a structural addition that doesn't change content bumps `schema_version` alone. As of schema_version 2.0, deployed sub-objects include `uscrn_validation` on soil-temp-anchored rules, `resolution_source` on bolt-threshold and heat-pause-anchored rules, and the four-field `source_quote` / `synthesis_note` / `design_note` / `source_disagreements` split on rule objects.

crops.name: Cherry Tomato
crops.description: The easiest tomato for beginners. Cherry tomatoes (including round cherry, pear-shaped, and cocktail types) are prolific, forgiving, and produce all season. Almost impossible to fail with.

3.notes: Short season -- choose varieties under 60 days like Tumbler or Sweet 100. Use black plastic mulch to warm soil.
3.zone_notes: Zone 3 is short-season but well-suited to cherry tomatoes. Cherry types (55-65 day) ripen before first frost even in Z3a. Start seeds 6 weeks before last frost. Choose Sungold, Sweet 100, or Tumbler for reliable harvest.

good.name: Basil
good.why: Repels aphids and whitefly, improves flavor

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Flavor-improvement claims are classic companion-planting tradition. Not documented in peer-reviewed research or extension literature.

good.name: Marigolds
good.why: Deter nematodes and whitefly in soil

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. The nematode component is extension-documented. The claim's additional assertions about deterring whiteflies are not supported in the extension literature on marigolds and should be read as traditional.

good.name: Carrots
good.why: Deep roots break up soil, minimal competition

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Root-zone partitioning is a real ecology concept. 'Carrots loosen soil for tomatoes' is a plausible mechanistic claim but not well-studied for specific pairs.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Flowering plants attracting predatory insects is a documented biological control mechanism (UC IPM, Cornell). Specific pairings vary in effectiveness.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: 'Fennel suppresses neighbors' is a common gardening-book claim. Limited research; allelopathy is real but specific claim pattern is traditional.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Inter-plant competition for N, P, K is a real agronomic concept. Specific 'bad pair' claims often extrapolate beyond what research has shown.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Bad companion claim, no pattern match. Default to traditional pending review.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Tomato hornworm
pests.symptoms: Large green caterpillars (up to 4 inches) stripping foliage. Leaves disappear rapidly. Black droppings on leaves.
pests.cause: Manduca quinquemaculata moth larvae. Mid to late summer pest.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick -- they are well camouflaged but easy to remove. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray. If white cocoons visible on back, leave them -- parasitic wasps are doing the work.
pests.prevention: Till soil in autumn to kill overwintering pupae. Plant dill and basil nearby to attract predatory wasps.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms: Tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings and young plants. Small shiny black beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause: Multiple flea beetle species. Most active in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment: Use row covers on seedlings. Apply diatomaceous earth. Neem oil spray.
pests.prevention: Delay transplanting until plants are large. Use transplants rather than seeds.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Early blight
diseases.symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings on lower leaves first. Affected leaves yellow and drop. Spreads upward through plant.
diseases.cause: Alternaria fungus. Favored by warm wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves immediately. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively. Mulch soil to prevent splash-up.
diseases.prevention: Rotate tomatoes every 3-4 years. Water at soil level. Space plants for airflow. Stake to keep foliage off ground.

diseases.name: Blossom end rot
diseases.symptoms: Dark, sunken, leathery patch at the bottom (blossom end) of fruit. Affects first fruits most. Not contagious.
diseases.cause: Calcium deficiency in developing fruit, caused by irregular watering or root damage -- not a pest or disease.
diseases.organic_treatment: Mulch to maintain even soil moisture. Water consistently. Foliar calcium spray provides some relief. Remove affected fruit.
diseases.prevention: Consistent watering is the key prevention. Avoid root disturbance. Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen.

diseases.name: Septoria leaf spot
diseases.symptoms: Small circular spots with dark borders and pale gray centers, starting on lower leaves. Spots may have yellow halos.
diseases.cause: Septoria lycopersici fungus. One of the most common tomato diseases.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Apply copper fungicide. Ensure good air circulation.
diseases.prevention: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Mulch around plants.

diseases.name: Late blight
diseases.symptoms: Water-soaked, rapidly expanding brown patches on leaves and stems. White fuzzy growth on undersides in humid conditions. Can destroy plants in days.
diseases.cause: Phytophthora infestans oomycete. The same pathogen that caused the Irish potato famine. Spreads rapidly in cool wet weather.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove and destroy all affected material immediately -- do not compost. Apply copper fungicide preventively in wet conditions.
diseases.prevention: Plant resistant varieties. Ensure excellent airflow. Never leave tomato debris in the garden over winter.

watering.frequency: Every 2-3 days in heat, weekly when cool
watering.method: At soil level -- wet foliage spreads disease
watering.signs_overwater: Yellow lower leaves, cracked fruit, soggy soil
watering.signs_underwater: Wilting leaves that recover at night, blossom drop, dry soil

crops.harvest_ready: Pick when fully colored (red, yellow, or orange depending on variety) and slightly soft to a gentle squeeze. They should detach from the vine with a slight twist -- no pulling needed. Flavor is at peak when skin starts to lose its sheen.

start_method.notes: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost. Harden off over 7-10 days before transplanting. Transplant deep -- bury stem up to lowest leaves to encourage roots.

container_notes.notes: Excellent container crop. Use 5-10 gallon pots. Determinate or compact varieties (Tumbling Tom, Tiny Tim) are ideal. Water daily in heat.

recommended: Tumbling Tom (compact-determinate, ideal for hanging baskets and containers)
Patio Choice (yellow, compact-determinate AAS winner, 18" plant)
varieties.note: Cherry-class tomatoes include round cherry, pear-shaped, and cocktail (elongated cherry) types -- cultivation is the same across all. Sungold is consistently rated the best-tasting cherry tomato by home gardeners worldwide. Juliet is the most common cocktail tomato.

rotation.avoid_after: Tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes -- all share blight and fusarium diseases
rotation.note: Always rotate nightshades to a fresh bed -- blight and fusarium can persist in soil for years.

storage.room_temp: 1-2 weeks at room temperature -- never refrigerate ripe tomatoes (cold destroys flavor)
storage.fridge: Refrigerate only if overripe and must be saved -- use within 1-2 days
storage.freezer: Freeze whole -- skins slip off when thawed. Best for cooking.
storage.notes: Keep tomatoes stem-side down at room temperature out of direct sun.

det_indet.detail: Cherry tomatoes are almost always indeterminate -- they grow, flower, and fruit all season until frost kills them. No stopping needed, but they need strong staking or caging. Some compact varieties (Tumbling Tom, Patio Choice) are technically determinate.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Tiny white root emerging from the seed, then a pale shoot pushing upward through the soil.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep soil temperature in the 70-85°F range. A heat mat makes a real difference for staying in the optimal zone. Cover with a humidity dome until sprouts appear.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Have you seen any sprouts yet?
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Tomato seeds need warm soil to sprout -- about as warm as a sunny windowsill, or 75°F if you have a soil thermometer. A heating mat under your seed tray is the easiest way to get there. Cover the tray with a clear plastic lid until the first green shoots appear, then take it off.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Two seed leaves open flat, then the first true leaves emerging between them -- they will look distinctly tomato-shaped.
growth_stages.user_action: Remove the humidity dome the moment sprouts appear. Get them as close to your brightest light source as possible -- leggy seedlings are caused by too little light, not too little water.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Strong stem, 3-4 sets of true leaves, deep green color. Ready to pot up or transplant.
growth_stages.user_action: Begin hardening off 7-10 days before your transplant date. A few hours outside each day, sheltered from wind. Plant deep -- bury the stem up to the lowest leaves and roots will form all along it.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Are they outside yet, or still hardening off?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small yellow flowers in clusters. Each flower is a potential fruit.
growth_stages.user_action: Switch from a balanced feed to a high-potassium fertilizer. Gently tap the flowering stems in the morning to help pollination -- or give them a gentle shake. This really does improve fruit set.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: When the first yellow flowers appear, change to a tomato fertilizer (those usually have more potassium, which the plant needs for fruit). Each morning, give the flowering stems a gentle shake or tap. This helps the flowers make fruit -- it really does work, especially indoors or in places without much wind.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Fully colored fruit that gives slightly to a gentle squeeze. The skin may start to lose its sheen when perfectly ripe.
growth_stages.user_action: Pick regularly -- every tomato you harvest signals the plant to produce more. Leaving ripe fruit on the vine slows production and attracts pests.
growth_stages.log_prompt: First tomatoes picked? Log your harvest.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Slowing production, yellowing lower leaves, nights cooling below 50°F.
growth_stages.user_action: Pinch out the growing tips to direct energy into existing fruit. Bring any nearly-ripe tomatoes inside if frost threatens -- they will ripen on a windowsill.
growth_stages.log_prompt: How was your season? Worth logging what worked.

notifications.title: Time to start your tomatoes indoors
notifications.body: Your last frost date is about {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks away -- the perfect window to get tomato seeds into trays. Find somewhere warm (70-80°F), keep the soil consistently moist, and cover with a dome until you see sprouts. This is where your season begins.

notifications.title: Start hardening off your tomatoes
notifications.body: Your last frost is {{days_until_anchor}} days away. Begin putting your plants outside for a few hours each day -- start sheltered, increase exposure gradually. This week of adjustment makes a real difference to how they settle in after transplanting.

notifications.title: Last frost has passed -- time to transplant
notifications.body: Your tomatoes are ready to go outside for good. Plant them deep -- bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves. Roots will form all along the buried stem and give you a stronger, more drought-tolerant plant.

notifications.title: Your tomatoes should be flowering soon
notifications.body: Small yellow flowers appearing means fruit is on the way. Switch to a high-potassium feed now, and give the flowering stems a gentle shake in the morning to help pollination. Each flower is a potential tomato.

notifications.title: First tomatoes should be nearly ready
notifications.body: Based on when you planted, you should be seeing ripe or nearly-ripe fruit about now. Pick when fully colored and slightly soft to the touch. The more you pick, the more the plant produces -- stay on top of it.

notifications.title: First frost in {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks -- finish strong
notifications.body: Your growing season is almost done. Pinch out the growing tips now so the plant puts all its remaining energy into the fruit already on the vine. Harvest anything you can and bring green tomatoes inside to ripen on a windowsill.

notifications.title: How are your tomatoes doing?
notifications.body: You have not logged anything in a couple of weeks. How is the plant looking? Any flowers, fruit, or pests worth noting? Regular check-ins help you catch problems early.

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- protect your tomatoes tonight
weather_triggers.body: Temperatures are dropping close to freezing tonight. Cover plants with fleece or old bedsheets, or bring containers inside. Tomatoes are frost-tender and one cold night can end your season early.

weather_triggers.title: Heat stress warning for your tomatoes
weather_triggers.body: Several very hot days ahead. Tomato flowers can drop when temperatures stay above 95°F. Water deeply in the early morning, add mulch around the base to retain moisture, and consider shade cloth during the hottest part of the day.

weather_triggers.title: Your tomatoes need deep watering
weather_triggers.body: It has been dry. Inconsistent watering at this stage causes blossom end rot and cracked fruit. Water deeply at the base -- aim for 1-2 inches this week. Mulching around the stem helps hold moisture.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- watch for blight
weather_triggers.body: Humid conditions are ideal for early and late blight. Check lower leaves for dark spots with yellow halos. Remove any affected leaves immediately and do not compost them. Good airflow around the plant is your best defense.

weather_triggers.title: Heavy rain -- harvest ripe tomatoes now
weather_triggers.body: A lot of rain in a short time can split ripe fruit. Pick anything that is nearly ready before it cracks, and check for soil splash on lower leaves which can spread disease.

germination.text: Bottom heat is the single biggest factor in germination speed. A heat mat, the top of your refrigerator, or anywhere consistently warm works well. Most tomato seeds germinate in 5-7 days at 75°F.
Cover your tray with a humidity dome or cling film until the first sprout appears. Remove it immediately when you see growth -- leaving it on causes damping off.

seedling.text: Leggy, stretched seedlings almost always mean not enough light -- not overwatering. Get them as close to a bright window as possible, or use a grow light 14-16 hours a day.
seedling.text_beginner: If your seedlings are tall and thin and look weak, they need more light -- not less water. Move them right next to a bright window (but pull them back a few inches at night if the window gets cold), or set up a grow light to shine on them for 14-16 hours each day. Pale color is a sign of the same problem.

seedling.text: Once you have two sets of true leaves, pot up into individual cells or small 3-inch pots. Tomatoes root all along their stems, so you can bury them deeper than they were -- it builds a stronger plant.

established.text: Harden off properly -- a week of outdoor time before transplanting, starting with just a couple of hours in a sheltered spot. Plants that skip this step sulk for weeks after transplanting.
Plant your tomatoes deeper than they sit in the pot. Bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves. Every bit of buried stem becomes roots.

flowering.text: A gentle shake of the flowering stem in the morning helps pollen transfer and improves fruit set. It sounds fussy but it genuinely makes a difference, especially in a sheltered spot without much breeze.
Stop high-nitrogen feeding the moment flowers appear. Nitrogen pushes leafy growth. What you want now is potassium -- switch to a tomato-specific or high-K feed.

harvest.text: Pick every ripe tomato you can find, every time you check the plant. The more you harvest, the more the plant produces. Leaving ripe fruit on the vine is the most common reason production slows mid-season.
Taste as you go. Different varieties peak at different moments -- some are best just before fully ripe, others need a few more days. Your palate is the best harvest indicator you have.

end_of_season.text: When nights drop below 50°F regularly, pinch out all the growing tips. The plant will stop trying to set new fruit and put everything into ripening what is already there.
Green tomatoes left on the plant when frost threatens can be brought inside to ripen. Lay them in a single layer somewhere cool and dark -- not the refrigerator, which kills flavor.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 4-8 lbs over the season per plant
yield_expectations.peak_production: A good plant at peak will give you a generous bowlful every 2-3 days
yield_expectations.first_year_note: First seasons are for learning. If you get enough for a salad, that is a success. You will get more each year as you learn what your specific garden needs.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Tomatoes are tropical plants and suffer the moment temperatures drop near freezing. Even a brief cold night can blacken leaves and kill young plants. If it happened at transplant, the plant was likely moved out too early -- soil temperature matters as much as air temperature.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Wait until both night temperatures are reliably above 50°F and soil temperature is above 60°F before transplanting. A cheap soil thermometer removes the guesswork.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Tomatoes are susceptible to blight, blossom end rot, and several common pests. Blight spreads fast in wet, humid conditions and usually starts at the lower leaves. Blossom end rot is caused by calcium deficiency triggered by irregular watering -- not a nutrient problem.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently at the base -- not overhead. Remove any affected leaves immediately. Rotate tomatoes to a different bed each year and stake plants to improve airflow.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Tomato plants can run into a few common problems. Blight is a leaf disease that shows up first on the bottom leaves and spreads fastest in wet, humid weather. Blossom end rot is the black or brown sunken spot on the bottom of the tomato -- it looks like a nutrient problem, but it's almost always caused by uneven watering (dry one day, soaked the next). Adding calcium won't fix it. Steady moisture will.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too much water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Overwatered tomatoes show yellowing lower leaves, cracked fruit, and roots that cannot get oxygen. Inconsistent watering -- dry then suddenly wet -- causes fruit splitting and blossom end rot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water deeply twice a week rather than a little every day. Mulching around the base dramatically improves moisture consistency.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too little water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress during flowering causes blossom drop -- no flowers, no fruit. During fruiting, inconsistent moisture causes blossom end rot and cracked skin.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Tomatoes need 1-2 inches of water per week. Mulch heavily to retain moisture, and water at the base never the leaves.

failure_diagnostics.label: Not enough sun
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Tomatoes need a minimum of 6-8 hours of direct sun to produce well. In shade they grow leafy but set little or no fruit, and are much more prone to disease.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Tomatoes are one of the most sun-hungry vegetables. If your current spot is marginal, prioritize this bed for tomatoes next season and move something more shade-tolerant elsewhere.

crops.description_beginner: The easiest tomato to start with. Cherry tomatoes -- the small bite-sized ones, including round, pear-shaped, and elongated types -- give you handfuls of fruit all summer. They forgive uneven watering and inconsistent care better than larger tomato types. A great choice if this is your first tomato.

crops.name: Beefsteak Tomato
crops.description: Large-fruited tomatoes perfect for slicing. Beefsteak-class includes true beefsteak-shape varieties, large globe slicers, and big heirloom slicers -- cultivation is the same across all. Need a long, warm season and sturdy support. Worth the effort for the flavor.

3.notes: Very challenging in Zone 3 -- 80+ day maturity leaves little margin. Choose Fast varieties like Jet Star. Use season extenders.
3.zone_notes: Zone 3 is marginal for large beefsteak varieties (80-100 day maturity). Choose a faster 75-day variety (Celebrity, Early Girl) or consider cherry tomatoes for more reliable harvest. Start 8 weeks before last frost.

good.name: Basil
good.why: Repels aphids and whitefly, improves flavor

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Flavor-improvement claims are classic companion-planting tradition. Not documented in peer-reviewed research or extension literature.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. This claim's nematode component aligns with the extension-documented mechanism, but the 'concurrent companion' application pattern reflects popular gardening practice rather than extension protocol.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Xerces Society documents borage as a pollinator-attractant plant that blooms concurrently with tomato, squash, and cucumber crops, drawing the same bees that pollinate those crops. Source: xerces.org/blog/plants-you-can-eat-are-pollinator-treat. The claim's additional assertions about deterring hornworm are not supported in extension literature; they recur widely in popular gardening sources but without rigorous backing and should be read as traditional.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Root-zone partitioning is a real ecology concept. 'Carrots loosen soil for tomatoes' is a plausible mechanistic claim but not well-studied for specific pairs.

provenance.label: traditional

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Tomato hornworm
pests.symptoms: Large green caterpillars (up to 4 inches) stripping foliage. Leaves disappear rapidly. Black droppings on leaves.
pests.cause: Manduca quinquemaculata moth larvae. Mid to late summer pest.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick -- they are well camouflaged but easy to remove. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray. If white cocoons visible on back, leave them -- parasitic wasps are doing the work.
pests.prevention: Till soil in autumn to kill overwintering pupae. Plant dill and basil nearby to attract predatory wasps.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms: Tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings and young plants. Small shiny black beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause: Multiple flea beetle species. Most active in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment: Use row covers on seedlings. Apply diatomaceous earth. Neem oil spray.
pests.prevention: Delay transplanting until plants are large. Use transplants rather than seeds.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Early blight
diseases.symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings on lower leaves first. Affected leaves yellow and drop. Spreads upward through plant.
diseases.cause: Alternaria fungus. Favored by warm wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves immediately. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively. Mulch soil to prevent splash-up.
diseases.prevention: Rotate tomatoes every 3-4 years. Water at soil level. Space plants for airflow. Stake to keep foliage off ground.

diseases.name: Blossom end rot
diseases.symptoms: Dark, sunken, leathery patch at the bottom (blossom end) of fruit. Affects first fruits most. Not contagious.
diseases.cause: Calcium deficiency in developing fruit, caused by irregular watering or root damage -- not a pest or disease.
diseases.organic_treatment: Mulch to maintain even soil moisture. Water consistently. Foliar calcium spray provides some relief. Remove affected fruit.
diseases.prevention: Consistent watering is the key prevention. Avoid root disturbance. Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen.

diseases.name: Septoria leaf spot
diseases.symptoms: Small circular spots with dark borders and pale gray centers, starting on lower leaves. Spots may have yellow halos.
diseases.cause: Septoria lycopersici fungus. One of the most common tomato diseases.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Apply copper fungicide. Ensure good air circulation.
diseases.prevention: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Mulch around plants.

diseases.name: Late blight
diseases.symptoms: Water-soaked, rapidly expanding brown patches on leaves and stems. White fuzzy growth on undersides in humid conditions. Can destroy plants in days.
diseases.cause: Phytophthora infestans oomycete. The same pathogen that caused the Irish potato famine. Spreads rapidly in cool wet weather.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove and destroy all affected material immediately -- do not compost. Apply copper fungicide preventively in wet conditions.
diseases.prevention: Plant resistant varieties. Ensure excellent airflow. Never leave tomato debris in the garden over winter.

watering.frequency: Every 2-3 days in heat, weekly when cool
watering.method: At soil level -- wet foliage spreads disease
watering.signs_overwater: Yellow lower leaves, cracked fruit, soggy soil
watering.signs_underwater: Wilting leaves that recover at night, blossom drop, dry soil

crops.harvest_ready: Pick when fully red (or variety color) all over, slightly soft to touch, and the skin has a slight give. Shoulder color change from green to red is the last indicator. Avoid waiting until very soft -- pick slightly firm and ripen indoors at room temperature.

start_method.notes: Start 8 weeks before last frost -- beefsteaks need a long season. Harden off carefully. Bury stem deep at transplant.

container_notes.notes: Can be grown in containers but needs very large pots (15+ gallons). Better in raised beds. Indeterminate varieties need strong staking.

varieties.note: Beefsteak-class tomatoes cover three rough sub-types: true beefsteak-shape large slicers (Big Boy, Mortgage Lifter), oblate globe slicers commonly sold under the beefsteak label (Celebrity), and large heirloom slicers (Brandywine). Cultivation is the same across all. Celebrity is the most disease-resistant option -- great for beginners in humid climates.

rotation.avoid_after: Tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes -- all share blight and fusarium diseases
rotation.note: Always rotate nightshades to a fresh bed -- blight and fusarium can persist in soil for years.

storage.room_temp: Up to 1 week at room temperature
storage.freezer: Slice and freeze on trays, then bag. Use for sauces and cooking.
storage.notes: Never refrigerate -- the cold breaks down the cell structure and kills flavor.

det_indet.detail: Beefsteak types are indeterminate -- they keep growing and need continuous support. Can reach 6-8 feet. Prune to 1-2 main stems for biggest fruit and better airflow. Compact-determinate exceptions exist for small spaces (Bush Beefsteak ~62 days, Bush Early Girl ~65 days).

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Tiny white root emerging from the seed, then a pale shoot pushing upward through the soil.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep soil temperature in the 70-85°F range. A heat mat makes a real difference for staying in the optimal zone. Cover with a humidity dome until sprouts appear.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Have you seen any sprouts yet?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Two seed leaves open flat, then the first true leaves emerging between them -- they will look distinctly tomato-shaped.
growth_stages.user_action: Remove the humidity dome the moment sprouts appear. Get them as close to your brightest light source as possible -- leggy seedlings are caused by too little light, not too little water.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Strong stem, 3-4 sets of true leaves, deep green color. Ready to pot up or transplant.
growth_stages.user_action: Begin hardening off 7-10 days before your transplant date. A few hours outside each day, sheltered from wind. Plant deep -- bury the stem up to the lowest leaves and roots will form all along it.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Are they outside yet, or still hardening off?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small yellow flowers in clusters. Each flower is a potential fruit.
growth_stages.user_action: Switch from a balanced feed to a high-potassium fertilizer. Gently tap the flowering stems in the morning to help pollination -- or give them a gentle shake. This really does improve fruit set.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Fully colored fruit that gives slightly to a gentle squeeze. The skin may start to lose its sheen when perfectly ripe.
growth_stages.user_action: Pick regularly -- every tomato you harvest signals the plant to produce more. Leaving ripe fruit on the vine slows production and attracts pests.
growth_stages.log_prompt: First tomatoes picked? Log your harvest.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Slowing production, yellowing lower leaves, nights cooling below 50°F.
growth_stages.user_action: Pinch out the growing tips to direct energy into existing fruit. Bring any nearly-ripe tomatoes inside if frost threatens -- they will ripen on a windowsill.
growth_stages.log_prompt: How was your season? Worth logging what worked.

notifications.title: Time to start your tomatoes indoors
notifications.body: Your last frost date is about {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks away -- the perfect window to get tomato seeds into trays. Find somewhere warm (70-80°F), keep the soil consistently moist, and cover with a dome until you see sprouts. This is where your season begins.

notifications.title: Start hardening off your tomatoes
notifications.body: Your last frost is {{days_until_anchor}} days away. Begin putting your plants outside for a few hours each day -- start sheltered, increase exposure gradually. This week of adjustment makes a real difference to how they settle in after transplanting.

notifications.title: Last frost has passed -- time to transplant
notifications.body: Your tomatoes are ready to go outside for good. Plant them deep -- bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves. Roots will form all along the buried stem and give you a stronger, more drought-tolerant plant.

notifications.title: Your tomatoes should be flowering soon
notifications.body: Small yellow flowers appearing means fruit is on the way. Switch to a high-potassium feed now, and give the flowering stems a gentle shake in the morning to help pollination. Each flower is a potential tomato.

notifications.title: First tomatoes should be nearly ready
notifications.body: Based on when you planted, you should be seeing ripe or nearly-ripe fruit about now. Pick when fully colored and slightly soft to the touch. The more you pick, the more the plant produces -- stay on top of it.

notifications.title: First frost in {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks -- finish strong
notifications.body: Your growing season is almost done. Pinch out the growing tips now so the plant puts all its remaining energy into the fruit already on the vine. Harvest anything you can and bring green tomatoes inside to ripen on a windowsill.

notifications.title: How are your tomatoes doing?
notifications.body: You have not logged anything in a couple of weeks. How is the plant looking? Any flowers, fruit, or pests worth noting? Regular check-ins help you catch problems early.

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- protect your tomatoes tonight
weather_triggers.body: Temperatures are dropping close to freezing tonight. Cover plants with fleece or old bedsheets, or bring containers inside. Tomatoes are frost-tender and one cold night can end your season early.

weather_triggers.title: Heat stress warning for your tomatoes
weather_triggers.body: Several very hot days ahead. Tomato flowers can drop when temperatures stay above 95°F. Water deeply in the early morning, add mulch around the base to retain moisture, and consider shade cloth during the hottest part of the day.

weather_triggers.title: Your tomatoes need deep watering
weather_triggers.body: It has been dry. Inconsistent watering at this stage causes blossom end rot and cracked fruit. Water deeply at the base -- aim for 1-2 inches this week. Mulching around the stem helps hold moisture.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- watch for blight
weather_triggers.body: Humid conditions are ideal for early and late blight. Check lower leaves for dark spots with yellow halos. Remove any affected leaves immediately and do not compost them. Good airflow around the plant is your best defense.

weather_triggers.title: Heavy rain -- harvest ripe tomatoes now
weather_triggers.body: A lot of rain in a short time can split ripe fruit. Pick anything that is nearly ready before it cracks, and check for soil splash on lower leaves which can spread disease.

germination.text: Bottom heat is the single biggest factor in germination speed. A heat mat, the top of your refrigerator, or anywhere consistently warm works well. Most tomato seeds germinate in 5-7 days at 75°F.
Cover your tray with a humidity dome or cling film until the first sprout appears. Remove it immediately when you see growth -- leaving it on causes damping off.

seedling.text: Leggy, stretched seedlings almost always mean not enough light -- not overwatering. Get them as close to a bright window as possible, or use a grow light 14-16 hours a day.

Once you have two sets of true leaves, pot up into individual cells or small 3-inch pots. Tomatoes root all along their stems, so you can bury them deeper than they were -- it builds a stronger plant.

established.text: Harden off properly -- a week of outdoor time before transplanting, starting with just a couple of hours in a sheltered spot. Plants that skip this step sulk for weeks after transplanting.
Plant your tomatoes deeper than they sit in the pot. Bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves. Every bit of buried stem becomes roots.

flowering.text: A gentle shake of the flowering stem in the morning helps pollen transfer and improves fruit set. It sounds fussy but it genuinely makes a difference, especially in a sheltered spot without much breeze.
Stop high-nitrogen feeding the moment flowers appear. Nitrogen pushes leafy growth. What you want now is potassium -- switch to a tomato-specific or high-K feed.

harvest.text: Pick every ripe tomato you can find, every time you check the plant. The more you harvest, the more the plant produces. Leaving ripe fruit on the vine is the most common reason production slows mid-season.
Taste as you go. Different varieties peak at different moments -- some are best just before fully ripe, others need a few more days. Your palate is the best harvest indicator you have.

end_of_season.text: When nights drop below 50°F regularly, pinch out all the growing tips. The plant will stop trying to set new fruit and put everything into ripening what is already there.
Green tomatoes left on the plant when frost threatens can be brought inside to ripen. Lay them in a single layer somewhere cool and dark -- not the refrigerator, which kills flavor.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 10-20 lbs over the season -- fewer but much larger fruit
yield_expectations.peak_production: A healthy beefsteak at peak produces 1-3 large fruits per week
yield_expectations.first_year_note: First seasons are for learning. If you get enough for a salad, that is a success. You will get more each year as you learn what your specific garden needs.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Tomatoes are tropical plants and suffer the moment temperatures drop near freezing. Even a brief cold night can blacken leaves and kill young plants. If it happened at transplant, the plant was likely moved out too early -- soil temperature matters as much as air temperature.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Wait until both night temperatures are reliably above 50°F and soil temperature is above 60°F before transplanting. A cheap soil thermometer removes the guesswork.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Tomatoes are susceptible to blight, blossom end rot, and several common pests. Blight spreads fast in wet, humid conditions and usually starts at the lower leaves. Blossom end rot is caused by calcium deficiency triggered by irregular watering -- not a nutrient problem.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently at the base -- not overhead. Remove any affected leaves immediately. Rotate tomatoes to a different bed each year and stake plants to improve airflow.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too much water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Overwatered tomatoes show yellowing lower leaves, cracked fruit, and roots that cannot get oxygen. Inconsistent watering -- dry then suddenly wet -- causes fruit splitting and blossom end rot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water deeply twice a week rather than a little every day. Mulching around the base dramatically improves moisture consistency.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too little water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress during flowering causes blossom drop -- no flowers, no fruit. During fruiting, inconsistent moisture causes blossom end rot and cracked skin.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Tomatoes need 1-2 inches of water per week. Mulch heavily to retain moisture, and water at the base never the leaves.

failure_diagnostics.label: Not enough sun
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Tomatoes need a minimum of 6-8 hours of direct sun to produce well. In shade they grow leafy but set little or no fruit, and are much more prone to disease.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Tomatoes are one of the most sun-hungry vegetables. If your current spot is marginal, prioritize this bed for tomatoes next season and move something more shade-tolerant elsewhere.

crops.name: Roma Tomato
crops.description: Paste tomato with meaty flesh and low moisture -- ideal for sauces, canning, and drying. Reliable producer with fewer disease issues than slicers.

3.notes: Choose Viva Italia or Sunrise Sauce for shortest days to maturity. Black plastic mulch is essential.
3.zone_notes: Short season -- start indoors early and choose fast-maturing varieties under 65 days.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: Many gardeners plant transplants the last week or two of May, after danger of frost has passed and air and soil temperatures warm. (MSU)
plant_out.synthesis_note: Start your warm season crops indoors for transplanting in mid-June, once the threat of frost has passed. Transplant outdoors after all danger of frost has passed and the soil has warmed. Don't be in a rush to transplant these tropical species. (UMaine, northern Maine Z3-4; UMN; NDSU)

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note: The seeds are sown six to eight weeks before the last frost date in your area. Roma and paste varieties are typically determinate (73-80 days to maturity); a 6-week indoor start is standard. (VCE 426-418; UMN Extension)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: Roma and paste tomatoes typically mature 73-80 days from transplant. Determinate growth means fruit ripens in a concentrated 2-3 week window. (UMN Extension; VCE 426-418)
harvest_start.design_note: Conservative placement uses 76 day mid-point.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.source_quote: Pick all the fruit and bring it indoors before the first frost at the end of summer. (UMN)
harvest_end.design_note: Conservative policy: harvest_end = first_frost - 5 days to buffer against frost-risk week.

4.notes: Roma's shorter season makes it more reliable than slicers in Zone 4. Harvest before frost threatens.
4.zone_notes: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost. Choose fast-maturing varieties for best yield.

plant_out.source_quote: Many gardeners plant transplants the last week or two of May, after danger of frost has passed and air and soil temperatures warm. (MSU)
plant_out.synthesis_note: Start your warm season crops indoors for transplanting in mid-June, once the threat of frost has passed. pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Tomato hornworm
pests.symptoms: Large green caterpillars (up to 4 inches) stripping foliage. Leaves disappear rapidly. Black droppings on leaves.
pests.cause: Manduca quinquemaculata moth larvae. Mid to late summer pest.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick -- they are well camouflaged but easy to remove. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray. If white cocoons visible on back, leave them -- parasitic wasps are doing the work.
pests.prevention: Till soil in autumn to kill overwintering pupae. Plant dill and basil nearby to attract predatory wasps.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms: Tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings and young plants. Small shiny black beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause: Multiple flea beetle species. Most active in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment: Use row covers on seedlings. Apply diatomaceous earth. Neem oil spray.
pests.prevention: Delay transplanting until plants are large. Use transplants rather than seeds.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Early blight
diseases.symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings on lower leaves first. Affected leaves yellow and drop. Spreads upward through plant.
diseases.cause: Alternaria fungus. Favored by warm wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves immediately. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively. Mulch soil to prevent splash-up.
diseases.prevention: Rotate tomatoes every 3-4 years. Water at soil level. Space plants for airflow. Stake to keep foliage off ground.

diseases.name: Blossom end rot
diseases.symptoms: Dark, sunken, leathery patch at the bottom (blossom end) of fruit. Affects first fruits most. Not contagious.
diseases.cause: Calcium deficiency in developing fruit, caused by irregular watering or root damage -- not a pest or disease.
diseases.organic_treatment: Mulch to maintain even soil moisture. Water consistently. Foliar calcium spray provides some relief. Remove affected fruit.
diseases.prevention: Consistent watering is the key prevention. Avoid root disturbance. Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen.

diseases.name: Septoria leaf spot
diseases.symptoms: Small circular spots with dark borders and pale gray centers, starting on lower leaves. Spots may have yellow halos.
diseases.cause: Septoria lycopersici fungus. One of the most common tomato diseases.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Apply copper fungicide. Ensure good air circulation.
diseases.prevention: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Mulch around plants.

diseases.name: Late blight
diseases.symptoms: Water-soaked, rapidly expanding brown patches on leaves and stems. White fuzzy growth on undersides in humid conditions. Can destroy plants in days.
diseases.cause: Phytophthora infestans oomycete. The same pathogen that caused the Irish potato famine. Spreads rapidly in cool wet weather.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove and destroy all affected material immediately -- do not compost. Apply copper fungicide preventively in wet conditions.
diseases.prevention: Plant resistant varieties. Ensure excellent airflow. Never leave tomato debris in the garden over winter.

crops.harvest_ready: Pick when deep red all over, firm but yielding to gentle squeeze. Roma skins are thicker so feel firmer than slicing tomatoes at peak ripeness.

start_method.notes: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost. Harden off over 7-10 days.

container_notes.notes: Good container tomato. 10-gallon pot minimum. Determinate types need less support.

varieties.note: Juliet is technically a plum type but more crack-resistant and easier to grow than San Marzano.

rotation.avoid_after: Tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes -- all share blight and fusarium diseases
rotation.note: Always rotate nightshades to a fresh bed -- blight and fusarium can persist in soil for years.

det_indet.detail: Most Roma varieties are determinate -- they grow to a set height (3-4 feet), produce a concentrated crop over 2-3 weeks, then stop. Less pruning needed. Good for sauce making -- all fruit ripens at once.

storage.room_temp: 1 week at room temperature -- never refrigerate
storage.freezer: Core, freeze whole for sauces -- or slice and freeze flat
storage.notes: Roma is the paste tomato -- freeze in large batches for winter sauce.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Tiny white root emerging from the seed, then a pale shoot pushing upward through the soil.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep soil temperature between 70-80°F. A heat mat makes a real difference. Cover with a humidity dome until sprouts appear.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Have you seen any sprouts yet?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Two seed leaves open flat, then the first true leaves emerging between them -- they will look distinctly tomato-shaped.
growth_stages.user_action: Remove the humidity dome the moment sprouts appear. Get them as close to your brightest light source as possible -- leggy seedlings are caused by too little light, not too little water.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Strong stem, 3-4 sets of true leaves, deep green color. Ready to pot up or transplant.
growth_stages.user_action: Begin hardening off 7-10 days before your transplant date. A few hours outside each day, sheltered from wind. Plant deep -- bury the stem up to the lowest leaves and roots will form all along it.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Are they outside yet, or still hardening off?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small yellow flowers in clusters. Each flower is a potential fruit.
growth_stages.user_action: Switch from a balanced feed to a high-potassium fertilizer. Gently tap the flowering stems in the morning to help pollination -- or give them a gentle shake. This really does improve fruit set.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Fully colored fruit that gives slightly to a gentle squeeze. The skin may start to lose its sheen when perfectly ripe.
growth_stages.user_action: Pick regularly -- every tomato you harvest signals the plant to produce more. Leaving ripe fruit on the vine slows production and attracts pests.
growth_stages.log_prompt: First tomatoes picked? Log your harvest.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Slowing production, yellowing lower leaves, nights cooling below 50°F.
growth_stages.user_action: Pinch out the growing tips to direct energy into existing fruit. Bring any nearly-ripe tomatoes inside if frost threatens -- they will ripen on a windowsill.
growth_stages.log_prompt: How was your season? Worth logging what worked.

notifications.title: Time to start your tomatoes indoors
notifications.body: Your last frost date is about {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks away -- the perfect window to get tomato seeds into trays. Find somewhere warm (70-80°F), keep the soil consistently moist, and cover with a dome until you see sprouts. This is where your season begins.

notifications.title: Start hardening off your tomatoes
notifications.body: Your last frost is {{days_until_anchor}} days away. Begin putting your plants outside for a few hours each day -- start sheltered, increase exposure gradually. This week of adjustment makes a real difference to how they settle in after transplanting.

notifications.title: Last frost has passed -- time to transplant
notifications.body: Your tomatoes are ready to go outside for good. Plant them deep -- bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves. Roots will form all along the buried stem and give you a stronger, more drought-tolerant plant.

notifications.title: Your tomatoes should be flowering soon
notifications.body: Small yellow flowers appearing means fruit is on the way. Switch to a high-potassium feed now, and give the flowering stems a gentle shake in the morning to help pollination. Each flower is a potential tomato.

notifications.title: First tomatoes should be nearly ready
notifications.body: Based on when you planted, you should be seeing ripe or nearly-ripe fruit about now. Pick when fully colored and slightly soft to the touch. The more you pick, the more the plant produces -- stay on top of it.

notifications.title: First frost in {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks -- finish strong
notifications.body: Your growing season is almost done. Pinch out the growing tips now so the plant puts all its remaining energy into the fruit already on the vine. Harvest anything you can and bring green tomatoes inside to ripen on a windowsill.

notifications.title: How are your tomatoes doing?
notifications.body: You have not logged anything in a couple of weeks. How is the plant looking? Any flowers, fruit, or pests worth noting? Regular check-ins help you catch problems early.

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- protect your tomatoes tonight
weather_triggers.body: Temperatures are dropping close to freezing tonight. Cover plants with fleece or old bedsheets, or bring containers inside. Tomatoes are frost-tender and one cold night can end your season early.

weather_triggers.title: Heat stress warning for your tomatoes
weather_triggers.body: Several very hot days ahead. Tomato flowers can drop when temperatures stay above 95°F. Water deeply in the early morning, add mulch around the base to retain moisture, and consider shade cloth during the hottest part of the day.

weather_triggers.title: Your tomatoes need deep watering
weather_triggers.body: It has been dry. Inconsistent watering at this stage causes blossom end rot and cracked fruit. Water deeply at the base -- aim for 1-2 inches this week. Mulching around the stem helps hold moisture.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- watch for blight
weather_triggers.body: Humid conditions are ideal for early and late blight. Check lower leaves for dark spots with yellow halos. Remove any affected leaves immediately and do not compost them. Good airflow around the plant is your best defense.

weather_triggers.title: Heavy rain -- harvest ripe tomatoes now
weather_triggers.body: A lot of rain in a short time can split ripe fruit. Pick anything that is nearly ready before it cracks, and check for soil splash on lower leaves which can spread disease.

germination.text: Bottom heat is the single biggest factor in germination speed. A heat mat, the top of your refrigerator, or anywhere consistently warm works well. Most tomato seeds germinate in 5-7 days at 75°F.
Cover your tray with a humidity dome or cling film until the first sprout appears. Remove it immediately when you see growth -- leaving it on causes damping off.

seedling.text: Leggy, stretched seedlings almost always mean not enough light -- not overwatering. Get them as close to a bright window as possible, or use a grow light 14-16 hours a day.

Once you have two sets of true leaves, pot up into individual cells or small 3-inch pots. Tomatoes root all along their stems, so you can bury them deeper than they were -- it builds a stronger plant.

established.text: Harden off properly -- a week of outdoor time before transplanting, starting with just a couple of hours in a sheltered spot. Plants that skip this step sulk for weeks after transplanting.
Plant your tomatoes deeper than they sit in the pot. Bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves. Every bit of buried stem becomes roots.

flowering.text: A gentle shake of the flowering stem in the morning helps pollen transfer and improves fruit set. It sounds fussy but it genuinely makes a difference, especially in a sheltered spot without much breeze.
Stop high-nitrogen feeding the moment flowers appear. Nitrogen pushes leafy growth. What you want now is potassium -- switch to a tomato-specific or high-K feed.

harvest.text: Pick every ripe tomato you can find, every time you check the plant. The more you harvest, the more the plant produces. Leaving ripe fruit on the vine is the most common reason production slows mid-season.
Taste as you go. Different varieties peak at different moments -- some are best just before fully ripe, others need a few more days. Your palate is the best harvest indicator you have.

end_of_season.text: When nights drop below 50°F regularly, pinch out all the growing tips. The plant will stop trying to set new fruit and put everything into ripening what is already there.
Green tomatoes left on the plant when frost threatens can be brought inside to ripen. Lay them in a single layer somewhere cool and dark -- not the refrigerator, which kills flavor.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 8-12 lbs over the season -- compact and prolific
yield_expectations.peak_production: Roma plants tend to set a lot of fruit at once -- perfect for batch cooking and preserving
yield_expectations.first_year_note: First seasons are for learning. If you get enough for a salad, that is a success. You will get more each year as you learn what your specific garden needs.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Tomatoes are tropical plants and suffer the moment temperatures drop near freezing. Even a brief cold night can blacken leaves and kill young plants. If it happened at transplant, the plant was likely moved out too early -- soil temperature matters as much as air temperature.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Wait until both night temperatures are reliably above 50°F and soil temperature is above 60°F before transplanting. A cheap soil thermometer removes the guesswork.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Tomatoes are susceptible to blight, blossom end rot, and several common pests. Blight spreads fast in wet, humid conditions and usually starts at the lower leaves. Blossom end rot is caused by calcium deficiency triggered by irregular watering -- not a nutrient problem.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently at the base -- not overhead. Remove any affected leaves immediately. Rotate tomatoes to a different bed each year and stake plants to improve airflow.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too much water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Overwatered tomatoes show yellowing lower leaves, cracked fruit, and roots that cannot get oxygen. Inconsistent watering -- dry then suddenly wet -- causes fruit splitting and blossom end rot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water deeply twice a week rather than a little every day. Mulching around the base dramatically improves moisture consistency.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too little water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress during flowering causes blossom drop -- no flowers, no fruit. During fruiting, inconsistent moisture causes blossom end rot and cracked skin.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Tomatoes need 1-2 inches of water per week. Mulch heavily to retain moisture, and water at the base never the leaves.

failure_diagnostics.label: Not enough sun
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Tomatoes need a minimum of 6-8 hours of direct sun to produce well. In shade they grow leafy but set little or no fruit, and are much more prone to disease.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Tomatoes are one of the most sun-hungry vegetables. If your current spot is marginal, prioritize this bed for tomatoes next season and move something more shade-tolerant elsewhere.

crops.name: Bell Pepper
crops.description: Sweet peppers that start green and ripen to red, yellow, or orange. Need warmth and patience -- green peppers are just unripe colored peppers.

3.notes: Very challenging in Zone 3. Choose California Wonder or Ace for shortest days. May not fully color before frost.
3.zone_notes: Zone 3 is marginal for peppers -- start 10+ weeks early indoors, use black plastic mulch to warm soil, and choose fast varieties under 70 days.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Tomato hornworm
pests.symptoms: Large green caterpillars (up to 4 inches) stripping foliage. Leaves disappear rapidly. Black droppings on leaves.
pests.cause: Manduca quinquemaculata moth larvae. Mid to late summer pest.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick -- they are well camouflaged but easy to remove. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray. If white cocoons visible on back, leave them -- parasitic wasps are doing the work.
pests.prevention: Till soil in autumn to kill overwintering pupae. Plant dill and basil nearby to attract predatory wasps.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms: Tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings and young plants. Small shiny black beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause: Multiple flea beetle species. Most active in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment: Use row covers on seedlings. Apply diatomaceous earth. Neem oil spray.
pests.prevention: Delay transplanting until plants are large. Use transplants rather than seeds.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Early blight
diseases.symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings on lower leaves first. Affected leaves yellow and drop. Spreads upward through plant.
diseases.cause: Alternaria fungus. Favored by warm wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves immediately. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively. Mulch soil to prevent splash-up.
diseases.prevention: Rotate tomatoes every 3-4 years. Water at soil level. Space plants for airflow. Stake to keep foliage off ground.

diseases.name: Late blight
diseases.symptoms: Water-soaked, rapidly expanding brown patches on leaves and stems. White fuzzy growth on undersides in humid conditions. Can destroy plants in days.
diseases.cause: Phytophthora infestans oomycete. The same pathogen that caused the Irish potato famine. Spreads rapidly in cool wet weather.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove and destroy all affected material immediately -- do not compost. Apply copper fungicide preventively in wet conditions.
diseases.prevention: Plant resistant varieties. Ensure excellent airflow. Never leave tomato debris in the garden over winter.

diseases.name: Anthracnose
diseases.symptoms: Dark sunken lesions on ripening fruit. Fruit rots on plant.
diseases.cause: Colletotrichum fungus. Favored by warm humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected fruit. Apply copper fungicide.
diseases.prevention: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Harvest promptly when ripe.

diseases.name: Blossom end rot
diseases.symptoms: Dark, sunken, leathery patch at the bottom (blossom end) of fruit. Affects first fruits most. Not contagious.
diseases.cause: Calcium deficiency in developing fruit, caused by irregular watering or root damage -- not a pest or disease.
diseases.organic_treatment: Mulch to maintain even soil moisture. Water consistently. Foliar calcium spray provides some relief. Remove affected fruit.
diseases.prevention: Consistent watering is the key prevention. Avoid root disturbance. Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen.

watering.signs_underwater: Wilting, flower drop, dry crumbly soil

crops.harvest_ready: Green peppers: pick when full sized and firm (any time). For colored peppers, leave until fully red/yellow/orange -- takes 2-3 more weeks. Colored peppers are sweeter.

start_method.notes: Start 8-10 weeks before last frost -- peppers are slow. Soil must be warm (70°F+) at transplant. Harden off over 10 days.

container_notes.notes: Very good container crop. 5-gallon pot. One plant per pot. Protect from wind.

varieties.note: Gypsy is a great early-maturing option for short seasons -- produces yellow-orange fruits.

rotation.avoid_after: Tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes -- all share blight and fusarium diseases
rotation.note: Always rotate nightshades to a fresh bed -- blight and fusarium can persist in soil for years.

storage.fridge: 1-2 weeks in fridge in a bag
storage.freezer: Slice and freeze raw -- excellent for cooking. No blanching needed.
storage.notes: Green peppers store longer than red/yellow. Frozen peppers are great for stir-fries.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: A small pale shoot pushing upward. Peppers are slower than tomatoes -- do not give up after a week.
growth_stages.user_action: Peppers need warmth more than any other vegetable. Keep soil at 80-85°F if possible. A heat mat is not optional with peppers -- it is the difference between 7 days and 21 days.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Two seed leaves, then the first true leaves which will be narrow and pointed.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep them warm and bright. Peppers are slow at this stage -- be patient. Do not overwater; they are prone to damping off.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Bushy plant with 4-6 sets of leaves, sturdy stem. Do not rush transplanting.
growth_stages.user_action: Peppers hate cold soil more than they hate cold air. Wait until nights are reliably above 55°F and the soil temperature is 65°F+. Cold-shocked peppers stall for weeks.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Outside yet, or still hardening off?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small white or purple flowers -- often the first one appears before you expect it.
growth_stages.user_action: Some growers remove the first flower (the 'king flower') to encourage bushier growth and more fruit. It is optional but can increase total yield.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Green peppers are ready to pick at full size. Leave them longer and they turn red, yellow or orange -- sweeter and more nutritious, but fewer total fruits.
growth_stages.user_action: Pick green to maximize total yield, or wait for color if flavor matters more. Use scissors or a knife -- pulling can snap branches.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Nights cooling, plant slowing down, remaining fruit taking longer to ripen.
growth_stages.user_action: Bring container peppers inside before the first frost -- they can overwinter as houseplants and come back stronger next year. In ground, harvest everything before frost.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Season wrapping up -- how did it go?

notifications.title: Time to start your peppers indoors
notifications.body: Peppers need 8-10 weeks indoors before transplanting -- start now. They germinate slowly, especially without bottom heat. Get a heat mat under them and keep soil temperature at 80-85°F. Patience pays off with peppers.

notifications.title: Last frost passed -- but check soil temperature first
notifications.body: The air temperature is safe, but peppers care more about soil warmth than air warmth. Check your soil temperature before transplanting -- it should be 65°F or warmer. Cold soil at transplant is the most common reason peppers stall.

notifications.title: Your peppers should be reaching full size
notifications.body: Green bell peppers are ready to pick at full size -- usually around now. If you want colored peppers, leave them another 2-3 weeks. They will turn red, orange or yellow and get sweeter, but the plant produces fewer total fruits the longer you wait.

notifications.title: Consider overwintering your pepper plants
notifications.body: Peppers are perennials in warm climates. Before frost arrives, you can bring container plants inside as houseplants. Cut them back by about a third, reduce watering, and keep in a bright spot. They will come back next spring faster and stronger.

notifications.title: Checking in on your peppers
notifications.body: You have not logged anything in a while. How are they looking? Peppers can be slow and frustrating mid-season -- they often seem to stall before suddenly taking off.

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- protect your peppers tonight
weather_triggers.body: Peppers are very frost-tender. Cover with fleece or bring containers inside tonight. Even a light frost can damage or kill the plant. Do not risk it.

weather_triggers.title: Heat stress -- your peppers may drop flowers
weather_triggers.body: Very high temperatures cause pepper flowers to drop before they can set fruit. Water deeply in the early morning and consider light shade cloth during peak afternoon heat. Hot peppers handle heat better than sweet varieties.

weather_triggers.title: Cold snap coming -- protect young pepper plants
weather_triggers.body: A sudden temperature drop can set pepper plants back significantly. Cover outdoor plants tonight and check soil temperature tomorrow. Peppers that get cold-shocked at transplant can stall for weeks.

weather_triggers.title: Dry spell -- your peppers need deep watering
weather_triggers.body: Drought stress during fruiting causes blossom drop and poor fruit development. Water deeply at the base twice a week and mulch heavily to retain moisture.

germination.text: Peppers are the most heat-dependent seed you will germinate. A heat mat is genuinely worth it -- germination at 85°F takes 7-10 days; at 65°F it can take 3-4 weeks or fail entirely.
Soak seeds in warm water for 8 hours before sowing. It softens the seed coat and speeds up germination.

seedling.text: Pepper seedlings are naturally slow. Do not panic if they seem stuck for a week after the seed leaves open -- they are putting energy into root development before visible growth.
Keep the heat mat going until they have 2 sets of true leaves. Peppers sulk in cool conditions at every stage.

established.text: The most common pepper mistake is transplanting too early. Soil temperature matters more than air temperature. A cheap soil thermometer is one of the most useful tools you can have for peppers.

Pinch out the very first flower bud you see (the king flower in the center fork of the plant). It redirects energy into bushy growth and more fruit overall -- though if you cannot bear to, leave it. You will still get peppers.

flowering.text: Hot peppers are often more reliable in the heat than sweet varieties. If your bells are struggling with flower drop in high temperatures, know that your chillies are probably loving it.
Peppers are self-pollinating but benefit from movement. A gentle breeze, or gently shaking the plant, helps pollen transfer.

harvest.text: Pick green peppers at full size to keep production going. Every pepper you leave on the plant to turn red reduces how many new ones it sets. Decide what matters more -- quantity or colored fruit.
Hot pepper heat intensifies as they ripen to red. Pick green for milder heat, red for maximum fire.

end_of_season.text: Pepper plants are true perennials -- they are only treated as annuals because of cold winters. A plant brought inside in autumn and overwintered will be much more productive the following year.
Harvest all remaining peppers before the first frost, even green ones. They can ripen slowly on a windowsill or be used green in cooking.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 6-10 bell peppers per plant, or 20-30+ hot peppers

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Peppers are even more cold-sensitive than tomatoes. Cold soil at transplant time is the most common cause of stunted, struggling plants -- the plant survives but sulks for weeks and never fully recovers its momentum.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Check soil temperature before transplanting -- it must be 65°F or warmer. A cold snap after transplant can be just as damaging. Keep fleece handy for the first few weeks.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Peppers can be affected by aphids, spider mites in hot dry weather, and bacterial spot in humid conditions. Spider mites thrive when plants are stressed -- usually by drought or heat.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Consistent watering prevents drought stress that invites spider mites. Good airflow around plants reduces humidity-related disease. Check undersides of leaves regularly.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too much water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Overwatered peppers show yellowing leaves and root rot. They prefer to dry out slightly between waterings -- unlike tomatoes they do not want consistently moist soil.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water when the top inch of soil is dry. Ensure excellent drainage -- peppers are more drought-tolerant than most vegetables once established.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too little water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress during flowering causes flowers to drop before setting fruit. This is one of the most common reasons for a pepper plant with no fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently during the flowering period. Deep watering twice a week is better than light daily watering.

failure_diagnostics.label: Not enough sun
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Peppers need full sun -- 8 hours minimum. In less sun they grow slowly, flower poorly, and are much more susceptible to disease.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: If your site gets less than 6 hours of direct sun, consider a different crop. Peppers planted in marginal light rarely justify the long season they require.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Pest-deterrent claim without matching established pattern. Default to traditional pending review.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. This claim's nematode component aligns with the extension-documented mechanism, but the 'concurrent companion' application pattern reflects popular gardening practice rather than extension protocol.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Root-zone partitioning is a real ecology concept. 'Carrots loosen soil for tomatoes' is a plausible mechanistic claim but not well-studied for specific pairs.
