pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Tomato hornworm
pests.symptoms: Large green caterpillars (up to 4 inches) stripping foliage. Leaves disappear rapidly. Black droppings on leaves.
pests.cause: Manduca quinquemaculata moth larvae. Mid to late summer pest.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick -- they are well camouflaged but easy to remove. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray. If white cocoons visible on back, leave them -- parasitic wasps are doing the work.
pests.prevention: Till soil in autumn to kill overwintering pupae. Plant dill and basil nearby to attract predatory wasps.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms: Tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings and young plants. Small shiny black beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause: Multiple flea beetle species. Most active in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment: Use row covers on seedlings. Apply diatomaceous earth. Neem oil spray.
pests.prevention: Delay transplanting until plants are large. Use transplants rather than seeds.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Early blight
diseases.symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings on lower leaves first. Affected leaves yellow and drop. Spreads upward through plant.
diseases.cause: Alternaria fungus. Favored by warm wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves immediately. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively. Mulch soil to prevent splash-up.
diseases.prevention: Rotate tomatoes every 3-4 years. Water at soil level. Space plants for airflow. Stake to keep foliage off ground.

diseases.name: Late blight
diseases.symptoms: Water-soaked, rapidly expanding brown patches on leaves and stems. White fuzzy growth on undersides in humid conditions. Can destroy plants in days.
diseases.cause: Phytophthora infestans oomycete. The same pathogen that caused the Irish potato famine. Spreads rapidly in cool wet weather.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove and destroy all affected material immediately -- do not compost. Apply copper fungicide preventively in wet conditions.
diseases.prevention: Plant resistant varieties. Ensure excellent airflow. Never leave tomato debris in the garden over winter.

diseases.name: Anthracnose
diseases.symptoms: Dark sunken lesions on ripening fruit. Fruit rots on plant.
diseases.cause: Colletotrichum fungus. Favored by warm humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected fruit. Apply copper fungicide.
diseases.prevention: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Harvest promptly when ripe.

diseases.name: Blossom end rot
diseases.symptoms: Dark, sunken, leathery patch at the bottom (blossom end) of fruit. Affects first fruits most. Not contagious.
diseases.cause: Calcium deficiency in developing fruit, caused by irregular watering or root damage -- not a pest or disease.
diseases.organic_treatment: Mulch to maintain even soil moisture. Water consistently. Foliar calcium spray provides some relief. Remove affected fruit.
diseases.prevention: Consistent watering is the key prevention. Avoid root disturbance. Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: A small pale shoot pushing upward. Peppers are slower than tomatoes -- do not give up after a week.
growth_stages.user_action: Peppers need warmth more than any other vegetable. Keep soil at 80-85°F if possible. A heat mat is not optional with peppers -- it is the difference between 7 days and 21 days.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Two seed leaves, then the first true leaves which will be narrow and pointed.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep them warm and bright. Peppers are slow at this stage -- be patient. Do not overwater; they are prone to damping off.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Bushy plant with 4-6 sets of leaves, sturdy stem. Do not rush transplanting.
growth_stages.user_action: Peppers hate cold soil more than they hate cold air. Wait until nights are reliably above 55°F and the soil temperature is 65°F+. Cold-shocked peppers stall for weeks.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Outside yet, or still hardening off?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small white or purple flowers -- often the first one appears before you expect it.
growth_stages.user_action: Some growers remove the first flower (the 'king flower') to encourage bushier growth and more fruit. It is optional but can increase total yield.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Green peppers are ready to pick at full size. Leave them longer and they turn red, yellow or orange -- sweeter and more nutritious, but fewer total fruits.
growth_stages.user_action: Pick green to maximize total yield, or wait for color if flavor matters more. Use scissors or a knife -- pulling can snap branches.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Nights cooling, plant slowing down, remaining fruit taking longer to ripen.
growth_stages.user_action: Bring container peppers inside before the first frost -- they can overwinter as houseplants and come back stronger next year. In ground, harvest everything before frost.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Season wrapping up -- how did it go?

notifications.title: Time to start your peppers indoors
notifications.body: Peppers need 8-10 weeks indoors before transplanting -- start now. They germinate slowly, especially without bottom heat. Get a heat mat under them and keep soil temperature at 80-85°F. Patience pays off with peppers.

notifications.title: Last frost passed -- but check soil temperature first
notifications.body: The air temperature is safe, but peppers care more about soil warmth than air warmth. Check your soil temperature before transplanting -- it should be 65°F or warmer. Cold soil at transplant is the most common reason peppers stall.

notifications.title: Your peppers should be reaching full size
notifications.body: Green bell peppers are ready to pick at full size -- usually around now. If you want colored peppers, leave them another 2-3 weeks. They will turn red, orange or yellow and get sweeter, but the plant produces fewer total fruits the longer you wait.

notifications.title: Consider overwintering your pepper plants
notifications.body: Peppers are perennials in warm climates. Before frost arrives, you can bring container plants inside as houseplants. Cut them back by about a third, reduce watering, and keep in a bright spot. They will come back next spring faster and stronger.

notifications.title: Checking in on your peppers
notifications.body: You have not logged anything in a while. How are they looking? Peppers can be slow and frustrating mid-season -- they often seem to stall before suddenly taking off.

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- protect your peppers tonight
weather_triggers.body: Peppers are very frost-tender. Cover with fleece or bring containers inside tonight. Even a light frost can damage or kill the plant. Do not risk it.

weather_triggers.title: Heat stress -- your peppers may drop flowers
weather_triggers.body: Very high temperatures cause pepper flowers to drop before they can set fruit. Water deeply in the early morning and consider light shade cloth during peak afternoon heat. Hot peppers handle heat better than sweet varieties.

weather_triggers.title: Cold snap coming -- protect young pepper plants
weather_triggers.body: A sudden temperature drop can set pepper plants back significantly. Cover outdoor plants tonight and check soil temperature tomorrow. Peppers that get cold-shocked at transplant can stall for weeks.

weather_triggers.title: Dry spell -- your peppers need deep watering
weather_triggers.body: Drought stress during fruiting causes blossom drop and poor fruit development. Water deeply at the base twice a week and mulch heavily to retain moisture.

germination.text: Peppers are the most heat-dependent seed you will germinate. A heat mat is genuinely worth it -- germination at 85°F takes 7-10 days; at 65°F it can take 3-4 weeks or fail entirely.
Soak seeds in warm water for 8 hours before sowing. It softens the seed coat and speeds up germination.

seedling.text: Pepper seedlings are naturally slow. Do not panic if they seem stuck for a week after the seed leaves open -- they are putting energy into root development before visible growth.
Keep the heat mat going until they have 2 sets of true leaves. Peppers sulk in cool conditions at every stage.

established.text: The most common pepper mistake is transplanting too early. Soil temperature matters more than air temperature. A cheap soil thermometer is one of the most useful tools you can have for peppers.

Pinch out the very first flower bud you see (the king flower in the center fork of the plant). It redirects energy into bushy growth and more fruit overall -- though if you cannot bear to, leave it. You will still get peppers.

flowering.text: Hot peppers are often more reliable in the heat than sweet varieties. If your bells are struggling with flower drop in high temperatures, know that your chillies are probably loving it.
Peppers are self-pollinating but benefit from movement. A gentle breeze, or gently shaking the plant, helps pollen transfer.

harvest.text: Pick green peppers at full size to keep production going. Every pepper you leave on the plant to turn red reduces how many new ones it sets. Decide what matters more -- quantity or colored fruit.
Hot pepper heat intensifies as they ripen to red. Pick green for milder heat, red for maximum fire.

end_of_season.text: Pepper plants are true perennials -- they are only treated as annuals because of cold winters. A plant brought inside in autumn and overwintered will be much more productive the following year.
Harvest all remaining peppers before the first frost, even green ones. They can ripen slowly on a windowsill or be used green in cooking.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 20-35+ peppers per plant -- jalapeno yields run lower than smaller hot peppers
yield_expectations.peak_production: Hot pepper plants at peak can produce faster than you can use them. Plan to dry, freeze or ferment the excess
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Peppers are one of the more challenging crops in cooler climates. A good harvest in year one is something to be genuinely proud of.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Peppers are even more cold-sensitive than tomatoes. Cold soil at transplant time is the most common cause of stunted, struggling plants -- the plant survives but sulks for weeks and never fully recovers its momentum.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Check soil temperature before transplanting -- it must be 65°F or warmer. A cold snap after transplant can be just as damaging. Keep fleece handy for the first few weeks.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Peppers can be affected by aphids, spider mites in hot dry weather, and bacterial spot in humid conditions. Spider mites thrive when plants are stressed -- usually by drought or heat.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Consistent watering prevents drought stress that invites spider mites. Good airflow around plants reduces humidity-related disease. Check undersides of leaves regularly.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too much water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Overwatered peppers show yellowing leaves and root rot. They prefer to dry out slightly between waterings -- unlike tomatoes they do not want consistently moist soil.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water when the top inch of soil is dry. Ensure excellent drainage -- peppers are more drought-tolerant than most vegetables once established.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too little water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress during flowering causes flowers to drop before setting fruit. This is one of the most common reasons for a pepper plant with no fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently during the flowering period. Deep watering twice a week is better than light daily watering.

failure_diagnostics.label: Not enough sun
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Peppers need full sun -- 8 hours minimum. In less sun they grow slowly, flower poorly, and are much more susceptible to disease.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: If your site gets less than 6 hours of direct sun, consider a different crop. Peppers planted in marginal light rarely justify the long season they require.

fertilizer.timing: switch to high-potassium at first flower
fertilizer.notes: Heavy feeder once fruiting starts. Consistent moisture and feeding prevents bitterness.

succession.tip: Sow every 3 weeks from last frost through early summer. Cucumber plants tire quickly -- after 6-8 weeks of heavy production they often become diseased, lose vigor, or slow dramatically. A succession planting coming in just as the first batch declines keeps harvests consistent all summer. Don't sow later than 3 months before your first fall frost -- cucumbers need warm soil and plenty of time.

good.name: Nasturtiums
good.why: Trap crop for aphids, attracts predators

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension 2022 and 2025 Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetable Crops; UConn IPM 'Perimeter Trap Cropping for Cole Crops'). Nasturtiums specifically are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and Utah State University Extension (Mohr et al., 'Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting'). Protocol caveat: UConn IPM explicitly notes trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents' -- so the aphid application here has a protocol-mismatch concern even though the companion is extension-named. The Cornell-IPM-specific attribution in earlier catalog reason text was not located in Cornell's published IPM material; actual backing is WSU/USU/UConn.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Xerces Society documents borage as a pollinator-attractant plant that blooms concurrently with tomato, squash, and cucumber crops, drawing the same bees that pollinate those crops. Source: xerces.org/blog/plants-you-can-eat-are-pollinator-treat. The claim's additional assertions about deterring cucumber beetle are not supported in extension literature; they recur widely in popular gardening sources but without rigorous backing and should be read as traditional.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Legume rhizobial nitrogen fixation is textbook plant science. The mechanism is real; the specific pairing benefit is mechanistically plausible but often not pair-tested.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Flowering plants attracting predatory insects is a documented biological control mechanism (UC IPM, Cornell). Specific pairings vary in effectiveness.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Bad companion claim, no pattern match. Default to traditional pending review.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Bad companion claim, no pattern match. Default to traditional pending review.

pests.name: Cucumber beetle
pests.symptoms: Yellow-green beetles with black spots or stripes feeding on leaves, flowers, and fruit. Plants wilt suddenly (bacterial wilt transmission). Holey leaves.
pests.cause: Spotted and striped cucumber beetles. Also transmit bacterial wilt disease.
pests.organic_treatment: Row covers until flowering. Yellow sticky traps. Neem oil spray. Spinosad-based insecticide.
pests.prevention: Delay planting until plants are large. Use row covers early season. Interplant with radishes and nasturtiums.

pests.name: Squash bug
pests.symptoms: Gray-brown flat insects on stems and undersides of leaves. Wilting leaves with yellow then brown patches. Bronze egg clusters on leaf undersides.
pests.cause: Anasa tristis. Overwinters as adults in garden debris.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick adults and egg masses. Trap under boards at night. Neem oil spray on nymphs.
pests.prevention: Remove all garden debris in autumn. Rotate cucurbit crops. Use row covers early season.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces, stems, and sometimes fruit. Leaves may yellow and die. Worst in warm days with cool nights.
diseases.cause: Fungal disease favored by humid conditions with poor air circulation.
diseases.organic_treatment: Spray with diluted neem oil or a baking soda solution (1 tsp per quart water). Apply potassium bicarbonate spray. Remove and destroy affected leaves.
diseases.prevention: Space plants for good airflow. Water at soil level, not on foliage. Choose resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation.

diseases.name: Bacterial wilt
diseases.symptoms: Sudden wilting of individual leaves, then whole stems, then entire plant. No recovery even with watering. Plants die within days.
diseases.cause: Erwinia tracheiphila bacteria spread by cucumber beetles feeding.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure -- remove and destroy infected plants immediately. Control cucumber beetles to prevent spread.
diseases.prevention: Use row covers to exclude cucumber beetles early in season. Plant resistant varieties.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms: Yellow-green patches on upper leaf surface with corresponding gray-purple fuzzy growth on leaf undersides. Leaves die rapidly.
diseases.cause: Pseudoperonospora cubensis fungus. Spreads rapidly in wet humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively.
diseases.prevention: Choose resistant varieties. Water at soil level. Ensure good air circulation.

watering.amount: 1 inch per week minimum, more in heat
watering.method: At soil level -- overhead watering encourages disease
watering.signs_overwater: Yellow leaves, root rot, soft stems

crops.harvest_ready: Pick at 6-8 inches before seeds harden. Firm and dark green. If yellowing starts at the base, you've waited too long -- this triggers the plant to stop producing.

start_method.notes: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F. Or start indoors 3-4 weeks before -- cucumbers dislike transplanting so use biodegradable pots.

container_notes.notes: Works in containers with a trellis. 5-gallon pot minimum. Compact or bushing varieties work best. Water frequently.

varieties.note: Diva is a top performer -- no bitterness, no need to peel, and resistant to most cucumber diseases.

rotation.avoid_after: Cucumbers, squash, pumpkins, melons -- share cucumber beetle, bacterial wilt, downy mildew
rotation.note: Rotate to prevent cucumber beetle and disease buildup.

storage.fridge: Up to 1 week wrapped in a paper towel in the fridge
storage.freezer: Not recommended -- becomes watery
storage.notes: Cucumbers are cold-sensitive -- ideal fridge temp is 50-55°F. Don't store near tomatoes (ethylene gas).

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Cucumbers germinate fast -- you should see the seed leaves pushing up within a week.
growth_stages.user_action: Sow seeds on their edge rather than flat -- it reduces rotting and speeds germination. Keep soil warm, 70°F+.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Large, round seed leaves, then the first true leaves which are rough and slightly lobed.
growth_stages.user_action: Cucumbers hate having their roots disturbed -- if starting indoors, use biodegradable pots you can plant whole. Transplant as little as possible.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Vines beginning to extend and tendrils reaching for support.
growth_stages.user_action: Get supports in place now before the vines get tangled. Cucumbers climbing a trellis produce straighter fruit, get better airflow, and are easier to harvest.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Yellow flowers appearing. Male flowers come first -- no fruit yet. Female flowers have a tiny swelling at the base that becomes the cucumber.
growth_stages.user_action: Do not panic when the first flowers drop without producing fruit -- those are males. Female flowers follow within a week or two.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Seeing flowers? Any tiny cucumbers forming?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Firm, dark green fruit at the size described for your variety. Skin should be smooth, not bumpy or yellowing.
growth_stages.user_action: Pick every 2-3 days without fail. A single missed cucumber that turns yellow and seedy signals the plant to stop producing. Regular picking is the most important thing you can do.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Slowing production, yellowing vines, powdery mildew appearing on leaves.
growth_stages.user_action: Powdery mildew at end of season is normal -- it does not mean you did anything wrong. Pull the plant before first frost and compost the vines.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Season done? How did it go?

notifications.title: Last frost passed -- sow your cucumbers now
notifications.body: Cucumbers go directly into warm soil after frost. Sow 2-3 seeds per spot and thin to the strongest. If starting indoors, use biodegradable pots -- cucumbers hate having their roots disturbed at transplant.

notifications.title: Time to set up your cucumber supports
notifications.body: Your cucumbers should be putting on growth now. Get a trellis or netting in place before the vines start sprawling -- it is much harder to do once they are tangled. Vertical growing gives you straighter fruit and better airflow.

notifications.title: Your cucumbers should be ready to pick
notifications.body: Check the vines carefully -- cucumbers hide under leaves and can go from perfect to overgrown very quickly. Pick every 2-3 days. A single yellow, seedy cucumber left on the plant tells it the job is done and production slows dramatically.

notifications.title: Check your cucumber vines
notifications.body: Cucumbers need checking every few days at harvest time. One overgrown fruit can slow down the whole plant. A quick look through the leaves is worth it.

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- cucumbers are extremely frost-tender
weather_triggers.body: Even a light frost kills cucumber plants. Cover with fleece tonight or bring containers inside. Do not risk it.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- watch for powdery mildew
weather_triggers.body: Cucumbers are prone to powdery mildew in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow around the vines, avoid watering the leaves, and pick regularly to keep the plant healthy.

weather_triggers.title: Heat stress -- keep your cucumbers well watered
weather_triggers.body: Cucumbers need consistent moisture in the heat -- stress during fruiting causes bitter, misshapen fruit. Water deeply at the base every day in very hot weather and mulch well.

germination.text: Sow cucumber seeds on their side -- the edge, not flat. It helps the root emerge more easily and reduces rotting.
Cucumbers germinate best at 70-95°F. They will not germinate well in cool soil -- wait for genuine warmth.

seedling.text: If starting indoors, use biodegradable pots. Cucumbers genuinely hate having their roots disturbed. Plant the whole pot when transplanting.
Thin to one plant per spot -- do not try to transplant the thinned seedlings. Cucumbers do not recover well from root disturbance.

established.text: Cucumbers climbing a trellis are easier to manage than sprawling on the ground. The fruit hangs straight, gets better airflow, and is much easier to spot at harvest.
Mulch heavily around the base. Cucumbers need consistent moisture and heat -- mulch provides both.

flowering.text: The first flowers are male -- they produce no fruit and will drop. This is normal. Female flowers follow, identifiable by the tiny cucumber shape at their base.
In a greenhouse or polytunnel, hand-pollinate by touching a small paintbrush to each flower. Outdoors, pollinators will do the work.

harvest.text: Pick every 2-3 days without exception during peak season. One overlarge, yellowing cucumber sends a signal to the whole plant that the season is done. Do not let that happen.
Harvest in the morning when cucumbers are at their crispest and coolest. Refrigerate immediately for best texture.

end_of_season.text: Powdery mildew appearing on leaves is normal at the end of cucumber season -- it is a sign of age, not failure. The plant has done its job.
Save seeds from an open-pollinated or heirloom variety for next year. Let one fruit go fully yellow and fat, scoop out the seeds, rinse and dry them.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 10-20 cucumbers over the season per plant
yield_expectations.peak_production: At peak, a healthy plant gives you 2-3 cucumbers every few days
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Cucumbers are one of the most rewarding first crops -- fast-growing, high-yielding, and delicious straight from the vine.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucurbits are tropical-origin tender annuals -- killed outright by even a light frost at any stage. Cold soil at planting (below 60 degrees) stunts seedlings for the rest of the season even if they survive. Late-summer frost ends the season abruptly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Wait to direct-sow or transplant until soil reaches 65 to 70 degrees and night temperatures stay above 50. In short-season zones, start transplants indoors 3 to 4 weeks before set-out, but disturb roots minimally -- cucurbits resent transplanting. Use black plastic mulch to warm soil. Have row cover ready for unexpected late-spring or early-fall frosts.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucumber beetles (striped and spotted) damage seedlings directly and transmit bacterial wilt -- a fatal disease that wilts vines from the tips inward. Squash bugs target squash and pumpkin (less so cucumber and melon). Powdery mildew shows up reliably late in the season as white powder on leaves. Downy mildew, anthracnose, and bacterial leaf spot are humidity-driven secondary problems.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Floating row cover from planting through first flower blocks cucumber beetles -- remove at flowering for pollination. Squash bug egg masses (orange-red, on undersides of leaves) crush easily by hand if caught early. For powdery mildew, choose resistant varieties (most modern cucumbers are bred for resistance) and water at the base, not overhead. Rotate cucurbits to a new bed each year.

failure_diagnostics.label: Watery fruit or vine collapse
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucurbits need consistent water but cannot tolerate waterlogged soil. Persistent saturation causes root rot, sudden vine collapse, and watery flavorless fruit. Heavy rain near harvest causes ripe melons to crack and split. Wet foliage drives powdery mildew, downy mildew, and bacterial leaf spot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil or raised mounds (the traditional 'cucurbit hill' approach exists for drainage reasons). Water deeply at the base 1 to 2 times per week rather than shallow daily. Mulch heavily to even out soil moisture and reduce splash-borne disease. Stop watering watermelons 2 weeks before expected harvest to concentrate flavor.

failure_diagnostics.label: Small or bitter fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress during flowering and fruit set produces small, misshapen, or bitter fruit. Cucurbits move large volumes of water through their tissues during fruit development -- a single mature watermelon plant can use 1 to 2 gallons of water per day in peak summer. Cucumber bitterness is often a drought-stress signal.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently and deeply -- 1 to 2 inches per week minimum during fruit development, more in heat. Drip irrigation outperforms overhead watering by both providing consistent water and keeping foliage dry. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture and reduce evaporation.

failure_diagnostics.label: Vines without fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucurbits need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum, ideally 8 or more -- to set and ripen fruit. In partial shade vines grow leaves and even bloom, but fruit set is poor and ripening is incomplete. A late-season fruit that never sweetens is often a sun problem more than a temperature problem.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in the sunniest spot available. Trellising vining cucurbits (vertical support for cucumbers and small-fruited squash) gets more leaf area into the sun and improves fruit set substantially. In partial-shade gardens, accept that cucurbits are not the right crop and grow leafy greens or herbs instead.

fertilizer.notes: Leafy crop that loves nitrogen. Feed monthly with a nitrogen-rich fertilizer. Reduce feeding in the final 4 weeks before harvest.
fertilizer.npk_hint: high N, e.g. 10-5-5 or fish emulsion
fertilizer.notify_message: Time to feed your kale -- leafy greens love nitrogen

succession.tip: Sow every 4 weeks from spring through midsummer. Like collards, kale is cut-and-come-again from the outer leaves -- one plant can produce for months. The most important succession is the late-summer sowing for autumn: kale planted 8-10 weeks before your first frost date will be at peak harvest when temperatures drop, and the flavor improves dramatically after frost. Don't skip this one.

good.name: Nasturtiums
good.why: Trap crop for aphids and caterpillars

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines; UConn IPM). Nasturtiums are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and USU Extension. Protocol caveats: UConn IPM notes that trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents.' Caterpillar deterrence (cabbage looper, imported cabbageworm) on brassicas is in secondary gardening literature but not specifically in the extension trap-cropping publications reviewed; the extension-recommended brassica trap crops for lepidopteran pests are collards (DBM) and radishes (flea beetles), not nasturtiums.

pests.name: Cabbage worm
pests.symptoms: Large irregular holes in leaves. Green caterpillars (1-1.5 inches) blending into foliage. White cabbage butterfly flying nearby is a warning sign.
pests.cause: Pieris rapae butterfly larvae. Lay eggs on leaf undersides.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick caterpillars and egg clusters. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray every 2 weeks. Row covers as barrier.
pests.prevention: Row covers from planting. White butterfly decoys (territorial behavior). Plant nasturtiums as trap crop.

pests.name: Cabbage aphid
pests.symptoms: Dense gray-green colonies on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl and pucker. Honeydew and sooty mold may follow.
pests.cause: Brevicoryne brassicae. Populations explode rapidly in cool weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Strong water blast. Insecticidal soap spray directly on colonies. Remove and compost heavily infested leaves.
pests.prevention: Avoid excess nitrogen. Encourage parasitic wasps with flowering herbs nearby.

pests.name: Flea beetle
pests.symptoms: Many tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings. Plants look peppered. Small shiny beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause: Multiple flea beetle species. Worst in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment: Row covers on seedlings. Diatomaceous earth. Kaolin clay spray.
pests.prevention: Delay planting. Use transplants. Interplant with aromatic herbs.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms: Plants wilt in hot weather despite watering. Stunted growth. Yellowing leaves. Roots are swollen, club-shaped, and deformed when dug up.
diseases.cause: Plasmodiophora brassicae soil pathogen. Survives in soil for up to 20 years. Thrives in acidic, wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure. Remove and destroy infected plants -- do not compost. Lime soil to raise pH to 7.0-7.2.
diseases.prevention: Minimum 7-year rotation away from brassicas in infected soil. Maintain soil pH above 6.5. Improve drainage.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms: Yellow patches on upper leaf surface with gray-purple fuzzy mold on undersides. Affects seedlings and mature plants.
diseases.cause: Peronospora brassicae fungus. Favored by cool moist conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Improve air circulation. Copper-based fungicide as preventive.
diseases.prevention: Avoid overhead watering. Space plants generously. Choose resistant varieties.

crops.harvest_ready: Pick outer leaves when 8-10 inches. Younger leaves are more tender. Kale sweetens after light frost. Never take more than 1/3 of the plant at once.

start_method.notes: Direct sow 4-6 weeks before last frost for spring crop, or in late summer for autumn. Can also transplant -- kale handles it well.

container_notes.notes: Great container crop. 3-5 gallon pot. Dwarf varieties (Dwarf Blue Curled) work especially well.

varieties.note: Red Russian is the most tender and least bitter -- best choice for raw salads.

rotation.avoid_after: Kale, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, turnip, kohlrabi -- share clubroot and downy mildew
rotation.note: Clubroot can persist 20 years -- in infected soil extend to 7-year rotation.

storage.fridge: Up to 1 week -- don't wash until ready to use. Store dry.
storage.freezer: Blanch 2-3 minutes, dry, freeze. Excellent for smoothies.
storage.notes: Kale continues to sweeten in cold storage -- like refrigerator "aging."

crops.soil_prep: Firm, fertile soil is key -- brassicas hate loose or acidic soil. Test pH and lime if below 6.5 (clubroot thrives in acidic conditions). Firm the soil by walking over it before planting -- transplants should feel solid, not loose. Dig in compost the previous autumn for spring planting.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small seed leaves pushing through the soil -- leafy greens germinate readily in cool, moist conditions.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged. Most leafy greens germinate best at 50-65°F -- they actually prefer cooler soil than tomatoes.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: True leaves developing, recognizable as the crop you planted.
growth_stages.user_action: Thin seedlings to the recommended spacing -- crowded leafy greens bolt faster and produce less. The thinnings are edible.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Leaves at a harvestable size, plant looking full and healthy.
growth_stages.user_action: Begin harvesting outer leaves now -- this encourages more growth from the center. Do not wait for the plant to be 'finished' before you start picking.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Ready to start harvesting outer leaves?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Leaves at good size, before any yellowing or flowering stem appears.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest cut-and-come-again -- remove outer leaves and let the center keep growing. For butterhead types, harvest the whole head when formed.

growth_stages.name: Bolting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: A central flower stalk shooting upward, leaves becoming smaller and more bitter.
growth_stages.user_action: Once bolting starts the flavor changes -- harvest everything immediately. Bolted leaves are still edible but more bitter. Remove the plant and either sow again or move on to a warm-season crop.

notifications.title: Time to sow your leafy greens
notifications.body: Leafy greens love cool weather and can go in the ground 4-6 weeks before your last frost. Sow directly into prepared soil or start indoors for transplanting. They are some of the first crops of the year -- enjoy the early start.

notifications.title: Your greens should be ready to start picking
notifications.body: Begin harvesting outer leaves now even if the plant seems small. Regular picking encourages more growth. Do not wait for the plant to be 'done' -- leafy greens are a harvest-as-you-go crop.

notifications.title: Heat incoming -- watch your greens for bolting
notifications.body: Hot weather triggers leafy greens to bolt -- sending up a flower stalk and turning bitter. Harvest everything you can now before the heat arrives. Consider sowing again in late summer for a fall crop.

notifications.title: Time to sow your fall leafy greens
notifications.body: Eight weeks before first frost is the window for a second sowing of leafy greens. A fall crop often outperforms spring -- the cooling temperatures mean slower bolting and sweeter flavor. Kale especially improves after a light frost.

notifications.title: How are your greens looking?
notifications.body: Leafy greens can bolt quickly in warm weather. A quick check every few days helps you catch the right harvest moment and spot any bolting before it is too late.

weather_triggers.title: Heat alert -- harvest your greens now
weather_triggers.body: Hot weather is the enemy of leafy greens. They bolt quickly and flavor turns bitter fast. Harvest as much as you can before the heat arrives. Shade cloth can buy you another week in marginal temperatures.

weather_triggers.title: Unexpected frost -- protect young greens
weather_triggers.body: Most leafy greens handle light frost well once established, but young seedlings need protection. Cover with fleece tonight if frost is forecast.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- watch for downy mildew
weather_triggers.body: Humid conditions encourage downy mildew on leafy greens. Ensure good airflow between plants and avoid watering late in the day. Pick regularly to keep the plant open.

germination.text: Leafy greens are some of the easiest crops to germinate -- cool, moist soil is all they need. Sow more thickly than you think you need and thin later.
The thinnings from leafy greens are completely edible -- use them as microgreens in salads. Thinning is harvesting.

seedling.text: Thin to the recommended spacing even though it feels wasteful. Crowded leafy greens bolt faster, get less airflow, and produce smaller leaves.
A light mulch around seedlings keeps moisture in and suppresses weeds -- both important for leafy greens which need consistent moisture.

established.text: Start harvesting outer leaves as soon as they reach a useful size -- this is how leafy greens work. The center keeps producing new growth as you remove the outer leaves.
Water consistently. Irregular watering is a major trigger for bolting in many leafy greens, especially lettuce and spinach.

harvest.text: Always harvest in the morning when leaves are full of water and at their crispest. Refrigerate immediately in a damp bag.
Leave at least half the plant intact when harvesting cut-and-come-again crops. Taking too much at once sets the plant back.

bolting.text: Once you see a flower stalk, harvest everything immediately. The leaves are still edible but will become more bitter every day.
Bolted leafy greens are not a failure -- it is the plant completing its lifecycle. A fall sowing often outperforms spring because the weather is cooling rather than warming.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 1-2 lbs of leaves per plant over the season, more with regular harvesting
yield_expectations.peak_production: A kale plant can produce for months if harvested correctly
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Kale is one of the most rewarding crops to grow. Pick it small for salads, larger for cooking.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Most leafy greens actually handle light frost well once established -- it can even improve flavor. But young seedlings are more vulnerable. If the damage happened at the seedling stage, a late frost likely caught them.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Cover seedlings with fleece if frost threatens in the first few weeks. Established leafy greens generally recover from light frost on their own.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Slugs love leafy green seedlings, especially in wet conditions. Downy mildew affects plants in humid, overcrowded conditions. Flea beetles leave tiny holes in leaves -- especially on arugula and kale.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Thin seedlings properly to allow airflow. Protect from slugs in the first few weeks. Row cover helps with flea beetles on susceptible varieties.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too much water or bolting
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Leafy greens in waterlogged soil develop root rot quickly. More commonly, warmth and long days trigger bolting -- the plant sends up a flower stalk and the leaves become bitter. This is the plant completing its lifecycle, not a failure of care.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Bolting is largely about timing. Sow earlier in spring or switch to a fall sowing -- cooling temperatures signal the plant to keep producing leaves rather than flowering.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too little water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Irregular watering is a major bolting trigger in lettuce and spinach. A dry spell followed by heat pushes them to flower and seed rapidly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Keep moisture consistent -- mulching around leafy greens makes a real difference. Water in the morning so leaves dry during the day.

failure_diagnostics.label: Bolted too quickly
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Heat and long days cause most leafy greens to bolt -- this is the most common reason they fail. The plant is not dying, it is doing what it is designed to do. Once bolted the leaves become bitter and inedible quickly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: The fall sowing is almost always more successful than spring for leafy greens. Cooling temperatures give you longer, slower-bolting plants. Shade cloth can also extend the spring crop by a couple of weeks.

crops.description: One of the fastest crops to harvest. Cold-hardy and can be direct sown as soon as ground can be worked. Bolts in heat -- time plantings for cool weather.

fertilizer.notes: Fast-growing, nitrogen-hungry crop. Liquid feed every 3 weeks keeps leaves large and dark green.

succession.tip: Sow every 2 weeks in spring until temperatures consistently reach 75°F, then pause and restart in late August for a fall crop. Spinach bolts fast in heat and is genuinely pointless to sow mid-summer in most zones. The fall succession is often better than spring -- cooler nights and shorter days keep it sweet longer. Count back from your first fall frost to time your last sowing.

pests.name: Leafminers
pests.symptoms: Pale winding tunnels or blotchy translucent patches between the upper and lower leaf surfaces. Affected tissue turns brown and the leaf is unusable even though the rest of the plant looks healthy.
pests.cause: Spinach leafminer (Pegomya hyoscyami) and vegetable leafminer larvae feed inside the leaf. Beets and Swiss chard host the same pest, so nearby plantings spread the problem.
pests.organic_treatment: Contact insecticides do not reach larvae inside the leaf. Remove and destroy infested leaves as soon as trails appear. Check 2-3 times a week in spring.
pests.prevention: Floating row cover from sowing through harvest -- the adult fly cannot lay eggs through it. Rotate away from beets, chard, and last year's spinach location. Till in old crop residue.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of small green or gray soft-bodied insects on undersides of leaves. Leaves curl and yellow. Sticky honeydew may develop into sooty mold.
pests.cause: Green peach aphid (Myzus persicae) is the primary species on spinach; cotton-melon aphid also occurs. Green peach aphid also vectors several spinach viruses, so even small populations can cause disproportionate damage.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with water. Insecticidal soap or neem oil on leaf undersides. Ladybugs and lacewings provide effective control on unprotected crops.
pests.prevention: Floating row cover excludes aphids and their virus transmission. Control weeds nearby, which host aphids in the off-season. Avoid excess nitrogen.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms: Large irregular holes chewed in leaves, often starting at the leaf margin. Silvery slime trails visible on leaves and soil in early morning. Damage worst in cool damp weather.
pests.cause: Several slug and snail species feed at night, hiding in mulch and debris during the day. Spinach's tender low-growing leaves are especially exposed.
pests.organic_treatment: Iron phosphate bait (labeled for vegetable gardens and safe around pets) scattered thinly around beds. Hand-pick at night with a flashlight. Beer traps set at soil level.
pests.prevention: Clean up leaf debris and boards where slugs hide. Water in the morning so soil surface dries by evening. Copper tape around raised beds deters crossings.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms: Yellow or pale green irregular patches on the upper leaf surface. Undersides show a fuzzy gray-violet mold in humid conditions. Badly infected leaves yellow entirely and collapse.
diseases.cause: Peronospora effusa (formerly P. farinosa f. sp. spinaciae), an oomycete. Favored by cool wet weather with long leaf-wetness periods. Overwinters on crop residue and seed.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove and destroy affected leaves at first sign. No effective organic fungicide cure once established.
diseases.prevention: Plant downy-mildew-resistant varieties -- resistance is widely available and is the single best control. Water at soil level, not overhead. Space plants for airflow. Rotate away from spinach for 2-3 years.

diseases.name: White rust
diseases.symptoms: Small white blister-like pustules on undersides of leaves, sometimes with yellow spots on the upper surface above each cluster. Heavily infected plants weaken and collapse.
diseases.cause: Albugo occidentalis, an oomycete. Favored by cool humid nights (optimum 54°F germination) and mild days. Overwinters as thick-walled oospores in soil. TAMU lists white rust as the major disease of spinach in parts of the South.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove infected plants. Copper-based fungicide labeled for spinach may slow spread if applied early.
diseases.prevention: Plant white-rust-resistant varieties; most modern varieties with white-rust resistance also carry Fusarium resistance. Rotate out of spinach for 3+ years. Avoid overhead irrigation.

diseases.name: Cercospora leaf spot
diseases.symptoms: Numerous small circular spots with pale tan to off-white centers and reddish-purple margins. Spots may coalesce and cause extensive leaf loss. Heavy pressure in late summer.
diseases.cause: Cercospora beticola fungus, the same pathogen that causes Cercospora leaf spot on beets and Swiss chard. Favored by warm temperatures (75-85°F), high humidity, and long nighttime leaf wetness.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Copper or biological fungicides (Bacillus subtilis products) applied preventively during humid stretches.
diseases.prevention: Rotate out of beets, chard, and spinach for 2-3 years. Control weeds in the Chenopodium family (lambsquarters, pigweed) that host the pathogen. Drip-irrigate rather than overhead.

diseases.name: Fusarium wilt
diseases.symptoms: Plants yellow and wilt starting with older lower leaves. Roots turn black. Stunted plants fail to head up. Worse on heavy soils and during warm weather stretches, which shorten the cool-season spinach window.
diseases.cause: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. spinaciae, a soil-borne fungus. Can persist in soil for years. Beets and Swiss chard can host the pathogen without showing symptoms, spreading it silently.
diseases.organic_treatment: No effective cure once plants are symptomatic. Remove and destroy infected plants.
diseases.prevention: Plant resistant varieties (most white-rust-resistant varieties are also Fusarium-resistant). Long rotations out of spinach, beets, and chard. Avoid waterlogged soils.

watering.frequency: Every 2-3 days -- spinach bolts in dry heat

crops.harvest_ready: Pick outer leaves continuously. Harvest entire plant once it shows signs of bolting (central stem elongates).

start_method.notes: Direct sow 4-6 weeks before last frost. Cold-tolerant -- sow very early. Poor transplant candidate.

container_notes.notes: Excellent container crop -- shallow roots. Even window boxes work. 6-8 inches deep minimum.

storage.freezer: Blanch 2 minutes, squeeze dry, freeze. Excellent.
storage.notes: Spinach wilts fast -- harvest and use promptly, or freeze.

bolting.triggers: Heat, long days -- very day-length sensitive
bolting.prevention: Plant very early (can handle frost). Choose slow-bolt varieties (Bloomsdale, Tyee). Autumn plantings last much longer. Shade cloth in spring heat.
bolting.note: Spinach is the most difficult to keep from bolting in warm weather -- succession sow and accept the short season.

varieties.note: Tyee is the most bolt-resistant variety available -- significantly extends the harvest window in spring.

thinning.method: Snip at soil level. Thinnings are edible.
thinning.tip: Spinach germinates in clusters -- each seed capsule contains multiple seeds. Thin promptly for best yield.

rotation.avoid_after: Beet family (same diseases)
rotation.good_after: Legumes (fix nitrogen that leafy crops need)
rotation.note: Rotate leafy greens to avoid leaf miner buildup.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small seed leaves pushing through the soil -- leafy greens germinate readily in cool, moist conditions.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged. Most leafy greens germinate best at 50-65°F -- they actually prefer cooler soil than tomatoes.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: True leaves developing, recognizable as the crop you planted.
growth_stages.user_action: Thin seedlings to the recommended spacing -- crowded leafy greens bolt faster and produce less. The thinnings are edible.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Leaves at a harvestable size, plant looking full and healthy.
growth_stages.user_action: Begin harvesting outer leaves now -- this encourages more growth from the center. Do not wait for the plant to be 'finished' before you start picking.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Ready to start harvesting outer leaves?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Leaves at good size, before any yellowing or flowering stem appears.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest cut-and-come-again -- remove outer leaves and let the center keep growing. For butterhead types, harvest the whole head when formed.

growth_stages.name: Bolting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: A central flower stalk shooting upward, leaves becoming smaller and more bitter.
growth_stages.user_action: Once bolting starts the flavor changes -- harvest everything immediately. Bolted leaves are still edible but more bitter. Remove the plant and either sow again or move on to a warm-season crop.

notifications.title: Time to sow your leafy greens
notifications.body: Leafy greens love cool weather and can go in the ground 4-6 weeks before your last frost. Sow directly into prepared soil or start indoors for transplanting. They are some of the first crops of the year -- enjoy the early start.

notifications.title: Your greens should be ready to start picking
notifications.body: Begin harvesting outer leaves now even if the plant seems small. Regular picking encourages more growth. Do not wait for the plant to be 'done' -- leafy greens are a harvest-as-you-go crop.

notifications.title: Heat incoming -- watch your greens for bolting
notifications.body: Hot weather triggers leafy greens to bolt -- sending up a flower stalk and turning bitter. Harvest everything you can now before the heat arrives. Consider sowing again in late summer for a fall crop.

notifications.title: Time to sow your fall leafy greens
notifications.body: Eight weeks before first frost is the window for a second sowing of leafy greens. A fall crop often outperforms spring -- the cooling temperatures mean slower bolting and sweeter flavor. Kale especially improves after a light frost.

notifications.title: How are your greens looking?
notifications.body: Leafy greens can bolt quickly in warm weather. A quick check every few days helps you catch the right harvest moment and spot any bolting before it is too late.

weather_triggers.title: Heat alert -- harvest your greens now
weather_triggers.body: Hot weather is the enemy of leafy greens. They bolt quickly and flavor turns bitter fast. Harvest as much as you can before the heat arrives. Shade cloth can buy you another week in marginal temperatures.

weather_triggers.title: Unexpected frost -- protect young greens
weather_triggers.body: Most leafy greens handle light frost well once established, but young seedlings need protection. Cover with fleece tonight if frost is forecast.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- watch for downy mildew
weather_triggers.body: Humid conditions encourage downy mildew on leafy greens. Ensure good airflow between plants and avoid watering late in the day. Pick regularly to keep the plant open.

germination.text: Leafy greens are some of the easiest crops to germinate -- cool, moist soil is all they need. Sow more thickly than you think you need and thin later.
The thinnings from leafy greens are completely edible -- use them as microgreens in salads. Thinning is harvesting.

seedling.text: Thin to the recommended spacing even though it feels wasteful. Crowded leafy greens bolt faster, get less airflow, and produce smaller leaves.
A light mulch around seedlings keeps moisture in and suppresses weeds -- both important for leafy greens which need consistent moisture.

established.text: Start harvesting outer leaves as soon as they reach a useful size -- this is how leafy greens work. The center keeps producing new growth as you remove the outer leaves.
Water consistently. Irregular watering is a major trigger for bolting in many leafy greens, especially lettuce and spinach.

harvest.text: Always harvest in the morning when leaves are full of water and at their crispest. Refrigerate immediately in a damp bag.
Leave at least half the plant intact when harvesting cut-and-come-again crops. Taking too much at once sets the plant back.

bolting.text: Once you see a flower stalk, harvest everything immediately. The leaves are still edible but will become more bitter every day.
Bolted leafy greens are not a failure -- it is the plant completing its lifecycle. A fall sowing often outperforms spring because the weather is cooling rather than warming.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 4-6 oz per plant before bolting
yield_expectations.peak_production: Spinach is a quick crop -- harvest everything within the window
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Spinach bolts fast in heat. Plan for a spring and a fall sowing rather than one long crop.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Most leafy greens actually handle light frost well once established -- it can even improve flavor. But young seedlings are more vulnerable. If the damage happened at the seedling stage, a late frost likely caught them.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Cover seedlings with fleece if frost threatens in the first few weeks. Established leafy greens generally recover from light frost on their own.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Slugs love leafy green seedlings, especially in wet conditions. Downy mildew affects plants in humid, overcrowded conditions. Flea beetles leave tiny holes in leaves -- especially on arugula and kale.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Thin seedlings properly to allow airflow. Protect from slugs in the first few weeks. Row cover helps with flea beetles on susceptible varieties.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too much water or bolting
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Leafy greens in waterlogged soil develop root rot quickly. More commonly, warmth and long days trigger bolting -- the plant sends up a flower stalk and the leaves become bitter. This is the plant completing its lifecycle, not a failure of care.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Bolting is largely about timing. Sow earlier in spring or switch to a fall sowing -- cooling temperatures signal the plant to keep producing leaves rather than flowering.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too little water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Irregular watering is a major bolting trigger in lettuce and spinach. A dry spell followed by heat pushes them to flower and seed rapidly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Keep moisture consistent -- mulching around leafy greens makes a real difference. Water in the morning so leaves dry during the day.

failure_diagnostics.label: Bolted too quickly
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Heat and long days cause most leafy greens to bolt -- this is the most common reason they fail. The plant is not dying, it is doing what it is designed to do. Once bolted the leaves become bitter and inedible quickly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: The fall sowing is almost always more successful than spring for leafy greens. Cooling temperatures give you longer, slower-bolting plants. Shade cloth can also extend the spring crop by a couple of weeks.

fertilizer.notes: Avoid high nitrogen -- it produces forked, hairy roots. A low-nitrogen feed worked into soil before sowing is ideal.

succession.tip: Sow every 3 weeks from early spring through midsummer. Carrots are slow to germinate (10-21 days) so keep the seedbed moist until sprouts appear. The key succession insight for carrots is that they store well in the ground -- you can leave a mature batch in place while a new one grows. But succession avoids having all your carrots mature in August heat, when they develop off flavors. Autumn-matured carrots from a late sowing are noticeably sweeter.

good.name: Rosemary
good.why: Deters carrot fly with strong scent

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Pest-deterrent claim without matching established pattern. Default to traditional pending review.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Allium sulfur-based volatile organic compounds have documented aphid-repellent effects (Durenne and Gosset, Insects 2018, 9(4):112). Chives-with-carrots for carrot fly deterrence is specifically described by Mississippi State University Extension ('Chives tend to repel aphids, but the chives also repel rust flies in carrots'). Utah State University Extension's 'Carrot Rust Fly' management page does NOT endorse allium interplanting as a primary control -- it lists timely harvest, delayed planting, crop rotation, crop residue removal, and row covers as the recommended tactics. The carrot-fly-by-allium mechanism is plausible (both aphids and carrot rust fly locate hosts by scent), but the extension protocol rigor is lower than the extension-documented controls. The earlier catalog attribution to 'UC IPM' does not match UC IPM's published aphid or carrot pest guidelines.

pests.name: Carrot fly
pests.symptoms: Rust-red tunnels and channels inside roots. Foliage yellows and wilts. Larvae (small white maggots) visible in roots.
pests.cause: Psila rosae. Female flies attracted by carrot scent to lay eggs near roots.
pests.organic_treatment: No cure once roots infested. Use fine mesh netting 60cm high as barrier -- flies are low-fliers.
pests.prevention: Grow under fine insect mesh. Sow alongside chives or rosemary to mask scent. Avoid thinning on still evenings when smell is strongest.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Willow-carrot aphids curl leaf tips and reduce vigor. Leaves distorted. Can transmit viruses.
pests.cause: Cavariella aegopodii. Arrives from willow trees in spring.
pests.organic_treatment: Insecticidal soap or neem oil spray.
pests.prevention: Grow under insect mesh. Avoid planting near willow trees.

diseases.name: Cavity spot
diseases.symptoms: Oval gray/brown sunken cavities on carrot roots. First appears as small lesions that enlarge.
diseases.cause: Pythium violae soil pathogen. Favored by compacted, poorly drained soil.
diseases.organic_treatment: No chemical control. Improve soil structure with organic matter.
diseases.prevention: Deep, well-drained, stone-free soil. Avoid waterlogging. Crop rotation.

watering.frequency: Every 3-4 days during germination, weekly once established
watering.method: Gentle overhead or drip -- a strong stream washes seeds out of loose seedbed during germination

crops.harvest_ready: Shoulder of carrot visible at soil level and ½ inch across. Green tops should be vibrant. Loosen soil first, then pull. Frost improves sweetness.

start_method.notes: Always direct sow -- carrots do not transplant. Sow thinly, firm soil well, and keep moist until germination (can take 2-3 weeks).

container_notes.notes: Works in deep containers (12+ inches). Choose short varieties (Chantenay, Danvers, Paris Market). 3-gallon minimum.

varieties.note: Chantenay is the best choice for heavy or rocky soil -- short and blunt rather than long and thin.

rotation.avoid_after: Carrots, parsnips, parsley, cilantro, dill, celery -- share carrot fly and Apiaceae diseases
rotation.note: Avoid planting carrots where parsnips (or vice versa) grew last year -- same pest pressures.

storage.fridge: 4-6 weeks -- remove tops first (tops draw moisture from root)
storage.freezer: Blanch and freeze for cooking
storage.notes: Carrots store best in damp sand in a cool place. Can be left in ground through mild frosts. Store away from apples, pears, and bananas -- ethylene from those fruits triggers isocoumarin formation in carrots, producing a bitter taste within days.

crops.soil_prep: Carrots need deep, light, stone-free soil to 12 inches. Remove all stones and break up clods. Never use fresh manure -- it causes forking and hairy roots. A light dressing of sand helps drainage. Firm the surface after sowing -- loose seedbed causes problems.

thinning.when: Thin when seedlings are 1 inch tall
thinning.method: Snip with scissors rather than pulling -- pulling disturbs neighbors. Thin again to 3-4 inches when 3 inches tall. Thinning is critical -- crowded carrots produce a mass of small forked roots.
thinning.tip: Thin on a still evening and firm soil around remaining plants to prevent carrot fly detecting the scent.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Thread-like shoots pushing up from the soil. Carrots and parsnips are notoriously slow -- do not give up.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep soil surface consistently moist -- the most common reason carrots fail is the surface drying out during the 2-3 week germination period. Lay a plank of wood over the row and check daily.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Feathery or distinctive first true leaves -- carrots look like tiny ferns, beetroot has deep red stems.
growth_stages.user_action: Thin seedlings carefully and promptly. Crowded root vegetables fork and stay small. Thin in stages -- once at 2 inches, again at 4 inches.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Strong leaf growth above ground. Roots are developing below -- resist the urge to dig and check.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep consistently watered -- irregular watering causes cracking and forking in root crops. Weed carefully to avoid disturbing roots.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Shoulders of root visible at soil surface, or reach the days to maturity for your variety. Test pull one before harvesting the row.
growth_stages.user_action: Water well before harvesting to loosen the soil. Pull at an angle rather than straight up to prevent snapping. Many root crops improve with frost.

growth_stages.name: In Storage
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Roots harvested and stored properly. Potatoes in a dark cool place. Carrots in damp sand.
growth_stages.user_action: Check stored roots monthly for any that are rotting -- one bad root can spread to others. Remove immediately.

notifications.title: Time to sow your root vegetables
notifications.body: Root vegetables go directly into the ground -- they do not transplant. Prepare your bed deeply, remove any stones that could cause forking, and sow thinly. Most root crops can go in 3-4 weeks before last frost.

notifications.title: Time to thin your root crops
notifications.body: Thinning is the most important thing you can do for root vegetables right now. Crowded roots fork and stay small. Thin to the recommended spacing -- eat the thinnings if they are big enough.

notifications.title: Your root vegetables should be approaching harvest
notifications.body: Do a test pull of one root before harvesting the row. Water the ground well first to loosen the soil. Most root crops can stay in the ground for several weeks after reaching full size -- they store well in situ.

notifications.title: Harvest before the ground freezes
notifications.body: Most root vegetables need to be out of the ground before it freezes solid. Carrots, parsnips, and beetroot can handle light frost -- it actually sweetens them. But harvest everything before a hard freeze locks them in.

notifications.title: Root check-in
notifications.body: Root vegetables mostly look after themselves once established, but it is worth checking for weeds and keeping the soil consistently moist. How are they looking above ground?

weather_triggers.title: Dry spell -- water your root crops consistently
weather_triggers.body: Irregular watering during root development causes carrots and parsnips to fork, beetroot to become woody, and potatoes to crack. Water deeply and consistently -- not a little every day but a good soak twice a week.

weather_triggers.title: Heavy rain -- check for waterlogging
weather_triggers.body: Root vegetables sitting in waterlogged soil can rot. Check drainage in your bed and consider harvesting any roots that are near maturity before they split from the rapid moisture uptake.

weather_triggers.title: Frost coming -- parsnips and carrots will thank you
weather_triggers.body: A light frost actually improves the flavor of carrots and parsnips by converting starch to sugar. Leave them in the ground through light frosts if you can. Potatoes and beetroot should be harvested before a hard frost.

germination.text: These crops are direct-sown -- transplanting damages the taproot and produces forked or stunted roots. Sow seeds shallowly (1/4 to 1/2 inch deep) and keep soil surface consistently moist for the 1 to 3 week germination window.
Carrot and parsnip seed is short-lived -- use fresh seed each year. Parsnip especially can take up to 3 weeks to germinate; do not give up early.

seedling.text: Thin to recommended spacing once seedlings have 2 true leaves -- crowded roots stay small and forked. Pull weaker seedlings rather than transplanting them.
Mulch lightly between rows once seedlings are established to suppress weeds. Hand-weed close to the row -- hoeing damages shallow seedling roots.

established.text: Water consistently. Uneven moisture causes carrot and parsnip roots to split as they swell during a wet period after dry conditions.
These crops feed lightly. Side-dress with compost mid-season if growth slows; avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers, which produce lush leafy tops at the expense of roots.

harvest.text: Harvest carrots, parsnips, beetroot, and turnips after the first frost for best flavor -- this is not folklore; the cold genuinely converts starch to sugar in the root. Parsnip especially needs frost exposure to develop its characteristic sweetness.

Loosen soil with a fork before pulling -- yanking by the tops snaps the root, especially on long carrots and parsnips. Cut tops off within an inch of the crown for storage; tops left on draw moisture out of the root.

storage.text: Store carrots, parsnips, beetroot, and turnips in layers of damp sand or sawdust in a cool location (32 to 40 degrees) at high humidity. Properly stored, these crops keep 4 to 6 months.

In zones with mild winters, you can leave the roots in the ground and harvest as needed -- mulch heavily over the row before the ground freezes. This is often easier than indoor storage and preserves quality longer.

yield_expectations.per_plant: One carrot per plant -- a 3-foot row gives you around 30-40 carrots
yield_expectations.peak_production: Carrots mature roughly all at once -- plan storage
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Homegrown carrots taste nothing like shop-bought ones. They are sweeter, more flavorful, and worth every bit of effort.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: These crops actively benefit from light to moderate frost -- it improves flavor by converting root starch to sugar. Damage from frost is rare and usually only happens to exposed leaf tops on a hard freeze; the roots are insulated by soil and survive even harsh winter conditions in many zones.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Time harvest to follow the first frost rather than precede it. In zones with mild winters, leave roots in the ground under heavy mulch and harvest as needed through winter.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Carrot rust fly (carrot, parsnip) is the headline pest -- larvae tunnel through roots leaving rusty trails. Cabbage maggot (turnip, sometimes beetroot) does similar damage to brassica roots. Leaf spot diseases and powdery mildew can hit foliage but rarely affect the root harvest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Floating row cover from sowing through harvest blocks both carrot rust fly and cabbage maggot -- this is the most effective home-garden defense. Rotate root crops to a new bed each year. Avoid planting carrot or parsnip after parsley or celery (same family, same pest).

failure_diagnostics.label: Cracked or rotten roots
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Uneven watering -- a dry spell followed by heavy water -- causes roots to split as they swell rapidly. Persistent waterlogging causes root rot, soft black tissue, and crown collapse. Beetroot and turnip handle wet soil better than carrot and parsnip, both of which need excellent drainage.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Maintain consistent moisture rather than letting soil dry out and then soaking it. On heavy clay, plant in a raised bed for carrot and parsnip especially. Mulch helps stabilize moisture.

failure_diagnostics.label: Small, woody, or strong-flavored roots
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought-stressed root crops produce small, fibrous roots with concentrated and often unpleasantly strong flavor. Parsnips become woody at the core; carrots become bitter; turnips become sharp; beetroot becomes earthy and tough.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water deeply and consistently -- 1 inch per week is the rough target. Mulch between rows to retain moisture. In hot weather, root crops appreciate light afternoon shade.

failure_diagnostics.label: Patchy germination
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Carrot, parsnip, and beetroot seeds need 1 to 3 weeks of consistent surface moisture to germinate. The most common reason for failed sowings is the soil surface drying out during germination -- not poor seed or bad soil. Parsnip seed in particular loses viability fast and old seed simply does not come up.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Sow into pre-moistened soil and cover with a board or burlap until the first seedlings emerge -- this keeps the surface consistently moist without daily watering. Use fresh parsnip seed each year. Pre-sprout difficult seed on damp paper towels indoors before sowing if needed.

crops.name: Basil
crops.description: The quintessential summer herb. Plant near tomatoes -- they're culinary and companion garden partners. Pinch flowers immediately to keep leaves producing.

3.notes: Start indoors 4 weeks before last frost. Cold kills basil instantly -- wait until nights are reliably above 50°F.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.source_quote: Sow basil seeds directly into the ground after the danger of frost has passed. (UMN Extension, 'Growing basil in home gardens')
direct_sow.synthesis_note: Basil is a warm-weather herb that cannot tolerate frost. Plant after last frost when soil has warmed to about 70 degrees F, typically 2 weeks after last frost. For an earlier start, seeds can be started indoors 4 weeks before last frost and transplanted out.

fertilizer.notes: Moderate feeder. Liquid balanced feed every 3 weeks keeps growth lush. Pinch out flowers to maintain leaf production.
fertilizer.npk_hint: 10-10-10 at half strength -- too much makes leaves bitter
fertilizer.notify_message: Light feed time for your basil

succession.tip: Sow every 3 weeks from last frost through midsummer. Basil bolts quickly in heat -- flowering stems become bitter and the plant redirects energy from leaves to seeds. Pinching flowers delays this but doesn't stop it. A fresh succession planting every 3 weeks means you always have young, leafy plants at peak flavor. If you're growing for pesto, succession means you can harvest entire plants rather than carefully pinching to delay bolt.
