pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Japanese beetle
pests.symptoms: Skeletonized leaves with only veins remaining. Metallic green beetles visible on plants in summer.
pests.cause: Popillia japonica. Adults feed on foliage July-August.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick beetles into soapy water in the morning when sluggish. Neem oil spray.
pests.prevention: Row covers during peak beetle season. Milky spore disease treatment targets larvae in lawn.

diseases.name: Fusarium wilt
diseases.symptoms: Sudden wilting of one or more stems, yellow leaves, streaking on stems. Plants die rapidly.
diseases.cause: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. basilici soil fungus.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure. Remove and destroy infected plants immediately.
diseases.prevention: Buy certified disease-free seed. Rotate basil crops. Improve soil drainage.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms: Yellowing leaves with fuzzy gray-purple coating on leaf undersides. Spreads rapidly in humid conditions.
diseases.cause: Peronospora belbahrii. A major basil disease, especially indoors.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Improve air circulation. Copper-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention: Do not wet foliage. Space plants well. Grow in full sun. Choose resistant varieties.

watering.frequency: Every 2-3 days -- wilts dramatically but recovers quickly
watering.method: At soil level -- wet leaves cause disease

crops.harvest_ready: Pick top leaves and stems before flowering. Once it flowers, flavor declines. Pinch flower heads to extend harvest.

start_method.notes: Start 4-6 weeks before last frost. Very cold-sensitive -- do not transplant until night temps stay above 50°F. Harden off over 7-10 days.

container_notes.notes: One of the best herbs for containers. Single large pot or window box. Keep in full sun and water regularly.

varieties.note: Genovese is the standard for pesto and Italian cooking. Spicy Globe stays compact and is ideal for containers.

storage.room_temp: On counter in a glass of water like flowers -- 1-2 weeks
storage.fridge: Avoid -- basil turns black in cold
storage.freezer: Blend with olive oil and freeze in ice cube trays. Excellent for winter cooking.
storage.notes: Never refrigerate fresh basil. Counter-top vase method is the best storage.

bolting.prevention: Pinch flower heads off immediately and consistently. Keep harvesting tips. Do not allow any flowers to set seed.
bolting.note: Basil that flowers drops leaf quality but doesn't become inedible. Aggressive pinching extends harvest by weeks.

rotation.avoid_after: Other herbs in the mint family
rotation.good_after: Tomatoes, peppers -- classic pairing and compatible rotation
rotation.note: Basil grown near tomatoes for companion benefit can follow tomatoes the next year.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small seedlings emerging. Annual herbs germinate readily in warm conditions.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep soil consistently moist. Most annual herbs germinate better in warmth -- 65-75°F is ideal.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: True leaves developing -- already recognizable as the herb you planted.
growth_stages.user_action: Thin to 6-9 inches. The thinnings are edible -- add them to salads.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: A bushy, fragrant plant ready for regular harvesting.
growth_stages.user_action: Begin harvesting by pinching out the growing tips -- this encourages bushy side growth rather than a tall, lanky plant.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Plenty of leafy growth, plant not yet showing flowering stems.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest little and often by pinching growing tips. Never remove more than a third of the plant at once. Regular harvesting is what keeps herbs producing.

growth_stages.name: Bolting / Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Central flower stem shooting up. Leaves becoming smaller and flavor intensifying or turning bitter depending on the herb.
growth_stages.user_action: Remove flower stems immediately on basil to extend harvest. For cilantro and dill, flowering is part of the lifecycle -- collect seeds for cooking or sowing.

notifications.title: Start your basil indoors
notifications.body: Basil is frost-tender and loves warmth. Start seeds indoors 3-4 weeks before last frost. Keep at 70°F+ -- basil sown in cold conditions germinates poorly and grows slowly.

notifications.title: Start pinching your basil
notifications.body: Begin pinching out the growing tips as soon as you have 4-6 sets of leaves. This is the most important technique for growing productive basil -- it forces bushy side growth instead of a single tall stem. Pinch every 2-3 weeks.

notifications.title: Remove basil flowers immediately
notifications.body: Pinch out any flower buds the moment you see them. Basil that flowers shifts all its energy to seed production and the leaves become smaller and less flavorful. Be diligent about this through summer.

notifications.title: Harvest all basil before first frost
notifications.body: Basil blackens and dies at the first frost. Harvest everything now. Make pesto, freeze leaves in olive oil ice cube trays, or dry stems for winter. Nothing from the basil plant should be left to frost.

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- protect tender herbs
weather_triggers.body: Basil, cilantro, and lemongrass are extremely frost-tender. Bring containers inside or cover with fleece tonight. Hardy herbs like thyme, rosemary, and mint are much more frost-tolerant.

weather_triggers.title: Heat alert -- herbs may bolt
weather_triggers.body: Heat triggers bolting in cilantro, dill, and parsley. Harvest as much as possible before temperatures peak. Basil, on the other hand, loves heat -- just remove any flowers that appear.

germination.text: These herbs are direct-sown or started indoors. Basil needs warm soil (70 degrees) for germination; dill and cilantro tolerate cooler soil (55 to 60 degrees) and actually germinate better in cool weather.
Sow shallowly -- 1/4 inch deep -- and keep soil surface moist. Cilantro and dill can be sown in succession every 2 to 3 weeks for continuous harvest, since both bolt fast.

seedling.text: Thin to recommended spacing once seedlings have 2 true leaves -- crowded plants bolt faster and produce less leaf. Pinch basil tops at 6 inches to encourage branching.
These herbs all benefit from light afternoon shade in hot summer climates. Cilantro especially bolts within weeks of warm weather hitting.

established.text: Pinch basil regularly to prevent flowering -- once basil flowers, leaf production slows and flavor changes. Removing flower buds extends the productive harvest by weeks.
Water consistently. Wilted plants recover but the stress accelerates bolting in cilantro and dill. Mulch to stabilize soil moisture.

harvest.text: Harvest by snipping outer leaves first, leaving the central growing tip intact. For basil, cut whole stems above a leaf pair to encourage two new shoots from each cut.
Cilantro is harvested as leaves OR seed (coriander). Same plant, same cycle: harvest leaves while plant is leafy, let it bolt, harvest dry seeds from the spent flower heads.

bolting.text: Bolting (going to flower) signals the end of useful leaf production for these herbs. Basil bolts in heat or after flowering; dill and cilantro bolt fast in any warm weather.

Once bolting starts, decide: pinch flowers to extend leaf harvest by 1 to 2 weeks (basil), or let the plant flower and self-seed for next year (dill, cilantro). Bolted cilantro is often the original planting and reseeds prolifically.

yield_expectations.per_plant: Continuous harvest of leaves all summer from one plant
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Basil from your own garden, still warm from the sun, is one of the great simple pleasures of growing food.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Basil is killed outright by light frost -- it is the most frost-sensitive culinary herb. Dill and cilantro are hardier; both tolerate light frost and cilantro actually grows better in cool weather. Basil also suffers chill damage (leaf blackening) below 50 degrees even without frost.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Wait to plant basil until soil is reliably 60 degrees and night temperatures stay above 50. For dill and cilantro, sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring -- they prefer cool conditions. Have row cover ready for cold nights with basil; in the fall, harvest basil heavily before the first cold snap because the plants will not recover.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Aphids cluster on tender new growth across all three. Basil downy mildew is the headline disease (yellowing and gray fuzz on leaf undersides) and has spread aggressively in recent years. Dill and cilantro may attract carrot family pests (carrot rust fly larvae, leaf miner). Powdery mildew occasionally hits all three in humid summers.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Choose downy-mildew-resistant basil varieties -- Rutgers Devotion DMR, Prospera, and similar bred for resistance. Space plants well for airflow. Hose off aphids with water; for serious infestations, insecticidal soap. Rotate herb-bed location each year.

failure_diagnostics.label: Root rot or yellowing
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: All three herbs need well-drained soil. Persistent waterlogging causes root rot, yellowing leaves, and crown collapse. Basil is especially sensitive to wet conditions and may collapse suddenly from Pythium or Fusarium in poorly-drained sites.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil. Use containers with drainage holes for indoor or balcony herbs. Water at the base, not overhead, and let the soil surface dry slightly between waterings. Avoid heavy clay sites for basil especially.

failure_diagnostics.label: Wilting or rapid bolting
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress accelerates bolting in cilantro and dill -- often by weeks -- and produces small, tough basil leaves with concentrated bitter flavor. Wilted herbs recover with watering but the stress shortens the productive cycle.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently, especially in heat. Mulch around plants to retain soil moisture. For cilantro and dill, succession-plant every 2 to 3 weeks rather than relying on one planting through the season -- this gives you continuous harvest even as individual plantings bolt.

failure_diagnostics.label: Leggy or sparse growth
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: These herbs need 6 hours of direct sun minimum for full flavor and growth. In partial shade, plants grow tall, leggy, and pale, with weaker flavor. Cilantro is a partial exception -- it tolerates partial shade in hot zones, where light shade actually slows bolting.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun in cool climates. In hot climates (zone 8 and warmer), cilantro and parsley tolerate and even prefer light afternoon shade. Basil and dill want full sun even in heat. For indoor growing, herbs need a sunny south-facing window or supplemental grow lights.

crops.description: The classic overproducer. Two plants feed a family -- three and you'll be leaving bags on neighbors' doorsteps. Plant in hills with lots of compost.

direct_sow.synthesis_note: Squash seeds will not germinate in cold soil. Black plastic mulch and row covers can raise soil temperature and allow earlier planting. Check soil temperature at the two-inch depth as summer squash seeds are planted deeper than cucumber seeds. (UMN Extension)

harvest_start.synthesis_note: In Georgia, the last practical direct-sow window for fall-maturing cucurbits and warm-season crops is around July 20 -- plantings after this date typically don't mature before first fall frost. UGA's Vegetable Garden Calendar names tomatoes, okra, corn, pole beans, lima beans, cucumbers, squash, and snap beans as the crops this cutoff applies to. (UGA Vegetable Garden Calendar)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: In warm zones (Z8+), cucurbit fruit quality declines in peak heat. Spring-planted fast cucurbits generally finish before the worst summer heat; secondary (fall) plantings harvest from late summer through first frost. (UGA Vegetable Garden Calendar; Clemson HGIC)
harvest_end.design_note: Use heat_pause_start - 5d for primary window end.

harvest_end.label: secondary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Harvest all cucurbit fruits before first fall frost. Vines are frost-tender; a light frost may kill foliage but fruit on the plant is usually still edible. A hard freeze will damage fruit. (UMN Extension; Iowa State Extension; UGA Vegetable Garden Calendar)

11.notes: Cool season crop in Zone 11. Avoid summer planting.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note: In south Florida, fast cucurbits are grown through the cool season and into spring. Plant from September through March for reliable harvest; summer heat reduces fruit set. (UF/IFAS pattern for cucurbits in tropical zones)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: In south Florida, fast cucurbits are grown through the cool season and into spring. Plant from September through March for reliable harvest; summer heat reduces fruit set. (UF/IFAS pattern for cucurbits in tropical zones)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: In south Florida, cucurbits are grown and harvested during the cool/dry season before summer heat and humidity reduce fruit set and quality. (UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar ENH1191; UF/IFAS VH021)

fertilizer.notes: Heavy feeder -- add generous compost at planting. Avoid excess nitrogen once flowering or you'll get lots of leaf and few fruit.

succession.tip: Sow a second batch 4 weeks after the first. One zucchini plant will produce more than most families can eat -- the reason for succession isn't quantity but quality. Younger plants produce more vigorously and with less disease pressure. Powdery mildew and squash vine borers typically hit older plants hard; a second generation sidesteps this. Two plants per succession, not a full bed.

good.name: Nasturtiums
good.why: Trap crop for aphids, attracts predators

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension 2022 and 2025 Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetable Crops; UConn IPM 'Perimeter Trap Cropping for Cole Crops'). Nasturtiums specifically are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and Utah State University Extension (Mohr et al., 'Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting'). Protocol caveat: UConn IPM explicitly notes trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents' -- so the aphid application here has a protocol-mismatch concern even though the companion is extension-named. The Cornell-IPM-specific attribution in earlier catalog reason text was not located in Cornell's published IPM material; actual backing is WSU/USU/UConn.

provenance.label: extension_backed

pests.name: Cucumber beetle
pests.symptoms: Yellow-green beetles with black spots or stripes feeding on leaves, flowers, and fruit. Plants wilt suddenly (bacterial wilt transmission). Holey leaves.
pests.cause: Spotted and striped cucumber beetles. Also transmit bacterial wilt disease.
pests.organic_treatment: Row covers until flowering. Yellow sticky traps. Neem oil spray. Spinosad-based insecticide.
pests.prevention: Delay planting until plants are large. Use row covers early season. Interplant with radishes and nasturtiums.

pests.name: Squash bug
pests.symptoms: Gray-brown flat insects on stems and undersides of leaves. Wilting leaves with yellow then brown patches. Bronze egg clusters on leaf undersides.
pests.cause: Anasa tristis. Overwinters as adults in garden debris.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick adults and egg masses. Trap under boards at night. Neem oil spray on nymphs.
pests.prevention: Remove all garden debris in autumn. Rotate cucurbit crops. Use row covers early season.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces, stems, and sometimes fruit. Leaves may yellow and die. Worst in warm days with cool nights.
diseases.cause: Fungal disease favored by humid conditions with poor air circulation.
diseases.organic_treatment: Spray with diluted neem oil or a baking soda solution (1 tsp per quart water). Apply potassium bicarbonate spray. Remove and destroy affected leaves.
diseases.prevention: Space plants for good airflow. Water at soil level, not on foliage. Choose resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation.

diseases.name: Bacterial wilt
diseases.symptoms: Sudden wilting of individual leaves, then whole stems, then entire plant. No recovery even with watering. Plants die within days.
diseases.cause: Erwinia tracheiphila bacteria spread by cucumber beetles feeding.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure -- remove and destroy infected plants immediately. Control cucumber beetles to prevent spread.
diseases.prevention: Use row covers to exclude cucumber beetles early in season. Plant resistant varieties.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms: Yellow-green patches on upper leaf surface with corresponding gray-purple fuzzy growth on leaf undersides. Leaves die rapidly.
diseases.cause: Pseudoperonospora cubensis fungus. Spreads rapidly in wet humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively.
diseases.prevention: Choose resistant varieties. Water at soil level. Ensure good air circulation.

watering.method: At soil level -- wet leaves cause powdery mildew

crops.harvest_ready: Best at 6-8 inches -- small zucchini have better flavor and texture. Overgrown zucchini (marrows) are still edible but become seedy and watery.

start_method.notes: Direct sow after last frost. Zucchini grows so fast that starting indoors offers little advantage. If starting indoors, use biodegradable pots -- 3 weeks before last frost maximum.

container_notes.notes: Possible in large containers (10+ gallons) but not ideal -- plants are large and thirsty. Raised beds are much better.

varieties.note: Patio Star and Bush Baby are excellent if space is limited -- compact plants, full yield.

rotation.avoid_after: Cucumbers, squash, pumpkins, melons -- share cucumber beetle, bacterial wilt, downy mildew
rotation.note: Rotate to prevent cucumber beetle and disease buildup.

storage.freezer: Slice or grate, blanch 2 minutes, freeze. Good for baking.
storage.notes: Small zucchini store much better than large ones.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Large seed leaves pushing up fast -- squash germinates quickly in warm soil.
growth_stages.user_action: Sow seeds on their edge to prevent rotting. Keep soil warm and moist.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Large, hairy true leaves developing rapidly. Squash grows fast once it gets going.
growth_stages.user_action: Give them space from the start -- squash plants get very large and do not like competition.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: A strong central crown with multiple large leaves. Bush varieties stay compact; vining types will start to sprawl.
growth_stages.user_action: If growing winter squash, direct the vines in the direction you want them to go now -- once established they are harder to redirect.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Growing well and in the right spot?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Large orange-yellow flowers. Male flowers come first on long straight stems. Female flowers have a swollen base -- the future squash.
growth_stages.user_action: Hand-pollinate female flowers in the early morning if you are not seeing good fruit set. Touch a male flower to each open female flower.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Flowers open? Any tiny squash forming?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Summer squash: harvest small and often at 6-8 inches. Winter squash: wait until skin is hard and stem is dry and corky.
growth_stages.user_action: Summer squash picked small tastes better and keeps production going. Winter squash left on the vine longer develops better flavor and storage life.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Slowing production on summer squash. Winter squash stems drying and corking -- the cue to harvest before frost.
growth_stages.user_action: Cure winter squash at room temperature for 10-14 days before storing -- it hardens the skin and sweetens the flesh. Summer squash plants can be composted after frost.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Season done? Worth noting what worked.

notifications.title: Time to sow your squash
notifications.body: Squash goes in a week after last frost, once the soil has had time to warm properly. Sow 2-3 seeds per spot and thin to the strongest plant. They grow fast -- you will see real progress within a week.

notifications.title: Check your squash flowers -- pollination time
notifications.body: Your squash should be flowering now. If you see flowers but no fruit forming, check whether you have both male and female flowers open at the same time. Female flowers have a small swollen base. Hand-pollinate in the morning if bees are scarce.

notifications.title: Summer squash ready -- pick small and often
notifications.body: Your courgettes or summer squash should be ready. Pick them at 6-8 inches -- they taste better small and the plant produces far more when you harvest regularly. A forgotten courgette turns into a marrow overnight.

notifications.title: Check your squash plants
notifications.body: Summer squash especially needs checking every few days -- they grow incredibly fast and a missed harvest sets back the whole plant.

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- protect your squash
weather_triggers.body: Squash is frost-tender. Cover with fleece tonight. Winter squash still on the vine must be harvested before a hard frost -- even one frosty night can damage stored winter squash.

weather_triggers.title: Powdery mildew risk for your squash
weather_triggers.body: Squash is very susceptible to powdery mildew in humid conditions. Ensure good spacing and airflow. If you see white powdery patches on leaves, remove affected leaves and spray with a dilute baking soda solution.

weather_triggers.title: Your squash needs deep watering
weather_triggers.body: Squash plants have large leaves and need a lot of water in dry conditions. Water deeply at the base -- not the leaves -- twice a week in drought conditions. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture.

germination.text: Sow squash seeds on their side, not flat. The root emerges from the pointed end and finds its way down more easily.
Squash germinates fast in warm soil -- sometimes in 4-5 days. In cold soil it rots. Wait for genuine warmth (60F+ minimum, 70F+ ideal).

seedling.text: Thin ruthlessly to one plant per spot. Squash planted too close together become a tangled mass that is prone to mildew and difficult to harvest.
Do not start squash indoors too early -- 3-4 weeks maximum. They outgrow their pots quickly and transplant shock is real.

established.text: Leave enough room -- a zucchini plant can easily cover 4-6 square feet. A butternut squash vine can run 6-10 feet. Plan for this before planting.
A thick layer of mulch around squash plants suppresses weeds, retains moisture, and keeps the fruit clean if it rests on the ground.

flowering.text: Male flowers come before female flowers -- this is normal and not something to worry about. Female flowers (with the swollen base behind the petals) follow within a week or two.
Early morning is when squash flowers are most receptive. If you are hand-pollinating, do it between 7-10am while flowers are fully open.

harvest.text: Pick zucchini and yellow summer squash young -- 6 to 8 inches is the sweet spot for tender flesh and best flavor. At full marrow size the seeds are tough and the skin gets bitter.
Harvest every 2 to 3 days during peak production. Summer squash plants stop setting new fruit if mature ones are left on the vine; constant picking keeps the plant producing.

end_of_season.text: Summer squash do not store. Use, freeze (grated, blanched), or give them away within a week of picking. Refrigerate at 45-50F at most -- below 40F they get pitted and chilled.
When production slows in late summer, pull the plant rather than nursing it. Powdery mildew sets in by then on most varieties; clear the bed and replant for fall greens or cover crop.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 10-20 lbs over the season -- zucchini is one of the most productive vegetables you can grow
yield_expectations.peak_production: At peak, one healthy zucchini plant produces 1-2 fruits every 2-3 days
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Zucchini is famously easy and productive. You will likely have more than you can eat -- plan to give some away.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucurbits are tropical-origin tender annuals -- killed outright by even a light frost at any stage. Cold soil at planting (below 60 degrees) stunts seedlings for the rest of the season even if they survive. Late-summer frost ends the season abruptly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Wait to direct-sow or transplant until soil reaches 65 to 70 degrees and night temperatures stay above 50. In short-season zones, start transplants indoors 3 to 4 weeks before set-out, but disturb roots minimally -- cucurbits resent transplanting. Use black plastic mulch to warm soil. Have row cover ready for unexpected late-spring or early-fall frosts.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucumber beetles (striped and spotted) damage seedlings directly and transmit bacterial wilt -- a fatal disease that wilts vines from the tips inward. Squash bugs target squash and pumpkin (less so cucumber and melon). Powdery mildew shows up reliably late in the season as white powder on leaves. Downy mildew, anthracnose, and bacterial leaf spot are humidity-driven secondary problems.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Floating row cover from planting through first flower blocks cucumber beetles -- remove at flowering for pollination. Squash bug egg masses (orange-red, on undersides of leaves) crush easily by hand if caught early. For powdery mildew, choose resistant varieties (most modern cucumbers are bred for resistance) and water at the base, not overhead. Rotate cucurbits to a new bed each year.

failure_diagnostics.label: Watery fruit or vine collapse
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucurbits need consistent water but cannot tolerate waterlogged soil. Persistent saturation causes root rot, sudden vine collapse, and watery flavorless fruit. Heavy rain near harvest causes ripe melons to crack and split. Wet foliage drives powdery mildew, downy mildew, and bacterial leaf spot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil or raised mounds (the traditional 'cucurbit hill' approach exists for drainage reasons). Water deeply at the base 1 to 2 times per week rather than shallow daily. Mulch heavily to even out soil moisture and reduce splash-borne disease. Stop watering watermelons 2 weeks before expected harvest to concentrate flavor.

failure_diagnostics.label: Small or bitter fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress during flowering and fruit set produces small, misshapen, or bitter fruit. Cucurbits move large volumes of water through their tissues during fruit development -- a single mature watermelon plant can use 1 to 2 gallons of water per day in peak summer. Cucumber bitterness is often a drought-stress signal.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently and deeply -- 1 to 2 inches per week minimum during fruit development, more in heat. Drip irrigation outperforms overhead watering by both providing consistent water and keeping foliage dry. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture and reduce evaporation.

failure_diagnostics.label: Vines without fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucurbits need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum, ideally 8 or more -- to set and ripen fruit. In partial shade vines grow leaves and even bloom, but fruit set is poor and ripening is incomplete. A late-season fruit that never sweetens is often a sun problem more than a temperature problem.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in the sunniest spot available. Trellising vining cucurbits (vertical support for cucumbers and small-fruited squash) gets more leaf area into the sun and improves fruit set substantially. In partial-shade gardens, accept that cucurbits are not the right crop and grow leafy greens or herbs instead.

fertilizer.notes: Beans fix their own nitrogen -- avoid high-nitrogen feeds or you'll get lots of leaf and few pods. A low-nitrogen feed at planting is all they need.
fertilizer.npk_hint: beans fix their own nitrogen -- use 5-10-10 only if soil is poor

succession.tip: Sow every 3 weeks from last frost through midsummer. Bush beans produce in a single flush over 2-3 weeks then decline -- succession is essential for a continuous harvest. Each sowing is a distinct new crop rather than a continuous one. Stop new sowings with enough growing season remaining before first frost: count back 60-70 days from your first expected frost date to find your last safe sowing date.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

pests.name: Bean seed fly
pests.symptoms: Seeds fail to germinate or seedlings die soon after emergence.
pests.cause: Delia platura maggots eat germinating seeds.
pests.organic_treatment: Sow when soil is warm (above 60°F) for rapid germination.
pests.prevention: Wait for warm soil. Start in pots and transplant. Pre-soak seeds to speed germination.

diseases.name: Bean rust
diseases.symptoms: Orange-brown powdery pustules on leaf undersides with corresponding pale spots on top.
diseases.cause: Uromyces appendiculatus fungus. Spreads in warm humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Sulfur-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Improve airflow.

diseases.name: Halo blight
diseases.symptoms: Water-soaked spots surrounded by yellow halo on leaves. Pods develop greasy patches.
diseases.cause: Pseudomonas syringae pv. phaseolicola bacteria. Seed-borne and spread by rain splash.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected plants. Copper-based bactericide spray.
diseases.prevention: Buy certified disease-free seed. Avoid working with wet plants. Rotate crops.

watering.frequency: Weekly -- avoid watering during flowering to prevent blossom drop

crops.harvest_ready: Pick when pods snap cleanly and are pencil thin. Seeds inside should barely be visible as bumps. Check daily -- over-mature beans signal the plant to stop producing.

start_method.notes: Direct sow only after last frost -- beans hate transplanting. Plant 1 inch deep in warm soil (60°F+).

container_notes.notes: Bush varieties work well in 5-gallon containers. Pole beans need a large pot with a trellis.

rotation.avoid_after: Beans, peas -- some shared diseases but generally disease pressure is lower
rotation.good_after: Brassicas, nightshades, corn -- legumes fix nitrogen that these heavy feeders need
rotation.note: Plant legumes before heavy feeders -- they'll leave nitrogen-rich soil behind.

storage.freezer: Blanch 3 minutes, freeze -- excellent
storage.notes: Best eaten fresh. Frozen green beans are nearly as good as fresh for cooking.

recommended: Purple Queen (purple pod, turns green when cooked)
varieties.note: Provider is the most reliable variety for difficult conditions -- very early, tolerates cool and warm soils.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: The fat seed leaf loop pushing up and then straightening. Beans germinate fast in warm soil.
growth_stages.user_action: Sow directly -- beans and peas dislike transplanting. Soil must be at least 60°F for beans, 45°F for peas.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: First true leaves developing, tendrils beginning to reach for support on climbing types.
growth_stages.user_action: Get supports in place for climbing varieties now. Pole beans and sugar snaps grow fast once established.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Strong growth with multiple sets of leaves. Climbing types reaching upward actively.
growth_stages.user_action: Pinch out the growing tips of broad beans when flowers appear at the top -- it deters blackfly, the most common pest.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Flowers along the stem or at growing tips. Beans are self-pollinating -- you do not need to do anything.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep plants well watered during flowering. Drought stress at this stage causes flowers to drop before setting pods.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Pods swelling and filling. Pick before the pods become tough and stringy. Seeds should be visible but not bulging.
growth_stages.user_action: Pick every 2-3 days. Regular picking is essential -- leaving pods to mature tells the plant its job is done and production stops dramatically.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Slowing production, pods becoming tougher, plants yellowing.
growth_stages.user_action: Leave the last few pods to dry fully on the plant and save the seeds for next year. Cut plants at the base and leave the roots -- they fix nitrogen into the soil.

notifications.title: Time to sow your peas
notifications.body: Peas are cold-hardy and can go in 6-8 weeks before your last frost. They actually prefer cool conditions -- sow directly into prepared soil as soon as the ground can be worked. Get supports in place at the same time.

notifications.title: Time to sow your beans
notifications.body: Beans need warm soil -- wait until a week after your last frost before sowing. Cold soil causes seeds to rot rather than germinate. Sow directly at 2-inch depth, supports already in place for pole types.

notifications.title: Pinch out your broad bean tips
notifications.body: As soon as your broad beans show flowers at the top of the stem, pinch out the top 4-6 inches of growth. This deters blackfly which love the soft tips, and also redirects energy to pod development. It feels drastic but it is the right thing to do.

notifications.title: Beans ready -- pick every 2-3 days
notifications.body: The single most important thing now is picking regularly. Beans that are left to mature on the plant signal it to stop producing new pods. Get out there every 2-3 days without fail.

notifications.title: Check your beans and peas
notifications.body: Beans and peas need picking every few days at harvest time. A few days of neglect can mean tough, stringy pods. How are they looking?

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- protect young beans
weather_triggers.body: Bean seedlings are frost-tender. Cover with fleece tonight. Peas handle light frost much better -- established pea plants usually survive without protection.

weather_triggers.title: Drought stress -- water your beans during flowering
weather_triggers.body: Drought during flowering is the most damaging thing for beans and peas. Flowers drop before setting pods and production suffers significantly. Water deeply at the base every 2-3 days in dry weather.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- watch for powdery mildew on peas
weather_triggers.body: Peas are prone to powdery mildew in humid conditions, especially later in the season. Ensure good airflow and harvest promptly. Late in the season this is normal -- the plant has done its job.

germination.text: Beans are direct-sown -- transplanting damages the brittle taproot. Wait until soil is 60 degrees minimum (65 to 70 is better) before sowing; cold soil rots seed before it germinates.

Sow 1 to 2 inches deep, 2 to 4 inches apart in rows. Inoculate seed with rhizobium bacteria at sowing if the bed has not grown beans recently -- this boosts the nitrogen-fixing nodulation that beans depend on.

seedling.text: Beans germinate fast in warm soil -- typically 7 to 10 days. Seedlings are vulnerable to slugs and bean leaf beetles in their first weeks; check daily.

Thin bush beans to 4 to 6 inches between plants once seedlings are 4 inches tall. Pole beans need a trellis or pole structure in place at this stage -- they grow fast and resent late-installed support.

established.text: Do not fertilize beans with nitrogen. Beans fix their own nitrogen via root nodules; high-N fertilizer suppresses nodulation and produces lush leafy plants with poor pod set.
Water consistently during flowering and pod-fill -- this is when water stress most reduces yield. Mulch heavily to stabilize soil moisture and suppress weeds.

flowering.text: Beans are self-pollinating and do not need pollinators. Flowers open and self-pollinate within hours; fruit set is fast.
Watch for bean leaf beetles and aphids during flowering -- both populations spike in this window. Check undersides of leaves daily.

harvest.text: Pick beans young and often -- bush and pole beans ready when pods snap cleanly and the seeds inside are still small. Edamame ready when pods are plump and fill 80 to 90 percent with bright green beans, before yellowing.
Harvest every 2 to 3 days during peak production. Beans left on the plant signal it to stop producing new pods. Edamame is harvested whole-pod, not shelled in the field.

end_of_season.text: After harvest, cut bean plants at ground level and leave roots in the soil -- the nitrogen-fixing root nodules become next year's slow-release nitrogen for the bed.
Rotate beans to a new bed each year. Bean diseases (anthracnose, halo blight, bean rust) survive in soil and infect next year's planting.

yield_expectations.per_plant: Half a pound per plant over the season -- plant generously
yield_expectations.peak_production: Bush beans produce in a flush -- all at once over 2-3 weeks, then done
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Bush beans are fast and reliable. Succession sow every 3 weeks for a continuous harvest.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Beans are warm-season tender annuals -- killed outright by light frost at any stage. Cold soil at sowing (below 60 degrees) rots seed; cool conditions during early growth produce stunted plants that never fully recover. Late summer frost ends the season abruptly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Wait to sow until soil is reliably 60 degrees minimum (65 to 70 is better). In short-season zones, choose early-maturing bush varieties and use black plastic mulch to warm soil. Have row cover ready for unexpected late-spring frosts. For fall harvests, time the planting so harvest finishes before first expected frost.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Mexican bean beetle (yellow with black spots, similar to ladybug but a pest) is the dominant bean pest east of the Rockies -- larvae skeletonize leaves. Bean leaf beetle damages seedlings and pods. Aphids cluster on tender new growth. Halo blight (water-soaked spots with yellow halo) and bean rust are the headline diseases. For edamame specifically, soybean aphid and Japanese beetle are also common.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: For Mexican bean beetle, hand-pick adults and crush yellow egg masses on leaf undersides; in heavy infestations, parasitic wasp release works for organic gardeners. Rotate to a new bed each year. Avoid working bean plants when foliage is wet -- this spreads halo blight and bean rust. Choose disease-resistant varieties for the next planting.

failure_diagnostics.label: Root rot or yellowing
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Persistent waterlogging causes root rot, yellowing leaves, and crown collapse. Beans are also susceptible to white mold (Sclerotinia) in cool wet conditions, which produces fluffy white growth at the soil line and kills plants quickly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil. Water at the base, not overhead, and water in the morning so foliage dries before evening. Space plants for airflow. For white mold, rotate at least 3 years between bean plantings in any one bed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor pod set or fill
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress during flowering and pod-fill is the leading cause of poor bean harvests. Plants drop flowers under water stress and produce small empty or partially-filled pods. Edamame is especially demanding of consistent water during the pod-fill window.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently during flowering and pod-fill -- 1 inch per week minimum, more in heat. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture. Drip irrigation is ideal because it provides consistent water without wetting foliage.

failure_diagnostics.label: Few flowers or pods
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Beans need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to flower and produce well. In partial shade plants grow leaves but flower sparsely and set few pods. Tall pole beans can shade their own lower leaves if not pinched at the top of the support.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun. For pole beans, pinch the growing tip when vines reach the top of the support to prevent excessive top growth and improve light penetration to lower flowering nodes.

fertilizer.notes: Peas fix nitrogen -- they don't need feeding and prefer leaner soil. Over-feeding produces lots of foliage at the expense of pods.

succession.tip: Sow every 2-3 weeks from early spring until temperatures consistently exceed 70°F. Peas hate heat and will stop producing and die when summer arrives -- don't fight it. The goal is to have multiple batches maturing through the cool spring window rather than one big planting that's all done at once. In zones 7+ you can also sow in autumn for a fall crop. Pause all sowings in summer.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

pests.name: Bean seed fly
pests.symptoms: Seeds fail to germinate or seedlings die soon after emergence.
pests.cause: Delia platura maggots eat germinating seeds.
pests.organic_treatment: Sow when soil is warm (above 60°F) for rapid germination.
pests.prevention: Wait for warm soil. Start in pots and transplant. Pre-soak seeds to speed germination.

diseases.name: Bean rust
diseases.symptoms: Orange-brown powdery pustules on leaf undersides with corresponding pale spots on top.
diseases.cause: Uromyces appendiculatus fungus. Spreads in warm humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Sulfur-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Improve airflow.

diseases.name: Halo blight
diseases.symptoms: Water-soaked spots surrounded by yellow halo on leaves. Pods develop greasy patches.
diseases.cause: Pseudomonas syringae pv. phaseolicola bacteria. Seed-borne and spread by rain splash.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected plants. Copper-based bactericide spray.
diseases.prevention: Buy certified disease-free seed. Avoid working with wet plants. Rotate crops.

watering.method: At soil level or overhead early in day

crops.harvest_ready: Pods are plump and round, seeds visible. Pod should snap cleanly. Sweet and crunchy. Don't wait until pods yellow.

start_method.notes: Direct sow 4-6 weeks before last frost -- peas prefer cool soil. Soak seeds overnight for faster germination.

container_notes.notes: Works in deep containers with trellis. 5-gallon minimum. Dwarf varieties are best.

rotation.avoid_after: Beans, peas -- some shared diseases but generally disease pressure is lower
rotation.good_after: Brassicas, nightshades, corn -- legumes fix nitrogen that these heavy feeders need
rotation.note: Plant legumes before heavy feeders -- they'll leave nitrogen-rich soil behind.

storage.freezer: Blanch 2 minutes, freeze -- good
storage.notes: Fresh is much better -- eat as soon as possible after harvest.

varieties.note: Cascadia is the best for small gardens -- compact 30-inch vines need no staking and produce heavily.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: The fat seed leaf loop pushing up and then straightening. Beans germinate fast in warm soil.
growth_stages.user_action: Sow directly -- beans and peas dislike transplanting. Soil must be at least 60°F for beans, 45°F for peas.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: First true leaves developing, tendrils beginning to reach for support on climbing types.
growth_stages.user_action: Get supports in place for climbing varieties now. Pole beans and sugar snaps grow fast once established.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Strong growth with multiple sets of leaves. Climbing types reaching upward actively.
growth_stages.user_action: Pinch out the growing tips of broad beans when flowers appear at the top -- it deters blackfly, the most common pest.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Flowers along the stem or at growing tips. Beans are self-pollinating -- you do not need to do anything.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep plants well watered during flowering. Drought stress at this stage causes flowers to drop before setting pods.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Pods swelling and filling. Pick before the pods become tough and stringy. Seeds should be visible but not bulging.
growth_stages.user_action: Pick every 2-3 days. Regular picking is essential -- leaving pods to mature tells the plant its job is done and production stops dramatically.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Slowing production, pods becoming tougher, plants yellowing.
growth_stages.user_action: Leave the last few pods to dry fully on the plant and save the seeds for next year. Cut plants at the base and leave the roots -- they fix nitrogen into the soil.

notifications.title: Time to sow your peas
notifications.body: Peas are cold-hardy and can go in 6-8 weeks before your last frost. They actually prefer cool conditions -- sow directly into prepared soil as soon as the ground can be worked. Get supports in place at the same time.

notifications.title: Time to sow your beans
notifications.body: Beans need warm soil -- wait until a week after your last frost before sowing. Cold soil causes seeds to rot rather than germinate. Sow directly at 2-inch depth, supports already in place for pole types.

notifications.title: Pinch out your broad bean tips
notifications.body: As soon as your broad beans show flowers at the top of the stem, pinch out the top 4-6 inches of growth. This deters blackfly which love the soft tips, and also redirects energy to pod development. It feels drastic but it is the right thing to do.

notifications.title: Beans ready -- pick every 2-3 days
notifications.body: The single most important thing now is picking regularly. Beans that are left to mature on the plant signal it to stop producing new pods. Get out there every 2-3 days without fail.

notifications.title: Check your beans and peas
notifications.body: Beans and peas need picking every few days at harvest time. A few days of neglect can mean tough, stringy pods. How are they looking?

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- protect young beans
weather_triggers.body: Bean seedlings are frost-tender. Cover with fleece tonight. Peas handle light frost much better -- established pea plants usually survive without protection.

weather_triggers.title: Drought stress -- water your beans during flowering
weather_triggers.body: Drought during flowering is the most damaging thing for beans and peas. Flowers drop before setting pods and production suffers significantly. Water deeply at the base every 2-3 days in dry weather.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- watch for powdery mildew on peas
weather_triggers.body: Peas are prone to powdery mildew in humid conditions, especially later in the season. Ensure good airflow and harvest promptly. Late in the season this is normal -- the plant has done its job.

germination.text: Peas are direct-sown 4 to 6 weeks before last frost -- they actually prefer cool soil (40 to 60 degrees) and germinate poorly above 75. In mild-winter zones, fall sowing for spring harvest works well.
Sow 1 to 1.5 inches deep, 2 inches apart. Inoculate seed with rhizobium bacteria if the bed has not grown peas recently. Soak seeds overnight before sowing in cool soil to speed germination.

seedling.text: Peas germinate in 7 to 14 days in cool soil. Seedlings tolerate light frost and even brief snow once established -- they are remarkably cold-hardy.
Install trellis or netting at sowing or as soon as seedlings emerge. Peas climb by tendrils and need something to grab. Even bush peas benefit from low brushwood support.

established.text: Do not fertilize with nitrogen. Peas fix their own nitrogen via root nodules; extra N produces leafy plants with poor pod production.
Water consistently. Peas have shallow roots and dry out fast -- mulch heavily to stabilize soil moisture and keep roots cool.

flowering.text: Peas are self-pollinating; flowers do not need insect pollinators. Cool weather during flowering produces the most flowers and highest yields.
Watch for pea aphids on flower clusters and tender new growth. Powdery mildew often shows up as flowering peaks, especially in still humid conditions.

harvest.text: Snow peas: pick when pods are flat and the peas inside are barely visible bumps. Sugar snap peas: pick when pods are plump and crisp but before peas inside become starchy. Both are best picked young and often.
Harvest every 1 to 2 days during peak production. Peas left on the plant signal it to stop producing new flowers; daily picking can extend the harvest by weeks.

end_of_season.text: Peas finish abruptly when daytime temperatures consistently exceed 75 to 80 degrees -- plants yellow, stop flowering, and decline. This is the natural cycle, not a problem.
Cut spent plants at ground level and leave roots in the soil for the nitrogen contribution. The freed-up bed is well-suited to a fall planting of cool-season crops or warm-season transplants.

yield_expectations.per_plant: A generous handful of pods per plant
yield_expectations.peak_production: Sugar snaps produce over several weeks in cool weather -- harvest daily at peak
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Fresh sugar snap peas eaten straight from the vine are one of the greatest garden rewards. They taste nothing like shop-bought.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Cold tolerance and heat-induced bolting
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Peas are unusual among annuals in being killed by HEAT, not cold. Young plants tolerate light frost and even brief snow; mature plants flower through cool spring weather but stop and decline once daytime temperatures consistently exceed 75 to 80 degrees. The end of pea season is heat, not cold.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Sow as early as possible -- 4 to 6 weeks before last frost in most zones. In mild-winter zones, fall sowing gives a long cool-season harvest. Choose heat-tolerant varieties (Wando, Sugar Sprint) for warmer zones. Plan succession plantings so harvest finishes before the heat hits.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Pea aphid (the headline pea pest) clusters on flower buds and tender new growth, weakening plants and reducing pod set. Pea weevil larvae bore into developing peas. Pea leaf miner damages leaves but rarely affects yield substantially. Powdery mildew is the headline disease, especially in cool humid conditions or as plants approach the heat-stress end of their cycle.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Hose off pea aphids with water; for serious infestations, insecticidal soap. Choose powdery-mildew-resistant varieties (most modern peas have some resistance). Space plants for airflow and avoid overhead watering. Rotate peas to a new bed each year.

failure_diagnostics.label: Root rot or yellowing
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Persistent waterlogging causes root rot and yellowing of inner leaves. Peas in heavy clay or low-lying spots are especially vulnerable. Wet foliage drives powdery mildew and ascochyta blight.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil. Use raised beds in heavy or wet sites. Water at the base, not overhead, and water early in the day so foliage dries before evening.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor pod set or fill
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress during flowering and pod-fill produces small empty pods or partially-filled pods. Peas have shallow roots and dry out fast; a few hot dry days during the critical flowering window can substantially reduce yield even on otherwise healthy plants.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently -- 1 inch per week minimum, more in heat. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture and keep roots cool. Drip irrigation works well for peas because it keeps foliage dry while providing consistent water.

failure_diagnostics.label: Sparse flowers or weak vines
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Peas need 6 hours of sun minimum, though they tolerate light shade better than beans. In deep shade, plants grow leggy with sparse flowers and reduced yield. Crowded planting can shade lower flowering nodes on tall pole peas.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun in cool climates; light afternoon shade is fine in warmer zones and may extend the bloom cycle by reducing heat stress. Space plants for airflow and light penetration. Trellis tall varieties properly so vines spread out rather than tangling.

fertilizer.timing: switch to balanced when heads form
fertilizer.notes: Heavy nitrogen feeder for leaf development. Switch to balanced feed once heads begin to form to avoid loose, leafy heads.

succession.tip: Start a spring crop and a separate late-summer crop for autumn harvest -- two distinct plantings rather than rolling succession. Spring broccoli planted after last frost and autumn broccoli started 10-12 weeks before first frost are your two windows. In between, broccoli struggles with bolting in summer heat. The autumn crop is often superior -- cool nights produce tighter, sweeter heads. Don't skip starting seeds for the autumn batch in July.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension 2022 and 2025 Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetable Crops; UConn IPM 'Perimeter Trap Cropping for Cole Crops'). Nasturtiums specifically are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and Utah State University Extension (Mohr et al., 'Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting'). Protocol caveat: UConn IPM explicitly notes trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents' -- so the aphid application here has a protocol-mismatch concern even though the companion is extension-named. The Cornell-IPM-specific attribution in earlier catalog reason text was not located in Cornell's published IPM material; actual backing is WSU/USU/UConn.

pests.name: Cabbage worm
pests.symptoms: Large irregular holes in leaves. Green caterpillars (1-1.5 inches) blending into foliage. White cabbage butterfly flying nearby is a warning sign.
pests.cause: Pieris rapae butterfly larvae. Lay eggs on leaf undersides.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick caterpillars and egg clusters. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray every 2 weeks. Row covers as barrier.
pests.prevention: Row covers from planting. White butterfly decoys (territorial behavior). Plant nasturtiums as trap crop.

pests.name: Cabbage aphid
pests.symptoms: Dense gray-green colonies on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl and pucker. Honeydew and sooty mold may follow.
pests.cause: Brevicoryne brassicae. Populations explode rapidly in cool weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Strong water blast. Insecticidal soap spray directly on colonies. Remove and compost heavily infested leaves.
pests.prevention: Avoid excess nitrogen. Encourage parasitic wasps with flowering herbs nearby.

pests.name: Flea beetle
pests.symptoms: Many tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings. Plants look peppered. Small shiny beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause: Multiple flea beetle species. Worst in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment: Row covers on seedlings. Diatomaceous earth. Kaolin clay spray.
pests.prevention: Delay planting. Use transplants. Interplant with aromatic herbs.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms: Plants wilt in hot weather despite watering. Stunted growth. Yellowing leaves. Roots are swollen, club-shaped, and deformed when dug up.
diseases.cause: Plasmodiophora brassicae soil pathogen. Survives in soil for up to 20 years. Thrives in acidic, wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure. Remove and destroy infected plants -- do not compost. Lime soil to raise pH to 7.0-7.2.
diseases.prevention: Minimum 7-year rotation away from brassicas in infected soil. Maintain soil pH above 6.5. Improve drainage.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms: Yellow patches on upper leaf surface with gray-purple fuzzy mold on undersides. Affects seedlings and mature plants.
diseases.cause: Peronospora brassicae fungus. Favored by cool moist conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Improve air circulation. Copper-based fungicide as preventive.
diseases.prevention: Avoid overhead watering. Space plants generously. Choose resistant varieties.

crops.harvest_ready: Pick when head is tight and dark green with no yellowing. Beads should still be closed. Size alone doesn't indicate readiness -- a large loose head is past peak.

start_method.notes: Start 6-8 weeks before transplant date. Harden off over 5-7 days. For fall crop, direct sow in midsummer.

container_notes.notes: Possible but challenging -- broccoli is large. 5-gallon minimum, one plant per pot.

varieties.note: Di Cicco produces smaller central heads but many side shoots over a long season -- great yield.

rotation.avoid_after: Kale, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, turnip, kohlrabi -- share clubroot and downy mildew
rotation.note: Clubroot can persist 20 years -- in infected soil extend to 7-year rotation.

bolting.triggers: Heat, transplant shock, wide temperature swings
bolting.prevention: Transplant carefully. Avoid temperature swings during head formation. Choose heat-tolerant varieties for summer crops.
bolting.note: Bolted broccoli (flowers opening) is still edible but quality drops. Harvest immediately when any yellowing appears.

storage.fridge: 3-5 days in a loosely wrapped bag -- don't seal tight, it needs airflow
storage.freezer: Cut to florets, blanch 3 minutes, freeze -- excellent, nearly as good as fresh
storage.notes: Yellowing comes from senescence, ethylene exposure, and warm storage -- not moisture. Store cold (32-40F) and humid in the crisper drawer; avoid storing near apples, bananas, or other ethylene-producing fruit. Use as soon as possible after harvest.

crops.soil_prep: Firm, fertile, slightly alkaline soil. Lime if pH below 6.5. Brassicas follow well after legumes (peas and beans fix nitrogen that feeds leafy brassicas). Firm the soil well before planting -- loose soil produces loose-headed broccoli.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Round seed leaves pushing up cleanly. Brassicas germinate readily in cool, moist conditions.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep soil consistently moist at 60-70°F. Brassicas do not need heat -- they prefer cool germination.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: True leaves developing -- slightly waxy and blue-green in color.
growth_stages.user_action: Watch for damping off -- good airflow and not overwatering prevents it. Thin to one plant per cell.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Sturdy plants with multiple leaf sets, ready to go outside.
growth_stages.user_action: Harden off well before transplanting. Net immediately after planting to protect from cabbage white butterflies -- do not delay on this.

growth_stages.name: Head Forming
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Central head beginning to form. On broccoli, a tight green dome. On cauliflower, a white curd appearing in the center.
growth_stages.user_action: For cauliflower, tie the outer leaves over the developing curd to blanch it and keep it white. Do this as soon as the curd is visible.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Broccoli: tight green head before any yellow flowers open. Cauliflower: firm white curd at full size. Cabbage: firm, dense head that does not give when squeezed.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest broccoli with a long stem cut -- side shoots will continue producing for weeks. Cauliflower and cabbage are once-and-done harvests.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Harvest time -- how did it look?

growth_stages.name: Side Shoots
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Broccoli only -- smaller side shoots developing from the stem after the main head is cut.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep harvesting side shoots regularly. A well-managed broccoli plant can produce for weeks after the main head is gone.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Getting side shoots from your broccoli?

notifications.title: Time to start your brassicas indoors
notifications.body: Broccoli, cauliflower, and cabbage need 6-8 weeks indoors before transplanting. Start now -- they grow slowly at first but reward the patience. Cool temperatures suit them perfectly.

notifications.title: Brassicas outside -- net them immediately
notifications.body: Cabbage white butterflies lay eggs on brassica leaves within hours of planting. Cover with fine mesh netting immediately after transplanting -- before you do anything else. Caterpillar damage can devastate an unprotected crop.

notifications.title: Cauliflower curd forming -- time to blanch
notifications.body: Tie a few outer leaves loosely over the developing curd now to protect it from light. This keeps the cauliflower white and tender. Check every few days -- once the curd is visible it develops quickly.

notifications.title: Check your broccoli heads
notifications.body: Broccoli heads that are ready to harvest look like tight green domes with no yellow showing. Once you see any flower buds opening it is past its best. Cut with a long stem and watch for side shoots to develop.

notifications.title: Start a fall brassica crop
notifications.body: Brassicas do well as a fall crop and often taste better -- frost sweetens cabbage and broccoli. Start seeds now for a crop that matures in the cooler autumn months.

notifications.title: How are your brassicas getting on?
notifications.body: Check under the netting for caterpillar damage -- they can strip a plant surprisingly fast. Also look at the developing head for any signs of bolting or discoloration.

weather_triggers.title: Heat stress -- brassicas may bolt
weather_triggers.body: Sustained high temperatures cause broccoli and cauliflower to bolt -- heads open into flowers before they are full size. Harvest anything that looks close to ready before the heat peaks.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- watch for clubroot and downy mildew
weather_triggers.body: Humid conditions favor several brassica diseases. Ensure good spacing and airflow. Check leaves for yellowing or powdery patches and remove affected material promptly.

weather_triggers.title: Late frost -- protect young brassicas
weather_triggers.body: Established brassicas handle frost well, but young transplants need protection for the first few weeks. Cover with fleece tonight.

germination.text: Brassicas are reliable germinators in cool conditions -- 60-70F is ideal. They do not need heat mats.
Sow into cells or modules rather than trays -- brassicas develop long tap roots and resent root disturbance.

seedling.text: Grow brassica seedlings in the coolest, brightest spot you have. Warmth makes them soft and leggy.
Feed with a dilute liquid feed once the first true leaves appear. Brassicas are hungry plants from the start.

established.text: Net immediately after transplanting. Cabbage white butterflies find brassicas within hours and lay clusters of yellow eggs on leaf undersides. Check the netting is secure all around -- one gap and caterpillars will find it.
Plant deeply -- broccoli forms roots along the buried stem like tomatoes and is more stable and drought-resistant for it.

head_forming.text: Watch the central head daily once it starts forming. The window between a tight, dense, perfectly-domed head and one that has begun to open into yellow flower buds is short -- often just 3-5 days in warm weather.
Steady moisture during head formation produces firmer, larger heads. Drought stress at this stage is the most common cause of small or loose heads.

harvest.text: Cut the main head with a long stem -- 6-8 inches. The remaining stem will produce side shoots over the following weeks. Harvest while the head is tight and green; once you see any yellow flower buds opening, the head is past its best.
Broccoli sugars convert quickly after harvest. For the best flavor, cut just before cooking; refrigerate immediately if not eating within a few hours.

side_shoots.text: Broccoli side shoots are sweeter and more tender than the main head. Keep the plant well watered and fed to encourage continuous production -- a single plant can yield for weeks after the main cut.
Some broccoli varieties are bred specifically for side shoot production. Purple sprouting broccoli is the best example -- it overwinters and produces all spring.

yield_expectations.per_plant: One large central head plus weeks of side shoots
yield_expectations.peak_production: Side shoots can be harvested every 1-2 weeks for 4-6 weeks after the main head
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Broccoli is one of the most satisfying crops -- a large green head you grew yourself is genuinely impressive.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Established brassicas handle frost well -- it actually sweetens them. But young transplants in their first 2-3 weeks are more vulnerable. A hard freeze can damage or kill recently transplanted seedlings.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Cover new transplants with fleece for the first 2-3 weeks after planting if frost is possible. Once established they are among the hardiest vegetables you can grow.

failure_diagnostics.label: Caterpillars or pests
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cabbage white butterflies lay eggs on brassica leaves and the caterpillars can strip a plant in days. This is by far the most common reason brassicas fail. If you did not net, this is almost certainly what happened.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Net immediately after transplanting -- before you do anything else. Fine mesh netting secured all the way around is the single most important thing you can do for brassicas. Check netting for gaps weekly.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too much water or clubroot
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Brassicas in waterlogged soil develop root problems. Clubroot -- a soil-borne disease -- causes swollen, distorted roots and wilting. Once present in soil it persists for many years.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Improve drainage before planting. If clubroot is suspected, rotate brassicas to a new bed and do not grow them in the affected soil for 4-5 years. Liming to raise soil pH above 7 discourages clubroot.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too little water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Brassicas need consistent moisture to develop good heads. Drought stress causes premature flowering in broccoli and cauliflower, and split heads in cabbage.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently and mulch around plants to retain moisture. A dry spell during head formation is the most damaging period.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor head development
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cauliflower is the most demanding -- it needs consistent temperatures and care to form a good curd. Broccoli heads opening into yellow flowers usually means the temperature swung too warm. Both benefit from 6+ hours of sun.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Cauliflower in particular needs a consistent, cool growing environment. Autumn sowings often perform better than spring ones in warmer zones. Shade cloth can help in warm spells.

crops.name: Garlic
crops.description: Plant in fall, harvest in summer. One of the most satisfying long-season crops -- almost no maintenance from October to June. Plant pointed end up, 2 inches deep.

3.notes: Plant before ground freezes. Mulch heavily after planting. Hardneck varieties like Rocambole do best in Zone 3.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: The standard UMN recommendation is to plant garlic cloves one to two weeks after first frost -- typically late September in northern Minnesota, early October in southern Minnesota. (UMN Extension) Planting too early risks shoot emergence above soil before winter; too late means roots don't develop before ground freezes. Plant garlic cloves in the fall, usually one or two weeks after the first killing frost. Cover with 3-4 inches of leaf or straw mulch after planting. (UMN)
