pests.name: Cucumber beetle
pests.symptoms: Yellow-green beetles with black spots or stripes feeding on leaves, flowers, and fruit. Plants wilt suddenly (bacterial wilt transmission). Holey leaves.
pests.cause: Spotted and striped cucumber beetles. Also transmit bacterial wilt disease.
pests.organic_treatment: Row covers until flowering. Yellow sticky traps. Neem oil spray. Spinosad-based insecticide.
pests.prevention: Delay planting until plants are large. Use row covers early season. Interplant with radishes and nasturtiums.

pests.name: Squash bug
pests.symptoms: Gray-brown flat insects on stems and undersides of leaves. Wilting leaves with yellow then brown patches. Bronze egg clusters on leaf undersides.
pests.cause: Anasa tristis. Overwinters as adults in garden debris.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick adults and egg masses. Trap under boards at night. Neem oil spray on nymphs.
pests.prevention: Remove all garden debris in autumn. Rotate cucurbit crops. Use row covers early season.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces, stems, and sometimes fruit. Leaves may yellow and die. Worst in warm days with cool nights.
diseases.cause: Fungal disease favored by humid conditions with poor air circulation.
diseases.organic_treatment: Spray with diluted neem oil or a baking soda solution (1 tsp per quart water). Apply potassium bicarbonate spray. Remove and destroy affected leaves.
diseases.prevention: Space plants for good airflow. Water at soil level, not on foliage. Choose resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation.

diseases.name: Bacterial wilt
diseases.symptoms: Sudden wilting of individual leaves, then whole stems, then entire plant. No recovery even with watering. Plants die within days.
diseases.cause: Erwinia tracheiphila bacteria spread by cucumber beetles feeding.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure -- remove and destroy infected plants immediately. Control cucumber beetles to prevent spread.
diseases.prevention: Use row covers to exclude cucumber beetles early in season. Plant resistant varieties.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms: Yellow-green patches on upper leaf surface with corresponding gray-purple fuzzy growth on leaf undersides. Leaves die rapidly.
diseases.cause: Pseudoperonospora cubensis fungus. Spreads rapidly in wet humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively.
diseases.prevention: Choose resistant varieties. Water at soil level. Ensure good air circulation.

crops.harvest_ready: Pick at 6-8 inches while skin is still tender. Firm to touch.

start_method.notes: Direct sow after last frost. Grows fast -- no need to start indoors.

rotation.avoid_after: Cucumbers, squash, pumpkins, melons -- share cucumber beetle, bacterial wilt, downy mildew
rotation.note: Rotate to prevent cucumber beetle and disease buildup.

storage.freezer: Slice or grate, blanch 2 minutes, freeze -- good for baking
storage.notes: Same as zucchini -- small squash store better than large ones.

varieties.note: Zephyr has outstanding flavor -- pale yellow with a green base, consistently sweet.

container_notes.notes: Possible in large containers (10+ gallons). Compact varieties like Patio Yellow work best. Water frequently.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Large seed leaves pushing up fast -- squash germinates quickly in warm soil.
growth_stages.user_action: Sow seeds on their edge to prevent rotting. Keep soil warm and moist.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Large, hairy true leaves developing rapidly. Squash grows fast once it gets going.
growth_stages.user_action: Give them space from the start -- squash plants get very large and do not like competition.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: A strong central crown with multiple large leaves. Bush varieties stay compact; vining types will start to sprawl.
growth_stages.user_action: If growing winter squash, direct the vines in the direction you want them to go now -- once established they are harder to redirect.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Growing well and in the right spot?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Large orange-yellow flowers. Male flowers come first on long straight stems. Female flowers have a swollen base -- the future squash.
growth_stages.user_action: Hand-pollinate female flowers in the early morning if you are not seeing good fruit set. Touch a male flower to each open female flower.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Flowers open? Any tiny squash forming?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Summer squash: harvest small and often at 6-8 inches. Winter squash: wait until skin is hard and stem is dry and corky.
growth_stages.user_action: Summer squash picked small tastes better and keeps production going. Winter squash left on the vine longer develops better flavor and storage life.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Slowing production on summer squash. Winter squash stems drying and corking -- the cue to harvest before frost.
growth_stages.user_action: Cure winter squash at room temperature for 10-14 days before storing -- it hardens the skin and sweetens the flesh. Summer squash plants can be composted after frost.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Season done? Worth noting what worked.

notifications.title: Time to sow your squash
notifications.body: Squash goes in a week after last frost, once the soil has had time to warm properly. Sow 2-3 seeds per spot and thin to the strongest plant. They grow fast -- you will see real progress within a week.

notifications.title: Check your squash flowers -- pollination time
notifications.body: Your squash should be flowering now. If you see flowers but no fruit forming, check whether you have both male and female flowers open at the same time. Female flowers have a small swollen base. Hand-pollinate in the morning if bees are scarce.

notifications.title: Summer squash ready -- pick small and often
notifications.body: Your courgettes or summer squash should be ready. Pick them at 6-8 inches -- they taste better small and the plant produces far more when you harvest regularly. A forgotten courgette turns into a marrow overnight.

notifications.title: Check your squash plants
notifications.body: Summer squash especially needs checking every few days -- they grow incredibly fast and a missed harvest sets back the whole plant.

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- protect your squash
weather_triggers.body: Squash is frost-tender. Cover with fleece tonight. Winter squash still on the vine must be harvested before a hard frost -- even one frosty night can damage stored winter squash.

weather_triggers.title: Powdery mildew risk for your squash
weather_triggers.body: Squash is very susceptible to powdery mildew in humid conditions. Ensure good spacing and airflow. If you see white powdery patches on leaves, remove affected leaves and spray with a dilute baking soda solution.

weather_triggers.title: Your squash needs deep watering
weather_triggers.body: Squash plants have large leaves and need a lot of water in dry conditions. Water deeply at the base -- not the leaves -- twice a week in drought conditions. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture.

germination.text: Sow squash seeds on their side, not flat. The root emerges from the pointed end and finds its way down more easily.
Squash germinates fast in warm soil -- sometimes in 4-5 days. In cold soil it rots. Wait for genuine warmth (60F+ minimum, 70F+ ideal).

seedling.text: Thin ruthlessly to one plant per spot. Squash planted too close together become a tangled mass that is prone to mildew and difficult to harvest.
Do not start squash indoors too early -- 3-4 weeks maximum. They outgrow their pots quickly and transplant shock is real.

established.text: Leave enough room -- a zucchini plant can easily cover 4-6 square feet. A butternut squash vine can run 6-10 feet. Plan for this before planting.
A thick layer of mulch around squash plants suppresses weeds, retains moisture, and keeps the fruit clean if it rests on the ground.

flowering.text: Male flowers come before female flowers -- this is normal and not something to worry about. Female flowers (with the swollen base behind the petals) follow within a week or two.
Early morning is when squash flowers are most receptive. If you are hand-pollinating, do it between 7-10am while flowers are fully open.

harvest.text: Pick zucchini and yellow summer squash young -- 6 to 8 inches is the sweet spot for tender flesh and best flavor. At full marrow size the seeds are tough and the skin gets bitter.
Harvest every 2 to 3 days during peak production. Summer squash plants stop setting new fruit if mature ones are left on the vine; constant picking keeps the plant producing.

end_of_season.text: Summer squash do not store. Use, freeze (grated, blanched), or give them away within a week of picking. Refrigerate at 45-50F at most -- below 40F they get pitted and chilled.
When production slows in late summer, pull the plant rather than nursing it. Powdery mildew sets in by then on most varieties; clear the bed and replant for fall greens or cover crop.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 10-20 lbs over the season -- zucchini is one of the most productive vegetables you can grow
yield_expectations.peak_production: At peak, one healthy zucchini plant produces 1-2 fruits every 2-3 days
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Zucchini is famously easy and productive. You will likely have more than you can eat -- plan to give some away.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucurbits are tropical-origin tender annuals -- killed outright by even a light frost at any stage. Cold soil at planting (below 60 degrees) stunts seedlings for the rest of the season even if they survive. Late-summer frost ends the season abruptly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Wait to direct-sow or transplant until soil reaches 65 to 70 degrees and night temperatures stay above 50. In short-season zones, start transplants indoors 3 to 4 weeks before set-out, but disturb roots minimally -- cucurbits resent transplanting. Use black plastic mulch to warm soil. Have row cover ready for unexpected late-spring or early-fall frosts.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucumber beetles (striped and spotted) damage seedlings directly and transmit bacterial wilt -- a fatal disease that wilts vines from the tips inward. Squash bugs target squash and pumpkin (less so cucumber and melon). Powdery mildew shows up reliably late in the season as white powder on leaves. Downy mildew, anthracnose, and bacterial leaf spot are humidity-driven secondary problems.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Floating row cover from planting through first flower blocks cucumber beetles -- remove at flowering for pollination. Squash bug egg masses (orange-red, on undersides of leaves) crush easily by hand if caught early. For powdery mildew, choose resistant varieties (most modern cucumbers are bred for resistance) and water at the base, not overhead. Rotate cucurbits to a new bed each year.

failure_diagnostics.label: Watery fruit or vine collapse
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucurbits need consistent water but cannot tolerate waterlogged soil. Persistent saturation causes root rot, sudden vine collapse, and watery flavorless fruit. Heavy rain near harvest causes ripe melons to crack and split. Wet foliage drives powdery mildew, downy mildew, and bacterial leaf spot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil or raised mounds (the traditional 'cucurbit hill' approach exists for drainage reasons). Water deeply at the base 1 to 2 times per week rather than shallow daily. Mulch heavily to even out soil moisture and reduce splash-borne disease. Stop watering watermelons 2 weeks before expected harvest to concentrate flavor.

failure_diagnostics.label: Small or bitter fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress during flowering and fruit set produces small, misshapen, or bitter fruit. Cucurbits move large volumes of water through their tissues during fruit development -- a single mature watermelon plant can use 1 to 2 gallons of water per day in peak summer. Cucumber bitterness is often a drought-stress signal.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently and deeply -- 1 to 2 inches per week minimum during fruit development, more in heat. Drip irrigation outperforms overhead watering by both providing consistent water and keeping foliage dry. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture and reduce evaporation.

failure_diagnostics.label: Vines without fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucurbits need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum, ideally 8 or more -- to set and ripen fruit. In partial shade vines grow leaves and even bloom, but fruit set is poor and ripening is incomplete. A late-season fruit that never sweetens is often a sun problem more than a temperature problem.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in the sunniest spot available. Trellising vining cucurbits (vertical support for cucumbers and small-fruited squash) gets more leaf area into the sun and improves fruit set substantially. In partial-shade gardens, accept that cucurbits are not the right crop and grow leafy greens or herbs instead.

good.name: Borage
good.why: Attracts bees for pollination, deters hornworm

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Xerces Society documents borage as a pollinator-attractant plant that blooms concurrently with tomato, squash, and cucumber crops, drawing the same bees that pollinate those crops. Source: xerces.org/blog/plants-you-can-eat-are-pollinator-treat. The claim's additional assertions about deterring hornworm are not supported in extension literature; they recur widely in popular gardening sources but without rigorous backing and should be read as traditional.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension 2022 and 2025 Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetable Crops; UConn IPM 'Perimeter Trap Cropping for Cole Crops'). Nasturtiums specifically are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and Utah State University Extension (Mohr et al., 'Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting'). Protocol caveat: UConn IPM explicitly notes trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents' -- so the aphid application here has a protocol-mismatch concern even though the companion is extension-named. The Cornell-IPM-specific attribution in earlier catalog reason text was not located in Cornell's published IPM material; actual backing is WSU/USU/UConn.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Pest-deterrent claim without matching established pattern. Default to traditional pending review.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Legume rhizobial nitrogen fixation is textbook plant science. The mechanism is real; the specific pairing benefit is mechanistically plausible but often not pair-tested.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Bad companion claim, no pattern match. Default to traditional pending review.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Inter-plant competition for N, P, K is a real agronomic concept. Specific 'bad pair' claims often extrapolate beyond what research has shown.

pests.name: Cucumber beetle
pests.symptoms: Yellow-green beetles with black spots or stripes feeding on leaves, flowers, and fruit. Plants wilt suddenly (bacterial wilt transmission). Holey leaves.
pests.cause: Spotted and striped cucumber beetles. Also transmit bacterial wilt disease.
pests.organic_treatment: Row covers until flowering. Yellow sticky traps. Neem oil spray. Spinosad-based insecticide.
pests.prevention: Delay planting until plants are large. Use row covers early season. Interplant with radishes and nasturtiums.

pests.name: Squash bug
pests.symptoms: Gray-brown flat insects on stems and undersides of leaves. Wilting leaves with yellow then brown patches. Bronze egg clusters on leaf undersides.
pests.cause: Anasa tristis. Overwinters as adults in garden debris.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick adults and egg masses. Trap under boards at night. Neem oil spray on nymphs.
pests.prevention: Remove all garden debris in autumn. Rotate cucurbit crops. Use row covers early season.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces, stems, and sometimes fruit. Leaves may yellow and die. Worst in warm days with cool nights.
diseases.cause: Fungal disease favored by humid conditions with poor air circulation.
diseases.organic_treatment: Spray with diluted neem oil or a baking soda solution (1 tsp per quart water). Apply potassium bicarbonate spray. Remove and destroy affected leaves.
diseases.prevention: Space plants for good airflow. Water at soil level, not on foliage. Choose resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation.

diseases.name: Bacterial wilt
diseases.symptoms: Sudden wilting of individual leaves, then whole stems, then entire plant. No recovery even with watering. Plants die within days.
diseases.cause: Erwinia tracheiphila bacteria spread by cucumber beetles feeding.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure -- remove and destroy infected plants immediately. Control cucumber beetles to prevent spread.
diseases.prevention: Use row covers to exclude cucumber beetles early in season. Plant resistant varieties.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms: Yellow-green patches on upper leaf surface with corresponding gray-purple fuzzy growth on leaf undersides. Leaves die rapidly.
diseases.cause: Pseudoperonospora cubensis fungus. Spreads rapidly in wet humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively.
diseases.prevention: Choose resistant varieties. Water at soil level. Ensure good air circulation.

crops.harvest_ready: Ready when skin is hard and beige-tan (no green). Stem dries and turns corky. Skin cannot be dented with a fingernail. Leave until first light frost for best sweetness.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Large seed leaves pushing up fast -- squash germinates quickly in warm soil.
growth_stages.user_action: Sow seeds on their edge to prevent rotting. Keep soil warm and moist.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Large, hairy true leaves developing rapidly. Squash grows fast once it gets going.
growth_stages.user_action: Give them space from the start -- squash plants get very large and do not like competition.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: A strong central crown with multiple large leaves. Bush varieties stay compact; vining types will start to sprawl.
growth_stages.user_action: If growing winter squash, direct the vines in the direction you want them to go now -- once established they are harder to redirect.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Growing well and in the right spot?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Large orange-yellow flowers. Male flowers come first on long straight stems. Female flowers have a swollen base -- the future squash.
growth_stages.user_action: Hand-pollinate female flowers in the early morning if you are not seeing good fruit set. Touch a male flower to each open female flower.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Flowers open? Any tiny squash forming?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Summer squash: harvest small and often at 6-8 inches. Winter squash: wait until skin is hard and stem is dry and corky.
growth_stages.user_action: Summer squash picked small tastes better and keeps production going. Winter squash left on the vine longer develops better flavor and storage life.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Slowing production on summer squash. Winter squash stems drying and corking -- the cue to harvest before frost.
growth_stages.user_action: Cure winter squash at room temperature for 10-14 days before storing -- it hardens the skin and sweetens the flesh. Summer squash plants can be composted after frost.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Season done? Worth noting what worked.

notifications.title: Time to sow your squash
notifications.body: Squash goes in a week after last frost, once the soil has had time to warm properly. Sow 2-3 seeds per spot and thin to the strongest plant. They grow fast -- you will see real progress within a week.

notifications.title: Check your squash flowers -- pollination time
notifications.body: Your squash should be flowering now. If you see flowers but no fruit forming, check whether you have both male and female flowers open at the same time. Female flowers have a small swollen base. Hand-pollinate in the morning if bees are scarce.

notifications.title: Summer squash ready -- pick small and often
notifications.body: Your courgettes or summer squash should be ready. Pick them at 6-8 inches -- they taste better small and the plant produces far more when you harvest regularly. A forgotten courgette turns into a marrow overnight.

notifications.title: Harvest your winter squash before frost
notifications.body: Frost is {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks away -- time to check your winter squash for harvest readiness. The stem should be dry and corky, and the skin should resist a thumbnail. Harvest all squash before frost and cure them for 10-14 days at room temperature.

notifications.title: Check your squash plants
notifications.body: Summer squash especially needs checking every few days -- they grow incredibly fast and a missed harvest sets back the whole plant.

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- protect your squash
weather_triggers.body: Squash is frost-tender. Cover with fleece tonight. Winter squash still on the vine must be harvested before a hard frost -- even one frosty night can damage stored winter squash.

weather_triggers.title: Powdery mildew risk for your squash
weather_triggers.body: Squash is very susceptible to powdery mildew in humid conditions. Ensure good spacing and airflow. If you see white powdery patches on leaves, remove affected leaves and spray with a dilute baking soda solution.

weather_triggers.title: Your squash needs deep watering
weather_triggers.body: Squash plants have large leaves and need a lot of water in dry conditions. Water deeply at the base -- not the leaves -- twice a week in drought conditions. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture.

germination.text: Sow squash seeds on their side, not flat. The root emerges from the pointed end and finds its way down more easily.
Squash germinates fast in warm soil -- sometimes in 4-5 days. In cold soil it rots. Wait for genuine warmth (60F+ minimum, 70F+ ideal).

seedling.text: Thin ruthlessly to one plant per spot. Squash planted too close together become a tangled mass that is prone to mildew and difficult to harvest.
Do not start squash indoors too early -- 3-4 weeks maximum. They outgrow their pots quickly and transplant shock is real.

established.text: Leave enough room -- a zucchini plant can easily cover 4-6 square feet. A butternut squash vine can run 6-10 feet. Plan for this before planting.
A thick layer of mulch around squash plants suppresses weeds, retains moisture, and keeps the fruit clean if it rests on the ground.

flowering.text: Male flowers come before female flowers -- this is normal and not something to worry about. Female flowers (with the swollen base behind the petals) follow within a week or two.
Early morning is when squash flowers are most receptive. If you are hand-pollinating, do it between 7-10am while flowers are fully open.

harvest.text: Winter squash is ready when the skin is hard enough that you cannot pierce it with a thumbnail and the stem has turned dry and corky. The fruit detaches easily but you should cut, not pull -- leaving 2 to 3 inches of stem dramatically extends storage life. Stemless squash rots from the wound within weeks.

Harvest before the first hard frost (28F or below). Light frost can be tolerated if the fruit is mature, but a hard freeze damages the flesh and ruins storage potential. Watch the forecast through autumn.

end_of_season.text: Cure freshly-cut winter squash for 10 to 14 days at 70-80F with good airflow before storing. Curing hardens the skin, heals minor stem wounds, and converts starches to sugars -- flavor improves dramatically over the cure window.

After curing, store at 50-60F in a dry, dark spot. A well-cured butternut keeps 3 to 6 months; acorn squash 1 to 2; spaghetti squash 2 to 3. Check periodically and use any squash showing soft spots first.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 3-6 fruits per plant for butternut and acorn types
yield_expectations.peak_production: Winter squash sets all its fruit within a window, then concentrates on ripening them
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Winter squash takes more patience than summer types -- the long growing season can feel slow. The payoff is months of stored vegetables.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucurbits are tropical-origin tender annuals -- killed outright by even a light frost at any stage. Cold soil at planting (below 60 degrees) stunts seedlings for the rest of the season even if they survive. Late-summer frost ends the season abruptly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Wait to direct-sow or transplant until soil reaches 65 to 70 degrees and night temperatures stay above 50. In short-season zones, start transplants indoors 3 to 4 weeks before set-out, but disturb roots minimally -- cucurbits resent transplanting. Use black plastic mulch to warm soil. Have row cover ready for unexpected late-spring or early-fall frosts.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucumber beetles (striped and spotted) damage seedlings directly and transmit bacterial wilt -- a fatal disease that wilts vines from the tips inward. Squash bugs target squash and pumpkin (less so cucumber and melon). Powdery mildew shows up reliably late in the season as white powder on leaves. Downy mildew, anthracnose, and bacterial leaf spot are humidity-driven secondary problems.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Floating row cover from planting through first flower blocks cucumber beetles -- remove at flowering for pollination. Squash bug egg masses (orange-red, on undersides of leaves) crush easily by hand if caught early. For powdery mildew, choose resistant varieties (most modern cucumbers are bred for resistance) and water at the base, not overhead. Rotate cucurbits to a new bed each year.

failure_diagnostics.label: Watery fruit or vine collapse
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucurbits need consistent water but cannot tolerate waterlogged soil. Persistent saturation causes root rot, sudden vine collapse, and watery flavorless fruit. Heavy rain near harvest causes ripe melons to crack and split. Wet foliage drives powdery mildew, downy mildew, and bacterial leaf spot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil or raised mounds (the traditional 'cucurbit hill' approach exists for drainage reasons). Water deeply at the base 1 to 2 times per week rather than shallow daily. Mulch heavily to even out soil moisture and reduce splash-borne disease. Stop watering watermelons 2 weeks before expected harvest to concentrate flavor.

failure_diagnostics.label: Small or bitter fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress during flowering and fruit set produces small, misshapen, or bitter fruit. Cucurbits move large volumes of water through their tissues during fruit development -- a single mature watermelon plant can use 1 to 2 gallons of water per day in peak summer. Cucumber bitterness is often a drought-stress signal.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently and deeply -- 1 to 2 inches per week minimum during fruit development, more in heat. Drip irrigation outperforms overhead watering by both providing consistent water and keeping foliage dry. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture and reduce evaporation.

failure_diagnostics.label: Vines without fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucurbits need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum, ideally 8 or more -- to set and ripen fruit. In partial shade vines grow leaves and even bloom, but fruit set is poor and ripening is incomplete. A late-season fruit that never sweetens is often a sun problem more than a temperature problem.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in the sunniest spot available. Trellising vining cucurbits (vertical support for cucumbers and small-fruited squash) gets more leaf area into the sun and improves fruit set substantially. In partial-shade gardens, accept that cucurbits are not the right crop and grow leafy greens or herbs instead.

good.name: Borage
good.why: Attracts bees for pollination, deters hornworm

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Xerces Society documents borage as a pollinator-attractant plant that blooms concurrently with tomato, squash, and cucumber crops, drawing the same bees that pollinate those crops. Source: xerces.org/blog/plants-you-can-eat-are-pollinator-treat. The claim's additional assertions about deterring hornworm are not supported in extension literature; they recur widely in popular gardening sources but without rigorous backing and should be read as traditional.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension 2022 and 2025 Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetable Crops; UConn IPM 'Perimeter Trap Cropping for Cole Crops'). Nasturtiums specifically are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and Utah State University Extension (Mohr et al., 'Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting'). Protocol caveat: UConn IPM explicitly notes trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents' -- so the aphid application here has a protocol-mismatch concern even though the companion is extension-named. The Cornell-IPM-specific attribution in earlier catalog reason text was not located in Cornell's published IPM material; actual backing is WSU/USU/UConn.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Pest-deterrent claim without matching established pattern. Default to traditional pending review.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Legume rhizobial nitrogen fixation is textbook plant science. The mechanism is real; the specific pairing benefit is mechanistically plausible but often not pair-tested.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Bad companion claim, no pattern match. Default to traditional pending review.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Inter-plant competition for N, P, K is a real agronomic concept. Specific 'bad pair' claims often extrapolate beyond what research has shown.

pests.name: Cucumber beetle
pests.symptoms: Yellow-green beetles with black spots or stripes feeding on leaves, flowers, and fruit. Plants wilt suddenly (bacterial wilt transmission). Holey leaves.
pests.cause: Spotted and striped cucumber beetles. Also transmit bacterial wilt disease.
pests.organic_treatment: Row covers until flowering. Yellow sticky traps. Neem oil spray. Spinosad-based insecticide.
pests.prevention: Delay planting until plants are large. Use row covers early season. Interplant with radishes and nasturtiums.

pests.name: Squash bug
pests.symptoms: Gray-brown flat insects on stems and undersides of leaves. Wilting leaves with yellow then brown patches. Bronze egg clusters on leaf undersides.
pests.cause: Anasa tristis. Overwinters as adults in garden debris.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick adults and egg masses. Trap under boards at night. Neem oil spray on nymphs.
pests.prevention: Remove all garden debris in autumn. Rotate cucurbit crops. Use row covers early season.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces, stems, and sometimes fruit. Leaves may yellow and die. Worst in warm days with cool nights.
diseases.cause: Fungal disease favored by humid conditions with poor air circulation.
diseases.organic_treatment: Spray with diluted neem oil or a baking soda solution (1 tsp per quart water). Apply potassium bicarbonate spray. Remove and destroy affected leaves.
diseases.prevention: Space plants for good airflow. Water at soil level, not on foliage. Choose resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation.

diseases.name: Bacterial wilt
diseases.symptoms: Sudden wilting of individual leaves, then whole stems, then entire plant. No recovery even with watering. Plants die within days.
diseases.cause: Erwinia tracheiphila bacteria spread by cucumber beetles feeding.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure -- remove and destroy infected plants immediately. Control cucumber beetles to prevent spread.
diseases.prevention: Use row covers to exclude cucumber beetles early in season. Plant resistant varieties.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms: Yellow-green patches on upper leaf surface with corresponding gray-purple fuzzy growth on leaf undersides. Leaves die rapidly.
diseases.cause: Pseudoperonospora cubensis fungus. Spreads rapidly in wet humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively.
diseases.prevention: Choose resistant varieties. Water at soil level. Ensure good air circulation.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Large seed leaves pushing up fast -- squash germinates quickly in warm soil.
growth_stages.user_action: Sow seeds on their edge to prevent rotting. Keep soil warm and moist.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Large, hairy true leaves developing rapidly. Squash grows fast once it gets going.
growth_stages.user_action: Give them space from the start -- squash plants get very large and do not like competition.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: A strong central crown with multiple large leaves. Bush varieties stay compact; vining types will start to sprawl.
growth_stages.user_action: If growing winter squash, direct the vines in the direction you want them to go now -- once established they are harder to redirect.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Growing well and in the right spot?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Large orange-yellow flowers. Male flowers come first on long straight stems. Female flowers have a swollen base -- the future squash.
growth_stages.user_action: Hand-pollinate female flowers in the early morning if you are not seeing good fruit set. Touch a male flower to each open female flower.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Flowers open? Any tiny squash forming?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Summer squash: harvest small and often at 6-8 inches. Winter squash: wait until skin is hard and stem is dry and corky.
growth_stages.user_action: Summer squash picked small tastes better and keeps production going. Winter squash left on the vine longer develops better flavor and storage life.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Slowing production on summer squash. Winter squash stems drying and corking -- the cue to harvest before frost.
growth_stages.user_action: Cure winter squash at room temperature for 10-14 days before storing -- it hardens the skin and sweetens the flesh. Summer squash plants can be composted after frost.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Season done? Worth noting what worked.

notifications.title: Time to sow your squash
notifications.body: Squash goes in a week after last frost, once the soil has had time to warm properly. Sow 2-3 seeds per spot and thin to the strongest plant. They grow fast -- you will see real progress within a week.

notifications.title: Check your squash flowers -- pollination time
notifications.body: Your squash should be flowering now. If you see flowers but no fruit forming, check whether you have both male and female flowers open at the same time. Female flowers have a small swollen base. Hand-pollinate in the morning if bees are scarce.

notifications.title: Summer squash ready -- pick small and often
notifications.body: Your courgettes or summer squash should be ready. Pick them at 6-8 inches -- they taste better small and the plant produces far more when you harvest regularly. A forgotten courgette turns into a marrow overnight.

notifications.title: Harvest your winter squash before frost
notifications.body: Frost is {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks away -- time to check your winter squash for harvest readiness. The stem should be dry and corky, and the skin should resist a thumbnail. Harvest all squash before frost and cure them for 10-14 days at room temperature.

notifications.title: Check your squash plants
notifications.body: Summer squash especially needs checking every few days -- they grow incredibly fast and a missed harvest sets back the whole plant.

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- protect your squash
weather_triggers.body: Squash is frost-tender. Cover with fleece tonight. Winter squash still on the vine must be harvested before a hard frost -- even one frosty night can damage stored winter squash.

weather_triggers.title: Powdery mildew risk for your squash
weather_triggers.body: Squash is very susceptible to powdery mildew in humid conditions. Ensure good spacing and airflow. If you see white powdery patches on leaves, remove affected leaves and spray with a dilute baking soda solution.

weather_triggers.title: Your squash needs deep watering
weather_triggers.body: Squash plants have large leaves and need a lot of water in dry conditions. Water deeply at the base -- not the leaves -- twice a week in drought conditions. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture.

germination.text: Sow squash seeds on their side, not flat. The root emerges from the pointed end and finds its way down more easily.
Squash germinates fast in warm soil -- sometimes in 4-5 days. In cold soil it rots. Wait for genuine warmth (60F+ minimum, 70F+ ideal).

seedling.text: Thin ruthlessly to one plant per spot. Squash planted too close together become a tangled mass that is prone to mildew and difficult to harvest.
Do not start squash indoors too early -- 3-4 weeks maximum. They outgrow their pots quickly and transplant shock is real.

established.text: Leave enough room -- a zucchini plant can easily cover 4-6 square feet. A butternut squash vine can run 6-10 feet. Plan for this before planting.
A thick layer of mulch around squash plants suppresses weeds, retains moisture, and keeps the fruit clean if it rests on the ground.

flowering.text: Male flowers come before female flowers -- this is normal and not something to worry about. Female flowers (with the swollen base behind the petals) follow within a week or two.
Early morning is when squash flowers are most receptive. If you are hand-pollinating, do it between 7-10am while flowers are fully open.

harvest.text: Winter squash is ready when the skin is hard enough that you cannot pierce it with a thumbnail and the stem has turned dry and corky. The fruit detaches easily but you should cut, not pull -- leaving 2 to 3 inches of stem dramatically extends storage life. Stemless squash rots from the wound within weeks.

Harvest before the first hard frost (28F or below). Light frost can be tolerated if the fruit is mature, but a hard freeze damages the flesh and ruins storage potential. Watch the forecast through autumn.

end_of_season.text: Cure freshly-cut winter squash for 10 to 14 days at 70-80F with good airflow before storing. Curing hardens the skin, heals minor stem wounds, and converts starches to sugars -- flavor improves dramatically over the cure window.

After curing, store at 50-60F in a dry, dark spot. A well-cured butternut keeps 3 to 6 months; acorn squash 1 to 2; spaghetti squash 2 to 3. Check periodically and use any squash showing soft spots first.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 3-6 fruits per plant for butternut and acorn types
yield_expectations.peak_production: Winter squash sets all its fruit within a window, then concentrates on ripening them
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Winter squash takes more patience than summer types -- the long growing season can feel slow. The payoff is months of stored vegetables.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucurbits are tropical-origin tender annuals -- killed outright by even a light frost at any stage. Cold soil at planting (below 60 degrees) stunts seedlings for the rest of the season even if they survive. Late-summer frost ends the season abruptly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Wait to direct-sow or transplant until soil reaches 65 to 70 degrees and night temperatures stay above 50. In short-season zones, start transplants indoors 3 to 4 weeks before set-out, but disturb roots minimally -- cucurbits resent transplanting. Use black plastic mulch to warm soil. Have row cover ready for unexpected late-spring or early-fall frosts.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucumber beetles (striped and spotted) damage seedlings directly and transmit bacterial wilt -- a fatal disease that wilts vines from the tips inward. Squash bugs target squash and pumpkin (less so cucumber and melon). Powdery mildew shows up reliably late in the season as white powder on leaves. Downy mildew, anthracnose, and bacterial leaf spot are humidity-driven secondary problems.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Floating row cover from planting through first flower blocks cucumber beetles -- remove at flowering for pollination. Squash bug egg masses (orange-red, on undersides of leaves) crush easily by hand if caught early. For powdery mildew, choose resistant varieties (most modern cucumbers are bred for resistance) and water at the base, not overhead. Rotate cucurbits to a new bed each year.

failure_diagnostics.label: Watery fruit or vine collapse
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucurbits need consistent water but cannot tolerate waterlogged soil. Persistent saturation causes root rot, sudden vine collapse, and watery flavorless fruit. Heavy rain near harvest causes ripe melons to crack and split. Wet foliage drives powdery mildew, downy mildew, and bacterial leaf spot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil or raised mounds (the traditional 'cucurbit hill' approach exists for drainage reasons). Water deeply at the base 1 to 2 times per week rather than shallow daily. Mulch heavily to even out soil moisture and reduce splash-borne disease. Stop watering watermelons 2 weeks before expected harvest to concentrate flavor.

failure_diagnostics.label: Small or bitter fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress during flowering and fruit set produces small, misshapen, or bitter fruit. Cucurbits move large volumes of water through their tissues during fruit development -- a single mature watermelon plant can use 1 to 2 gallons of water per day in peak summer. Cucumber bitterness is often a drought-stress signal.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently and deeply -- 1 to 2 inches per week minimum during fruit development, more in heat. Drip irrigation outperforms overhead watering by both providing consistent water and keeping foliage dry. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture and reduce evaporation.

failure_diagnostics.label: Vines without fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucurbits need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum, ideally 8 or more -- to set and ripen fruit. In partial shade vines grow leaves and even bloom, but fruit set is poor and ripening is incomplete. A late-season fruit that never sweetens is often a sun problem more than a temperature problem.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in the sunniest spot available. Trellising vining cucurbits (vertical support for cucumbers and small-fruited squash) gets more leaf area into the sun and improves fruit set substantially. In partial-shade gardens, accept that cucurbits are not the right crop and grow leafy greens or herbs instead.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension 2022 and 2025 Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetable Crops; UConn IPM 'Perimeter Trap Cropping for Cole Crops'). Nasturtiums specifically are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and Utah State University Extension (Mohr et al., 'Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting'). Protocol caveat: UConn IPM explicitly notes trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents' -- so the aphid application here has a protocol-mismatch concern even though the companion is extension-named. The Cornell-IPM-specific attribution in earlier catalog reason text was not located in Cornell's published IPM material; actual backing is WSU/USU/UConn.

pests.name: Cucumber beetle
pests.symptoms: Yellow-green beetles with black spots or stripes feeding on leaves, flowers, and fruit. Plants wilt suddenly (bacterial wilt transmission). Holey leaves.
pests.cause: Spotted and striped cucumber beetles. Also transmit bacterial wilt disease.
pests.organic_treatment: Row covers until flowering. Yellow sticky traps. Neem oil spray. Spinosad-based insecticide.
pests.prevention: Delay planting until plants are large. Use row covers early season. Interplant with radishes and nasturtiums.

pests.name: Squash bug
pests.symptoms: Gray-brown flat insects on stems and undersides of leaves. Wilting leaves with yellow then brown patches. Bronze egg clusters on leaf undersides.
pests.cause: Anasa tristis. Overwinters as adults in garden debris.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick adults and egg masses. Trap under boards at night. Neem oil spray on nymphs.
pests.prevention: Remove all garden debris in autumn. Rotate cucurbit crops. Use row covers early season.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces, stems, and sometimes fruit. Leaves may yellow and die. Worst in warm days with cool nights.
diseases.cause: Fungal disease favored by humid conditions with poor air circulation.
diseases.organic_treatment: Spray with diluted neem oil or a baking soda solution (1 tsp per quart water). Apply potassium bicarbonate spray. Remove and destroy affected leaves.
diseases.prevention: Space plants for good airflow. Water at soil level, not on foliage. Choose resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation.

diseases.name: Bacterial wilt
diseases.symptoms: Sudden wilting of individual leaves, then whole stems, then entire plant. No recovery even with watering. Plants die within days.
diseases.cause: Erwinia tracheiphila bacteria spread by cucumber beetles feeding.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure -- remove and destroy infected plants immediately. Control cucumber beetles to prevent spread.
diseases.prevention: Use row covers to exclude cucumber beetles early in season. Plant resistant varieties.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms: Yellow-green patches on upper leaf surface with corresponding gray-purple fuzzy growth on leaf undersides. Leaves die rapidly.
diseases.cause: Pseudoperonospora cubensis fungus. Spreads rapidly in wet humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively.
diseases.prevention: Choose resistant varieties. Water at soil level. Ensure good air circulation.

rotation.avoid_after: Cucumbers, squash, pumpkins, melons -- share cucumber beetle, bacterial wilt, downy mildew
rotation.note: Rotate to prevent cucumber beetle and disease buildup.

storage.freezer: Cook, rake into strands, freeze -- good
storage.notes: Spaghetti squash stores well. The hollow interior protects the flesh.

varieties.note: Small Wonder produces smaller fruits that cook faster and fit in most microwaves -- much easier to handle than standard.

container_notes.notes: Not suited to containers -- vines grow very long. Ground or large raised bed only.

start_method.notes: Direct sow after last frost. In zones 3-5, start indoors 3-4 weeks before in biodegradable pots.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Large seed leaves pushing up fast -- squash germinates quickly in warm soil.
growth_stages.user_action: Sow seeds on their edge to prevent rotting. Keep soil warm and moist.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Large, hairy true leaves developing rapidly. Squash grows fast once it gets going.
growth_stages.user_action: Give them space from the start -- squash plants get very large and do not like competition.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: A strong central crown with multiple large leaves. Bush varieties stay compact; vining types will start to sprawl.
growth_stages.user_action: If growing winter squash, direct the vines in the direction you want them to go now -- once established they are harder to redirect.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Growing well and in the right spot?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Large orange-yellow flowers. Male flowers come first on long straight stems. Female flowers have a swollen base -- the future squash.
growth_stages.user_action: Hand-pollinate female flowers in the early morning if you are not seeing good fruit set. Touch a male flower to each open female flower.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Flowers open? Any tiny squash forming?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Summer squash: harvest small and often at 6-8 inches. Winter squash: wait until skin is hard and stem is dry and corky.
growth_stages.user_action: Summer squash picked small tastes better and keeps production going. Winter squash left on the vine longer develops better flavor and storage life.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Slowing production on summer squash. Winter squash stems drying and corking -- the cue to harvest before frost.
growth_stages.user_action: Cure winter squash at room temperature for 10-14 days before storing -- it hardens the skin and sweetens the flesh. Summer squash plants can be composted after frost.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Season done? Worth noting what worked.

notifications.title: Time to sow your squash
notifications.body: Squash goes in a week after last frost, once the soil has had time to warm properly. Sow 2-3 seeds per spot and thin to the strongest plant. They grow fast -- you will see real progress within a week.

notifications.title: Check your squash flowers -- pollination time
notifications.body: Your squash should be flowering now. If you see flowers but no fruit forming, check whether you have both male and female flowers open at the same time. Female flowers have a small swollen base. Hand-pollinate in the morning if bees are scarce.

notifications.title: Summer squash ready -- pick small and often
notifications.body: Your courgettes or summer squash should be ready. Pick them at 6-8 inches -- they taste better small and the plant produces far more when you harvest regularly. A forgotten courgette turns into a marrow overnight.

notifications.title: Harvest your winter squash before frost
notifications.body: Frost is {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks away -- time to check your winter squash for harvest readiness. The stem should be dry and corky, and the skin should resist a thumbnail. Harvest all squash before frost and cure them for 10-14 days at room temperature.

notifications.title: Check your squash plants
notifications.body: Summer squash especially needs checking every few days -- they grow incredibly fast and a missed harvest sets back the whole plant.

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- protect your squash
weather_triggers.body: Squash is frost-tender. Cover with fleece tonight. Winter squash still on the vine must be harvested before a hard frost -- even one frosty night can damage stored winter squash.

weather_triggers.title: Powdery mildew risk for your squash
weather_triggers.body: Squash is very susceptible to powdery mildew in humid conditions. Ensure good spacing and airflow. If you see white powdery patches on leaves, remove affected leaves and spray with a dilute baking soda solution.

weather_triggers.title: Your squash needs deep watering
weather_triggers.body: Squash plants have large leaves and need a lot of water in dry conditions. Water deeply at the base -- not the leaves -- twice a week in drought conditions. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture.

germination.text: Sow squash seeds on their side, not flat. The root emerges from the pointed end and finds its way down more easily.
Squash germinates fast in warm soil -- sometimes in 4-5 days. In cold soil it rots. Wait for genuine warmth (60F+ minimum, 70F+ ideal).

seedling.text: Thin ruthlessly to one plant per spot. Squash planted too close together become a tangled mass that is prone to mildew and difficult to harvest.
Do not start squash indoors too early -- 3-4 weeks maximum. They outgrow their pots quickly and transplant shock is real.

established.text: Leave enough room -- a zucchini plant can easily cover 4-6 square feet. A butternut squash vine can run 6-10 feet. Plan for this before planting.
A thick layer of mulch around squash plants suppresses weeds, retains moisture, and keeps the fruit clean if it rests on the ground.

flowering.text: Male flowers come before female flowers -- this is normal and not something to worry about. Female flowers (with the swollen base behind the petals) follow within a week or two.
Early morning is when squash flowers are most receptive. If you are hand-pollinating, do it between 7-10am while flowers are fully open.

harvest.text: Winter squash is ready when the skin is hard enough that you cannot pierce it with a thumbnail and the stem has turned dry and corky. The fruit detaches easily but you should cut, not pull -- leaving 2 to 3 inches of stem dramatically extends storage life. Stemless squash rots from the wound within weeks.

Harvest before the first hard frost (28F or below). Light frost can be tolerated if the fruit is mature, but a hard freeze damages the flesh and ruins storage potential. Watch the forecast through autumn.

end_of_season.text: Cure freshly-cut winter squash for 10 to 14 days at 70-80F with good airflow before storing. Curing hardens the skin, heals minor stem wounds, and converts starches to sugars -- flavor improves dramatically over the cure window.

After curing, store at 50-60F in a dry, dark spot. A well-cured butternut keeps 3 to 6 months; acorn squash 1 to 2; spaghetti squash 2 to 3. Check periodically and use any squash showing soft spots first.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 3-6 fruits per plant for butternut and acorn types
yield_expectations.peak_production: Winter squash sets all its fruit within a window, then concentrates on ripening them
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Winter squash takes more patience than summer types -- the long growing season can feel slow. The payoff is months of stored vegetables.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucurbits are tropical-origin tender annuals -- killed outright by even a light frost at any stage. Cold soil at planting (below 60 degrees) stunts seedlings for the rest of the season even if they survive. Late-summer frost ends the season abruptly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Wait to direct-sow or transplant until soil reaches 65 to 70 degrees and night temperatures stay above 50. In short-season zones, start transplants indoors 3 to 4 weeks before set-out, but disturb roots minimally -- cucurbits resent transplanting. Use black plastic mulch to warm soil. Have row cover ready for unexpected late-spring or early-fall frosts.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucumber beetles (striped and spotted) damage seedlings directly and transmit bacterial wilt -- a fatal disease that wilts vines from the tips inward. Squash bugs target squash and pumpkin (less so cucumber and melon). Powdery mildew shows up reliably late in the season as white powder on leaves. Downy mildew, anthracnose, and bacterial leaf spot are humidity-driven secondary problems.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Floating row cover from planting through first flower blocks cucumber beetles -- remove at flowering for pollination. Squash bug egg masses (orange-red, on undersides of leaves) crush easily by hand if caught early. For powdery mildew, choose resistant varieties (most modern cucumbers are bred for resistance) and water at the base, not overhead. Rotate cucurbits to a new bed each year.

failure_diagnostics.label: Watery fruit or vine collapse
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucurbits need consistent water but cannot tolerate waterlogged soil. Persistent saturation causes root rot, sudden vine collapse, and watery flavorless fruit. Heavy rain near harvest causes ripe melons to crack and split. Wet foliage drives powdery mildew, downy mildew, and bacterial leaf spot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil or raised mounds (the traditional 'cucurbit hill' approach exists for drainage reasons). Water deeply at the base 1 to 2 times per week rather than shallow daily. Mulch heavily to even out soil moisture and reduce splash-borne disease. Stop watering watermelons 2 weeks before expected harvest to concentrate flavor.

failure_diagnostics.label: Small or bitter fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress during flowering and fruit set produces small, misshapen, or bitter fruit. Cucurbits move large volumes of water through their tissues during fruit development -- a single mature watermelon plant can use 1 to 2 gallons of water per day in peak summer. Cucumber bitterness is often a drought-stress signal.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently and deeply -- 1 to 2 inches per week minimum during fruit development, more in heat. Drip irrigation outperforms overhead watering by both providing consistent water and keeping foliage dry. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture and reduce evaporation.

failure_diagnostics.label: Vines without fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucurbits need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum, ideally 8 or more -- to set and ripen fruit. In partial shade vines grow leaves and even bloom, but fruit set is poor and ripening is incomplete. A late-season fruit that never sweetens is often a sun problem more than a temperature problem.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in the sunniest spot available. Trellising vining cucurbits (vertical support for cucumbers and small-fruited squash) gets more leaf area into the sun and improves fruit set substantially. In partial-shade gardens, accept that cucurbits are not the right crop and grow leafy greens or herbs instead.

fertilizer.notes: Like bush beans, pole beans fix nitrogen. Over-feeding produces lush vines with poor pod set.
fertilizer.npk_hint: 5-10-10 only if needed -- beans fix nitrogen

succession.tip: Sow every 3-4 weeks from last frost through early summer. Pole beans produce longer than bush beans -- a single planting can yield for 6-8 weeks of picking. But succession still helps: when the first planting hits peak production, the second is getting established. Use the longer interval (4 weeks) in zones with shorter seasons. Count back 65-80 days from first frost for your last sowing.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

pests.name: Bean seed fly
pests.symptoms: Seeds fail to germinate or seedlings die soon after emergence.
pests.cause: Delia platura maggots eat germinating seeds.
pests.organic_treatment: Sow when soil is warm (above 60°F) for rapid germination.
pests.prevention: Wait for warm soil. Start in pots and transplant. Pre-soak seeds to speed germination.

diseases.name: Bean rust
diseases.symptoms: Orange-brown powdery pustules on leaf undersides with corresponding pale spots on top.
diseases.cause: Uromyces appendiculatus fungus. Spreads in warm humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Sulfur-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Improve airflow.

diseases.name: Halo blight
diseases.symptoms: Water-soaked spots surrounded by yellow halo on leaves. Pods develop greasy patches.
diseases.cause: Pseudomonas syringae pv. phaseolicola bacteria. Seed-borne and spread by rain splash.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected plants. Copper-based bactericide spray.
diseases.prevention: Buy certified disease-free seed. Avoid working with wet plants. Rotate crops.

rotation.note: Plant legumes before heavy feeders -- they'll leave nitrogen-rich soil behind.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: The fat seed leaf loop pushing up and then straightening. Beans germinate fast in warm soil.
growth_stages.user_action: Sow directly -- beans and peas dislike transplanting. Soil must be at least 60°F for beans, 45°F for peas.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: First true leaves developing, tendrils beginning to reach for support on climbing types.
growth_stages.user_action: Get supports in place for climbing varieties now. Pole beans and sugar snaps grow fast once established.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Strong growth with multiple sets of leaves. Climbing types reaching upward actively.
growth_stages.user_action: Pinch out the growing tips of broad beans when flowers appear at the top -- it deters blackfly, the most common pest.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Flowers along the stem or at growing tips. Beans are self-pollinating -- you do not need to do anything.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep plants well watered during flowering. Drought stress at this stage causes flowers to drop before setting pods.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Pods swelling and filling. Pick before the pods become tough and stringy. Seeds should be visible but not bulging.
growth_stages.user_action: Pick every 2-3 days. Regular picking is essential -- leaving pods to mature tells the plant its job is done and production stops dramatically.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Slowing production, pods becoming tougher, plants yellowing.
growth_stages.user_action: Leave the last few pods to dry fully on the plant and save the seeds for next year. Cut plants at the base and leave the roots -- they fix nitrogen into the soil.

notifications.title: Time to sow your peas
notifications.body: Peas are cold-hardy and can go in 6-8 weeks before your last frost. They actually prefer cool conditions -- sow directly into prepared soil as soon as the ground can be worked. Get supports in place at the same time.

notifications.title: Time to sow your beans
notifications.body: Beans need warm soil -- wait until a week after your last frost before sowing. Cold soil causes seeds to rot rather than germinate. Sow directly at 2-inch depth, supports already in place for pole types.

notifications.title: Pinch out your broad bean tips
notifications.body: As soon as your broad beans show flowers at the top of the stem, pinch out the top 4-6 inches of growth. This deters blackfly which love the soft tips, and also redirects energy to pod development. It feels drastic but it is the right thing to do.

notifications.title: Beans ready -- pick every 2-3 days
notifications.body: The single most important thing now is picking regularly. Beans that are left to mature on the plant signal it to stop producing new pods. Get out there every 2-3 days without fail.

notifications.title: Check your beans and peas
notifications.body: Beans and peas need picking every few days at harvest time. A few days of neglect can mean tough, stringy pods. How are they looking?

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- protect young beans
weather_triggers.body: Bean seedlings are frost-tender. Cover with fleece tonight. Peas handle light frost much better -- established pea plants usually survive without protection.

weather_triggers.title: Drought stress -- water your beans during flowering
weather_triggers.body: Drought during flowering is the most damaging thing for beans and peas. Flowers drop before setting pods and production suffers significantly. Water deeply at the base every 2-3 days in dry weather.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- watch for powdery mildew on peas
weather_triggers.body: Peas are prone to powdery mildew in humid conditions, especially later in the season. Ensure good airflow and harvest promptly. Late in the season this is normal -- the plant has done its job.

germination.text: Beans are direct-sown -- transplanting damages the brittle taproot. Wait until soil is 60 degrees minimum (65 to 70 is better) before sowing; cold soil rots seed before it germinates.

Sow 1 to 2 inches deep, 2 to 4 inches apart in rows. Inoculate seed with rhizobium bacteria at sowing if the bed has not grown beans recently -- this boosts the nitrogen-fixing nodulation that beans depend on.

seedling.text: Beans germinate fast in warm soil -- typically 7 to 10 days. Seedlings are vulnerable to slugs and bean leaf beetles in their first weeks; check daily.

Thin bush beans to 4 to 6 inches between plants once seedlings are 4 inches tall. Pole beans need a trellis or pole structure in place at this stage -- they grow fast and resent late-installed support.

established.text: Do not fertilize beans with nitrogen. Beans fix their own nitrogen via root nodules; high-N fertilizer suppresses nodulation and produces lush leafy plants with poor pod set.
Water consistently during flowering and pod-fill -- this is when water stress most reduces yield. Mulch heavily to stabilize soil moisture and suppress weeds.

flowering.text: Beans are self-pollinating and do not need pollinators. Flowers open and self-pollinate within hours; fruit set is fast.
Watch for bean leaf beetles and aphids during flowering -- both populations spike in this window. Check undersides of leaves daily.

harvest.text: Pick beans young and often -- bush and pole beans ready when pods snap cleanly and the seeds inside are still small. Edamame ready when pods are plump and fill 80 to 90 percent with bright green beans, before yellowing.
Harvest every 2 to 3 days during peak production. Beans left on the plant signal it to stop producing new pods. Edamame is harvested whole-pod, not shelled in the field.

end_of_season.text: After harvest, cut bean plants at ground level and leave roots in the soil -- the nitrogen-fixing root nodules become next year's slow-release nitrogen for the bed.
Rotate beans to a new bed each year. Bean diseases (anthracnose, halo blight, bean rust) survive in soil and infect next year's planting.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 1-2 lbs per plant over a long season
yield_expectations.peak_production: Pole beans produce continuously for months -- far more total yield than bush beans
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Pole beans are the most productive choice if you have a support structure. They keep going all summer with regular picking.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Beans are warm-season tender annuals -- killed outright by light frost at any stage. Cold soil at sowing (below 60 degrees) rots seed; cool conditions during early growth produce stunted plants that never fully recover. Late summer frost ends the season abruptly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Wait to sow until soil is reliably 60 degrees minimum (65 to 70 is better). In short-season zones, choose early-maturing bush varieties and use black plastic mulch to warm soil. Have row cover ready for unexpected late-spring frosts. For fall harvests, time the planting so harvest finishes before first expected frost.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Mexican bean beetle (yellow with black spots, similar to ladybug but a pest) is the dominant bean pest east of the Rockies -- larvae skeletonize leaves. Bean leaf beetle damages seedlings and pods. Aphids cluster on tender new growth. Halo blight (water-soaked spots with yellow halo) and bean rust are the headline diseases. For edamame specifically, soybean aphid and Japanese beetle are also common.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: For Mexican bean beetle, hand-pick adults and crush yellow egg masses on leaf undersides; in heavy infestations, parasitic wasp release works for organic gardeners. Rotate to a new bed each year. Avoid working bean plants when foliage is wet -- this spreads halo blight and bean rust. Choose disease-resistant varieties for the next planting.

failure_diagnostics.label: Root rot or yellowing
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Persistent waterlogging causes root rot, yellowing leaves, and crown collapse. Beans are also susceptible to white mold (Sclerotinia) in cool wet conditions, which produces fluffy white growth at the soil line and kills plants quickly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil. Water at the base, not overhead, and water in the morning so foliage dries before evening. Space plants for airflow. For white mold, rotate at least 3 years between bean plantings in any one bed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor pod set or fill
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress during flowering and pod-fill is the leading cause of poor bean harvests. Plants drop flowers under water stress and produce small empty or partially-filled pods. Edamame is especially demanding of consistent water during the pod-fill window.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently during flowering and pod-fill -- 1 inch per week minimum, more in heat. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture. Drip irrigation is ideal because it provides consistent water without wetting foliage.

failure_diagnostics.label: Few flowers or pods
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Beans need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to flower and produce well. In partial shade plants grow leaves but flower sparsely and set few pods. Tall pole beans can shade their own lower leaves if not pinched at the top of the support.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun. For pole beans, pinch the growing tip when vines reach the top of the support to prevent excessive top growth and improve light penetration to lower flowering nodes.
