pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

pests.name: Bean seed fly
pests.symptoms: Seeds fail to germinate or seedlings die soon after emergence.
pests.cause: Delia platura maggots eat germinating seeds.
pests.organic_treatment: Sow when soil is warm (above 60°F) for rapid germination.
pests.prevention: Wait for warm soil. Start in pots and transplant. Pre-soak seeds to speed germination.

diseases.name: Bean rust
diseases.symptoms: Orange-brown powdery pustules on leaf undersides with corresponding pale spots on top.
diseases.cause: Uromyces appendiculatus fungus. Spreads in warm humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Sulfur-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Improve airflow.

diseases.name: Halo blight
diseases.symptoms: Water-soaked spots surrounded by yellow halo on leaves. Pods develop greasy patches.
diseases.cause: Pseudomonas syringae pv. phaseolicola bacteria. Seed-borne and spread by rain splash.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected plants. Copper-based bactericide spray.
diseases.prevention: Buy certified disease-free seed. Avoid working with wet plants. Rotate crops.

crops.harvest_ready: Pods flat, seeds barely visible. Pick before seeds swell. More tender when small.

start_method.notes: Direct sow in cool weather, 4-6 weeks before last frost.

rotation.avoid_after: Beans, peas -- some shared diseases but generally disease pressure is lower
rotation.good_after: Brassicas, nightshades, corn -- legumes fix nitrogen that these heavy feeders need
rotation.note: Plant legumes before heavy feeders -- they'll leave nitrogen-rich soil behind.

storage.freezer: Blanch 1-2 minutes, freeze -- very good
storage.notes: Snow peas freeze better than sugar snap peas due to thinner walls.

varieties.note: Oregon Sugar Pod II has the best disease package -- resistant to enation mosaic virus and powdery mildew.

container_notes.notes: Good container crop with a trellis. 3-gallon minimum. Dwarf varieties need less support.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: The fat seed leaf loop pushing up and then straightening. Beans germinate fast in warm soil.
growth_stages.user_action: Sow directly -- beans and peas dislike transplanting. Soil must be at least 60°F for beans, 45°F for peas.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: First true leaves developing, tendrils beginning to reach for support on climbing types.
growth_stages.user_action: Get supports in place for climbing varieties now. Pole beans and sugar snaps grow fast once established.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Strong growth with multiple sets of leaves. Climbing types reaching upward actively.
growth_stages.user_action: Pinch out the growing tips of broad beans when flowers appear at the top -- it deters blackfly, the most common pest.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Flowers along the stem or at growing tips. Beans are self-pollinating -- you do not need to do anything.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep plants well watered during flowering. Drought stress at this stage causes flowers to drop before setting pods.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Pods swelling and filling. Pick before the pods become tough and stringy. Seeds should be visible but not bulging.
growth_stages.user_action: Pick every 2-3 days. Regular picking is essential -- leaving pods to mature tells the plant its job is done and production stops dramatically.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Slowing production, pods becoming tougher, plants yellowing.
growth_stages.user_action: Leave the last few pods to dry fully on the plant and save the seeds for next year. Cut plants at the base and leave the roots -- they fix nitrogen into the soil.

notifications.title: Time to sow your peas
notifications.body: Peas are cold-hardy and can go in 6-8 weeks before your last frost. They actually prefer cool conditions -- sow directly into prepared soil as soon as the ground can be worked. Get supports in place at the same time.

notifications.title: Time to sow your beans
notifications.body: Beans need warm soil -- wait until a week after your last frost before sowing. Cold soil causes seeds to rot rather than germinate. Sow directly at 2-inch depth, supports already in place for pole types.

notifications.title: Pinch out your broad bean tips
notifications.body: As soon as your broad beans show flowers at the top of the stem, pinch out the top 4-6 inches of growth. This deters blackfly which love the soft tips, and also redirects energy to pod development. It feels drastic but it is the right thing to do.

notifications.title: Beans ready -- pick every 2-3 days
notifications.body: The single most important thing now is picking regularly. Beans that are left to mature on the plant signal it to stop producing new pods. Get out there every 2-3 days without fail.

notifications.title: Check your beans and peas
notifications.body: Beans and peas need picking every few days at harvest time. A few days of neglect can mean tough, stringy pods. How are they looking?

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- protect young beans
weather_triggers.body: Bean seedlings are frost-tender. Cover with fleece tonight. Peas handle light frost much better -- established pea plants usually survive without protection.

weather_triggers.title: Drought stress -- water your beans during flowering
weather_triggers.body: Drought during flowering is the most damaging thing for beans and peas. Flowers drop before setting pods and production suffers significantly. Water deeply at the base every 2-3 days in dry weather.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- watch for powdery mildew on peas
weather_triggers.body: Peas are prone to powdery mildew in humid conditions, especially later in the season. Ensure good airflow and harvest promptly. Late in the season this is normal -- the plant has done its job.

germination.text: Peas are direct-sown 4 to 6 weeks before last frost -- they actually prefer cool soil (40 to 60 degrees) and germinate poorly above 75. In mild-winter zones, fall sowing for spring harvest works well.
Sow 1 to 1.5 inches deep, 2 inches apart. Inoculate seed with rhizobium bacteria if the bed has not grown peas recently. Soak seeds overnight before sowing in cool soil to speed germination.

seedling.text: Peas germinate in 7 to 14 days in cool soil. Seedlings tolerate light frost and even brief snow once established -- they are remarkably cold-hardy.
Install trellis or netting at sowing or as soon as seedlings emerge. Peas climb by tendrils and need something to grab. Even bush peas benefit from low brushwood support.

established.text: Do not fertilize with nitrogen. Peas fix their own nitrogen via root nodules; extra N produces leafy plants with poor pod production.
Water consistently. Peas have shallow roots and dry out fast -- mulch heavily to stabilize soil moisture and keep roots cool.

flowering.text: Peas are self-pollinating; flowers do not need insect pollinators. Cool weather during flowering produces the most flowers and highest yields.
Watch for pea aphids on flower clusters and tender new growth. Powdery mildew often shows up as flowering peaks, especially in still humid conditions.

harvest.text: Snow peas: pick when pods are flat and the peas inside are barely visible bumps. Sugar snap peas: pick when pods are plump and crisp but before peas inside become starchy. Both are best picked young and often.
Harvest every 1 to 2 days during peak production. Peas left on the plant signal it to stop producing new flowers; daily picking can extend the harvest by weeks.

end_of_season.text: Peas finish abruptly when daytime temperatures consistently exceed 75 to 80 degrees -- plants yellow, stop flowering, and decline. This is the natural cycle, not a problem.
Cut spent plants at ground level and leave roots in the soil for the nitrogen contribution. The freed-up bed is well-suited to a fall planting of cool-season crops or warm-season transplants.

yield_expectations.per_plant: A good handful of pods per plant per week at peak
yield_expectations.peak_production: Snow peas produce over several weeks -- harvest when flat and before seeds bulge
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Snow peas are delicious raw and one of the easiest crops to get right.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Cold tolerance and heat-induced bolting
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Peas are unusual among annuals in being killed by HEAT, not cold. Young plants tolerate light frost and even brief snow; mature plants flower through cool spring weather but stop and decline once daytime temperatures consistently exceed 75 to 80 degrees. The end of pea season is heat, not cold.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Sow as early as possible -- 4 to 6 weeks before last frost in most zones. In mild-winter zones, fall sowing gives a long cool-season harvest. Choose heat-tolerant varieties (Wando, Sugar Sprint) for warmer zones. Plan succession plantings so harvest finishes before the heat hits.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Pea aphid (the headline pea pest) clusters on flower buds and tender new growth, weakening plants and reducing pod set. Pea weevil larvae bore into developing peas. Pea leaf miner damages leaves but rarely affects yield substantially. Powdery mildew is the headline disease, especially in cool humid conditions or as plants approach the heat-stress end of their cycle.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Hose off pea aphids with water; for serious infestations, insecticidal soap. Choose powdery-mildew-resistant varieties (most modern peas have some resistance). Space plants for airflow and avoid overhead watering. Rotate peas to a new bed each year.

failure_diagnostics.label: Root rot or yellowing
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Persistent waterlogging causes root rot and yellowing of inner leaves. Peas in heavy clay or low-lying spots are especially vulnerable. Wet foliage drives powdery mildew and ascochyta blight.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil. Use raised beds in heavy or wet sites. Water at the base, not overhead, and water early in the day so foliage dries before evening.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor pod set or fill
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress during flowering and pod-fill produces small empty pods or partially-filled pods. Peas have shallow roots and dry out fast; a few hot dry days during the critical flowering window can substantially reduce yield even on otherwise healthy plants.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently -- 1 inch per week minimum, more in heat. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture and keep roots cool. Drip irrigation works well for peas because it keeps foliage dry while providing consistent water.

failure_diagnostics.label: Sparse flowers or weak vines
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Peas need 6 hours of sun minimum, though they tolerate light shade better than beans. In deep shade, plants grow leggy with sparse flowers and reduced yield. Crowded planting can shade lower flowering nodes on tall pole peas.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun in cool climates; light afternoon shade is fine in warmer zones and may extend the bloom cycle by reducing heat stress. Space plants for airflow and light penetration. Trellis tall varieties properly so vines spread out rather than tangling.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

pests.name: Bean seed fly
pests.symptoms: Seeds fail to germinate or seedlings die soon after emergence.
pests.cause: Delia platura maggots eat germinating seeds.
pests.organic_treatment: Sow when soil is warm (above 60°F) for rapid germination.
pests.prevention: Wait for warm soil. Start in pots and transplant. Pre-soak seeds to speed germination.

diseases.name: Bean rust
diseases.symptoms: Orange-brown powdery pustules on leaf undersides with corresponding pale spots on top.
diseases.cause: Uromyces appendiculatus fungus. Spreads in warm humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Sulfur-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Improve airflow.

diseases.name: Halo blight
diseases.symptoms: Water-soaked spots surrounded by yellow halo on leaves. Pods develop greasy patches.
diseases.cause: Pseudomonas syringae pv. phaseolicola bacteria. Seed-borne and spread by rain splash.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected plants. Copper-based bactericide spray.
diseases.prevention: Buy certified disease-free seed. Avoid working with wet plants. Rotate crops.

crops.harvest_ready: Pods 6-8 inches, firm and plump. Press thumbnail into a bean -- if it leaves a mark, they're ready. For best texture, pick before beans turn mealy.

start_method.notes: Direct sow in autumn (mild climates) or very early spring. Cold-tolerant -- among the first things to sow.

rotation.avoid_after: Beans, peas -- some shared diseases but generally disease pressure is lower
rotation.good_after: Brassicas, nightshades, corn -- legumes fix nitrogen that these heavy feeders need
rotation.note: Plant legumes before heavy feeders -- they'll leave nitrogen-rich soil behind.

storage.freezer: Shell, blanch 3 minutes, freeze -- excellent, traditional preservation method
storage.notes: Double-pod if beans are large (remove gray skin after blanching) for smoother texture.

varieties.note: The Sutton is the best compact variety -- 12 inches tall, no staking, good for exposed or windy gardens.

container_notes.notes: Can be grown in containers. 5-gallon minimum per plant. Dwarf varieties like The Sutton are best.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: The fat seed leaf loop pushing up and then straightening. Beans germinate fast in warm soil.
growth_stages.user_action: Sow directly -- beans and peas dislike transplanting. Soil must be at least 60°F for beans, 45°F for peas.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: First true leaves developing, tendrils beginning to reach for support on climbing types.
growth_stages.user_action: Get supports in place for climbing varieties now. Pole beans and sugar snaps grow fast once established.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Strong growth with multiple sets of leaves. Climbing types reaching upward actively.
growth_stages.user_action: Pinch out the growing tips of broad beans when flowers appear at the top -- it deters blackfly, the most common pest.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Flowers along the stem or at growing tips. Beans are self-pollinating -- you do not need to do anything.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep plants well watered during flowering. Drought stress at this stage causes flowers to drop before setting pods.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Pods swelling and filling. Pick before the pods become tough and stringy. Seeds should be visible but not bulging.
growth_stages.user_action: Pick every 2-3 days. Regular picking is essential -- leaving pods to mature tells the plant its job is done and production stops dramatically.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Slowing production, pods becoming tougher, plants yellowing.
growth_stages.user_action: Leave the last few pods to dry fully on the plant and save the seeds for next year. Cut plants at the base and leave the roots -- they fix nitrogen into the soil.

notifications.title: Time to sow your peas
notifications.body: Peas are cold-hardy and can go in 6-8 weeks before your last frost. They actually prefer cool conditions -- sow directly into prepared soil as soon as the ground can be worked. Get supports in place at the same time.

notifications.title: Time to sow your beans
notifications.body: Beans need warm soil -- wait until a week after your last frost before sowing. Cold soil causes seeds to rot rather than germinate. Sow directly at 2-inch depth, supports already in place for pole types.

notifications.title: Pinch out your broad bean tips
notifications.body: As soon as your broad beans show flowers at the top of the stem, pinch out the top 4-6 inches of growth. This deters blackfly which love the soft tips, and also redirects energy to pod development. It feels drastic but it is the right thing to do.

notifications.title: Beans ready -- pick every 2-3 days
notifications.body: The single most important thing now is picking regularly. Beans that are left to mature on the plant signal it to stop producing new pods. Get out there every 2-3 days without fail.

notifications.title: Check your beans and peas
notifications.body: Beans and peas need picking every few days at harvest time. A few days of neglect can mean tough, stringy pods. How are they looking?

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- protect young beans
weather_triggers.body: Bean seedlings are frost-tender. Cover with fleece tonight. Peas handle light frost much better -- established pea plants usually survive without protection.

weather_triggers.title: Drought stress -- water your beans during flowering
weather_triggers.body: Drought during flowering is the most damaging thing for beans and peas. Flowers drop before setting pods and production suffers significantly. Water deeply at the base every 2-3 days in dry weather.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- watch for powdery mildew on peas
weather_triggers.body: Peas are prone to powdery mildew in humid conditions, especially later in the season. Ensure good airflow and harvest promptly. Late in the season this is normal -- the plant has done its job.

germination.text: Broad beans (fava beans) are cool-season legumes -- the opposite of warm-season beans. Sow in late fall in mild-winter zones (zones 8+) for spring harvest, or as early in spring as soil can be worked in colder zones. The plants tolerate light frost throughout their cycle.
Sow seeds 1.5 to 2 inches deep, 6 to 8 inches apart in rows 2 to 3 feet apart. Inoculate with rhizobium bacteria at sowing for nitrogen-fixing nodulation.

seedling.text: Broad bean seedlings emerge in 7 to 14 days and are remarkably cold-hardy -- they tolerate light frost and even brief snow without damage in most cases.
Stake or support tall varieties as they grow -- mature plants reach 3 to 5 feet and topple in wind without support. A simple twine-and-stake corral around the planting works well.

established.text: Do not fertilize with nitrogen. Broad beans fix their own nitrogen via root nodules; high-N fertilizer suppresses nodulation and produces lush leafy plants with poor pod set.
Water consistently during flowering and pod-fill. Mulch heavily to stabilize soil moisture and suppress weeds. Black bean aphids show up first on the growing tips at this stage.

flowering.text: Broad bean flowers are white with distinctive black markings -- attractive to pollinators and often the first major nectar source of spring. Bumblebees especially favor them.

Pinch out the top 4 to 6 inches of growing tips once the lowest flowers begin to set pods. This is the single most effective control for black bean aphid (which clusters on the tender growing tips) and concentrates the plant's energy into pod fill.

harvest.text: Harvest pods when the beans inside have swollen but the pods are still bright green and tender. Pods left too long become tough and the beans inside develop a bitter outer skin that needs blanching to remove.
Harvest every 3 to 4 days during peak production. Broad beans are usually shelled before cooking; some varieties (Aquadulce especially) can be eaten pod-and-all when very young.

end_of_season.text: After harvest, cut plants at ground level and leave roots in the soil -- the nitrogen-fixing root nodules become next year's slow-release nitrogen contribution to the bed.
Broad beans are a traditional cover crop for this reason. The bed where they grew is well-suited to nitrogen-loving warm-season crops (corn, leafy greens, brassicas) the following season.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 30-50 beans per plant across multiple pods
yield_expectations.peak_production: Broad beans produce over 3-4 weeks then are done -- a proper seasonal crop
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Fresh broad beans double-podded and eaten immediately are extraordinary -- completely different from frozen or tinned.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Cold tolerance
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Broad beans are unusual among legumes in being substantially cold-tolerant -- young plants survive light frost and even brief snow. The threats at the cold end are sustained hard freezes (below about 15 degrees) and frost during flowering or pod-fill, which damages the tender flowers and pods. Hot summer weather, not cold, ends the broad-bean cycle.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: In mild-winter zones (8 and warmer), sow in late fall for spring harvest -- the plants overwinter and produce earlier and heavier than spring-sown plants. In colder zones, sow as early in spring as soil can be worked. Cover with row cover during sustained hard freezes if attempting to overwinter in marginal zones.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Black bean aphid (Aphis fabae, sometimes called blackfly) is the dominant broad-bean pest -- dense black colonies cluster on the growing tips during flowering and can stunt or kill plants if uncontrolled. Chocolate spot (Botrytis fabae) is the headline disease, producing characteristic chocolate-brown spots on leaves in cool wet weather. Broad bean weevil and pea aphid are secondary pests.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Pinch out the top 4 to 6 inches of growing tips at first flowering -- this single action removes the aphid's preferred habitat and concentrates plant energy into pods. Hose off remaining aphids with water; encourage ladybugs and lacewings. For chocolate spot, choose resistant varieties, space plants for airflow, and avoid overhead watering.

failure_diagnostics.label: Root rot or chocolate spot
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Broad beans tolerate moderate moisture but suffer in waterlogged soil. Persistent saturation causes root rot. Wet humid conditions during flowering and pod-fill drive chocolate spot disease, which can defoliate plants and reduce yield substantially.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil. Water at the base, not overhead. Space plants for airflow. In wet climates, choose chocolate-spot-resistant varieties and consider trellising plants to lift foliage off the ground.

failure_diagnostics.label: Small or empty pods
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress during flowering and pod-fill produces small pods or pods with poorly-developed beans inside. Broad beans tolerate dry conditions better than most legumes once established but still need consistent water during the critical flowering and pod-fill window.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently during flowering and pod-fill -- 1 inch per week minimum. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture and keep roots cool. The cool-weather growing window means water demands are lower than for warm-season beans, but consistent water still matters.

failure_diagnostics.label: Tall weak plants with few pods
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Broad beans need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to set pods well. In partial shade plants grow tall and weak with sparse flowering and few pods. Plants that lean or topple from inadequate support similarly suffer reduced yield.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun. Stake or support tall varieties as they grow -- mature plants reach 3 to 5 feet and need anchoring. A simple twine-and-stake corral around the planting prevents wind damage.

crops.name: Lettuce (Leaf)
crops.description: One of the fastest crops in the garden. Sow directly, harvest outer leaves as cut-and-come-again. Bolts in heat -- succession sow every 2 weeks through spring and again in fall.

3.notes: Direct sow early. Succession sow every 2 weeks for steady supply. Use cold frame for earliest and latest harvests.

succession.tip: Sow every 2 weeks from your last frost date through early summer, then again from late summer through autumn. Pause in the heat of summer -- lettuce bolts above 75°F and turns bitter. A 2-week interval means you always have a row coming in as the previous one peaks. Sow just enough for 1-2 weeks of salads per batch rather than a full bed at once.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Structural-category claim has a mechanistic basis. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Root-zone partitioning is a real ecology concept. 'Carrots loosen soil for tomatoes' is a plausible mechanistic claim but not well-studied for specific pairs.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Allium sulfur-based volatile organic compounds have documented aphid-repellent effects (Durenne and Gosset, 'Companion Plants for Aphid Pest Management,' Insects 2018, 9(4):112). The companion application is described by several extensions at home-gardening rigor: Mississippi State University Extension ('Companion planting improves gardens,' Snyder via Reeves) explicitly states 'Chives tend to repel aphids'; Utah State University Extension ('Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting,' Mohr et al.) lists onions, garlic, and chives as repelling common garden pests; UC Cooperative Extension Master Gardener publications (Butte County 'Best Friends in the Garden' and Fresno County 'Winter companion planting to repel insects') likewise list allium VOCs among aphid-repellent companions. These extension sources describe the pairing at tradition-plus-plausible-mechanism rigor rather than validated protocol -- the Kansas State Extension / Johnson County 'Companion Planting' page caveats that allium sulfur repellency is 'centralized to the garlic itself -- and only with certain pests.' The earlier catalog attribution to 'UC IPM' does not match UC IPM's Pest Notes on aphids (pn7404), which focus on reflective mulches, water sprays, soaps, and natural enemies rather than allium interplanting.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension 2022 and 2025 Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetable Crops; UConn IPM 'Perimeter Trap Cropping for Cole Crops'). Nasturtiums specifically are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and Utah State University Extension (Mohr et al., 'Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting'). Protocol caveat: UConn IPM explicitly notes trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents' -- so the aphid application here has a protocol-mismatch concern even though the companion is extension-named. The Cornell-IPM-specific attribution in earlier catalog reason text was not located in Cornell's published IPM material; actual backing is WSU/USU/UConn.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Bad companion claim, no pattern match. Default to traditional pending review.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Inter-plant competition for N, P, K is a real agronomic concept. Specific 'bad pair' claims often extrapolate beyond what research has shown.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

pests.name: Lettuce root aphid
pests.symptoms: Plants wilt and die despite adequate watering. White waxy deposits on roots when plant pulled up. Difficult to detect above ground.
pests.cause: Pemphigus bursarius. Lives underground on lettuce roots.
pests.organic_treatment: Remove affected plants. Drench soil with insecticidal soap solution. Rotate lettuce crops.
pests.prevention: Crop rotation. Grow resistant varieties labeled LR (Lettuce root aphid resistant).

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms: Yellow patches on older leaves with gray-purple mold on undersides. Spreads rapidly in wet cool conditions.
diseases.cause: Bremia lactucae fungus. Very common in cool damp weather.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Improve airflow. Copper fungicide preventively.
diseases.prevention: Water at soil level. Space plants well. Choose resistant varieties. Avoid autumn/winter planting under cover without ventilation.

diseases.name: Tipburn
diseases.symptoms: Brown papery edges on inner leaves. Not contagious. Common in cos/romaine types.
diseases.cause: Calcium deficiency in inner leaves due to poor circulation -- not a disease. Worse in hot weather.
diseases.organic_treatment: Ensure consistent watering. Improve air movement around plants.
diseases.prevention: Harvest before heads are fully mature in summer. Choose heat-tolerant varieties.

watering.frequency: Every 2-3 days -- shallow roots dry out quickly
watering.signs_overwater: Slime at base, yellow outer leaves

crops.harvest_ready: Pick outer leaves as needed, or harvest whole head when full. Harvest before heat causes bolting -- once the central stem elongates, leaves turn bitter.

start_method.notes: Direct sow outdoors 3-4 weeks before last frost. Or start indoors 4 weeks before for transplanting. Very easy to transplant.

container_notes.notes: One of the best container crops. Shallow roots -- any container 6+ inches deep works, including window boxes and grow bags.

varieties.note: Buttercrunch is the most forgiving variety -- heat tolerant and slow to bolt.

storage.fridge: 3-5 days wrapped in damp paper towel in a bag
storage.freezer: Not suitable
storage.notes: Don't wash until ready to eat. Store away from apples and pears (ethylene ripeners).

bolting.triggers: Heat above 75°F, long days (>14 hours), stress
bolting.prevention: Choose slow-bolt varieties (Buttercrunch, Batavian types). Provide afternoon shade in summer. Succession sow every 2-3 weeks rather than large single planting. Harvest outer leaves constantly.
bolting.note: Once bolted, harvest quickly -- central leaves are still edible before bitterness sets in fully.

thinning.to_spacing: 6-8 inches for leaf lettuce, 10-12 for heads
thinning.method: Snip extras at soil level -- thinnings are edible as salad.
thinning.tip: Successive thinning works well -- thin loosely first, then use thinnings as baby salad, thin again as they grow.

rotation.avoid_after: Other lettuce, endive, chicory -- share lettuce root aphid
rotation.note: Rotate lettuce to avoid lettuce root aphid buildup in soil.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small seed leaves pushing through the soil -- leafy greens germinate readily in cool, moist conditions.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged. Most leafy greens germinate best at 50-65°F -- they actually prefer cooler soil than tomatoes.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: True leaves developing, recognizable as the crop you planted.
growth_stages.user_action: Thin seedlings to the recommended spacing -- crowded leafy greens bolt faster and produce less. The thinnings are edible.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Leaves at a harvestable size, plant looking full and healthy.
growth_stages.user_action: Begin harvesting outer leaves now -- this encourages more growth from the center. Do not wait for the plant to be 'finished' before you start picking.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Ready to start harvesting outer leaves?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Leaves at good size, before any yellowing or flowering stem appears.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest cut-and-come-again -- remove outer leaves and let the center keep growing. For butterhead types, harvest the whole head when formed.

growth_stages.name: Bolting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: A central flower stalk shooting upward, leaves becoming smaller and more bitter.
growth_stages.user_action: Once bolting starts the flavor changes -- harvest everything immediately. Bolted leaves are still edible but more bitter. Remove the plant and either sow again or move on to a warm-season crop.

notifications.title: Time to sow your leafy greens
notifications.body: Leafy greens love cool weather and can go in the ground 4-6 weeks before your last frost. Sow directly into prepared soil or start indoors for transplanting. They are some of the first crops of the year -- enjoy the early start.

notifications.title: Your greens should be ready to start picking
notifications.body: Begin harvesting outer leaves now even if the plant seems small. Regular picking encourages more growth. Do not wait for the plant to be 'done' -- leafy greens are a harvest-as-you-go crop.

notifications.title: Heat incoming -- watch your greens for bolting
notifications.body: Hot weather triggers leafy greens to bolt -- sending up a flower stalk and turning bitter. Harvest everything you can now before the heat arrives. Consider sowing again in late summer for a fall crop.

notifications.title: Time to sow your fall leafy greens
notifications.body: Eight weeks before first frost is the window for a second sowing of leafy greens. A fall crop often outperforms spring -- the cooling temperatures mean slower bolting and sweeter flavor. Kale especially improves after a light frost.

notifications.title: How are your greens looking?
notifications.body: Leafy greens can bolt quickly in warm weather. A quick check every few days helps you catch the right harvest moment and spot any bolting before it is too late.

weather_triggers.title: Heat alert -- harvest your greens now
weather_triggers.body: Hot weather is the enemy of leafy greens. They bolt quickly and flavor turns bitter fast. Harvest as much as you can before the heat arrives. Shade cloth can buy you another week in marginal temperatures.

weather_triggers.title: Unexpected frost -- protect young greens
weather_triggers.body: Most leafy greens handle light frost well once established, but young seedlings need protection. Cover with fleece tonight if frost is forecast.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- watch for downy mildew
weather_triggers.body: Humid conditions encourage downy mildew on leafy greens. Ensure good airflow between plants and avoid watering late in the day. Pick regularly to keep the plant open.

germination.text: Leafy greens are some of the easiest crops to germinate -- cool, moist soil is all they need. Sow more thickly than you think you need and thin later.
The thinnings from leafy greens are completely edible -- use them as microgreens in salads. Thinning is harvesting.

seedling.text: Thin to the recommended spacing even though it feels wasteful. Crowded leafy greens bolt faster, get less airflow, and produce smaller leaves.
A light mulch around seedlings keeps moisture in and suppresses weeds -- both important for leafy greens which need consistent moisture.

established.text: Start harvesting outer leaves as soon as they reach a useful size -- this is how leafy greens work. The center keeps producing new growth as you remove the outer leaves.
Water consistently. Irregular watering is a major trigger for bolting in many leafy greens, especially lettuce and spinach.

harvest.text: Always harvest in the morning when leaves are full of water and at their crispest. Refrigerate immediately in a damp bag.
Leave at least half the plant intact when harvesting cut-and-come-again crops. Taking too much at once sets the plant back.

bolting.text: Once you see a flower stalk, harvest everything immediately. The leaves are still edible but will become more bitter every day.
Bolted leafy greens are not a failure -- it is the plant completing its lifecycle. A fall sowing often outperforms spring because the weather is cooling rather than warming.

yield_expectations.per_plant: Multiple harvests over 6-8 weeks before bolting
yield_expectations.peak_production: A well-managed lettuce plant gives you a harvest every 1-2 weeks
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Leaf lettuce is one of the easiest and fastest crops you can grow. You can be eating it within 30 days of sowing.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Most leafy greens actually handle light frost well once established -- it can even improve flavor. But young seedlings are more vulnerable. If the damage happened at the seedling stage, a late frost likely caught them.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Cover seedlings with fleece if frost threatens in the first few weeks. Established leafy greens generally recover from light frost on their own.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Slugs love leafy green seedlings, especially in wet conditions. Downy mildew affects plants in humid, overcrowded conditions. Flea beetles leave tiny holes in leaves -- especially on arugula and kale.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Thin seedlings properly to allow airflow. Protect from slugs in the first few weeks. Row cover helps with flea beetles on susceptible varieties.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too much water or bolting
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Leafy greens in waterlogged soil develop root rot quickly. More commonly, warmth and long days trigger bolting -- the plant sends up a flower stalk and the leaves become bitter. This is the plant completing its lifecycle, not a failure of care.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Bolting is largely about timing. Sow earlier in spring or switch to a fall sowing -- cooling temperatures signal the plant to keep producing leaves rather than flowering.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too little water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Irregular watering is a major bolting trigger in lettuce and spinach. A dry spell followed by heat pushes them to flower and seed rapidly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Keep moisture consistent -- mulching around leafy greens makes a real difference. Water in the morning so leaves dry during the day.

failure_diagnostics.label: Bolted too quickly
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Heat and long days cause most leafy greens to bolt -- this is the most common reason they fail. The plant is not dying, it is doing what it is designed to do. Once bolted the leaves become bitter and inedible quickly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: The fall sowing is almost always more successful than spring for leafy greens. Cooling temperatures give you longer, slower-bolting plants. Shade cloth can also extend the spring crop by a couple of weeks.

diseases.symptoms: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces, stems, and sometimes fruit. Leaves may yellow and die. Worst in warm days with cool nights.
diseases.cause: Fungal disease favored by humid conditions with poor air circulation.
diseases.organic_treatment: Spray with diluted neem oil or a baking soda solution (1 tsp per quart water). Apply potassium bicarbonate spray. Remove and destroy affected leaves.
diseases.prevention: Space plants for good airflow. Water at soil level, not on foliage. Choose resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation.

crops.harvest_ready: Pick outer stalks at any size. Younger leaves are more tender.

container_notes.notes: Good container crop. 3-gallon pot minimum. Colorful varieties make attractive container plantings.

storage.fridge: 3-5 days -- don't wash until ready to use
storage.freezer: Blanch 2 minutes, freeze -- excellent for cooking
storage.notes: Chard wilts quickly. Store dry and unwashed.

recommended: Bright Lights (similar to Rainbow, very productive)
varieties.note: Rainbow and Bright Lights are identical in all but name -- extremely productive and visually stunning.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Legume rhizobial nitrogen fixation is textbook plant science. The mechanism is real; the specific pairing benefit is mechanistically plausible but often not pair-tested.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Pest-deterrent claim without matching established pattern. Default to traditional pending review.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Inter-plant competition for N, P, K is a real agronomic concept. Specific 'bad pair' claims often extrapolate beyond what research has shown.

start_method.notes: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost. Or start indoors 4 weeks before and transplant -- chard handles transplanting well.

rotation.avoid_after: Beetroot, spinach -- share leaf miner, Cercospora leaf spot
rotation.note: Rotate to a different bed each season to prevent disease and pest buildup.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small seed leaves pushing through the soil -- leafy greens germinate readily in cool, moist conditions.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged. Most leafy greens germinate best at 50-65°F -- they actually prefer cooler soil than tomatoes.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: True leaves developing, recognizable as the crop you planted.
growth_stages.user_action: Thin seedlings to the recommended spacing -- crowded leafy greens bolt faster and produce less. The thinnings are edible.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Leaves at a harvestable size, plant looking full and healthy.
growth_stages.user_action: Begin harvesting outer leaves now -- this encourages more growth from the center. Do not wait for the plant to be 'finished' before you start picking.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Ready to start harvesting outer leaves?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Leaves at good size, before any yellowing or flowering stem appears.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest cut-and-come-again -- remove outer leaves and let the center keep growing. For butterhead types, harvest the whole head when formed.

growth_stages.name: Bolting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: A central flower stalk shooting upward, leaves becoming smaller and more bitter.
growth_stages.user_action: Once bolting starts the flavor changes -- harvest everything immediately. Bolted leaves are still edible but more bitter. Remove the plant and either sow again or move on to a warm-season crop.

notifications.title: Time to sow your leafy greens
notifications.body: Leafy greens love cool weather and can go in the ground 4-6 weeks before your last frost. Sow directly into prepared soil or start indoors for transplanting. They are some of the first crops of the year -- enjoy the early start.

notifications.title: Your greens should be ready to start picking
notifications.body: Begin harvesting outer leaves now even if the plant seems small. Regular picking encourages more growth. Do not wait for the plant to be 'done' -- leafy greens are a harvest-as-you-go crop.

notifications.title: Heat incoming -- watch your greens for bolting
notifications.body: Hot weather triggers leafy greens to bolt -- sending up a flower stalk and turning bitter. Harvest everything you can now before the heat arrives. Consider sowing again in late summer for a fall crop.

notifications.title: Time to sow your fall leafy greens
notifications.body: Eight weeks before first frost is the window for a second sowing of leafy greens. A fall crop often outperforms spring -- the cooling temperatures mean slower bolting and sweeter flavor. Kale especially improves after a light frost.

notifications.title: How are your greens looking?
notifications.body: Leafy greens can bolt quickly in warm weather. A quick check every few days helps you catch the right harvest moment and spot any bolting before it is too late.

weather_triggers.title: Heat alert -- harvest your greens now
weather_triggers.body: Hot weather is the enemy of leafy greens. They bolt quickly and flavor turns bitter fast. Harvest as much as you can before the heat arrives. Shade cloth can buy you another week in marginal temperatures.

weather_triggers.title: Unexpected frost -- protect young greens
weather_triggers.body: Most leafy greens handle light frost well once established, but young seedlings need protection. Cover with fleece tonight if frost is forecast.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- watch for downy mildew
weather_triggers.body: Humid conditions encourage downy mildew on leafy greens. Ensure good airflow between plants and avoid watering late in the day. Pick regularly to keep the plant open.

germination.text: Leafy greens are some of the easiest crops to germinate -- cool, moist soil is all they need. Sow more thickly than you think you need and thin later.
The thinnings from leafy greens are completely edible -- use them as microgreens in salads. Thinning is harvesting.

seedling.text: Thin to the recommended spacing even though it feels wasteful. Crowded leafy greens bolt faster, get less airflow, and produce smaller leaves.
A light mulch around seedlings keeps moisture in and suppresses weeds -- both important for leafy greens which need consistent moisture.

established.text: Start harvesting outer leaves as soon as they reach a useful size -- this is how leafy greens work. The center keeps producing new growth as you remove the outer leaves.
Water consistently. Irregular watering is a major trigger for bolting in many leafy greens, especially lettuce and spinach.

harvest.text: Always harvest in the morning when leaves are full of water and at their crispest. Refrigerate immediately in a damp bag.
Leave at least half the plant intact when harvesting cut-and-come-again crops. Taking too much at once sets the plant back.

bolting.text: Once you see a flower stalk, harvest everything immediately. The leaves are still edible but will become more bitter every day.
Bolted leafy greens are not a failure -- it is the plant completing its lifecycle. A fall sowing often outperforms spring because the weather is cooling rather than warming.

yield_expectations.per_plant: Continuous harvest for the whole season -- chard is one of the most productive leafy greens
yield_expectations.peak_production: A chard plant at full size gives generous harvests every 1-2 weeks all season
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Chard is more heat-tolerant than spinach or lettuce -- a good bridge crop for summer.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Most leafy greens actually handle light frost well once established -- it can even improve flavor. But young seedlings are more vulnerable. If the damage happened at the seedling stage, a late frost likely caught them.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Cover seedlings with fleece if frost threatens in the first few weeks. Established leafy greens generally recover from light frost on their own.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Slugs love leafy green seedlings, especially in wet conditions. Downy mildew affects plants in humid, overcrowded conditions. Flea beetles leave tiny holes in leaves -- especially on arugula and kale.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Thin seedlings properly to allow airflow. Protect from slugs in the first few weeks. Row cover helps with flea beetles on susceptible varieties.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too much water or bolting
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Leafy greens in waterlogged soil develop root rot quickly. More commonly, warmth and long days trigger bolting -- the plant sends up a flower stalk and the leaves become bitter. This is the plant completing its lifecycle, not a failure of care.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Bolting is largely about timing. Sow earlier in spring or switch to a fall sowing -- cooling temperatures signal the plant to keep producing leaves rather than flowering.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too little water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Irregular watering is a major bolting trigger in lettuce and spinach. A dry spell followed by heat pushes them to flower and seed rapidly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Keep moisture consistent -- mulching around leafy greens makes a real difference. Water in the morning so leaves dry during the day.

failure_diagnostics.label: Bolted too quickly
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Heat and long days cause most leafy greens to bolt -- this is the most common reason they fail. The plant is not dying, it is doing what it is designed to do. Once bolted the leaves become bitter and inedible quickly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: The fall sowing is almost always more successful than spring for leafy greens. Cooling temperatures give you longer, slower-bolting plants. Shade cloth can also extend the spring crop by a couple of weeks.

pests.name: Cabbage worm
pests.symptoms: Large irregular holes in leaves. Green caterpillars (1-1.5 inches) blending into foliage. White cabbage butterfly flying nearby is a warning sign.
pests.cause: Pieris rapae butterfly larvae. Lay eggs on leaf undersides.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick caterpillars and egg clusters. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray every 2 weeks. Row covers as barrier.
pests.prevention: Row covers from planting. White butterfly decoys (territorial behavior). Plant nasturtiums as trap crop.

pests.name: Cabbage aphid
pests.symptoms: Dense gray-green colonies on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl and pucker. Honeydew and sooty mold may follow.
pests.cause: Brevicoryne brassicae. Populations explode rapidly in cool weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Strong water blast. Insecticidal soap spray directly on colonies. Remove and compost heavily infested leaves.
pests.prevention: Avoid excess nitrogen. Encourage parasitic wasps with flowering herbs nearby.

pests.name: Flea beetle
pests.symptoms: Many tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings. Plants look peppered. Small shiny beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause: Multiple flea beetle species. Worst in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment: Row covers on seedlings. Diatomaceous earth. Kaolin clay spray.
pests.prevention: Delay planting. Use transplants. Interplant with aromatic herbs.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms: Plants wilt in hot weather despite watering. Stunted growth. Yellowing leaves. Roots are swollen, club-shaped, and deformed when dug up.
diseases.cause: Plasmodiophora brassicae soil pathogen. Survives in soil for up to 20 years. Thrives in acidic, wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure. Remove and destroy infected plants -- do not compost. Lime soil to raise pH to 7.0-7.2.
diseases.prevention: Minimum 7-year rotation away from brassicas in infected soil. Maintain soil pH above 6.5. Improve drainage.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms: Yellow patches on upper leaf surface with gray-purple fuzzy mold on undersides. Affects seedlings and mature plants.
diseases.cause: Peronospora brassicae fungus. Favored by cool moist conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Improve air circulation. Copper-based fungicide as preventive.
diseases.prevention: Avoid overhead watering. Space plants generously. Choose resistant varieties.

crops.harvest_ready: Pick leaves at 2-4 inches for mild flavor. Larger leaves are more peppery. Harvest whole plant before it bolts.

start_method.notes: Direct sow -- arugula bolts easily and prefers not to be transplanted.

container_notes.notes: Excellent container crop. Very shallow roots -- window boxes ideal.

rotation.avoid_after: Kale, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, turnip, kohlrabi -- share clubroot and downy mildew
rotation.note: Clubroot can persist 20 years -- in infected soil extend to 7-year rotation.

bolting.prevention: Plant in early spring or autumn. Provide shade. Keep well-watered. Harvest very frequently.
bolting.note: Arugula bolt is not the end -- flowers are edible and peppery. But leaves become very spicy once bolting begins.

storage.freezer: Not suitable for fresh eating -- blanch and freeze for cooking only
storage.notes: Arugula is very perishable. Eat fresh -- freezing destroys the peppery flavor.

varieties.note: Astro is the best all-round choice -- milder than wild types and significantly slower to bolt than standard arugula.

good.name: Nasturtiums
good.why: Trap crop for flea beetles that attack arugula

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines; UConn IPM 'Perimeter Trap Cropping for Cole Crops'). Nasturtiums are specifically named as a flea beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and USU Extension (Mohr et al.). Flea beetles have intermediate mobility, so the trap cropping protocol is a better fit here than for aphids. Note: WSU, USU, and UConn identify radishes or collards as the more heavily-documented trap crops for flea beetles on brassicas; nasturtiums are mentioned alongside but with less-specific protocol guidance.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small seed leaves pushing through the soil -- leafy greens germinate readily in cool, moist conditions.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged. Most leafy greens germinate best at 50-65°F -- they actually prefer cooler soil than tomatoes.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: True leaves developing, recognizable as the crop you planted.
growth_stages.user_action: Thin seedlings to the recommended spacing -- crowded leafy greens bolt faster and produce less. The thinnings are edible.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Leaves at a harvestable size, plant looking full and healthy.
growth_stages.user_action: Begin harvesting outer leaves now -- this encourages more growth from the center. Do not wait for the plant to be 'finished' before you start picking.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Ready to start harvesting outer leaves?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Leaves at good size, before any yellowing or flowering stem appears.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest cut-and-come-again -- remove outer leaves and let the center keep growing. For butterhead types, harvest the whole head when formed.

growth_stages.name: Bolting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: A central flower stalk shooting upward, leaves becoming smaller and more bitter.
growth_stages.user_action: Once bolting starts the flavor changes -- harvest everything immediately. Bolted leaves are still edible but more bitter. Remove the plant and either sow again or move on to a warm-season crop.

notifications.title: Time to sow your leafy greens
notifications.body: Leafy greens love cool weather and can go in the ground 4-6 weeks before your last frost. Sow directly into prepared soil or start indoors for transplanting. They are some of the first crops of the year -- enjoy the early start.

notifications.title: Your greens should be ready to start picking
notifications.body: Begin harvesting outer leaves now even if the plant seems small. Regular picking encourages more growth. Do not wait for the plant to be 'done' -- leafy greens are a harvest-as-you-go crop.

notifications.title: Heat incoming -- watch your greens for bolting
notifications.body: Hot weather triggers leafy greens to bolt -- sending up a flower stalk and turning bitter. Harvest everything you can now before the heat arrives. Consider sowing again in late summer for a fall crop.

notifications.title: Time to sow your fall leafy greens
notifications.body: Eight weeks before first frost is the window for a second sowing of leafy greens. A fall crop often outperforms spring -- the cooling temperatures mean slower bolting and sweeter flavor. Kale especially improves after a light frost.

notifications.title: How are your greens looking?
notifications.body: Leafy greens can bolt quickly in warm weather. A quick check every few days helps you catch the right harvest moment and spot any bolting before it is too late.

weather_triggers.title: Heat alert -- harvest your greens now
weather_triggers.body: Hot weather is the enemy of leafy greens. They bolt quickly and flavor turns bitter fast. Harvest as much as you can before the heat arrives. Shade cloth can buy you another week in marginal temperatures.

weather_triggers.title: Unexpected frost -- protect young greens
weather_triggers.body: Most leafy greens handle light frost well once established, but young seedlings need protection. Cover with fleece tonight if frost is forecast.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- watch for downy mildew
weather_triggers.body: Humid conditions encourage downy mildew on leafy greens. Ensure good airflow between plants and avoid watering late in the day. Pick regularly to keep the plant open.

germination.text: Leafy greens are some of the easiest crops to germinate -- cool, moist soil is all they need. Sow more thickly than you think you need and thin later.
The thinnings from leafy greens are completely edible -- use them as microgreens in salads. Thinning is harvesting.

seedling.text: Thin to the recommended spacing even though it feels wasteful. Crowded leafy greens bolt faster, get less airflow, and produce smaller leaves.
A light mulch around seedlings keeps moisture in and suppresses weeds -- both important for leafy greens which need consistent moisture.

established.text: Start harvesting outer leaves as soon as they reach a useful size -- this is how leafy greens work. The center keeps producing new growth as you remove the outer leaves.
Water consistently. Irregular watering is a major trigger for bolting in many leafy greens, especially lettuce and spinach.

harvest.text: Always harvest in the morning when leaves are full of water and at their crispest. Refrigerate immediately in a damp bag.
Leave at least half the plant intact when harvesting cut-and-come-again crops. Taking too much at once sets the plant back.

bolting.text: Once you see a flower stalk, harvest everything immediately. The leaves are still edible but will become more bitter every day.
Bolted leafy greens are not a failure -- it is the plant completing its lifecycle. A fall sowing often outperforms spring because the weather is cooling rather than warming.

yield_expectations.per_plant: Quick, fast crops -- 2-3 harvests before bolting in warmth
yield_expectations.peak_production: Arugula is best as a succession crop -- sow small amounts every 3 weeks for continuous supply
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Arugula is fast and rewarding. It can be ready in 21 days and goes brilliantly with almost everything.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Most leafy greens actually handle light frost well once established -- it can even improve flavor. But young seedlings are more vulnerable. If the damage happened at the seedling stage, a late frost likely caught them.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Cover seedlings with fleece if frost threatens in the first few weeks. Established leafy greens generally recover from light frost on their own.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Slugs love leafy green seedlings, especially in wet conditions. Downy mildew affects plants in humid, overcrowded conditions. Flea beetles leave tiny holes in leaves -- especially on arugula and kale.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Thin seedlings properly to allow airflow. Protect from slugs in the first few weeks. Row cover helps with flea beetles on susceptible varieties.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too much water or bolting
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Leafy greens in waterlogged soil develop root rot quickly. More commonly, warmth and long days trigger bolting -- the plant sends up a flower stalk and the leaves become bitter. This is the plant completing its lifecycle, not a failure of care.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Bolting is largely about timing. Sow earlier in spring or switch to a fall sowing -- cooling temperatures signal the plant to keep producing leaves rather than flowering.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too little water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Irregular watering is a major bolting trigger in lettuce and spinach. A dry spell followed by heat pushes them to flower and seed rapidly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Keep moisture consistent -- mulching around leafy greens makes a real difference. Water in the morning so leaves dry during the day.

failure_diagnostics.label: Bolted too quickly
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Heat and long days cause most leafy greens to bolt -- this is the most common reason they fail. The plant is not dying, it is doing what it is designed to do. Once bolted the leaves become bitter and inedible quickly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: The fall sowing is almost always more successful than spring for leafy greens. Cooling temperatures give you longer, slower-bolting plants. Shade cloth can also extend the spring crop by a couple of weeks.

fertilizer.notify_message: Time to feed your collard greens

succession.tip: Sow every 4 weeks from spring through midsummer. Collards are more heat-tolerant than most brassicas and can be harvested as cut-and-come-again from the lower leaves. A summer sowing started 8-10 weeks before first frost will produce the best harvest -- collards genuinely improve in flavor after light frost. Start the autumn batch earlier than you think you need to.

good.name: Nasturtiums
good.why: Trap crop for aphids and caterpillars

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines; UConn IPM). Nasturtiums are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and USU Extension. Protocol caveats: UConn IPM notes that trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents.' Caterpillar deterrence (cabbage looper, imported cabbageworm) on brassicas is in secondary gardening literature but not specifically in the extension trap-cropping publications reviewed; the extension-recommended brassica trap crops for lepidopteran pests are collards (DBM) and radishes (flea beetles), not nasturtiums.

pests.name: Cabbage worm
pests.symptoms: Large irregular holes in leaves. Green caterpillars (1-1.5 inches) blending into foliage. White cabbage butterfly flying nearby is a warning sign.
pests.cause: Pieris rapae butterfly larvae. Lay eggs on leaf undersides.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick caterpillars and egg clusters. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray every 2 weeks. Row covers as barrier.
pests.prevention: Row covers from planting. White butterfly decoys (territorial behavior). Plant nasturtiums as trap crop.

pests.name: Cabbage aphid
pests.symptoms: Dense gray-green colonies on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl and pucker. Honeydew and sooty mold may follow.
pests.cause: Brevicoryne brassicae. Populations explode rapidly in cool weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Strong water blast. Insecticidal soap spray directly on colonies. Remove and compost heavily infested leaves.
pests.prevention: Avoid excess nitrogen. Encourage parasitic wasps with flowering herbs nearby.

pests.name: Flea beetle
pests.symptoms: Many tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings. Plants look peppered. Small shiny beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause: Multiple flea beetle species. Worst in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment: Row covers on seedlings. Diatomaceous earth. Kaolin clay spray.
pests.prevention: Delay planting. Use transplants. Interplant with aromatic herbs.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms: Plants wilt in hot weather despite watering. Stunted growth. Yellowing leaves. Roots are swollen, club-shaped, and deformed when dug up.
diseases.cause: Plasmodiophora brassicae soil pathogen. Survives in soil for up to 20 years. Thrives in acidic, wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure. Remove and destroy infected plants -- do not compost. Lime soil to raise pH to 7.0-7.2.
diseases.prevention: Minimum 7-year rotation away from brassicas in infected soil. Maintain soil pH above 6.5. Improve drainage.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms: Yellow patches on upper leaf surface with gray-purple fuzzy mold on undersides. Affects seedlings and mature plants.
diseases.cause: Peronospora brassicae fungus. Favored by cool moist conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Improve air circulation. Copper-based fungicide as preventive.
diseases.prevention: Avoid overhead watering. Space plants generously. Choose resistant varieties.

crops.harvest_ready: Pick outer leaves at 8-10 inches. Like kale, sweeten after frost.

start_method.notes: Direct sow 4-6 weeks before last frost. Or transplant -- collards are resilient.

rotation.avoid_after: Kale, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, turnip, kohlrabi -- share clubroot and downy mildew
rotation.note: Clubroot can persist 20 years -- in infected soil extend to 7-year rotation.

storage.freezer: Blanch 3 minutes, freeze -- excellent. Traditional Southern preservation.
storage.notes: Blanched frozen collards are nearly as good as fresh for cooking.

varieties.note: Georgia Southern is the traditional standard -- large leaves, mild flavor when cooked with pork.

container_notes.notes: Good container crop. 3-gallon minimum. Large plants -- one per pot.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small seed leaves pushing through the soil -- leafy greens germinate readily in cool, moist conditions.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged. Most leafy greens germinate best at 50-65°F -- they actually prefer cooler soil than tomatoes.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: True leaves developing, recognizable as the crop you planted.
growth_stages.user_action: Thin seedlings to the recommended spacing -- crowded leafy greens bolt faster and produce less. The thinnings are edible.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Leaves at a harvestable size, plant looking full and healthy.
growth_stages.user_action: Begin harvesting outer leaves now -- this encourages more growth from the center. Do not wait for the plant to be 'finished' before you start picking.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Ready to start harvesting outer leaves?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Leaves at good size, before any yellowing or flowering stem appears.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest cut-and-come-again -- remove outer leaves and let the center keep growing. For butterhead types, harvest the whole head when formed.

growth_stages.name: Bolting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: A central flower stalk shooting upward, leaves becoming smaller and more bitter.
growth_stages.user_action: Once bolting starts the flavor changes -- harvest everything immediately. Bolted leaves are still edible but more bitter. Remove the plant and either sow again or move on to a warm-season crop.

notifications.title: Time to sow your leafy greens
notifications.body: Leafy greens love cool weather and can go in the ground 4-6 weeks before your last frost. Sow directly into prepared soil or start indoors for transplanting. They are some of the first crops of the year -- enjoy the early start.

notifications.title: Your greens should be ready to start picking
notifications.body: Begin harvesting outer leaves now even if the plant seems small. Regular picking encourages more growth. Do not wait for the plant to be 'done' -- leafy greens are a harvest-as-you-go crop.

notifications.title: Heat incoming -- watch your greens for bolting
notifications.body: Hot weather triggers leafy greens to bolt -- sending up a flower stalk and turning bitter. Harvest everything you can now before the heat arrives. Consider sowing again in late summer for a fall crop.

notifications.title: Time to sow your fall leafy greens
notifications.body: Eight weeks before first frost is the window for a second sowing of leafy greens. A fall crop often outperforms spring -- the cooling temperatures mean slower bolting and sweeter flavor. Kale especially improves after a light frost.

notifications.title: How are your greens looking?
notifications.body: Leafy greens can bolt quickly in warm weather. A quick check every few days helps you catch the right harvest moment and spot any bolting before it is too late.

weather_triggers.title: Heat alert -- harvest your greens now
weather_triggers.body: Hot weather is the enemy of leafy greens. They bolt quickly and flavor turns bitter fast. Harvest as much as you can before the heat arrives. Shade cloth can buy you another week in marginal temperatures.

weather_triggers.title: Unexpected frost -- protect young greens
weather_triggers.body: Most leafy greens handle light frost well once established, but young seedlings need protection. Cover with fleece tonight if frost is forecast.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- watch for downy mildew
weather_triggers.body: Humid conditions encourage downy mildew on leafy greens. Ensure good airflow between plants and avoid watering late in the day. Pick regularly to keep the plant open.

germination.text: Leafy greens are some of the easiest crops to germinate -- cool, moist soil is all they need. Sow more thickly than you think you need and thin later.
The thinnings from leafy greens are completely edible -- use them as microgreens in salads. Thinning is harvesting.

seedling.text: Thin to the recommended spacing even though it feels wasteful. Crowded leafy greens bolt faster, get less airflow, and produce smaller leaves.
A light mulch around seedlings keeps moisture in and suppresses weeds -- both important for leafy greens which need consistent moisture.

established.text: Start harvesting outer leaves as soon as they reach a useful size -- this is how leafy greens work. The center keeps producing new growth as you remove the outer leaves.
Water consistently. Irregular watering is a major trigger for bolting in many leafy greens, especially lettuce and spinach.

harvest.text: Always harvest in the morning when leaves are full of water and at their crispest. Refrigerate immediately in a damp bag.
Leave at least half the plant intact when harvesting cut-and-come-again crops. Taking too much at once sets the plant back.

bolting.text: Once you see a flower stalk, harvest everything immediately. The leaves are still edible but will become more bitter every day.
Bolted leafy greens are not a failure -- it is the plant completing its lifecycle. A fall sowing often outperforms spring because the weather is cooling rather than warming.

yield_expectations.per_plant: Long-season crop -- one plant can feed a family for months
yield_expectations.peak_production: Collards are productive and heat-tolerant compared to most leafy greens
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Collards are more forgiving than most leafy greens. They handle both heat and frost better than spinach or lettuce.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Most leafy greens actually handle light frost well once established -- it can even improve flavor. But young seedlings are more vulnerable. If the damage happened at the seedling stage, a late frost likely caught them.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Cover seedlings with fleece if frost threatens in the first few weeks. Established leafy greens generally recover from light frost on their own.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Slugs love leafy green seedlings, especially in wet conditions. Downy mildew affects plants in humid, overcrowded conditions. Flea beetles leave tiny holes in leaves -- especially on arugula and kale.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Thin seedlings properly to allow airflow. Protect from slugs in the first few weeks. Row cover helps with flea beetles on susceptible varieties.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too much water or bolting
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Leafy greens in waterlogged soil develop root rot quickly. More commonly, warmth and long days trigger bolting -- the plant sends up a flower stalk and the leaves become bitter. This is the plant completing its lifecycle, not a failure of care.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Bolting is largely about timing. Sow earlier in spring or switch to a fall sowing -- cooling temperatures signal the plant to keep producing leaves rather than flowering.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too little water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Irregular watering is a major bolting trigger in lettuce and spinach. A dry spell followed by heat pushes them to flower and seed rapidly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Keep moisture consistent -- mulching around leafy greens makes a real difference. Water in the morning so leaves dry during the day.

failure_diagnostics.label: Bolted too quickly
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Heat and long days cause most leafy greens to bolt -- this is the most common reason they fail. The plant is not dying, it is doing what it is designed to do. Once bolted the leaves become bitter and inedible quickly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: The fall sowing is almost always more successful than spring for leafy greens. Cooling temperatures give you longer, slower-bolting plants. Shade cloth can also extend the spring crop by a couple of weeks.

crops.name: Bok Choy
crops.description: Fast, productive, and delicious stir-fried or in soups. Baby bok choy can be harvested whole at 30 days or left to mature as full heads. Cool-season crop that tolerates light frost.
