pests.name: Cabbage worm
pests.symptoms: Large irregular holes in leaves. Green caterpillars (1-1.5 inches) blending into foliage. White cabbage butterfly flying nearby is a warning sign.
pests.cause: Pieris rapae butterfly larvae. Lay eggs on leaf undersides.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick caterpillars and egg clusters. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray every 2 weeks. Row covers as barrier.
pests.prevention: Row covers from planting. White butterfly decoys (territorial behavior). Plant nasturtiums as trap crop.

pests.name: Cabbage aphid
pests.symptoms: Dense gray-green colonies on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl and pucker. Honeydew and sooty mold may follow.
pests.cause: Brevicoryne brassicae. Populations explode rapidly in cool weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Strong water blast. Insecticidal soap spray directly on colonies. Remove and compost heavily infested leaves.
pests.prevention: Avoid excess nitrogen. Encourage parasitic wasps with flowering herbs nearby.

pests.name: Flea beetle
pests.symptoms: Many tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings. Plants look peppered. Small shiny beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause: Multiple flea beetle species. Worst in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment: Row covers on seedlings. Diatomaceous earth. Kaolin clay spray.
pests.prevention: Delay planting. Use transplants. Interplant with aromatic herbs.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms: Plants wilt in hot weather despite watering. Stunted growth. Yellowing leaves. Roots are swollen, club-shaped, and deformed when dug up.
diseases.cause: Plasmodiophora brassicae soil pathogen. Survives in soil for up to 20 years. Thrives in acidic, wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure. Remove and destroy infected plants -- do not compost. Lime soil to raise pH to 7.0-7.2.
diseases.prevention: Minimum 7-year rotation away from brassicas in infected soil. Maintain soil pH above 6.5. Improve drainage.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms: Yellow patches on upper leaf surface with gray-purple fuzzy mold on undersides. Affects seedlings and mature plants.
diseases.cause: Peronospora brassicae fungus. Favored by cool moist conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Improve air circulation. Copper-based fungicide as preventive.
diseases.prevention: Avoid overhead watering. Space plants generously. Choose resistant varieties.

watering.frequency: Every 3-4 days -- consistent moisture prevents loose curds

crops.harvest_ready: Pick when head is firm, white, and compact -- typically 6-8 inches across. Any yellowing or separation of curds means over-mature.

start_method.notes: Start 6-8 weeks before last frost. Harden off carefully -- cauliflower is sensitive to temperature swings which can cause buttoning (tiny premature heads).

rotation.avoid_after: Kale, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, turnip, kohlrabi -- share clubroot and downy mildew
rotation.note: Clubroot can persist 20 years -- in infected soil extend to 7-year rotation.

bolting.triggers: Temperature swings, especially cold snaps during head formation
bolting.prevention: Consistent temperatures are key. Avoid transplanting when cold snaps are forecast. Keep well watered.
bolting.note: Buttoning (tiny premature heads) is a form of bolting triggered by cold stress on young plants.

storage.freezer: Cut to florets, blanch 3 minutes, freeze -- good
storage.notes: Wrap head loosely -- tight wrapping traps ethylene gas and speeds deterioration.

recommended: Graffiti (vivid purple, retains color when cooked)
varieties.note: Colored varieties (Cheddar, Graffiti) are more heat-tolerant than white types and hold color well.

crops.soil_prep: Firm, fertile, consistent soil is critical -- cauliflower is very sensitive to nutrient fluctuation. Lime if pH below 6.5. Follow legumes in rotation. Do not over-manure -- excess nitrogen causes loose, leafy curds.

container_notes.notes: Possible but challenging -- cauliflower is large and sensitive. 5-gallon minimum, one plant per pot.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Round seed leaves pushing up cleanly. Brassicas germinate readily in cool, moist conditions.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep soil consistently moist at 60-70°F. Brassicas do not need heat -- they prefer cool germination.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: True leaves developing -- slightly waxy and blue-green in color.
growth_stages.user_action: Watch for damping off -- good airflow and not overwatering prevents it. Thin to one plant per cell.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Sturdy plants with multiple leaf sets, ready to go outside.
growth_stages.user_action: Harden off well before transplanting. Net immediately after planting to protect from cabbage white butterflies -- do not delay on this.

growth_stages.name: Head Forming
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Central head beginning to form. On broccoli, a tight green dome. On cauliflower, a white curd appearing in the center.
growth_stages.user_action: For cauliflower, tie the outer leaves over the developing curd to blanch it and keep it white. Do this as soon as the curd is visible.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Broccoli: tight green head before any yellow flowers open. Cauliflower: firm white curd at full size. Cabbage: firm, dense head that does not give when squeezed.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest broccoli with a long stem cut -- side shoots will continue producing for weeks. Cauliflower and cabbage are once-and-done harvests.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Harvest time -- how did it look?

notifications.title: Time to start your brassicas indoors
notifications.body: Broccoli, cauliflower, and cabbage need 6-8 weeks indoors before transplanting. Start now -- they grow slowly at first but reward the patience. Cool temperatures suit them perfectly.

notifications.title: Brassicas outside -- net them immediately
notifications.body: Cabbage white butterflies lay eggs on brassica leaves within hours of planting. Cover with fine mesh netting immediately after transplanting -- before you do anything else. Caterpillar damage can devastate an unprotected crop.

notifications.title: Cauliflower curd forming -- time to blanch
notifications.body: Tie a few outer leaves loosely over the developing curd now to protect it from light. This keeps the cauliflower white and tender. Check every few days -- once the curd is visible it develops quickly.

notifications.title: Check your broccoli heads
notifications.body: Broccoli heads that are ready to harvest look like tight green domes with no yellow showing. Once you see any flower buds opening it is past its best. Cut with a long stem and watch for side shoots to develop.

notifications.title: Start a fall brassica crop
notifications.body: Brassicas do well as a fall crop and often taste better -- frost sweetens cabbage and broccoli. Start seeds now for a crop that matures in the cooler autumn months.

notifications.title: How are your brassicas getting on?
notifications.body: Check under the netting for caterpillar damage -- they can strip a plant surprisingly fast. Also look at the developing head for any signs of bolting or discoloration.

weather_triggers.title: Heat stress -- brassicas may bolt
weather_triggers.body: Sustained high temperatures cause broccoli and cauliflower to bolt -- heads open into flowers before they are full size. Harvest anything that looks close to ready before the heat peaks.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- watch for clubroot and downy mildew
weather_triggers.body: Humid conditions favor several brassica diseases. Ensure good spacing and airflow. Check leaves for yellowing or powdery patches and remove affected material promptly.

weather_triggers.title: Late frost -- protect young brassicas
weather_triggers.body: Established brassicas handle frost well, but young transplants need protection for the first few weeks. Cover with fleece tonight.

germination.text: Brassicas are reliable germinators in cool conditions -- 60-70F is ideal. They do not need heat mats.
Sow into cells or modules rather than trays -- brassicas develop long tap roots and resent root disturbance.

seedling.text: Grow brassica seedlings in the coolest, brightest spot you have. Warmth makes them soft and leggy.
Feed with a dilute liquid feed once the first true leaves appear. Brassicas are hungry plants from the start.

established.text: Net immediately after transplanting. Cabbage white butterflies find brassicas within hours and lay clusters of yellow eggs on leaf undersides. Check the netting is secure all around -- one gap and caterpillars will find it.

Cauliflower is the fussiest of the head brassicas. Steady moisture and consistent feeding through the whole season prevent the small, loose, button-shaped curds ("buttoning") that come from any check in growth.

head_forming.text: As soon as the curd is visible at the center of the plant -- about the size of an egg -- tie a few of the outer leaves loosely over it with twine or a clothes pin. This is called blanching: it shields the curd from sunlight, which keeps it white and prevents the bitter, off-flavor that develops in light-exposed curds.

Self-blanching varieties wrap their own leaves over the curd; colored varieties (purple, orange, green Romanesco) do not need blanching at all and develop their color from light. Check the seed packet to know which you are growing.

harvest.text: Cut the head when the curd reaches full size for the variety -- usually 6 to 8 inches across -- and is still tight and dense. Once the curd starts to separate into visible florets ("ricing"), it is past its best for eating fresh, though still good cooked.
Cauliflower is a once-and-done harvest -- the plant produces one main curd and is finished. Most varieties do not produce a meaningful second flush; pull the plant and replant the bed.

yield_expectations.per_plant: One head per plant
yield_expectations.peak_production: Cauliflower is a once-and-done crop -- plan the timing carefully
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Cauliflower is the most challenging of the brassicas -- temperature-sensitive and unforgiving of irregular care. Getting a good head is an achievement.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Established brassicas handle frost well -- it actually sweetens them. But young transplants in their first 2-3 weeks are more vulnerable. A hard freeze can damage or kill recently transplanted seedlings.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Cover new transplants with fleece for the first 2-3 weeks after planting if frost is possible. Once established they are among the hardiest vegetables you can grow.

failure_diagnostics.label: Caterpillars or pests
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cabbage white butterflies lay eggs on brassica leaves and the caterpillars can strip a plant in days. This is by far the most common reason brassicas fail. If you did not net, this is almost certainly what happened.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Net immediately after transplanting -- before you do anything else. Fine mesh netting secured all the way around is the single most important thing you can do for brassicas. Check netting for gaps weekly.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too much water or clubroot
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Brassicas in waterlogged soil develop root problems. Clubroot -- a soil-borne disease -- causes swollen, distorted roots and wilting. Once present in soil it persists for many years.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Improve drainage before planting. If clubroot is suspected, rotate brassicas to a new bed and do not grow them in the affected soil for 4-5 years. Liming to raise soil pH above 7 discourages clubroot.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too little water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Brassicas need consistent moisture to develop good heads. Drought stress causes premature flowering in broccoli and cauliflower, and split heads in cabbage.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently and mulch around plants to retain moisture. A dry spell during head formation is the most damaging period.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor head development
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cauliflower is the most demanding -- it needs consistent temperatures and care to form a good curd. Broccoli heads opening into yellow flowers usually means the temperature swung too warm. Both benefit from 6+ hours of sun.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Cauliflower in particular needs a consistent, cool growing environment. Autumn sowings often perform better than spring ones in warmer zones. Shade cloth can help in warm spells.

crops.name: Cabbage
crops.description: Solid, reliable and stores well -- whole cabbages last months in a cool cellar. Two crops per year in most zones. More forgiving than cauliflower about temperature swings.

succession.tip: Sow a spring crop and a late-summer crop. Cabbage takes too long for rapid succession -- 70-90 days from transplant -- so it's a two-crop seasonal approach rather than staggered sowings. Spring cabbage matures before summer heat; late-summer planting (started July or August depending on your zone) matures into autumn and can be stored in a cool cellar for weeks. Pick between early varieties (smaller heads, faster) for spring and storage types for the autumn batch.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension 2022 and 2025 Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetable Crops; UConn IPM 'Perimeter Trap Cropping for Cole Crops'). Nasturtiums specifically are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and Utah State University Extension (Mohr et al., 'Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting'). Protocol caveat: UConn IPM explicitly notes trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents' -- so the aphid application here has a protocol-mismatch concern even though the companion is extension-named. The Cornell-IPM-specific attribution in earlier catalog reason text was not located in Cornell's published IPM material; actual backing is WSU/USU/UConn.

pests.name: Cabbage worm
pests.symptoms: Large irregular holes in leaves. Green caterpillars (1-1.5 inches) blending into foliage. White cabbage butterfly flying nearby is a warning sign.
pests.cause: Pieris rapae butterfly larvae. Lay eggs on leaf undersides.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick caterpillars and egg clusters. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray every 2 weeks. Row covers as barrier.
pests.prevention: Row covers from planting. White butterfly decoys (territorial behavior). Plant nasturtiums as trap crop.

pests.name: Cabbage aphid
pests.symptoms: Dense gray-green colonies on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl and pucker. Honeydew and sooty mold may follow.
pests.cause: Brevicoryne brassicae. Populations explode rapidly in cool weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Strong water blast. Insecticidal soap spray directly on colonies. Remove and compost heavily infested leaves.
pests.prevention: Avoid excess nitrogen. Encourage parasitic wasps with flowering herbs nearby.

pests.name: Flea beetle
pests.symptoms: Many tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings. Plants look peppered. Small shiny beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause: Multiple flea beetle species. Worst in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment: Row covers on seedlings. Diatomaceous earth. Kaolin clay spray.
pests.prevention: Delay planting. Use transplants. Interplant with aromatic herbs.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms: Plants wilt in hot weather despite watering. Stunted growth. Yellowing leaves. Roots are swollen, club-shaped, and deformed when dug up.
diseases.cause: Plasmodiophora brassicae soil pathogen. Survives in soil for up to 20 years. Thrives in acidic, wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure. Remove and destroy infected plants -- do not compost. Lime soil to raise pH to 7.0-7.2.
diseases.prevention: Minimum 7-year rotation away from brassicas in infected soil. Maintain soil pH above 6.5. Improve drainage.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms: Yellow patches on upper leaf surface with gray-purple fuzzy mold on undersides. Affects seedlings and mature plants.
diseases.cause: Peronospora brassicae fungus. Favored by cool moist conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Improve air circulation. Copper-based fungicide as preventive.
diseases.prevention: Avoid overhead watering. Space plants generously. Choose resistant varieties.

crops.harvest_ready: Firm, solid head that doesn't give when squeezed. Heads will split if left too long -- harvest promptly when solid.

start_method.notes: Start 6-8 weeks before last frost. Harden off over 7-10 days.

rotation.avoid_after: Kale, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, turnip, kohlrabi -- share clubroot and downy mildew
rotation.note: Clubroot can persist 20 years -- in infected soil extend to 7-year rotation.

storage.freezer: Blanch and freeze for cooking -- raw freezing not recommended
storage.notes: Cabbage is one of the best-keeping vegetables. Outer leaves protect inner head.

varieties.note: January King is exceptional for winter harvesting -- extremely frost-hardy with beautiful purple-green coloring.

container_notes.notes: Can be grown in containers. 5-gallon minimum. Compact varieties like Gonzales work best.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Round seed leaves pushing up cleanly. Brassicas germinate readily in cool, moist conditions.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep soil consistently moist at 60-70°F. Brassicas do not need heat -- they prefer cool germination.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: True leaves developing -- slightly waxy and blue-green in color.
growth_stages.user_action: Watch for damping off -- good airflow and not overwatering prevents it. Thin to one plant per cell.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Sturdy plants with multiple leaf sets, ready to go outside.
growth_stages.user_action: Harden off well before transplanting. Net immediately after planting to protect from cabbage white butterflies -- do not delay on this.

growth_stages.name: Head Forming
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Central head beginning to form. On broccoli, a tight green dome. On cauliflower, a white curd appearing in the center.
growth_stages.user_action: For cauliflower, tie the outer leaves over the developing curd to blanch it and keep it white. Do this as soon as the curd is visible.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Broccoli: tight green head before any yellow flowers open. Cauliflower: firm white curd at full size. Cabbage: firm, dense head that does not give when squeezed.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest broccoli with a long stem cut -- side shoots will continue producing for weeks. Cauliflower and cabbage are once-and-done harvests.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Harvest time -- how did it look?

notifications.title: Time to start your brassicas indoors
notifications.body: Broccoli, cauliflower, and cabbage need 6-8 weeks indoors before transplanting. Start now -- they grow slowly at first but reward the patience. Cool temperatures suit them perfectly.

notifications.title: Brassicas outside -- net them immediately
notifications.body: Cabbage white butterflies lay eggs on brassica leaves within hours of planting. Cover with fine mesh netting immediately after transplanting -- before you do anything else. Caterpillar damage can devastate an unprotected crop.

notifications.title: Cauliflower curd forming -- time to blanch
notifications.body: Tie a few outer leaves loosely over the developing curd now to protect it from light. This keeps the cauliflower white and tender. Check every few days -- once the curd is visible it develops quickly.

notifications.title: Check your broccoli heads
notifications.body: Broccoli heads that are ready to harvest look like tight green domes with no yellow showing. Once you see any flower buds opening it is past its best. Cut with a long stem and watch for side shoots to develop.

notifications.title: Start a fall brassica crop
notifications.body: Brassicas do well as a fall crop and often taste better -- frost sweetens cabbage and broccoli. Start seeds now for a crop that matures in the cooler autumn months.

notifications.title: How are your brassicas getting on?
notifications.body: Check under the netting for caterpillar damage -- they can strip a plant surprisingly fast. Also look at the developing head for any signs of bolting or discoloration.

weather_triggers.title: Heat stress -- brassicas may bolt
weather_triggers.body: Sustained high temperatures cause broccoli and cauliflower to bolt -- heads open into flowers before they are full size. Harvest anything that looks close to ready before the heat peaks.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- watch for clubroot and downy mildew
weather_triggers.body: Humid conditions favor several brassica diseases. Ensure good spacing and airflow. Check leaves for yellowing or powdery patches and remove affected material promptly.

weather_triggers.title: Late frost -- protect young brassicas
weather_triggers.body: Established brassicas handle frost well, but young transplants need protection for the first few weeks. Cover with fleece tonight.

germination.text: Brassicas are reliable germinators in cool conditions -- 60-70F is ideal. They do not need heat mats.
Sow into cells or modules rather than trays -- brassicas develop long tap roots and resent root disturbance.

seedling.text: Grow brassica seedlings in the coolest, brightest spot you have. Warmth makes them soft and leggy.
Feed with a dilute liquid feed once the first true leaves appear. Brassicas are hungry plants from the start.

established.text: Net immediately after transplanting. Cabbage white butterflies find brassicas within hours and lay clusters of yellow eggs on leaf undersides. Check the netting is secure all around -- one gap and caterpillars will find it.
Cabbage is a heavy feeder. Side-dress with compost or a balanced fertilizer once heads start to form -- nitrogen drives leaf production through head formation.

head_forming.text: The outer leaves of cabbage form a loose rosette first; the head begins to form when the inner leaves start cupping inward and overlapping. From that point, leaves continue to wrap tightly until the head is firm.
Even moisture during head formation prevents splitting later. Sudden water after a dry spell -- including heavy rain near maturity -- causes mature heads to crack open.

harvest.text: Cabbage is ready when the head feels firm and dense to a gentle squeeze, and does not give. Cut the head off at the base with a sharp knife, leaving the lower leaves and root in the soil.

If you leave the stub in place after cutting, several small loose secondary heads sometimes form on the cut stem -- worth picking for slaws even though they will not match the main head. The single best harvest window is when the head is firm; leave it too long and it splits.

yield_expectations.per_plant: One head per plant, 2-4 lbs for most varieties
yield_expectations.peak_production: Cabbage stores well in the ground -- can be left until needed
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Cabbage is slower and more patient than most crops. The payoff is a vegetable that stores in the ground until you are ready for it.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Established brassicas handle frost well -- it actually sweetens them. But young transplants in their first 2-3 weeks are more vulnerable. A hard freeze can damage or kill recently transplanted seedlings.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Cover new transplants with fleece for the first 2-3 weeks after planting if frost is possible. Once established they are among the hardiest vegetables you can grow.

failure_diagnostics.label: Caterpillars or pests
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cabbage white butterflies lay eggs on brassica leaves and the caterpillars can strip a plant in days. This is by far the most common reason brassicas fail. If you did not net, this is almost certainly what happened.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Net immediately after transplanting -- before you do anything else. Fine mesh netting secured all the way around is the single most important thing you can do for brassicas. Check netting for gaps weekly.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too much water or clubroot
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Brassicas in waterlogged soil develop root problems. Clubroot -- a soil-borne disease -- causes swollen, distorted roots and wilting. Once present in soil it persists for many years.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Improve drainage before planting. If clubroot is suspected, rotate brassicas to a new bed and do not grow them in the affected soil for 4-5 years. Liming to raise soil pH above 7 discourages clubroot.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too little water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Brassicas need consistent moisture to develop good heads. Drought stress causes premature flowering in broccoli and cauliflower, and split heads in cabbage.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently and mulch around plants to retain moisture. A dry spell during head formation is the most damaging period.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor head development
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cauliflower is the most demanding -- it needs consistent temperatures and care to form a good curd. Broccoli heads opening into yellow flowers usually means the temperature swung too warm. Both benefit from 6+ hours of sun.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Cauliflower in particular needs a consistent, cool growing environment. Autumn sowings often perform better than spring ones in warmer zones. Shade cloth can help in warm spells.

fertilizer.timing: switch to high-potassium 6 weeks before harvest
fertilizer.notes: Feed nitrogen monthly until bulbs start to form, then switch to high-potassium feed to encourage bulb sizing.

succession.reason: Single harvest crop with a long growing season. Not practical for succession.

pests.name: Onion fly
pests.symptoms: Plants wilt and die. White maggots at the base of bulb eating roots and inner leaves.
pests.cause: Delia antiqua fly. Lays eggs near onion seedlings in spring.
pests.organic_treatment: Insect mesh over bed. Remove and destroy affected plants.
pests.prevention: Grow under fine mesh. Rotate alliums every 3 years. Interplant with carrots -- mutual pest confusion.

pests.name: Thrips
pests.symptoms: Silver streaking and speckling on leaves. Stunted growth. Tiny yellow-brown insects visible.
pests.cause: Thrips tabaci. Worse in hot dry summers.
pests.organic_treatment: Neem oil spray. Insecticidal soap.
pests.prevention: Reflective mulch. Adequate watering in dry weather.

diseases.name: White rot
diseases.symptoms: Plants yellow and die. White fluffy growth at base with small black seed-like sclerotia. Roots and base rotted.
diseases.cause: Sclerotium cepivorum soil fungus. Persists in soil for 20+ years.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure. Remove all plant material. Do not replant alliums in infected soil.
diseases.prevention: Strict crop rotation. Buy allium seed sets from reputable sources.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms: Gray-purple fuzzy growth on leaves. Leaves yellow and collapse. Worst in wet cool springs.
diseases.cause: Peronospora destructor fungus.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Copper-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention: Avoid overhead watering. Space plants for airflow. Rotate crops.

watering.amount: 1 inch per week -- stop watering when tops fall over

crops.harvest_ready: Tops fall over naturally -- this is the signal. Leave for 2 weeks then harvest. Skin should be papery and dry.

start_method.notes: Easiest from sets (small bulbs). From seed, start 10-12 weeks indoors before transplanting. From transplants, harden off over 5 days.

container_notes.notes: Possible in containers, 6+ inches deep. Better in raised beds.

rotation.avoid_after: Onions, garlic, leeks, shallots -- share white rot and onion fly
rotation.note: White rot can persist indefinitely in soil -- strict rotation is essential once present.

storage.room_temp: Months in cool dry place with good airflow -- ideal 35-50°F
storage.freezer: Chop and freeze raw -- excellent for cooking
storage.notes: Store in mesh bags or hang in braids. Never store with potatoes -- mutual spoilage.

varieties.note: Patterson is the best storage onion -- keeps 9-12 months. Walla Walla is sweetest but stores only 1-2 months.

thinning.method: Gently pull or snip. Thinnings make excellent spring onions.
thinning.tip: Onion spacing directly determines bulb size -- 4 inches produces medium bulbs, 6 inches produces large bulbs.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Cloves, sets, or seeds in the ground. No visible growth yet.
growth_stages.user_action: Plant garlic and onion sets pointed end up, just below the surface. For leeks, sow seeds in modules and transplant as pencil-thin seedlings.

growth_stages.name: Early Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Green shoots pushing up from sets or cloves. Slow growth initially -- alliums establish roots first.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep weed-free -- alliums are poor competitors with weeds, especially in early growth.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Strong upright leaves, healthy green color. Onions and garlic developing the bulb underground.
growth_stages.user_action: Stop feeding garlic and onions with nitrogen once the bulb starts forming -- it encourages leafy growth at the expense of the bulb.

growth_stages.name: Bulb Forming
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: For garlic: scapes curling upward on hardneck varieties. For onions: leaves beginning to yellow from the tips and fall over.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest garlic scapes when curled -- they are delicious and removing them redirects energy to the bulb. For onions, bending down any remaining upright leaves once half have fallen speeds final ripening.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Seeing scapes on garlic, or leaves beginning to fall?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Garlic: leaves 2/3 brown. Onions: all leaves yellow and fallen. Leeks: any size -- harvest young for mild flavor.
growth_stages.user_action: Lift carefully with a fork to avoid bruising. Cure in a warm, airy spot for 2-4 weeks before storing -- this is essential for long storage life.

growth_stages.name: Curing and Storage
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Skin papery and tight, neck dry and closed.
growth_stages.user_action: Hang or lay in a single layer in good airflow, out of direct rain, for 2-4 weeks. Garlic and onions not properly cured will not store well.

notifications.title: Time to plant your garlic
notifications.body: Garlic is planted in autumn and overwinters in the ground -- it needs a cold period to develop properly. Plant cloves now, pointed end up, 2 inches deep and 6 inches apart. You will not see much happen until spring, and that is exactly right.

notifications.title: Time to plant your onion sets
notifications.body: Onion sets can go in 3-4 weeks before last frost. Plant pointed end up with just the tip showing at the surface. They establish quickly and are more reliable than growing from seed.

notifications.title: Harvest your garlic scapes
notifications.body: Hardneck garlic sends up curled green shoots called scapes in early summer. Cut them off now -- they are delicious in stir fries and pestos, and removing them directs energy back into the bulb for a larger harvest.

notifications.title: Check your garlic for harvest readiness
notifications.body: When two thirds of the leaves have turned brown, your garlic is ready. Do not wait for all leaves to die -- the outer wrapper deteriorates. Lift carefully with a fork, do not pull by the stem, and handle gently to avoid bruising.

notifications.title: Cure your alliums properly -- it is worth it
notifications.body: Garlic and onions not properly cured will not store through winter. Hang or lay them in a single layer in a warm, airy space out of rain for 3-4 weeks. The necks should be completely dry before storage. This step makes the difference between 3-month storage and 6-month storage.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- watch for rust on your alliums
weather_triggers.body: Allium rust appears as orange powder on leaves in humid conditions. It weakens the plant but rarely kills it. Remove badly affected leaves and ensure good airflow. Rotate alliums to a different bed next year.

weather_triggers.title: Keep curing alliums dry
weather_triggers.body: Rain on curing garlic and onions undoes the drying process and encourages rot. Make sure they are under cover -- a shed, garage, or covered porch is ideal.

planting.text: Plant garlic in your best, most fertile bed. It is in the ground for 9 months -- give it good conditions from the start.
Save the largest cloves from each bulb for planting and eat the small ones. Larger cloves produce larger bulbs.

early_growth.text: Keep allium beds completely weed-free. Onions and garlic have poor, shallow root systems and are easily out-competed. Even small weeds reduce yields significantly.
No need to water garlic in autumn and winter -- rainfall is usually sufficient. Begin watering in spring if it is dry.

established.text: Stop feeding with nitrogen once bulbs start to form. High nitrogen at this stage produces soft, poorly-stored bulbs with thick necks.
Leeks can be earthed up as they grow to blanch the lower stem -- this gives you a longer white shaft and milder flavor.

bulb_forming.text: When onion leaves begin to yellow and fall over, stop watering. The plant is telling you it is finishing -- let it dry down naturally.
Do not bend onion tops manually until at least half the leaves have yellowed on their own. Bending them too early exposes the neck to disease.

harvest.text: Lift rather than pull. A garden fork under the bulb loosens the roots and prevents the stem tearing -- which exposes the bulb to rot during curing.
Harvest on a dry day and leave on top of the soil for a few hours before bringing in. The sun begins the drying process.

curing.text: Curing is the most important step most gardeners skip. 3-4 weeks in warm, airy conditions transforms a perishable vegetable into one that stores for 6-9 months.
Braid garlic and onions for storage if you have enough -- it looks beautiful and is functional. Store in a cool, dry, dark place.

yield_expectations.per_plant: One medium-large onion per set
yield_expectations.peak_production: Onions give a single harvest -- quantity comes from how many you plant
yield_expectations.first_year_note: A row of properly cured onions hanging in a shed will last through most of winter. Few things feel more satisfying.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Established alliums are among the hardiest vegetables and handle frost well. Garlic overwintering in the ground is designed for frost. Young onion seedlings are more vulnerable to late hard freezes.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Protect young onion sets if a hard freeze threatens in the first few weeks after planting. Established plants need no protection from ordinary frost.

failure_diagnostics.label: Allium rust or white rot
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Allium rust appears as orange powder on leaves in humid summers -- it weakens but rarely kills the plant. White rot is more serious: a soil-borne fungus that causes bulbs to rot at the base. Once white rot is in soil it persists for decades.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Rotate alliums to a new bed every year. White rot cannot be eliminated from infected soil -- grow alliums elsewhere if you see it. Rust is largely cosmetic -- harvest early and the bulbs are usually fine.

failure_diagnostics.label: Rotting bulbs
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Garlic and onion bulbs rot in waterlogged soil, especially during curing. Rain on curing alliums reverses the drying process and causes neck rot -- one of the most common storage failures.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Ensure excellent drainage. Cure garlic and onions under cover -- a shed or garage with good airflow. Even a few hours of rain on curing bulbs can significantly reduce storage life.

failure_diagnostics.label: Small bulbs
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Alliums that experience drought stress during bulb development produce small, tight bulbs. Irregular watering is a common cause of disappointing allium harvests.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently during bulb formation -- from spring until leaves begin to yellow. Stop watering completely once leaves start to die back naturally.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor bulb development
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Alliums need full sun for good bulb development. The bulbing trigger in onions and garlic is day length -- both need long days combined with warmth to form bulbs. In shade or under trees, they often produce only small, undeveloped bulbs.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant alliums in your sunniest, most open bed. Weed competition also significantly reduces yield -- keep allium beds completely weed-free from early spring.

fertilizer.notes: Light, consistent feeding produces tender green tops. Liquid feed every 3 weeks.
fertilizer.notify_message: Time to feed your spring onions

succession.tip: Sow every 2 weeks from early spring through summer. Spring onions mature in 60-70 days and are ready for a short window before they start to bulb and toughen. Frequent small sowings -- a short row every two weeks -- give you a steady supply of tender young onions through the season. They can also be grown between other crops as space-fillers, since their narrow profile doesn't compete.

pests.name: Onion fly
pests.symptoms: Plants wilt and die. White maggots at the base of bulb eating roots and inner leaves.
pests.cause: Delia antiqua fly. Lays eggs near onion seedlings in spring.
pests.organic_treatment: Insect mesh over bed. Remove and destroy affected plants.
pests.prevention: Grow under fine mesh. Rotate alliums every 3 years. Interplant with carrots -- mutual pest confusion.

pests.name: Thrips
pests.symptoms: Silver streaking and speckling on leaves. Stunted growth. Tiny yellow-brown insects visible.
pests.cause: Thrips tabaci. Worse in hot dry summers.
pests.organic_treatment: Neem oil spray. Insecticidal soap.
pests.prevention: Reflective mulch. Adequate watering in dry weather.

diseases.name: White rot
diseases.symptoms: Plants yellow and die. White fluffy growth at base with small black seed-like sclerotia. Roots and base rotted.
diseases.cause: Sclerotium cepivorum soil fungus. Persists in soil for 20+ years.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure. Remove all plant material. Do not replant alliums in infected soil.
diseases.prevention: Strict crop rotation. Buy allium seed sets from reputable sources.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms: Gray-purple fuzzy growth on leaves. Leaves yellow and collapse. Worst in wet cool springs.
diseases.cause: Peronospora destructor fungus.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Copper-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention: Avoid overhead watering. Space plants for airflow. Rotate crops.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Cloves, sets, or seeds in the ground. No visible growth yet.
growth_stages.user_action: Plant garlic and onion sets pointed end up, just below the surface. For leeks, sow seeds in modules and transplant as pencil-thin seedlings.

growth_stages.name: Early Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Green shoots pushing up from sets or cloves. Slow growth initially -- alliums establish roots first.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep weed-free -- alliums are poor competitors with weeds, especially in early growth.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Strong upright leaves, healthy green color. Onions and garlic developing the bulb underground.
growth_stages.user_action: Stop feeding garlic and onions with nitrogen once the bulb starts forming -- it encourages leafy growth at the expense of the bulb.

growth_stages.name: Bulb Forming
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: For garlic: scapes curling upward on hardneck varieties. For onions: leaves beginning to yellow from the tips and fall over.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest garlic scapes when curled -- they are delicious and removing them redirects energy to the bulb. For onions, bending down any remaining upright leaves once half have fallen speeds final ripening.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Seeing scapes on garlic, or leaves beginning to fall?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Garlic: leaves 2/3 brown. Onions: all leaves yellow and fallen. Leeks: any size -- harvest young for mild flavor.
growth_stages.user_action: Lift carefully with a fork to avoid bruising. Cure in a warm, airy spot for 2-4 weeks before storing -- this is essential for long storage life.

growth_stages.name: Curing and Storage
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Skin papery and tight, neck dry and closed.
growth_stages.user_action: Hang or lay in a single layer in good airflow, out of direct rain, for 2-4 weeks. Garlic and onions not properly cured will not store well.

notifications.title: Time to plant your garlic
notifications.body: Garlic is planted in autumn and overwinters in the ground -- it needs a cold period to develop properly. Plant cloves now, pointed end up, 2 inches deep and 6 inches apart. You will not see much happen until spring, and that is exactly right.

notifications.title: Time to plant your onion sets
notifications.body: Onion sets can go in 3-4 weeks before last frost. Plant pointed end up with just the tip showing at the surface. They establish quickly and are more reliable than growing from seed.

notifications.title: Harvest your garlic scapes
notifications.body: Hardneck garlic sends up curled green shoots called scapes in early summer. Cut them off now -- they are delicious in stir fries and pestos, and removing them directs energy back into the bulb for a larger harvest.

notifications.title: Check your garlic for harvest readiness
notifications.body: When two thirds of the leaves have turned brown, your garlic is ready. Do not wait for all leaves to die -- the outer wrapper deteriorates. Lift carefully with a fork, do not pull by the stem, and handle gently to avoid bruising.

notifications.title: Cure your alliums properly -- it is worth it
notifications.body: Garlic and onions not properly cured will not store through winter. Hang or lay them in a single layer in a warm, airy space out of rain for 3-4 weeks. The necks should be completely dry before storage. This step makes the difference between 3-month storage and 6-month storage.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- watch for rust on your alliums
weather_triggers.body: Allium rust appears as orange powder on leaves in humid conditions. It weakens the plant but rarely kills it. Remove badly affected leaves and ensure good airflow. Rotate alliums to a different bed next year.

weather_triggers.title: Keep curing alliums dry
weather_triggers.body: Rain on curing garlic and onions undoes the drying process and encourages rot. Make sure they are under cover -- a shed, garage, or covered porch is ideal.

planting.text: Plant garlic in your best, most fertile bed. It is in the ground for 9 months -- give it good conditions from the start.
Save the largest cloves from each bulb for planting and eat the small ones. Larger cloves produce larger bulbs.

early_growth.text: Keep allium beds completely weed-free. Onions and garlic have poor, shallow root systems and are easily out-competed. Even small weeds reduce yields significantly.
No need to water garlic in autumn and winter -- rainfall is usually sufficient. Begin watering in spring if it is dry.

established.text: Stop feeding with nitrogen once bulbs start to form. High nitrogen at this stage produces soft, poorly-stored bulbs with thick necks.
Leeks can be earthed up as they grow to blanch the lower stem -- this gives you a longer white shaft and milder flavor.

bulb_forming.text: When onion leaves begin to yellow and fall over, stop watering. The plant is telling you it is finishing -- let it dry down naturally.
Do not bend onion tops manually until at least half the leaves have yellowed on their own. Bending them too early exposes the neck to disease.

harvest.text: Lift rather than pull. A garden fork under the bulb loosens the roots and prevents the stem tearing -- which exposes the bulb to rot during curing.
Harvest on a dry day and leave on top of the soil for a few hours before bringing in. The sun begins the drying process.

curing.text: Curing is the most important step most gardeners skip. 3-4 weeks in warm, airy conditions transforms a perishable vegetable into one that stores for 6-9 months.
Braid garlic and onions for storage if you have enough -- it looks beautiful and is functional. Store in a cool, dry, dark place.

yield_expectations.per_plant: One spring onion per seed -- fast at 8 weeks
yield_expectations.peak_production: Succession sow every 3 weeks from early spring for continuous supply
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Spring onions are one of the fastest crops in the garden and endlessly useful in the kitchen.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Established alliums are among the hardiest vegetables and handle frost well. Garlic overwintering in the ground is designed for frost. Young onion seedlings are more vulnerable to late hard freezes.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Protect young onion sets if a hard freeze threatens in the first few weeks after planting. Established plants need no protection from ordinary frost.

failure_diagnostics.label: Allium rust or white rot
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Allium rust appears as orange powder on leaves in humid summers -- it weakens but rarely kills the plant. White rot is more serious: a soil-borne fungus that causes bulbs to rot at the base. Once white rot is in soil it persists for decades.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Rotate alliums to a new bed every year. White rot cannot be eliminated from infected soil -- grow alliums elsewhere if you see it. Rust is largely cosmetic -- harvest early and the bulbs are usually fine.

failure_diagnostics.label: Rotting bulbs
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Garlic and onion bulbs rot in waterlogged soil, especially during curing. Rain on curing alliums reverses the drying process and causes neck rot -- one of the most common storage failures.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Ensure excellent drainage. Cure garlic and onions under cover -- a shed or garage with good airflow. Even a few hours of rain on curing bulbs can significantly reduce storage life.

failure_diagnostics.label: Small bulbs
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Alliums that experience drought stress during bulb development produce small, tight bulbs. Irregular watering is a common cause of disappointing allium harvests.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently during bulb formation -- from spring until leaves begin to yellow. Stop watering completely once leaves start to die back naturally.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor bulb development
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Alliums need full sun for good bulb development. The bulbing trigger in onions and garlic is day length -- both need long days combined with warmth to form bulbs. In shade or under trees, they often produce only small, undeveloped bulbs.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant alliums in your sunniest, most open bed. Weed competition also significantly reduces yield -- keep allium beds completely weed-free from early spring.

crops.name: Sweet Corn
crops.description: The three sisters classic. Needs to be grown in blocks (minimum 4×4) for wind pollination -- a single row gives no ears. Sweetness drops fast after picking -- eat within 30 minutes of harvest.

3.notes: Direct sow after last frost. Short-season varieties like Earlivee or Polar Vee essential. One crop only.

fertilizer.notes: Heavy feeder -- apply nitrogen-rich fertilizer at planting and again when plants reach knee height. Tasseling onwards needs less nitrogen.
fertilizer.npk_hint: heavy feeder -- high N side-dress at knee height, e.g. 10-5-5
fertilizer.notify_message: Time to side-dress your corn with nitrogen

succession.tip: Sow every 2 weeks from last frost through early summer, or plant early-, mid-, and late-maturing varieties simultaneously. Sweet corn is only good for a 3-5 day window at peak ripeness -- succession planting means you have ears ready over weeks rather than a single overwhelming harvest. Each block needs to be large enough for pollination (at least 3-4 rows of 3-4 plants). Count back 75-90 days from first frost for your last sowing.

good.name: Beans
good.why: Three Sisters -- fix nitrogen for hungry corn

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Legume rhizobial nitrogen fixation is textbook plant science. The mechanism is real; the specific pairing benefit is mechanistically plausible but often not pair-tested.

good.name: Squash
good.why: Three Sisters -- ground cover, moisture retention

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Ground cover effects on soil temperature and moisture are real; specific pairings not well-studied.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension 2022 and 2025 Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetable Crops; UConn IPM 'Perimeter Trap Cropping for Cole Crops'). Nasturtiums specifically are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and Utah State University Extension (Mohr et al., 'Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting'). Protocol caveat: UConn IPM explicitly notes trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents' -- so the aphid application here has a protocol-mismatch concern even though the companion is extension-named. The Cornell-IPM-specific attribution in earlier catalog reason text was not located in Cornell's published IPM material; actual backing is WSU/USU/UConn.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Bad companion claim, no pattern match. Default to traditional pending review.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Inter-plant competition for N, P, K is a real agronomic concept. Specific 'bad pair' claims often extrapolate beyond what research has shown.

pests.name: Corn earworm
pests.symptoms: Caterpillar boring into silk and tip of ear. Frass visible at tip. Damaged kernels at ear tip.
pests.cause: Helicoverpa zea moth larvae. A major corn pest.
pests.organic_treatment: Apply mineral oil to silk 5-6 days after silk emergence. Bt spray on silk. Trichogramma wasp release.
pests.prevention: Choose tight-husked varieties. Monitor with pheromone traps.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

diseases.name: Gray leaf spot
diseases.symptoms: Rectangular gray-brown lesions running along leaf veins. Severe infection yellows entire plant.
diseases.cause: Cercospora zeae-maydis fungus. Worst in warm humid regions.
diseases.organic_treatment: No practical organic treatment for home gardens.
diseases.prevention: Choose resistant hybrids. Rotate corn crops. Till crop residue after harvest.

watering.frequency: Weekly, increase during silking and ear fill
watering.method: At soil level -- overhead at silking helps pollination

crops.harvest_ready: Silks brown and dry. Pull back husk -- kernels should be plump and milky when pierced with thumbnail. The window is 1-2 days. Eat immediately after picking.

start_method.notes: Direct sow after last frost in blocks (not rows) for pollination. Plant 4+ rows minimum. Soil must be above 60°F.

storage.room_temp: Same day -- sugars convert to starch within hours
storage.freezer: Blanch 4 minutes, cut from cob, freeze -- very good
storage.notes: The famous rule: put water on to boil before you pick. Modern super-sweet varieties hold a little longer.

varieties.note: Super-sweet varieties (SH2 types) hold their sugar much longer after picking than regular sweet corn -- good for home gardeners who can't rush to the pot.

crops.soil_prep: Corn is a heavy feeder. Dig in generous amounts of well-rotted manure or compost the autumn before planting. Top-dress with balanced fertilizer before planting. Soil pH 6.0-6.8. Corn grows best in warm, well-drained soil -- wait until soil temperature is above 60°F.

thinning.to_spacing: 12-15 inches between plants in rows 30 inches apart
thinning.method: Thin by cutting at soil level -- corn roots intertwine and pulling disturbs neighbors.
thinning.tip: Plant in blocks of at least 4 rows rather than long single rows -- corn is wind-pollinated and needs dense planting for good ear fill.

container_notes.notes: Not suitable for containers -- corn needs to be grown in blocks for wind pollination, which requires too many large pots to be practical.

rotation.avoid_after: Corn -- buildup of corn rootworm and smut diseases
rotation.good_after: Excellent after legumes (beans, peas) which fix nitrogen for heavy-feeding corn
rotation.note: Classic rotation: corn after beans is the most efficient use of nitrogen fixation.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: A strong shoot pushing up. Corn germinates fast in warm soil.
growth_stages.user_action: Sow directly when soil temperature reaches 60°F. Corn does not transplant well. Sow in blocks rather than rows for wind pollination.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Tall narrow seedlings pushing up vigorously.
growth_stages.user_action: Thin to 12 inches if sown thickly. Water consistently -- corn is a heavy water user.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Plants 2-3 feet tall, growing strongly. Knee-high by the Fourth of July is the traditional gauge.
growth_stages.user_action: Feed with a high-nitrogen fertilizer now. Corn is a very hungry plant. Side-dress with compost if available.

growth_stages.name: Tasseling and Silking
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Tassels appearing at the top of the plant, silk emerging from developing ears.
growth_stages.user_action: This is the pollination window. Wind carries pollen from tassels to silk. A block planting of at least 4x4 plants gives adequate pollination. Dry weather during silking causes poor kernel set.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Silks turned brown and dry. Pull back the husk to check -- kernels should be full and release milky juice when pierced.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest immediately and cook immediately. Sweet corn begins converting sugar to starch the moment it is picked. The difference between corn eaten within an hour of picking and corn bought from a shop is remarkable.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: All ears harvested, stalks turning brown and beginning to dry. Plants are 6-8 feet tall and slow to break down if left whole.
growth_stages.user_action: Cut stalks at ground level and chop into the compost or directly till in. Mark the bed in your rotation log -- corn is a heavy nitrogen feeder and should not follow itself next season.

notifications.title: Time to sow your sweet corn
notifications.body: Corn goes directly into warm soil a week after last frost. Sow in a block -- at least 4 plants wide in each direction. Wind pollination is how corn sets kernels, and a single row pollinates very poorly. Expect gaps and poor cobs from a single row.

notifications.title: Corn is silking -- keep it well watered
notifications.body: This is the most critical watering window for sweet corn. Drought stress when silks are emerging causes incomplete kernel set -- you end up with gappy, poorly-filled cobs. Water deeply every 2-3 days if it is not raining.

notifications.title: Check your corn for harvest readiness
notifications.body: Pull back the husk on one ear and press a kernel with your thumbnail. Milky juice means perfect harvest time. Clear juice means too early. No juice and it is past peak. Cook within hours of picking for the best flavor you have ever tasted from sweet corn.

weather_triggers.title: Drought during silking -- water immediately
weather_triggers.body: Drought stress when corn silk is emerging is the most damaging moment for the crop. Incomplete pollination means gaps in the cob. Water deeply today.

germination.text: Sow corn in a block at least 4 rows wide, not in a single long row. Corn is wind-pollinated -- pollen drifts from tassel to silk -- and a block planting catches pollen efficiently while a row planting wastes most of it.

Wait for soil to reach 60 degrees minimum (65 to 70 for supersweet varieties) before direct-sowing. Cold soil rots seed; supersweet types in cold soil simply do not germinate. Pre-germinate seeds on damp paper towels in cold zones if needed.

seedling.text: Thin to 8 to 12 inches between plants once seedlings are 4 inches tall. Crowded corn produces small ears. Resist transplanting -- corn resents root disturbance and seedlings rarely catch up after transplanting.
Side-dress with nitrogen at the 4-leaf stage and again at knee-high. Corn is a heavy feeder; deficiency shows as yellowing of older leaves first.

established.text: Hill soil up around the base of plants once they are 12 to 18 inches tall. This gives wind support and encourages prop-root development -- the brace roots that prevent toppling in summer storms.
Continue consistent watering; corn ear fill depends heavily on water during the silking and ear-development weeks. Drought during this window produces missing kernels.

tasseling.text: Tassels emerge from the top of each stalk and shed pollen for about a week. Watch for the silk emerging from each developing ear at the same time -- proper timing of these two stages is what makes a full ear.
If the block is small or wind is limited, hand-pollinate by gently shaking tassels over the silks. This dramatically improves kernel fill in small home plantings.

harvest.text: Use the milk test: peel back a husk, puncture a kernel with a fingernail. Clear liquid means under-ripe; milky liquid means perfect; pasty means over-ripe. Sweet corn moves from under-ripe to over-ripe in 2 to 3 days; check daily during peak.

Eat or refrigerate within hours of picking -- the sugar-to-starch conversion begins immediately and accelerates at room temperature. Supersweet varieties hold their sweetness longer (days) than older sugary varieties (hours).

end_of_season.text: After harvest, cut stalks at ground level and chop into the compost or till in. Corn stalks are large and slow to break down; chopping accelerates decomposition.
Rotate corn to a new bed next year -- it is a heavy nitrogen feeder and should not follow itself.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 1-2 ears per plant
yield_expectations.peak_production: All ears mature within a 1-2 week window -- the whole harvest happens at once
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Corn eaten within an hour of picking tastes like a different vegetable from anything sold in a shop. That moment alone justifies growing it.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Sweet corn is a tender annual and damaged by even a light frost at any stage. Cold soil at planting (below 60 degrees, or below 65 to 70 for supersweet types) rots seed before it germinates. Late-summer frost ends the season abruptly -- ears in the milk stage at first frost are still edible but those still developing are lost.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Wait for soil to reach 60 degrees (65 to 70 for supersweet varieties) before sowing. Use black plastic mulch to warm soil in cool zones. In short-season zones, choose early-maturing varieties (60 to 70 days) and time the sowing so harvest finishes well before expected first frost.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Corn earworm is the headline pest -- adult moths lay eggs on silks; larvae enter the ear tip and eat developing kernels. European corn borer tunnels into stalks. Common smut produces grotesque gray-black galls on ears (delicacy in some cuisines, ruined ear in others). Stewart's wilt is bacterial and transmitted by flea beetles in some regions.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: For corn earworm, drop a few drops of vegetable oil onto the silk channel after pollination -- this physically blocks larval entry. For European corn borer, chop and compost stalks at end of season to break the overwintering cycle. Choose smut-resistant varieties. Rotate corn to a new bed each year.

failure_diagnostics.label: Root issues or poor ears
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Corn tolerates more water than most vegetables but cannot handle persistent waterlogging -- roots rot and plants topple from weakened anchorage. Excessive water at silking can dilute kernel sweetness, especially in supersweet varieties.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil. Hill soil up around stalks at knee-high stage to encourage prop-root development and improve drainage. In flood-prone gardens, plant on raised berms.

failure_diagnostics.label: Missing kernels or short ears
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress during silking and ear-development is the leading cause of poor ears in home-grown corn. Each kernel forms only when a pollen grain successfully lands on a silk and grows down it -- water stress shortens or browns silks, producing ears with rows of missing kernels (the gap-toothed ear).
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water deeply and consistently from tasseling through ear development -- 1 to 2 inches per week minimum, more in heat. Mulch heavily between rows to retain soil moisture. Drip irrigation is ideal for corn during the critical pollination window.

failure_diagnostics.label: Weak stalks or small ears
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Corn needs full sun -- 8 hours minimum, ideally more. In partial shade plants grow tall and weak with small or no ears. Corn shaded by larger plants or buildings simply will not produce a meaningful crop.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in the sunniest spot available. Plant blocks (not rows) to maximize wind pollination. Avoid planting downwind of fences or buildings that block wind movement during tasseling.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

pests.name: Bean seed fly
pests.symptoms: Seeds fail to germinate or seedlings die soon after emergence.
pests.cause: Delia platura maggots eat germinating seeds.
pests.organic_treatment: Sow when soil is warm (above 60°F) for rapid germination.
pests.prevention: Wait for warm soil. Start in pots and transplant. Pre-soak seeds to speed germination.

diseases.name: Bean rust
diseases.symptoms: Orange-brown powdery pustules on leaf undersides with corresponding pale spots on top.
diseases.cause: Uromyces appendiculatus fungus. Spreads in warm humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Sulfur-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Improve airflow.

diseases.name: Halo blight
diseases.symptoms: Water-soaked spots surrounded by yellow halo on leaves. Pods develop greasy patches.
diseases.cause: Pseudomonas syringae pv. phaseolicola bacteria. Seed-borne and spread by rain splash.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected plants. Copper-based bactericide spray.
diseases.prevention: Buy certified disease-free seed. Avoid working with wet plants. Rotate crops.

crops.harvest_ready: Pods plump and bright green, beans filling pods. Pick before pods yellow.

start_method.notes: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm. Like other beans, dislikes transplanting.

rotation.avoid_after: Beans, peas -- some shared diseases but generally disease pressure is lower
rotation.good_after: Brassicas, nightshades, corn -- legumes fix nitrogen that these heavy feeders need
rotation.note: Plant legumes before heavy feeders -- they'll leave nitrogen-rich soil behind.

storage.freezer: Blanch in pod 3 minutes, freeze -- excellent, this is what commercial frozen edamame is
storage.notes: Edamame frozen in the pod keeps flavor best. Boil from frozen in salted water.

varieties.note: Envy is the best choice for short-season gardens -- 75 days maturity vs 85-90 for most varieties.

container_notes.notes: Good container crop. 3-gallon minimum, 2-3 plants per pot. Compact varieties work well.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: A strong shoot pushing up. Corn germinates fast in warm soil.
growth_stages.user_action: Sow directly when soil temperature reaches 60°F. Corn does not transplant well. Sow in blocks rather than rows for wind pollination.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Tall narrow seedlings pushing up vigorously.
growth_stages.user_action: Thin to 12 inches if sown thickly. Water consistently -- corn is a heavy water user.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Plants 2-3 feet tall, growing strongly. Knee-high by the Fourth of July is the traditional gauge.
growth_stages.user_action: Feed with a high-nitrogen fertilizer now. Corn is a very hungry plant. Side-dress with compost if available.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small white or pale-purple flowers in the leaf axils. Edamame is self-pollinating, so flowers come and go quickly -- often opening and setting fruit within hours. Tiny pods begin forming directly behind successful flowers within days.
growth_stages.user_action: Maintain consistent moisture from flowering through pod-fill -- this is the critical irrigation window for yield. Watch for bean leaf beetles and aphids during the flowering window; both populations spike then. Do not fertilize with nitrogen.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Silks turned brown and dry. Pull back the husk to check -- kernels should be full and release milky juice when pierced.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest immediately and cook immediately. Sweet corn begins converting sugar to starch the moment it is picked. The difference between corn eaten within an hour of picking and corn bought from a shop is remarkable.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Pods harvested, plant senescing -- leaves yellowing and dropping, stem stiff and dry. Edamame finishes its life cycle quickly once pods are mature.
growth_stages.user_action: Cut plants at ground level rather than pulling. Leave the roots in the soil -- the nitrogen-fixing nodules become next season's slow-release nitrogen for whichever crop follows. Mark the bed in your rotation log.

notifications.title: Time to sow your edamame
notifications.body: Edamame goes directly into warm soil a week or two after last frost -- wait until soil is at least 60F (65-70F is better). If this is your first time growing soybeans in this bed, dust the seed with rhizobium inoculant at sowing. The bacteria settle into the root nodules and fix nitrogen for the plant; without them, edamame yield drops sharply on bean-naive soil.

notifications.title: Edamame is flowering -- keep it consistently watered
notifications.body: This is the start of the critical irrigation window for edamame. Water stress from flowering through pod-fill is the single biggest cause of poor yield -- pods that abort before they fill, or fill unevenly. Water deeply every 2-3 days if it is not raining, and mulch to stabilize soil moisture. Skip nitrogen fertilizer; beans fix their own and high-N suppresses nodulation.

notifications.title: Check your edamame pods for harvest readiness
notifications.body: Squeeze a pod between thumb and finger -- when it feels plump and the beans inside fill 80 to 90 percent of the pod, it is ready. Pods should still be bright green; once they start yellowing, the beans inside have moved past their tender sweet stage. Harvest the whole pod (don't shell in the field) and either eat fresh, or blanch for 3-5 minutes and freeze whole-pod.

weather_triggers.title: Drought during flowering or pod-fill -- water immediately
weather_triggers.body: Drought stress during flowering and pod-fill is the most damaging moment for edamame. Water stress now causes pods to abort or fill unevenly. Water deeply today and mulch heavily if you have not already.

germination.text: Beans are direct-sown -- transplanting damages the brittle taproot. Wait until soil is 60 degrees minimum (65 to 70 is better) before sowing; cold soil rots seed before it germinates.

Sow 1 to 2 inches deep, 2 to 4 inches apart in rows. Inoculate seed with rhizobium bacteria at sowing if the bed has not grown beans recently -- this boosts the nitrogen-fixing nodulation that beans depend on.

seedling.text: Beans germinate fast in warm soil -- typically 7 to 10 days. Seedlings are vulnerable to slugs and bean leaf beetles in their first weeks; check daily.

Thin bush beans to 4 to 6 inches between plants once seedlings are 4 inches tall. Pole beans need a trellis or pole structure in place at this stage -- they grow fast and resent late-installed support.

Rabbits favor young soybean over most garden crops -- a single rabbit can clip an entire row of seedlings to the ground in one night. Cover seedlings with hardware cloth, chicken-wire cages, or row cover until plants are 8-10 inches tall and the stems have toughened. Damage rarely continues once plants are past the seedling stage.

established.text: Do not fertilize beans with nitrogen. Beans fix their own nitrogen via root nodules; high-N fertilizer suppresses nodulation and produces lush leafy plants with poor pod set.
Water consistently during flowering and pod-fill -- this is when water stress most reduces yield. Mulch heavily to stabilize soil moisture and suppress weeds.

flowering.text: Beans are self-pollinating and do not need pollinators. Flowers open and self-pollinate within hours; fruit set is fast.
Watch for bean leaf beetles and aphids during flowering -- both populations spike in this window. Check undersides of leaves daily.

harvest.text: Pick beans young and often -- bush and pole beans ready when pods snap cleanly and the seeds inside are still small. Edamame ready when pods are plump and fill 80 to 90 percent with bright green beans, before yellowing.
Harvest every 2 to 3 days during peak production. Beans left on the plant signal it to stop producing new pods. Edamame is harvested whole-pod, not shelled in the field.

end_of_season.text: After harvest, cut bean plants at ground level and leave roots in the soil -- the nitrogen-fixing root nodules become next year's slow-release nitrogen for the bed.
Rotate beans to a new bed each year. Bean diseases (anthracnose, halo blight, bean rust) survive in soil and infect next year's planting.

yield_expectations.per_plant: Pods ripen in a single 7-10 day window; whole-plant harvest yields a generous bowlful from each plant
yield_expectations.peak_production: Edamame plants ripen all pods within a 1-2 week window -- the whole harvest happens at once
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Fresh-picked edamame is sweeter and more tender than anything you can buy frozen. The whole-plant single-harvest model is unusual but easy.
factors: harvest timing within the 7-10 day window

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Beans are warm-season tender annuals -- killed outright by light frost at any stage. Cold soil at sowing (below 60 degrees) rots seed; cool conditions during early growth produce stunted plants that never fully recover. Late summer frost ends the season abruptly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Wait to sow until soil is reliably 60 degrees minimum (65 to 70 is better). In short-season zones, choose early-maturing bush varieties and use black plastic mulch to warm soil. Have row cover ready for unexpected late-spring frosts. For fall harvests, time the planting so harvest finishes before first expected frost.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Mexican bean beetle (yellow with black spots, similar to ladybug but a pest) is the dominant bean pest east of the Rockies -- larvae skeletonize leaves. Bean leaf beetle damages seedlings and pods. Aphids cluster on tender new growth. Halo blight (water-soaked spots with yellow halo) and bean rust are the headline diseases. For edamame specifically, soybean aphid and Japanese beetle are also common.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: For Mexican bean beetle, hand-pick adults and crush yellow egg masses on leaf undersides; in heavy infestations, parasitic wasp release works for organic gardeners. Rotate to a new bed each year. Avoid working bean plants when foliage is wet -- this spreads halo blight and bean rust. Choose disease-resistant varieties for the next planting.

failure_diagnostics.label: Root rot or yellowing
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Persistent waterlogging causes root rot, yellowing leaves, and crown collapse. Beans are also susceptible to white mold (Sclerotinia) in cool wet conditions, which produces fluffy white growth at the soil line and kills plants quickly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil. Water at the base, not overhead, and water in the morning so foliage dries before evening. Space plants for airflow. For white mold, rotate at least 3 years between bean plantings in any one bed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor pod set or fill
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress during flowering and pod-fill is the leading cause of poor bean harvests. Plants drop flowers under water stress and produce small empty or partially-filled pods. Edamame is especially demanding of consistent water during the pod-fill window.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently during flowering and pod-fill -- 1 inch per week minimum, more in heat. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture. Drip irrigation is ideal because it provides consistent water without wetting foliage.

failure_diagnostics.label: Few flowers or pods
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Beans need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to flower and produce well. In partial shade plants grow leaves but flower sparsely and set few pods. Tall pole beans can shade their own lower leaves if not pinched at the top of the support.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun. For pole beans, pinch the growing tip when vines reach the top of the support to prevent excessive top growth and improve light penetration to lower flowering nodes.
