fertilizer.notes: Biennial -- feeds moderately. Monthly balanced feed. Avoid high nitrogen which reduces flavor intensity.

succession.tip: Sow a second batch 4 weeks after the first. Parsley is slow to germinate (3-4 weeks) and biennial -- in its second year it bolts immediately. For practical purposes treat it as an annual and sow a fresh batch mid-season. The second sowing will be producing vigorously through autumn and into early winter in mild zones. Soak seeds overnight before sowing to improve germination speed.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Carrot fly
pests.symptoms: Root damage and wilting. Cilantro and dill are in carrot family and attract same pests.
pests.cause: Psila rosae. Affects all members of the carrot family.
pests.organic_treatment: Grow under fine insect mesh.
pests.prevention: Insect mesh. Grow away from carrots and parsnips.

diseases.name: Leaf spot
diseases.symptoms: Dark brown spots on leaves. Affected leaves yellow and die.
diseases.cause: Bacterial or fungal leaf spot. Favored by wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Copper-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention: Water at soil level. Good spacing.

crops.harvest_ready: Snip outer stems at any time once plant has 6+ stems.

storage.freezer: Blanch briefly, squeeze dry, freeze -- or blend into oil cubes
storage.notes: Flat-leaf parsley stores better than curly. The water-glass fridge method is highly effective.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small seedlings emerging. Annual herbs germinate readily in warm conditions.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep soil consistently moist. Most annual herbs germinate better in warmth -- 65-75°F is ideal.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: True leaves developing -- already recognizable as the herb you planted.
growth_stages.user_action: Thin to 6-9 inches. The thinnings are edible -- add them to salads.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: A bushy, fragrant plant ready for regular harvesting.
growth_stages.user_action: Begin harvesting by pinching out the growing tips -- this encourages bushy side growth rather than a tall, lanky plant.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Plenty of leafy growth, plant not yet showing flowering stems.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest little and often by pinching growing tips. Never remove more than a third of the plant at once. Regular harvesting is what keeps herbs producing.

growth_stages.name: Bolting (Year 1)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: A central flower stalk shooting up from a year-one parsley plant. Leaves become smaller, sparser, and increasingly bitter as the plant redirects energy from leaf production to seed-set. This is not normal -- parsley should not bolt in its first year.
growth_stages.user_action: Year-one bolting is usually a stress response: seedlings exposed to prolonged cold before transplanting (vernalization), or sustained heat stress in zones 9-11. The plant is unlikely to recover meaningfully -- pull and replace with a fresh sowing of slow-bolt varieties, sown direct, mulched heavily for cooler soil. Note the cause for next year.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Bolting in year 1 -- pulling for a fresh sowing?

growth_stages.name: Second-Year Bolting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Year-2 plants sending up a tall central flower stalk in spring or early summer, followed by umbel-shaped flowers and seed development. Leaves become sparse and bitter as the plant redirects energy to reproduction. This is the normal end of parsley's biennial lifecycle.
growth_stages.user_action: Decide whether to pull the plant for a fresh year-1 sowing, or let it flower for seed-saving and pollinator support. Once parsley bolts in year 2, the plant dies after seed-set and is finished.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Bolting in year 2 -- pulling or letting it seed?

notifications.title: Start your parsley indoors or direct sow
notifications.body: Parsley can be sown indoors 4 weeks before last frost or directly outside after it. It is notoriously slow to germinate -- 3 weeks is normal. Do not give up. Once it gets going it produces abundantly all season.

notifications.title: Parsley in its second year will bolt
notifications.body: Parsley is biennial -- it flowers in its second year and then dies. Harvest as much as you can now if this is a second-year plant, and sow fresh seed for this season's main crop.

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- protect tender herbs
weather_triggers.body: Basil, cilantro, and lemongrass are extremely frost-tender. Bring containers inside or cover with fleece tonight. Hardy herbs like thyme, rosemary, and mint are much more frost-tolerant.

weather_triggers.title: Heat alert -- herbs may bolt
weather_triggers.body: Heat triggers bolting in cilantro, dill, and parsley. Harvest as much as possible before temperatures peak. Basil, on the other hand, loves heat -- just remove any flowers that appear.

germination.text: Parsley is famously slow to germinate -- 2 to 4 weeks is normal. Soak seeds overnight before sowing to soften the hard seed coat. Sow in early spring for summer harvest, or in fall in mild zones for winter and spring harvest.

Sow shallowly (1/4 inch) and keep the soil surface consistently moist for the entire germination window. The most common parsley failure is letting the surface dry out during the long germination period.

seedling.text: Thin to 6-inch spacing once seedlings have 2 true leaves. Parsley has a taproot and resents transplanting -- direct-sown plants outperform transplants over the season.
Mulch lightly between plants to suppress weeds. Hand-weed close to plants -- parsley roots are shallow and easily damaged.

established.text: Harvest outer leaves first, leaving the central growing tip intact. The plant continues producing new leaves from the center for months, even into mild winters.
Side-dress with compost mid-season for sustained leaf production. Water consistently -- parsley wilts quickly in heat and the recovery uses energy that could go into leaves.

harvest.text: Cut individual stems at the base; do not harvest more than a third of the plant at once. Used cut-and-come-again, a single parsley plant can produce a generous harvest from spring through fall, and into winter in mild zones.
Parsley flavor concentrates in cool weather -- fall and early spring harvests are the best of the year in most zones. Hot summer growth is milder.

bolting.text: Year-1 bolting is a stress response, not a normal stage. The most common cause is transplanting seedlings that were exposed to extended cold (a few weeks below 50F) -- the plant interprets the cold as winter and bolts the following spring as if it were year 2.

Heat stress in zones 9-11 can also trigger early bolt. Once bolting starts, the plant rarely produces useful leaves again. Pull and resow with a slow-bolt variety like Giant of Italy or Krausa, sown direct after the soil warms past 50F so the seedlings never see vernalization-triggering cold.

second_year_bolting.text: Parsley is biennial -- in its second year, it bolts to flower and produces seed, then dies. The leaves that grow in the second year are sparse, bitter, and not worth harvesting.

Most home gardeners treat parsley as an annual: pull it at the end of year 1, replant fresh seed in year 2. Some growers let one or two plants bolt in year 2 specifically to save seed; the umbel-shaped flowers also attract beneficial insects to the garden.

yield_expectations.per_plant: Continuous harvest from one plant for the whole season
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Parsley is slow to germinate but patient once established -- one plant keeps producing all season.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost tolerance
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Parsley is one of the more cold-tolerant culinary herbs. Mature plants survive light frost without damage and tolerate sustained cold weather better than basil, dill, or cilantro. In zones 7 and warmer, parsley often overwinters and resumes growth in early spring before bolting in its second year.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant parsley early in spring -- it tolerates light frost as a young transplant. In mild zones, fall planting gives an extended cool-season harvest. Cover with row cover in zone 6 and below for winter protection if attempting to overwinter.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Parsley shares many pests with carrot (Apiaceae family): carrot rust fly larvae tunnel into roots; parsleyworm (the spectacular striped caterpillar that becomes the black swallowtail butterfly) eats foliage but rarely seriously damages the plant. Septoria leaf spot can hit foliage in wet weather.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Floating row cover during the carrot rust fly emergence windows blocks the pest. Parsleyworm is generally tolerated by experienced gardeners -- the swallowtail caterpillars are striking and the damage is usually minor; relocate them to a sacrificial parsley plant if there are too many. For Septoria, water at the base and provide good airflow.

failure_diagnostics.label: Root rot or yellowing
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Parsley needs consistent moisture but well-drained soil. Persistent waterlogging causes root rot and yellowing of inner leaves. Containerized parsley in pots without drainage fails the same way.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil. Use pots with drainage holes for container culture. Water deeply at the base rather than shallow overhead, and let the soil surface dry slightly between waterings.

failure_diagnostics.label: Wilting and small leaves
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Parsley wilts dramatically in heat and drought. Mild wilting recovers without lasting damage, but repeated severe drought stress produces small, tough, strongly-flavored leaves and accelerates bolt risk in second-year plants.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently -- 1 inch per week minimum, more in heat. Mulch around plants to retain soil moisture. In hot climates, parsley appreciates light afternoon shade.

failure_diagnostics.label: Leggy or sparse growth
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Parsley needs 4 to 6 hours of direct sun minimum -- it tolerates more shade than most herbs but produces sparse, leggy growth in deep shade. Indoor parsley on a windowsill often disappoints for this reason.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full to partial sun outdoors. For indoor growing, place near the brightest available window or supplement with a grow light. Light afternoon shade is fine and even helpful in hot climates.

crops.name: Cilantro / Coriander
crops.description: Fast to bolt in heat. Succession sow every 3 weeks through cool weather. Let some plants go to seed -- you'll always have a supply, and the seeds (coriander) are a spice in their own right.

3.notes: Direct sow. Cool weather is key -- bolts quickly in heat. Sow a fresh batch every 3 weeks.

direct_sow.design_note: Plant early in cool weather; harvest before heat triggers bolting.

fertilizer.notes: Fast-growing and light feeder. One application at sowing is enough. Over-feeding speeds bolting.
fertilizer.notify_message: Light feed time for your cilantro

succession.tip: Sow every 2 weeks from spring through autumn. Cilantro is the most determined bolter in the herb garden -- it can go from seedling to flower in 3-4 weeks in warm weather. There is no saving a bolted cilantro plant for leaf harvest. The only reliable approach is frequent new sowings. In summer, choose slow-bolt varieties and still expect faster cycling than in spring. Let a few plants go to seed -- coriander seed is a useful spice and the plants will self-sow.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Carrot fly
pests.symptoms: Root damage and wilting. Cilantro and dill are in carrot family and attract same pests.
pests.cause: Psila rosae. Affects all members of the carrot family.
pests.organic_treatment: Grow under fine insect mesh.
pests.prevention: Insect mesh. Grow away from carrots and parsnips.

diseases.name: Leaf spot
diseases.symptoms: Dark brown spots on leaves. Affected leaves yellow and die.
diseases.cause: Bacterial or fungal leaf spot. Favored by wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Copper-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention: Water at soil level. Good spacing.

crops.harvest_ready: Pick leaves before flowering. Once it bolts, leaves become lacy and bitter.

start_method.notes: Direct sow -- cilantro bolts quickly and dislikes transplanting. Sow every 2-3 weeks for continuous harvest.

container_notes.notes: Good container herb. Deep pots preferred (taproot). At least 8 inches deep.

bolting.prevention: Choose slow-bolt varieties (Leisure, Calypso). Plant in cool season. Keep well watered. Succession sow every 2 weeks. Provide shade.
bolting.note: Once bolting starts, harvest all leaves immediately and let it go to coriander seed -- equally useful.

storage.room_temp: 3-5 days in a glass of water like flowers
storage.fridge: 1 week in a glass of water in the fridge, covered with a bag
storage.freezer: Blend with water, freeze in ice cube trays -- excellent for curries
storage.notes: Cilantro is one of the most perishable herbs. The water-glass method in the fridge is the most effective.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small seedlings emerging. Annual herbs germinate readily in warm conditions.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep soil consistently moist. Most annual herbs germinate better in warmth -- 65-75°F is ideal.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: True leaves developing -- already recognizable as the herb you planted.
growth_stages.user_action: Thin to 6-9 inches. The thinnings are edible -- add them to salads.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: A bushy, fragrant plant ready for regular harvesting.
growth_stages.user_action: Begin harvesting by pinching out the growing tips -- this encourages bushy side growth rather than a tall, lanky plant.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Plenty of leafy growth, plant not yet showing flowering stems.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest little and often by pinching growing tips. Never remove more than a third of the plant at once. Regular harvesting is what keeps herbs producing.

growth_stages.name: Bolting / Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Central flower stem shooting up. Leaves becoming smaller and flavor intensifying or turning bitter depending on the herb.
growth_stages.user_action: Remove flower stems immediately on basil to extend harvest. For cilantro and dill, flowering is part of the lifecycle -- collect seeds for cooking or sowing.

notifications.title: Cilantro bolting -- sow your next batch
notifications.body: Cilantro bolts fast, especially in warm weather. When you see the first flower stem, sow your next batch immediately. Succession sowing every 3-4 weeks is the only way to have continuous cilantro through the season.

notifications.title: Cilantro seeds -- coriander for cooking
notifications.body: The seeds of bolted cilantro are coriander -- a completely different flavor and equally useful in the kitchen. Let some plants go to seed, collect them when the plant dries and browns, and use them whole or ground.

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- protect tender herbs
weather_triggers.body: Basil, cilantro, and lemongrass are extremely frost-tender. Bring containers inside or cover with fleece tonight. Hardy herbs like thyme, rosemary, and mint are much more frost-tolerant.

weather_triggers.title: Heat alert -- herbs may bolt
weather_triggers.body: Heat triggers bolting in cilantro, dill, and parsley. Harvest as much as possible before temperatures peak. Basil, on the other hand, loves heat -- just remove any flowers that appear.

germination.text: These herbs are direct-sown or started indoors. Basil needs warm soil (70 degrees) for germination; dill and cilantro tolerate cooler soil (55 to 60 degrees) and actually germinate better in cool weather.
Sow shallowly -- 1/4 inch deep -- and keep soil surface moist. Cilantro and dill can be sown in succession every 2 to 3 weeks for continuous harvest, since both bolt fast.

seedling.text: Thin to recommended spacing once seedlings have 2 true leaves -- crowded plants bolt faster and produce less leaf. Pinch basil tops at 6 inches to encourage branching.
These herbs all benefit from light afternoon shade in hot summer climates. Cilantro especially bolts within weeks of warm weather hitting.

established.text: Pinch basil regularly to prevent flowering -- once basil flowers, leaf production slows and flavor changes. Removing flower buds extends the productive harvest by weeks.
Water consistently. Wilted plants recover but the stress accelerates bolting in cilantro and dill. Mulch to stabilize soil moisture.

harvest.text: Harvest by snipping outer leaves first, leaving the central growing tip intact. For basil, cut whole stems above a leaf pair to encourage two new shoots from each cut.
Cilantro is harvested as leaves OR seed (coriander). Same plant, same cycle: harvest leaves while plant is leafy, let it bolt, harvest dry seeds from the spent flower heads.

bolting.text: Bolting (going to flower) signals the end of useful leaf production for these herbs. Basil bolts in heat or after flowering; dill and cilantro bolt fast in any warm weather.

Once bolting starts, decide: pinch flowers to extend leaf harvest by 1 to 2 weeks (basil), or let the plant flower and self-seed for next year (dill, cilantro). Bolted cilantro is often the original planting and reseeds prolifically.

yield_expectations.per_plant: Multiple harvests before bolting -- succession sow for continuous supply
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Cilantro is a fast, generous herb. The secret is succession sowing rather than trying to keep one plant going all season.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Basil is killed outright by light frost -- it is the most frost-sensitive culinary herb. Dill and cilantro are hardier; both tolerate light frost and cilantro actually grows better in cool weather. Basil also suffers chill damage (leaf blackening) below 50 degrees even without frost.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Wait to plant basil until soil is reliably 60 degrees and night temperatures stay above 50. For dill and cilantro, sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring -- they prefer cool conditions. Have row cover ready for cold nights with basil; in the fall, harvest basil heavily before the first cold snap because the plants will not recover.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Aphids cluster on tender new growth across all three. Basil downy mildew is the headline disease (yellowing and gray fuzz on leaf undersides) and has spread aggressively in recent years. Dill and cilantro may attract carrot family pests (carrot rust fly larvae, leaf miner). Powdery mildew occasionally hits all three in humid summers.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Choose downy-mildew-resistant basil varieties -- Rutgers Devotion DMR, Prospera, and similar bred for resistance. Space plants well for airflow. Hose off aphids with water; for serious infestations, insecticidal soap. Rotate herb-bed location each year.

failure_diagnostics.label: Root rot or yellowing
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: All three herbs need well-drained soil. Persistent waterlogging causes root rot, yellowing leaves, and crown collapse. Basil is especially sensitive to wet conditions and may collapse suddenly from Pythium or Fusarium in poorly-drained sites.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil. Use containers with drainage holes for indoor or balcony herbs. Water at the base, not overhead, and let the soil surface dry slightly between waterings. Avoid heavy clay sites for basil especially.

failure_diagnostics.label: Wilting or rapid bolting
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress accelerates bolting in cilantro and dill -- often by weeks -- and produces small, tough basil leaves with concentrated bitter flavor. Wilted herbs recover with watering but the stress shortens the productive cycle.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently, especially in heat. Mulch around plants to retain soil moisture. For cilantro and dill, succession-plant every 2 to 3 weeks rather than relying on one planting through the season -- this gives you continuous harvest even as individual plantings bolt.

failure_diagnostics.label: Leggy or sparse growth
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: These herbs need 6 hours of direct sun minimum for full flavor and growth. In partial shade, plants grow tall, leggy, and pale, with weaker flavor. Cilantro is a partial exception -- it tolerates partial shade in hot zones, where light shade actually slows bolting.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun in cool climates. In hot climates (zone 8 and warmer), cilantro and parsley tolerate and even prefer light afternoon shade. Basil and dill want full sun even in heat. For indoor growing, herbs need a sunny south-facing window or supplemental grow lights.

pests.name: Onion thrips
pests.symptoms: Silvery streaks or white blotches on leaves, giving a sandblasted appearance. Leaves may yellow and dry at the tips. Tiny (under 1/16 inch) yellow to brown insects hide between leaf blades and in leaf axils.
pests.cause: Thrips tabaci, the primary allium thrips. Multiple generations per year, worst in hot dry weather. Populations build quickly and can move between chives and nearby onions, garlic, and weeds.
pests.organic_treatment: Blue sticky cards monitor population. Insecticidal soap or spinosad applied into the leaf axils where thrips hide. Treat in evening to protect pollinators visiting chive flowers.
pests.prevention: Water regularly during hot weather -- drought-stressed chives are more attractive to thrips. Remove crop debris in fall where thrips overwinter.

pests.name: Onion maggot
pests.symptoms: Plants yellow and wilt for no apparent reason. Digging up the clump reveals small white legless larvae tunneling in roots and bulb bases, often with secondary rot. Heaviest damage on spring-planted clumps.
pests.cause: Delia antiqua larvae. The adult fly lays eggs at the base of alliums in spring. UMN notes onion maggot attacks only the Alliaceae family, including chives. Cool moist conditions favor egg survival.
pests.organic_treatment: No effective rescue once larvae are in the bulb. Remove and destroy infested clumps.
pests.prevention: Floating row cover from spring emergence through early summer blocks egg-laying. Rotate chives away from last year's allium beds by at least half a mile where possible -- flies travel far. Destroy cull onions and allium debris in fall.

pests.name: Allium leafminer
pests.symptoms: Rows of small round white spots along leaf blades (from adult female feeding punctures). Later, pale tunnels inside the hollow leaves. Plants may rot from secondary infection. Distorted wavy foliage.
pests.cause: Phytomyza gymnostoma, an invasive fly established in the Northeast since 2015. Two generations per year, active in spring (April-May) and fall (September-November). Cornell notes it now occurs throughout New York allium country.
pests.organic_treatment: Row covers timed to the two flight periods. Spinosad during active flights is the primary organic tool. Remove and destroy infested leaves.
pests.prevention: Check county extension alerts for local flight timing. Harvest chives heavily before spring flight to reduce tender target tissue. Less of a concern outside the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms: Pale yellow or light green oval patches on leaves with fuzzy gray-violet growth on undersides in humid mornings. Leaves collapse and the clump thins out. Worst in cool wet spring weather.
diseases.cause: Peronospora destructor, an oomycete that also affects onions and garlic. Overwinters in infected plant material and soil. Long dew periods favor infection.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove and destroy affected foliage. Cut back the clump hard to remove infected tissue and allow regrowth. Copper fungicides provide partial prevention.
diseases.prevention: Water at soil level, not overhead. Divide crowded clumps every 3-4 years to improve airflow. Rotate allium plantings.

diseases.name: Rust
diseases.symptoms: Small orange or reddish-brown pustules on leaves that release powdery spores when rubbed. Leaves yellow and die back from tips. Clump looks weakened and bloom is reduced.
diseases.cause: Puccinia allii, a fungus specific to the Alliaceae. Spread by wind-blown spores. Most severe in damp mild weather.
diseases.organic_treatment: Shear the clump back to the ground and dispose of infected foliage. New growth usually comes in clean.
diseases.prevention: Avoid overcrowding. Water at the soil line. Remove volunteer alliums and garlic mustard nearby.

diseases.name: Fusarium basal rot
diseases.symptoms: Yellowing and dieback of outer leaves. The base of the clump softens and rots, often with a white or pink fungal growth. Whole clump eventually collapses.
diseases.cause: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cepae, a soil-borne fungus that infects onion, garlic, shallot, and chives. Persists in soil for many years and often enters through root damage caused by onion maggot or cultivation.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove and destroy affected clumps with surrounding soil. No effective rescue.
diseases.prevention: Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds -- Fusarium is much worse in wet ground. Do not replant chives in the same spot for at least 4 years (UMN guideline for alliums). Control onion maggot to avoid the entry wounds Fusarium exploits.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Plant settling in after planting or propagation.
growth_stages.user_action: Most perennial herbs prefer poor, well-drained soil -- do not over-fertilize. Good drainage is more important than rich soil.

growth_stages.name: Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: New growth appearing, roots establishing.
growth_stages.user_action: Water regularly in the first season to establish roots. Once established, most perennial herbs are drought-tolerant.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Abundant leafy growth -- harvest anytime the plant has plenty.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest by cutting stems back by a third. Never cut into old woody growth on rosemary, sage, and thyme -- they do not regenerate from old wood.

growth_stages.name: Winter
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Plant slowing down or going dormant. Hardy perennials stay evergreen; tender ones die back.
growth_stages.user_action: Give a light haircut before winter to tidy up but avoid heavy pruning -- leave it for spring. Mulch around the base in colder zones.

growth_stages.name: Spring Cutback
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: New green growth beginning to push from the base or lower stems.
growth_stages.user_action: Cut back last year's growth by about half once new growth appears. This annual cutback keeps perennial herbs from going woody and keeps them productive.

notifications.title: Spring cutback time for your herbs
notifications.body: Once new growth is clearly showing, cut back last year's growth by about half. Always cut into green growth -- never into old brown wood on rosemary, sage, and thyme, as they do not regenerate from old wood. This annual trim keeps your herbs productive and compact.

notifications.title: Harvest your herbs before they flower
notifications.body: The flavor of most culinary herbs is strongest just before they flower. Harvest generous amounts now -- dry, freeze, or use fresh. Once flowers open the essential oil content changes.

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- protect tender herbs
weather_triggers.body: Basil, cilantro, and lemongrass are extremely frost-tender. Bring containers inside or cover with fleece tonight. Hardy herbs like thyme, rosemary, and mint are much more frost-tolerant.

weather_triggers.title: Heat alert -- herbs may bolt
weather_triggers.body: Heat triggers bolting in cilantro, dill, and parsley. Harvest as much as possible before temperatures peak. Basil, on the other hand, loves heat -- just remove any flowers that appear.

planting.text: Chives and mint prefer fertile, consistently moist soil and tolerate partial shade -- the opposite of Mediterranean herbs. A standard compost-amended garden bed suits them well.

Mint spreads aggressively by underground runners and will take over a bed within 2 years. Plant mint in a sunken pot or contained bed unless you have unlimited space to give it. Chives stays politely in clumps.

establishment.text: Water consistently through the first season. Both crops establish quickly and produce harvestable foliage within weeks of planting.
Mulch with compost or shredded leaves to retain moisture. Both herbs respond well to consistent moisture and benefit from organic mulch (the opposite of Mediterranean herbs).

harvest.text: Harvest chives by cutting whole leaves at the base with scissors -- avoid pulling individual leaves, which damages the bulb cluster. Cut close to the ground; the leaves regrow.
Harvest mint by snipping stems above a leaf node, which encourages branching. Frequent harvest keeps mint productive and bushy; unharvested mint becomes leggy and woody.

winter.text: Both crops die back to the ground after hard frost. The crowns are fully hardy through USDA zone 4 (chives) and zone 3 (most mints). The dieback is normal and complete -- the plant disappears underground until spring.

Do not try to keep these herbs harvestable through winter outdoors -- they are not evergreen. For winter harvest, dig a small clump in fall and pot it for the windowsill, or simply do without and welcome the spring regrowth.

spring_cutback.text: Cut the dead foliage to ground level in early spring before new growth emerges. Both crops regrow vigorously from the crown.

Spring is also the time to divide established clumps. Chives clumps benefit from division every 3 to 4 years; mint should be reset every 2 to 3 years to prevent decline. Lift, split, and replant the most vigorous portions; compost the rest.

yield_expectations.per_plant: Continuous harvest all season -- snip and they regrow
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Chives are one of the easiest perennials you can grow. Divide clumps every few years to keep them vigorous.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Chives and mint die back to the ground after the first hard frost -- this is normal and complete. The crowns are deeply hardy (mint to zone 3, chives to zone 4) and survive winter underground without protection. There is no frost damage to worry about; the dieback is the plant's normal life cycle, not a failure.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Expect complete dieback and welcome regrowth in spring. Mulch lightly over the dormant crowns in zones 3 and 4 to insulate against repeated freeze-thaw cycles, but no special protection is needed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Chives can develop allium rust (orange pustules on leaves) in humid summers. Mint occasionally suffers mint rust (similar orange pustules) and verticillium wilt. Aphids cluster on chive flower stalks. Pest pressure is otherwise low -- both herbs deter many insects with their volatile oils.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Cut affected foliage to the ground at first sign of rust -- both crops regrow clean. Remove and destroy verticillium-affected mint plants; do not replant mint in the same spot for 4 years. For aphids, hose off with water or wait for ladybugs to find them.

failure_diagnostics.label: Root rot or yellowing
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: These herbs prefer moist soil but cannot tolerate sustained waterlogging. Symptoms are yellowing leaves and crown rot in poorly-drained soil, especially over winter when growth is dormant.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Improve drainage if soil holds water through winter. Container-grown chives and mint need pots with drainage holes and never need to sit in a saucer of water. Adjust watering by season -- much less in winter, when growth is dormant.

failure_diagnostics.label: Wilting or stunted growth
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Both herbs prefer consistent moisture and stress quickly under drought. Mint especially wilts dramatically when dry -- it usually recovers when watered, but repeated drought stress reduces the harvest and toughens the leaves. Chives in dry soil produces narrow, fibrous leaves.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently. Mulch to retain soil moisture. In hot weather, light afternoon shade benefits both herbs. Mint thrives in moisture conditions that would rot Mediterranean herbs.

failure_diagnostics.label: Leggy growth or weak flavor
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Both herbs prefer full sun but tolerate partial shade -- chives accepts as little as 4 hours of sun, and mint actively prefers afternoon shade in hot climates. In deep shade both grow leggy and lose flavor strength.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun to partial shade. Chives placed in light shade in hot summers stays more tender. Mint in dry sunny spots needs more water; mint in shade needs less.

crops.hardiness_notes: One of the most cold-hardy culinary herbs. Reliably perennial across nearly all US zones. Dies back in winter and returns from clump each spring. Divide every 2-4 years.

fertilizer.notify_message: Time for a light feed for your mint

succession.reason: Perennial -- one planting provides harvests for years. Succession isn't needed.

tasks.description: Cut back hard to 2 inches in fall to prevent woodiness. Divide and replant every 2-3 years to refresh. Contains roots to prevent spreading.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Rosemary beetle
pests.symptoms: Metallic striped beetles eating leaves and flowers. Most active autumn and spring.
pests.cause: Chrysolina americana. Affects lavender, rosemary, sage, thyme, marjoram.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick adults and larvae. Shake over a sheet. Pyrethrum spray.
pests.prevention: Check plants regularly. Avoid hiding spots at base.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms: White coating on leaves. Leaves yellow and drop. Common on sage and mint.
diseases.cause: Various Erysiphe fungi.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Improve airflow. Neem oil spray.
diseases.prevention: Water at soil level. Ensure good spacing.

crops.harvest_ready: Pick stems just before flowering for maximum flavor. Harvest regularly to prevent spreading.

start_method.notes: Easiest from cuttings or division -- mint seeds are unreliable. Grow in containers to prevent spreading.

container_notes.notes: Containers are the preferred way to grow mint -- it spreads aggressively in the ground. Any size pot.

storage.room_temp: 3-5 days in a glass of water like flowers
storage.fridge: 1 week wrapped in damp paper towel
storage.freezer: Blanch briefly, freeze on a tray, bag -- or make mint oil cubes
storage.notes: Mint dries well -- hang bunches upside down for 2 weeks for long-term storage.

varieties.note: Grow each variety in its own container -- mint varieties cross-pollinate and lose their character when mixed.

rotation.avoid_after: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note: Perennial herbs don't need annual rotation, but they can be divided and moved if needed. Choose a permanent-ish spot with the right sun and drainage; plan to divide every 3-4 years to keep plants vigorous.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Plant settling in after planting or propagation.
growth_stages.user_action: Most perennial herbs prefer poor, well-drained soil -- do not over-fertilize. Good drainage is more important than rich soil.

growth_stages.name: Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: New growth appearing, roots establishing.
growth_stages.user_action: Water regularly in the first season to establish roots. Once established, most perennial herbs are drought-tolerant.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Abundant leafy growth -- harvest anytime the plant has plenty.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest by cutting stems back by a third. Never cut into old woody growth on rosemary, sage, and thyme -- they do not regenerate from old wood.

growth_stages.name: Winter
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Plant slowing down or going dormant. Hardy perennials stay evergreen; tender ones die back.
growth_stages.user_action: Give a light haircut before winter to tidy up but avoid heavy pruning -- leave it for spring. Mulch around the base in colder zones.

growth_stages.name: Spring Cutback
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: New green growth beginning to push from the base or lower stems.
growth_stages.user_action: Cut back last year's growth by about half once new growth appears. This annual cutback keeps perennial herbs from going woody and keeps them productive.

notifications.title: Plant your mint in a container
notifications.body: Mint spreads aggressively by underground runners and will take over a bed within a season. Plant in a pot sunk into the ground, or in a dedicated container. This is not optional advice -- it is the most important thing to know about mint.

notifications.title: Cut mint back for winter
notifications.body: Cut mint back hard to a few inches above the soil as it dies back in autumn. It will come back strongly from the roots in spring. Mulch the container or bed to protect the roots in colder zones.

weather_triggers.body: Basil, cilantro, and lemongrass are extremely frost-tender. Bring containers inside or cover with fleece tonight. Hardy herbs like thyme, rosemary, and mint are much more frost-tolerant.

fertilizer.notes: Light feeder -- excess feeding reduces aromatic oils. One light feed in spring when growth begins is all that's needed.
fertilizer.npk_hint: low N -- over-feeding reduces flavor intensity

succession.reason: Perennial herb -- one plant produces year after year.

tasks.description: Cut back by one-third in spring as new growth emerges. Never cut into woody stems. Replace plants every 4-5 years as productivity declines.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Rosemary beetle
pests.symptoms: Metallic striped beetles eating leaves and flowers. Most active autumn and spring.
pests.cause: Chrysolina americana. Affects lavender, rosemary, sage, thyme, marjoram.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick adults and larvae. Shake over a sheet. Pyrethrum spray.
pests.prevention: Check plants regularly. Avoid hiding spots at base.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms: White coating on leaves. Leaves yellow and drop. Common on sage and mint.
diseases.cause: Various Erysiphe fungi.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Improve airflow. Neem oil spray.
diseases.prevention: Water at soil level. Ensure good spacing.

watering.signs_overwater: Root rot, yellowing -- very common mistake

crops.harvest_ready: Pick before flowering. Morning harvest when oils are highest.

rotation.avoid_after: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note: Perennial herbs don't need annual rotation, but they can be divided and moved if needed. Choose a permanent-ish spot with the right sun and drainage; plan to divide every 3-4 years to keep plants vigorous.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Plant settling in after planting or propagation.
growth_stages.user_action: Most perennial herbs prefer poor, well-drained soil -- do not over-fertilize. Good drainage is more important than rich soil.

growth_stages.name: Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: New growth appearing, roots establishing.
growth_stages.user_action: Water regularly in the first season to establish roots. Once established, most perennial herbs are drought-tolerant.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Abundant leafy growth -- harvest anytime the plant has plenty.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest by cutting stems back by a third. Never cut into old woody growth on rosemary, sage, and thyme -- they do not regenerate from old wood.

growth_stages.name: Winter
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Plant slowing down or going dormant. Hardy perennials stay evergreen; tender ones die back.
growth_stages.user_action: Give a light haircut before winter to tidy up but avoid heavy pruning -- leave it for spring. Mulch around the base in colder zones.

growth_stages.name: Spring Cutback
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: New green growth beginning to push from the base or lower stems.
growth_stages.user_action: Cut back last year's growth by about half once new growth appears. This annual cutback keeps perennial herbs from going woody and keeps them productive.

notifications.title: Spring cutback time for your herbs
notifications.body: Once new growth is clearly showing, cut back last year's growth by about half. Always cut into green growth -- never into old brown wood on rosemary, sage, and thyme, as they do not regenerate from old wood. This annual trim keeps your herbs productive and compact.

notifications.title: Harvest your herbs before they flower
notifications.body: The flavor of most culinary herbs is strongest just before they flower. Harvest generous amounts now -- dry, freeze, or use fresh. Once flowers open the essential oil content changes.

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- protect tender herbs
weather_triggers.body: Basil, cilantro, and lemongrass are extremely frost-tender. Bring containers inside or cover with fleece tonight. Hardy herbs like thyme, rosemary, and mint are much more frost-tolerant.

weather_triggers.title: Heat alert -- herbs may bolt
weather_triggers.body: Heat triggers bolting in cilantro, dill, and parsley. Harvest as much as possible before temperatures peak. Basil, on the other hand, loves heat -- just remove any flowers that appear.

planting.text: Mediterranean herbs prefer poor, well-drained soil and full sun. Skip the compost amendment and the rich potting mix -- these herbs evolved on dry rocky hillsides and produce stronger flavor on lean soil. A handful of grit or coarse sand in the planting hole helps drainage.
Plant in spring after the last frost, or in fall in mild-winter zones. Space generously -- mature rosemary and sage can spread 3 to 4 feet across; thyme and oregano spread by creeping stems.

establishment.text: Water regularly through the first season to establish roots, then step back. Established Mediterranean herbs need very little supplemental water and actively dislike consistently moist soil.
Mulch with gravel or coarse sand around the base rather than organic mulch -- organic mulch holds moisture against the crown and invites rot in these herbs.

harvest.text: Harvest by snipping the top 2 to 3 inches of stem rather than pulling individual leaves. Regular harvest encourages bushy compact growth; unharvested plants become woody and sparse.
Harvest is most intense in early-to-mid summer when leaves carry peak essential oil. A morning harvest after dew has dried but before the heat of the day captures the strongest flavor.

winter.text: Hardy Mediterranean herbs (thyme, oregano, sage, hardy rosemary varieties) overwinter outdoors through USDA zone 6 or 7 and can be harvested through mild winters -- the leaves stay green and usable. Less-hardy rosemary varieties need protection or container culture in zones 6 and below.
Avoid wet feet in winter -- waterlogged dormant roots are the most common cause of Mediterranean herb death. A thick gravel mulch and excellent drainage matter more in winter than in summer.

spring_cutback.text: In early spring before new growth starts, cut back about a third of the previous year's growth. Never cut into old brown wood -- new growth comes only from green-stemmed wood, and a hard cut into the woody base often kills the plant.

Older plants (4 to 5 years and up) become woody and sparse despite annual cutback. When the woody portion exceeds the productive portion, replace the plant rather than trying to rejuvenate it -- propagate replacements from cuttings the previous fall.

yield_expectations.per_plant: Generous continuous harvest from established plants
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Thyme is one of the hardiest and most forgiving of all herbs. Once established it looks after itself.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Cold or winter damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Mediterranean herbs vary widely in cold tolerance. Thyme and oregano are hardy through USDA zone 4 or 5. Hardy sage varieties survive zone 5; tender varieties only zone 7. Common rosemary is reliably hardy only to zone 7 or 8; hardy varieties (Arp, Madeline Hill) extend to zone 6 with protection. Cold damage shows as blackened tips and dieback the following spring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Confirm your variety's hardiness range and choose hardy varieties for cold zones. In marginal zones, plant on the south side of a wall or in a sheltered spot, and mulch crown with gravel before winter. For rosemary in zones 5 and below, treat as a container plant and overwinter indoors near a sunny window.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Mediterranean herbs are remarkably pest-resistant -- their essential oils deter most insects and they evolved without typical garden pest pressure. The main problems are root rot (from too much water), powdery mildew (in humid conditions or shade), and spider mites (in dry hot conditions, especially indoors).
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Improve drainage and reduce watering -- nearly all disease problems on Mediterranean herbs trace back to wet feet. Increase airflow with light pruning. For spider mites on indoor plants, increase humidity and rinse foliage occasionally.

failure_diagnostics.label: Root rot
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Root rot from overwatering or poor drainage is the single most common killer of Mediterranean herbs. Symptoms are yellowing leaves at the base, sudden wilting despite moist soil, and a rotten smell at the crown. The damage is often irreversible by the time symptoms show.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil, on a slope or raised bed if necessary. Water only when the top 2 inches of soil are dry; in cool weather and through winter, water rarely or not at all. Use gravel mulch instead of organic mulch.

failure_diagnostics.label: Wilting or leaf drop
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Mediterranean herbs are drought-tolerant but not drought-immune. Severe drought during the first establishing season kills young plants. Established plants drop older leaves as a normal response to prolonged drought; this is recoverable but reduces the harvest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water young plants regularly through their first season. Established plants need water only during prolonged dry spells -- a deep watering once every 2 to 3 weeks is plenty. A well-established Mediterranean herb thrives on neglect once roots are deep.

failure_diagnostics.label: Leggy or weak growth
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: These herbs need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to develop strong essential oils and compact growth. In partial shade plants stretch toward the light, become leggy and floppy, lose their characteristic flavor intensity, and become more disease-prone.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun. If your only sunny spots are filled, container-grown Mediterranean herbs do well on a sunny patio or balcony. Move pots seasonally to track the sun if needed.

crops.hardiness_notes: English / common thyme is reliably perennial in Z4-Z9. French thyme is less hardy (Z6+). Needs well-drained soil; wet winter roots cause more losses than cold.

crops.name: Dill
crops.description: Fast, feathery, and self-seeding. Plant once and you'll have it forever -- it reseeds prolifically. Harvest young leaves for flavor; let some plants set seed for pickling.

fertilizer.notes: Light feeder. A single balanced feed at planting is sufficient. Over-feeding reduces aromatic oils.
fertilizer.notify_message: Light feed time for your dill

succession.tip: Sow every 3 weeks from spring through midsummer. Dill bolts in heat but more slowly than cilantro -- you get 4-6 weeks of good leaf production before flowering. Succession keeps a supply of fresh feathery fronds through the season. Note that dill at different stages serves different purposes: young plants for fronds, mature plants for flower heads (great with cucumbers), seeds for pickling. Plan your succession with the end use in mind.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Carrot fly
pests.symptoms: Root damage and wilting. Cilantro and dill are in carrot family and attract same pests.
pests.cause: Psila rosae. Affects all members of the carrot family.
pests.organic_treatment: Grow under fine insect mesh.
pests.prevention: Insect mesh. Grow away from carrots and parsnips.

diseases.name: Leaf spot
diseases.symptoms: Dark brown spots on leaves. Affected leaves yellow and die.
diseases.cause: Bacterial or fungal leaf spot. Favored by wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Copper-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention: Water at soil level. Good spacing.

crops.harvest_ready: Pick feathery leaves any time. For seeds, wait until seed heads turn brown.

start_method.notes: Direct sow -- taproots dislike disturbance. Succession sow every 3 weeks.

container_notes.notes: Works in deep pots (taproot). 8-12 inches deep minimum. Can grow tall -- stake if needed.

storage.freezer: Freeze fronds dry on a tray, then bag -- very good. Or freeze in oil cubes.
storage.notes: Dried dill loses flavor quickly. Freezing is better for preserving the green, fresh taste.

varieties.note: Fernleaf is the best container dill -- compact and slower to bolt than standard varieties.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small seedlings emerging. Annual herbs germinate readily in warm conditions.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep soil consistently moist. Most annual herbs germinate better in warmth -- 65-75°F is ideal.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: True leaves developing -- already recognizable as the herb you planted.
growth_stages.user_action: Thin to 6-9 inches. The thinnings are edible -- add them to salads.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: A bushy, fragrant plant ready for regular harvesting.
growth_stages.user_action: Begin harvesting by pinching out the growing tips -- this encourages bushy side growth rather than a tall, lanky plant.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Plenty of leafy growth, plant not yet showing flowering stems.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest little and often by pinching growing tips. Never remove more than a third of the plant at once. Regular harvesting is what keeps herbs producing.

growth_stages.name: Bolting / Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Central flower stem shooting up. Leaves becoming smaller and flavor intensifying or turning bitter depending on the herb.
growth_stages.user_action: Remove flower stems immediately on basil to extend harvest. For cilantro and dill, flowering is part of the lifecycle -- collect seeds for cooking or sowing.

notifications.title: Cilantro bolting -- sow your next batch
notifications.body: Cilantro bolts fast, especially in warm weather. When you see the first flower stem, sow your next batch immediately. Succession sowing every 3-4 weeks is the only way to have continuous cilantro through the season.

notifications.title: Cilantro seeds -- coriander for cooking
notifications.body: The seeds of bolted cilantro are coriander -- a completely different flavor and equally useful in the kitchen. Let some plants go to seed, collect them when the plant dries and browns, and use them whole or ground.

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- protect tender herbs
weather_triggers.body: Basil, cilantro, and lemongrass are extremely frost-tender. Bring containers inside or cover with fleece tonight. Hardy herbs like thyme, rosemary, and mint are much more frost-tolerant.

weather_triggers.title: Heat alert -- herbs may bolt
weather_triggers.body: Heat triggers bolting in cilantro, dill, and parsley. Harvest as much as possible before temperatures peak. Basil, on the other hand, loves heat -- just remove any flowers that appear.

germination.text: These herbs are direct-sown or started indoors. Basil needs warm soil (70 degrees) for germination; dill and cilantro tolerate cooler soil (55 to 60 degrees) and actually germinate better in cool weather.
Sow shallowly -- 1/4 inch deep -- and keep soil surface moist. Cilantro and dill can be sown in succession every 2 to 3 weeks for continuous harvest, since both bolt fast.

seedling.text: Thin to recommended spacing once seedlings have 2 true leaves -- crowded plants bolt faster and produce less leaf. Pinch basil tops at 6 inches to encourage branching.
These herbs all benefit from light afternoon shade in hot summer climates. Cilantro especially bolts within weeks of warm weather hitting.

established.text: Pinch basil regularly to prevent flowering -- once basil flowers, leaf production slows and flavor changes. Removing flower buds extends the productive harvest by weeks.
Water consistently. Wilted plants recover but the stress accelerates bolting in cilantro and dill. Mulch to stabilize soil moisture.

harvest.text: Harvest by snipping outer leaves first, leaving the central growing tip intact. For basil, cut whole stems above a leaf pair to encourage two new shoots from each cut.
Cilantro is harvested as leaves OR seed (coriander). Same plant, same cycle: harvest leaves while plant is leafy, let it bolt, harvest dry seeds from the spent flower heads.

bolting.text: Bolting (going to flower) signals the end of useful leaf production for these herbs. Basil bolts in heat or after flowering; dill and cilantro bolt fast in any warm weather.

Once bolting starts, decide: pinch flowers to extend leaf harvest by 1 to 2 weeks (basil), or let the plant flower and self-seed for next year (dill, cilantro). Bolted cilantro is often the original planting and reseeds prolifically.

yield_expectations.per_plant: Generous leaf harvest before bolting, then seeds for cooking
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Dill self-seeds prolifically -- once you grow it, you may have it forever.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Basil is killed outright by light frost -- it is the most frost-sensitive culinary herb. Dill and cilantro are hardier; both tolerate light frost and cilantro actually grows better in cool weather. Basil also suffers chill damage (leaf blackening) below 50 degrees even without frost.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Wait to plant basil until soil is reliably 60 degrees and night temperatures stay above 50. For dill and cilantro, sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring -- they prefer cool conditions. Have row cover ready for cold nights with basil; in the fall, harvest basil heavily before the first cold snap because the plants will not recover.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Aphids cluster on tender new growth across all three. Basil downy mildew is the headline disease (yellowing and gray fuzz on leaf undersides) and has spread aggressively in recent years. Dill and cilantro may attract carrot family pests (carrot rust fly larvae, leaf miner). Powdery mildew occasionally hits all three in humid summers.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Choose downy-mildew-resistant basil varieties -- Rutgers Devotion DMR, Prospera, and similar bred for resistance. Space plants well for airflow. Hose off aphids with water; for serious infestations, insecticidal soap. Rotate herb-bed location each year.

failure_diagnostics.label: Root rot or yellowing
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: All three herbs need well-drained soil. Persistent waterlogging causes root rot, yellowing leaves, and crown collapse. Basil is especially sensitive to wet conditions and may collapse suddenly from Pythium or Fusarium in poorly-drained sites.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil. Use containers with drainage holes for indoor or balcony herbs. Water at the base, not overhead, and let the soil surface dry slightly between waterings. Avoid heavy clay sites for basil especially.

failure_diagnostics.label: Wilting or rapid bolting
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress accelerates bolting in cilantro and dill -- often by weeks -- and produces small, tough basil leaves with concentrated bitter flavor. Wilted herbs recover with watering but the stress shortens the productive cycle.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently, especially in heat. Mulch around plants to retain soil moisture. For cilantro and dill, succession-plant every 2 to 3 weeks rather than relying on one planting through the season -- this gives you continuous harvest even as individual plantings bolt.

failure_diagnostics.label: Leggy or sparse growth
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: These herbs need 6 hours of direct sun minimum for full flavor and growth. In partial shade, plants grow tall, leggy, and pale, with weaker flavor. Cilantro is a partial exception -- it tolerates partial shade in hot zones, where light shade actually slows bolting.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun in cool climates. In hot climates (zone 8 and warmer), cilantro and parsley tolerate and even prefer light afternoon shade. Basil and dill want full sun even in heat. For indoor growing, herbs need a sunny south-facing window or supplemental grow lights.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Plant settling in after planting or propagation.
growth_stages.user_action: Most perennial herbs prefer poor, well-drained soil -- do not over-fertilize. Good drainage is more important than rich soil.

growth_stages.name: Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: New growth appearing, roots establishing.
growth_stages.user_action: Water regularly in the first season to establish roots. Once established, most perennial herbs are drought-tolerant.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Abundant leafy growth -- harvest anytime the plant has plenty.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest by cutting stems back by a third. Never cut into old woody growth on rosemary, sage, and thyme -- they do not regenerate from old wood.

growth_stages.name: Winter
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Plant slowing down or going dormant. Hardy perennials stay evergreen; tender ones die back.
growth_stages.user_action: Give a light haircut before winter to tidy up but avoid heavy pruning -- leave it for spring. Mulch around the base in colder zones.

growth_stages.name: Spring Cutback
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: New green growth beginning to push from the base or lower stems.
growth_stages.user_action: Cut back last year's growth by about half once new growth appears. This annual cutback keeps perennial herbs from going woody and keeps them productive.

notifications.title: Prune your rosemary in spring
notifications.body: Trim rosemary back by a third once new growth begins in spring. Cut back to healthy green growth -- never into old brown wood, which does not regenerate. Regular light pruning keeps rosemary compact and productive for years.

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- protect tender herbs
weather_triggers.body: Basil, cilantro, and lemongrass are extremely frost-tender. Bring containers inside or cover with fleece tonight. Hardy herbs like thyme, rosemary, and mint are much more frost-tolerant.

weather_triggers.title: Heat alert -- herbs may bolt
weather_triggers.body: Heat triggers bolting in cilantro, dill, and parsley. Harvest as much as possible before temperatures peak. Basil, on the other hand, loves heat -- just remove any flowers that appear.

planting.text: Mediterranean herbs prefer poor, well-drained soil and full sun. Skip the compost amendment and the rich potting mix -- these herbs evolved on dry rocky hillsides and produce stronger flavor on lean soil. A handful of grit or coarse sand in the planting hole helps drainage.
Plant in spring after the last frost, or in fall in mild-winter zones. Space generously -- mature rosemary and sage can spread 3 to 4 feet across; thyme and oregano spread by creeping stems.

establishment.text: Water regularly through the first season to establish roots, then step back. Established Mediterranean herbs need very little supplemental water and actively dislike consistently moist soil.
Mulch with gravel or coarse sand around the base rather than organic mulch -- organic mulch holds moisture against the crown and invites rot in these herbs.

harvest.text: Harvest by snipping the top 2 to 3 inches of stem rather than pulling individual leaves. Regular harvest encourages bushy compact growth; unharvested plants become woody and sparse.
Harvest is most intense in early-to-mid summer when leaves carry peak essential oil. A morning harvest after dew has dried but before the heat of the day captures the strongest flavor.

winter.text: Hardy Mediterranean herbs (thyme, oregano, sage, hardy rosemary varieties) overwinter outdoors through USDA zone 6 or 7 and can be harvested through mild winters -- the leaves stay green and usable. Less-hardy rosemary varieties need protection or container culture in zones 6 and below.
Avoid wet feet in winter -- waterlogged dormant roots are the most common cause of Mediterranean herb death. A thick gravel mulch and excellent drainage matter more in winter than in summer.

spring_cutback.text: In early spring before new growth starts, cut back about a third of the previous year's growth. Never cut into old brown wood -- new growth comes only from green-stemmed wood, and a hard cut into the woody base often kills the plant.

Older plants (4 to 5 years and up) become woody and sparse despite annual cutback. When the woody portion exceeds the productive portion, replace the plant rather than trying to rejuvenate it -- propagate replacements from cuttings the previous fall.

failure_diagnostics.label: Cold or winter damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Mediterranean herbs vary widely in cold tolerance. Thyme and oregano are hardy through USDA zone 4 or 5. Hardy sage varieties survive zone 5; tender varieties only zone 7. Common rosemary is reliably hardy only to zone 7 or 8; hardy varieties (Arp, Madeline Hill) extend to zone 6 with protection. Cold damage shows as blackened tips and dieback the following spring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Confirm your variety's hardiness range and choose hardy varieties for cold zones. In marginal zones, plant on the south side of a wall or in a sheltered spot, and mulch crown with gravel before winter. For rosemary in zones 5 and below, treat as a container plant and overwinter indoors near a sunny window.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Mediterranean herbs are remarkably pest-resistant -- their essential oils deter most insects and they evolved without typical garden pest pressure. The main problems are root rot (from too much water), powdery mildew (in humid conditions or shade), and spider mites (in dry hot conditions, especially indoors).
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Improve drainage and reduce watering -- nearly all disease problems on Mediterranean herbs trace back to wet feet. Increase airflow with light pruning. For spider mites on indoor plants, increase humidity and rinse foliage occasionally.

failure_diagnostics.label: Root rot
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Root rot from overwatering or poor drainage is the single most common killer of Mediterranean herbs. Symptoms are yellowing leaves at the base, sudden wilting despite moist soil, and a rotten smell at the crown. The damage is often irreversible by the time symptoms show.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil, on a slope or raised bed if necessary. Water only when the top 2 inches of soil are dry; in cool weather and through winter, water rarely or not at all. Use gravel mulch instead of organic mulch.

failure_diagnostics.label: Wilting or leaf drop
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Mediterranean herbs are drought-tolerant but not drought-immune. Severe drought during the first establishing season kills young plants. Established plants drop older leaves as a normal response to prolonged drought; this is recoverable but reduces the harvest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water young plants regularly through their first season. Established plants need water only during prolonged dry spells -- a deep watering once every 2 to 3 weeks is plenty. A well-established Mediterranean herb thrives on neglect once roots are deep.

failure_diagnostics.label: Leggy or weak growth
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: These herbs need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to develop strong essential oils and compact growth. In partial shade plants stretch toward the light, become leggy and floppy, lose their characteristic flavor intensity, and become more disease-prone.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun. If your only sunny spots are filled, container-grown Mediterranean herbs do well on a sunny patio or balcony. Move pots seasonally to track the sun if needed.

growth_stages.user_action: Water regularly in the first season to establish roots. Once established, most perennial herbs are drought-tolerant.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Abundant leafy growth -- harvest anytime the plant has plenty.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest by cutting stems back by a third. Never cut into old woody growth on rosemary, sage, and thyme -- they do not regenerate from old wood.

growth_stages.name: Winter
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Plant slowing down or going dormant. Hardy perennials stay evergreen; tender ones die back.
growth_stages.user_action: Give a light haircut before winter to tidy up but avoid heavy pruning -- leave it for spring. Mulch around the base in colder zones.

growth_stages.name: Spring Cutback
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: New green growth beginning to push from the base or lower stems.
growth_stages.user_action: Cut back last year's growth by about half once new growth appears. This annual cutback keeps perennial herbs from going woody and keeps them productive.

notifications.title: Spring cutback time for your herbs
notifications.body: Once new growth is clearly showing, cut back last year's growth by about half. Always cut into green growth -- never into old brown wood on rosemary, sage, and thyme, as they do not regenerate from old wood. This annual trim keeps your herbs productive and compact.

notifications.title: Harvest your herbs before they flower
notifications.body: The flavor of most culinary herbs is strongest just before they flower. Harvest generous amounts now -- dry, freeze, or use fresh. Once flowers open the essential oil content changes.

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- protect tender herbs
weather_triggers.body: Basil, cilantro, and lemongrass are extremely frost-tender. Bring containers inside or cover with fleece tonight. Hardy herbs like thyme, rosemary, and mint are much more frost-tolerant.

weather_triggers.title: Heat alert -- herbs may bolt
weather_triggers.body: Heat triggers bolting in cilantro, dill, and parsley. Harvest as much as possible before temperatures peak. Basil, on the other hand, loves heat -- just remove any flowers that appear.

planting.text: Mediterranean herbs prefer poor, well-drained soil and full sun. Skip the compost amendment and the rich potting mix -- these herbs evolved on dry rocky hillsides and produce stronger flavor on lean soil. A handful of grit or coarse sand in the planting hole helps drainage.
Plant in spring after the last frost, or in fall in mild-winter zones. Space generously -- mature rosemary and sage can spread 3 to 4 feet across; thyme and oregano spread by creeping stems.

establishment.text: Water regularly through the first season to establish roots, then step back. Established Mediterranean herbs need very little supplemental water and actively dislike consistently moist soil.
Mulch with gravel or coarse sand around the base rather than organic mulch -- organic mulch holds moisture against the crown and invites rot in these herbs.

harvest.text: Harvest by snipping the top 2 to 3 inches of stem rather than pulling individual leaves. Regular harvest encourages bushy compact growth; unharvested plants become woody and sparse.
Harvest is most intense in early-to-mid summer when leaves carry peak essential oil. A morning harvest after dew has dried but before the heat of the day captures the strongest flavor.

winter.text: Hardy Mediterranean herbs (thyme, oregano, sage, hardy rosemary varieties) overwinter outdoors through USDA zone 6 or 7 and can be harvested through mild winters -- the leaves stay green and usable. Less-hardy rosemary varieties need protection or container culture in zones 6 and below.
Avoid wet feet in winter -- waterlogged dormant roots are the most common cause of Mediterranean herb death. A thick gravel mulch and excellent drainage matter more in winter than in summer.

spring_cutback.text: In early spring before new growth starts, cut back about a third of the previous year's growth. Never cut into old brown wood -- new growth comes only from green-stemmed wood, and a hard cut into the woody base often kills the plant.

Older plants (4 to 5 years and up) become woody and sparse despite annual cutback. When the woody portion exceeds the productive portion, replace the plant rather than trying to rejuvenate it -- propagate replacements from cuttings the previous fall.

yield_expectations.per_plant: Generous harvest, best before flowering
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Greek oregano varieties have the strongest flavor. Harvest before the flowers open for maximum essential oil content.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Cold or winter damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Mediterranean herbs vary widely in cold tolerance. Thyme and oregano are hardy through USDA zone 4 or 5. Hardy sage varieties survive zone 5; tender varieties only zone 7. Common rosemary is reliably hardy only to zone 7 or 8; hardy varieties (Arp, Madeline Hill) extend to zone 6 with protection. Cold damage shows as blackened tips and dieback the following spring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Confirm your variety's hardiness range and choose hardy varieties for cold zones. In marginal zones, plant on the south side of a wall or in a sheltered spot, and mulch crown with gravel before winter. For rosemary in zones 5 and below, treat as a container plant and overwinter indoors near a sunny window.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Mediterranean herbs are remarkably pest-resistant -- their essential oils deter most insects and they evolved without typical garden pest pressure. The main problems are root rot (from too much water), powdery mildew (in humid conditions or shade), and spider mites (in dry hot conditions, especially indoors).
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Improve drainage and reduce watering -- nearly all disease problems on Mediterranean herbs trace back to wet feet. Increase airflow with light pruning. For spider mites on indoor plants, increase humidity and rinse foliage occasionally.

failure_diagnostics.label: Root rot
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Root rot from overwatering or poor drainage is the single most common killer of Mediterranean herbs. Symptoms are yellowing leaves at the base, sudden wilting despite moist soil, and a rotten smell at the crown. The damage is often irreversible by the time symptoms show.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil, on a slope or raised bed if necessary. Water only when the top 2 inches of soil are dry; in cool weather and through winter, water rarely or not at all. Use gravel mulch instead of organic mulch.

failure_diagnostics.label: Wilting or leaf drop
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Mediterranean herbs are drought-tolerant but not drought-immune. Severe drought during the first establishing season kills young plants. Established plants drop older leaves as a normal response to prolonged drought; this is recoverable but reduces the harvest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water young plants regularly through their first season. Established plants need water only during prolonged dry spells -- a deep watering once every 2 to 3 weeks is plenty. A well-established Mediterranean herb thrives on neglect once roots are deep.

failure_diagnostics.label: Leggy or weak growth
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: These herbs need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to develop strong essential oils and compact growth. In partial shade plants stretch toward the light, become leggy and floppy, lose their characteristic flavor intensity, and become more disease-prone.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun. If your only sunny spots are filled, container-grown Mediterranean herbs do well on a sunny patio or balcony. Move pots seasonally to track the sun if needed.

fertilizer.npk_hint: low N -- poor soil actually improves flavor

succession.reason: Perennial herb. One plant produces for many years.

tasks.description: Prune lightly in spring after new growth appears. Remove about one-third of growth. Replace every 4-5 years when plants become woody and unproductive.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Rosemary beetle
pests.symptoms: Metallic striped beetles eating leaves and flowers. Most active autumn and spring.
pests.cause: Chrysolina americana. Affects lavender, rosemary, sage, thyme, marjoram.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick adults and larvae. Shake over a sheet. Pyrethrum spray.
pests.prevention: Check plants regularly. Avoid hiding spots at base.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms: White coating on leaves. Leaves yellow and drop. Common on sage and mint.
diseases.cause: Various Erysiphe fungi.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Improve airflow. Neem oil spray.
diseases.prevention: Water at soil level. Ensure good spacing.

crops.harvest_ready: Pick young leaves before flowering. Most flavorful in spring.

start_method.notes: Start 6-8 weeks before last frost or buy plants. Harden off over 7 days.

storage.freezer: Freeze leaves individually on a tray then bag -- or fry in butter and freeze
