failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Mediterranean herbs are drought-tolerant but not drought-immune. Severe drought during the first establishing season kills young plants. Established plants drop older leaves as a normal response to prolonged drought; this is recoverable but reduces the harvest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water young plants regularly through their first season. Established plants need water only during prolonged dry spells -- a deep watering once every 2 to 3 weeks is plenty. A well-established Mediterranean herb thrives on neglect once roots are deep.

failure_diagnostics.label: Leggy or weak growth
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: These herbs need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to develop strong essential oils and compact growth. In partial shade plants stretch toward the light, become leggy and floppy, lose their characteristic flavor intensity, and become more disease-prone.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun. If your only sunny spots are filled, container-grown Mediterranean herbs do well on a sunny patio or balcony. Move pots seasonally to track the sun if needed.

fertilizer.timing: switch to high-potassium at first flower
fertilizer.notes: Heavy feeder like peppers and tomatoes. Start with balanced feed, switch to high-potassium when flowers appear. Consistent feeding produces larger, more tender fruit.

succession.reason: Long DTM (70-85 days) and produces continuously from one planting. Succession isn't practical.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Tomato hornworm
pests.symptoms: Large green caterpillars (up to 4 inches) stripping foliage. Leaves disappear rapidly. Black droppings on leaves.
pests.cause: Manduca quinquemaculata moth larvae. Mid to late summer pest.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick -- they are well camouflaged but easy to remove. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray. If white cocoons visible on back, leave them -- parasitic wasps are doing the work.
pests.prevention: Till soil in autumn to kill overwintering pupae. Plant dill and basil nearby to attract predatory wasps.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms: Tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings and young plants. Small shiny black beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause: Multiple flea beetle species. Most active in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment: Use row covers on seedlings. Apply diatomaceous earth. Neem oil spray.
pests.prevention: Delay transplanting until plants are large. Use transplants rather than seeds.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Early blight
diseases.symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings on lower leaves first. Affected leaves yellow and drop. Spreads upward through plant.
diseases.cause: Alternaria fungus. Favored by warm wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves immediately. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively. Mulch soil to prevent splash-up.
diseases.prevention: Rotate tomatoes every 3-4 years. Water at soil level. Space plants for airflow. Stake to keep foliage off ground.

diseases.name: Blossom end rot
diseases.symptoms: Dark, sunken, leathery patch at the bottom (blossom end) of fruit. Affects first fruits most. Not contagious.
diseases.cause: Calcium deficiency in developing fruit, caused by irregular watering or root damage -- not a pest or disease.
diseases.organic_treatment: Mulch to maintain even soil moisture. Water consistently. Foliar calcium spray provides some relief. Remove affected fruit.
diseases.prevention: Consistent watering is the key prevention. Avoid root disturbance. Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen.

diseases.name: Septoria leaf spot
diseases.symptoms: Small circular spots with dark borders and pale gray centers, starting on lower leaves. Spots may have yellow halos.
diseases.cause: Septoria lycopersici fungus. One of the most common tomato diseases.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Apply copper fungicide. Ensure good air circulation.
diseases.prevention: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Mulch around plants.

diseases.name: Late blight
diseases.symptoms: Water-soaked, rapidly expanding brown patches on leaves and stems. White fuzzy growth on undersides in humid conditions. Can destroy plants in days.
diseases.cause: Phytophthora infestans oomycete. The same pathogen that caused the Irish potato famine. Spreads rapidly in cool wet weather.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove and destroy all affected material immediately -- do not compost. Apply copper fungicide preventively in wet conditions.
diseases.prevention: Plant resistant varieties. Ensure excellent airflow. Never leave tomato debris in the garden over winter.

crops.harvest_ready: Skin is shiny and tight. Flesh yields slightly when pressed and springs back. Dull skin means over-mature and bitter.

start_method.notes: Start 8-10 weeks before last frost. Eggplant loves heat -- don't rush transplanting.

rotation.avoid_after: Tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes -- all share blight and fusarium diseases
rotation.note: Always rotate nightshades to a fresh bed -- blight and fusarium can persist in soil for years.

storage.freezer: Roast/cook first, then freeze -- raw frozen eggplant is poor quality
storage.notes: Eggplant deteriorates rapidly. Cook it or freeze as a cooked dish (baba ganoush, caponata).

varieties.note: Ichiban is excellent for beginners -- sets fruit in cool conditions better than many varieties, very prolific.

good.name: Marigolds
good.why: Deter Colorado beetle, nematodes, and aphids

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. The nematode component is extension-documented. The claim's additional assertions about deterring aphids, Colorado beetle are not supported in the extension literature on marigolds and should be read as traditional.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension 2022 and 2025 Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetable Crops; UConn IPM 'Perimeter Trap Cropping for Cole Crops'). Nasturtiums specifically are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and Utah State University Extension (Mohr et al., 'Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting'). Protocol caveat: UConn IPM explicitly notes trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents' -- so the aphid application here has a protocol-mismatch concern even though the companion is extension-named. The Cornell-IPM-specific attribution in earlier catalog reason text was not located in Cornell's published IPM material; actual backing is WSU/USU/UConn.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Pest-deterrent claim without matching established pattern. Default to traditional pending review.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Structural-category claim has a mechanistic basis. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small seedlings emerging. Eggplant germinates more slowly than tomatoes.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep at 80-85°F. Heat mat essential. Eggplant is even more heat-demanding than peppers at germination.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: True leaves with a distinctive purple sheen on the underside.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep consistently warm. Eggplant is slow -- do not worry if progress seems minimal in the first few weeks.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Compact, sturdy plant ready for outdoor conditions.
growth_stages.user_action: Do not transplant until nights are reliably above 60°F. Eggplant is more cold-sensitive than peppers.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Purple star-shaped flowers with yellow centers.
growth_stages.user_action: Feed with a high-potassium fertilizer. Tap flowering stems gently to aid pollination.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Glossy, firm skin -- harvest before the shine fades. Eggplant past its prime becomes bitter and seedy.
growth_stages.user_action: Cut rather than pull -- eggplants have thorny calyx. Use secateurs. Pick when the skin is shiny and the fruit gives slightly to pressure.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Slowing fruit set, smaller fruit, nights cooling below 55 degrees F.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest any remaining fruit before first frost -- eggplant does not ripen off the plant. Pull and compost spent plants; the stems can be tough so chop or shred before composting.
growth_stages.log_prompt: How was your eggplant season? Worth logging what worked.

notifications.title: Start your eggplant indoors -- 10 weeks before last frost
notifications.body: Eggplant is even slower than peppers and needs 10-12 weeks indoors. Start now with a heat mat at 80-85°F. They are rewarding once established but demand patience early on.

weather_triggers.title: Cold snap -- protect your eggplant
weather_triggers.body: Eggplant is more cold-sensitive than any other common vegetable. Even temperatures in the 50s at night slow them significantly. Cover with fleece tonight.

germination.text: Eggplant needs warm soil to germinate -- 75 to 85 degrees is the sweet spot. Start indoors 8 to 10 weeks before last frost; eggplant is even more heat-loving than peppers and gets a slow start.
Use a heat mat under the seed tray for reliable germination -- room temperature is too cold for fast germination. Seedlings emerge in 7 to 14 days at the right temperature.

seedling.text: Pot up seedlings to 4-inch pots once they have 2 true leaves. Eggplant resents cold and slow growth; keep seedlings warm (70+ degrees day, 60+ night) until transplant.
Harden off slowly over 7 to 10 days before transplanting outdoors. Eggplant transplanted into cold soil sulks for weeks and may never fully recover.

established.text: Transplant outdoors only after night temperatures stay reliably above 55 degrees and soil reaches 65. Black plastic mulch and row cover help substantially in cool zones.
Eggplant prefers more consistent soil moisture than peppers -- closer to tomato needs. Water deeply 1 to 2 times per week and mulch heavily. Side-dress with compost or balanced fertilizer mid-season.

harvest.text: Pick eggplant when the skin is glossy and the fruit feels firm but yields slightly to thumb pressure. Dull skin means the fruit is overripe -- the seeds inside have hardened and the flesh has turned bitter.
Use pruners or a sharp knife to cut the stem cleanly -- eggplant stems are tough and twisting damages the plant. Harvest every 3 to 5 days during peak production to encourage continued fruit set.

end_of_season.text: Eggplant production drops as nights cool below 55 degrees. Harvest all developing fruit before first expected frost -- frost kills the plant and damages fruit.
Pull and compost spent plants. Rotate eggplant to a new bed each year; avoid planting in any spot where tomato, pepper, or potato grew last year (Solanaceae rotation).

yield_expectations.per_plant: 4-8 fruits per plant over the season
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Eggplant is challenging in cooler climates but deeply satisfying when it works.
yield_expectations.peak_production: A productive plant front-loads in late summer -- expect a steady run of fruit for 4 to 6 weeks before cooler nights slow it down.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Eggplant is one of the most heat-loving and frost-sensitive vegetables. Cold soil at transplant (below 65 degrees) stunts plants for the rest of the season. Light frost kills the plant outright. Cool nights below 55 degrees during fruit set reduce yield substantially even without frost.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Wait to transplant until soil reaches 65 degrees and night temperatures stay above 55. Use black plastic mulch to warm soil and row cover for the first weeks. In short-season zones, choose early-maturing varieties (Patio Baby, Hansel) and start indoors 8 to 10 weeks before transplant date.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Flea beetles are the headline eggplant pest -- they make countless tiny shotholes in leaves, especially on young plants. Heavy flea-beetle damage on seedlings can kill plants outright. Colorado potato beetle, tomato hornworm, and aphids also attack eggplant. Verticillium wilt and bacterial wilt are the headline diseases in long-rotation gardens.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Floating row cover at transplant blocks flea beetles -- remove at flowering for pollination. Hand-pick larger pests (Colorado potato beetle, hornworm). Rotate eggplant to a new bed and avoid spots where Solanaceae grew last year. Choose disease-resistant varieties for areas with verticillium history.

failure_diagnostics.label: Yellowing or weak growth
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Eggplant prefers more consistent moisture than peppers but cannot tolerate waterlogged soil. Persistent saturation causes root rot, yellowing leaves, and fruit drop. Wet humid conditions also drive flea beetle and Colorado potato beetle activity.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil. Water at the base, not overhead, and water early in the day so foliage dries before evening. Mulch heavily to stabilize soil moisture. Avoid heavy clay sites for eggplant.

failure_diagnostics.label: Bitter fruit or blossom drop
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress during flowering and fruit development causes blossom drop and produces small, bitter, often misshapen fruit. Eggplant is more sensitive to inconsistent watering than peppers -- the fruit develops fast and water-stressed plants cannot fill them properly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water deeply 1 to 2 times per week and increase frequency in heat. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture. Drip irrigation works well for eggplant by providing consistent water without wetting foliage.

failure_diagnostics.label: Few flowers or fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Eggplant needs full sun -- 8 hours minimum -- and serious heat to set fruit well. In partial shade or cool conditions, plants may grow leaves but flower sparsely and set few fruit. Eggplant in cool coastal climates often disappoints for this reason.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in the sunniest, hottest spot available. Plant against a south-facing wall or fence for reflected heat in cool climates. In genuinely cool-summer regions, grow in containers that can be moved or accept that eggplant is not the right crop.

crops.name: Tomatillo
crops.description: Salsa verde essential. Very productive, heat-tolerant, and easier than tomatoes. Plant two for pollination -- a single plant produces no fruit. The papery husk is the giveaway it's ready.

3.notes: Start 6 weeks early. Must plant two plants for fruit set. Short season works with fast varieties.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Wait to transplant tomatillos outdoors until soil temperatures reach 60 degrees F and the danger of frost has passed. (SDSU Extension; Utah State Extension)

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note: Allow six to eight weeks to grow tomatillo transplants from seed. Plants should have five to seven leaves and a well-developed root system before transplanting outdoors. (USU Extension)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: Expect to begin harvesting fruit about 60 to 75 days from transplanting. Tomatillos will be ready to harvest 65 to 100 days after transplanting. (SDSU Extension). (Utah State Extension)
harvest_start.design_note: Conservative mid-point 70 days used.

fertilizer.notes: Moderate feeder. Switch to low-nitrogen feed once flowers appear to encourage fruiting.

succession.reason: Produces continuously from one planting. Single sowing is sufficient.

pests.name: Three-lined potato beetle
pests.symptoms: Adults (1/4 inch, yellow with three black stripes running lengthwise) feed on leaves and flowers. Larvae look like small slugs covered in their own dark excrement -- they cluster in rows and skeletonize leaves, leaving only the midvein. A single infestation can defoliate a young tomatillo plant in days.
pests.cause: Lema daturaphila (formerly L. trilinea). UMN, UNH, and SDSU extensions all identify this as the most damaging and characteristic tomatillo pest. Uncommon on tomato and potato despite the common name. Overwinters as adults or larvae in garden debris.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick adults, larvae, and the bright orange egg clusters from leaf undersides -- check plants daily during peak activity. Spinosad is effective on larvae if applied to leaf undersides. Bt is not effective (beetle, not caterpillar).
pests.prevention: Remove ground-cherry (Physalis spp.) and jimsonweed (Datura) near the garden -- these are alternate hosts that carry the beetle between seasons. Rotate tomatillos to a new spot each year. Floating row cover until flowering blocks the overwintering generation.

pests.name: Tomatillo fruitworm
pests.symptoms: Tiny entry hole in the fruit husk (often between pinprick and pinhead size). Inside, a small caterpillar tunnels through the developing fruit. Infested fruits may ripen prematurely, drop early, or discolor internally even when the outside looks fine.
pests.cause: Heliothis subflexa moth larvae, closely related to corn earworm but specialized on Physalis. Less widely distributed than the three-lined potato beetle but can destroy much of a crop where present.
pests.organic_treatment: Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis var. kurstaki) applied to young fruits every 7 days during peak moth flight. Spinosad is also effective. Remove and destroy fallen or damaged fruits so larvae cannot complete development.
pests.prevention: Scout fruit husks for entry holes weekly. Pheromone traps help time Bt applications. Rotate plantings and clean up Physalis volunteers.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of small green or black insects on tender new growth. Curled distorted leaves. Sticky honeydew followed by sooty mold.
pests.cause: Green peach aphid (Myzus persicae) and potato aphid (Macrosiphum euphorbiae) are the primary species. Heavy populations can vector viruses shared across the nightshade family.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with water. Insecticidal soap or neem oil on undersides. Ladybugs and lacewings usually keep populations below damaging levels in home gardens.
pests.prevention: Avoid excess nitrogen. Tolerate small populations; beneficial insects need prey to stay around.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms: Small round shot-holes in leaves, worst on seedlings and transplants. Tiny shiny black beetles jump when disturbed. Established tomatillos easily outgrow the damage.
pests.cause: Several flea beetle species feed across the nightshade family. Most active in spring and early summer.
pests.organic_treatment: Row cover seedlings until they are 8-10 inches tall. Kaolin clay spray deters feeding. Neem oil for persistent infestations.
pests.prevention: Transplant rather than direct-seed. Keep garden edges weed-free to reduce overwintering cover.

diseases.name: Early blight
diseases.symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings (target pattern) on lower leaves first. Yellow halo around each spot. Affected leaves yellow and drop; plant defoliates from the bottom up.
diseases.cause: Alternaria solani and related species. Favored by warm wet weather. Overwinters on crop residue and in soil; splashes onto lower leaves during rainfall.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves immediately and dispose (do not compost). Copper-based fungicide or Bacillus subtilis applied preventively during wet stretches.
diseases.prevention: Rotate tomatillos, tomatoes, peppers, and eggplants on a 3-4 year cycle. Mulch to prevent soil splash. Water at soil level. Stake plants for airflow.

diseases.name: Anthracnose fruit rot
diseases.symptoms: Sunken, circular, water-soaked lesions on ripening fruits. Lesions may show concentric rings and eventually produce pinkish-orange spore masses in humid weather. Fruits rot on the plant.
diseases.cause: Colletotrichum coccodes and related species. Spreads by rain splash in warm wet weather. Overwinters on debris and in soil.
diseases.organic_treatment: Pick and destroy affected fruits. Copper fungicide during extended wet weather near harvest.
diseases.prevention: Mulch under plants. Avoid overhead irrigation. Rotate out of solanaceous crops. Pick fruits promptly once they fill the husk.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms: White powdery patches on upper and lower leaf surfaces. Affected leaves yellow and may drop. Plant vigor and fruit set decline.
diseases.cause: Several Leveillula and Podosphaera species. Favored by warm days and cool humid nights, unlike most fungal diseases that need leaf wetness.
diseases.organic_treatment: Potassium bicarbonate, neem oil, or milk spray (1 part milk to 9 parts water) applied at first signs. Remove badly affected leaves.
diseases.prevention: Full sun site with good airflow. Avoid overcrowding. Water in the morning.

crops.harvest_ready: Husk papery and brown, splitting at base. Fruit feels firm inside. Green color is correct at harvest.

start_method.notes: Start 6 weeks before last frost. Plant 2 tomatillos minimum -- they need cross-pollination. Harden off over 7 days.

rotation.avoid_after: Tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes -- all share blight and fusarium diseases
rotation.note: Always rotate nightshades to a fresh bed -- blight and fusarium can persist in soil for years.

storage.room_temp: 2-3 weeks in husk at room temperature
storage.fridge: Up to 1 month in husk in fridge
storage.freezer: Roast then freeze, or freeze raw whole -- good for salsas
storage.notes: Keep husks on until ready to use -- the papery husk extends shelf life dramatically.

recommended: Toma Verde (classic green, reliable -- our tier-1 reference)
Purple de Milpa (small, traditional Mexican heirloom)
varieties.note: Toma Verde is the reliable starter choice -- easy, productive, and reasonably early. Always plant at least 2 plants (tomatillos are self-incompatible). For more variety detail see the Varieties section. Pineapple Tomatillo is actually a ground cherry (Physalis pruinosa) and is covered under the Ground Cherry crop.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Pest-deterrent claim without matching established pattern. Default to traditional pending review.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. The nematode component is extension-documented. The claim's additional assertions about deterring aphids are not supported in the extension literature on marigolds and should be read as traditional.

good.name: Tomatoes
good.why: Same growing requirements, compatible spacing -- must plant 2 tomatillos for cross-pollination

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Structural-category claim has a mechanistic basis. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: 'Fennel suppresses neighbors' is a common gardening-book claim. Limited research; allelopathy is real but specific claim pattern is traditional.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Inter-plant competition for N, P, K is a real agronomic concept. Specific 'bad pair' claims often extrapolate beyond what research has shown.

container_notes.notes: Works in containers -- 5-gallon minimum. Remember: you need at least 2 plants for pollination, so 2 containers minimum.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small seedlings emerging. Eggplant germinates more slowly than tomatoes.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep at 80-85°F. Heat mat essential. Eggplant is even more heat-demanding than peppers at germination.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: True leaves with a distinctive purple sheen on the underside.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep consistently warm. Eggplant is slow -- do not worry if progress seems minimal in the first few weeks.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Compact, sturdy plant ready for outdoor conditions.
growth_stages.user_action: Do not transplant until nights are reliably above 60°F. Eggplant is more cold-sensitive than peppers.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Purple star-shaped flowers with yellow centers.
growth_stages.user_action: Feed with a high-potassium fertilizer. Tap flowering stems gently to aid pollination.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Glossy, firm skin -- harvest before the shine fades. Eggplant past its prime becomes bitter and seedy.
growth_stages.user_action: Cut rather than pull -- eggplants have thorny calyx. Use secateurs. Pick when the skin is shiny and the fruit gives slightly to pressure.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Husks browning and splitting, fruit dropping to the ground, nights cooling below 50 degrees F.
growth_stages.user_action: Pick up dropped fruit promptly -- tomatillos that overwinter on the ground can self-seed aggressively next year. Pull spent plants after harvest and compost.
growth_stages.log_prompt: How was your tomatillo season? Worth logging what worked.

notifications.title: Plant at least two tomatillo plants
notifications.body: Tomatillos need two plants for pollination -- they are self-incompatible, meaning a single plant produces almost no fruit. Two plants from different sources gives you a full harvest.

germination.text: Tomatillo seeds germinate fast in warm soil (70 to 80 degrees) -- typically 7 to 10 days. Start indoors 6 to 8 weeks before last frost, similar timing to tomato.
Tomatillo is closely related to tomato (both Solanaceae) and treated similarly through germination. Use a heat mat for reliable warm-soil germination.

seedling.text: Pot up seedlings to 4-inch pots once they have 2 true leaves. Plant deeper than they sat in the seed tray -- tomatillo, like tomato, develops adventitious roots from the buried stem.
Harden off over 7 to 10 days before transplanting. Tomatillo tolerates light cool weather better than tomato but still prefers warm conditions.

established.text: Plant at least 2 tomatillo plants -- a single plant produces few or no fruit because tomatillo requires cross-pollination from a genetically different plant. This is the single most important fact about growing tomatillo.
Water consistently and feed every 2 weeks with a balanced fertilizer. Tomatillo plants get large -- 3 to 4 feet wide and tall -- and benefit from staking or caging like tomato.

harvest.text: Tomatillos are ready when the papery husk is fully filled or just beginning to split, and the fruit inside has shifted color (green for green varieties, purple for purple varieties). Pick before the husk splits fully.
Tomatillos that fall to the ground are usually ripe. Many gardeners harvest by spreading a sheet under the plant and shaking. The plant continues producing through fall until first frost.

end_of_season.text: Tomatillo is killed by light frost. Harvest all developing fruit before first expected frost -- ripening can continue indoors at room temperature in the husks.

Self-seeded tomatillo seedlings often appear the following spring from dropped fruit. These can be transplanted or thinned out depending on garden plans. Rotate tomatillo to a new bed each year (Solanaceae rotation).

yield_expectations.per_plant: 50-100 fruits per plant in a good season
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Tomatillos are prolific once established -- you will have more than enough for salsa verde.
yield_expectations.peak_production: Late summer is when the husks fill and drop -- expect a heavy 3 to 4 week window once the first fruits ripen, with fruits ready to pick when they fill the husk.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Tomatillo is a tender annual killed by light frost at any stage. Cold soil at transplant (below 60 degrees) stunts plants. The first fall frost ends production abruptly, though harvested fruit ripens in the husk indoors.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Wait to transplant until soil reaches 60 degrees and night temperatures stay above 50. Have row cover ready for unexpected late-spring frosts. In fall, harvest all developing fruit before first expected frost -- the husks protect ripening fruit at room temperature for weeks.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Tomatillo shares pests with tomato: tomato hornworm, Colorado potato beetle, aphids, and three-lined potato beetle. Diseases are generally less serious than tomato; early blight and septoria leaf spot are the main concerns. Tomatillo seems more resistant to many tomato diseases than tomato itself.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Hand-pick larger pests (hornworm, potato beetle). Rotate tomatillo to a new bed and avoid spots where tomato, pepper, eggplant, or potato grew last year. Mulch to reduce splash-borne disease. Tomatillo is generally lower-maintenance than tomato for pest and disease management.

failure_diagnostics.label: Splitting or rotting fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Persistent waterlogging causes root rot and weak growth. Heavy rain near harvest causes tomatillo fruit to split inside the husk. Wet humid conditions drive early blight and septoria.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil. Water at the base, not overhead, and water early in the day. Mulch heavily to stabilize soil moisture. Stake or cage plants to keep foliage off the ground.

failure_diagnostics.label: Small or empty husks
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress reduces fruit set and produces small fruit that does not fully fill the husk. Severely drought-stressed tomatillo produces husks that look mature but are mostly empty -- a frustrating discovery at harvest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently -- 1 to 2 inches per week, more in heat. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture. Tomatillo tolerates more drought than tomato but produces best with consistent water through the fruit-development window.

failure_diagnostics.label: Few flowers or fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Tomatillo needs full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to flower and fruit well. In partial shade plants grow large and leafy but produce few fruit. Single-plant plantings (with no cross-pollination partner) also produce few or no fruit, regardless of sun.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun. Plant at least 2 plants for cross-pollination -- this is the single most consequential planting decision for tomatillo yield. Space plants 3 to 4 feet apart to allow each room to develop fully.

varieties_detail.origin_note: No single documented introduction year, breeder, or region of first selection has been located for Toma Verde. The name appears to be a commercial compression of 'tomate verde' (Spanish for green tomatillo) applied to a traditional open-pollinated selection that has been in continuous US seed-network circulation for decades. It is labeled heirloom by Harvesting History and treated as a heritage variety by multiple long-standing seed catalogs, which is why we classify it as such. We have left the detailed origin fields absent rather than invent a history.
varieties_detail.fruit_color: bright green at maturity, paling to soft green with a golden blush as fully ripe
varieties_detail.flavor_notes: sweet and citrusy; described as a cross between lemon, pineapple, and tomato. Sweeter and less sharply tart than most green tomatillos, especially when allowed to ripen fully.
varieties_detail.growth_habit_notes: Bushier and less sprawling than standard indeterminate tomatillos, but still benefits from a large cage or wire support. Plants typically reach 3-4 feet tall and 3-4 feet across.
varieties_detail.short_season_notes: Among the earliest-maturing tomatillos; recommended for Zone 4-5 gardeners for this reason.
varieties_detail.pollination_notes: Like all tomatillos, Toma Verde is self-incompatible -- you must plant at least two plants for any fruit to set. Two different tomatillo varieties flowering together give the best fruit set. A single plant will produce empty husks.
varieties_detail.seed_saving_notes: Open-pollinated variety, so seed saves true. Because tomatillos are insect-pollinated and self-incompatible, isolate from other tomatillo varieties by at least 150 feet or use cage isolation if you want to save seed pure.
varieties_detail.description: An early-maturing, open-pollinated green tomatillo that has become the home-garden standard. Sweet-tart flavor, reliable production, and easier to grow than tomatoes.
varieties_detail.notes:
Toma Verde is the most widely recommended tomatillo for first-time growers and the variety most commonly stocked by Johnny's Selected Seeds, Kitchen Garden Seeds, Hoss, Harvesting History, and similar US seed catalogs. It is valued for three reasons: earliness (60-70 days from transplant, faster than most), semi-determinate growth habit (more manageable than sprawling indeterminate heirlooms like Purple de Milpa), and flavor described across sources as sweet rather than sharply tart. The classic application is salsa verde; ripe fruit can also be eaten out of hand.

On days to maturity: the 60-70 day range reflects the consensus of Johnny's Selected Seeds and Utah State University Extension. South Dakota State University Extension reports 65-100 days from transplant for tomatillos as a group (covering later varieties); some retail listings report 55 days (Deep Harvest Farm) or 85 days (Harvesting History). Neither outlier is well-supported for this specific variety, so the published range here reflects the best-supported central cluster.

On growth habit: USU Extension's tomatillo bulletin groups Toma Verde with sprawling-habit varieties (alongside Gigante, Tamayo, Gulliver Hybrid). Our classification of 'semi-determinate' follows Johnny's Selected Seeds, Kitchen Garden Seeds, and Hoss Tools -- seed catalogs closer to the commercial selection lineage of this variety -- who describe it as bushier and more manageable than standard indeterminate tomatillos. We cite Johnny's as the more specific source for this variety's growth habit, while noting the legitimate disagreement with USU's broader classification.

varieties_detail.history: Purple de Milpa is a traditional Mexican heirloom tomatillo selected and preserved within the milpa system -- the Mesoamerican intercropping tradition in which corn, beans, squash, and other food crops are grown together in family cornfields. The 'de milpa' in the name literally means 'of the cornfield.' Unlike modern commercial tomatillo selections, Purple de Milpa has been grown semi-wild for generations, often reseeding itself year-to-year in Mexican agricultural landscapes. It reached US seed commerce through heritage seed preservation networks; Seed Savers Exchange and similar heirloom-focused catalogs have maintained it as a living-heritage variety. No single introduction date or named breeder exists, as is typical for varieties carried forward through traditional seed saving rather than commercial breeding programs.
varieties_detail.fruit_size: 3/4 to 1 inch diameter (notably smaller than Toma Verde and most modern varieties)
varieties_detail.fruit_color: deep purple-tinged skin with green flesh; fully ripe fruit is rich purple
varieties_detail.flavor_notes: sharp and tangy-sweet, with a richer and more complex flavor than green tomatillos. SDSU Extension describes the purple tomatillos as 'much sweeter than the green varieties.' Some cooks prefer the sharper, more intense flavor for salsa verde depth; others find it too assertive and prefer it mixed with green varieties.
varieties_detail.growth_habit_notes: Sprawling rather than bushy. Plants reach 3-4 feet tall and spread widely. Seed Savers Exchange notes 'the trellised vines were not as productive as the ones that spread' -- suggesting that in this variety, generous ground space outperforms tight caging. Still benefits from some support to keep fruit off the soil.
varieties_detail.short_season_notes: Despite the 70-90 day range suggesting mid-season timing, growers in cooler zones (e.g., Z4-5 Connecticut) report that Purple de Milpa continues producing late into fall and through early light frosts -- consistent with its milpa heritage as a hardy, semi-wild variety. Gardeners in short-season zones should still start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and expect main harvest to come in a late rush.
varieties_detail.pollination_notes: Self-incompatible, like all tomatillos -- plant at least two tomatillo plants for fruit set. Because Purple de Milpa can cross-pollinate with other tomatillo varieties grown nearby, seed savers who want to maintain the variety pure should isolate by at least 150 feet or use cage isolation.
varieties_detail.seed_saving_notes: Open-pollinated heirloom; seed saves true when isolated from other tomatillo varieties. Per Seed Savers Exchange and Saanich Organics, wet-processing is the standard method: blend fruit with water, let viable seeds sink, rinse and dry. This variety is noted for self-seeding readily -- fruit that drops to the ground in fall will often produce volunteers the following year.
varieties_detail.description: The heirloom Mexican tomatillo that grows wild in traditional milpa cornfields. Small purple-tinged fruit with a sharper, more complex flavor than modern green varieties. Prolific, hardy, and reliably self-seeding.
varieties_detail.notes:
Purple de Milpa is the tomatillo most closely associated with traditional Mexican milpa agriculture -- the Mesoamerican intercropping system in which multiple food crops share a family cornfield. It is the variety that heirloom-focused seed savers (Seed Savers Exchange, Mary's Heirloom Seeds, Annie's Heirloom Seeds) consistently preserve and promote. Relative to Toma Verde and other modern green tomatillos, fruits are smaller (3/4 to 1 inch vs. 1.5 to 2 inches), flavor is sharper and more intense, and growth habit is more sprawling and semi-wild.

Growers comparing purple tomatillos should be aware that 'Purple Tomatillo' sold generically by seed houses is often not the same as named Purple de Milpa. The generic purple types (sometimes also labeled Purple Coban, Purple Blush, or Morado) typically have larger fruit and less pronounced milpa characteristics. Purple de Milpa is specifically the small-fruited heirloom selection.

On days to maturity: the 70-90 day range reflects Seed Savers Exchange and multiple heirloom-focused catalogs. SDSU Extension reports 75-100 days for tomatillos as a group, which covers this variety's range. The variety matures later than Toma Verde, but in practice its extended production window (often cropping into late fall and tolerating light frosts better than modern varieties) offsets the later start in many growers' experience.

On heirloom classification: Purple de Milpa meets the full standard for heirloom, including documented cultural origin. It is labeled heirloom consistently across all consulted sources. This is a tier-1 heritage variety with authentic milpa lineage; see our methodology page on how we classify heirlooms.

varieties_detail.origin_note: Verde Puebla is consistently sold by US and international heritage seed companies as an old Mexican heirloom associated with the Puebla region of Mexico -- a region with deep tomatillo-growing tradition. Australian Seed describes it as 'an old Mexican heirloom variety'; Hudson Valley Seed Company and Tomato Growers Supply Company sell it as a heritage variety with the 'Puebla Verde' name. However, no specific introduction date, breeder, or primary-source documentation of a selection history has been located. We have left the detailed origin fields absent and classify Verde Puebla as an heirloom (per our methodology's consumer-world heirloom standard) but without a documented heritage story. See our methodology page on how we classify heirlooms.
varieties_detail.fruit_size: 1.5-2 inches diameter (approximately 1-2 ounces per fruit; notably larger than Toma Verde)
varieties_detail.fruit_color: golden-green to yellowish-green when ripe; paler and more yellow-tinted than Toma Verde and most other green tomatillos
varieties_detail.flavor_notes: sweet-tart, balanced; SDSU Extension describes it as 'sweet/tart flavor.' The flavor profile sits between the sharp tartness of smaller tomatillos and the sweetness of fully-ripe golden varieties -- a versatile middle ground for salsa verde, sauces, and cooked applications.
varieties_detail.growth_habit_notes: Sprawling indeterminate plant. Hudson Valley Seed Company and Tomato Growers Supply both note the plant benefits from staking -- a simple 4-foot stake per plant works well, or basket-weave staking like tomatoes when growing several. Plants can reach 4+ feet tall and spread widely; fruit-laden branches are prone to drooping without support.
varieties_detail.short_season_notes: At 70-80 days from transplant, Verde Puebla is later than Toma Verde (60-70 days) and roughly matches Purple de Milpa (70-90 days). Growers in Zone 4-5 should start indoors 6-7 weeks before last frost and use season extension (row covers, black plastic mulch) to ensure a useful harvest window. In short seasons, Toma Verde is the safer choice; Verde Puebla rewards warmer-zone growers with larger fruit and higher yield per plant.
varieties_detail.pollination_notes: Self-incompatible like all tomatillos -- plant at least two tomatillo plants for fruit set. Cross-pollination between Verde Puebla and another tomatillo variety (Toma Verde works well) gives best production.
varieties_detail.seed_saving_notes: Open-pollinated heirloom; seed saves true when isolated. Because tomatillos are insect-pollinated and self-incompatible, isolate from other tomatillo varieties by at least 150 feet to maintain variety purity. Standard tomatillo wet-processing applies (blend with water, let seeds sink, rinse and dry).
varieties_detail.description: A traditional Mexican heirloom tomatillo from the Puebla region, producing notably larger and more golden-green fruit than most. Sweet-tart flavor and high yields make it a salsa-verde workhorse for growers with longer seasons.
varieties_detail.notes:
Verde Puebla is the tomatillo to choose when fruit size matters -- its 1-2 oz golden-green fruits are roughly double the weight of typical green tomatillos, reducing the husking effort per pound and producing meaningful salsa yields from a couple of plants. It trades earliness for size: at 70-80 days from transplant, it matures later than Toma Verde, so it's better suited to zones with longer warm seasons (Z6 and warmer, or Z5 with season extension).

Among the three tier-1 tomatillos in our database, the picks are: Toma Verde for earliness and short-season reliability; Purple de Milpa for small-fruit sharpness and traditional milpa heritage; Verde Puebla for large-fruit yield and versatile sweet-tart flavor. All three cross-pollinate well, and many gardeners plant Toma Verde + Verde Puebla together as a complementary pair.

On days to maturity: the 70-80 day range reflects Tomato Growers Supply (75 days) and consistent reporting across heritage seed catalogs. SDSU Extension's 65-100 day range for tomatillos as a group encompasses this variety. Verde Puebla is on the later end of the green-tomatillo spectrum but within normal expectations.

On heirloom classification: Verde Puebla is labeled heirloom by multiple heritage-focused seed houses (Australian Seed explicitly uses 'old Mexican heirloom'; Hudson Valley and Tomato Growers Supply treat it as a heritage variety). It meets the consumer-world standard for heirloom (open-pollinated, traditional, long seed-network circulation). We have classified it as heirloom on that basis, while noting in the origin fields that specific introduction documentation could not be located.

varieties_detail.origin_note: Gigante is a traditional green tomatillo selection valued for its large fruit size. No single documented introduction year, breeder, or region of first selection has been located. It is consistently labeled heirloom by open-pollinated seed catalogs including Gardeners Basics, and USU Extension lists it among green tomatillo varieties with sprawling growth habit. Similar large-fruited Mexican tomatillo selections circulate under various names (Plaza Latina Giant Green from Adaptive Seeds has a documented 2005 Oregon seed-saving origin from Mexican market fruit; whether Gigante and Plaza Latina Giant Green are the same stock is unclear). We classify Gigante as heirloom based on its open-pollinated status and long seed-trade circulation, and leave detailed origin fields absent.
varieties_detail.fruit_size: 2-4 inches diameter; the largest green tomatillo commonly available, up to twice the size of standard varieties
varieties_detail.fruit_color: bright green, ripening to paler green with golden cast
varieties_detail.flavor_notes: sweet-tart, with less sharp acidity than smaller-fruited tomatillos. The sweetness-to-tartness ratio favors sweet compared to Miltomate or Purple de Milpa.
varieties_detail.growth_habit_notes: Large sprawling plant, bushy habit per seed-catalog descriptions. Grows to 3-4 feet or taller and spreads widely. Staking or caging strongly recommended; fruit-laden branches will droop without support.
varieties_detail.short_season_notes: At 75-85 days from transplant and with large fruit that takes time to fully size up, Gigante is best for Zone 6 and warmer with long warm seasons. Zone 4-5 growers should either start indoors 8 weeks before last frost or choose Toma Verde instead.
varieties_detail.pollination_notes: Self-incompatible -- plant at least two tomatillo plants for fruit set. Pairs well with Toma Verde or Verde Puebla as cross-pollinators.
varieties_detail.seed_saving_notes: Open-pollinated; seeds save true when isolated from other tomatillo varieties by at least 150 feet or via cage isolation.
varieties_detail.description: The largest green tomatillo, producing 2-4 inch sweet-tart fruit on sprawling plants. For growers who want maximum fruit size and yield per plant in longer seasons.
varieties_detail.notes:
Gigante is the tomatillo to choose for sheer size. Its fruits are roughly double the diameter and several times the weight of typical green tomatillos, which significantly reduces husking time per pound of salsa. The tradeoff is a longer season requirement: at 75-85 days from transplant, it's among the later tomatillos.

Growers should note that 'Gigante' is sometimes used as a descriptor rather than a strict variety name in the seed trade, and similar large-fruited tomatillos circulate under names like Plaza Latina Giant Green (from Adaptive Seeds). If strict variety purity matters, check the supplier's seed-source lineage.

On days to maturity: the 75-85 day range is a consensus estimate from seed catalogs; SDSU Extension's 65-100 day range for tomatillos as a group covers this variety.

varieties_detail.history: Miltomate is the traditional Mexican name -- derived from the Nahuatl words 'milli' (cornfield) and 'tomatl' (tomato) -- for tomatillos grown within the milpa intercropping system. The word literally means 'field tomato' and is still used in Mexican and Central American agriculture to refer to small, tart, traditional tomatillos that grow semi-wild among corn, beans, and squash. As a named commercial variety in the US seed trade, Miltomate has become associated with one-inch diameter, sharply tart fruit -- a selection preserved from traditional milpa cultivation. Like Purple de Milpa, the variety's identity is rooted in the milpa agricultural system rather than a single introduction event; the name itself predates Spanish contact with Mesoamerica.
varieties_detail.fruit_size: approximately 1 inch diameter; notably smaller than modern commercial tomatillos
varieties_detail.fruit_color: bright green ripening to pale green; occasionally with faint purple tinge
varieties_detail.flavor_notes: sharply tart, more acidic than sweeter modern varieties. SDSU Extension describes it as '1-inch diameter fruit with a tart flavor.' The intense acidity is valued in traditional Mexican salsa verde recipes where the sharpness balances chili heat and fat.
varieties_detail.growth_habit_notes: Traditional semi-wild growth pattern. Plants sprawl broadly and self-seed readily -- behaviors consistent with milpa-heritage varieties that have been maintained through generations of casual cultivation rather than tight commercial selection. Staking helps but isn't essential; volunteers the following year are common.
varieties_detail.short_season_notes: The smaller fruit size helps Miltomate mature reliably in shorter seasons than Gigante or Verde Puebla. Zone 4-5 growers who want a traditional-tasting tomatillo should consider Miltomate alongside Toma Verde and Purple de Milpa.
varieties_detail.pollination_notes: Self-incompatible; plant at least two tomatillo plants. Miltomate pairs well with any other tomatillo variety for cross-pollination.
varieties_detail.seed_saving_notes: Open-pollinated heirloom; seed saves true when isolated. The variety is known for self-seeding reliably -- fallen fruit in fall produces volunteer plants the following spring, making Miltomate well-suited to seed-saving beginners.
varieties_detail.description: The traditional Mexican milpa-grown tomatillo -- small, tart, and culturally tied to Mesoamerican intercropping. The name itself means 'field tomato' in Nahuatl.
varieties_detail.notes:
Miltomate represents one of the oldest continuously-cultivated tomatillo types in the world -- the small, sharply tart fruit that has been grown in Mexican cornfields for centuries. While Toma Verde and Gigante reflect modern selection for larger sweeter fruit, Miltomate preserves the traditional flavor profile that authentic Mexican salsa verde recipes were built around.

It complements Purple de Milpa nicely -- both are milpa-system heirlooms, but where Purple de Milpa offers purple color and sweet-tart complexity, Miltomate offers the sharp acidic baseline flavor. Growing both together gives a complete picture of traditional tomatillo agriculture.

On days to maturity: the 70-90 day range reflects catalog reporting; SDSU Extension's general 65-100 day range applies. Small-fruited milpa-style tomatillos often mature earlier than their DTM figures suggest when fruit is harvested at 1-inch size rather than waiting for larger development.

varieties_detail.origin_note: Rendidora is a Mexican commercial tomatillo variety, distinguished from other green tomatillos primarily by its upright growth habit -- USU Extension specifically calls out Rendidora as the upright-growing high-yield variety in contrast to sprawling types like Toma Verde and Gigante. No specific breeder, introduction year, or heritage narrative has been located. Because the variety's value proposition is its growth habit and yield (modern breeding characteristics) rather than traditional lineage, we classify it as open-pollinated rather than heirloom.
varieties_detail.fruit_size: approximately 1.5-2 inches diameter; similar to Toma Verde
varieties_detail.fruit_color: bright green ripening to pale green
varieties_detail.flavor_notes: typical green tomatillo sweet-tart balance; less distinctive in flavor profile than named heirloom varieties, but well-suited to standard salsa verde use.
varieties_detail.growth_habit_notes: The defining feature of Rendidora is its notably upright growth habit, distinct from the sprawling/bushy character of Toma Verde, Verde Puebla, Purple de Milpa, and Gigante. This makes Rendidora particularly useful for gardeners with limited space or who want a more tidy garden appearance; a simple single stake per plant is typically sufficient support, versus the full cage required for sprawling varieties. Yield per plant is high despite the smaller footprint.
varieties_detail.short_season_notes: Rendidora is a moderate-season variety at 70-80 days from transplant, not specifically bred for short seasons. The upright growth habit allows tighter spacing in compact garden layouts but does not shorten the time-to-harvest. Z4-5 growers who want a reliably early tomatillo should choose Toma Verde instead.
varieties_detail.pollination_notes: Self-incompatible -- plant at least two tomatillo plants. A good companion to the sprawling varieties for cross-pollination since it occupies vertical rather than horizontal space.
varieties_detail.seed_saving_notes: Open-pollinated; seed saves true when isolated by at least 150 feet or via cage isolation from other tomatillo varieties.
varieties_detail.description: A Mexican commercial tomatillo distinguished by upright growth habit and high yields. The space-efficient choice for compact gardens.
varieties_detail.notes:
Rendidora fills a specific role in the tomatillo lineup: it's the variety to choose when garden space is tight and you don't want sprawling plants taking over beds. USU Extension singles out its upright growth habit as the defining characteristic that distinguishes it from the more common sprawling tomatillo varieties.

In a diversified home tomatillo planting, Rendidora works well as the vertical partner to a sprawling heirloom like Purple de Milpa or Verde Puebla -- together they make efficient use of both vertical and horizontal garden space while giving the cross-pollination needed for good fruit set.

On days to maturity: the 70-80 day range reflects catalog consensus for mid-season green tomatillos. Falls within SDSU Extension's 65-100 day range for tomatillos generally.

crops.disease_resistance_notes_default: Tomatillos rarely suffer from disease or pest damage (USU Extension). Pest pressure is modest in most home-garden conditions. Per-variety resistance claims are unusual for tomatillos and are noted on individual varieties only when specific documentation exists.

good.name: Borage
good.why: Attracts bees -- critical for watermelon pollination

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Xerces Society documents borage as a pollinator-attractant plant that blooms concurrently with tomato, squash, and cucumber crops, drawing the same bees that pollinate those crops. Source: xerces.org/blog/plants-you-can-eat-are-pollinator-treat.

good.name: Nasturtiums
good.why: Trap crop for aphids and cucumber beetles

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic. Nasturtiums are named as an aphid trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and USU Extension. However, the extension-documented trap crop for cucumber beetles is Blue Hubbard squash, not nasturtiums (Pinero, University of Missouri / Lincoln University IPM, 2017). The combined aphid-plus-cucumber-beetle framing in this claim pairs one extension-named mechanism (nasturtium + aphid) with a popular-gardening mechanism (nasturtium + cucumber beetle) that is not extension-documented. Protocol caveat: UConn IPM notes trap cropping is a weak fit for aphids due to passive air dispersal.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. This claim's nematode component aligns with the extension-documented mechanism, but the 'concurrent companion' application pattern reflects popular gardening practice rather than extension protocol.

pests.name: Cucumber beetle
pests.symptoms: Yellow-green beetles with black spots or stripes feeding on leaves, flowers, and fruit. Plants wilt suddenly (bacterial wilt transmission). Holey leaves.
pests.cause: Spotted and striped cucumber beetles. Also transmit bacterial wilt disease.
pests.organic_treatment: Row covers until flowering. Yellow sticky traps. Neem oil spray. Spinosad-based insecticide.
pests.prevention: Delay planting until plants are large. Use row covers early season. Interplant with radishes and nasturtiums.

pests.name: Squash bug
pests.symptoms: Gray-brown flat insects on stems and undersides of leaves. Wilting leaves with yellow then brown patches. Bronze egg clusters on leaf undersides.
pests.cause: Anasa tristis. Overwinters as adults in garden debris.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick adults and egg masses. Trap under boards at night. Neem oil spray on nymphs.
pests.prevention: Remove all garden debris in autumn. Rotate cucurbit crops. Use row covers early season.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces, stems, and sometimes fruit. Leaves may yellow and die. Worst in warm days with cool nights.
diseases.cause: Fungal disease favored by humid conditions with poor air circulation.
diseases.organic_treatment: Spray with diluted neem oil or a baking soda solution (1 tsp per quart water). Apply potassium bicarbonate spray. Remove and destroy affected leaves.
diseases.prevention: Space plants for good airflow. Water at soil level, not on foliage. Choose resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation.

diseases.name: Bacterial wilt
diseases.symptoms: Sudden wilting of individual leaves, then whole stems, then entire plant. No recovery even with watering. Plants die within days.
diseases.cause: Erwinia tracheiphila bacteria spread by cucumber beetles feeding.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure -- remove and destroy infected plants immediately. Control cucumber beetles to prevent spread.
diseases.prevention: Use row covers to exclude cucumber beetles early in season. Plant resistant varieties.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms: Yellow-green patches on upper leaf surface with corresponding gray-purple fuzzy growth on leaf undersides. Leaves die rapidly.
diseases.cause: Pseudoperonospora cubensis fungus. Spreads rapidly in wet humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively.
diseases.prevention: Choose resistant varieties. Water at soil level. Ensure good air circulation.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Large seed leaves pushing up fast. Melons germinate quickly in warmth.
growth_stages.user_action: Melons need warmth above everything -- 75-85°F for germination. A heat mat is essential in all but the hottest climates.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Large, rough true leaves developing rapidly.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep warm. Melons sulk badly in cold temperatures -- below 60°F slows them dramatically and sets them back.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Vines beginning to run. Melons need space -- a lot of it.
growth_stages.user_action: Direct the vines in the direction you want them to grow. Melons need full sun and warm soil -- black plastic mulch makes a real difference in cooler zones.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Yellow flowers. Male flowers first, female flowers with a swollen base following.
growth_stages.user_action: Hand-pollinate female flowers in the morning for better fruit set. Touch a male flower to each open female flower.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Flowers appearing? Any small melons forming?

growth_stages.name: Fruit Setting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small melons developing after successful pollination.
growth_stages.user_action: Once fruit sets, limit to 2-3 fruits per plant. More than this and none of them will reach their potential size or sweetness.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Watermelon: thump test gives a deep hollow sound, tendril nearest the fruit is brown and dead. Cantaloupe: slips easily from the vine, smell is intensely fragrant. Honeydew: skin turns creamy yellow, slight give at the blossom end.
growth_stages.user_action: Underripe melon is disappointing. Learn the ripeness cues for your variety and wait. A day or two of patience makes a huge difference.

notifications.title: Start your melons indoors
notifications.body: Melons need a long warm season -- start them indoors 3-4 weeks before last frost. Use biodegradable pots to minimize root disturbance at transplant. Do not rush transplanting -- melon seedlings in cold soil stall badly.

notifications.title: Thin your melon fruits
notifications.body: Limit each plant to 2-3 fruits. More than this and you will get small, bland melons. Choose the best-positioned fruits and pinch off the rest. More space per fruit means more sugar, more size, more flavor.

notifications.title: Check your melons for ripeness
notifications.body: Learning to read ripeness is the most important melon skill. For watermelons, find the dead brown tendril nearest the fruit -- if it is dead and dry, the melon is ready. Thump it -- a deep hollow sound confirms it. Do not rely on size alone.

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- protect your melons immediately
weather_triggers.body: Melons are extremely frost-tender. Even a light frost kills them. Cover immediately or bring containers inside. If fruit is nearly ripe, harvest it -- it will continue ripening indoors.

weather_triggers.title: Extreme heat -- water melons deeply
weather_triggers.body: Melons love heat but need consistent moisture in very high temperatures. Water deeply at the base every day in extreme heat. Inconsistent watering causes hollow hearts and blossom end rot.

germination.text: Melons germinate best at 80-85F. A heat mat is not optional in most climates -- without bottom heat germination is slow and unreliable.
Sow two seeds per pot and thin to the stronger one. Do not transplant the thinned seedling -- melons hate root disturbance.

seedling.text: Keep melon seedlings consistently warm. A single cold night below 55F can set them back by weeks.
Do not over-pot. Keep in a small pot until the roots are just filling it, then plant out rather than potting up again -- each pot change is a disruption.

established.text: Black plastic mulch over the soil warms it and conserves moisture -- it makes a meaningful difference to melon yields in cooler zones.
Melons need more space than any other common vegetable. One watermelon vine needs 6-8 square feet of ground. Plan accordingly.

flowering.text: Hand-pollinate female flowers in the early morning using a small paintbrush, or by removing a male flower and touching it directly to the female. This dramatically improves fruit set in a polytunnel or cool season.
The window for pollination is short -- flowers are receptive for only a few hours in the morning.

fruit_set.text: Thin to 2-3 fruits per vine. This is the decision that determines melon quality. Spreading the plant's energy across too many fruits gives you several mediocre ones instead of a few excellent ones.
Place a tile or board under developing melons to keep them off the soil. This prevents rotting and pests getting to the vulnerable underside.

harvest.text: Watermelon does not slip from the vine -- it must be cut. The most reliable ripeness indicator is the tendril nearest the fruit: when that small curly tendril is brown and dried, the melon is ripe. Combine with the ground-spot check (the patch resting on the soil should turn from white to creamy yellow) for confidence.

A second cue is the thump test: a ripe watermelon gives a deep, hollow thunk when tapped, while an underripe one sounds higher and tighter. This takes practice -- it is more reliable as a confirmation than as a primary signal.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 1-3 melons per plant depending on thinning
yield_expectations.peak_production: Melons produce over a concentrated period -- plan to use them quickly
yield_expectations.first_year_note: A homegrown melon eaten warm from the vine on a hot day is one of the peak garden experiences. Worth every bit of the long season.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucurbits are tropical-origin tender annuals -- killed outright by even a light frost at any stage. Cold soil at planting (below 60 degrees) stunts seedlings for the rest of the season even if they survive. Late-summer frost ends the season abruptly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Wait to direct-sow or transplant until soil reaches 65 to 70 degrees and night temperatures stay above 50. In short-season zones, start transplants indoors 3 to 4 weeks before set-out, but disturb roots minimally -- cucurbits resent transplanting. Use black plastic mulch to warm soil. Have row cover ready for unexpected late-spring or early-fall frosts.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucumber beetles (striped and spotted) damage seedlings directly and transmit bacterial wilt -- a fatal disease that wilts vines from the tips inward. Squash bugs target squash and pumpkin (less so cucumber and melon). Powdery mildew shows up reliably late in the season as white powder on leaves. Downy mildew, anthracnose, and bacterial leaf spot are humidity-driven secondary problems.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Floating row cover from planting through first flower blocks cucumber beetles -- remove at flowering for pollination. Squash bug egg masses (orange-red, on undersides of leaves) crush easily by hand if caught early. For powdery mildew, choose resistant varieties (most modern cucumbers are bred for resistance) and water at the base, not overhead. Rotate cucurbits to a new bed each year.

failure_diagnostics.label: Watery fruit or vine collapse
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucurbits need consistent water but cannot tolerate waterlogged soil. Persistent saturation causes root rot, sudden vine collapse, and watery flavorless fruit. Heavy rain near harvest causes ripe melons to crack and split. Wet foliage drives powdery mildew, downy mildew, and bacterial leaf spot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil or raised mounds (the traditional 'cucurbit hill' approach exists for drainage reasons). Water deeply at the base 1 to 2 times per week rather than shallow daily. Mulch heavily to even out soil moisture and reduce splash-borne disease. Stop watering watermelons 2 weeks before expected harvest to concentrate flavor.

failure_diagnostics.label: Small or bitter fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress during flowering and fruit set produces small, misshapen, or bitter fruit. Cucurbits move large volumes of water through their tissues during fruit development -- a single mature watermelon plant can use 1 to 2 gallons of water per day in peak summer. Cucumber bitterness is often a drought-stress signal.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently and deeply -- 1 to 2 inches per week minimum during fruit development, more in heat. Drip irrigation outperforms overhead watering by both providing consistent water and keeping foliage dry. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture and reduce evaporation.

failure_diagnostics.label: Vines without fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucurbits need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum, ideally 8 or more -- to set and ripen fruit. In partial shade vines grow leaves and even bloom, but fruit set is poor and ripening is incomplete. A late-season fruit that never sweetens is often a sun problem more than a temperature problem.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in the sunniest spot available. Trellising vining cucurbits (vertical support for cucumbers and small-fruited squash) gets more leaf area into the sun and improves fruit set substantially. In partial-shade gardens, accept that cucurbits are not the right crop and grow leafy greens or herbs instead.
