pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Peachtree borer
pests.symptoms: Gummy, amber-colored sap mixed with sawdust at base of trunk near soil line. Weakened, declining tree.
pests.cause: Synanthedon exitiosa clear-wing moth larvae. Bore into trunk near soil.
pests.organic_treatment: Dig out larvae by hand in autumn. Apply beneficial nematodes around trunk base in autumn.
pests.prevention: Keep base of trunk clear of mulch and debris. Apply pyrethrin spray to trunk base in early September.

diseases.name: Brown rot
diseases.symptoms: Brown soft spots on ripening fruit, rapidly expanding. Fuzzy gray-brown spore masses develop. Fruit mummifies on tree.
diseases.cause: Monilinia fructicola/laxa fungus. Spreads rapidly in warm humid conditions near harvest.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove and destroy all affected fruit immediately -- do not compost. Apply sulfur fungicide preventively near harvest.
diseases.prevention: Remove mummified fruit from tree and ground. Improve air circulation with pruning. Avoid fruit injury.

diseases.name: Black knot
diseases.symptoms: Hard black galls/swellings on branches and twigs. Galls enlarge each year. Severe infection kills branches.
diseases.cause: Apiosporina morbosa fungus. Affects plum, cherry, and related stone fruits.
diseases.organic_treatment: Prune out knots 4 inches below visible growth in winter. Destroy -- do not compost.
diseases.prevention: Remove wild plum/cherry trees nearby. Annual inspection and removal of small knots.

watering.frequency: Weekly young, drought tolerant when mature

crops.harvest_ready: Orange all over, slight give near stem, detaches easily, sweet aroma. Ripen quickly once picked.

storage.freezer: Halve, stone, freeze flat -- excellent for jam and baking
storage.notes: Apricots have the shortest shelf life of stone fruits. Freeze immediately at peak ripeness.

varieties.note: Goldcot is the most reliable for northern gardens -- significantly more cold-hardy than Moorpark.

start_method.notes: Plant bare-root trees in late winter/early spring while dormant. Container trees can go in spring through early autumn. Stake against wind for the first 2 years.

container_notes.notes: Fruit trees need to be grown in the ground. Dwarf varieties on very dwarfing rootstocks can be tried in very large (30+ gallon) containers but are challenging and rarely as productive.

rotation.avoid_after: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Bare-root or potted tree just planted. Base of the trunk right at soil level, and the graft union -- the knobby joint where the variety was grafted onto the rootstock -- sits 2 to 4 inches above the ground.
growth_stages.user_action: Dig the hole twice as wide as the roots and the same depth. Spread the roots over a small mound in the bottom of the hole. Stake firmly against wind. Don't add fertilizer to the planting hole. Water in deeply.

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: First leaves breaking from the dormant branches. New shoot tips extending. The tree is putting almost everything into root growth.
growth_stages.user_action: Water deeply once a week through the first summer. Pinch off any flowers that form -- year-one fruit costs the tree more strength than it returns. Keep weeds and grass cleared 2 to 3 feet around the trunk.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Strong shoot extension from the trunk. The first major side branches are starting to take shape.
growth_stages.user_action: Stone fruit trees are trained to an open-vase form: 3 to 5 main branches angled outward at roughly 45 degrees, evenly spaced around the trunk, with no central leader. Pick those 3 to 5 main branches and remove everything else cleanly back to the trunk. Use branch spreaders (small props that hold a branch at a wider angle) or hanging weights so the chosen branches stay angled outward as they grow.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Leaves fully dropped, buds tight on the stems. The tree is in true winter dormancy.
growth_stages.user_action: First-year dormancy is a holding period -- the work happens later. Mulch heavily around the base before hard freeze. Wrap the trunk in young-tree wrap to prevent sunscald and rodent damage. Major pruning waits until late winter (the next stage).
growth_stages.log_prompt: Tree wrapped and mulched for winter?

growth_stages.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Tree fully dormant; buds tight; late winter into early spring.
growth_stages.user_action: Maintain an open-center (vase) form: 3 to 5 main scaffold branches angled outward from a short trunk, with no central leader. Stone fruit needs sun and air movement through the canopy. Remove dead, diseased, damaged wood, then anything growing inward.

growth_stages.name: Blossom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Pink or white bloom opening. Apricot is earliest and most frost-exposed.
growth_stages.user_action: Watch overnight temperatures closely -- stone fruit blooms ahead of apple. Cover smaller trees with fleece on frost nights. Avoid sprays while pollinators are active.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Petal fall complete; small green fruitlets visible. A natural drop reduces the load in late spring.
growth_stages.user_action: Thin to one fruit every 4 to 6 inches on the branch (peach and nectarine especially). Stone fruit overload makes the fruit small and breaks branches.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Background color shift complete (yellow on peach/nectarine; full color on plum/cherry); fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure.
growth_stages.user_action: Pick when fruit lifts and twists free with a gentle motion -- forced fruit is not yet ripe. Stone fruit ripens fast and over a short window; check daily during peak.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest Sanitation
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Mummified fruit hanging on tree or fallen below; leaves yellowing.
growth_stages.user_action: Remove every mummified fruit from the tree and the ground -- these are the brown rot spore source for next year. Apply a potassium feed after harvest while leaves are still working.

notifications.title: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text: Set the graft union a few inches above final soil level. Burying it lets the scion root and you lose the dwarfing rootstock effect.
Stake securely for the first two seasons. Drive the stake into the hole before the tree goes in to avoid root damage later.

establishment.text: Water deeply once a week through the first growing season. Roots are still inside the original root ball and dry out quickly.
Mulch a 3-foot circle around the trunk to hold moisture. Keep mulch a few inches clear of the trunk to prevent collar rot.

first_growth.text: Stone fruit trains to an open-center form, not a central leader. Choose 3 to 5 scaffolds angled outward from a short trunk and remove the central leader once the scaffolds are set.
Wide-angled scaffolds are stronger and let light into the interior. Use spreaders or weights to set the angle in the first two seasons.

dormancy.text: First dormancy is when you commit to the open-center form. Stand back and look at the structure before you cut.
Make clean cuts just above an outward-facing bud. Ragged stubs invite disease, especially Cytospora canker on stone fruit.

dormant_prune.text: Maintain the open-center vase: no central leader, 3 to 5 scaffolds, an open interior. Light and air through the canopy is the main brown rot control you have.
Work the three Ds first -- dead, diseased, damaged -- then thin to keep the open form. Stone fruit tolerates and rewards heavier annual pruning than pome fruit.

blossom.text: Stone fruit blooms ahead of apple, so spring frost risk is higher. Watch overnight forecasts and cover small trees with fleece on frost nights. Apricot is the earliest bloomer and the most frost-exposed.
Do not spray during bloom. Pollinators are working and the flower window is short.

fruit_set.text: Thin peach and nectarine to one fruit every 4 to 6 inches along the branch. Unthinned stone fruit stays small and the weight breaks limbs.
Plum and cherry usually self-thin reasonably well, but a heavy set is still worth thinning by hand to improve fruit size.

harvest.text: Stone fruit ripens fast and over a short window -- check daily during peak. Fruit should lift and twist free with a gentle motion; if it resists, leave it another day.
Pick into shallow containers to avoid bruising the fruit underneath. Stone fruit does not finish ripening off the tree the way pears do.

post_harvest.text: Remove every mummified fruit -- those leathery brown remnants on branches and ground are the spore source for next year's brown rot. This is the single most important post-harvest task on stone fruit.
Apply a potassium feed while leaves are still working. The feed goes into next year's flower buds, not this year's growth.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 80-150 lbs from a mature standard tree, less on dwarf rootstocks
yield_expectations.peak_production: Full production hits around year 4 to 6 on standard rootstocks, year 3 to 4 on dwarfing stocks. A well-thinned mature stone-fruit tree produces a heavy crop over a 1 to 2 week harvest window.
yield_expectations.first_year_note: No fruit in year one. The tree puts everything into roots and scaffold structure. Remove any flowers that form -- they cost more in tree vigor than they return in fruit.
factors: open-vase pruning for sun and air
consistent water from pit-hardening through harvest

crops.hardiness_notes: Apricots present a significant disconnect between tree survival and fruit production. The tree itself is genuinely cold-hardy -- standard varieties survive to zone 5a, and Manchurian-type apricots (Mandan, Sungold, Moongold) survive to zone 3. However, apricots are notorious early bloomers, often flowering a full month before the official last-frost date. Late spring frosts frequently kill the blossoms even though the tree is unharmed, making reliable crops rare north of zone 6a. In marginal zones, growers report harvesting a full crop only once every 3-5 years. Strategies to improve fruit production include late-blooming varieties (Harglow, Goldrich, Harlayne, Canadian White Blenheim), north-facing siting to delay bloom, and frost-protection coverings during bloom. Apricots need well-drained soil -- they are particularly susceptible to root rot in heavy or wet soils. Most varieties are self-fertile. In warm climates (zones 8-9), low-chill varieties (Katy, Gold Kist, Royal Rosa) are required since standard apricots need 600-900 chill hours to break dormancy properly.

varieties_detail.notes: Manchurian-type apricot (Prunus armeniaca mandshurica). One of the cold-hardiest apricots available. Fruit is smaller and less refined than standard cultivars but reliable in the coldest zones. Good for drying, canning, preserves.
Canadian-bred cultivar, considered the go-to apricot for zone 4 growers. Produces good-quality fruit by cold-climate standards. Self-fertile but better with a pollinator. Ripens early August.
Late-blooming cultivar from Canada's Harrow research station. The late bloom significantly reduces spring frost crop losses. Firm, medium-sized orange fruit with good flavor. Self-pollinating.
Classic heirloom apricot, prized for exceptional flavor. Large fruit with distinctive speckled skin. Self-pollinating. Best fresh-eating apricot but susceptible to split stones and uneven ripening.
Low-chill California-bred apricot. For warm climates where standard apricots fail to break dormancy. Large yellow fruit with red blush. Early ripening (May-June). Self-fertile.

crops.chill_hours_note: Flowers early -- late frost risk is higher concern than chill hours in most zones

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost killed the blossom
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Stone fruit blooms before apple, often when frost is still common. A single hard frost during the brief bloom window can eliminate the year's crop. Apricot is the earliest-blooming and most frost-exposed -- in colder zones it can lose the crop most years.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Watch overnight forecasts through bloom and cover smaller trees with horticultural fleece on frost nights. In frost-prone sites, choose later-blooming varieties on your next planting -- apricot in particular has varieties selected for late bloom that ride out spring frost better.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Brown rot (Monilinia) is the headline disease on stone fruit -- it turns ripening fruit into soft brown lesions, then leathery mummies. Plum curculio leaves crescent-shaped scars on young fruit. Peach leaf curl distorts new leaves in spring. Cherry fruit fly maggots ruin cherries near harvest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Sanitation drives brown rot control: remove every mummified fruit from tree and ground at the end of the season. For peach leaf curl, a single dormant copper spray before bud-swell prevents the season's infection. Open-center pruning helps everything by drying the canopy faster after rain.

failure_diagnostics.label: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Pollination needs vary by stone fruit type. Peach, nectarine, and sour cherry are usually self-fertile and set fruit alone. Sweet cherry and many plums and apricots need a compatible second variety with overlapping bloom. A self-sterile tree alone will bloom heavily and set nothing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Check the pollination requirement of your variety before assuming poor weather. If a partner is needed, plant a compatible second variety within 100 feet -- a neighbor's tree counts if it is close enough. Bloom-time charts from extension publications help match pollinators.

failure_diagnostics.label: Root problems or waterlogging
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Stone fruit is unusually intolerant of wet feet. Trees in saturated soil show yellowing leaves, weak shoots, and gummy bark splits at the base (Phytophthora collar rot). Decline can be rapid -- a stone-fruit tree can fail in a single wet spring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Drainage is set at planting. On a wet site, plant the next tree on a 12-inch raised mound or move sites entirely. Stone fruit on its own roots tolerates wet less than pome fruit -- choose a Phytophthora-resistant rootstock if available.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Stone fruit needs 6 to 8 hours of direct sun to color, sweeten, and ripen evenly. In shade or in a crowded canopy, fruit stays small and pale and brown rot pressure increases because the canopy stays wet longer.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Maintain the open-center form with annual pruning -- this is more important on stone fruit than on any other tree fruit. Light and air through the canopy is both a yield driver and a disease control. Site new trees in full sun, away from buildings or larger trees that will shade them as they mature.

crops.name: Pear (European)
crops.description: Long-lived, productive tree that outlasts its planter. Harvest slightly underripe and ripen indoors -- tree-ripened pears go mealy. Bartlett, Bosc, and Anjou are the classics. Needs cross-pollination.

3.notes: Hardy varieties like Luscious and Summercrisp are best for Zone 3.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Plant bare root fruit trees in early spring while they are still dormant, as soon as the soil can be worked. In Minnesota, this is April or May. Bare root plants suffer severely from transplanting shock -- plant as soon as soil is workable and before bud break. (UMN Extension 'Growing apples in the home garden'; UMN Extension 'Growing stone fruits in the home garden')

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.source_quote: The most common mistake novice pear growers make is to let the fruit ripen on the tree. Fruit that ripens on the tree ends up gritty and unpleasant. Instead, fruit should be picked at a mature stage and then allowed to ripen indoors. (UMN Extension)
harvest_start.synthesis_note: European pear harvest window is August through October in cold and temperate zones, with exact timing by variety. Pick fruit when mature (full size) but still firm, not when fully ripe. Use a gentle lift-and-twist motion to detach the fruit from the spur. Ripen indoors at room temperature for 5 to 10 days, or cold-store winter varieties (Anjou, Bosc, Comice) for 2 to 3 months before ripening. First significant harvest occurs 3 to 5 years after planting per crop-level years_to_first_harvest field. (UMN Extension; UMD Extension; UMaine Extension)

crops.pollinator_notes: Partially self-fertile but yields much better with a second variety. Bartlett and Anjou are common pairs.

tasks.description: Prune in late winter to central leader shape. Pears are prone to fire blight -- disinfect tools between cuts.

crops.year_one_notes: Remove blossoms years 1-2. Pears are slow -- patience in early years means decades of production.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Pollinator category is mechanistically grounded. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Ground cover effects on soil temperature and moisture are real; specific pairings not well-studied.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: The aphid-repellent element is mechanism-plausible: allium sulfur VOCs have documented aphid-repellent effects (Durenne and Gosset, Insects 2018, 9(4):112) and are described at home-gardening rigor by Mississippi State and USU Extension. However, the 'repel scab fungus' element is mechanism-fabricated. Apple scab (Venturia inaequalis) is a fungal disease whose extension-recommended management (UMN Extension 'Apple scab of apples and crabapples'; Cornell apple IPM guidelines) consists of resistant-variety selection, fallen-leaf sanitation, canopy pruning for rapid leaf-drying, and fungicide timing. No extension source endorses chives or other alliums as a scab management tactic, and there is no documented mechanism by which allium VOCs would suppress a foliar fungal pathogen that requires leaf surface moisture to infect. The scab-repellent claim is folk-remedy framing rather than extension-backed. Downgraded from extension_backed because the composite why-text mixes a mechanism-real aphid component with a mechanism-fabricated scab component.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Codling moth
pests.symptoms: Small entry holes in fruit with brown frass (sawdust-like droppings). Maggot inside apple tunnelling to core. Often mistaken for worm in apple.
pests.cause: Cydia pomonella moth. Larvae tunnel into developing fruit from June-August.
pests.organic_treatment: Pheromone traps to monitor and disrupt mating. Apply kaolin clay to fruit. Remove fallen fruit daily.
pests.prevention: Hang pheromone traps from late May. Use sticky tree bands to trap crawling larvae.

diseases.name: Fire blight
diseases.symptoms: Blossoms and shoots wilt and turn black/brown. Shepherd's crook shape. Spreads rapidly in warm wet weather.
diseases.cause: Erwinia amylovora bacteria. Pears are more susceptible than apples.
diseases.organic_treatment: Prune infected wood 12 inches below infection. Sterilize tools. Copper spray before bloom.
diseases.prevention: Plant resistant varieties. Avoid excess nitrogen. Improve airflow.

diseases.name: Pear scab
diseases.symptoms: Dark olive-green/black spots on leaves and fruit. Cracked, deformed fruit.
diseases.cause: Venturia pirina fungus. Similar to apple scab.
diseases.organic_treatment: Copper or sulfur fungicide from bud break. Rake and destroy leaves.
diseases.prevention: Plant resistant varieties. Remove leaf debris in autumn.

crops.harvest_ready: Pears ripen from the inside out. Pick while still firm and green/yellow. Ripen at room temperature. Check by pressing near the stem -- ready when it yields slightly.

storage.room_temp: Pick firm and green, ripen on counter 3-5 days
storage.fridge: Once ripe: 3-5 days. Unripe pears: 1-3 months in fridge -- they ripen on removal
storage.freezer: Peel, slice, poach lightly and freeze -- good for cooking
storage.notes: Never ripen pears on the tree -- pick firm. Fridge storage actually ripens them slowly over months.

varieties.note: Conference is the most reliable for backyard growers -- heavy cropper, partial self-fertile, and excellent disease resistance.

start_method.notes: Plant bare-root trees in late winter/early spring while dormant. Container trees can go in spring through early autumn. Stake against wind for the first 2 years.

container_notes.notes: Fruit trees need to be grown in the ground. Dwarf varieties on very dwarfing rootstocks can be tried in very large (30+ gallon) containers but are challenging and rarely as productive.

rotation.avoid_after: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Bare-root or potted tree planted. The graft union -- the knobby joint where the variety was grafted onto the rootstock -- sits 2 to 4 inches above the soil. Trunk vertical and supported by a stake.
growth_stages.user_action: Dig the hole twice as wide as the roots, same depth. Plant so the graft union is clearly above ground -- if it gets buried, the dwarfing rootstock stops working and the tree gets too big. Stake firmly. Water in deeply.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Tree planted with graft union above soil?

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: First buds breaking on the young tree. Slow start -- pome fruits put almost all year-one energy into roots, not visible top growth.
growth_stages.user_action: Water deeply once a week through the first summer. Pinch off all year-one flowers and any fruit that sets. Keep grass and weeds cleared in a 3-foot circle around the trunk.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Trunk extending. Side branches developing. The early structure of the tree is taking shape.
growth_stages.user_action: Pome fruit trees are trained to a central-leader form: one strong vertical trunk with side branches angled outward at roughly 60 to 80 degrees and spaced along it. Pick the first set of side branches about 2 to 3 feet off the ground. Use branch spreaders (small props that hold a branch at a wider angle) -- narrow branch angles break under fruit weight.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Main trunk and first side branches chosen?

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Leaves fallen, buds tight. Tree is fully dormant and frost-hardy.
growth_stages.user_action: First-year dormancy is a holding period -- the real pruning happens later. Wrap the trunk in young-tree wrap to prevent sunscald and rodent damage. Mulch deeply around the base, keeping mulch a few inches off the trunk. Hold off on major pruning until late winter.

growth_stages.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Tree fully dormant -- no green tissue, buds tight. Late winter, before bud-break.
growth_stages.user_action: Maintain a central-leader form: one dominant vertical leader, with scaffold branches spaced along it. Remove dead, diseased, damaged wood first; then crossing branches and water sprouts. Aim for an open, airy canopy.

growth_stages.name: Blossom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Pink-bud opening into white or pale-pink bloom; pollinators active on warm days.
growth_stages.user_action: Watch the forecast for frost. Avoid all sprays during bloom -- pollinators are working. If frost is forecast, cover smaller trees with horticultural fleece overnight.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set and June Drop
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Petals fall, small green fruitlets visible. A natural drop of excess fruitlets follows in early summer (the 'June drop').
growth_stages.user_action: After June drop, thin remaining fruit to one per cluster, spaced about 6 inches apart. Hand-thinning sets next year's bud quality.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Fruit color shift complete, seeds darkening when sliced (apple), background color shift from green to yellow (pear). Fruit lifts and twists free easily when ready.
growth_stages.user_action: Pick over multiple visits as fruit ripens unevenly. Cup the fruit, lift, and twist; do not pull. Place in baskets gently -- bruises shorten storage.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest Sanitation
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Leaves yellowing or dropped; fallen fruit on ground.
growth_stages.user_action: Rake and remove all fallen fruit and leaves. Codling moth larvae and apple/pear scab spores overwinter in this debris. Apply a potassium feed once leaves have dropped to support next year's bud.

notifications.title: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text: Position the graft union -- the swollen knob low on the trunk -- a few inches above final soil level. Burying it lets the scion root and you lose the dwarfing rootstock effect.
Stake firmly for the first two seasons. Drive the stake into the planting hole before the tree goes in to avoid damaging roots later.

establishment.text: Water deeply once a week through the first growing season, even in summer rain. Roots have not yet reached out of the planting hole and the original root ball dries quickly.
Mulch a 3-foot circle around the trunk to hold moisture and suppress competing weeds. Keep mulch a few inches clear of the trunk to prevent collar rot.

first_growth.text: Choose 3 or 4 scaffold branches evenly spaced up the trunk and around the compass. Remove competing leaders so a single central trunk dominates.
Train scaffolds to wide angles with spreaders or weights. Wide-angled branches are stronger and bear more fruit than narrow upright ones.

dormancy.text: First dormancy is when you set the tree's permanent shape. Stand back and look at the structure before you cut.
Make every cut clean and just above an outward-facing bud. Ragged cuts and stubs invite disease.

dormant_prune.text: Work the three Ds first: dead, diseased, damaged. Then thin crossing branches and remove inward-pointing growth. The goal is an open canopy that light and spray can reach.
Maintain a central leader: one dominant vertical with scaffolds stepping out and down. On older trees, remove no more than a quarter of total wood in any one winter.

blossom.text: Frost during bloom is the single largest risk to the year's crop. Watch the overnight forecast and cover small trees with fleece if frost threatens.
Do not spray anything -- including organic options -- while the tree is in bloom. Pollinators are at work and the flower window is short.

fruit_set.text: Thin to one fruit per cluster, spaced about 6 inches apart, after the June drop has finished. Unthinned trees produce many small fruit and tend toward biennial bearing.
The June drop is the tree shedding what it cannot ripen. It looks alarming but is healthy -- additional hand-thinning is still usually needed afterward.

harvest.text: Apples and pears ripen unevenly across the tree. Walk the tree every few days and pick what lifts and twists free with a gentle motion.
Pears finish ripening off the tree -- pick when the background color shifts from deep green toward yellow but the fruit is still firm. Apples ripen on the tree.

post_harvest.text: Clear all fallen fruit and leaves from under the tree. This debris is where codling moth larvae overwinter and where apple/pear scab spores survive to reinfect next spring.
Apply a potassium-rich feed after harvest while leaves are still working. This is the feed that goes into next year's flower buds, not this year's growth.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 50-150 lbs on a mature dwarf, 150-300 lbs on a mature standard tree
yield_expectations.peak_production: Dwarf rootstocks bear at year 2 to 4 and reach full production by year 5 to 7. Semi-dwarf and standard trees take longer (year 4 to 8 for first crop, year 8 to 12 for full production) but carry larger crops for far longer.
yield_expectations.first_year_note: No fruit in year one. Pome fruits are the slowest of the common backyard fruits to come into bearing. Remove any first-year flowers so energy goes to the trunk and scaffold.
factors: annual fruit thinning to one fruit per cluster
cross-pollination -- almost all varieties need a different variety nearby
fire blight, codling moth, and apple scab management
rootstock choice (dwarf bears earlier, standard bears longer)

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

crops.hardiness_notes: European pears (Pyrus communis) are hardy across a wide range but fire blight is the defining limitation in humid eastern zones. Susceptible varieties (Bartlett, Bosc) can be killed outright by fire blight in warm humid climates where the bacterial disease thrives. Resistant varieties (Kieffer, Moonglow, Warren, Harrow Delight) are the practical choice for the South and humid Midwest. European pears also require 2-8 weeks of cold storage after harvest before they develop proper flavor and texture -- they ripen from the inside out and are picked green, unlike Asian pears which ripen on the tree. Almost all European pears require cross-pollination with a compatible variety; pollen-incompatible pairs exist (Bartlett and Seckel cannot pollinate each other). Asian pears can cross-pollinate European pears when bloom times overlap. Trees begin bearing in year 4-6 and can produce for 50+ years.

varieties_detail.notes: The world's most widely grown pear. Classic bell-shaped yellow fruit. Requires pollinator. Highly susceptible to fire blight -- avoid in humid eastern zones. Best in Pacific Northwest and California.
Long-necked russet-brown pear with sweet-spicy flavor. Excellent for baking and poaching. Moderately fire-blight susceptible. Requires pollinator. Cold-hardier than Bartlett.
Green or red skin varieties. Smooth-textured, mild sweet flavor. Long storage life (up to 6 months). Moderate fire blight resistance. Requires pollinator.
The gift-box gourmet pear. Considered the best-tasting European pear -- rich buttery flavor. Greenish-yellow with red blush. Moderate fire blight resistance. Requires pollinator.

European x Asian hybrid. Strong fire blight resistance, tolerates heat and humidity. Partially self-fertile. Large golden pears best for cooking, canning, preserves. The safest pear for the humid South.
Fire-blight resistant with Bartlett-like quality. Yellow skin with red blush. Good universal pollinator for other European pears. Released by USDA in 1960. Excellent beginner pear.
Small 'sugar pear' -- intensely sweet, snack-size. Late-blooming reduces frost risk. Fire blight resistant. Note: cannot cross-pollinate with Bartlett (shared S-alleles). Pair with Bosc or Anjou.

crops.chill_hours_note: High chill requirement -- best in zones 4-7

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost killed the blossom
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: A frost during bloom kills the open flowers and any fruitlets just set. Apple and pear bloom in early to mid spring, often when frost is still possible. A single hard frost during the brief bloom window can eliminate the year's crop.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Watch the overnight forecast through the bloom window and cover small trees with horticultural fleece on frost nights. For a frost-prone site, choose later-blooming varieties on your next planting -- bloom timing varies by variety by 1 to 3 weeks.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Codling moth larvae tunnel into apples and pears, leaving small holes with frass at the entry. Apple scab and pear scab cause olive-brown lesions on leaves and fruit. Fire blight on pear blackens shoots from the tip down. These three are the dominant pome problems across the country.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Clear all fallen fruit and leaves at the end of each season -- this is where codling moth and scab overwinter. For codling moth, pheromone traps and well-timed sprays during the egg-hatch windows are the standard home-orchard tools. Prune for an open canopy that dries quickly after rain to suppress scab.

failure_diagnostics.label: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Most apples and pears need pollen from a different but compatible variety to set fruit. A single tree alone, or two trees of the same variety, will bloom heavily and set little or no fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant a second variety with overlapping bloom time within about 100 feet -- a neighbor's tree counts if it is in range. Crabapple is an effective universal pollinator for apple. For pear, European and Asian pears can cross-pollinate if bloom overlaps.

failure_diagnostics.label: Root problems or waterlogging
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Pome fruit trees in saturated soil show yellowing leaves, weak shoot growth, and dieback that worsens through the season. The roots suffocate and cannot take up water or nutrients, so the tree behaves as if it is drought-stressed even with wet feet.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Drainage is set at planting and is hard to improve afterward. If the site holds water, plant the next tree on a 12-inch raised mound or move to a different site. Avoid amending only the planting hole -- this creates a sump.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Pome fruit needs 6 to 8 hours of direct sun to color and sweeten properly. In shade, trees flower and set fruit but the fruit is small, pale, and low in sugar. A dense, unpruned canopy creates the same problem within a sunny site by shading its own interior.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site new trees in full sun. On established trees, prune to open the canopy: remove inward-growing branches and water sprouts so light reaches every fruiting spur. A well-pruned tree in full sun outyields a crowded one of the same age.

crops.name: Pear (Asian)
crops.description: Apple-like texture, crisp and sweet. Harvested tree-ripe (unlike European pears). Earlier bearing than European pears -- often fruit in 2-3 years. Shinseiki and 20th Century are popular varieties.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Pollinator category is mechanistically grounded. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Ground cover effects on soil temperature and moisture are real; specific pairings not well-studied.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Allium sulfur-based volatile organic compounds have documented aphid-repellent effects (Durenne and Gosset, 'Companion Plants for Aphid Pest Management,' Insects 2018, 9(4):112). The companion application is described by several extensions at home-gardening rigor: Mississippi State University Extension ('Companion planting improves gardens,' Snyder via Reeves) explicitly states 'Chives tend to repel aphids'; Utah State University Extension ('Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting,' Mohr et al.) lists onions, garlic, and chives as repelling common garden pests; UC Cooperative Extension Master Gardener publications (Butte County 'Best Friends in the Garden' and Fresno County 'Winter companion planting to repel insects') likewise list allium VOCs among aphid-repellent companions. These extension sources describe the pairing at tradition-plus-plausible-mechanism rigor rather than validated protocol -- the Kansas State Extension / Johnson County 'Companion Planting' page caveats that allium sulfur repellency is 'centralized to the garlic itself -- and only with certain pests.' The earlier catalog attribution to 'UC IPM' does not match UC IPM's Pest Notes on aphids (pn7404), which focus on reflective mulches, water sprays, soaps, and natural enemies rather than allium interplanting.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Bad companion claim, no pattern match. Default to traditional pending review.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Codling moth
pests.symptoms: Small entry holes in fruit with brown frass (sawdust-like droppings). Maggot inside apple tunnelling to core. Often mistaken for worm in apple.
pests.cause: Cydia pomonella moth. Larvae tunnel into developing fruit from June-August.
pests.organic_treatment: Pheromone traps to monitor and disrupt mating. Apply kaolin clay to fruit. Remove fallen fruit daily.
pests.prevention: Hang pheromone traps from late May. Use sticky tree bands to trap crawling larvae.

diseases.name: Fire blight
diseases.symptoms: Blossoms and shoots wilt and turn black/brown. Shepherd's crook shape. Spreads rapidly in warm wet weather.
diseases.cause: Erwinia amylovora bacteria. Pears are more susceptible than apples.
diseases.organic_treatment: Prune infected wood 12 inches below infection. Sterilize tools. Copper spray before bloom.
diseases.prevention: Plant resistant varieties. Avoid excess nitrogen. Improve airflow.

diseases.name: Pear scab
diseases.symptoms: Dark olive-green/black spots on leaves and fruit. Cracked, deformed fruit.
diseases.cause: Venturia pirina fungus. Similar to apple scab.
diseases.organic_treatment: Copper or sulfur fungicide from bud break. Rake and destroy leaves.
diseases.prevention: Plant resistant varieties. Remove leaf debris in autumn.

start_method.notes: Plant bare-root trees in late winter/early spring while dormant. Container trees can go in spring through early autumn. Stake against wind for the first 2 years.

container_notes.notes: Fruit trees need to be grown in the ground. Dwarf varieties on very dwarfing rootstocks can be tried in very large (30+ gallon) containers but are challenging and rarely as productive.

rotation.avoid_after: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Bare-root or potted tree planted. The graft union -- the knobby joint where the variety was grafted onto the rootstock -- sits 2 to 4 inches above the soil. Trunk vertical and supported by a stake.
growth_stages.user_action: Dig the hole twice as wide as the roots, same depth. Plant so the graft union is clearly above ground -- if it gets buried, the dwarfing rootstock stops working and the tree gets too big. Stake firmly. Water in deeply.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Tree planted with graft union above soil?

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: First buds breaking on the young tree. Slow start -- pome fruits put almost all year-one energy into roots, not visible top growth.
growth_stages.user_action: Water deeply once a week through the first summer. Pinch off all year-one flowers and any fruit that sets. Keep grass and weeds cleared in a 3-foot circle around the trunk.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Trunk extending. Side branches developing. The early structure of the tree is taking shape.
growth_stages.user_action: Pome fruit trees are trained to a central-leader form: one strong vertical trunk with side branches angled outward at roughly 60 to 80 degrees and spaced along it. Pick the first set of side branches about 2 to 3 feet off the ground. Use branch spreaders (small props that hold a branch at a wider angle) -- narrow branch angles break under fruit weight.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Main trunk and first side branches chosen?

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Leaves fallen, buds tight. Tree is fully dormant and frost-hardy.
growth_stages.user_action: First-year dormancy is a holding period -- the real pruning happens later. Wrap the trunk in young-tree wrap to prevent sunscald and rodent damage. Mulch deeply around the base, keeping mulch a few inches off the trunk. Hold off on major pruning until late winter.

growth_stages.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Tree fully dormant -- no green tissue, buds tight. Late winter, before bud-break.
growth_stages.user_action: Maintain a central-leader form: one dominant vertical leader, with scaffold branches spaced along it. Remove dead, diseased, damaged wood first; then crossing branches and water sprouts. Aim for an open, airy canopy.

growth_stages.name: Blossom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Pink-bud opening into white or pale-pink bloom; pollinators active on warm days.
growth_stages.user_action: Watch the forecast for frost. Avoid all sprays during bloom -- pollinators are working. If frost is forecast, cover smaller trees with horticultural fleece overnight.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set and June Drop
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Petals fall, small green fruitlets visible. A natural drop of excess fruitlets follows in early summer (the 'June drop').
growth_stages.user_action: After June drop, thin remaining fruit to one per cluster, spaced about 6 inches apart. Hand-thinning sets next year's bud quality.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Fruit color shift complete, seeds darkening when sliced (apple), background color shift from green to yellow (pear). Fruit lifts and twists free easily when ready.
growth_stages.user_action: Pick over multiple visits as fruit ripens unevenly. Cup the fruit, lift, and twist; do not pull. Place in baskets gently -- bruises shorten storage.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest Sanitation
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Leaves yellowing or dropped; fallen fruit on ground.
growth_stages.user_action: Rake and remove all fallen fruit and leaves. Codling moth larvae and apple/pear scab spores overwinter in this debris. Apply a potassium feed once leaves have dropped to support next year's bud.

notifications.title: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text: Position the graft union -- the swollen knob low on the trunk -- a few inches above final soil level. Burying it lets the scion root and you lose the dwarfing rootstock effect.
Stake firmly for the first two seasons. Drive the stake into the planting hole before the tree goes in to avoid damaging roots later.

establishment.text: Water deeply once a week through the first growing season, even in summer rain. Roots have not yet reached out of the planting hole and the original root ball dries quickly.
Mulch a 3-foot circle around the trunk to hold moisture and suppress competing weeds. Keep mulch a few inches clear of the trunk to prevent collar rot.

first_growth.text: Choose 3 or 4 scaffold branches evenly spaced up the trunk and around the compass. Remove competing leaders so a single central trunk dominates.
Train scaffolds to wide angles with spreaders or weights. Wide-angled branches are stronger and bear more fruit than narrow upright ones.

dormancy.text: First dormancy is when you set the tree's permanent shape. Stand back and look at the structure before you cut.
Make every cut clean and just above an outward-facing bud. Ragged cuts and stubs invite disease.

dormant_prune.text: Work the three Ds first: dead, diseased, damaged. Then thin crossing branches and remove inward-pointing growth. The goal is an open canopy that light and spray can reach.
Maintain a central leader: one dominant vertical with scaffolds stepping out and down. On older trees, remove no more than a quarter of total wood in any one winter.

blossom.text: Frost during bloom is the single largest risk to the year's crop. Watch the overnight forecast and cover small trees with fleece if frost threatens.
Do not spray anything -- including organic options -- while the tree is in bloom. Pollinators are at work and the flower window is short.

fruit_set.text: Thin to one fruit per cluster, spaced about 6 inches apart, after the June drop has finished. Unthinned trees produce many small fruit and tend toward biennial bearing.
The June drop is the tree shedding what it cannot ripen. It looks alarming but is healthy -- additional hand-thinning is still usually needed afterward.

harvest.text: Apples and pears ripen unevenly across the tree. Walk the tree every few days and pick what lifts and twists free with a gentle motion.
Pears finish ripening off the tree -- pick when the background color shifts from deep green toward yellow but the fruit is still firm. Apples ripen on the tree.

post_harvest.text: Clear all fallen fruit and leaves from under the tree. This debris is where codling moth larvae overwinter and where apple/pear scab spores survive to reinfect next spring.
Apply a potassium-rich feed after harvest while leaves are still working. This is the feed that goes into next year's flower buds, not this year's growth.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 100-300 lbs on a mature standard tree, with each fruit larger and heavier than European pears
yield_expectations.peak_production: Dwarf rootstocks bear at year 2 to 4 and reach full production by year 5 to 7. Semi-dwarf and standard trees take longer (year 4 to 8 for first crop, year 8 to 12 for full production) but carry larger crops for far longer.
yield_expectations.first_year_note: No fruit in year one. Pome fruits are the slowest of the common backyard fruits to come into bearing. Remove any first-year flowers so energy goes to the trunk and scaffold.
factors: annual fruit thinning to one fruit per cluster
cross-pollination -- almost all varieties need a different variety nearby
fire blight, codling moth, and apple scab management
rootstock choice (dwarf bears earlier, standard bears longer)

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

crops.hardiness_notes: Asian pears (Pyrus pyrifolia) are crisp like apples rather than buttery like European pears, and ripen on the tree rather than off. They have generally lower chill requirements (300-600 hours) than European pears, making them more adaptable to zones 8-9. They also have better fire blight resistance as a group, though no Asian pear is truly immune. Most are partially self-fertile but produce significantly larger crops with a compatible pollinator -- Asian pears can cross-pollinate each other or compatible European pears (Bartlett and 20th Century have overlapping bloom, Chojuro blooms with Anjou). Asian pears bruise easily and don't ship well, which makes them a home-garden-favorable fruit that rarely appears in grocery stores. Trees begin bearing in year 3-4, earlier than European pears. Prune aggressively -- Asian pears set more fruit than the tree can properly size without thinning.

varieties_detail.notes: Most popular Asian pear in the US. Large russeted golden fruit with brandy-like aroma and low acid. Bears young. Susceptible to fire blight despite Asian pear reputation. Partially self-fertile; better with Shinseiki or 20th Century as pollinator.
Yellow-skinned, crisp, mild-flavored fruit. Self-fertile (one of the few). Moderate fire blight resistance. Vigorous, reliable producer. Good beginner Asian pear. Ripens late August.
World's most widely-grown Asian pear. Yellow-green skin, juicy sweet-tart flesh. Self-fertile. Stores 4-5 months refrigerated. Fire-blight susceptible. Excellent cold hardiness for an Asian pear.

Old variety with distinctive butterscotch flavor. Russeted brown skin, flat shape. Moderate fire blight resistance. Stores up to 5 months. Earliest-blooming Asian pear -- pairs well with Anjou for pollination.

crops.chill_hours_note: Lower chill than European pears -- better suited to zones 6-9

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost killed the blossom
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: A frost during bloom kills the open flowers and any fruitlets just set. Apple and pear bloom in early to mid spring, often when frost is still possible. A single hard frost during the brief bloom window can eliminate the year's crop.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Watch the overnight forecast through the bloom window and cover small trees with horticultural fleece on frost nights. For a frost-prone site, choose later-blooming varieties on your next planting -- bloom timing varies by variety by 1 to 3 weeks.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Codling moth larvae tunnel into apples and pears, leaving small holes with frass at the entry. Apple scab and pear scab cause olive-brown lesions on leaves and fruit. Fire blight on pear blackens shoots from the tip down. These three are the dominant pome problems across the country.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Clear all fallen fruit and leaves at the end of each season -- this is where codling moth and scab overwinter. For codling moth, pheromone traps and well-timed sprays during the egg-hatch windows are the standard home-orchard tools. Prune for an open canopy that dries quickly after rain to suppress scab.

failure_diagnostics.label: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Most apples and pears need pollen from a different but compatible variety to set fruit. A single tree alone, or two trees of the same variety, will bloom heavily and set little or no fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant a second variety with overlapping bloom time within about 100 feet -- a neighbor's tree counts if it is in range. Crabapple is an effective universal pollinator for apple. For pear, European and Asian pears can cross-pollinate if bloom overlaps.

failure_diagnostics.label: Root problems or waterlogging
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Pome fruit trees in saturated soil show yellowing leaves, weak shoot growth, and dieback that worsens through the season. The roots suffocate and cannot take up water or nutrients, so the tree behaves as if it is drought-stressed even with wet feet.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Drainage is set at planting and is hard to improve afterward. If the site holds water, plant the next tree on a 12-inch raised mound or move to a different site. Avoid amending only the planting hole -- this creates a sump.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Pome fruit needs 6 to 8 hours of direct sun to color and sweeten properly. In shade, trees flower and set fruit but the fruit is small, pale, and low in sugar. A dense, unpruned canopy creates the same problem within a sunny site by shading its own interior.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site new trees in full sun. On established trees, prune to open the canopy: remove inward-growing branches and water sprouts so light reaches every fruiting spur. A well-pruned tree in full sun outyields a crowded one of the same age.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Pollinator category is mechanistically grounded. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. The nematode component is extension-documented. The claim's additional assertions about deterring whiteflies are not supported in the extension literature on marigolds and should be read as traditional.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Soil-category claim has a mechanistic basis. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: 'Fennel suppresses neighbors' is a common gardening-book claim. Limited research; allelopathy is real but specific claim pattern is traditional.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Scale insects
pests.symptoms: Flat brown or white waxy lumps on stems and leaves. Sooty black mold follows from honeydew. Leaves yellow.
pests.cause: Various scale species. Common on indoor/container citrus.
pests.organic_treatment: Scrape off by hand. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap. Horticultural oil spray in winter.
pests.prevention: Inspect regularly. Keep plants healthy and well-fed. Good air circulation.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Citrus greening (HLB)
diseases.symptoms: Mottled yellow-green leaves in blotchy pattern. Small, lopsided, bitter fruit. Tree slowly declines. No cure.
diseases.cause: Candidatus Liberibacter bacteria spread by Asian citrus psyllid insect. A devastating citrus disease.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure. Remove affected trees.
diseases.prevention: Control Asian citrus psyllid with neem oil or spinosad. Inspect purchased trees before planting.

diseases.name: Root rot (Phytophthora)
diseases.symptoms: Yellow leaves, declining vigor, branch dieback. Bark at soil line may show brown discoloration.
diseases.cause: Phytophthora root rot from waterlogged or poorly drained soil.
diseases.organic_treatment: Improve drainage. Avoid overwatering. Apply phosphonate fungicide.
diseases.prevention: Well-drained soil essential. Never let roots sit in water. Graft onto resistant rootstock.
