rotation.avoid_after: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Container-grown tree just planted. The graft union -- the knobby joint where the variety was grafted onto the rootstock -- sits well above soil level. Trunk often staked briefly to support against wind.
growth_stages.user_action: Dig the hole the same depth as the rootball but twice as wide. Plant high -- the top of the rootball should sit slightly above ground level. Don't add fertilizer at planting. Water deeply, then mulch around the base, keeping mulch a few inches off the trunk.

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: New leaves emerging in the first weeks after planting. Citrus pushes growth in flushes rather than steadily.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep soil consistently moist (not soggy) through year one. Begin a light citrus-specific feeding once new growth appears. Remove any first-year flowers so the tree builds its leafy canopy before fruiting.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Tree filling out with leaves and side branches. Canopy taking shape; some shoots may appear from below the graft union.
growth_stages.user_action: Citrus needs almost no training -- it builds its own canopy. Remove any shoots growing from below the graft union and any tall vertical shoots from inside the canopy. Keep pruning light; citrus fruits at the outer edges of the canopy, so a dense outer leaf surface matters more than a defined branch structure.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Citrus does not lose its leaves -- it's evergreen. Growth slows in cool weather, foliage may darken slightly, and the tree holds its shape.
growth_stages.user_action: Citrus's version of dormancy is a winter slowdown, not a leaf-fall. In marginal zones, watch overnight forecasts and protect with frost cloth or warm holiday lights when temperatures approach 28 degrees F. Reduce watering frequency but don't let the rootball go bone-dry.

growth_stages.name: Light Annual Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: After main harvest, before spring flush. Citrus does not truly go dormant.
growth_stages.user_action: Light shape pruning: remove dead wood, suckers from below the graft union, water sprouts, crossing branches. Avoid heavy heading -- citrus fruits at the canopy edge.

growth_stages.name: Main Bloom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Honey-scented spring bloom. Smaller flushes possible in summer or fall on healthy trees.
growth_stages.user_action: Avoid sprays during bloom. The smell brings pollinators from a distance.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small fruit forming after petal fall. Heavy early-summer drop is the tree shedding excess set, normal.
growth_stages.user_action: Citrus is self-fertile; no thinning needed in most cases. Maintain consistent moisture to limit drop.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Variable -- some types ripen for months. Citrus does not ripen off the tree; pick when the fruit tastes right, not when it colors.
growth_stages.user_action: Use clippers or a gentle twist; do not pull, which tears bark. Most citrus can hang on the tree for weeks or months once ripe -- treat the tree as the storage.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest Feeding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Main harvest done. Tree preparing for next bloom flush.
growth_stages.user_action: Apply citrus-specific fertilizer (higher in nitrogen, with iron, zinc, manganese micronutrients). Inspect for scale and consider a horticultural oil application.

notifications.title: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text: Citrus is grafted on rootstock chosen for cold tolerance, disease resistance, and tree size. The graft union must sit 2 to 4 inches above soil level -- buried unions defeat the purpose of the rootstock and invite Phytophthora.
Plant in spring once soil is reliably above 60 degrees. Skip nitrogen fertilizer in the planting hole; a thin layer of compost is enough.

establishment.text: Water deeply once a week through the first season. Citrus has shallow roots and dries out faster than other tree fruit -- but also rots faster in standing water. Aim for evenly moist, never soggy.
Mulch a 3-foot circle but keep mulch 6 inches back from the trunk. Citrus collar and crown rot from Phytophthora is the single most common young-tree killer.

first_growth.text: Citrus is grown as a balanced canopy or hedge form, not as central-leader or open-center. Do not strip lower branches -- those are where most of the fruit will come from.
Remove suckers from below the graft union immediately. Rootstock suckers grow fast and have wicked thorns; left in place they take over the tree.

dormancy.text: Citrus does not have true dormancy -- it is evergreen and grows year-round wherever frost does not knock it back. There is no winter pruning window in the way deciduous fruit has.
In the colder end of citrus range, freeze protection (frost cloth, string lights, banking soil around the trunk) is the winter task rather than pruning.

dormant_prune.text: Citrus pruning is light and shape-focused, done after the main harvest in late winter or early spring before new growth. Remove dead wood, suckers, water sprouts, and crossing branches.
Avoid heavy heading cuts. Citrus fruits on previous and current-year growth at the canopy edge -- removing that growth removes next year's fruit.

blossom.text: Citrus often blooms multiple times per year. The main bloom in spring is the largest, but a healthy tree may also flush in summer or fall. Honey-scented flowers are normal.
Do not spray insecticide during bloom. The smell brings pollinators from a distance.

fruit_set.text: Most citrus is self-fertile and a single tree fruits well. Some mandarin varieties are seedy when cross-pollinated and seedless when isolated -- check your variety preference.
Heavy fruit drop in early summer is normal -- the tree sheds excess set. Persistent drop later in the season usually indicates water stress.

harvest.text: Citrus does not ripen off the tree. Pick when the fruit tastes right, not when it colors -- many citrus types color before they are sweet, and others stay green when ripe.
Use clippers or a gentle twist; do not pull, which can tear bark. Most citrus can hang on the tree for weeks or months once ripe -- treat the tree as the storage.

post_harvest.text: Apply citrus-specific fertilizer (higher in nitrogen, micronutrients including iron, zinc, manganese) after the main harvest. Citrus is heavier-feeding than other fruit trees.
Inspect for scale and ant trails year-round; the post-harvest window is a good time for a horticultural-oil application before the next bloom.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 20-50 lbs from a mature dooryard tree, smaller fruit but heavy bearer
yield_expectations.peak_production: Grafted citrus typically reaches full production in 3 to 5 years and stays productive for decades. Many varieties hold ripe fruit on the tree for months, so harvest is often a slow steady pick rather than a single window.
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Light or no fruit in year one is normal. Grafted citrus can flower early; remove early blossoms in year one so the tree builds canopy and roots first.
factors: consistent moisture through bloom and fruit set
nitrogen feeding split across the year
iron and zinc availability (citrus leaves yellow when these are deficient)

crops.hardiness_notes: Limes (Citrus aurantiifolia and C. latifolia) are the least cold-hardy common citrus -- leaves are damaged at 30F, trees killed at 24-28F. True Key limes (C. aurantiifolia) are more cold-sensitive than Persian/Bearss limes (C. latifolia). In zones 8-9, grow in containers and move indoors for winter. Limes are year-round producers in true tropical conditions but have a strong winter/spring harvest peak in subtropical zones. Most limes are self-fertile. Key limes are thorny, small-fruited, and have the classic intense lime flavor; Persian limes are thornless, larger, less acidic, and are the commercial standard. The Kaffir lime is grown for its leaves (used in Thai cooking) rather than its fruit. Lime trees are smaller than lemon trees (10-15 feet) and work well in containers. Begin bearing in year 3-4 from grafted trees.

varieties_detail.notes: Thornless commercial standard Persian lime. Large seedless green fruit. Self-fertile. More cold-hardy than Key lime. The practical choice for California and Florida home growers.

Classic small yellow-green lime with intense aromatic flavor. Thorny shrubby tree. Self-fertile. The true Key lime from Key Lime Pie fame. Less cold-hardy than Bearss -- Florida Keys and South Florida only.

Grown primarily for aromatic leaves used in Thai and Southeast Asian cooking. Distinctive double-lobed leaves. Small bumpy fruit is minimally juicy. Self-fertile. Essential herb tree for Asian cooking.

Lime x kumquat hybrid -- much more cold-hardy than true limes, surviving to about 20F. Small oval yellow fruit with lime-like flavor. Self-fertile. The only way to grow a lime-flavored fruit in zones 8-9.
Sweet non-acidic lime, eaten like an orange rather than juiced. Yellow-green skin. Popular in Middle Eastern and South Asian cuisines. Self-fertile. Interesting specialty citrus.

crops.chill_hours_note: No chill requirement -- among the least cold-hardy citrus

failure_diagnostics.label: Freeze damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Citrus is evergreen and does not become fully dormant, so freeze damage is a whole-tree phenomenon (leaves, twigs, fruit) rather than the blossom-frost issue deciduous fruit faces. Lemons and limes are most cold-sensitive (damaged below about 30 degrees); oranges and grapefruit tolerate brief drops to about 26 degrees; mandarins are typically the hardiest. Damage shows as leaf drop, blackened twigs, and split or mushy fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Cover with frost cloth on freeze nights and string old-style incandescent lights through the canopy if possible. Bank soil up around the graft union before winter so the rootstock survives even if the top is killed. In marginal zones, choose the most cold-hardy varieties (satsuma mandarin, kumquat, calamondin) or grow in a movable container.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Scale insects (cottony cushion scale, citrus mealybug, California red scale) and Asian citrus psyllid are the dominant citrus pests. Asian citrus psyllid spreads Huanglongbing (HLB, citrus greening), the disease threatening commercial citrus in Florida, Texas, and California. Phytophthora root and crown rot kills more young trees than any insect.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Inspect for scale year-round and treat with horticultural oil. In HLB-affected areas, follow your state's quarantine guidance; healthy trees on resistant rootstock and aggressive psyllid control are the home-garden defense. For Phytophthora prevention, keep mulch off the trunk and avoid overwatering.

failure_diagnostics.label: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Most citrus is self-fertile -- a single tree should fruit well. Heavy bloom with no fruit set is more often a water-stress, temperature-extreme, or alternate-bearing issue than a pollination one. Some mandarin varieties produce seedless fruit only when isolated from other citrus.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Maintain consistent moisture through bloom and fruit set. If the tree blooms heavily one year and barely the next, it is alternate-bearing -- thinning fruit in the heavy year levels the cycle out. Avoid moving citrus during bloom; flowers and small fruit drop from stress.

failure_diagnostics.label: Phytophthora root or crown rot
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Citrus is more prone to Phytophthora than any other backyard fruit tree. The pathogen thrives in waterlogged soil and at the trunk-soil interface. Symptoms are yellowing leaves with green veins, dieback, gum oozing from the lower trunk, and bark that lifts off the wood at the base.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant on a raised mound on heavy or poorly-drained soil. Keep mulch a hand-width back from the trunk. Water deeply but infrequently, and let the top inch of soil dry between waterings. There is no good cure once Phytophthora is established.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Citrus needs full sun, 6 to 8 hours minimum, to develop sugar and color. In shade the tree grows leaves and may bloom but fruit stays small, sour, and green. South or southwest exposure is ideal in most US citrus zones.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun -- if a wall or building is reflecting heat, even better. Light pruning to keep the inside of the canopy open helps inner fruit ripen. In containers, rotate the pot a quarter turn every few weeks for even growth.

crops.name: Orange (Navel)
crops.description: Classic seedless eating orange. Needs warm days, cool nights, and a long growing season to develop sweetness. Washington Navel is most widely grown. Harvest Dec-Apr for peak flavor.

3.notes: Too cold for oranges outdoors.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: In zones too cold for in-ground citrus (Z3-Z7), grow citrus in containers and move outdoors in spring once nights are reliably above 40 degrees F, then back indoors before fall frost. In Zone 8 or colder, citrus should be grown in containers and brought indoors before first frost. Meyer Lemon and kumquats are the most reliable container citrus for cold-climate gardeners. provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Pollinator category is mechanistically grounded. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. The nematode component is extension-documented. The claim's additional assertions about deterring whiteflies are not supported in the extension literature on marigolds and should be read as traditional.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Scale insects
pests.symptoms: Flat brown or white waxy lumps on stems and leaves. Sooty black mold follows from honeydew. Leaves yellow.
pests.cause: Various scale species. Common on indoor/container citrus.
pests.organic_treatment: Scrape off by hand. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap. Horticultural oil spray in winter.
pests.prevention: Inspect regularly. Keep plants healthy and well-fed. Good air circulation.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Citrus greening (HLB)
diseases.symptoms: Mottled yellow-green leaves in blotchy pattern. Small, lopsided, bitter fruit. Tree slowly declines. No cure.
diseases.cause: Candidatus Liberibacter bacteria spread by Asian citrus psyllid insect. A devastating citrus disease.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure. Remove affected trees.
diseases.prevention: Control Asian citrus psyllid with neem oil or spinosad. Inspect purchased trees before planting.

diseases.name: Root rot (Phytophthora)
diseases.symptoms: Yellow leaves, declining vigor, branch dieback. Bark at soil line may show brown discoloration.
diseases.cause: Phytophthora root rot from waterlogged or poorly drained soil.
diseases.organic_treatment: Improve drainage. Avoid overwatering. Apply phosphonate fungicide.
diseases.prevention: Well-drained soil essential. Never let roots sit in water. Graft onto resistant rootstock.

crops.harvest_ready: Deep orange skin, heavy for size. Taste is the best test -- a navel that looks orange can still be tart inside.

storage.freezer: Juice in ice cube trays. Segments freeze well.
storage.notes: Navel oranges have the thickest peel and best keeping quality of citrus.

varieties.note: Cara Cara is gaining rapidly in popularity -- pink flesh with low acidity and a distinctive berry note.

start_method.notes: Buy as a container plant. Harden off if moving from indoors to outdoors in spring. In zones below 9, grow in a large pot and bring indoors before first frost.

container_notes.notes: Excellent container plants in cold climates -- bring indoors before frost. Use citrus-specific potting mix. 15-gallon minimum for productive fruiting.

rotation.avoid_after: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Container-grown tree just planted. The graft union -- the knobby joint where the variety was grafted onto the rootstock -- sits well above soil level. Trunk often staked briefly to support against wind.
growth_stages.user_action: Dig the hole the same depth as the rootball but twice as wide. Plant high -- the top of the rootball should sit slightly above ground level. Don't add fertilizer at planting. Water deeply, then mulch around the base, keeping mulch a few inches off the trunk.

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: New leaves emerging in the first weeks after planting. Citrus pushes growth in flushes rather than steadily.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep soil consistently moist (not soggy) through year one. Begin a light citrus-specific feeding once new growth appears. Remove any first-year flowers so the tree builds its leafy canopy before fruiting.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Tree filling out with leaves and side branches. Canopy taking shape; some shoots may appear from below the graft union.
growth_stages.user_action: Citrus needs almost no training -- it builds its own canopy. Remove any shoots growing from below the graft union and any tall vertical shoots from inside the canopy. Keep pruning light; citrus fruits at the outer edges of the canopy, so a dense outer leaf surface matters more than a defined branch structure.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Citrus does not lose its leaves -- it's evergreen. Growth slows in cool weather, foliage may darken slightly, and the tree holds its shape.
growth_stages.user_action: Citrus's version of dormancy is a winter slowdown, not a leaf-fall. In marginal zones, watch overnight forecasts and protect with frost cloth or warm holiday lights when temperatures approach 28 degrees F. Reduce watering frequency but don't let the rootball go bone-dry.

growth_stages.name: Light Annual Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: After main harvest, before spring flush. Citrus does not truly go dormant.
growth_stages.user_action: Light shape pruning: remove dead wood, suckers from below the graft union, water sprouts, crossing branches. Avoid heavy heading -- citrus fruits at the canopy edge.

growth_stages.name: Main Bloom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Honey-scented spring bloom. Smaller flushes possible in summer or fall on healthy trees.
growth_stages.user_action: Avoid sprays during bloom. The smell brings pollinators from a distance.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small fruit forming after petal fall. Heavy early-summer drop is the tree shedding excess set, normal.
growth_stages.user_action: Citrus is self-fertile; no thinning needed in most cases. Maintain consistent moisture to limit drop.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Variable -- some types ripen for months. Citrus does not ripen off the tree; pick when the fruit tastes right, not when it colors.
growth_stages.user_action: Use clippers or a gentle twist; do not pull, which tears bark. Most citrus can hang on the tree for weeks or months once ripe -- treat the tree as the storage.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest Feeding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Main harvest done. Tree preparing for next bloom flush.
growth_stages.user_action: Apply citrus-specific fertilizer (higher in nitrogen, with iron, zinc, manganese micronutrients). Inspect for scale and consider a horticultural oil application.

notifications.title: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text: Citrus is grafted on rootstock chosen for cold tolerance, disease resistance, and tree size. The graft union must sit 2 to 4 inches above soil level -- buried unions defeat the purpose of the rootstock and invite Phytophthora.
Plant in spring once soil is reliably above 60 degrees. Skip nitrogen fertilizer in the planting hole; a thin layer of compost is enough.

establishment.text: Water deeply once a week through the first season. Citrus has shallow roots and dries out faster than other tree fruit -- but also rots faster in standing water. Aim for evenly moist, never soggy.
Mulch a 3-foot circle but keep mulch 6 inches back from the trunk. Citrus collar and crown rot from Phytophthora is the single most common young-tree killer.

first_growth.text: Citrus is grown as a balanced canopy or hedge form, not as central-leader or open-center. Do not strip lower branches -- those are where most of the fruit will come from.
Remove suckers from below the graft union immediately. Rootstock suckers grow fast and have wicked thorns; left in place they take over the tree.

dormancy.text: Citrus does not have true dormancy -- it is evergreen and grows year-round wherever frost does not knock it back. There is no winter pruning window in the way deciduous fruit has.
In the colder end of citrus range, freeze protection (frost cloth, string lights, banking soil around the trunk) is the winter task rather than pruning.

dormant_prune.text: Citrus pruning is light and shape-focused, done after the main harvest in late winter or early spring before new growth. Remove dead wood, suckers, water sprouts, and crossing branches.
Avoid heavy heading cuts. Citrus fruits on previous and current-year growth at the canopy edge -- removing that growth removes next year's fruit.

blossom.text: Citrus often blooms multiple times per year. The main bloom in spring is the largest, but a healthy tree may also flush in summer or fall. Honey-scented flowers are normal.
Do not spray insecticide during bloom. The smell brings pollinators from a distance.

fruit_set.text: Most citrus is self-fertile and a single tree fruits well. Some mandarin varieties are seedy when cross-pollinated and seedless when isolated -- check your variety preference.
Heavy fruit drop in early summer is normal -- the tree sheds excess set. Persistent drop later in the season usually indicates water stress.

harvest.text: Citrus does not ripen off the tree. Pick when the fruit tastes right, not when it colors -- many citrus types color before they are sweet, and others stay green when ripe.
Use clippers or a gentle twist; do not pull, which can tear bark. Most citrus can hang on the tree for weeks or months once ripe -- treat the tree as the storage.

post_harvest.text: Apply citrus-specific fertilizer (higher in nitrogen, micronutrients including iron, zinc, manganese) after the main harvest. Citrus is heavier-feeding than other fruit trees.
Inspect for scale and ant trails year-round; the post-harvest window is a good time for a horticultural-oil application before the next bloom.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 100-200 lbs from a mature dooryard tree at full production
yield_expectations.peak_production: Grafted citrus typically reaches full production in 3 to 5 years and stays productive for decades. Many varieties hold ripe fruit on the tree for months, so harvest is often a slow steady pick rather than a single window.
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Light or no fruit in year one is normal. Grafted citrus can flower early; remove early blossoms in year one so the tree builds canopy and roots first.
factors: consistent moisture through bloom and fruit set
nitrogen feeding split across the year
iron and zinc availability (citrus leaves yellow when these are deficient)

crops.hardiness_notes: Navel oranges (Citrus sinensis) are moderately cold-hardy among citrus -- mature trees tolerate 20-22F, making them viable in zones 8b-9a with protection. Navels are the winter-eating orange (peel-and-eat, no juice); Valencia oranges are the juice orange (tougher peel, more juice, summer harvest). Navels produce seedless fruit because the flowers cannot produce viable pollen -- they are seedless by nature. This also means they're self-fertile by definition (no pollination needed). They set fruit from late fall through early winter, with the classic winter-holiday ripening pattern. Cold stress actually improves flavor by increasing sugar content -- warm climates like Florida produce less-flavorful navel oranges than cooler climates like California. Trees are sensitive to wet feet and alkaline soils. Most commercial navels are grafted on trifoliate orange rootstock which increases cold-hardiness by 5-10F. Begin bearing year 3-5.

varieties_detail.notes: The original navel orange (1870s California). Large seedless fruit with classic flavor. Peak ripeness December-February. Self-fertile by nature. The commercial standard for winter-harvest oranges in California.
Pink-fleshed navel with berry-like flavor notes. Medium-large fruit. Same ripening period as Washington (December-February). Self-fertile. Popular premium variety at farmers markets.
Earlier-ripening navel (October-December). Heavy bearing. Self-fertile. Good for growers wanting fresh oranges before the Washington navel season.
Late-ripening navel (March-June). Extends the navel orange season. Fruit holds on the tree for months. Self-fertile. Plant alongside Washington for continuous harvest fall through summer.
Technically not a navel -- a true sweet orange. Summer harvest (May-October). Excellent juice orange. Self-fertile. Pair with a Washington navel for year-round oranges from just two trees.

crops.chill_hours_note: Minimal chill -- suited to zones 9-11

failure_diagnostics.label: Freeze damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Citrus is evergreen and does not become fully dormant, so freeze damage is a whole-tree phenomenon (leaves, twigs, fruit) rather than the blossom-frost issue deciduous fruit faces. Lemons and limes are most cold-sensitive (damaged below about 30 degrees); oranges and grapefruit tolerate brief drops to about 26 degrees; mandarins are typically the hardiest. Damage shows as leaf drop, blackened twigs, and split or mushy fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Cover with frost cloth on freeze nights and string old-style incandescent lights through the canopy if possible. Bank soil up around the graft union before winter so the rootstock survives even if the top is killed. In marginal zones, choose the most cold-hardy varieties (satsuma mandarin, kumquat, calamondin) or grow in a movable container.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Scale insects (cottony cushion scale, citrus mealybug, California red scale) and Asian citrus psyllid are the dominant citrus pests. Asian citrus psyllid spreads Huanglongbing (HLB, citrus greening), the disease threatening commercial citrus in Florida, Texas, and California. Phytophthora root and crown rot kills more young trees than any insect.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Inspect for scale year-round and treat with horticultural oil. In HLB-affected areas, follow your state's quarantine guidance; healthy trees on resistant rootstock and aggressive psyllid control are the home-garden defense. For Phytophthora prevention, keep mulch off the trunk and avoid overwatering.

failure_diagnostics.label: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Most citrus is self-fertile -- a single tree should fruit well. Heavy bloom with no fruit set is more often a water-stress, temperature-extreme, or alternate-bearing issue than a pollination one. Some mandarin varieties produce seedless fruit only when isolated from other citrus.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Maintain consistent moisture through bloom and fruit set. If the tree blooms heavily one year and barely the next, it is alternate-bearing -- thinning fruit in the heavy year levels the cycle out. Avoid moving citrus during bloom; flowers and small fruit drop from stress.

failure_diagnostics.label: Phytophthora root or crown rot
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Citrus is more prone to Phytophthora than any other backyard fruit tree. The pathogen thrives in waterlogged soil and at the trunk-soil interface. Symptoms are yellowing leaves with green veins, dieback, gum oozing from the lower trunk, and bark that lifts off the wood at the base.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant on a raised mound on heavy or poorly-drained soil. Keep mulch a hand-width back from the trunk. Water deeply but infrequently, and let the top inch of soil dry between waterings. There is no good cure once Phytophthora is established.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Citrus needs full sun, 6 to 8 hours minimum, to develop sugar and color. In shade the tree grows leaves and may bloom but fruit stays small, sour, and green. South or southwest exposure is ideal in most US citrus zones.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun -- if a wall or building is reflecting heat, even better. Light pruning to keep the inside of the canopy open helps inner fruit ripen. In containers, rotate the pot a quarter turn every few weeks for even growth.

crops.description: More cold-tolerant than oranges, easier to peel, and beloved by kids. Satsuma mandarin is the hardiest type -- survives down to 20°F for short periods. Great container plant.

3.notes: Container only. Satsuma in large pot, indoors Nov-Apr.

fertilizer.notes: Citrus fertilizer three times a year. Container plants need more frequent light feeding.

succession.reason: Tree crop -- not applicable for succession planting.

crops.pollinator_notes: Self-fertile. Some varieties (Clementine) produce seedless fruit when isolated from other citrus.

tasks.description: Light prune in early spring. Remove dead wood, suckers, and branches below the graft union.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Pollinator category is mechanistically grounded. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Pest-deterrent claim without matching established pattern. Default to traditional pending review.

provenance.reason: Soil-category claim has a mechanistic basis. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.reason: 'Fennel suppresses neighbors' is a common gardening-book claim. Limited research; allelopathy is real but specific claim pattern is traditional.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Scale insects
pests.symptoms: Flat brown or white waxy lumps on stems and leaves. Sooty black mold follows from honeydew. Leaves yellow.
pests.cause: Various scale species. Common on indoor/container citrus.
pests.organic_treatment: Scrape off by hand. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap. Horticultural oil spray in winter.
pests.prevention: Inspect regularly. Keep plants healthy and well-fed. Good air circulation.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Citrus greening (HLB)
diseases.symptoms: Mottled yellow-green leaves in blotchy pattern. Small, lopsided, bitter fruit. Tree slowly declines. No cure.
diseases.cause: Candidatus Liberibacter bacteria spread by Asian citrus psyllid insect. A devastating citrus disease.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure. Remove affected trees.
diseases.prevention: Control Asian citrus psyllid with neem oil or spinosad. Inspect purchased trees before planting.

diseases.name: Root rot (Phytophthora)
diseases.symptoms: Yellow leaves, declining vigor, branch dieback. Bark at soil line may show brown discoloration.
diseases.cause: Phytophthora root rot from waterlogged or poorly drained soil.
diseases.organic_treatment: Improve drainage. Avoid overwatering. Apply phosphonate fungicide.
diseases.prevention: Well-drained soil essential. Never let roots sit in water. Graft onto resistant rootstock.

crops.harvest_ready: Deep orange, easy to peel, skin slightly loose. Segments separate easily.

storage.freezer: Freeze peeled segments -- good for smoothies
storage.notes: Mandarins dry out faster than oranges. Best eaten fresh within 1 week.

varieties.note: Owari Satsuma is the most cold-hardy mandarin -- reliable in zones 7-8 where most citrus fails.

start_method.notes: Buy as a container plant. Harden off if moving from indoors to outdoors in spring. In zones below 9, grow in a large pot and bring indoors before first frost.

container_notes.notes: Excellent container plants in cold climates -- bring indoors before frost. Use citrus-specific potting mix. 15-gallon minimum for productive fruiting.

rotation.avoid_after: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Container-grown tree just planted. The graft union -- the knobby joint where the variety was grafted onto the rootstock -- sits well above soil level. Trunk often staked briefly to support against wind.
growth_stages.user_action: Dig the hole the same depth as the rootball but twice as wide. Plant high -- the top of the rootball should sit slightly above ground level. Don't add fertilizer at planting. Water deeply, then mulch around the base, keeping mulch a few inches off the trunk.

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: New leaves emerging in the first weeks after planting. Citrus pushes growth in flushes rather than steadily.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep soil consistently moist (not soggy) through year one. Begin a light citrus-specific feeding once new growth appears. Remove any first-year flowers so the tree builds its leafy canopy before fruiting.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Tree filling out with leaves and side branches. Canopy taking shape; some shoots may appear from below the graft union.
growth_stages.user_action: Citrus needs almost no training -- it builds its own canopy. Remove any shoots growing from below the graft union and any tall vertical shoots from inside the canopy. Keep pruning light; citrus fruits at the outer edges of the canopy, so a dense outer leaf surface matters more than a defined branch structure.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Citrus does not lose its leaves -- it's evergreen. Growth slows in cool weather, foliage may darken slightly, and the tree holds its shape.
growth_stages.user_action: Citrus's version of dormancy is a winter slowdown, not a leaf-fall. In marginal zones, watch overnight forecasts and protect with frost cloth or warm holiday lights when temperatures approach 28 degrees F. Reduce watering frequency but don't let the rootball go bone-dry.

growth_stages.name: Light Annual Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: After main harvest, before spring flush. Citrus does not truly go dormant.
growth_stages.user_action: Light shape pruning: remove dead wood, suckers from below the graft union, water sprouts, crossing branches. Avoid heavy heading -- citrus fruits at the canopy edge.

growth_stages.name: Main Bloom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Honey-scented spring bloom. Smaller flushes possible in summer or fall on healthy trees.
growth_stages.user_action: Avoid sprays during bloom. The smell brings pollinators from a distance.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small fruit forming after petal fall. Heavy early-summer drop is the tree shedding excess set, normal.
growth_stages.user_action: Citrus is self-fertile; no thinning needed in most cases. Maintain consistent moisture to limit drop.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Variable -- some types ripen for months. Citrus does not ripen off the tree; pick when the fruit tastes right, not when it colors.
growth_stages.user_action: Use clippers or a gentle twist; do not pull, which tears bark. Most citrus can hang on the tree for weeks or months once ripe -- treat the tree as the storage.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest Feeding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Main harvest done. Tree preparing for next bloom flush.
growth_stages.user_action: Apply citrus-specific fertilizer (higher in nitrogen, with iron, zinc, manganese micronutrients). Inspect for scale and consider a horticultural oil application.

notifications.title: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text: Citrus is grafted on rootstock chosen for cold tolerance, disease resistance, and tree size. The graft union must sit 2 to 4 inches above soil level -- buried unions defeat the purpose of the rootstock and invite Phytophthora.
Plant in spring once soil is reliably above 60 degrees. Skip nitrogen fertilizer in the planting hole; a thin layer of compost is enough.

establishment.text: Water deeply once a week through the first season. Citrus has shallow roots and dries out faster than other tree fruit -- but also rots faster in standing water. Aim for evenly moist, never soggy.
Mulch a 3-foot circle but keep mulch 6 inches back from the trunk. Citrus collar and crown rot from Phytophthora is the single most common young-tree killer.

first_growth.text: Citrus is grown as a balanced canopy or hedge form, not as central-leader or open-center. Do not strip lower branches -- those are where most of the fruit will come from.
Remove suckers from below the graft union immediately. Rootstock suckers grow fast and have wicked thorns; left in place they take over the tree.

dormancy.text: Citrus does not have true dormancy -- it is evergreen and grows year-round wherever frost does not knock it back. There is no winter pruning window in the way deciduous fruit has.
In the colder end of citrus range, freeze protection (frost cloth, string lights, banking soil around the trunk) is the winter task rather than pruning.

dormant_prune.text: Citrus pruning is light and shape-focused, done after the main harvest in late winter or early spring before new growth. Remove dead wood, suckers, water sprouts, and crossing branches.
Avoid heavy heading cuts. Citrus fruits on previous and current-year growth at the canopy edge -- removing that growth removes next year's fruit.

blossom.text: Citrus often blooms multiple times per year. The main bloom in spring is the largest, but a healthy tree may also flush in summer or fall. Honey-scented flowers are normal.
Do not spray insecticide during bloom. The smell brings pollinators from a distance.

fruit_set.text: Most citrus is self-fertile and a single tree fruits well. Some mandarin varieties are seedy when cross-pollinated and seedless when isolated -- check your variety preference.
Heavy fruit drop in early summer is normal -- the tree sheds excess set. Persistent drop later in the season usually indicates water stress.

harvest.text: Citrus does not ripen off the tree. Pick when the fruit tastes right, not when it colors -- many citrus types color before they are sweet, and others stay green when ripe.
Use clippers or a gentle twist; do not pull, which can tear bark. Most citrus can hang on the tree for weeks or months once ripe -- treat the tree as the storage.

post_harvest.text: Apply citrus-specific fertilizer (higher in nitrogen, micronutrients including iron, zinc, manganese) after the main harvest. Citrus is heavier-feeding than other fruit trees.
Inspect for scale and ant trails year-round; the post-harvest window is a good time for a horticultural-oil application before the next bloom.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 50-100 lbs from a mature dooryard tree, often with a concentrated winter harvest window
yield_expectations.peak_production: Grafted citrus typically reaches full production in 3 to 5 years and stays productive for decades. Many varieties hold ripe fruit on the tree for months, so harvest is often a slow steady pick rather than a single window.
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Light or no fruit in year one is normal. Grafted citrus can flower early; remove early blossoms in year one so the tree builds canopy and roots first.
factors: consistent moisture through bloom and fruit set
nitrogen feeding split across the year
iron and zinc availability (citrus leaves yellow when these are deficient)

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

crops.hardiness_notes: Mandarins and clementines (Citrus reticulata) are the most cold-hardy of the sweet citrus -- Satsuma mandarins tolerate 15-18F when mature, making them viable in zone 8a. This hardiness makes mandarins the right citrus for Gulf Coast growers (Louisiana, Alabama, Mississippi, Florida Panhandle) where winters are too cold for oranges or lemons. Fruit characteristics vary widely across varieties: Satsumas are early-ripening and virtually seedless with loose peels; clementines are small and very sweet; Tangerines have more intense flavor and tighter peels. Most mandarins require cross-pollination from another citrus variety for heavy fruit set; pollination by bees from neighboring citrus is usually sufficient. Fruit matures fall through winter depending on variety. Trees are small (8-15 feet) and well-suited to container growing. Begin bearing year 3-4 from grafted trees. Satsumas are particularly forgiving and make good beginner citrus for cold-winter zones.

varieties_detail.notes: Most cold-hardy sweet citrus -- survives to 15F when mature. Loose-peeled easy-peeling fruit ripens October-December. Essentially seedless. Self-fertile. The go-to citrus for the Gulf Coast and zone 8 growers.
Small very sweet fruit with loose peel. The 'Cuties' marketing name. Requires cross-pollination for heavy bearing. Sensitive to heat and humidity -- best in Mediterranean climates.
Classic Christmas tangerine. Deep red-orange skin and flesh, tight peel but snap-peel type. Heavy bearing. Self-fertile. The traditional Florida tangerine.
Miniature seedless mandarin, bite-size fruit with intense sweet flavor. Ripens December-January. Self-fertile. Premium variety at high-end markets.
Clementine x Minneola tangelo cross. Medium red-orange fruit with exceptional sweet-tart flavor and rich aroma. Requires cross-pollination. Ripens November-January. Popular home-garden variety.

crops.chill_hours_note: Minimal chill -- one of the more cold-tolerant citrus varieties

failure_diagnostics.label: Freeze damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Citrus is evergreen and does not become fully dormant, so freeze damage is a whole-tree phenomenon (leaves, twigs, fruit) rather than the blossom-frost issue deciduous fruit faces. Lemons and limes are most cold-sensitive (damaged below about 30 degrees); oranges and grapefruit tolerate brief drops to about 26 degrees; mandarins are typically the hardiest. Damage shows as leaf drop, blackened twigs, and split or mushy fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Cover with frost cloth on freeze nights and string old-style incandescent lights through the canopy if possible. Bank soil up around the graft union before winter so the rootstock survives even if the top is killed. In marginal zones, choose the most cold-hardy varieties (satsuma mandarin, kumquat, calamondin) or grow in a movable container.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Scale insects (cottony cushion scale, citrus mealybug, California red scale) and Asian citrus psyllid are the dominant citrus pests. Asian citrus psyllid spreads Huanglongbing (HLB, citrus greening), the disease threatening commercial citrus in Florida, Texas, and California. Phytophthora root and crown rot kills more young trees than any insect.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Inspect for scale year-round and treat with horticultural oil. In HLB-affected areas, follow your state's quarantine guidance; healthy trees on resistant rootstock and aggressive psyllid control are the home-garden defense. For Phytophthora prevention, keep mulch off the trunk and avoid overwatering.

failure_diagnostics.label: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Most citrus is self-fertile -- a single tree should fruit well. Heavy bloom with no fruit set is more often a water-stress, temperature-extreme, or alternate-bearing issue than a pollination one. Some mandarin varieties produce seedless fruit only when isolated from other citrus.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Maintain consistent moisture through bloom and fruit set. If the tree blooms heavily one year and barely the next, it is alternate-bearing -- thinning fruit in the heavy year levels the cycle out. Avoid moving citrus during bloom; flowers and small fruit drop from stress.

failure_diagnostics.label: Phytophthora root or crown rot
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Citrus is more prone to Phytophthora than any other backyard fruit tree. The pathogen thrives in waterlogged soil and at the trunk-soil interface. Symptoms are yellowing leaves with green veins, dieback, gum oozing from the lower trunk, and bark that lifts off the wood at the base.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant on a raised mound on heavy or poorly-drained soil. Keep mulch a hand-width back from the trunk. Water deeply but infrequently, and let the top inch of soil dry between waterings. There is no good cure once Phytophthora is established.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Citrus needs full sun, 6 to 8 hours minimum, to develop sugar and color. In shade the tree grows leaves and may bloom but fruit stays small, sour, and green. South or southwest exposure is ideal in most US citrus zones.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun -- if a wall or building is reflecting heat, even better. Light pruning to keep the inside of the canopy open helps inner fruit ripen. In containers, rotate the pot a quarter turn every few weeks for even growth.

good.name: Borage
good.why: Attracts pollinators, improves general garden health

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Xerces Society documents borage as a pollinator-attractant plant. While Xerces specifically names tomato, squash, and cucumber crops, the pollinator-attraction mechanism generalizes reasonably to other insect-pollinated crops. Source: xerces.org/blog/plants-you-can-eat-are-pollinator-treat.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Soil-category claim has a mechanistic basis. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. This claim's nematode component aligns with the extension-documented mechanism, but the 'concurrent companion' application pattern reflects popular gardening practice rather than extension protocol.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: 'Fennel suppresses neighbors' is a common gardening-book claim. Limited research; allelopathy is real but specific claim pattern is traditional.

pests.name: Mealybugs
pests.symptoms: White cottony masses along stems, at leaf axils, and inside ripening fruit eyes. Sticky honeydew on leaves and ground below, followed by sooty mold. Ants often tend the colonies.
pests.cause: Several mealybug species, including Pseudococcus longispinus and Planococcus species. UF/IFAS lists mealybug as one of the most common fig insects. Heaviest in warm humid weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Spray colonies with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, focusing on leaf axils and fruit clusters. Control ants (which farm mealybugs) with sticky bands on the trunk. Prune out heavily infested branches.
pests.prevention: Inspect new plants before planting. Avoid over-fertilizing with nitrogen. Remove fruit mummies where mealybugs overwinter.

pests.name: Fig mites
pests.symptoms: Yellow or russet discoloration on leaves, curled or distorted new growth, and reduced vigor. Most important as vectors of fig mosaic virus, which causes permanent yellow mottling and leaf distortion.
pests.cause: Aceria ficus (fig blister mite) and related eriophyid mites. Too small to see without magnification. Transmit fig mosaic virus from infected trees to healthy ones.
pests.organic_treatment: Horticultural oil or sulfur sprays applied in late winter or early spring (before bud break) are the standard control. Remove and destroy severely virus-infected trees -- there is no cure for mosaic.
pests.prevention: Only propagate cuttings from symptom-free trees. Disinfect pruning tools between trees. Control is especially important if mites were a problem the previous year.

pests.name: Fig beetle
pests.symptoms: Large (1 inch) iridescent green beetles feed on ripe figs, chewing into fruits from the eye. Birds often follow beetle damage and finish off the fruit.
pests.cause: Cotinis mutabilis (green fig beetle) in the West and Cotinis nitida (green June beetle) in the Southeast. Attracted to ripe and overripe fruit.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick beetles in early morning when they are sluggish. Drop into soapy water. Bag developing fruit in fine-mesh organza bags to exclude beetles.
pests.prevention: Pick fruit daily as it ripens. Remove fallen and overripe figs so beetles move elsewhere. Closed-eye varieties are less vulnerable.

pests.name: Ants
pests.symptoms: Ants trailing up the trunk and through the canopy. Ants tending mealybugs and scale, protecting them from natural enemies. May enter fruit through the eye.
pests.cause: Argentine ants and other species are attracted by honeydew produced by mealybugs and scale. UF/IFAS lists ants among the most common fig pests.
pests.organic_treatment: Sticky trunk bands (Tanglefoot on tree wrap, not directly on bark) block ants from climbing. Bait stations with boric acid along ant trails.
pests.prevention: Keep tree base clear of mulch and weeds that shelter ants. Control the sap-sucking insects (mealybugs, scale) that ants tend.

diseases.name: Fig rust
diseases.symptoms: Small yellow to yellow-green spots on upper leaf surface that turn reddish-brown as they enlarge. Undersides of leaves develop small blister-like pustules. Heavy infection causes leaves to yellow and drop prematurely, weakening the tree and reducing cold tolerance.
diseases.cause: Cerotelium fici, a fungus. UF/IFAS identifies fig rust as the most common fig disease in the southeastern US. Favored by warm humid weather.
diseases.organic_treatment: Once leaves show symptoms, no cure -- focus on sanitation. Rake and dispose of fallen leaves in fall (they harbor overwintering spores).
diseases.prevention: Prune for good air circulation. Water at soil level -- avoid overhead irrigation. Apply 5-5-50 Bordeaux spray (copper sulfate + lime + water) preventively during the growing season in high-pressure areas. 2-3 inches of mulch under the tree. Fig rust resistance varies by variety.

diseases.name: Fig mosaic virus
diseases.symptoms: Yellow mottling or mosaic pattern on leaves, often with diffuse margins that blend into green. Older lesions may develop a brown-red band. Leaf distortion and reduced vigor. No cure.
diseases.cause: One or more viruses transmitted by fig mites (Aceria ficus) and through infected cuttings. Widespread in backyard figs.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure. Severely affected trees should be removed and replaced.
diseases.prevention: Only take cuttings from trees with no mosaic symptoms. Control fig mites with horticultural oil or sulfur. Many tolerant varieties carry low-level virus without major yield loss.

diseases.name: Thread blight
diseases.symptoms: Fine white fungal threads run along twigs and leaf undersides, matting leaves together. Leaves turn brown and die but remain attached, hanging in the canopy.
diseases.cause: Pellicularia koleroga (syn. Rhizoctonia), a fungus favored by humid summer conditions and dense canopies. Listed by UF/IFAS as a regional fig disease.
diseases.organic_treatment: Prune out affected branches well back into healthy wood. Dispose of prunings; do not compost.
diseases.prevention: Thin canopy annually to improve airflow. Avoid overhead watering. Space trees for light penetration.
