growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Container-grown or bare-root fig just planted. Often a multi-stem shrub-like form rather than a single trunk.
growth_stages.user_action: Plant in the warmest, most sheltered spot you have -- against a south-facing wall is ideal in cold zones. Dig wide, plant at the original soil line, water in deeply. In zone 6 and colder, plant in a large container so you can move it into shelter for winter.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Fig planted in sheltered spot or container?

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Leaves emerging from the dormant stems. Fig often pushes new growth quickly once warm weather arrives.
growth_stages.user_action: Water consistently through the first summer; figs handle drought once established but need steady moisture in year one. Remove any small fruit that sets in year one. In containers, keep the rootball moist but never standing in water.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Multiple stems extending from the base or main trunk. Fig can grow as a single-trunk tree or a multi-stem bush.
growth_stages.user_action: Decide on the form now: single-trunk for warm zones (more vertical growth, easier to harvest), multi-stem for cold zones (insurance -- if one stem dies back, others survive). Remove competing growth to settle the form. Pinch the tips of long shoots to encourage side branching.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Leaves drop. In warm zones (8-10) figs may hold leaves into early winter; in colder zones they go fully dormant by the first hard freeze.
growth_stages.user_action: Cold-zone protection is critical for fig. Wrap the trunk and main stems with burlap or insulation, mound mulch deeply over the root zone, or move container figs into an unheated garage or shed. The colder the zone, the more aggressive the wrapping should be. Light pruning is OK now but main pruning waits until late winter.

growth_stages.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Tree fully dormant. Late-winter window.
growth_stages.user_action: Heavy pruning OK. Hard prune in cold zones (sacrifices breba crop); light prune in warm zones to keep both crops.

growth_stages.name: (No Visible Bloom)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Fig has no visible flowers -- the syconium is the flower structure.
growth_stages.user_action: Most home varieties are parthenocarpic; no pollinator needed.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Development
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Breba crop on year-old wood, main crop on current-year wood.
growth_stages.user_action: Maintain consistent moisture to prevent fruit drop.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Neck softens, fruit hangs down, nectar at eye.
growth_stages.user_action: Pick daily during peak; ripe figs go over fast.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest & Winter Prep
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Fruit done; tree heading to dormancy.
growth_stages.user_action: Clear drops. Mulch refresh. Wrap trunk in cold zones.

notifications.title: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text: Fig is grown on its own roots in home gardens -- there is no graft union to worry about. Plant with the crown at the original soil line.
Plant in spring after frost danger passes. Fig is more tolerant of poor and alkaline soil than most fruit trees but appreciates a generous compost amendment at planting.

establishment.text: Water deeply once a week through the first season. Established figs are remarkably drought-tolerant but young trees need consistent moisture for the first two years.
Mulch a 3-foot circle around the base. Fig roots are shallow and benefit from a deep organic mulch year-round.

first_growth.text: Fig can be grown as a single-trunk tree, a multi-stemmed shrub, or even an espalier against a wall. Multi-stem form is common in cold zones because it allows the tree to regenerate from the crown after winter dieback.
Pinch the growing tips at 24 to 30 inches to encourage branching. Otherwise fig grows fast and gangly.

dormancy.text: Fig is fully deciduous and goes dormant in winter. In the warmer end of fig range, dormancy is brief; in cold zones the tree may die back to the ground each winter and regrow from the crown.
In USDA zones 6 and below, wrap the trunk and main scaffolds with insulating material before winter, or grow as a multi-stem so regeneration from the crown is easy.

dormant_prune.text: Fig tolerates heavy pruning. Most varieties bear two crops per year: an early 'breba' crop on previous-year wood and a main crop on current-year wood. Heavy winter pruning reduces the breba crop but does not affect the main crop.
In cold zones where the breba crop rarely ripens before frost anyway, prune hard to maintain a manageable size. In warm zones, prune lightly to preserve the breba crop.

blossom.text: Fig has no visible flowers -- the 'fruit' is actually a syconium, an enclosed structure with the flowers inside. There is no bloom stage to protect from frost.

Most home-garden fig varieties (Common figs) are parthenocarpic, meaning they set fruit without pollination. Some varieties (Smyrna, San Pedro types) need a specific wasp pollinator that is not present in most US gardens -- avoid these unless you live in California's fig belt.

fruit_set.text: Fruit develops over several months. A breba crop ripens in early summer on year-old wood; the main crop ripens in late summer to early fall on current-year wood.
Heavy early fruit drop indicates water stress. Fig is drought-tolerant but drops fruit before it drops leaves when water-stressed.

harvest.text: Fig is ripe when the fruit hangs down on its stem (the neck softens), the skin gives to gentle pressure, and a tiny drop of nectar may appear at the eye. Underripe figs are starchy and disappointing; ripe figs are floral and intensely sweet.
Harvest daily during peak ripening. Ripe figs do not hold on the tree -- they go from underripe to over-ripe in 24 to 48 hours and attract birds, wasps, and yellow jackets fast.

post_harvest.text: Clean up dropped fruit immediately. Fermenting figs attract wasps, yellow jackets, and dried-fruit beetles in serious numbers.
Apply mulch refresh and a balanced feed in fall before dormancy. In cold zones, this is also when to wrap the trunk for winter protection.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 20-50 lbs from a mature in-ground tree in a warm zone; 5-15 lbs from a mature container fig
yield_expectations.peak_production: Full production typically by year 3 to 5. A mature in-ground fig in a warm zone produces heavily; a container fig produces more modestly but gives reliable fruit even in cold zones.
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Light or no harvest in year one. Figs are precocious for a fruit tree and may set a few in year two. Year one is still a root and trunk year.
factors: winter protection in zones 6 and colder (wrap, mulch heavy, or grow in container)
consistent moisture during fruit sizing -- drought causes drop
balance between breba (year-old wood) and main crop (current-year wood) when pruning
container growing for cold zones extends viable range significantly

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

crops.hardiness_notes: Figs (Ficus carica) have a unique hardiness pattern: roots are significantly more cold-tolerant than the above-ground canes. In zones 5-6, the top growth frequently dies back to the ground in winter, but the roots survive and resprout vigorously in spring, fruiting on new wood the same year. This makes figs genuinely viable in zones 5-6 as die-back-and-regrow shrubs (expect 6-8 feet of growth per season), though crop timing gets tight in zones 5a-5b. In zones 7+, figs grow as full-sized trees (15-25 feet) with normal fig tree habit. Common figs (the type grown for backyard fruit) are parthenocarpic -- they produce fruit without pollination and don't need another tree. Many varieties produce two crops: an early breba crop on previous-year wood in June-July, and a main crop on current-year wood in August-October. In cold zones where canes die back, only the main crop is possible. Winter protection (wrapping, mulching, or the Minnesota Tip method of burying canes) is essential in zones 5-6 and recommended in zone 7. Trees begin bearing in year 2-3.

varieties_detail.notes: The gold standard for cold-climate fig growing. Roots survive to -20F even when top growth dies back. Medium purple-mahogany fruit with sweet berry flavor. Self-fertile. The safest fig for zones 5-6.
Small sweet brown-purple fruit -- one of the sweetest figs. Closed eye keeps out moisture in rainy climates, reducing spoilage. Self-fertile. Heat-tolerant and southern-adapted.
Most widely planted fig in the southern US. Large medium-brown fruit, sometimes produces two crops per year. Self-fertile. Heat-tolerant. Less cold-hardy than Chicago Hardy.
Naturally dwarf (6-10 feet), ideal for containers and small spaces. Small purple-black fruit with intense strawberry-like flavor. Self-fertile. A 17th-century French heirloom still prized for flavor.

Louisiana State University release. Heavy producer of medium dark-purple fruit. Bred for hot humid southern conditions. Self-fertile. Fast-growing and productive. Top choice for the Gulf Coast and Southeast.

crops.chill_hours_note: Essentially no chill requirement -- ideal for zones 7-11

failure_diagnostics.label: Cold or frost damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Fig blooms inside the syconium (no exposed flowers), so spring frost during bloom is not an issue. The cold problem for fig is winter dieback at the edge of its hardiness range -- USDA zone 7 reliably, zones 6 and 5 with protection. Cold-damaged trees often regenerate from the crown but lose the breba crop and may produce only the late main crop.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: In cold zones, grow as a multi-stem shrub so regeneration from the crown is easy. Wrap the trunk and main scaffolds with insulation in fall, or bend young trees over and bury them under mulch for winter (the traditional 'fig coffin' approach).

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Fig has remarkably few serious pests in most of the US. Fig rust (orange spots on leaves leading to defoliation) shows up in humid climates. Fig mites cause leaf curling but rarely affect crop. Birds, wasps, and yellow jackets are often more destructive than insects -- they go after ripe fruit hard.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: For fig rust, rake and destroy fallen leaves in fall to break the cycle. For wasps and yellow jackets, harvest daily and clean up drops immediately. Bird netting helps in serious bird-pressure areas; a single ripe fig can attract a flock.

failure_diagnostics.label: Bloom but no fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Pollination is not the issue for fig in most home gardens. Common fig varieties are parthenocarpic and set fruit without pollination. Smyrna and San Pedro varieties need a specific fig wasp (only present in California's fig belt and a few similar areas); planting one of these outside its range gives you a tree that flowers internally but never sets fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Confirm your variety is a Common fig (parthenocarpic) before planting. Brown Turkey, Celeste, Chicago Hardy, Black Mission, and Kadota are all Common figs. Persistent fruit drop is more often water stress than pollination failure.

failure_diagnostics.label: Waterlogging or root problems
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Fig tolerates a wider moisture range than most fruit trees but cannot survive standing water. Roots in waterlogged soil suffocate; symptoms include yellowing leaves and dieback. Excessive irrigation in summer can also reduce fruit quality (less sugar, more cracking).
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil. Once established, water deeply but infrequently -- weekly is plenty in most climates. Avoid the daily-shallow-watering pattern that suits some other fruit.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Fig needs full sun, 6 to 8 hours minimum, to ripen fruit properly. In partial shade the tree grows leaves but produces fewer and lower-quality figs that may not reach full sweetness before fall.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun -- a south or southwest wall provides reflected heat that helps in cooler zones. Light pruning to open the canopy helps inner fruit ripen.

crops.name: Pomegranate
crops.description: Stunning in autumn with orange-red fruit and fiery foliage. Drought-tolerant, heat-loving, and long-lived. Needs a long hot summer (200+ frost-free days) for fruit to ripen fully.

7.notes: Russian varieties (Salavatski) are most cold-hardy. Ripen before first frost.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Fig, pomegranate, and persimmon are warm-climate perennials. Plant bare-root or container stock in spring after last frost, or in fall in mild-winter zones. Fig is hardy to Zone 6 with winter protection (die-back hardy to Z5). Pomegranate Z7+. Persimmon (American) Z5+, Asian Z7+. Harvest late summer through fall once trees reach bearing age (2-4 years for fig and persimmon, 2-3 years for pomegranate). (UGA Extension Fig Production; Clemson HGIC Fig; UF/IFAS Pomegranate; UC Master Gardeners Persimmon)

fertilizer.notes: Light feeder once established. Two balanced feeds a year is plenty. Over-feeding reduces fruit quality.

succession.reason: Tree crop -- not applicable for succession planting.

crops.pollinator_notes: Self-fertile. Single tree bears well. Bees improve fruit set.

tasks.description: Prune in late winter. Train as multi-stem shrub or single-trunk tree. Remove suckers from base regularly throughout growing season.

crops.year_one_notes: No fruit expected years 1-2. Plant in full sun -- location drives everything with pomegranates.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of small soft-bodied insects on new growth. Curled and yellowed young leaves. Sticky honeydew on lower leaves and fruit, followed by sooty mold that disfigures the skin.
pests.cause: Cotton/melon aphid (Aphis gossypii) is most common. UF/IFAS CREC notes aphids are common to most pomegranate-growing regions, especially on young plants and at the propagation stage.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast with water. Insecticidal soap or neem oil. Ladybugs and lacewings provide strong control. Tolerate light populations -- natural enemies need prey to stay around.
pests.prevention: Avoid over-fertilizing. Control ants that tend aphid colonies. Protect young plants most carefully.

pests.name: Leaffooted bug
pests.symptoms: Hard darkened spots or sunken areas on fruit rind where bugs have fed. Fruit may develop internal browning and off-flavors. Long narrow brown bugs (3/4 inch) with flared hind legs visible on fruit clusters, often in groups.
pests.cause: Leptoglossus zonatus and related species. Major warm-region fruit pest. Feeds by piercing the rind and sucking juice from arils.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick adults and nymphs in morning when sluggish. Knock clusters into soapy water. Pyrethrin products if infestations are heavy.
pests.prevention: Scout fruit weekly. Remove weedy borders where bugs overwinter. Netting fruit clusters when fruits begin to size up protects against both bugs and birds.

pests.name: Mealybugs
pests.symptoms: White cottony masses in leaf axils, on fruit, and inside the calyx. Sticky honeydew and sooty mold. Fruit may crack at the calyx where mealybugs feed.
pests.cause: Several mealybug species affect pomegranate. Often farmed by ants.
pests.organic_treatment: Horticultural oil or insecticidal soap sprayed into calyx and leaf axils. Control ants with sticky trunk bands.
pests.prevention: Inspect nursery stock. Prune for airflow so spray coverage reaches hidden areas.

pests.name: Thrips
pests.symptoms: Silvery or bronzy scarring on fruit skin where thrips have rasped the surface. Distorted new leaves. Heaviest damage during bloom and early fruit development.
pests.cause: Several thrips species including Scirtothrips and Frankliniella. Active during warm dry weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blue sticky traps to monitor. Spinosad applied in the evening during bloom (to protect bees). Reflective mulch deters thrips from landing.
pests.prevention: Maintain even irrigation to reduce stress. Remove weedy hosts around the orchard.

diseases.name: Anthracnose fruit rot
diseases.symptoms: Circular brown or black sunken lesions on fruit skin that may show concentric rings. Lesions spread rapidly in warm wet weather. Fruit drops prematurely or rots on the tree. Leaves may show dark spots.
diseases.cause: Colletotrichum gloeosporioides fungus. UF/IFAS research identifies this as the most damaging pomegranate disease in the humid Southeast, causing severe fruit rot and premature fruit drop.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove and destroy affected fruits. Copper-based fungicide during extended wet weather.
diseases.prevention: Plant resistant varieties where available -- UF/IFAS trials show significant variation. Prune for airflow. Rake and remove fallen fruit and leaves. Avoid overhead irrigation. Mulch under canopy.

diseases.name: Cercospora leaf spot & fruit blemish
diseases.symptoms: Dark brown to black circular leaf spots, sometimes coalescing. Early leaf drop. On fruit, small dark blemishes that may enlarge into sunken lesions. Fruit quality and appearance reduced.
diseases.cause: Cercospora punicae fungus. UF/IFAS CREC lists this as a primary pomegranate concern in humid climates. Spreads by rain splash.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves and fruits. Copper fungicide may reduce spread during wet periods.
diseases.prevention: Space plants for air circulation. Water at soil level. Rake and destroy fallen leaves in winter.

diseases.name: Branch canker & dieback
diseases.symptoms: Sudden wilting and dieback of individual branches. Elliptical cankers on branches that may ooze sap. Interior wood shows brown streaking. Whole branches may die back from the tip.
diseases.cause: Neofusicoccum parvum, Lasiodiplodia theobromae, and related fungi in the Botryosphaeriaceae. UF/IFAS surveys isolate these regularly from diseased branches. Stressed and pruning-wounded trees are most vulnerable.
diseases.organic_treatment: Prune affected branches well below the cankered tissue (at least 6 inches into healthy wood). Disinfect pruning tools between cuts. Burn or dispose of prunings; do not compost.
diseases.prevention: Prune during dry weather with clean cuts at a slight angle so water drains. Avoid pruning in wet weather when spores are active. Keep trees unstressed -- healthy vigorous trees resist canker.

diseases.name: Fruit heart rot (Alternaria)
diseases.symptoms: Fruit looks normal from outside but interior arils are rotted dark brown or black when cut open. Often no external symptoms -- the first sign is biting into a ruined fruit.
diseases.cause: Alternaria alternata infects flowers and developing fruit during wet bloom weather, then grows inside the fruit undetected. Worse in years with heavy spring rain.
diseases.organic_treatment: No effective organic rescue once infection is internal. Discard affected fruits.
diseases.prevention: Plant less-susceptible varieties where possible. Avoid overhead irrigation during bloom. Thin fruit clusters to improve airflow.

crops.harvest_ready: Deep red skin, fruit feels heavy for its size, skin begins to crack slightly. Tap -- sounds metallic rather than dull.

storage.freezer: Freeze arils (seeds) in a bag -- excellent, lasts 6 months
storage.notes: Whole pomegranates have remarkable shelf life. The thick skin is nature's packaging.

varieties.note: Sienevyi is the most cold-hardy pomegranate -- recommended for zones 6-7 where Wonderful is unreliable.

start_method.notes: Plant bare-root trees in late winter/early spring while dormant. Container trees can go in spring through early autumn. Stake against wind for the first 2 years.

container_notes.notes: Fruit trees need to be grown in the ground. Dwarf varieties on very dwarfing rootstocks can be tried in very large (30+ gallon) containers but are challenging and rarely as productive.

rotation.avoid_after: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Tree or multi-trunk shrub just planted. Pomegranate often arrives as a multi-stem clump; mulberry and persimmon as single-trunk trees.
growth_stages.user_action: Plant high in well-drained soil. Stake mulberry and persimmon firmly; pomegranate usually doesn't need staking once the multi-trunk form is set. Water in deeply, mulch around the base, and avoid burying the lowest stems.

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: First leaves breaking. Pomegranate often pushes new shoots from the base in a clump; mulberry and persimmon push from existing stems.
growth_stages.user_action: Water deeply once a week through the first summer. Remove any first-year flowers or developing fruit. For pomegranate, decide now whether to keep the multi-trunk form (let 3 to 5 main trunks grow) or train it to a single trunk; remove the extra base shoots accordingly.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Strong shoot extension. Mulberry grows quickly and may need its first directional pruning. Persimmon is slower. Pomegranate fills its multi-trunk clump.
growth_stages.user_action: Mulberry: pick one main vertical trunk and remove low side branches you don't want long-term -- mulberry grows large fast. Persimmon: light shaping only; both American and Asian persimmons fruit on last year's wood, so heavy pruning costs you crops. Pomegranate: keep the chosen 3 to 5 main trunks clear of small side shoots below knee height.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Mulberry, persimmon, and pomegranate all drop their leaves in late fall. Frost-hardy when fully dormant.
growth_stages.user_action: Mulch around the base before hard freeze. Pomegranate benefits from extra mulch over the root zone in zone 7 and colder. Wrap young trunks in young-tree wrap if rabbits or sunscald are concerns. Major pruning waits until late winter.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Mulch and trunk protection in place?

growth_stages.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Tree fully dormant, leaves down. Late-winter window.
growth_stages.user_action: Light structural pruning only on mulberry and persimmon -- both fruit on previous-year wood. Pomegranate suckers freely; remove suckers and limit to 3 to 5 main trunks.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Late-spring or early-summer bloom -- well after main spring frost risk has passed.
growth_stages.user_action: These crops bloom late, so frost protection is rarely needed. Avoid spraying during bloom.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small green fruit forming after petal fall. Most home varieties are self-fertile.
growth_stages.user_action: Thinning is rarely needed for this group. On heavy pomegranate set, thin lightly to prevent limb breakage.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Mulberry summer-ripens over weeks; persimmon and pomegranate ripen in fall.
growth_stages.user_action: Mulberry: lay a sheet under the tree and shake, or pick ripe fruit daily. Persimmon: astringent types after first frost; non-astringent when fully colored. Pomegranate: when fruit cracks slightly or sounds metallic when tapped.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Last fruit picked. Drops attract wasps and yellow jackets in late summer.
growth_stages.user_action: Clear fallen fruit. Apply a balanced or potassium-rich feed. Refresh mulch before winter.

notifications.title: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text: These trees are typically grown on their own roots in home gardens, so there is no graft union to worry about. Plant with the crown at the original soil line.
Water in well at planting and mulch a 3-foot circle around the base, kept a few inches back from the trunk. Staking is usually not needed unless the site is very windy.

establishment.text: Water deeply once a week through the first season -- even after rain. Establishment takes one to two years; do not skip irrigation just because the tree looks fine.
These crops are slow to bear -- mulberry typically 2 to 3 years, persimmon 3 to 5, pomegranate 2 to 3. Patience is the main first-season skill.

first_growth.text: Train to a modified central-leader or open-vase form depending on the species. Pomegranate is often grown as a multi-stemmed shrub; mulberry and persimmon take well to a single-trunk form.
Remove low water sprouts and any suckers. Pomegranate especially suckers freely and needs annual sucker removal.

dormancy.text: Winter pruning is the rule for this group. Wait until leaves are fully down and the tree is dormant.
A mulch refresh and a deep watering before the ground freezes help winter survival, especially in the colder end of each species' hardiness range.

dormant_prune.text: Light structural pruning only on mulberry and persimmon. Both bear on previous-year wood and heavy heading reduces the next crop. Remove dead, diseased, damaged, and crossing branches; leave the rest.
Pomegranate is the exception -- it tolerates and benefits from heavier annual pruning to limit suckers and keep the canopy open. Limit to 3 to 5 main trunks if growing as a multi-stem.

blossom.text: These crops bloom later than pome and stone fruit, so spring frost is rarely the problem. Mulberry, persimmon, and pomegranate flower from late spring into early summer in most zones.
Avoid spraying during bloom. Pollinators are doing the year's most important work in this window even on self-fertile crops.

fruit_set.text: Most home varieties of these crops are self-fertile (American persimmon needs a male; Asian persimmon does not; pomegranate and mulberry are self-fertile). Confirm your variety before assuming.
Thinning is rarely needed -- the tree's natural set is usually appropriate. A heavy pomegranate set on a young tree may benefit from light thinning to avoid limb breakage.

harvest.text: Mulberry ripens over 3 to 4 weeks; harvest by laying a sheet under the tree and shaking, or by picking ripe fruit daily. Persimmon and pomegranate ripen later -- persimmon is best after the first frost (astringent types) and pomegranate when the fruit cracks slightly or sounds metallic when tapped.
Handle ripe fruit gently. Mulberry and ripe persimmon stain badly and bruise even more easily than stone fruit.

post_harvest.text: Clear fallen fruit from under the tree. Sticky drops attract wasps and yellow jackets in late summer.
Apply a balanced or potassium-rich feed after harvest to build reserves. Refresh mulch before winter.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 30-60 lbs from a mature multi-trunk shrub, typically 50-100 fruits
yield_expectations.peak_production: Full production in year 4 to 6. Mature plants produce reliably for decades with very little intervention compared to deciduous fruit trees.
yield_expectations.first_year_note: No useful crop in year one. These are tough, low-input plants once established, but year one is still a root-building year. Remove fruit if any sets.
factors: light structural pruning -- these crops fruit on previous-year wood (mulberry, persimmon) or freely from suckers (pomegranate)
fruit drop when stressed in pomegranate

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

crops.hardiness_notes: Pomegranates (Punica granatum) are remarkably drought-tolerant and adaptable to the arid Southwest and Mediterranean-climate California. They need a hot dry summer to properly develop fruit sugars -- in humid climates, fruit may split and rot before ripening. Cold hardiness varies significantly by variety: the standard 'Wonderful' is hardy to about 15F (zone 8a+), while 'Salavatski' and other Russian-bred varieties survive to 0F (zone 7a). Most pomegranates are self-fertile. They flower heavily but drop most blossoms; don't panic at a pile of fallen flowers. Fruit matures 5-7 months after flowering. Trees are multi-stemmed shrubs or small trees (10-15 feet) and tolerate significant pruning. Begin bearing in year 2-3. In humid climates, fruit cracking and fungal disease limit success even where winter temperatures are adequate.

varieties_detail.notes: The commercial standard -- the pomegranate you see in grocery stores. Large deep-red fruit with tart-sweet juice. Self-fertile. Hardy to 15F. Best in California and Arizona climates.
Russian-bred cold-hardy variety. Survives to 0F. Large red fruit with sweet-tart flavor. Self-fertile. The top choice for zone 7 growers and anywhere winter cold limits standard pomegranates.
Another Russian-bred cold-hardy variety. Medium orange-red fruit with exceptional sweet flavor. Self-fertile. Lower chill requirement makes it productive in moderate-winter zones.
Modern variety bred for superior flavor -- often ranked the best-tasting pomegranate. Soft seeds (edible without spitting). Medium-large red fruit. Self-fertile. Popular with culinary growers.
Virtually seedless variety with sweet non-acidic juice. Unique clear non-staining juice. Self-fertile. Less cold-hardy than Salavatski. Best for California coastal growers.

crops.chill_hours_note: Very low chill -- thrives in zones 7-10 with hot summers

failure_diagnostics.label: Cold or frost damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: These crops bloom late enough that spring frost during bloom is rarely the problem -- the more common cold issue is winter cold damage at the edge of each species' hardiness range. Pomegranate is hardy to about USDA zone 7; persimmon and mulberry are hardier (zones 4 to 5 for hardy varieties). Cold-damaged wood shows as dieback the following spring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Confirm your variety is hardy to your zone -- there is wide variation within each species. In marginal zones, plant in a sheltered south-facing site, mulch heavily before winter, and accept some annual dieback on pomegranate.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Pest pressure on this group is generally lower than on pome or stone fruit. Mulberry attracts birds heavily once fruit ripens. Persimmon is sometimes hit by persimmon psyllid (curling new growth) or persimmon wilt. Pomegranate can suffer leaffooted bug damage and heart rot in humid summers.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Bird netting on mulberry once fruit colors. For persimmon psyllid, a dormant horticultural oil spray reduces overwintering populations. For pomegranate heart rot, choose resistant varieties and improve airflow with light pruning.

failure_diagnostics.label: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Most home varieties of these crops are self-fertile. American persimmon (Diospyros virginiana) is the main exception -- it needs a male tree nearby. Asian persimmon (Diospyros kaki), which is what most named varieties sold in the US are, sets fruit without a pollinator (sometimes seedless).
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Confirm whether your variety is American or Asian persimmon and whether it needs a male. For pomegranate and mulberry, persistent fruit-drop usually points to drought stress or extreme heat at bloom rather than pollination.

failure_diagnostics.label: Root problems or waterlogging
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: These crops want well-drained soil. Pomegranate is the most drought-tolerant; mulberry tolerates a wider moisture range; persimmon prefers consistent moisture but hates standing water. Symptoms of waterlogging are yellowing leaves, dieback, and root rot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Improve drainage before planting on heavy or low-lying soil -- plant on a 12-inch mound if needed. Pomegranate especially does best on the dry side once established.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: All three need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to ripen and develop sugar. Pomegranate especially struggles in shade and may flower without setting fruit. Persimmon ripens unevenly without enough sun.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun. Light pruning to keep the canopy open helps fruit ripen on the inside of the tree -- particularly important for pomegranate and persimmon.

crops.name: Raspberry
crops.description: One of the most productive garden shrubs. Summer-bearing (one big crop) or everbearing (two crops). Manage with a simple T-trellis and annual cane pruning. Very cold-hardy.

3.notes: Excellent cold-hardy fruit. Boyne and Latham are proven Zone 3 varieties.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Plant raspberry and blackberry canes (container or bare-root) in early spring. Container plants can be planted after last frost. Prune all canes to 6 inches at planting. (UMN Extension, Cornell Extension)
plant_out.design_note: Bare-root plants may be planted as early as the ground is workable -- approximately last_frost - 14 days.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: Summer-bearing (floricane) raspberries and blackberries fruit on second-year canes, so first significant harvest occurs in year 2 after planting. (UMN Extension) Typical harvest: July through August for summer-bearing; August through first frost for everbearing. Everbearing (primocane) varieties fruit on first-year canes but yield is lighter. (UMN Extension)

fertilizer.notes: Feed in spring as growth begins. After fruiting, apply sulphate of potash to build next year's canes.

succession.reason: Perennial canes -- not applicable for succession planting.

crops.pollinator_notes: Self-fertile. Bees improve yield.

tasks.description: Summer-bearing: cut all fruited canes to ground after harvest. Leave new green canes for next year. Everbearing: cut all canes to ground in late winter for one big fall crop.

crops.planting_method_notes: Plant bare-root canes in late fall through early spring. Spring planting preferred in cold zones.
crops.year_one_notes: First-year canes (primocanes) don't fruit in summer types. Let them grow -- they'll fruit next year as floricanes.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. The nematode component is extension-documented. The claim's additional assertions about deterring aphids are not supported in the extension literature on marigolds and should be read as traditional.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: The aphid-repellent element is mechanism-plausible: allium sulfur VOCs have documented aphid-repellent effects (Durenne and Gosset, Insects 2018, 9(4):112) at home-gardening extension rigor (Mississippi State, USU). However, the 'repel beetles' sub-claim for garlic on raspberry is not extension-documented. Raspberry beetle/cane borer/Japanese beetle management in extension publications (Cornell Berry Diagnostic Tool, PNW Extension) relies on cultural controls, pruning, and targeted insecticides; allium interplanting is not listed. Downgraded from extension_backed because the composite claim mixes a mechanism-real aphid component with an unbacked beetle component.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Spotted wing drosophila
pests.symptoms: Soft, collapsing fruit before full ripeness. Tiny maggots inside ripening berries.
pests.cause: Drosophila suzukii fly. Major pest of soft fruit.
pests.organic_treatment: Fine mesh netting (1mm) over plants during ripening. Spinosad spray. Harvest frequently.
pests.prevention: Fine netting is most effective. Remove overripe fruit promptly.

diseases.name: Cane diseases (botrytis/anthracnose)
diseases.symptoms: Purple/brown spots on canes. Die-back of canes. Gray mold on fruit in wet conditions.
diseases.cause: Botrytis and Elsinoe fungal diseases.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove and destroy affected canes. Copper-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention: Prune out old canes after fruiting. Improve airflow. Avoid overhead irrigation.

crops.harvest_ready: Deep red (or yellow/black by variety). Pulls away from white core easily with no resistance. Soft and fragrant. Harvest daily.

storage.freezer: Freeze flat then bag -- excellent quality preserved
storage.notes: The most perishable fruit. Freeze immediately if not eating same day.

varieties.note: Heritage is the most widely planted home raspberry -- reliable, prolific, two crops per year.

start_method.notes: Plant from container in spring. Bare-root plants available in winter -- plant immediately on receipt.

container_notes.notes: Fruit trees need to be grown in the ground. Dwarf varieties on very dwarfing rootstocks can be tried in very large (30+ gallon) containers but are challenging and rarely as productive.

rotation.avoid_after: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Bare-root or potted plant just set. Soil level matches the original line on the stems -- not buried deeper.
growth_stages.user_action: Blueberry: plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5 to 5.5), mix peat moss or pine fines into the hole, and mulch with pine needles or wood chips. Cane fruits (raspberry, blackberry): plant alongside a trellis or post-and-wire support so the canes have something to grow on. Elderberry: tolerates wetter ground than the others. Water in deeply.

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: New leaves breaking. Blueberry pushes new shoots from the base; cane fruits send up new canes from the ground.
growth_stages.user_action: Water consistently through the first summer -- berries have shallow roots and dry out fast. Remove all flowers in year one so the plant builds its roots and a strong base. For raspberries and blackberries, pinch off the tip of each new cane once it reaches your trellis height; this encourages side branches that will carry fruit.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Multiple stems or canes coming up from the base. Blueberry fills out as a many-stemmed bush; cane fruits send up vigorous new canes; elderberry bushes out widely.
growth_stages.user_action: Berries don't get scaffold-branch training the way trees do -- they're naturally multi-stemmed. Blueberry: keep the strongest 4 to 6 stems and remove weak twiggy growth. Raspberry and blackberry: train new canes onto the trellis and thin them to about 4 to 6 strong canes per linear foot. Elderberry: let it bush out freely; remove only crossed or weak growth.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Blueberry leaves turn red-purple and drop. Raspberry and blackberry canes go fully bare. Elderberry drops cleanly. All are dormant and frost-hardy.
growth_stages.user_action: Top up the mulch before deep freeze, especially for shallow-rooted blueberry. In cold zones, consider laying down trailing blackberry canes and covering them with mulch or burlap. Real pruning waits until late winter (the next stage).

growth_stages.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Bush or canes fully dormant. Late-winter window before bud break.
growth_stages.user_action: Blueberry: cane-renewal -- remove 1 or 2 of the oldest, thickest canes at ground level each winter. Caneberries: remove last year's spent floricanes; thin remaining primocanes to 4 to 6 per linear foot.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Late-spring bloom on blueberry, raspberry, blackberry; early-summer bloom on elderberry. Frost risk usually past.
growth_stages.user_action: Avoid sprays during bloom. Wild bumblebees are the main blueberry pollinators.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set & Bird Netting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Berries forming. Bird pressure ramps up as fruit colors.
growth_stages.user_action: Drape bird netting after fruit colors and before any berry softens fully. Cross-pollination boosts blueberry yield -- a second variety nearby helps.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Ripe fruit pulls free with gentle pressure. Bushes and canes are hand-height -- no ladders.
growth_stages.user_action: Pick every 1 to 2 days during peak. Wear long sleeves for thorny canes. Refrigerate immediately; berries do not store at room temperature.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest Cleanup
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Last fruit picked. Spent floricanes on caneberries dying back.
growth_stages.user_action: Cut spent floricanes at ground level if not done in late winter. Apply a potassium-rich feed (use an acidic blueberry-specific fertilizer for blueberry). Refresh mulch.

notifications.title: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text: These crops are typically grown on their own roots -- there is no graft union. Plant with the crown at the original soil line. Blueberry needs acidic soil (pH 4.5 to 5.5); test before planting and amend with elemental sulfur if needed.
Caneberries (raspberry, blackberry) need a trellis or support system from year one. Build it before planting; retrofitting around established canes is awkward.

establishment.text: Water deeply once a week through the first season -- berries are shallow-rooted and dry out fast. Blueberry especially needs steady moisture and acidic mulch (pine bark, pine needles).
Remove flowers in year one on caneberries and blueberry. The energy goes into root and cane development; you will get more fruit from years two onward by skipping year one.

first_growth.text: Blueberry develops as a multi-stemmed shrub. Let 5 to 7 main canes establish in the first 2 to 3 years; do not prune for shape, only remove damaged wood.
Caneberries put up new canes (primocanes) from the crown each year. In year one, let everything grow -- those are next year's fruiting canes (floricanes).

dormancy.text: These crops are deciduous and go fully dormant in winter. Pruning is done in late winter or very early spring before bud break.
Refresh mulch before winter. For caneberries, tip-prune any canes that did not harden off (still green and floppy at the tip).

dormant_prune.text: Blueberry uses cane-renewal pruning. Each winter, remove 1 or 2 of the oldest, thickest, least-productive canes at ground level to push new cane growth from the crown. By year 5 or 6 the bush has a rotating set of young productive canes.

Caneberries: remove all canes that fruited last summer (floricanes) -- they die after fruiting and harbor disease. Leave the new green canes (primocanes) for next year. Thin remaining canes to 4 to 6 strong canes per linear foot of row.

blossom.text: Blueberry, raspberry, and blackberry bloom late enough that spring frost is rarely the problem -- usually mid-to-late spring, after most frost danger is past. Elderberry blooms even later, in early summer.
Pollinators love these flowers. Do not spray during bloom. Wild bumblebees in particular are major pollinators of blueberry.

fruit_set.text: Most blueberry varieties benefit from a second variety blooming at the same time for cross-pollination -- a single bush will fruit but a pair fruits much more heavily. Caneberries and elderberry are mostly self-fertile.
Drape bird netting after fruit colors and before any berry softens fully. Once birds find the patch they keep coming back.

harvest.text: Pick fruit at hand height -- no ladders here. Ripe blueberries pull off with a gentle roll of the thumb; fruit that resists is not yet ripe (color is not enough -- some varieties color days before they sweeten).

Caneberries shatter when over-ripe -- pick every 1 to 2 days during peak. Wear long sleeves for blackberry and the thorny raspberries. Eat or refrigerate immediately; berries do not store at room temperature.

post_harvest.text: After caneberry harvest, cut the spent floricanes (now dying or dead) at ground level if you did not get them in late winter. This removes overwintering sites for cane disease and the spotted wing drosophila.
A potassium-rich feed and a mulch refresh after harvest sets up next year's bloom. For blueberry, use an acidic fertilizer formulated for ericaceous plants.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 1-2 lbs per cane, or roughly 4-8 lbs per mature plant grown on a trellis
yield_expectations.peak_production: Full production typically arrives in year 4 to 7 depending on type. Berries ripen unevenly across a 2 to 4 week window, so expect to pick every few days at peak.
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Plan on no harvest in year one. Remove all flowers so the plant invests in roots and new canes. Year-two harvest is small; full production comes in year three or later.
factors: soil pH (especially blueberry, which needs 4.5 to 5.5)
trellis or stake support for canes

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

crops.hardiness_notes: Raspberries come in two bearing types that affect pruning and harvest timing. Summer-bearing (floricane) raspberries produce on 2-year-old canes, yielding one large crop in early summer. Everbearing (primocane) raspberries produce on first-year canes, yielding a fall crop and (if canes are left standing) a smaller summer crop the following year. For simplicity, cut primocane varieties to the ground each winter and enjoy one heavy fall harvest. Red and yellow raspberries are the most cold-hardy (zones 3-9). Black and purple raspberries are slightly less hardy (zones 4-8) and more disease-prone. Raspberries prefer cool summers -- fruit quality declines sharply above 85F at ripening. In warm zones (8-9), grow in dappled afternoon shade. Plants spread by underground rhizomes and can become invasive; contain with a root barrier or mow around the patch. Establishment is fast: expect light crops in year 2, full crops in year 3.

varieties_detail.notes: The most widely grown everbearing raspberry. Medium-large firm red berries with good flavor. Heavy fall crop late August to frost. Self-fertile. Vigorous and adaptable. Good beginner variety.
Extremely cold-hardy -- developed for Manitoba. Heavy producer of medium-sized sweet berries. Summer harvest in early July. Self-fertile. Top choice for zones 3-4.
Pale yellow berries with distinctive sweet banana-apricot flavor. Fall-bearing. Self-fertile. Ornamental as well as productive. Birds ignore yellow berries, reducing crop losses.

Highest-quality black raspberry available. Glossy black berries with rich flavor, ripen in July. Self-fertile. More disease-resistant than most black raspberries. Susceptible to anthracnose in humid years.
Heat-tolerant everbearing red -- better than Heritage in zones 7-9. Large sweet berries. Heavy fall crop. Self-fertile. Root rot resistant. Good choice for the Mid-Atlantic and upper South.

crops.chill_hours_note: Good chill requirement -- zones 4-8 ideal. Ever-bearing varieties more adaptable

failure_diagnostics.label: Cold or frost damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: These crops bloom late enough that spring frost during bloom is rarely the problem. The more common cold issues are winter cane dieback on caneberries (canes that did not harden off in fall die back from the tips) and winter damage at the edge of blueberry's hardiness range. Some blackberry varieties are only hardy to USDA zone 6 or 7.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Choose varieties hardy to your zone. For caneberries, stop fertilizing by midsummer so canes harden off properly before winter. Mulch heavily in fall. In marginal zones for blackberry, lay primocanes flat under mulch for winter.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Spotted wing drosophila (SWD) is now the dominant berry pest across most of the US -- it lays eggs in ripening fruit and the larvae make berries unsalvageable. Cane diseases (anthracnose, spur blight, cane blight) affect caneberries and survive in old floricanes. Blueberry maggot and mummy berry are blueberry-specific.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Remove and destroy spent floricanes immediately after harvest -- this is the main defense against cane disease and SWD overwintering. Pick ripe fruit promptly so SWD has less to lay eggs in. For blueberry mummy berry, mulch heavily in fall to bury fallen mummies.

failure_diagnostics.label: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Caneberries and elderberry are self-fertile and a single plant fruits. Blueberry is technically self-fertile but yields much more heavily with a second variety blooming at the same time -- a single bush often produces small or sparse berries. Cool wet weather during bloom keeps pollinators (especially bumblebees) grounded even when a partner is present.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant at least two compatible blueberry varieties for cross-pollination. Encourage native bumblebees with flowering plants nearby. Avoid spraying anything during bloom.

failure_diagnostics.label: Root problems or waterlogging
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: These crops want consistent moisture but well-drained soil. Blueberry hates wet feet and dies quickly in waterlogged soil; root rot from poorly-drained sites is a leading killer. Caneberries tolerate slightly more moisture but still suffer in standing water.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: On heavy or low-lying soil, plant in a raised bed or mound. Blueberry especially does best in a 12-inch raised bed with bark-amended acidic soil. Ensure water drains away from the root zone.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: These crops need full sun, 6 to 8 hours minimum, to fruit well. Elderberry tolerates partial shade better than the others but still fruits more heavily in sun. Shaded canes and bushes grow leaves but produce few or small berries.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun. For caneberries, avoid letting the row become a dense thicket -- thin canes to 4 to 6 per linear foot so light reaches all the fruiting wood.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. The nematode component is extension-documented. The claim's additional assertions about deterring aphids are not supported in the extension literature on marigolds and should be read as traditional.
