pests.name: Persea mite
pests.symptoms: Circular yellow spots on leaf undersides that become brown necrotic patches. Fine webbing on leaf undersides visible with a hand lens. Severe infestations cause widespread leaf browning and premature leaf drop, exposing fruit and trunk to sunburn.
pests.cause: Oligonychus perseae. UC ANR identifies this as a key California avocado pest. Populations build April-June, peak July-August on the undersides of mature leaves.
pests.organic_treatment: Horticultural oil or narrow-range summer oil applied to leaf undersides. Direct water sprays to knock down populations. Predatory mites (Neoseiulus californicus) provide biological control.
pests.prevention: Monitor leaf undersides from spring onward. Avoid dusty conditions near groves. Protect beneficial mite populations by avoiding broad-spectrum miticides.

pests.name: Avocado thrips
pests.symptoms: Silvery or tan scarring on fruit skin with a leathery 'alligator skin' appearance as fruit expands. Damage occurs while fruit is 5-15 mm long (early spring). Internal fruit quality is unaffected but market appearance is ruined. Tiny (2 mm) brown-orange insects on new leaves and young fruit.
pests.cause: Scirtothrips perseae. UC ANR cites avocado thrips as responsible for large California industry losses. Each female lays up to 300 eggs; multiple generations per season.
pests.organic_treatment: Spinosad (evening applications to protect bees) during early fruit set. Horticultural oil reduces populations. Protect native predatory thrips (Franklinothrips spp.).
pests.prevention: Scout weekly during bloom and early fruit development. Reduce tender flush growth that thrips prefer -- careful pruning and moderate nitrogen help.

pests.name: Armored scale
pests.symptoms: Small circular or oval raised bumps on leaves, twigs, and sometimes fruit. Yellowing and premature leaf drop in heavy infestations. Unlike soft scales, armored scales do not produce honeydew.
pests.cause: Latania scale, greedy scale, and oleander scale are most commonly found on avocado per UC ANR. Protected under their waxy covers, they are hard to control with contact sprays.
pests.organic_treatment: Narrow-range horticultural oil at delayed-dormant timing and again as needed during the growing season. Parasitic wasps provide biological control if not disrupted by broad-spectrum sprays.
pests.prevention: Inspect nursery stock. Avoid ant-tended areas (ants protect scale from parasitoid wasps). Control dust, which interferes with parasitic wasps.

pests.name: Avocado lace bug
pests.symptoms: Yellow stippling visible on upper leaf surfaces. Undersides of leaves show dark spots of lace bug excrement and tiny clear-winged insects. In severe infestations, whole leaves brown and drop.
pests.cause: Pseudacysta perseae. Most damaging during hot dry weather. An established pest in Florida and increasing in California.
pests.organic_treatment: Insecticidal soap or horticultural oil sprayed on leaf undersides where lace bugs live. Multiple applications during population buildup. Remove heavily infested leaves.
pests.prevention: Monitor leaf undersides starting in early summer. Maintain consistent irrigation -- drought-stressed trees suffer worse damage.

diseases.name: Phytophthora root rot
diseases.symptoms: Small pale leaves that wilt in afternoon heat. Sparse canopy with many small leaves. Twig dieback from the tips inward. Fruit small and misshapen. Digging reveals dark, rotted, sparse feeder roots instead of the healthy white mat a healthy tree should have.
diseases.cause: Phytophthora cinnamomi, a soil-borne oomycete. UC ANR and international sources identify this as the single most destructive avocado disease worldwide. Thrives in waterlogged soils.
diseases.organic_treatment: No effective cure. Reduce tree stress with careful irrigation (avoid waterlogging) and mulching. Phosphonate products (systemic, available to commercial growers) can slow decline but do not eliminate the pathogen.
diseases.prevention: Plant on resistant rootstocks (Duke 7, Dusa, Toro Canyon) -- this is the single most important prevention step. Plant on well-drained sites or mounded beds. Do not over-irrigate. Inspect nursery stock carefully; do not introduce infested soil or plants.

diseases.name: Anthracnose
diseases.symptoms: Small sunken dark lesions on fruit, often first appearing at the stem end and expanding as fruit ripens. May show concentric ring pattern. Black spots on stems and leaves. Severely affected fruit rots on the tree or in storage.
diseases.cause: Colletotrichum gloeosporioides. Infects during humid weather but may remain latent until fruit ripens, which is why losses often appear post-harvest. Overwinters on infected twigs, leaves, and mummified fruit.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove infected fruit from tree and ground. Copper fungicide preventively during wet weather. Handle fruit carefully -- bruises invite anthracnose.
diseases.prevention: Prune for airflow. Rake fallen leaves and remove mummified fruit. Avoid overhead irrigation. Plant anthracnose-resistant varieties if available.

diseases.name: Branch canker & dieback
diseases.symptoms: Dead or dying branches with discolored bark. Dark staining visible in the wood beneath. Small white or pink spore masses may appear on infected wood. Whole branches die back from the tip over weeks to months.
diseases.cause: Neofusicoccum and related Botryosphaeriaceae fungi (formerly called Dothiorella canker). Enter through pruning wounds and stressed tissue. Drought-stressed trees are most vulnerable.
diseases.organic_treatment: Prune out affected branches well below visible damage. Disinfect tools between cuts. Dispose of prunings; do not compost.
diseases.prevention: Keep trees adequately irrigated but not waterlogged. Prune during dry weather. Avoid sunburn by whitewashing exposed trunks on young trees.

diseases.name: Laurel wilt (regional)
diseases.symptoms: Sudden wilting of upper canopy followed by rapid whole-tree death, sometimes within weeks. Dark blue-black streaks visible in the sapwood. Small entry holes from the beetle vector on the trunk. Primarily a Florida concern.
diseases.cause: Raffaelea lauricola fungus vectored by the redbay ambrosia beetle (Xyleborus glabratus). UF/IFAS documents laurel wilt as a major and devastating Florida avocado disease since roughly 2012. Not yet established in California.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure. Affected trees must be removed and destroyed to slow spread to neighboring trees. Systemic fungicide injections may give temporary protection for high-value trees but are not a home-gardener treatment.
diseases.prevention: Plant disease-free nursery stock. Remove dying laurel-family trees (redbay, swampbay, camphor) nearby, which serve as beetle reservoirs. Contact local extension if you suspect laurel wilt -- it is a reportable disease in some states.

watering.amount: Deep soak -- avocados are sensitive to both over and underwatering
watering.method: At soil level, good drainage essential
watering.signs_overwater: Yellowing, root rot -- very common problem

crops.harvest_ready: Pick when full sized. Leave on tree until needed -- they ripen after harvest. Test by picking one and ripening at room temperature -- takes 5-7 days.

storage.room_temp: Ripen at room temperature -- hard avocados take 3-5 days
storage.fridge: Once ripe: 2-3 days. Unripe: up to 2 weeks
storage.freezer: Mash with lemon juice and freeze -- good for guacamole
storage.notes: Speed ripening by placing next to a banana in a paper bag.

varieties.note: Bacon is the most cold-tolerant Guatemalan-type avocado -- reliable in Z8 where Hass struggles. Wurtz stays under 8 feet -- ideal for containers.

start_method.notes: Plant bare-root trees in late winter/early spring while dormant. Container trees can go in spring through early autumn. Stake against wind for the first 2 years.

container_notes.notes: Avocados grow in containers in cold climates but need very large pots (25+ gallons) and excellent drainage. Use avocado/citrus potting mix. They rarely fruit in containers outside tropical zones.

rotation.avoid_after: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Container-grown grafted tree just planted. The graft union -- the knobby joint where the variety was grafted onto the rootstock -- sits well above soil. Often staked briefly while establishing.
growth_stages.user_action: Avocado has fragile roots and is prone to root rot -- plant on a small mound to ensure good drainage, with the top of the rootball slightly above ground level. Avoid lawn locations; avocado roots compete poorly with turfgrass. Water deeply, mulch generously, keeping mulch off the trunk.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Tree planted on mound with good drainage?

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: New leaf flush emerging. Avocado pushes growth in flushes rather than steadily.
growth_stages.user_action: Water 2 to 3 times a week the first summer, less near the coast. Check soil moisture before each watering -- avocado hates wet feet. Begin light nitrogen feeding once new growth appears. Remove any first-year flowers (most won't set fruit anyway).
growth_stages.log_prompt: New flush and watering schedule set?

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Tree filling out with leaves; lower branches sometimes drooping. Canopy taking shape.
growth_stages.user_action: Avocado needs almost no training. Fruit forms at the outer edges of the canopy, so a wide, dense canopy matters more than a defined branch structure. Pinch the tips of long lanky shoots to encourage side branching. Remove any shoots growing from below the graft union. Avoid heavy pruning -- avocado wood is brittle and exposed bark sunburns easily.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Avocado is evergreen and does not drop its leaves. Growth slows in cool weather; the tree holds its shape and color.
growth_stages.user_action: Avocado's version of dormancy is a winter slowdown, not a leaf-fall. Frost is the year-one killer -- young trees are damaged below 30 degrees F and killed below 25. Cover with frost cloth or string warm holiday lights through the canopy when overnight lows threaten. Reduce watering frequency but don't let the rootball dry out.

growth_stages.name: Light Annual Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: After main harvest or in late winter.
growth_stages.user_action: Light shape pruning. Remove dead wood, suckers, ground-dragging branches.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Heavy bloom in spring. A-type or B-type pattern.
growth_stages.user_action: Plant both A and B types nearby for best set. Do not spray.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small fruit forming. Heavy early-summer drop is normal.
growth_stages.user_action: Thin fruit in heavy years to level alternate bearing.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Mature fruit by size and variety-specific color. Tree is the storage.
growth_stages.user_action: Pick mature fruit, ripen at room temperature.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest Feeding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Main harvest done.
growth_stages.user_action: Apply fertilizer with extra zinc and iron. Refresh mulch.

notifications.title: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text: Avocado is grafted on rootstock chosen for soil tolerance and disease resistance, especially Phytophthora resistance. The graft union must sit 2 to 4 inches above soil level -- buried unions invite root rot.
Plant in spring once nights are reliably above 50 degrees. Avocado roots are extremely sensitive to disturbance -- handle the root ball gently and avoid loosening the bottom of the hole.

establishment.text: Water deeply but infrequently. Avocado has shallow brittle roots that drown easily in waterlogged soil and die quickly in drought -- the sweet spot is moist-but-never-soggy. Aim for the top 2 inches of soil to dry slightly between waterings.
Mulch heavily with coarse organic mulch (wood chips, bark) but keep mulch 6 inches back from the trunk. Avocado evolved in tropical leaf-litter environments and the deep mulch genuinely matters.

first_growth.text: Avocado is grown as a balanced canopy or pyramidal tree, not as central-leader or open-center. Do not strip lower branches -- avocado fruits at the canopy edge and the lower limbs are productive.
Pinch the growing tip at 24 to 30 inches to encourage branching. Otherwise avocado tends to grow as a tall whip with few side branches.

dormancy.text: Avocado is evergreen and does not have true dormancy. Growth slows in winter but the tree is never bare.

In the cooler end of avocado range, freeze protection (frost cloth, banking soil around the trunk, string lights) is the winter task. Mature trees of cold-hardy varieties (Mexican-race) survive brief drops to about 24 degrees; tropical varieties die at 30.

dormant_prune.text: Avocado pruning is light and shape-focused, done in late winter or after the main harvest. Remove dead wood, suckers from below the graft union, and any branches dragging on the ground.
Avoid heavy heading cuts. Avocado fruits on the previous year's wood at the canopy edge -- removing that growth removes next year's fruit.

blossom.text: Avocado has an unusual bloom system: each flower opens twice, once as functionally female and once as functionally male, but a tree's flowers are synchronized to be female and male at different times. 'A-type' varieties are female in the morning; 'B-type' varieties are female in the afternoon.
A single tree of either type sets fruit because flowers overlap in many conditions, but planting both types nearby boosts fruit set significantly. Do not spray during bloom.

fruit_set.text: Avocado often shows alternate bearing -- a heavy crop year followed by a light year. This is partly genetic and partly fixable by thinning fruit on heavy years.
Persistent fruit drop in early summer is normal -- the tree sheds excess set. Drop later in the season usually indicates water stress or boron deficiency.

harvest.text: Avocado does not ripen on the tree. Pick mature fruit (size and skin color appropriate to the variety) and ripen at room temperature -- 5 to 14 days depending on the variety. The tree is the storage; mature fruit can hang on the tree for weeks or months.
Use a picking pole with a basket on the end for high fruit, or a clipper for low fruit. Twist gently rather than pulling; pulling tears bark.

post_harvest.text: Avocado is heavy-feeding -- apply a balanced fertilizer with extra zinc and iron after the main harvest. Yellowing leaves between green veins indicates iron deficiency, especially in alkaline soil.
Refresh mulch annually. Avocado roots need the leaf-litter environment year-round.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 60-200 lbs from a mature dooryard tree in a typical year, with strong alternate-bearing common -- a heavy year followed by a much lighter one
yield_expectations.peak_production: Grafted trees bear in year 3 to 4 and reach full production around year 5 to 8. Mature trees often alternate -- a heavy crop one year followed by a lighter crop the next.
yield_expectations.first_year_note: No fruit in year one. Avocado trees produce huge numbers of flowers but only about 1 in 10,000 sets fruit even at maturity, so first-year flowers can be ignored or removed without loss.

crops.hardiness_notes: Avocados (Persea americana) come in three racial types with dramatically different cold tolerances. Mexican varieties (Persea americana var. drymifolia) are the most cold-hardy, tolerating 16-18F -- these are the practical choice for zone 8-9 growers. Guatemalan varieties tolerate to 24F and are zone 10. West Indian varieties are true tropicals, damaged below 32F, and are really only for zone 11. Commercial Hass is a Guatemalan-Mexican hybrid hardy to about 24F (zone 9b). Most avocados require cross-pollination between Type A and Type B varieties (flowers open as female one day and male the next on complementary schedules); this is why commercial orchards always have pollinator trees interspersed. Home growers often plant a Type A + Type B pair. Avocados are shallow-rooted, drought-sensitive once bearing, and intolerant of wet feet. Trees begin bearing in year 3-5 from grafted trees, 7-10 years from seed. Seed-grown trees produce fruit but usually not true to type.

varieties_detail.notes: Most cold-hardy commonly available avocado. Small black-skinned fruit with excellent rich flavor -- many consider it superior to Hass. Type A. Self-fertile. The avocado for zone 8 growers.

The commercial standard -- the avocado you buy in stores. Medium-large pebbly-skinned fruit that blackens when ripe. Type A. Partially self-fertile but bears heavier with a Type B pollinator (Fuerte works well).
Green-skinned pear-shaped avocado. Milder and creamier than Hass, stays green at ripeness. Type B. Classic pollinator for Hass in home orchards. More cold-hardy than Hass.
Medium green-skinned fruit, earlier ripening than most avocados. Type B. Good pollinator for Hass. More cold-hardy than Hass, making it a better zone 9a choice. Mild flavor.

Purple-black-skinned fruit with rich flavor. Cold-hardy for a Mexican-West Indian type. Type A. Good choice for Gulf Coast growers (Texas, Louisiana, Florida Panhandle) where heat and humidity defeat California varieties.

crops.chill_hours_note: No chill requirement -- frost protection critical. Zones 9-11

failure_diagnostics.label: Freeze damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Avocado is evergreen and does not become fully dormant; freeze damage is whole-tree (leaves, twigs, fruit, and even bark splitting) rather than blossom-frost. Mexican-race varieties (Bacon, Mexicola, Stewart) tolerate brief drops to about 24 degrees; West Indian varieties die at 30 to 32. Damage shows as leaf drop, blackened twigs, and split bark.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Cover with frost cloth on freeze nights; bank soil up around the graft union before winter so the rootstock survives even if the top is killed. In marginal zones, choose the most cold-hardy varieties or grow in a movable container.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Phytophthora root rot is by far the most serious avocado problem -- it kills more avocados than any other cause. Persea mite and avocado lace bug damage leaves but rarely kill trees. Laurel wilt (a fungal disease spread by an invasive beetle) is now killing avocados in parts of Florida.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Choose Phytophthora-resistant rootstock (Dusa, Toro Canyon) when planting. Keep mulch off the trunk and ensure excellent drainage. For persea mite, encourage predatory mites with reduced spraying. In Florida, follow state guidance on laurel wilt.

failure_diagnostics.label: Bloom but no fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Avocado has the unusual A-type / B-type flower system: a single tree's flowers are synchronized male or female at different times of day, so any one tree's pollen is rarely available when its own flowers are receptive. A single tree often sets some fruit (because conditions can shift the timing) but pairs of A and B types crank up the set substantially.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant an A-type and a B-type nearby (within 30 feet). Hass is A-type; Bacon, Fuerte, and Zutano are B-type. Encourage native bees and avoid spraying during the long bloom window.

failure_diagnostics.label: Phytophthora root rot
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Avocado is more prone to Phytophthora root rot than any other backyard fruit tree. The pathogen thrives in wet soil and kills feeder roots; the tree slowly declines with yellowing leaves, dieback, and eventually death. Once established it cannot be cured.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant on a 12-inch raised mound on heavy or poorly-drained soil. Choose Phytophthora-resistant rootstock. Water deeply but infrequently and let the top inch of soil dry between waterings. Keep mulch off the trunk.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Avocado needs full sun, 6 to 8 hours minimum, to bloom and ripen fruit properly. In partial shade the tree grows leaves but bears poorly. Wind exposure also hurts -- avocado leaves and fruit damage easily in strong wind.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun in a wind-sheltered spot. South or southwest exposure is ideal. Avoid planting close to eucalyptus or other trees with allelopathic root chemistry.

pests.name: Mulberry whitefly
pests.symptoms: Small white winged insects flush up in clouds when leaves are disturbed. Oval dark nymphs fringed with white wax cling to leaf undersides. Sticky honeydew and sooty mold on lower foliage. Light to moderate infestations rarely threaten an established tree.
pests.cause: Tetraleurodes mori, named for mulberry although it feeds on other hosts. The Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station identifies this as a mulberry-specific pest, though control is rarely needed.
pests.organic_treatment: Strong water spray to knock down adults. Insecticidal soap or horticultural oil on leaf undersides. Yellow sticky traps for monitoring. Beneficial wasps usually keep populations in check.
pests.prevention: Avoid broad-spectrum sprays that kill parasitic wasps. Most home trees never need treatment.

pests.name: Scale insects
pests.symptoms: Raised bumps (light tan to gray) on twigs, branches, and sometimes leaf stems. Yellowing leaves, twig dieback, and reduced vigor in heavy infestations. Sometimes sticky honeydew from soft-scale species.
pests.cause: Armored scales in the family Diaspididae are common on mulberry. Protected under waxy covers that resist contact sprays. Crawlers (the mobile juvenile stage) are the vulnerable stage.
pests.organic_treatment: Dormant horticultural oil in late winter smothers overwintering scale. Summer oil at reduced rate during crawler activity (typically early summer). Prune out heavily infested branches.
pests.prevention: Inspect trunk and branches annually. Control ants that farm scale. Prune for airflow.

pests.name: Mealybugs
pests.symptoms: White cottony masses at leaf axils and on twigs. Slowed plant growth, twig dieback, premature leaf drop. Sooty mold on lower leaves. Worst on young trees and in warm climates.
pests.cause: Several Pseudococcus species. Often tended by ants, which protect them from parasitic wasps.
pests.organic_treatment: Horticultural oil or insecticidal soap, focusing on hidden areas. Control ants with sticky trunk bands.
pests.prevention: Inspect new trees before planting. Maintain healthy tree vigor -- stressed mulberries attract more pests.

pests.name: Japanese beetles
pests.symptoms: Skeletonized leaves (only the major veins remain), starting at the top of the tree and moving downward. Masses of metallic green-and-copper beetles feeding together, especially in sunny weather. July is the usual peak.
pests.cause: Popillia japonica adults. Mulberry is listed among the 275+ plants they attack. Damage is usually cosmetic on a mature tree but can defoliate young trees.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick in early morning when beetles are sluggish -- knock into soapy water. Avoid pheromone traps in the home garden (they attract more beetles than they catch). Neem oil deters feeding on young trees.
pests.prevention: Encourage ground-nesting predators by leaving some bare ground. Healthy lawns with parasitic nematodes have fewer grubs.

diseases.name: Bacterial blight
diseases.symptoms: Water-soaked spots on young leaves that turn brown or black with yellow halos. Leaf distortion. Black stripes or lesions on young shoots. Twig tip dieback. Heaviest in cool wet spring weather. On fruit: dark irregular spots.
diseases.cause: Pseudomonas syringae pv. mori. TAMU and PNW Handbook both identify this as the primary bacterial disease of mulberry. Favored by cool, wet weather. Young leaves are most susceptible.
diseases.organic_treatment: Prune out and destroy affected shoots during dry weather. Copper-based bactericide at late-dormant timing and again at bud break in high-pressure years.
diseases.prevention: Avoid overhead watering. Prune only in dry weather. Minimize wounds to limbs and new shoots. Mulch to reduce soil splash.

diseases.name: Leaf spot (false mildew)
diseases.symptoms: Whitish indefinite patches on undersides of leaves appearing in mid-summer. Yellowish spores emerge from leaf stomata, spreading out as a white cobweb-like coating. Leaves yellow and fall prematurely. In the South this can be severe.
diseases.cause: Mycosphaerella mori fungus. TAMU notes this is a significant disease on mulberries growing in southern states. Overwinters on fallen leaves.
diseases.organic_treatment: Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn to reduce overwintering inoculum. Copper fungicide at first sign of infection in high-pressure areas.
diseases.prevention: Prune for airflow. Water at soil level. Gather and remove or compost fallen leaves in fall.

diseases.name: Cankers & branch dieback
diseases.symptoms: Sunken discolored areas on twigs and branches. Black masses of spores sometimes visible in infected bark. Branches beyond the canker die back. Cankers on main trunks can kill the tree.
diseases.cause: Multiple fungi including Cytospora, Dothiorella, Gibberella, and Fusarium species per TAMU. Often follows freeze damage, pruning wounds, or drought stress.
diseases.organic_treatment: Prune out cankered branches well below the visible damage. Disinfect pruning tools between cuts. Trees with trunk cankers generally cannot be saved.
diseases.prevention: Prune in dry weather with clean, sharp cuts. Avoid wounding the trunk (mower and string-trimmer damage). Keep the tree watered during drought but not waterlogged.

diseases.name: Root-knot nematodes
diseases.symptoms: Stunted, slow-growing young trees. Yellowing leaves. Afternoon wilting despite adequate water. Pulling a young tree reveals galled, knobby roots. Less impact on established mature trees.
diseases.cause: Meloidogyne spp., microscopic roundworms. TAMU notes seedling mulberries in the East and Southwest are vulnerable. Sandy soils favor the pest.
diseases.organic_treatment: No effective in-ground chemical treatment for home growers. Amend with compost to support beneficial soil microbes.
diseases.prevention: Test soil for nematodes before planting. In known-infested soils, plant elsewhere or use resistant rootstocks where available. French marigolds as a cover crop before planting can reduce population.

crops.harvest_ready: Berries turn from red to deep purple-black. Pick by spreading a sheet and shaking branches. Stain everything -- wear old clothes.

storage.freezer: Freeze immediately -- lasts 6 months, excellent quality
storage.notes: Mulberries are one of the most perishable fruits. The reason you never see them in stores. Freeze everything you can't eat same day.

varieties.note: Illinois Everbearing is the most reliable backyard mulberry -- productive over 6-8 weeks rather than 2 weeks for other varieties.

start_method.notes: Plant bare-root trees in late winter/early spring while dormant. Container trees can go in spring through early autumn. Stake against wind for the first 2 years.

container_notes.notes: Fruit trees need to be grown in the ground. Dwarf varieties on very dwarfing rootstocks can be tried in very large (30+ gallon) containers but are challenging and rarely as productive.

rotation.avoid_after: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Tree or multi-trunk shrub just planted. Pomegranate often arrives as a multi-stem clump; mulberry and persimmon as single-trunk trees.
growth_stages.user_action: Plant high in well-drained soil. Stake mulberry and persimmon firmly; pomegranate usually doesn't need staking once the multi-trunk form is set. Water in deeply, mulch around the base, and avoid burying the lowest stems.

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: First leaves breaking. Pomegranate often pushes new shoots from the base in a clump; mulberry and persimmon push from existing stems.
growth_stages.user_action: Water deeply once a week through the first summer. Remove any first-year flowers or developing fruit. For pomegranate, decide now whether to keep the multi-trunk form (let 3 to 5 main trunks grow) or train it to a single trunk; remove the extra base shoots accordingly.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Strong shoot extension. Mulberry grows quickly and may need its first directional pruning. Persimmon is slower. Pomegranate fills its multi-trunk clump.
growth_stages.user_action: Mulberry: pick one main vertical trunk and remove low side branches you don't want long-term -- mulberry grows large fast. Persimmon: light shaping only; both American and Asian persimmons fruit on last year's wood, so heavy pruning costs you crops. Pomegranate: keep the chosen 3 to 5 main trunks clear of small side shoots below knee height.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Mulberry, persimmon, and pomegranate all drop their leaves in late fall. Frost-hardy when fully dormant.
growth_stages.user_action: Mulch around the base before hard freeze. Pomegranate benefits from extra mulch over the root zone in zone 7 and colder. Wrap young trunks in young-tree wrap if rabbits or sunscald are concerns. Major pruning waits until late winter.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Mulch and trunk protection in place?

growth_stages.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Tree fully dormant, leaves down. Late-winter window.
growth_stages.user_action: Light structural pruning only on mulberry and persimmon -- both fruit on previous-year wood. Pomegranate suckers freely; remove suckers and limit to 3 to 5 main trunks.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Late-spring or early-summer bloom -- well after main spring frost risk has passed.
growth_stages.user_action: These crops bloom late, so frost protection is rarely needed. Avoid spraying during bloom.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small green fruit forming after petal fall. Most home varieties are self-fertile.
growth_stages.user_action: Thinning is rarely needed for this group. On heavy pomegranate set, thin lightly to prevent limb breakage.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Mulberry summer-ripens over weeks; persimmon and pomegranate ripen in fall.
growth_stages.user_action: Mulberry: lay a sheet under the tree and shake, or pick ripe fruit daily. Persimmon: astringent types after first frost; non-astringent when fully colored. Pomegranate: when fruit cracks slightly or sounds metallic when tapped.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Last fruit picked. Drops attract wasps and yellow jackets in late summer.
growth_stages.user_action: Clear fallen fruit. Apply a balanced or potassium-rich feed. Refresh mulch before winter.

notifications.title: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text: These trees are typically grown on their own roots in home gardens, so there is no graft union to worry about. Plant with the crown at the original soil line.
Water in well at planting and mulch a 3-foot circle around the base, kept a few inches back from the trunk. Staking is usually not needed unless the site is very windy.

establishment.text: Water deeply once a week through the first season -- even after rain. Establishment takes one to two years; do not skip irrigation just because the tree looks fine.
These crops are slow to bear -- mulberry typically 2 to 3 years, persimmon 3 to 5, pomegranate 2 to 3. Patience is the main first-season skill.

first_growth.text: Train to a modified central-leader or open-vase form depending on the species. Pomegranate is often grown as a multi-stemmed shrub; mulberry and persimmon take well to a single-trunk form.
Remove low water sprouts and any suckers. Pomegranate especially suckers freely and needs annual sucker removal.

dormancy.text: Winter pruning is the rule for this group. Wait until leaves are fully down and the tree is dormant.
A mulch refresh and a deep watering before the ground freezes help winter survival, especially in the colder end of each species' hardiness range.

dormant_prune.text: Light structural pruning only on mulberry and persimmon. Both bear on previous-year wood and heavy heading reduces the next crop. Remove dead, diseased, damaged, and crossing branches; leave the rest.
Pomegranate is the exception -- it tolerates and benefits from heavier annual pruning to limit suckers and keep the canopy open. Limit to 3 to 5 main trunks if growing as a multi-stem.

blossom.text: These crops bloom later than pome and stone fruit, so spring frost is rarely the problem. Mulberry, persimmon, and pomegranate flower from late spring into early summer in most zones.
Avoid spraying during bloom. Pollinators are doing the year's most important work in this window even on self-fertile crops.

fruit_set.text: Most home varieties of these crops are self-fertile (American persimmon needs a male; Asian persimmon does not; pomegranate and mulberry are self-fertile). Confirm your variety before assuming.
Thinning is rarely needed -- the tree's natural set is usually appropriate. A heavy pomegranate set on a young tree may benefit from light thinning to avoid limb breakage.

harvest.text: Mulberry ripens over 3 to 4 weeks; harvest by laying a sheet under the tree and shaking, or by picking ripe fruit daily. Persimmon and pomegranate ripen later -- persimmon is best after the first frost (astringent types) and pomegranate when the fruit cracks slightly or sounds metallic when tapped.
Handle ripe fruit gently. Mulberry and ripe persimmon stain badly and bruise even more easily than stone fruit.

post_harvest.text: Clear fallen fruit from under the tree. Sticky drops attract wasps and yellow jackets in late summer.
Apply a balanced or potassium-rich feed after harvest to build reserves. Refresh mulch before winter.

yield_expectations.per_plant: Heavy bearer once mature -- expect 50+ lbs from a mature tree, ripening over a 2 to 6 week window with daily pickings
yield_expectations.peak_production: Full production in year 4 to 6. Mature plants produce reliably for decades with very little intervention compared to deciduous fruit trees.
yield_expectations.first_year_note: No useful crop in year one. These are tough, low-input plants once established, but year one is still a root-building year. Remove fruit if any sets.
factors: light structural pruning -- these crops fruit on previous-year wood (mulberry, persimmon) or freely from suckers (pomegranate)
fruit drop when stressed in pomegranate

crops.hardiness_notes: Mulberry (Morus species) is an easy, adaptable fruit tree that fits well in a backyard but has two quirks worth knowing. First, ripe mulberries drop readily and stain hard surfaces -- don't plant over a patio, sidewalk, or driveway. Second, fruit doesn't ripen uniformly on the tree, so harvest happens daily over 4-6 weeks rather than in one big pick. Three main species are grown: White mulberry (Morus alba) is the Asian import, very hardy, less flavorful fruit, considered invasive in some regions. Red mulberry (Morus rubra) is the North American native, better-flavored, zones 5-9. Black mulberry (Morus nigra) has the best flavor of all but is only hardy to zone 7-8. Most varieties sold in US nurseries are red-white hybrids chosen for cold hardiness and flavor. Mulberries are self-fertile; one tree produces abundantly. Trees bear in year 2-3 and are long-lived (100+ years). In zones 4-5, choose named varieties bred for cold hardiness rather than seedling trees.

varieties_detail.notes: Most popular mulberry for US home gardens. Large sweet dark berries over a long bearing season (6+ weeks). Self-fertile. Cold-hardy. Produces heavily even in light shade. Nearly seedless.
Produces enormous berries (3-4 inches long) with excellent sweet flavor. Self-fertile. Requires warm climate. Not hardy in cold zones. The most impressive mulberry for warm-climate growers.
Compact tree (6-10 feet) suitable for containers or small gardens. Self-fertile. Small sweet black berries over long season. More cold-hardy than most black mulberries. Good patio tree.
Cold-hardy cultivar from Minnesota. Very productive with large sweet black-purple fruit. Self-fertile. Good choice for zone 4-5 growers where Illinois Everbearing may struggle in severe winters.
True black mulberry with the species' legendary flavor -- widely regarded as the best-tasting mulberry. Compact tree (10-15 feet). Self-fertile. Only for warm-winter zones; not cold-hardy.

crops.chill_hours_note: Low to moderate chill -- adaptable across zones 5-10

failure_diagnostics.label: Cold or frost damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: These crops bloom late enough that spring frost during bloom is rarely the problem -- the more common cold issue is winter cold damage at the edge of each species' hardiness range. Pomegranate is hardy to about USDA zone 7; persimmon and mulberry are hardier (zones 4 to 5 for hardy varieties). Cold-damaged wood shows as dieback the following spring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Confirm your variety is hardy to your zone -- there is wide variation within each species. In marginal zones, plant in a sheltered south-facing site, mulch heavily before winter, and accept some annual dieback on pomegranate.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Pest pressure on this group is generally lower than on pome or stone fruit. Mulberry attracts birds heavily once fruit ripens. Persimmon is sometimes hit by persimmon psyllid (curling new growth) or persimmon wilt. Pomegranate can suffer leaffooted bug damage and heart rot in humid summers.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Bird netting on mulberry once fruit colors. For persimmon psyllid, a dormant horticultural oil spray reduces overwintering populations. For pomegranate heart rot, choose resistant varieties and improve airflow with light pruning.

failure_diagnostics.label: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Most home varieties of these crops are self-fertile. American persimmon (Diospyros virginiana) is the main exception -- it needs a male tree nearby. Asian persimmon (Diospyros kaki), which is what most named varieties sold in the US are, sets fruit without a pollinator (sometimes seedless).
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Confirm whether your variety is American or Asian persimmon and whether it needs a male. For pomegranate and mulberry, persistent fruit-drop usually points to drought stress or extreme heat at bloom rather than pollination.

failure_diagnostics.label: Root problems or waterlogging
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: These crops want well-drained soil. Pomegranate is the most drought-tolerant; mulberry tolerates a wider moisture range; persimmon prefers consistent moisture but hates standing water. Symptoms of waterlogging are yellowing leaves, dieback, and root rot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Improve drainage before planting on heavy or low-lying soil -- plant on a 12-inch mound if needed. Pomegranate especially does best on the dry side once established.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: All three need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to ripen and develop sugar. Pomegranate especially struggles in shade and may flower without setting fruit. Persimmon ripens unevenly without enough sun.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun. Light pruning to keep the canopy open helps fruit ripen on the inside of the tree -- particularly important for pomegranate and persimmon.

crops.pollinator_notes: Requires cross-pollination from a different pawpaw variety or seedling. Flowers are pollinated by flies and beetles, not bees. Hand-pollination improves fruit set significantly.

tasks.description: Minimal pruning. Remove suckers and dead wood in late winter. Pawpaw forms a natural pyramid shape.

pests.name: Pawpaw peduncle borer
pests.symptoms: Individual flowers wither, dry, and drop shortly after opening. Cutting open an affected flower reveals a small (5 mm) whitish larva tunneling through the flower tissue and into the peduncle (the flower stem) at the base. In bad years, most of a crop's flowers can be destroyed.
pests.cause: Talponia plummeriana, a small native moth. Kentucky State University identifies this as the single most damaging pawpaw pest. Typically provides a beneficial thinning effect in normal years; destructive only in outbreak years.
pests.organic_treatment: No reliable organic spray -- larvae are protected inside the flower tissue. Hand-remove and destroy affected flowers when damage appears.
pests.prevention: Scout flowers daily during bloom. Clean up flower debris under trees to reduce overwintering population. Avoid broad-spectrum sprays that kill parasitic wasps.

pests.name: Zebra swallowtail larvae
pests.symptoms: Chewed young leaves on new growth. Green-and-black striped caterpillars (up to 1 1/2 inches) on young foliage. Damage is almost always minor on established trees and does not affect fruit yield.
pests.cause: Eurytides marcellus. Pawpaw is the exclusive host plant for this butterfly's larvae. Kentucky State notes the adult butterfly is of such beauty that this should be considered a blessing rather than a curse.
pests.organic_treatment: Generally not recommended -- the damage is minor and the adult butterfly is ecologically valuable. On young seedlings only, hand-relocate caterpillars to mature trees.
pests.prevention: Generally not needed. Established pawpaws tolerate this feeding easily.

pests.name: Asimina webworm
pests.symptoms: Leaves at branch tips pulled together with silk webbing to form a shelter. Caterpillars feed inside the webbing. Damage is unsightly but occurs late in the season after growth has finished, so impact is minimal.
pests.cause: Omphalocera munroei, reported as an occasional pawpaw pest by Ohio State extension. Appears in late summer or early fall.
pests.organic_treatment: Prune out and destroy affected branch tips with their webbing. Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) is effective on caterpillars if treatment is warranted.
pests.prevention: Rarely needed. Clean up leaf litter under trees in fall.

diseases.name: Phyllosticta leaf spot
diseases.symptoms: Small circular brown or black spots on leaves, sometimes with a lighter center ('bordered' spots). In high-pressure years, fruit may also develop spots that can crack. Usually a cosmetic issue on a healthy tree.
diseases.cause: Phyllosticta species, fungi. Ohio State lists this among the common pawpaw diseases. Spreads by rain splash in wet weather. Overwinters on fallen leaves.
diseases.organic_treatment: Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn. Copper fungicide only in severe cases; most pawpaw leaf spot does not warrant treatment.
diseases.prevention: Prune for air circulation. Water at soil level. Remove leaf litter annually.

diseases.name: Sooty blotch & flyspeck
diseases.symptoms: Dark smudgy patches (sooty blotch) and tiny black dots grouped in flyspeck patterns on fruit skin. Surface blemish only -- does not penetrate the fruit or affect flavor.
diseases.cause: Complex of surface fungi, including Zygophiala and Schizothyrium species, favored by warm humid weather and dense canopies. Reported by Ohio State on pawpaw fruit.
diseases.organic_treatment: Gently wipe fruit with a damp cloth at harvest -- much of the blemish washes off. Copper fungicide may suppress in high-pressure orchards but is rarely needed in home plantings.
diseases.prevention: Prune for better air circulation and light penetration. Thin heavy fruit clusters to improve airflow.

crops.harvest_ready: Skin softens and yellows. Strong tropical aroma. Slight give to thumb pressure. Short shelf life -- eat within days.

storage.freezer: Scoop out flesh, mash with lemon juice, freeze in portions -- excellent
storage.notes: Pawpaws are the most perishable large temperate fruit -- freeze surplus immediately.

varieties.note: Shenandoah is the most widely recommended introduction variety -- milder flavor appeals to beginners, reliable producer.

start_method.notes: Plant bare-root trees in late winter/early spring while dormant. Container trees can go in spring through early autumn. Stake against wind for the first 2 years.

container_notes.notes: Fruit trees need to be grown in the ground. Dwarf varieties on very dwarfing rootstocks can be tried in very large (30+ gallon) containers but are challenging and rarely as productive.

rotation.avoid_after: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Container-grown tree just planted. Pawpaw seedlings have a long tap root; potted trees may show some root circling.
growth_stages.user_action: Plant carefully -- pawpaw doesn't like root disturbance. Loosen any roots that are circling the rootball. Plant at the original soil line, water in well, mulch deeply. Plant at least two genetically different pawpaws within 30 feet of each other so the flowers can cross-pollinate.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Two or more pawpaws planted within range?

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: First leaves emerging. Pawpaw is famously slow to start -- most year-one energy goes into the tap root, with little visible top growth.
growth_stages.user_action: Pawpaw needs partial shade in years 1 to 2 -- full sun can scorch young leaves. Use a shade cloth or plant on the east side of a taller plant. Water consistently. Don't expect dramatic top growth; the tree is building an exceptional root system underground.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Tree finally putting on visible top growth. Tropical-looking long leaves; growth shape is naturally pyramidal.
growth_stages.user_action: Pawpaw needs almost no training. The natural pyramidal shape is the right shape. Pick one main vertical trunk if two are competing, and clear any shoots from the base. The shade requirement ends around year 3 -- by then the tree handles full sun fine.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Leaves turn yellow and drop -- pawpaw is fully deciduous. Buds tight on the stems through winter.
growth_stages.user_action: Pawpaw is generally cold-hardy through zone 5 once established, so first-year dormancy needs only standard care: mulch the root zone, wrap young trunks if rodents are a concern. The shade cloth comes off if it was up. Pawpaw shrugs off cold winters.

growth_stages.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Tree fully dormant. Late-winter window.
growth_stages.user_action: Light pruning only: dead, diseased, damaged. Pawpaw needs little structural pruning.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Maroon bell flowers before leaves emerge. Faintly fetid smell -- normal.
growth_stages.user_action: Hand-pollinate between trees with a small brush to boost fruit set.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small green fruit forming. Self-incompatible -- need 2+ trees.
growth_stages.user_action: Confirm cross-pollination from different variety nearby.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Late summer to early fall. Fruit gives to pressure and often falls.
growth_stages.user_action: Catch falling fruit on a sheet or pick daily. Refrigerate or pulp-freeze immediately.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Fruit done; tree heading toward dormancy.
growth_stages.user_action: Minimal cleanup. Light spring feeding.

notifications.title: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text: Pawpaw is grown from grafted named varieties or from seedlings. Both are own-rooted in practice -- there is no dwarfing rootstock concern. Plant with the crown at the original soil line.
Young pawpaws need shade for the first 2 to 3 years. Plant under existing tree shade or set up shade cloth on stakes; full sun on a young pawpaw burns the foliage.

establishment.text: Water deeply once a week through the first two seasons. Pawpaw roots are notoriously slow to establish and the tree may look like it is sulking for the first year -- this is normal, not a problem.
Mulch a 3-foot circle around the base. Pawpaw thrives in a forest-floor environment of deep leaf litter; replicate that with an inch of compost annually under the mulch.

first_growth.text: Pawpaw grows naturally as a small understory tree with a pyramidal form. No structural pruning is needed in the first few years; let the tree establish its natural shape.
Once established, gradually reduce shade -- pawpaw needs increasing sun as it matures to set fruit. By year 3 or 4 it should be in mostly full sun.

dormancy.text: Pawpaw is fully deciduous and goes dormant in winter. It is one of the latest trees to leaf out in spring -- do not panic if neighboring trees have leaves and yours does not yet.
Refresh mulch before the ground freezes. Pawpaw is hardy through USDA zone 5; no special winter protection needed in zone.

dormant_prune.text: Pawpaw needs little pruning. Remove dead, diseased, damaged wood and any low suckers. Avoid heavy structural pruning -- the tree's natural shape is what you want.
Pawpaw fruits on previous-year wood. Heavy heading reduces the next crop. Less is more.

blossom.text: Pawpaw flowers are dark maroon, bell-shaped, and faintly fetid -- they are pollinated by flies and beetles, not bees. The smell is the point and is normal.
Bloom happens before the leaves emerge in mid-spring. Frost during bloom can damage flowers but is rarely catastrophic; pawpaw blooms over a 2 to 3 week window.

fruit_set.text: Pawpaw is self-incompatible -- a single tree, even a grafted named variety, will produce little or no fruit. You need at least two genetically different trees (different varieties, or seedlings from different parents) within about 30 feet for pollination.

Hand-pollination with a small brush significantly boosts fruit set in home gardens. Move pollen between flowers on different trees during the bloom window. Many serious pawpaw growers do this every year.

harvest.text: Pawpaw ripens in late summer to early fall. Ripe fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure (like a ripe peach) and often falls from the tree on its own. Catch ripening fruit by laying a sheet under the canopy or check daily.

Pawpaw does not store. Refrigerate immediately for up to a week, or pulp and freeze for use in baking or smoothies. The flavor is best at peak ripeness; under-ripe fruit is starchy and over-ripe fruit ferments quickly.

post_harvest.text: Pawpaw is one of the lowest-maintenance fruit trees once established -- no major post-harvest cleanup is needed. Clear any fallen leaves from the immediate trunk area.
A balanced organic fertilizer in early spring is usually sufficient. Pawpaw is a light feeder compared to most fruit trees.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 25-50 lbs from a mature grafted tree, harvested over a 2 to 4 week window in late summer or fall
yield_expectations.peak_production: First fruit typically in year 5 to 7 from grafted trees, longer from seedlings. Mature pawpaws produce a moderate but very reliable crop with almost no spray or thinning input.
yield_expectations.first_year_note: No fruit in year one. Pawpaws are slow to establish, often putting almost all their first-year energy into a tap root. Don't expect visible top growth until the root system is set.
factors: shade in years 1 to 2 (pawpaw seedlings are shade-obligate when young)
cross-pollination -- pawpaws need at least two genetically different trees
fly pollination, not bee -- some growers hang carrion bait near trees
very few pest or disease problems once established

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

crops.hardiness_notes: Pawpaw (Asimina triloba) is North America's largest native fruit and one of the most interesting tree fruits a home grower can plant. It tolerates shade better than almost any fruiting tree, thrives in humid eastern zones where stone fruits struggle with disease, and has essentially no serious pests or diseases in the US. The fruit has a tropical custard flavor (compared to banana, mango, and pineapple) but the trees are fully hardy to zone 5 and marginal in zone 4. Pawpaws require cross-pollination between two different varieties -- a single pawpaw tree will not fruit. Pollination is by flies and beetles rather than bees, as the maroon flowers smell mildly of rotting meat; some growers hand-pollinate for better fruit set. Pawpaws need protection from direct sunlight in their first 2-3 years; they are naturally understory trees. Mature trees tolerate full sun. Fruit doesn't store -- it must be eaten within a few days of ripening, which is why you rarely see pawpaws in grocery stores. Trees begin bearing in year 5-8 from seed, year 3-5 from grafted trees.

varieties_detail.notes: Partially self-fertile (still better with a pollinator). Medium-large fruit with rich custardy flavor and relatively few seeds. Kansas-origin variety. The pawpaw for beginners who want reliable fruit from a single tree.
Peterson Pawpaws release. Mild sweet flavor and relatively firm flesh -- considered the best pawpaw for people who are new to the fruit's tropical flavor. Requires pollinator. Released 2003.
Peterson Pawpaws release. Large fruit (up to a pound each) with rich deep flavor. The fruit-quality benchmark among modern pawpaws. Requires pollinator. Ripens late.
Florida-origin variety, the best low-chill pawpaw for the southern end of the range. Medium fruit with distinctive mango-tropical flavor. Requires pollinator. Earlier ripening than most varieties.
Indiana-origin heirloom. Large fruit with excellent flavor. Cold-hardy. Requires pollinator. Classic variety available from most specialty fruit nurseries. A good reliable choice for zones 5-7.

crops.chill_hours_note: Native to eastern US -- zones 5-8. Needs a pollinator partner

failure_diagnostics.label: Cold or frost damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Pawpaw is hardy through USDA zone 5 -- one of the most cold-hardy fruit trees in this group. Spring frost during bloom can damage some flowers but rarely eliminates the crop because pawpaw blooms over a 2 to 3 week window. Winter cold is rarely the limiting factor.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Pawpaw needs little frost protection in its zone range. If you are at the southern edge of its range, ensure the tree gets enough winter chill (over 400 hours below 45 degrees) for proper bloom.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Pawpaw is famously pest-resistant -- deer leave it alone, and the leaves contain natural insecticides. The main pest is pawpaw peduncle borer, which causes premature fruit drop. Phyllosticta leaf spot may show up in wet years but rarely affects the crop.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Clear and destroy any prematurely-dropped fruit to break the peduncle borer cycle. No spraying is generally needed. Pawpaw's pest profile is one of the reasons to plant it -- it needs less intervention than nearly any other backyard fruit.

failure_diagnostics.label: Bloom but no fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Pawpaw is self-incompatible. A single tree -- including a grafted named variety -- will not set significant fruit. Even two seedlings with the same parent may share enough genes to be incompatible. This is the single most common reason pawpaws bloom heavily but fruit poorly in home gardens.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant at least two genetically different pawpaws within 30 feet -- two different named varieties, or seedlings from different sources. Hand-pollinate with a small brush between trees during bloom; this can multiply fruit set several times over.

failure_diagnostics.label: Waterlogging or root problems
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Pawpaw tolerates moist soil better than most fruit trees -- it is naturally a streambank species. Standing water still damages roots, but pawpaw fails more often from drought during establishment than from waterlogging.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Maintain consistent moisture, especially during the first 2 to 3 years. Mulch deeply with leaf litter or compost to mimic the forest-floor environment pawpaw evolved in.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Pawpaw is unusual in needing shade as a young tree but full sun as a mature tree. A mature pawpaw in deep shade grows leaves but bears little or no fruit. A young pawpaw in full sun burns and may die.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Provide shade for the first 2 to 3 years (existing tree shade or shade cloth on stakes), then gradually reduce shade as the tree matures. By year 4 or 5 the tree should be in mostly full sun.

crops.description: A 2,000-year track record. Incredibly drought-tolerant and long-lived -- trees can produce for centuries. Needs cold winters for flowering. Arbequina is self-fertile and the most popular home variety.
