pests.name: Olive fruit fly
pests.symptoms: Small brown puncture (sting) on olive fruit that darkens as the larva tunnels inside. Cut fruit shows tan tunnels and sometimes a small cream-colored maggot. Fruit drops early or rots on the tree. Affected fruit ruins oil quality and cannot be cured.
pests.cause: Bactrocera oleae. UC ANR identifies this as the most damaging pest of California olives and the most important olive pest worldwide. Regional -- primarily a California concern in the US. Multiple generations per season.
pests.organic_treatment: Hang yellow sticky traps baited with ammonium carbonate for monitoring. Spinosad-based GF-120 NF Naturalyte bait (OMRI-listed) applied weekly to a few branches during fruit development attracts and kills egg-laying females. Kaolin clay spray (Surround WP) deters egg-laying.
pests.prevention: Pick up and destroy all dropped olives -- they harbor pupae. Consider not leaving fruit on trees past January. Strip unpicked olives at season end on ornamental (non-fruiting) trees to deny the fly a breeding site. Regionally, protected or closed fruit clusters help.

pests.name: Black scale
pests.symptoms: Dark brown to black domed bumps on twigs, branches, and leaves -- about 1/8 inch across with a characteristic H-shaped ridge on the back. Copious sticky honeydew coating leaves and fruit, followed by heavy sooty mold that reduces photosynthesis. Leaf drop and twig dieback.
pests.cause: Saissetia oleae, a soft scale listed by UC ANR as a key olive pest. Worse in humid coastal conditions and in dense canopies. Farmed by ants.
pests.organic_treatment: Narrow-range horticultural oil timed to crawler emergence (typically late spring into summer). Prune out heavily infested branches. Control ants with sticky trunk bands.
pests.prevention: Prune to open the canopy -- scale populations crash in well-ventilated trees. Protect parasitic wasps (Metaphycus spp.) that provide biological control.

pests.name: Olive psyllid (regional)
pests.symptoms: Waxy white filaments on new growth tips. Distorted, curled young leaves. Flower buds malformed or dropping. Sticky honeydew and sooty mold. Most severe on flush growth in spring.
pests.cause: Euphyllura olivina, an invasive psyllid established in California since roughly 2007. UC ANR lists it as a regional olive pest. Multiple generations per year.
pests.organic_treatment: Horticultural oil or insecticidal soap during the spring flush. Parasitic wasps provide partial control.
pests.prevention: Prune out infested tips in spring. Support natural enemies by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays.

pests.name: Olive mite
pests.symptoms: Pale stippling or silvery discoloration on leaves. Heavy infestations cause leaf bronzing and early leaf drop. Visible only with a hand lens.
pests.cause: Oxycenus maxwelli and related eriophyid mites. UC ANR lists this as an olive pest, mostly a concern on stressed trees and in hot dry weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Sulfur dust or horticultural oil (not together -- they interact). Most established trees tolerate mite damage.
pests.prevention: Maintain even irrigation. Avoid drought stress, which favors mite buildup.

diseases.name: Olive knot
diseases.symptoms: Rough, woody, gall-like swellings on twigs, branches, and occasionally trunk and leaves. Knots start as small swellings and grow to 1-2 inches or more. Branches beyond heavy knots lose vigor, fail to leaf out, and die back. Fruit from infected trees may carry off-flavors.
diseases.cause: Pseudomonas savastanoi pv. savastanoi, a bacterium. UC ANR identifies this as a primary olive disease, with incidence strongly tied to rainfall and freeze injury (openings that let the bacteria in). Spreads by water and contaminated pruning tools.
diseases.organic_treatment: Prune out knotted tissue during dry weather, cutting 6-12 inches into healthy wood. Disinfect tools between cuts with 10% bleach or 70% alcohol. Destroy (burn or bag) all prunings. No effective bactericide registered for home use.
diseases.prevention: Only prune in dry weather. Avoid injuring bark with mowers, pruners, or picking equipment. Plant disease-free nursery stock (pathogen exclusion is the primary defense). Protect trees from freeze damage in marginal zones. Copper sprays before winter rains can reduce new infections in commercial orchards.

diseases.name: Peacock spot
diseases.symptoms: Circular dark olive-green to black spots (1/10 to 1/2 inch) on upper leaf surfaces, sometimes with a yellow halo -- the 'peacock eye' or 'bird's eye' pattern. Lower-canopy leaves most affected. Heavy infection causes defoliation, weakening the tree and reducing bloom the following year.
diseases.cause: Spilocaea oleaginea (also called Cycloconium oleaginum), a fungus. UC ANR and oliveoilsource.com both document this as a common olive disease worldwide. Infection occurs in cool wet fall and winter weather (35-80°F); inactive in hot dry summer.
diseases.organic_treatment: Copper-based fungicide applied in late October before winter rains, and again in spring if wet weather persists. Rake and destroy fallen leaves that harbor overwintering spores.
diseases.prevention: Plant on well-drained sites with good air circulation. Avoid overhead irrigation. Prune to open the canopy. Cultivar resistance varies but no variety is immune.

diseases.name: Verticillium wilt
diseases.symptoms: Sudden wilting and yellowing of leaves on one side of the tree or on individual branches. Dark vascular streaking visible when a cut is made in affected wood. Leaves may remain attached after dying (unlike frost damage, which drops leaves). Young trees often die; mature trees may decline over years.
diseases.cause: Verticillium dahliae, a soil-borne fungus with a very wide host range (tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, cotton, many others). Persists in soil for over a decade. Particularly bad on sites previously planted to susceptible annual crops.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure. Prune out affected branches. Severely infected young trees should be removed.
diseases.prevention: Do not plant olives where solanaceous crops (tomatoes, peppers, eggplants) have grown recently. Plant on verticillium-tested soil in replant situations. Some rootstocks show tolerance. Avoid over-irrigation.

diseases.name: Botryosphaeria blight
diseases.symptoms: Dead flower clusters that fail to emerge in spring, or blighted clusters with blackened rachises appearing in late spring. Fruit rot with silvery covering. Elliptical cankers on branches that girdle and kill twigs.
diseases.cause: Neofusicoccum parvum, Diplodia, and related Botryosphaeriaceae fungi. Often enters through olive knot galls, pruning wounds, or freeze-damaged tissue. Compounds the damage caused by olive knot.
diseases.organic_treatment: Prune out dead branches and blighted clusters. Disinfect pruning tools between cuts. Dispose of prunings; do not compost.
diseases.prevention: Control olive knot (which provides entry points). Prune during dry weather with clean cuts. Keep trees adequately watered but not waterlogged.

watering.signs_overwater: Root rot -- most common olive killer

crops.harvest_ready: Green olives: firm and green, bitter but curable. Black olives: shrivelled and very dark. Both need curing before eating.

storage.room_temp: Freshly picked olives must be cured immediately -- they are inedible raw
storage.freezer: Freeze cured olives in brine -- quality drops somewhat but acceptable
storage.notes: Cure in brine (12-18 months), lye (1-2 weeks), or dry salt (6 weeks). Home-cured olives are very satisfying.

varieties.note: Arbequina is the best choice for most backyard growers -- self-fertile (no partner needed), compact, and produces oil and table olives.

start_method.notes: Plant bare-root trees in late winter/early spring while dormant. Container trees can go in spring through early autumn. Stake against wind for the first 2 years.

container_notes.notes: Olive is a classic container tree for cold-zone growers. Use a 15+ gallon container with excellent drainage. In zones below 8, bring indoors to an unheated but frost-free space for winter (olives need a cool dormancy -- don't keep in a heated room). Choose dwarf varieties like Arbequina for best container performance. Expect reduced vigor and fruit set versus in-ground trees in warm zones.

rotation.avoid_after: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Container-grown olive just planted. Often a small multi-stem form or a single-trunk young tree.
growth_stages.user_action: Plant in well-drained soil -- olives die fast in wet feet. Site in full sun and a sheltered spot if your zone is marginal for cold. Water in deeply, mulch generously, but keep mulch off the trunk. Stake briefly if the tree was tall and slim from the nursery.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Olive planted in well-drained sunny spot?

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Leaves greening up and new shoots extending. Olive is slow but steady in year one.
growth_stages.user_action: Water deeply but infrequently -- about every 10 to 14 days, depending on heat and soil. Olive prefers a deep soak followed by drying out over constant moisture. Remove any first-year flowers or olives. Watch for olive fruit fly if you're in a warm coastal zone.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Branch structure becoming visible. Olive naturally wants to be multi-stemmed unless trained otherwise.
growth_stages.user_action: Olive trains to an open-vase form similar to stone fruit -- 3 to 5 main branches angled outward, no central trunk. Decide on the form now: single-trunk for an orchard look, multi-stem for ornamental use or as insurance against cold damage. Remove any shoots from below the soil line and any crossing growth.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Form decided and main branches chosen?

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Olive is evergreen -- leaves stay on through winter. Growth slows visibly; the silver-green foliage may darken slightly.
growth_stages.user_action: Olive's version of dormancy is a winter slowdown, not true leaf-fall. Cold-hardiness varies sharply by variety -- some olives tolerate brief drops to about 15 degrees F, others lose wood at 25. Check your variety's cold tolerance and don't rely on the tree past its limit. Use frost cloth or warm holiday lights if a hard freeze threatens. Reduce watering frequency.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Variety cold limit known and protection ready?

growth_stages.name: Late Winter Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Late winter, before bloom.
growth_stages.user_action: Light pruning. Open canopy. Remove dead wood, suckers, water sprouts.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Late-spring creamy-yellow flower clusters. Wind-pollinated.
growth_stages.user_action: Plant a second variety nearby for boosted set.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small green fruit. Heavy early-summer drop is normal.
growth_stages.user_action: Thin in heavy years to level alternate-bearing cycle.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Green for table olives, fully-darkened for oil or black-cured.
growth_stages.user_action: Pick by hand or net-shake. Plan 6+ weeks of curing.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Main harvest done.
growth_stages.user_action: Light feeding only. Refresh coarse mulch.

notifications.title: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text: Olive is grown on its own roots or grafted -- both are common. The graft union, if present, should sit at or just above soil level. Olive tolerates planting depth better than most fruit trees.
Plant in spring after frost danger passes. Olive thrives in poor, rocky, alkaline soil -- do not over-amend with compost or manure. Excellent drainage matters more than fertility.

establishment.text: Water deeply once a week through the first season. Once established (2 to 3 years), olive is among the most drought-tolerant fruit trees and thrives on infrequent deep watering.
Mulch a 3-foot circle but use a coarse, dry mulch (gravel works well). Olive resents the moist organic mulch that other fruit trees prefer.

first_growth.text: Olive can be trained as a single-trunk tree or a multi-stemmed shrub. Both are traditional. For single-trunk form, select a strong leader and remove competing trunks at the base.
Olive grows slowly. Do not over-fertilize trying to push growth -- excess nitrogen produces vegetative growth at the expense of fruit and shortens the tree's life.

dormancy.text: Olive is evergreen and never fully dormant. Growth pauses through winter cold but the tree is never bare.

Olive needs winter chill (above freezing but below about 50 degrees) to set fruit -- about 200 to 300 hours below 50 in winter. In subtropical zones with no winter chill, olive grows but rarely fruits.

dormant_prune.text: Olive pruning is done in late winter or early spring before bloom. Olive fruits on previous-year wood; heavy heading reduces the next crop substantially.
Open the canopy enough that light reaches all the fruiting wood. Olive can become a thicket if left unpruned. Remove dead wood, suckers, and water sprouts.

blossom.text: Olive blooms in late spring with creamy-yellow flower clusters. The bloom is wind-pollinated -- bees rarely visit -- so isolation from pollinator gardens does not matter.
Most olive varieties are self-fertile but most also benefit from a second variety nearby. Mission and Manzanillo are good cross-pollinators.

fruit_set.text: Olive is famously alternate-bearing -- a heavy crop year followed by a light year. Thinning fruit in heavy years partly evens the cycle out.
Heavy early-summer fruit drop is normal -- the tree sheds excess set. Persistent later drop usually means drought stress.

harvest.text: Harvest timing depends on use. For green olives, pick when fruit is fully sized but still green-yellow. For oil or black-cured olives, wait until fruit darkens fully.
All raw olives are bitter from oleuropein and inedible without curing. Plan for a 6-week minimum cure (lye, brine, or salt) before eating.

post_harvest.text: Light feeding only after harvest -- a balanced organic fertilizer at half the usual rate. Olive is a light feeder and over-fertilizing causes problems.
Refresh mulch with coarse material. Inspect for olive fruit fly damage in the harvested fruit and remove any infested drops from under the tree.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 20-60 lbs from a mature dooryard tree in an on year, much less in an off year (alternate-bearing is the norm)
yield_expectations.peak_production: Full production in year 5 to 8 and continuing for decades. Mature olives often alternate, with a heavy crop one year and a lighter one the next.
yield_expectations.first_year_note: No useful crop in year one. Olives are slow to bear but very long-lived. Year one is canopy and root development.
factors: cold-hardiness varies sharply by variety -- some tolerate brief drops to about 15 degrees F, others lose wood at 25 degrees F
drought-tolerant once established but moisture during fruit sizing improves yield
olive fruit fly in warm coastal zones

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

crops.hardiness_notes: Olives (Olea europaea) need a Mediterranean climate to produce fruit properly: hot dry summers, mild winters with 200-400 chill hours, and minimal rainfall during fruit ripening in fall. Trees survive to about 15F when mature (zone 8b), but fruit buds are damaged at higher temperatures -- reliable fruit production really starts in zone 9a. In humid climates like the US Southeast, olives grow as ornamentals but fruit production is minimal due to inadequate summer heat accumulation and fungal disease pressure. California, Arizona, Texas Hill Country, and New Mexico are the practical US olive-growing regions. Most olives require cross-pollination from a second variety for fruit set, though 'self-fertile' Arbequina is a reasonable exception. Fresh olives are inedibly bitter; all olive varieties require brining or curing before eating. Trees are slow to begin bearing (year 4-8) but extraordinarily long-lived (centuries) and drought-tolerant. Pollen is heavily wind-dispersed and can cause severe allergies; reduced-pollen varieties exist for landscape use in populated areas.

varieties_detail.notes: Spanish variety. Partially self-fertile -- one of few olive varieties that fruits alone. Small brown-purple fruit, excellent for oil production. Cold-hardy. The home-garden standard olive. Earlier bearing than most varieties.
Classic California olive, brought by Franciscan missionaries in the 1700s. Medium black fruit, dual-purpose for table olives and oil. Requires pollinator. The cultural heritage olive of California.

Spanish variety, the classic green table olive. Large oval fruit. Requires pollinator (Sevillano, Mission). Most widely-planted table olive variety globally. Lower oil content; grown specifically for eating.
Greek variety producing the famous purple-black Kalamata olives. Large almond-shaped fruit. Requires pollinator. Classic Mediterranean table olive with distinctive rich flavor. Good cold tolerance.
Italian oil olive, the standard for premium Tuscan olive oil. Small black fruit with very high oil content. Requires pollinator. Top choice for serious home oil production.

crops.chill_hours_note: Moderate chill requirement -- needs cool winters but not freezing. Zones 8-11

failure_diagnostics.label: Cold or freeze damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Olive is evergreen and tolerates light frost but is killed back by hard freezes -- mature trees suffer leaf and twig damage at about 22 degrees and severe damage below about 15. Olive needs some winter chill (200 to 300 hours below 50 degrees) to set fruit, so subtropical zones grow olive trees that rarely fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: In marginal zones, plant in the warmest microclimate available (south wall, sheltered courtyard) and choose cold-hardy varieties (Arbequina, Mission). In no-chill zones, accept that olive is an ornamental tree.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Olive fruit fly is the headline pest in California and increasingly in other Western states -- it lays eggs in developing fruit, ruining the crop for table or oil use. Olive knot bacteria causes warty growths on twigs and branches. Verticillium wilt is an occasional serious problem.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: For olive fruit fly, hang yellow sticky traps and bait traps from late spring through harvest. Pick up all dropped fruit. For olive knot, prune out infected branches in dry weather and disinfect tools. Verticillium has no cure -- avoid planting in soil where tomatoes or other susceptible crops have suffered the disease.

failure_diagnostics.label: Bloom but no fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Olive is wind-pollinated and most varieties are self-fertile, so missing pollination is rarely the issue. Heavy bloom with no fruit set is more often insufficient winter chill, drought stress, or alternate bearing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Confirm your zone provides enough winter chill (below 50 degrees for several hundred hours). Plant a second variety nearby (Mission, Manzanillo) for cross-pollination boost. In hot windy sites, irrigate during bloom.

failure_diagnostics.label: Waterlogging or root problems
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Olive evolved in poor, rocky, dry-summer Mediterranean soils. It cannot tolerate waterlogged soil; standing water kills roots quickly and the tree never recovers. Over-irrigation also produces vegetative growth at the expense of fruit and shortens the tree's productive life.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant on a 12-inch raised mound on heavy or poorly-drained soil. Water deeply but infrequently once established; many mature olives do well with no irrigation at all in their native climate range.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Olive needs full sun, all day if possible. In partial shade the tree grows leaves but barely fruits. Olive is also the most heat-tolerant common backyard fruit tree -- the hottest spot in the yard is usually the right spot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in the sunniest, hottest spot available. Light pruning to open the canopy helps inner fruit ripen. Reflective surfaces (white walls, gravel mulch) can help in marginal zones.

crops.name: Parsnip
crops.soil: Deep, loose, sandy loam -- same as carrots
crops.description: Slow to germinate, long to mature -- but worth it. Frost turns starch to sugar; the sweetest parsnips are dug after a hard freeze. Needs deep, loose soil just like carrots.

3.notes: Direct sow early. Long season barely fits -- choose 100-day varieties. Frost dramatically improves flavor.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note: Parsnips need warmer soil than other root crops to germinate well; optimal soil temperature is 50-70 degrees F. (MSU Extension; UMN Extension) Seeds are slow to germinate, taking up to 3 weeks even in ideal conditions. Sow 2-3 weeks before last frost as soon as soil can be worked. In Minnesota, start planting parsnips beginning May 1, about 2 weeks before last frost. (UMN Extension; Iowa State, harvesttotable)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: Parsnip flavor is greatly enhanced by a few hard touches of frost (cold converts starches to sugars). Spring-planted parsnips come to harvest after first frost in autumn. The longer parsnips stay in the ground in the fall, the sweeter they will be. Roots left in the ground all winter have the best flavor. harvest_end extends well past first_frost; practically, harvest through winter in zones with workable ground, or before frost locks soil. (UMN, Iowa State)

Roots left in the ground all winter have the best flavor. harvest_end extends well past first_frost; practically, harvest through winter in zones with workable ground, or before frost locks soil. (UMN, Iowa State)

fertilizer.notes: Like carrots, avoid excess nitrogen. Prepare the bed with a low-nitrogen fertilizer before sowing for best root development.

succession.reason: Very long DTM and improved by frost -- sow once, harvest through winter.

pests.name: Carrot fly
pests.symptoms: Rust-red tunnels and channels inside roots. Foliage yellows and wilts. Larvae (small white maggots) visible in roots.
pests.cause: Psila rosae. Female flies attracted by carrot scent to lay eggs near roots.
pests.organic_treatment: No cure once roots infested. Use fine mesh netting 60cm high as barrier -- flies are low-fliers.
pests.prevention: Grow under fine insect mesh. Sow alongside chives or rosemary to mask scent. Avoid thinning on still evenings when smell is strongest.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Willow-carrot aphids curl leaf tips and reduce vigor. Leaves distorted. Can transmit viruses.
pests.cause: Cavariella aegopodii. Arrives from willow trees in spring.
pests.organic_treatment: Insecticidal soap or neem oil spray.
pests.prevention: Grow under insect mesh. Avoid planting near willow trees.

diseases.name: Cavity spot
diseases.symptoms: Oval gray/brown sunken cavities on carrot roots. First appears as small lesions that enlarge.
diseases.cause: Pythium violae soil pathogen. Favored by compacted, poorly drained soil.
diseases.organic_treatment: No chemical control. Improve soil structure with organic matter.
diseases.prevention: Deep, well-drained, stone-free soil. Avoid waterlogging. Crop rotation.

crops.harvest_ready: Harvest after first hard frost for maximum sweetness -- frost converts starches to sugar. Roots should be firm.

start_method.notes: Always direct sow. Parsnip seeds are short-lived -- use fresh seed each year. Germination slow (2-4 weeks) -- mark rows.

rotation.avoid_after: Carrots, parsnips, parsley, cilantro, dill, celery -- share carrot fly and Apiaceae diseases
rotation.note: Avoid planting carrots where parsnips (or vice versa) grew last year -- same pest pressures.

storage.freezer: Blanch and freeze for cooking
storage.notes: Can be left in the ground through frost -- flavor improves with cold. Cover with straw to access through winter. Store away from apples, pears, and bananas -- ethylene from those fruits causes parsnips to turn bitter, the same way it affects carrots.

varieties.note: Javelin has good canker resistance -- important for wet soils where canker is common.

crops.soil_prep: Similar to carrots -- deep, stone-free, loose soil to 12-15 inches. Never fresh manure. Add only well-rotted compost from 2+ years ago. Parsnips tolerate heavier soil than carrots if well-dug.

thinning.when: Thin when seedlings are 1 inch tall
thinning.method: Snip with scissors. Parsnip seedlings are delicate -- pulling causes too much disturbance.
thinning.tip: Parsnip germination is slow and patchy. Mark rows with a fast-germinating radish to avoid losing the row.

good.name: Radishes
good.why: Break up soil for deep parsnip roots

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Root-zone partitioning is a real ecology concept. 'Carrots loosen soil for tomatoes' is a plausible mechanistic claim but not well-studied for specific pairs.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Legume rhizobial nitrogen fixation is textbook plant science. The mechanism is real; the specific pairing benefit is mechanistically plausible but often not pair-tested.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Inter-plant competition for N, P, K is a real agronomic concept. Specific 'bad pair' claims often extrapolate beyond what research has shown.

container_notes.notes: Possible in very deep containers (15+ inches). Short varieties (Gladiator) work better than long types. 5-gallon deep pot minimum.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Thread-like shoots pushing up from the soil. Carrots and parsnips are notoriously slow -- do not give up.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep soil surface consistently moist -- the most common reason carrots fail is the surface drying out during the 2-3 week germination period. Lay a plank of wood over the row and check daily.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Feathery or distinctive first true leaves -- carrots look like tiny ferns, beetroot has deep red stems.
growth_stages.user_action: Thin seedlings carefully and promptly. Crowded root vegetables fork and stay small. Thin in stages -- once at 2 inches, again at 4 inches.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Strong leaf growth above ground. Roots are developing below -- resist the urge to dig and check.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep consistently watered -- irregular watering causes cracking and forking in root crops. Weed carefully to avoid disturbing roots.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Shoulders of root visible at soil surface, or reach the days to maturity for your variety. Test pull one before harvesting the row.
growth_stages.user_action: Water well before harvesting to loosen the soil. Pull at an angle rather than straight up to prevent snapping. Many root crops improve with frost.

growth_stages.name: In Storage
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Roots harvested and stored properly. Potatoes in a dark cool place. Carrots in damp sand.
growth_stages.user_action: Check stored roots monthly for any that are rotting -- one bad root can spread to others. Remove immediately.

notifications.title: Time to sow your root vegetables
notifications.body: Root vegetables go directly into the ground -- they do not transplant. Prepare your bed deeply, remove any stones that could cause forking, and sow thinly. Most root crops can go in 3-4 weeks before last frost.

notifications.title: Time to thin your root crops
notifications.body: Thinning is the most important thing you can do for root vegetables right now. Crowded roots fork and stay small. Thin to the recommended spacing -- eat the thinnings if they are big enough.

notifications.title: Your root vegetables should be approaching harvest
notifications.body: Do a test pull of one root before harvesting the row. Water the ground well first to loosen the soil. Most root crops can stay in the ground for several weeks after reaching full size -- they store well in situ.

notifications.title: Harvest before the ground freezes
notifications.body: Most root vegetables need to be out of the ground before it freezes solid. Carrots, parsnips, and beetroot can handle light frost -- it actually sweetens them. But harvest everything before a hard freeze locks them in.

notifications.title: Root check-in
notifications.body: Root vegetables mostly look after themselves once established, but it is worth checking for weeds and keeping the soil consistently moist. How are they looking above ground?

weather_triggers.title: Dry spell -- water your root crops consistently
weather_triggers.body: Irregular watering during root development causes carrots and parsnips to fork, beetroot to become woody, and potatoes to crack. Water deeply and consistently -- not a little every day but a good soak twice a week.

weather_triggers.title: Heavy rain -- check for waterlogging
weather_triggers.body: Root vegetables sitting in waterlogged soil can rot. Check drainage in your bed and consider harvesting any roots that are near maturity before they split from the rapid moisture uptake.

weather_triggers.title: Frost coming -- parsnips and carrots will thank you
weather_triggers.body: A light frost actually improves the flavor of carrots and parsnips by converting starch to sugar. Leave them in the ground through light frosts if you can. Potatoes and beetroot should be harvested before a hard frost.

germination.text: These crops are direct-sown -- transplanting damages the taproot and produces forked or stunted roots. Sow seeds shallowly (1/4 to 1/2 inch deep) and keep soil surface consistently moist for the 1 to 3 week germination window.
Carrot and parsnip seed is short-lived -- use fresh seed each year. Parsnip especially can take up to 3 weeks to germinate; do not give up early.

seedling.text: Thin to recommended spacing once seedlings have 2 true leaves -- crowded roots stay small and forked. Pull weaker seedlings rather than transplanting them.
Mulch lightly between rows once seedlings are established to suppress weeds. Hand-weed close to the row -- hoeing damages shallow seedling roots.

established.text: Water consistently. Uneven moisture causes carrot and parsnip roots to split as they swell during a wet period after dry conditions.
These crops feed lightly. Side-dress with compost mid-season if growth slows; avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers, which produce lush leafy tops at the expense of roots.

harvest.text: Harvest carrots, parsnips, beetroot, and turnips after the first frost for best flavor -- this is not folklore; the cold genuinely converts starch to sugar in the root. Parsnip especially needs frost exposure to develop its characteristic sweetness.

Loosen soil with a fork before pulling -- yanking by the tops snaps the root, especially on long carrots and parsnips. Cut tops off within an inch of the crown for storage; tops left on draw moisture out of the root.

storage.text: Store carrots, parsnips, beetroot, and turnips in layers of damp sand or sawdust in a cool location (32 to 40 degrees) at high humidity. Properly stored, these crops keep 4 to 6 months.

In zones with mild winters, you can leave the roots in the ground and harvest as needed -- mulch heavily over the row before the ground freezes. This is often easier than indoor storage and preserves quality longer.

yield_expectations.per_plant: One parsnip per plant -- a 3-foot row gives you around 15-20 parsnips
yield_expectations.peak_production: Parsnips can stay in the ground all winter, improving with frost
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Parsnips are slow and demand patience, but a roasted homegrown parsnip after the first frost is extraordinary.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: These crops actively benefit from light to moderate frost -- it improves flavor by converting root starch to sugar. Damage from frost is rare and usually only happens to exposed leaf tops on a hard freeze; the roots are insulated by soil and survive even harsh winter conditions in many zones.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Time harvest to follow the first frost rather than precede it. In zones with mild winters, leave roots in the ground under heavy mulch and harvest as needed through winter.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Carrot rust fly (carrot, parsnip) is the headline pest -- larvae tunnel through roots leaving rusty trails. Cabbage maggot (turnip, sometimes beetroot) does similar damage to brassica roots. Leaf spot diseases and powdery mildew can hit foliage but rarely affect the root harvest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Floating row cover from sowing through harvest blocks both carrot rust fly and cabbage maggot -- this is the most effective home-garden defense. Rotate root crops to a new bed each year. Avoid planting carrot or parsnip after parsley or celery (same family, same pest).

failure_diagnostics.label: Cracked or rotten roots
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Uneven watering -- a dry spell followed by heavy water -- causes roots to split as they swell rapidly. Persistent waterlogging causes root rot, soft black tissue, and crown collapse. Beetroot and turnip handle wet soil better than carrot and parsnip, both of which need excellent drainage.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Maintain consistent moisture rather than letting soil dry out and then soaking it. On heavy clay, plant in a raised bed for carrot and parsnip especially. Mulch helps stabilize moisture.

failure_diagnostics.label: Small, woody, or strong-flavored roots
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought-stressed root crops produce small, fibrous roots with concentrated and often unpleasantly strong flavor. Parsnips become woody at the core; carrots become bitter; turnips become sharp; beetroot becomes earthy and tough.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water deeply and consistently -- 1 inch per week is the rough target. Mulch between rows to retain moisture. In hot weather, root crops appreciate light afternoon shade.

failure_diagnostics.label: Patchy germination
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Carrot, parsnip, and beetroot seeds need 1 to 3 weeks of consistent surface moisture to germinate. The most common reason for failed sowings is the soil surface drying out during germination -- not poor seed or bad soil. Parsnip seed in particular loses viability fast and old seed simply does not come up.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Sow into pre-moistened soil and cover with a board or burlap until the first seedlings emerge -- this keeps the surface consistently moist without daily watering. Use fresh parsnip seed each year. Pre-sprout difficult seed on damp paper towels indoors before sowing if needed.

crops.name: Kohlrabi
crops.description: The alien-looking brassica that deserves far more attention. Crisp, mild, sweet flavor -- eat raw like an apple or cooked. Very fast-maturing and easier than broccoli or cabbage.

3.notes: Direct sow spring through summer. Multiple successions fit in Zone 3's season.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note: Kohlrabi is a fast-maturing brassica (45-60 days) typically direct-sown. Plant spring crop when soil reaches 40 degrees F, about 3-4 weeks before last frost. Plant fall crop in late summer for October harvest. Harvest when bulbs are 2-3 inches diameter; larger bulbs become woody. (Cornell, UMN)

fertilizer.notes: Moderate feeder. Consistent balanced feeding produces well-formed bulbs. Avoid excess nitrogen.

succession.tip: Sow every 3 weeks from early spring through early summer, then again in late summer for autumn. Kohlrabi is fast (45-60 days) and must be harvested promptly -- left too long it becomes woody. Spring and autumn sowings work well; skip midsummer plantings in most zones as it bolts in heat. Each sowing gives you a tight 1-2 week harvest window, so small frequent batches beat one big sowing.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension 2022 and 2025 Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetable Crops; UConn IPM 'Perimeter Trap Cropping for Cole Crops'). Nasturtiums specifically are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and Utah State University Extension (Mohr et al., 'Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting'). Protocol caveat: UConn IPM explicitly notes trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents' -- so the aphid application here has a protocol-mismatch concern even though the companion is extension-named. The Cornell-IPM-specific attribution in earlier catalog reason text was not located in Cornell's published IPM material; actual backing is WSU/USU/UConn.

pests.name: Cabbage worm
pests.symptoms: Large irregular holes in leaves. Green caterpillars (1-1.5 inches) blending into foliage. White cabbage butterfly flying nearby is a warning sign.
pests.cause: Pieris rapae butterfly larvae. Lay eggs on leaf undersides.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick caterpillars and egg clusters. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray every 2 weeks. Row covers as barrier.
pests.prevention: Row covers from planting. White butterfly decoys (territorial behavior). Plant nasturtiums as trap crop.

pests.name: Cabbage aphid
pests.symptoms: Dense gray-green colonies on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl and pucker. Honeydew and sooty mold may follow.
pests.cause: Brevicoryne brassicae. Populations explode rapidly in cool weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Strong water blast. Insecticidal soap spray directly on colonies. Remove and compost heavily infested leaves.
pests.prevention: Avoid excess nitrogen. Encourage parasitic wasps with flowering herbs nearby.

pests.name: Flea beetle
pests.symptoms: Many tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings. Plants look peppered. Small shiny beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause: Multiple flea beetle species. Worst in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment: Row covers on seedlings. Diatomaceous earth. Kaolin clay spray.
pests.prevention: Delay planting. Use transplants. Interplant with aromatic herbs.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms: Plants wilt in hot weather despite watering. Stunted growth. Yellowing leaves. Roots are swollen, club-shaped, and deformed when dug up.
diseases.cause: Plasmodiophora brassicae soil pathogen. Survives in soil for up to 20 years. Thrives in acidic, wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure. Remove and destroy infected plants -- do not compost. Lime soil to raise pH to 7.0-7.2.
diseases.prevention: Minimum 7-year rotation away from brassicas in infected soil. Maintain soil pH above 6.5. Improve drainage.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms: Yellow patches on upper leaf surface with gray-purple fuzzy mold on undersides. Affects seedlings and mature plants.
diseases.cause: Peronospora brassicae fungus. Favored by cool moist conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Improve air circulation. Copper-based fungicide as preventive.
diseases.prevention: Avoid overhead watering. Space plants generously. Choose resistant varieties.

crops.harvest_ready: Pick when bulb is 2-3 inches. Larger kohlrabi becomes woody and tough.

rotation.avoid_after: Kale, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, turnip, kohlrabi -- share clubroot and downy mildew
rotation.note: Clubroot can persist 20 years -- in infected soil extend to 7-year rotation.

storage.freezer: Peel, cube, blanch 2 minutes, freeze -- good for soups
storage.notes: Remove leaves before storing -- they draw moisture from the bulb.

recommended: Superschmelz (giant type, stays tender even large)
varieties.note: Superschmelz can grow to 10 inches across while staying tender -- the most forgiving if you miss harvest.

thinning.tip: Thinnings are edible. Crowded kohlrabi produces small tough bulbs.

container_notes.notes: Good container crop. 2-gallon minimum. Space 6 inches apart. Fast-maturing and compact.

start_method.notes: Direct sow 4-6 weeks before last frost for spring, or in late summer for autumn harvest.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Round seed leaves pushing up cleanly. Brassicas germinate readily in cool, moist conditions.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep soil consistently moist at 60-70°F. Brassicas do not need heat -- they prefer cool germination.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: True leaves developing -- slightly waxy and blue-green in color.
growth_stages.user_action: Watch for damping off -- good airflow and not overwatering prevents it. Thin to one plant per cell.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Sturdy plants with multiple leaf sets, ready to go outside.
growth_stages.user_action: Harden off well before transplanting. Net immediately after planting to protect from cabbage white butterflies -- do not delay on this.

growth_stages.name: Head Forming
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Central head beginning to form. On broccoli, a tight green dome. On cauliflower, a white curd appearing in the center.
growth_stages.user_action: For cauliflower, tie the outer leaves over the developing curd to blanch it and keep it white. Do this as soon as the curd is visible.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Broccoli: tight green head before any yellow flowers open. Cauliflower: firm white curd at full size. Cabbage: firm, dense head that does not give when squeezed.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest broccoli with a long stem cut -- side shoots will continue producing for weeks. Cauliflower and cabbage are once-and-done harvests.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Harvest time -- how did it look?

notifications.title: Time to start your brassicas indoors
notifications.body: Broccoli, cauliflower, and cabbage need 6-8 weeks indoors before transplanting. Start now -- they grow slowly at first but reward the patience. Cool temperatures suit them perfectly.

notifications.title: Brassicas outside -- net them immediately
notifications.body: Cabbage white butterflies lay eggs on brassica leaves within hours of planting. Cover with fine mesh netting immediately after transplanting -- before you do anything else. Caterpillar damage can devastate an unprotected crop.

notifications.title: Cauliflower curd forming -- time to blanch
notifications.body: Tie a few outer leaves loosely over the developing curd now to protect it from light. This keeps the cauliflower white and tender. Check every few days -- once the curd is visible it develops quickly.

notifications.title: Check your broccoli heads
notifications.body: Broccoli heads that are ready to harvest look like tight green domes with no yellow showing. Once you see any flower buds opening it is past its best. Cut with a long stem and watch for side shoots to develop.

notifications.title: Start a fall brassica crop
notifications.body: Brassicas do well as a fall crop and often taste better -- frost sweetens cabbage and broccoli. Start seeds now for a crop that matures in the cooler autumn months.

notifications.title: How are your brassicas getting on?
notifications.body: Check under the netting for caterpillar damage -- they can strip a plant surprisingly fast. Also look at the developing head for any signs of bolting or discoloration.

weather_triggers.title: Heat stress -- brassicas may bolt
weather_triggers.body: Sustained high temperatures cause broccoli and cauliflower to bolt -- heads open into flowers before they are full size. Harvest anything that looks close to ready before the heat peaks.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- watch for clubroot and downy mildew
weather_triggers.body: Humid conditions favor several brassica diseases. Ensure good spacing and airflow. Check leaves for yellowing or powdery patches and remove affected material promptly.

weather_triggers.title: Late frost -- protect young brassicas
weather_triggers.body: Established brassicas handle frost well, but young transplants need protection for the first few weeks. Cover with fleece tonight.

germination.text: Brassicas are reliable germinators in cool conditions -- 60-70F is ideal. They do not need heat mats.
Sow into cells or modules rather than trays -- brassicas develop long tap roots and resent root disturbance.

seedling.text: Grow brassica seedlings in the coolest, brightest spot you have. Warmth makes them soft and leggy.
Feed with a dilute liquid feed once the first true leaves appear. Brassicas are hungry plants from the start.

established.text: Net immediately after transplanting. Cabbage white butterflies find brassicas within hours and lay clusters of yellow eggs on leaf undersides. Check the netting is secure all around -- one gap and caterpillars will find it.
Kohlrabi is the fastest of the head brassicas -- many varieties are ready in 50-60 days. It does not need the long season the others do, which makes it a useful succession-planting crop.

head_forming.text: The edible part of kohlrabi is the swollen stem just above the soil line, not a head or curd. It begins as a small bulge on the stem and enlarges over a few weeks as the plant matures.
Keep moisture even during bulb formation. Drought stress produces tough, fibrous bulbs that woody up unpleasantly. The leaves are also edible and good cooked like collards.

harvest.text: Harvest when the swollen stem reaches 2 to 3 inches across (3 to 4 for the larger storage varieties like Superschmelz). Pull the whole plant or cut just above the root with a knife.
Smaller is sweeter -- baby kohlrabi at 1.5-2 inches is the most tender, and successive sowings give you a long harvest window of small bulbs rather than a glut of woody big ones.

yield_expectations.per_plant: One bulb per plant -- fast crop, 45-60 days
yield_expectations.peak_production: Succession sow every 3 weeks for continuous supply
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Kohlrabi is one of the fastest-maturing brassicas and underrated as a vegetable. Sweet and crunchy when harvested young.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Established brassicas handle frost well -- it actually sweetens them. But young transplants in their first 2-3 weeks are more vulnerable. A hard freeze can damage or kill recently transplanted seedlings.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Cover new transplants with fleece for the first 2-3 weeks after planting if frost is possible. Once established they are among the hardiest vegetables you can grow.

failure_diagnostics.label: Caterpillars or pests
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cabbage white butterflies lay eggs on brassica leaves and the caterpillars can strip a plant in days. This is by far the most common reason brassicas fail. If you did not net, this is almost certainly what happened.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Net immediately after transplanting -- before you do anything else. Fine mesh netting secured all the way around is the single most important thing you can do for brassicas. Check netting for gaps weekly.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too much water or clubroot
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Brassicas in waterlogged soil develop root problems. Clubroot -- a soil-borne disease -- causes swollen, distorted roots and wilting. Once present in soil it persists for many years.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Improve drainage before planting. If clubroot is suspected, rotate brassicas to a new bed and do not grow them in the affected soil for 4-5 years. Liming to raise soil pH above 7 discourages clubroot.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too little water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Brassicas need consistent moisture to develop good heads. Drought stress causes premature flowering in broccoli and cauliflower, and split heads in cabbage.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently and mulch around plants to retain moisture. A dry spell during head formation is the most damaging period.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor head development
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cauliflower is the most demanding -- it needs consistent temperatures and care to form a good curd. Broccoli heads opening into yellow flowers usually means the temperature swung too warm. Both benefit from 6+ hours of sun.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Cauliflower in particular needs a consistent, cool growing environment. Autumn sowings often perform better than spring ones in warmer zones. Shade cloth can help in warm spells.

good.name: Borage
good.why: Attracts bees -- critical for watermelon pollination

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Xerces Society documents borage as a pollinator-attractant plant that blooms concurrently with tomato, squash, and cucumber crops, drawing the same bees that pollinate those crops. Source: xerces.org/blog/plants-you-can-eat-are-pollinator-treat.

good.name: Nasturtiums
good.why: Trap crop for aphids and cucumber beetles

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic. Nasturtiums are named as an aphid trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and USU Extension. However, the extension-documented trap crop for cucumber beetles is Blue Hubbard squash, not nasturtiums (Pinero, University of Missouri / Lincoln University IPM, 2017). The combined aphid-plus-cucumber-beetle framing in this claim pairs one extension-named mechanism (nasturtium + aphid) with a popular-gardening mechanism (nasturtium + cucumber beetle) that is not extension-documented. Protocol caveat: UConn IPM notes trap cropping is a weak fit for aphids due to passive air dispersal.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. This claim's nematode component aligns with the extension-documented mechanism, but the 'concurrent companion' application pattern reflects popular gardening practice rather than extension protocol.

pests.name: Cucumber beetle
pests.symptoms: Yellow-green beetles with black spots or stripes feeding on leaves, flowers, and fruit. Plants wilt suddenly (bacterial wilt transmission). Holey leaves.
pests.cause: Spotted and striped cucumber beetles. Also transmit bacterial wilt disease.
pests.organic_treatment: Row covers until flowering. Yellow sticky traps. Neem oil spray. Spinosad-based insecticide.
pests.prevention: Delay planting until plants are large. Use row covers early season. Interplant with radishes and nasturtiums.

pests.name: Squash bug
pests.symptoms: Gray-brown flat insects on stems and undersides of leaves. Wilting leaves with yellow then brown patches. Bronze egg clusters on leaf undersides.
pests.cause: Anasa tristis. Overwinters as adults in garden debris.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick adults and egg masses. Trap under boards at night. Neem oil spray on nymphs.
pests.prevention: Remove all garden debris in autumn. Rotate cucurbit crops. Use row covers early season.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces, stems, and sometimes fruit. Leaves may yellow and die. Worst in warm days with cool nights.
diseases.cause: Fungal disease favored by humid conditions with poor air circulation.
diseases.organic_treatment: Spray with diluted neem oil or a baking soda solution (1 tsp per quart water). Apply potassium bicarbonate spray. Remove and destroy affected leaves.
diseases.prevention: Space plants for good airflow. Water at soil level, not on foliage. Choose resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation.

diseases.name: Bacterial wilt
diseases.symptoms: Sudden wilting of individual leaves, then whole stems, then entire plant. No recovery even with watering. Plants die within days.
diseases.cause: Erwinia tracheiphila bacteria spread by cucumber beetles feeding.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure -- remove and destroy infected plants immediately. Control cucumber beetles to prevent spread.
diseases.prevention: Use row covers to exclude cucumber beetles early in season. Plant resistant varieties.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms: Yellow-green patches on upper leaf surface with corresponding gray-purple fuzzy growth on leaf undersides. Leaves die rapidly.
diseases.cause: Pseudoperonospora cubensis fungus. Spreads rapidly in wet humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively.
diseases.prevention: Choose resistant varieties. Water at soil level. Ensure good air circulation.

watering.frequency: Weekly -- reduce water as fruit ripens

crops.harvest_ready: Skin turns creamy white-yellow. Slight give at blossom end. Sweet aroma. Stem separation becomes easy.

rotation.avoid_after: Cucumbers, squash, pumpkins, melons -- share cucumber beetle, bacterial wilt, downy mildew
rotation.note: Rotate to prevent cucumber beetle and disease buildup.

storage.room_temp: Up to 1 week unripe. Once ripe: 2-3 days
storage.freezer: Cube and freeze -- good for smoothies
storage.notes: Honeydew ripens slowly -- store at room temperature until the stem end yields slightly.

container_notes.notes: Not well-suited to containers -- needs significant space for vines.

start_method.notes: Direct sow 2 weeks after last frost. In short-season zones, start indoors 3-4 weeks before in biodegradable pots.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Large seed leaves pushing up fast. Melons germinate quickly in warmth.
growth_stages.user_action: Melons need warmth above everything -- 75-85°F for germination. A heat mat is essential in all but the hottest climates.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Large, rough true leaves developing rapidly.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep warm. Melons sulk badly in cold temperatures -- below 60°F slows them dramatically and sets them back.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Vines beginning to run. Melons need space -- a lot of it.
growth_stages.user_action: Direct the vines in the direction you want them to grow. Melons need full sun and warm soil -- black plastic mulch makes a real difference in cooler zones.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Yellow flowers. Male flowers first, female flowers with a swollen base following.
growth_stages.user_action: Hand-pollinate female flowers in the morning for better fruit set. Touch a male flower to each open female flower.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Flowers appearing? Any small melons forming?

growth_stages.name: Fruit Setting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small melons developing after successful pollination.
growth_stages.user_action: Once fruit sets, limit to 2-3 fruits per plant. More than this and none of them will reach their potential size or sweetness.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Watermelon: thump test gives a deep hollow sound, tendril nearest the fruit is brown and dead. Cantaloupe: slips easily from the vine, smell is intensely fragrant. Honeydew: skin turns creamy yellow, slight give at the blossom end.
growth_stages.user_action: Underripe melon is disappointing. Learn the ripeness cues for your variety and wait. A day or two of patience makes a huge difference.

notifications.title: Start your melons indoors
notifications.body: Melons need a long warm season -- start them indoors 3-4 weeks before last frost. Use biodegradable pots to minimize root disturbance at transplant. Do not rush transplanting -- melon seedlings in cold soil stall badly.

notifications.title: Thin your melon fruits
notifications.body: Limit each plant to 2-3 fruits. More than this and you will get small, bland melons. Choose the best-positioned fruits and pinch off the rest. More space per fruit means more sugar, more size, more flavor.

notifications.title: Check your melons for ripeness
notifications.body: Learning to read ripeness is the most important melon skill. For watermelons, find the dead brown tendril nearest the fruit -- if it is dead and dry, the melon is ready. Thump it -- a deep hollow sound confirms it. Do not rely on size alone.

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- protect your melons immediately
weather_triggers.body: Melons are extremely frost-tender. Even a light frost kills them. Cover immediately or bring containers inside. If fruit is nearly ripe, harvest it -- it will continue ripening indoors.

weather_triggers.title: Extreme heat -- water melons deeply
weather_triggers.body: Melons love heat but need consistent moisture in very high temperatures. Water deeply at the base every day in extreme heat. Inconsistent watering causes hollow hearts and blossom end rot.

germination.text: Melons germinate best at 80-85F. A heat mat is not optional in most climates -- without bottom heat germination is slow and unreliable.
Sow two seeds per pot and thin to the stronger one. Do not transplant the thinned seedling -- melons hate root disturbance.

seedling.text: Keep melon seedlings consistently warm. A single cold night below 55F can set them back by weeks.
Do not over-pot. Keep in a small pot until the roots are just filling it, then plant out rather than potting up again -- each pot change is a disruption.

established.text: Black plastic mulch over the soil warms it and conserves moisture -- it makes a meaningful difference to melon yields in cooler zones.
Melons need more space than any other common vegetable. One watermelon vine needs 6-8 square feet of ground. Plan accordingly.

flowering.text: Hand-pollinate female flowers in the early morning using a small paintbrush, or by removing a male flower and touching it directly to the female. This dramatically improves fruit set in a polytunnel or cool season.
The window for pollination is short -- flowers are receptive for only a few hours in the morning.

fruit_set.text: Thin to 2-3 fruits per vine. This is the decision that determines melon quality. Spreading the plant's energy across too many fruits gives you several mediocre ones instead of a few excellent ones.
Place a tile or board under developing melons to keep them off the soil. This prevents rotting and pests getting to the vulnerable underside.

harvest.text: Honeydew does not slip from the vine reliably and must be cut. The primary ripeness cue is rind color: it shifts from pale green to creamy yellow or cream-white as the melon matures. Skin texture also turns slightly waxy or velvety.

Smell the blossom end (opposite the stem) -- a ripe honeydew has a faint sweet aroma there. Honeydew can be slightly underripe at harvest and continue ripening on the counter for 2-4 days, unlike most melons. This makes timing more forgiving than for cantaloupe or watermelon.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 1-3 melons per plant depending on thinning
yield_expectations.peak_production: Melons produce over a concentrated period -- plan to use them quickly
yield_expectations.first_year_note: A homegrown melon eaten warm from the vine on a hot day is one of the peak garden experiences. Worth every bit of the long season.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucurbits are tropical-origin tender annuals -- killed outright by even a light frost at any stage. Cold soil at planting (below 60 degrees) stunts seedlings for the rest of the season even if they survive. Late-summer frost ends the season abruptly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Wait to direct-sow or transplant until soil reaches 65 to 70 degrees and night temperatures stay above 50. In short-season zones, start transplants indoors 3 to 4 weeks before set-out, but disturb roots minimally -- cucurbits resent transplanting. Use black plastic mulch to warm soil. Have row cover ready for unexpected late-spring or early-fall frosts.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucumber beetles (striped and spotted) damage seedlings directly and transmit bacterial wilt -- a fatal disease that wilts vines from the tips inward. Squash bugs target squash and pumpkin (less so cucumber and melon). Powdery mildew shows up reliably late in the season as white powder on leaves. Downy mildew, anthracnose, and bacterial leaf spot are humidity-driven secondary problems.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Floating row cover from planting through first flower blocks cucumber beetles -- remove at flowering for pollination. Squash bug egg masses (orange-red, on undersides of leaves) crush easily by hand if caught early. For powdery mildew, choose resistant varieties (most modern cucumbers are bred for resistance) and water at the base, not overhead. Rotate cucurbits to a new bed each year.

failure_diagnostics.label: Watery fruit or vine collapse
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucurbits need consistent water but cannot tolerate waterlogged soil. Persistent saturation causes root rot, sudden vine collapse, and watery flavorless fruit. Heavy rain near harvest causes ripe melons to crack and split. Wet foliage drives powdery mildew, downy mildew, and bacterial leaf spot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil or raised mounds (the traditional 'cucurbit hill' approach exists for drainage reasons). Water deeply at the base 1 to 2 times per week rather than shallow daily. Mulch heavily to even out soil moisture and reduce splash-borne disease. Stop watering watermelons 2 weeks before expected harvest to concentrate flavor.

failure_diagnostics.label: Small or bitter fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress during flowering and fruit set produces small, misshapen, or bitter fruit. Cucurbits move large volumes of water through their tissues during fruit development -- a single mature watermelon plant can use 1 to 2 gallons of water per day in peak summer. Cucumber bitterness is often a drought-stress signal.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently and deeply -- 1 to 2 inches per week minimum during fruit development, more in heat. Drip irrigation outperforms overhead watering by both providing consistent water and keeping foliage dry. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture and reduce evaporation.

failure_diagnostics.label: Vines without fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cucurbits need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum, ideally 8 or more -- to set and ripen fruit. In partial shade vines grow leaves and even bloom, but fruit set is poor and ripening is incomplete. A late-season fruit that never sweetens is often a sun problem more than a temperature problem.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in the sunniest spot available. Trellising vining cucurbits (vertical support for cucumbers and small-fruited squash) gets more leaf area into the sun and improves fruit set substantially. In partial-shade gardens, accept that cucurbits are not the right crop and grow leafy greens or herbs instead.

tasks.description: Light prune after harvest. Remove dead wood and crossing branches to improve air circulation.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Pollinator category is mechanistically grounded. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. The nematode component is extension-documented. The claim's additional assertions about deterring whiteflies are not supported in the extension literature on marigolds and should be read as traditional.

provenance.label: traditional
