pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Scale insects
pests.symptoms: Flat brown or white waxy lumps on stems and leaves. Sooty black mold follows from honeydew. Leaves yellow.
pests.cause: Various scale species. Common on indoor/container citrus.
pests.organic_treatment: Scrape off by hand. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap. Horticultural oil spray in winter.
pests.prevention: Inspect regularly. Keep plants healthy and well-fed. Good air circulation.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Citrus greening (HLB)
diseases.symptoms: Mottled yellow-green leaves in blotchy pattern. Small, lopsided, bitter fruit. Tree slowly declines. No cure.
diseases.cause: Candidatus Liberibacter bacteria spread by Asian citrus psyllid insect. A devastating citrus disease.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure. Remove affected trees.
diseases.prevention: Control Asian citrus psyllid with neem oil or spinosad. Inspect purchased trees before planting.

diseases.name: Root rot (Phytophthora)
diseases.symptoms: Yellow leaves, declining vigor, branch dieback. Bark at soil line may show brown discoloration.
diseases.cause: Phytophthora root rot from waterlogged or poorly drained soil.
diseases.organic_treatment: Improve drainage. Avoid overwatering. Apply phosphonate fungicide.
diseases.prevention: Well-drained soil essential. Never let roots sit in water. Graft onto resistant rootstock.

crops.harvest_ready: Full sized and heavy. Yellow or pink blush depending on variety. Taste test -- only way to confirm sweetness.

storage.freezer: Juice in ice cube trays. Segments freeze well.
storage.notes: Grapefruits have the best shelf life of all citrus -- can last months in a cool room.

recommended: Star Ruby (most red flesh, low acid)
varieties.note: Oro Blanco (a pummelo-grapefruit hybrid) has much less bitterness than true grapefruit -- great for people who find grapefruit too harsh.

start_method.notes: Buy as a container plant. Harden off if moving from indoors to outdoors in spring. In zones below 9, grow in a large pot and bring indoors before first frost.

container_notes.notes: Excellent container plants in cold climates -- bring indoors before frost. Use citrus-specific potting mix. 15-gallon minimum for productive fruiting.

rotation.avoid_after: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Container-grown tree just planted. The graft union -- the knobby joint where the variety was grafted onto the rootstock -- sits well above soil level. Trunk often staked briefly to support against wind.
growth_stages.user_action: Dig the hole the same depth as the rootball but twice as wide. Plant high -- the top of the rootball should sit slightly above ground level. Don't add fertilizer at planting. Water deeply, then mulch around the base, keeping mulch a few inches off the trunk.

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: New leaves emerging in the first weeks after planting. Citrus pushes growth in flushes rather than steadily.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep soil consistently moist (not soggy) through year one. Begin a light citrus-specific feeding once new growth appears. Remove any first-year flowers so the tree builds its leafy canopy before fruiting.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Tree filling out with leaves and side branches. Canopy taking shape; some shoots may appear from below the graft union.
growth_stages.user_action: Citrus needs almost no training -- it builds its own canopy. Remove any shoots growing from below the graft union and any tall vertical shoots from inside the canopy. Keep pruning light; citrus fruits at the outer edges of the canopy, so a dense outer leaf surface matters more than a defined branch structure.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Citrus does not lose its leaves -- it's evergreen. Growth slows in cool weather, foliage may darken slightly, and the tree holds its shape.
growth_stages.user_action: Citrus's version of dormancy is a winter slowdown, not a leaf-fall. In marginal zones, watch overnight forecasts and protect with frost cloth or warm holiday lights when temperatures approach 28 degrees F. Reduce watering frequency but don't let the rootball go bone-dry.

growth_stages.name: Light Annual Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: After main harvest, before spring flush. Citrus does not truly go dormant.
growth_stages.user_action: Light shape pruning: remove dead wood, suckers from below the graft union, water sprouts, crossing branches. Avoid heavy heading -- citrus fruits at the canopy edge.

growth_stages.name: Main Bloom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Honey-scented spring bloom. Smaller flushes possible in summer or fall on healthy trees.
growth_stages.user_action: Avoid sprays during bloom. The smell brings pollinators from a distance.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Small fruit forming after petal fall. Heavy early-summer drop is the tree shedding excess set, normal.
growth_stages.user_action: Citrus is self-fertile; no thinning needed in most cases. Maintain consistent moisture to limit drop.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Variable -- some types ripen for months. Citrus does not ripen off the tree; pick when the fruit tastes right, not when it colors.
growth_stages.user_action: Use clippers or a gentle twist; do not pull, which tears bark. Most citrus can hang on the tree for weeks or months once ripe -- treat the tree as the storage.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest Feeding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Main harvest done. Tree preparing for next bloom flush.
growth_stages.user_action: Apply citrus-specific fertilizer (higher in nitrogen, with iron, zinc, manganese micronutrients). Inspect for scale and consider a horticultural oil application.

notifications.title: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text: Citrus is grafted on rootstock chosen for cold tolerance, disease resistance, and tree size. The graft union must sit 2 to 4 inches above soil level -- buried unions defeat the purpose of the rootstock and invite Phytophthora.
Plant in spring once soil is reliably above 60 degrees. Skip nitrogen fertilizer in the planting hole; a thin layer of compost is enough.

establishment.text: Water deeply once a week through the first season. Citrus has shallow roots and dries out faster than other tree fruit -- but also rots faster in standing water. Aim for evenly moist, never soggy.
Mulch a 3-foot circle but keep mulch 6 inches back from the trunk. Citrus collar and crown rot from Phytophthora is the single most common young-tree killer.

first_growth.text: Citrus is grown as a balanced canopy or hedge form, not as central-leader or open-center. Do not strip lower branches -- those are where most of the fruit will come from.
Remove suckers from below the graft union immediately. Rootstock suckers grow fast and have wicked thorns; left in place they take over the tree.

dormancy.text: Citrus does not have true dormancy -- it is evergreen and grows year-round wherever frost does not knock it back. There is no winter pruning window in the way deciduous fruit has.
In the colder end of citrus range, freeze protection (frost cloth, string lights, banking soil around the trunk) is the winter task rather than pruning.

dormant_prune.text: Citrus pruning is light and shape-focused, done after the main harvest in late winter or early spring before new growth. Remove dead wood, suckers, water sprouts, and crossing branches.
Avoid heavy heading cuts. Citrus fruits on previous and current-year growth at the canopy edge -- removing that growth removes next year's fruit.

blossom.text: Citrus often blooms multiple times per year. The main bloom in spring is the largest, but a healthy tree may also flush in summer or fall. Honey-scented flowers are normal.
Do not spray insecticide during bloom. The smell brings pollinators from a distance.

fruit_set.text: Most citrus is self-fertile and a single tree fruits well. Some mandarin varieties are seedy when cross-pollinated and seedless when isolated -- check your variety preference.
Heavy fruit drop in early summer is normal -- the tree sheds excess set. Persistent drop later in the season usually indicates water stress.

harvest.text: Citrus does not ripen off the tree. Pick when the fruit tastes right, not when it colors -- many citrus types color before they are sweet, and others stay green when ripe.
Use clippers or a gentle twist; do not pull, which can tear bark. Most citrus can hang on the tree for weeks or months once ripe -- treat the tree as the storage.

post_harvest.text: Apply citrus-specific fertilizer (higher in nitrogen, micronutrients including iron, zinc, manganese) after the main harvest. Citrus is heavier-feeding than other fruit trees.
Inspect for scale and ant trails year-round; the post-harvest window is a good time for a horticultural-oil application before the next bloom.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 100-200 lbs from a mature dooryard tree, with fruit holding on the tree for months
yield_expectations.peak_production: Grafted citrus typically reaches full production in 3 to 5 years and stays productive for decades. Many varieties hold ripe fruit on the tree for months, so harvest is often a slow steady pick rather than a single window.
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Light or no fruit in year one is normal. Grafted citrus can flower early; remove early blossoms in year one so the tree builds canopy and roots first.
factors: consistent moisture through bloom and fruit set
nitrogen feeding split across the year
iron and zinc availability (citrus leaves yellow when these are deficient)

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

crops.hardiness_notes: Grapefruit (Citrus paradisi) is moderately cold-hardy citrus, tolerating 22-24F when mature. It is the slowest citrus to ripen -- fruit stays on the tree 12-18 months and sweetens slowly. Like oranges, grapefruit quality is actually better in slightly cooler climates where winter cold increases sugar content, which is why Texas Rio Grande Valley and California desert grapefruit have better flavor than Florida grapefruit. Grapefruit trees are large (15-20 feet) and produce heavily, often yielding hundreds of pounds from a mature tree. Self-fertile. Seedless varieties (Rio Red, Star Ruby, Ruby Red) are the modern commercial standard. Fruit can hang on the tree for months without dropping. Commercial production has declined significantly due to citrus greening disease (HLB) which is currently devastating citrus across the southeastern US. Choose HLB-tolerant varieties where available. Begin bearing year 4-6.

varieties_detail.notes: Classic pink-fleshed grapefruit -- the commercial standard for decades. Medium-large yellow fruit with pink flesh. Sweet-tart with less bitterness than white grapefruit. Self-fertile. Texas grapefruit.
Improved Ruby Red with deeper red flesh that holds color longer. Sweeter than Ruby Red. Self-fertile. The modern commercial standard for Texas Rio Grande Valley production.
Deepest red flesh of any grapefruit. Excellent sweet-tart flavor. More cold-tender than Ruby Red. Self-fertile. Premium variety at specialty markets.
Pummelo x white grapefruit hybrid. Very sweet, no bitterness. More cold-hardy than standard grapefruit. Self-fertile. Good choice for borderline zones where grapefruit struggles.
Classic white-fleshed grapefruit. More acidic and traditionally 'grapefruit-bitter' flavor. Seedless. Self-fertile. The original commercial grapefruit from which most modern varieties descend.

crops.chill_hours_note: No chill requirement -- zones 9-11 only

failure_diagnostics.label: Freeze damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Citrus is evergreen and does not become fully dormant, so freeze damage is a whole-tree phenomenon (leaves, twigs, fruit) rather than the blossom-frost issue deciduous fruit faces. Lemons and limes are most cold-sensitive (damaged below about 30 degrees); oranges and grapefruit tolerate brief drops to about 26 degrees; mandarins are typically the hardiest. Damage shows as leaf drop, blackened twigs, and split or mushy fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Cover with frost cloth on freeze nights and string old-style incandescent lights through the canopy if possible. Bank soil up around the graft union before winter so the rootstock survives even if the top is killed. In marginal zones, choose the most cold-hardy varieties (satsuma mandarin, kumquat, calamondin) or grow in a movable container.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Scale insects (cottony cushion scale, citrus mealybug, California red scale) and Asian citrus psyllid are the dominant citrus pests. Asian citrus psyllid spreads Huanglongbing (HLB, citrus greening), the disease threatening commercial citrus in Florida, Texas, and California. Phytophthora root and crown rot kills more young trees than any insect.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Inspect for scale year-round and treat with horticultural oil. In HLB-affected areas, follow your state's quarantine guidance; healthy trees on resistant rootstock and aggressive psyllid control are the home-garden defense. For Phytophthora prevention, keep mulch off the trunk and avoid overwatering.

failure_diagnostics.label: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Most citrus is self-fertile -- a single tree should fruit well. Heavy bloom with no fruit set is more often a water-stress, temperature-extreme, or alternate-bearing issue than a pollination one. Some mandarin varieties produce seedless fruit only when isolated from other citrus.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Maintain consistent moisture through bloom and fruit set. If the tree blooms heavily one year and barely the next, it is alternate-bearing -- thinning fruit in the heavy year levels the cycle out. Avoid moving citrus during bloom; flowers and small fruit drop from stress.

failure_diagnostics.label: Phytophthora root or crown rot
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Citrus is more prone to Phytophthora than any other backyard fruit tree. The pathogen thrives in waterlogged soil and at the trunk-soil interface. Symptoms are yellowing leaves with green veins, dieback, gum oozing from the lower trunk, and bark that lifts off the wood at the base.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant on a raised mound on heavy or poorly-drained soil. Keep mulch a hand-width back from the trunk. Water deeply but infrequently, and let the top inch of soil dry between waterings. There is no good cure once Phytophthora is established.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Citrus needs full sun, 6 to 8 hours minimum, to develop sugar and color. In shade the tree grows leaves and may bloom but fruit stays small, sour, and green. South or southwest exposure is ideal in most US citrus zones.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun -- if a wall or building is reflecting heat, even better. Light pruning to keep the inside of the canopy open helps inner fruit ripen. In containers, rotate the pot a quarter turn every few weeks for even growth.

crops.name: Cherry (Sweet)
crops.description: The most spectacular fruit tree in bloom. Needs cross-pollination from another variety. Birds will compete for every fruit -- netting is essential before fruit colors. Needs 700-1,200 chill hours.

3.notes: Sour cherry is more reliable in Zone 3. Sweet cherry marginal -- try Stella (self-fertile).

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Plant bare root fruit trees in early spring while they are still dormant, as soon as the soil can be worked. In Minnesota, this is April or May. Bare root plants suffer severely from transplanting shock -- plant as soon as soil is workable and before bud break. (UMN Extension 'Growing apples in the home garden'; UMN Extension 'Growing stone fruits in the home garden')

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: Stone fruit harvest runs June through August for most varieties. Peaches and nectarines ripen mid-to-late summer; apricots earliest (June-July); sweet cherries June-July; sour cherries July; plums July-September depending on type (Japanese types earlier, European types later). This month-by-month synthesis of stone fruit harvest windows follows Iowa State University Extension's commercial-orchard reference material on peach, plum, and cherry harvest timing. UMN Extension is cited for complementary climate-zone guidance on northern-Midwest stone fruit cultivation.

crops.pollinator_notes: Requires a compatible sweet cherry variety for cross-pollination. Bing, Rainier, and Stella are popular combinations. Stella is self-fertile and pollinates others.

tasks.description: Prune after harvest in summer (not winter) to reduce silver leaf disease risk. Remove crossing and dead branches.

crops.year_one_notes: No harvest years 1-3. Focus on building scaffold. Stake tree in first year.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Allium sulfur-based volatile organic compounds have documented aphid-repellent effects (Durenne and Gosset, 'Companion Plants for Aphid Pest Management,' Insects 2018, 9(4):112). The companion application is described by several extensions at home-gardening rigor: Mississippi State University Extension ('Companion planting improves gardens,' Snyder via Reeves) explicitly states 'Chives tend to repel aphids'; Utah State University Extension ('Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting,' Mohr et al.) lists onions, garlic, and chives as repelling common garden pests; UC Cooperative Extension Master Gardener publications (Butte County 'Best Friends in the Garden' and Fresno County 'Winter companion planting to repel insects') likewise list allium VOCs among aphid-repellent companions. These extension sources describe the pairing at tradition-plus-plausible-mechanism rigor rather than validated protocol -- the Kansas State Extension / Johnson County 'Companion Planting' page caveats that allium sulfur repellency is 'centralized to the garlic itself -- and only with certain pests.' The earlier catalog attribution to 'UC IPM' does not match UC IPM's Pest Notes on aphids (pn7404), which focus on reflective mulches, water sprays, soaps, and natural enemies rather than allium interplanting.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Peachtree borer
pests.symptoms: Gummy, amber-colored sap mixed with sawdust at base of trunk near soil line. Weakened, declining tree.
pests.cause: Synanthedon exitiosa clear-wing moth larvae. Bore into trunk near soil.
pests.organic_treatment: Dig out larvae by hand in autumn. Apply beneficial nematodes around trunk base in autumn.
pests.prevention: Keep base of trunk clear of mulch and debris. Apply pyrethrin spray to trunk base in early September.

diseases.name: Brown rot
diseases.symptoms: Brown soft spots on ripening fruit, rapidly expanding. Fuzzy gray-brown spore masses develop. Fruit mummifies on tree.
diseases.cause: Monilinia fructicola/laxa fungus. Spreads rapidly in warm humid conditions near harvest.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove and destroy all affected fruit immediately -- do not compost. Apply sulfur fungicide preventively near harvest.
diseases.prevention: Remove mummified fruit from tree and ground. Improve air circulation with pruning. Avoid fruit injury.

diseases.name: Black knot
diseases.symptoms: Hard black galls/swellings on branches and twigs. Galls enlarge each year. Severe infection kills branches.
diseases.cause: Apiosporina morbosa fungus. Affects plum, cherry, and related stone fruits.
diseases.organic_treatment: Prune out knots 4 inches below visible growth in winter. Destroy -- do not compost.
diseases.prevention: Remove wild plum/cherry trees nearby. Annual inspection and removal of small knots.

crops.harvest_ready: Deep red-black color, firm but giving to squeeze. Glossy skin. Taste a few -- best indicator is flavor.

storage.fridge: 1-2 weeks in a sealed bag -- don't wash until ready to eat
storage.freezer: Freeze with stones on a tray, then bag -- very good quality preserved
storage.notes: Sweet cherries keep surprisingly well in the fridge unwashed. Freeze surplus immediately.

recommended: Rainier (yellow with pink blush, very sweet)
varieties.note: Lapins and Stella are self-fertile -- if you can only plant one tree, these are your only choices.

start_method.notes: Plant bare-root trees in late winter/early spring while dormant. Container trees can go in spring through early autumn. Stake against wind for the first 2 years.

container_notes.notes: Fruit trees need to be grown in the ground. Dwarf varieties on very dwarfing rootstocks can be tried in very large (30+ gallon) containers but are challenging and rarely as productive.

rotation.avoid_after: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Bare-root or potted tree just planted. Base of the trunk right at soil level, and the graft union -- the knobby joint where the variety was grafted onto the rootstock -- sits 2 to 4 inches above the ground.
growth_stages.user_action: Dig the hole twice as wide as the roots and the same depth. Spread the roots over a small mound in the bottom of the hole. Stake firmly against wind. Don't add fertilizer to the planting hole. Water in deeply.

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: First leaves breaking from the dormant branches. New shoot tips extending. The tree is putting almost everything into root growth.
growth_stages.user_action: Water deeply once a week through the first summer. Pinch off any flowers that form -- year-one fruit costs the tree more strength than it returns. Keep weeds and grass cleared 2 to 3 feet around the trunk.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Strong shoot extension from the trunk. The first major side branches are starting to take shape.
growth_stages.user_action: Stone fruit trees are trained to an open-vase form: 3 to 5 main branches angled outward at roughly 45 degrees, evenly spaced around the trunk, with no central leader. Pick those 3 to 5 main branches and remove everything else cleanly back to the trunk. Use branch spreaders (small props that hold a branch at a wider angle) or hanging weights so the chosen branches stay angled outward as they grow.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Leaves fully dropped, buds tight on the stems. The tree is in true winter dormancy.
growth_stages.user_action: First-year dormancy is a holding period -- the work happens later. Mulch heavily around the base before hard freeze. Wrap the trunk in young-tree wrap to prevent sunscald and rodent damage. Major pruning waits until late winter (the next stage).
growth_stages.log_prompt: Tree wrapped and mulched for winter?

growth_stages.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Tree fully dormant; buds tight; late winter into early spring.
growth_stages.user_action: Maintain an open-center (vase) form: 3 to 5 main scaffold branches angled outward from a short trunk, with no central leader. Stone fruit needs sun and air movement through the canopy. Remove dead, diseased, damaged wood, then anything growing inward.

growth_stages.name: Blossom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Pink or white bloom opening. Apricot is earliest and most frost-exposed.
growth_stages.user_action: Watch overnight temperatures closely -- stone fruit blooms ahead of apple. Cover smaller trees with fleece on frost nights. Avoid sprays while pollinators are active.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Petal fall complete; small green fruitlets visible. A natural drop reduces the load in late spring.
growth_stages.user_action: Thin to one fruit every 4 to 6 inches on the branch (peach and nectarine especially). Stone fruit overload makes the fruit small and breaks branches.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Background color shift complete (yellow on peach/nectarine; full color on plum/cherry); fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure.
growth_stages.user_action: Pick when fruit lifts and twists free with a gentle motion -- forced fruit is not yet ripe. Stone fruit ripens fast and over a short window; check daily during peak.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest Sanitation
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Mummified fruit hanging on tree or fallen below; leaves yellowing.
growth_stages.user_action: Remove every mummified fruit from the tree and the ground -- these are the brown rot spore source for next year. Apply a potassium feed after harvest while leaves are still working.

notifications.title: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text: Set the graft union a few inches above final soil level. Burying it lets the scion root and you lose the dwarfing rootstock effect.
Stake securely for the first two seasons. Drive the stake into the hole before the tree goes in to avoid root damage later.

establishment.text: Water deeply once a week through the first growing season. Roots are still inside the original root ball and dry out quickly.
Mulch a 3-foot circle around the trunk to hold moisture. Keep mulch a few inches clear of the trunk to prevent collar rot.

first_growth.text: Stone fruit trains to an open-center form, not a central leader. Choose 3 to 5 scaffolds angled outward from a short trunk and remove the central leader once the scaffolds are set.
Wide-angled scaffolds are stronger and let light into the interior. Use spreaders or weights to set the angle in the first two seasons.

dormancy.text: First dormancy is when you commit to the open-center form. Stand back and look at the structure before you cut.
Make clean cuts just above an outward-facing bud. Ragged stubs invite disease, especially Cytospora canker on stone fruit.

dormant_prune.text: Maintain the open-center vase: no central leader, 3 to 5 scaffolds, an open interior. Light and air through the canopy is the main brown rot control you have.
Work the three Ds first -- dead, diseased, damaged -- then thin to keep the open form. Stone fruit tolerates and rewards heavier annual pruning than pome fruit.

blossom.text: Stone fruit blooms ahead of apple, so spring frost risk is higher. Watch overnight forecasts and cover small trees with fleece on frost nights. Apricot is the earliest bloomer and the most frost-exposed.
Do not spray during bloom. Pollinators are working and the flower window is short.

fruit_set.text: Thin peach and nectarine to one fruit every 4 to 6 inches along the branch. Unthinned stone fruit stays small and the weight breaks limbs.
Plum and cherry usually self-thin reasonably well, but a heavy set is still worth thinning by hand to improve fruit size.

harvest.text: Stone fruit ripens fast and over a short window -- check daily during peak. Fruit should lift and twist free with a gentle motion; if it resists, leave it another day.
Pick into shallow containers to avoid bruising the fruit underneath. Stone fruit does not finish ripening off the tree the way pears do.

post_harvest.text: Remove every mummified fruit -- those leathery brown remnants on branches and ground are the spore source for next year's brown rot. This is the single most important post-harvest task on stone fruit.
Apply a potassium feed while leaves are still working. The feed goes into next year's flower buds, not this year's growth.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 30-50 lbs from a mature semi-standard tree
yield_expectations.peak_production: Full production hits around year 4 to 6 on standard rootstocks, year 3 to 4 on dwarfing stocks. A well-thinned mature stone-fruit tree produces a heavy crop over a 1 to 2 week harvest window.
yield_expectations.first_year_note: No fruit in year one. The tree puts everything into roots and scaffold structure. Remove any flowers that form -- they cost more in tree vigor than they return in fruit.
factors: open-vase pruning for sun and air
consistent water from pit-hardening through harvest

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

crops.hardiness_notes: Sweet cherries are among the fussiest stone fruits about climate. Traditional varieties thrive in zones 5-7 with dry summers and cold-but-not-frigid winters -- conditions found in the Pacific Northwest and inland California. In humid eastern zones, summer rain during ripening causes fruit cracking that ruins crops. In warmer zones (8+), most varieties fail to get enough chill hours (700-800) to break dormancy properly. Newer cold-hardy varieties (Kristin, Whitegold, BlackGold, Lapins) push the cold limit to zone 4 with reliable survival, though reliable fruit production remains marginal. Sweet cherries are self-sterile and typically require a pollination partner; self-fertile varieties (Stella, Lapins, Black Gold) are a relatively recent breeding achievement and are the practical choice for home growers with limited space. Sensitivity to summer heat above 95F and winter bud damage below -20F are both common. Trees typically begin bearing in year 4 and produce 30-50 quarts at maturity.

varieties_detail.notes: Cold-hardiest named sweet cherry, bred in Geneva NY and field-tested in Montana and Norway. Large dark-red fruit. Requires pollinator. Pick this for zone 4 or challenging continental climates.

Self-pollinating Canadian-bred Stella x Van cross. Large dark-red crack-resistant fruit. Late-ripening. One of the best all-around sweet cherries for home growers -- tolerates late frost and is hardier than Bing.

First self-fertile sweet cherry widely available. Dark red heart-shaped fruit. Acts as universal pollinator for many other sweet cherries including Bing. Cornell notes some cold-sensitivity in harsh winters.

Classic commercial sweet cherry and quality benchmark. Large firm dark-red fruit with superior flavor. Requires pollinator (Stella works well). Highly susceptible to rain-cracking and brown rot -- not recommended for humid eastern zones.
Low-chill cherry bred for warm climates where standard cherries fail to break dormancy. Medium-large red heart-shaped fruit. Requires Minnie Royal as pollinator. Makes cherries possible in zones 8-9.

crops.chill_hours_note: High chill requirement -- best in zones 5-7. Struggle in zones 8+

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost killed the blossom
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Stone fruit blooms before apple, often when frost is still common. A single hard frost during the brief bloom window can eliminate the year's crop. Apricot is the earliest-blooming and most frost-exposed -- in colder zones it can lose the crop most years.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Watch overnight forecasts through bloom and cover smaller trees with horticultural fleece on frost nights. In frost-prone sites, choose later-blooming varieties on your next planting -- apricot in particular has varieties selected for late bloom that ride out spring frost better.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Brown rot (Monilinia) is the headline disease on stone fruit -- it turns ripening fruit into soft brown lesions, then leathery mummies. Plum curculio leaves crescent-shaped scars on young fruit. Peach leaf curl distorts new leaves in spring. Cherry fruit fly maggots ruin cherries near harvest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Sanitation drives brown rot control: remove every mummified fruit from tree and ground at the end of the season. For peach leaf curl, a single dormant copper spray before bud-swell prevents the season's infection. Open-center pruning helps everything by drying the canopy faster after rain.

failure_diagnostics.label: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Pollination needs vary by stone fruit type. Peach, nectarine, and sour cherry are usually self-fertile and set fruit alone. Sweet cherry and many plums and apricots need a compatible second variety with overlapping bloom. A self-sterile tree alone will bloom heavily and set nothing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Check the pollination requirement of your variety before assuming poor weather. If a partner is needed, plant a compatible second variety within 100 feet -- a neighbor's tree counts if it is close enough. Bloom-time charts from extension publications help match pollinators.

failure_diagnostics.label: Root problems or waterlogging
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Stone fruit is unusually intolerant of wet feet. Trees in saturated soil show yellowing leaves, weak shoots, and gummy bark splits at the base (Phytophthora collar rot). Decline can be rapid -- a stone-fruit tree can fail in a single wet spring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Drainage is set at planting. On a wet site, plant the next tree on a 12-inch raised mound or move sites entirely. Stone fruit on its own roots tolerates wet less than pome fruit -- choose a Phytophthora-resistant rootstock if available.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Stone fruit needs 6 to 8 hours of direct sun to color, sweeten, and ripen evenly. In shade or in a crowded canopy, fruit stays small and pale and brown rot pressure increases because the canopy stays wet longer.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Maintain the open-center form with annual pruning -- this is more important on stone fruit than on any other tree fruit. Light and air through the canopy is both a yield driver and a disease control. Site new trees in full sun, away from buildings or larger trees that will shade them as they mature.

succession.reason: Perennial plant -- harvested seasonally year after year from the same crown.

tasks.description: Cut stalks to 8-10 inches after harvest season ends and after first frost. Mulch crowns with 4 inches of straw to protect through winter.
Divide clumps every 3-4 years in early spring. Replant offsets (suckers) 4 feet apart.

crops.year_one_notes: May produce a small harvest in year one from annual varieties. Perennial types fruit more heavily from year two.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Artichoke plume moth
pests.symptoms: Larvae tunnel into stems and buds. Wilting shoots. Entry holes in base.
pests.cause: Platyptilia carduidactyla moth. Western US pest.
pests.organic_treatment: Remove and destroy infested buds. Bt spray.
pests.prevention: Cut plants to ground level after harvest to remove overwintering sites.

diseases.name: Botrytis (gray mold)
diseases.symptoms: Gray fuzzy mold on leaves and buds in wet cool weather.
diseases.cause: Botrytis cinerea.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected tissue. Copper-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention: Good air circulation. Avoid overhead watering.

watering.frequency: Every 3-5 days -- heavy feeder and drinker

crops.harvest_ready: Cut bud when plump and tight, before scales begin to open. Size varies by position on plant -- central bud is largest.

start_method.notes: Start 8-10 weeks before last frost. Briefly expose to cold (vernalization) by putting near a window on cold nights -- this triggers better budding. Harden off over 7 days.

storage.fridge: 1 week in a bag with a few drops of water
storage.freezer: Blanch hearts, freeze -- good for cooking
storage.notes: Trim the stem end and spritz with water before refrigerating to keep fresh.

varieties.note: Imperial Star produces in year one if started early -- essential for zones 3-6 where artichokes are grown as annuals.

crops.soil_prep: Artichokes are heavy feeders. Dig in generous amounts of well-rotted manure or compost. They prefer a rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil. pH 6.5-7.5. In cold climates, raised beds help warm soil earlier.

container_notes.notes: Not practical in containers -- artichokes grow to 4-6 feet tall and wide. Ground planting only.

rotation.avoid_after: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note: Perennial herbs don't need annual rotation, but they can be divided and moved if needed. Choose a permanent-ish spot with the right sun and drainage; plan to divide every 3-4 years to keep plants vigorous.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Established plant or germinating seed.
growth_stages.user_action: Artichokes grown from seed are variable -- buy named variety plants for reliable results. Plant in a permanent spot with excellent drainage.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Large, deeply lobed silver-green leaves developing.
growth_stages.user_action: Water generously. Artichokes are large plants and heavy feeders -- they benefit from regular feeding with a balanced fertilizer.

growth_stages.name: Flower Buds Forming
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Tight, scaly buds forming at the top of stems.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest the central bud first and largest. Side buds follow -- they will be smaller but just as delicious.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Buds tight and firm before the scales begin to open. Once scales open the heart becomes fibrous.
growth_stages.user_action: Cut with 2-3 inches of stem. Cook immediately or store in water in the refrigerator for up to a week.

failure_diagnostics.label: Cold tolerance and dormancy
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: These three perennials handle winter cold differently. Asparagus is fully cold-hardy through zone 3, dies back to the ground each winter, and emerges from the crown each spring. Strawberry is cold-hardy through zone 3 with mulch, sometimes loses leaves but the crown survives. Artichoke is the cold-tender one -- hardy only to zone 7 reliably, often grown as an annual in colder zones. Late spring frost can damage emerging asparagus spears and strawberry blossoms.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: For asparagus, cover emerging spears with row cover during late spring frosts; damaged spears are tough and bitter. For strawberry, mulch heavily over the crowns before winter and uncover in early spring. For artichoke in zones 6 and below, grow as an annual or dig and overwinter the crown indoors. Hardy artichoke varieties (Imperial Star) survive zone 6 with heavy mulching.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Each of these crops has its own primary pest: asparagus beetle (both common and spotted) chews ferns and lays eggs on spears; spotted wing drosophila (SWD), slugs, and gray mold (Botrytis) are the headline strawberry problems; artichoke is generally low-pest but artichoke aphid clusters in the bracts and slugs damage tender new growth. Asparagus rust and Fusarium crown rot affect asparagus over time; strawberry is also vulnerable to verticillium wilt.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: For asparagus beetle, hand-pick adults and crush egg masses; in heavy infestations, neem or pyrethrin sprays in the cool of the day work. For SWD on strawberry, harvest ripe fruit promptly and clean up drops; row cover during fruit ripening helps. For artichoke aphid, hose off with water or use insecticidal soap. Choose disease-resistant strawberry varieties and renovate beds every 3 to 4 years.

failure_diagnostics.label: Crown rot or root rot
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: All three crops fail in waterlogged soil. Asparagus crowns rot in standing water -- a single wet season can kill an established bed. Strawberry crowns rot at the soil-stem interface in persistently wet conditions, and the fruit develops gray mold in damp weather. Artichoke is similarly intolerant of wet feet.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds. For asparagus, the bed is a multi-year commitment -- excellent drainage at planting prevents 20 years of disappointment. For strawberry, raised beds and straw mulch (the source of the name) keep fruit and crowns dry. For artichoke, mound up the planting site if drainage is marginal.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor establishment or poor yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress in the establishment year is the leading cause of failed asparagus and artichoke plantings. Strawberry tolerates short drought once established but fruit size and number drop substantially with water stress during fruiting. Asparagus that goes dry in summer produces fewer and smaller spears the following spring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water deeply through the establishment season for all three. Asparagus needs consistent moisture in summer (when it is feeding the crown for next year's spears) more than in spring (when it is producing spears from already-stored energy). Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture for all three.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor yield or weak growth
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: All three want full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to produce well. Shaded asparagus produces fewer and thinner spears; shaded strawberry produces small pale fruit with weak flavor; shaded artichoke grows leaves but produces few or no buds. These are not shade-tolerant crops.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun. Asparagus is a long-term commitment (15 to 20 years productive life), so the site choice matters more than for annual crops. For strawberry, full sun is also better for disease management because foliage dries faster after rain or dew.

crops.hardiness_notes: Perennial in Z7-Z11. In Z3-Z6 typically grown as an annual from transplants started early indoors, or mulched heavily to attempt overwintering (inconsistent results).

crops.name: Turnip
crops.description: One of the fastest root crops -- baby turnips in 35 days. Both root and greens are edible. Cool-season crop that tolerates light frost.

3.notes: Direct sow early. Two short seasons possible.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note: Direct seed cool-season root vegetables (carrots, beets, radishes, turnips) when soil reaches 40 degrees F, typically 2-4 weeks before last frost. (UMN Extension) Roots do not transplant -- their long taproots develop early and transplanting damages and misdirects root growth. In Minnesota, start planting carrots beginning April 15. (UMN Extension)

direct_sow.label: secondary
direct_sow.synthesis_note: Plant a fall crop when summer heat subsides, approximately 2-3 months before first fall frost. Fall-matured roots are sweeter due to cool-weather sugar accumulation. fertilizer.notes: Light feeder. Work a balanced fertilizer into the bed before sowing. No additional feeding needed.

succession.tip: Sow every 3 weeks from early spring and again from late summer. Turnips mature in 40-60 days and taste best pulled young and small. Like radishes, they're a quick-turnaround crop that benefits from small frequent sowings. The autumn succession is often the better season -- cool nights sweeten the flavor. Stop spring sowings when temperatures consistently exceed 75°F.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension 2022 and 2025 Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetable Crops; UConn IPM 'Perimeter Trap Cropping for Cole Crops'). Nasturtiums specifically are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and Utah State University Extension (Mohr et al., 'Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting'). Protocol caveat: UConn IPM explicitly notes trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents' -- so the aphid application here has a protocol-mismatch concern even though the companion is extension-named. The Cornell-IPM-specific attribution in earlier catalog reason text was not located in Cornell's published IPM material; actual backing is WSU/USU/UConn.

pests.name: Cabbage worm
pests.symptoms: Large irregular holes in leaves. Green caterpillars (1-1.5 inches) blending into foliage. White cabbage butterfly flying nearby is a warning sign.
pests.cause: Pieris rapae butterfly larvae. Lay eggs on leaf undersides.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick caterpillars and egg clusters. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray every 2 weeks. Row covers as barrier.
pests.prevention: Row covers from planting. White butterfly decoys (territorial behavior). Plant nasturtiums as trap crop.

pests.name: Cabbage aphid
pests.symptoms: Dense gray-green colonies on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl and pucker. Honeydew and sooty mold may follow.
pests.cause: Brevicoryne brassicae. Populations explode rapidly in cool weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Strong water blast. Insecticidal soap spray directly on colonies. Remove and compost heavily infested leaves.
pests.prevention: Avoid excess nitrogen. Encourage parasitic wasps with flowering herbs nearby.

pests.name: Flea beetle
pests.symptoms: Many tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings. Plants look peppered. Small shiny beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause: Multiple flea beetle species. Worst in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment: Row covers on seedlings. Diatomaceous earth. Kaolin clay spray.
pests.prevention: Delay planting. Use transplants. Interplant with aromatic herbs.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms: Plants wilt in hot weather despite watering. Stunted growth. Yellowing leaves. Roots are swollen, club-shaped, and deformed when dug up.
diseases.cause: Plasmodiophora brassicae soil pathogen. Survives in soil for up to 20 years. Thrives in acidic, wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure. Remove and destroy infected plants -- do not compost. Lime soil to raise pH to 7.0-7.2.
diseases.prevention: Minimum 7-year rotation away from brassicas in infected soil. Maintain soil pH above 6.5. Improve drainage.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms: Yellow patches on upper leaf surface with gray-purple fuzzy mold on undersides. Affects seedlings and mature plants.
diseases.cause: Peronospora brassicae fungus. Favored by cool moist conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Improve air circulation. Copper-based fungicide as preventive.
diseases.prevention: Avoid overhead watering. Space plants generously. Choose resistant varieties.

crops.harvest_ready: Pick roots at 2-3 inches -- any bigger and they get woody and peppery. Leaves can be harvested any time.

rotation.avoid_after: Kale, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, turnip, kohlrabi -- share clubroot and downy mildew
rotation.note: Clubroot can persist 20 years -- in infected soil extend to 7-year rotation.

storage.freezer: Cube, blanch, freeze -- good for soups and mash
storage.notes: Can be left in the ground through light frosts -- flavor improves with cold.

varieties.note: Hakurei is exceptional eaten raw -- sweet and crisp with no bitterness. Completely different from standard turnips.

thinning.method: Snip at soil level. Thinnings edible.
thinning.tip: Thinning is especially important for turnip -- they bulk up quickly and need the space.

container_notes.notes: Works in deep containers. 3-gallon minimum, 8 inches deep. Compact varieties like Tokyo Cross work well.

start_method.notes: Direct sow 4-6 weeks before last frost for spring, or in late summer. Fast-maturing -- no need to start indoors.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Thread-like shoots pushing up from the soil. Carrots and parsnips are notoriously slow -- do not give up.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep soil surface consistently moist -- the most common reason carrots fail is the surface drying out during the 2-3 week germination period. Lay a plank of wood over the row and check daily.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Feathery or distinctive first true leaves -- carrots look like tiny ferns, beetroot has deep red stems.
growth_stages.user_action: Thin seedlings carefully and promptly. Crowded root vegetables fork and stay small. Thin in stages -- once at 2 inches, again at 4 inches.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Strong leaf growth above ground. Roots are developing below -- resist the urge to dig and check.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep consistently watered -- irregular watering causes cracking and forking in root crops. Weed carefully to avoid disturbing roots.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Shoulders of root visible at soil surface, or reach the days to maturity for your variety. Test pull one before harvesting the row.
growth_stages.user_action: Water well before harvesting to loosen the soil. Pull at an angle rather than straight up to prevent snapping. Many root crops improve with frost.

growth_stages.name: In Storage
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Roots harvested and stored properly. Potatoes in a dark cool place. Carrots in damp sand.
growth_stages.user_action: Check stored roots monthly for any that are rotting -- one bad root can spread to others. Remove immediately.

notifications.title: Time to sow your root vegetables
notifications.body: Root vegetables go directly into the ground -- they do not transplant. Prepare your bed deeply, remove any stones that could cause forking, and sow thinly. Most root crops can go in 3-4 weeks before last frost.

notifications.title: Time to thin your root crops
notifications.body: Thinning is the most important thing you can do for root vegetables right now. Crowded roots fork and stay small. Thin to the recommended spacing -- eat the thinnings if they are big enough.

notifications.title: Your root vegetables should be approaching harvest
notifications.body: Do a test pull of one root before harvesting the row. Water the ground well first to loosen the soil. Most root crops can stay in the ground for several weeks after reaching full size -- they store well in situ.

notifications.title: Harvest before the ground freezes
notifications.body: Most root vegetables need to be out of the ground before it freezes solid. Carrots, parsnips, and beetroot can handle light frost -- it actually sweetens them. But harvest everything before a hard freeze locks them in.

notifications.title: Root check-in
notifications.body: Root vegetables mostly look after themselves once established, but it is worth checking for weeds and keeping the soil consistently moist. How are they looking above ground?

weather_triggers.title: Dry spell -- water your root crops consistently
weather_triggers.body: Irregular watering during root development causes carrots and parsnips to fork, beetroot to become woody, and potatoes to crack. Water deeply and consistently -- not a little every day but a good soak twice a week.

weather_triggers.title: Heavy rain -- check for waterlogging
weather_triggers.body: Root vegetables sitting in waterlogged soil can rot. Check drainage in your bed and consider harvesting any roots that are near maturity before they split from the rapid moisture uptake.

weather_triggers.title: Frost coming -- parsnips and carrots will thank you
weather_triggers.body: A light frost actually improves the flavor of carrots and parsnips by converting starch to sugar. Leave them in the ground through light frosts if you can. Potatoes and beetroot should be harvested before a hard frost.

germination.text: These crops are direct-sown -- transplanting damages the taproot and produces forked or stunted roots. Sow seeds shallowly (1/4 to 1/2 inch deep) and keep soil surface consistently moist for the 1 to 3 week germination window.
Carrot and parsnip seed is short-lived -- use fresh seed each year. Parsnip especially can take up to 3 weeks to germinate; do not give up early.

seedling.text: Thin to recommended spacing once seedlings have 2 true leaves -- crowded roots stay small and forked. Pull weaker seedlings rather than transplanting them.
Mulch lightly between rows once seedlings are established to suppress weeds. Hand-weed close to the row -- hoeing damages shallow seedling roots.

established.text: Water consistently. Uneven moisture causes carrot and parsnip roots to split as they swell during a wet period after dry conditions.
These crops feed lightly. Side-dress with compost mid-season if growth slows; avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers, which produce lush leafy tops at the expense of roots.

harvest.text: Harvest carrots, parsnips, beetroot, and turnips after the first frost for best flavor -- this is not folklore; the cold genuinely converts starch to sugar in the root. Parsnip especially needs frost exposure to develop its characteristic sweetness.

Loosen soil with a fork before pulling -- yanking by the tops snaps the root, especially on long carrots and parsnips. Cut tops off within an inch of the crown for storage; tops left on draw moisture out of the root.

storage.text: Store carrots, parsnips, beetroot, and turnips in layers of damp sand or sawdust in a cool location (32 to 40 degrees) at high humidity. Properly stored, these crops keep 4 to 6 months.

In zones with mild winters, you can leave the roots in the ground and harvest as needed -- mulch heavily over the row before the ground freezes. This is often easier than indoor storage and preserves quality longer.

yield_expectations.per_plant: One turnip per plant -- fast crop at 40-60 days
yield_expectations.peak_production: Best harvested young at golf ball size for best flavor
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Young turnips are sweet and delicious -- a world away from the woody, bitter specimens you might remember. Pick them small.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: These crops actively benefit from light to moderate frost -- it improves flavor by converting root starch to sugar. Damage from frost is rare and usually only happens to exposed leaf tops on a hard freeze; the roots are insulated by soil and survive even harsh winter conditions in many zones.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Time harvest to follow the first frost rather than precede it. In zones with mild winters, leave roots in the ground under heavy mulch and harvest as needed through winter.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Carrot rust fly (carrot, parsnip) is the headline pest -- larvae tunnel through roots leaving rusty trails. Cabbage maggot (turnip, sometimes beetroot) does similar damage to brassica roots. Leaf spot diseases and powdery mildew can hit foliage but rarely affect the root harvest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Floating row cover from sowing through harvest blocks both carrot rust fly and cabbage maggot -- this is the most effective home-garden defense. Rotate root crops to a new bed each year. Avoid planting carrot or parsnip after parsley or celery (same family, same pest).

failure_diagnostics.label: Cracked or rotten roots
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Uneven watering -- a dry spell followed by heavy water -- causes roots to split as they swell rapidly. Persistent waterlogging causes root rot, soft black tissue, and crown collapse. Beetroot and turnip handle wet soil better than carrot and parsnip, both of which need excellent drainage.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Maintain consistent moisture rather than letting soil dry out and then soaking it. On heavy clay, plant in a raised bed for carrot and parsnip especially. Mulch helps stabilize moisture.

failure_diagnostics.label: Small, woody, or strong-flavored roots
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought-stressed root crops produce small, fibrous roots with concentrated and often unpleasantly strong flavor. Parsnips become woody at the core; carrots become bitter; turnips become sharp; beetroot becomes earthy and tough.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water deeply and consistently -- 1 inch per week is the rough target. Mulch between rows to retain moisture. In hot weather, root crops appreciate light afternoon shade.

failure_diagnostics.label: Patchy germination
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Carrot, parsnip, and beetroot seeds need 1 to 3 weeks of consistent surface moisture to germinate. The most common reason for failed sowings is the soil surface drying out during germination -- not poor seed or bad soil. Parsnip seed in particular loses viability fast and old seed simply does not come up.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Sow into pre-moistened soil and cover with a board or burlap until the first seedlings emerge -- this keeps the surface consistently moist without daily watering. Use fresh parsnip seed each year. Pre-sprout difficult seed on damp paper towels indoors before sowing if needed.

fertilizer.notes: Heavy nitrogen feeder for long, thick stems. Feed monthly throughout the season.

succession.reason: Very long DTM (100-120 days) and single harvest. Not practical for succession planting.

pests.name: Onion fly
pests.symptoms: Plants wilt and die. White maggots at the base of bulb eating roots and inner leaves.
pests.cause: Delia antiqua fly. Lays eggs near onion seedlings in spring.
pests.organic_treatment: Insect mesh over bed. Remove and destroy affected plants.
pests.prevention: Grow under fine mesh. Rotate alliums every 3 years. Interplant with carrots -- mutual pest confusion.

pests.name: Thrips
pests.symptoms: Silver streaking and speckling on leaves. Stunted growth. Tiny yellow-brown insects visible.
pests.cause: Thrips tabaci. Worse in hot dry summers.
pests.organic_treatment: Neem oil spray. Insecticidal soap.
pests.prevention: Reflective mulch. Adequate watering in dry weather.

diseases.name: White rot
diseases.symptoms: Plants yellow and die. White fluffy growth at base with small black seed-like sclerotia. Roots and base rotted.
diseases.cause: Sclerotium cepivorum soil fungus. Persists in soil for 20+ years.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure. Remove all plant material. Do not replant alliums in infected soil.
diseases.prevention: Strict crop rotation. Buy allium seed sets from reputable sources.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms: Gray-purple fuzzy growth on leaves. Leaves yellow and collapse. Worst in wet cool springs.
diseases.cause: Peronospora destructor fungus.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Copper-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention: Avoid overhead watering. Space plants for airflow. Rotate crops.

crops.harvest_ready: Harvest at any size from pencil-thin. Pull when shaft is firm and white. Can leave in ground through winter.

start_method.notes: Start 10-12 weeks before transplant. Harden off over 7 days. Transplant into deep holes -- drop in and water, don't fill with soil. This blanches the stems.

rotation.avoid_after: Onions, garlic, leeks, shallots -- share white rot and onion fly
rotation.note: White rot can persist indefinitely in soil -- strict rotation is essential once present.

storage.freezer: Slice, blanch 1 minute, freeze -- good for soups and cooking
storage.notes: Leeks can be left in the ground through mild frosts as living storage.

varieties.note: Musselburgh is the standout variety for cold hardiness -- can be harvested through winter in zones 5-7.
