growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Cloves, sets, or seeds in the ground. No visible growth yet.
growth_stages.user_action: Plant garlic and onion sets pointed end up, just below the surface. For leeks, sow seeds in modules and transplant as pencil-thin seedlings.

growth_stages.name: Early Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Green shoots pushing up from sets or cloves. Slow growth initially -- alliums establish roots first.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep weed-free -- alliums are poor competitors with weeds, especially in early growth.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Strong upright leaves, healthy green color. Onions and garlic developing the bulb underground.
growth_stages.user_action: Stop feeding garlic and onions with nitrogen once the bulb starts forming -- it encourages leafy growth at the expense of the bulb.

growth_stages.name: Bulb Forming
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: For garlic: scapes curling upward on hardneck varieties. For onions: leaves beginning to yellow from the tips and fall over.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest garlic scapes when curled -- they are delicious and removing them redirects energy to the bulb. For onions, bending down any remaining upright leaves once half have fallen speeds final ripening.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Seeing scapes on garlic, or leaves beginning to fall?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Garlic: leaves 2/3 brown. Onions: all leaves yellow and fallen. Leeks: any size -- harvest young for mild flavor.
growth_stages.user_action: Lift carefully with a fork to avoid bruising. Cure in a warm, airy spot for 2-4 weeks before storing -- this is essential for long storage life.

growth_stages.name: Curing and Storage
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Skin papery and tight, neck dry and closed.
growth_stages.user_action: Hang or lay in a single layer in good airflow, out of direct rain, for 2-4 weeks. Garlic and onions not properly cured will not store well.

notifications.title: Time to plant your garlic
notifications.body: Garlic is planted in autumn and overwinters in the ground -- it needs a cold period to develop properly. Plant cloves now, pointed end up, 2 inches deep and 6 inches apart. You will not see much happen until spring, and that is exactly right.

notifications.title: Time to plant your onion sets
notifications.body: Onion sets can go in 3-4 weeks before last frost. Plant pointed end up with just the tip showing at the surface. They establish quickly and are more reliable than growing from seed.

notifications.title: Harvest your garlic scapes
notifications.body: Hardneck garlic sends up curled green shoots called scapes in early summer. Cut them off now -- they are delicious in stir fries and pestos, and removing them directs energy back into the bulb for a larger harvest.

notifications.title: Check your garlic for harvest readiness
notifications.body: When two thirds of the leaves have turned brown, your garlic is ready. Do not wait for all leaves to die -- the outer wrapper deteriorates. Lift carefully with a fork, do not pull by the stem, and handle gently to avoid bruising.

notifications.title: Cure your alliums properly -- it is worth it
notifications.body: Garlic and onions not properly cured will not store through winter. Hang or lay them in a single layer in a warm, airy space out of rain for 3-4 weeks. The necks should be completely dry before storage. This step makes the difference between 3-month storage and 6-month storage.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- watch for rust on your alliums
weather_triggers.body: Allium rust appears as orange powder on leaves in humid conditions. It weakens the plant but rarely kills it. Remove badly affected leaves and ensure good airflow. Rotate alliums to a different bed next year.

weather_triggers.title: Keep curing alliums dry
weather_triggers.body: Rain on curing garlic and onions undoes the drying process and encourages rot. Make sure they are under cover -- a shed, garage, or covered porch is ideal.

planting.text: Plant garlic in your best, most fertile bed. It is in the ground for 9 months -- give it good conditions from the start.
Save the largest cloves from each bulb for planting and eat the small ones. Larger cloves produce larger bulbs.

early_growth.text: Keep allium beds completely weed-free. Onions and garlic have poor, shallow root systems and are easily out-competed. Even small weeds reduce yields significantly.
No need to water garlic in autumn and winter -- rainfall is usually sufficient. Begin watering in spring if it is dry.

established.text: Stop feeding with nitrogen once bulbs start to form. High nitrogen at this stage produces soft, poorly-stored bulbs with thick necks.
Leeks can be earthed up as they grow to blanch the lower stem -- this gives you a longer white shaft and milder flavor.

bulb_forming.text: When onion leaves begin to yellow and fall over, stop watering. The plant is telling you it is finishing -- let it dry down naturally.
Do not bend onion tops manually until at least half the leaves have yellowed on their own. Bending them too early exposes the neck to disease.

harvest.text: Lift rather than pull. A garden fork under the bulb loosens the roots and prevents the stem tearing -- which exposes the bulb to rot during curing.
Harvest on a dry day and leave on top of the soil for a few hours before bringing in. The sun begins the drying process.

curing.text: Curing is the most important step most gardeners skip. 3-4 weeks in warm, airy conditions transforms a perishable vegetable into one that stores for 6-9 months.
Braid garlic and onions for storage if you have enough -- it looks beautiful and is functional. Store in a cool, dry, dark place.

yield_expectations.per_plant: One leek per plant -- sizeable at full growth
yield_expectations.peak_production: Leeks stand in the ground all winter and are harvested as needed
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Leeks are a genuinely useful winter vegetable. They store in the ground and you can harvest all winter as you need them.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Established alliums are among the hardiest vegetables and handle frost well. Garlic overwintering in the ground is designed for frost. Young onion seedlings are more vulnerable to late hard freezes.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Protect young onion sets if a hard freeze threatens in the first few weeks after planting. Established plants need no protection from ordinary frost.

failure_diagnostics.label: Allium rust or white rot
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Allium rust appears as orange powder on leaves in humid summers -- it weakens but rarely kills the plant. White rot is more serious: a soil-borne fungus that causes bulbs to rot at the base. Once white rot is in soil it persists for decades.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Rotate alliums to a new bed every year. White rot cannot be eliminated from infected soil -- grow alliums elsewhere if you see it. Rust is largely cosmetic -- harvest early and the bulbs are usually fine.

failure_diagnostics.label: Rotting bulbs
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Garlic and onion bulbs rot in waterlogged soil, especially during curing. Rain on curing alliums reverses the drying process and causes neck rot -- one of the most common storage failures.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Ensure excellent drainage. Cure garlic and onions under cover -- a shed or garage with good airflow. Even a few hours of rain on curing bulbs can significantly reduce storage life.

failure_diagnostics.label: Small bulbs
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Alliums that experience drought stress during bulb development produce small, tight bulbs. Irregular watering is a common cause of disappointing allium harvests.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently during bulb formation -- from spring until leaves begin to yellow. Stop watering completely once leaves start to die back naturally.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor bulb development
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Alliums need full sun for good bulb development. The bulbing trigger in onions and garlic is day length -- both need long days combined with warmth to form bulbs. In shade or under trees, they often produce only small, undeveloped bulbs.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant alliums in your sunniest, most open bed. Weed competition also significantly reduces yield -- keep allium beds completely weed-free from early spring.

crops.name: Brussels Sprouts
crops.description: The most patient brassica -- needs cold to form tight buttons. Flavor dramatically improves after frost. Definitely a fall crop.

3.notes: Start indoors. Choose 90-day varieties. Frost improves flavor.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Brussels sprouts are a long-season cool-weather crop (90-110 days from transplant). Cold-zone growers can produce a spring crop planted 4 weeks before last frost and a fall crop planted in June. Sprouts improve in flavor after light frost exposure; cold-hardy mature plants survive temperatures down to about 20 degrees F. (UMN Extension, Old Farmer's Almanac)

fertilizer.notify_message: Time to feed your Brussels sprouts

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension 2022 and 2025 Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetable Crops; UConn IPM 'Perimeter Trap Cropping for Cole Crops'). Nasturtiums specifically are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and Utah State University Extension (Mohr et al., 'Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting'). Protocol caveat: UConn IPM explicitly notes trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents' -- so the aphid application here has a protocol-mismatch concern even though the companion is extension-named. The Cornell-IPM-specific attribution in earlier catalog reason text was not located in Cornell's published IPM material; actual backing is WSU/USU/UConn.

pests.name: Cabbage worm
pests.symptoms: Large irregular holes in leaves. Green caterpillars (1-1.5 inches) blending into foliage. White cabbage butterfly flying nearby is a warning sign.
pests.cause: Pieris rapae butterfly larvae. Lay eggs on leaf undersides.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick caterpillars and egg clusters. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray every 2 weeks. Row covers as barrier.
pests.prevention: Row covers from planting. White butterfly decoys (territorial behavior). Plant nasturtiums as trap crop.

pests.name: Cabbage aphid
pests.symptoms: Dense gray-green colonies on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl and pucker. Honeydew and sooty mold may follow.
pests.cause: Brevicoryne brassicae. Populations explode rapidly in cool weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Strong water blast. Insecticidal soap spray directly on colonies. Remove and compost heavily infested leaves.
pests.prevention: Avoid excess nitrogen. Encourage parasitic wasps with flowering herbs nearby.

pests.name: Flea beetle
pests.symptoms: Many tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings. Plants look peppered. Small shiny beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause: Multiple flea beetle species. Worst in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment: Row covers on seedlings. Diatomaceous earth. Kaolin clay spray.
pests.prevention: Delay planting. Use transplants. Interplant with aromatic herbs.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms: Plants wilt in hot weather despite watering. Stunted growth. Yellowing leaves. Roots are swollen, club-shaped, and deformed when dug up.
diseases.cause: Plasmodiophora brassicae soil pathogen. Survives in soil for up to 20 years. Thrives in acidic, wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure. Remove and destroy infected plants -- do not compost. Lime soil to raise pH to 7.0-7.2.
diseases.prevention: Minimum 7-year rotation away from brassicas in infected soil. Maintain soil pH above 6.5. Improve drainage.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms: Yellow patches on upper leaf surface with gray-purple fuzzy mold on undersides. Affects seedlings and mature plants.
diseases.cause: Peronospora brassicae fungus. Favored by cool moist conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Improve air circulation. Copper-based fungicide as preventive.
diseases.prevention: Avoid overhead watering. Space plants generously. Choose resistant varieties.

crops.harvest_ready: Pick sprouts from the bottom up as they reach 1-1.5 inches. They should be tight and firm. Harvest after first frost for sweeter flavor.

start_method.notes: Start 6-8 weeks before transplant date. Brussels need a long season -- in zones 3-5, start early indoors.

rotation.avoid_after: Kale, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, turnip, kohlrabi -- share clubroot and downy mildew
rotation.note: Clubroot can persist 20 years -- in infected soil extend to 7-year rotation.

storage.fridge: 3-5 days on the stalk -- much longer than off
storage.freezer: Blanch 3-5 minutes depending on size, freeze -- excellent. Most commercial frozen sprouts are excellent quality.
storage.notes: Leave on the stalk in the fridge for longest shelf life. Freeze surplus immediately -- frozen sprouts are genuinely excellent.

varieties.note: Gustus is consistently rated for flavor -- less bitter than older varieties.

container_notes.notes: Possible in large containers. 5-gallon minimum, one plant per pot. Tall plants may need staking.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Round seed leaves pushing up cleanly. Brassicas germinate readily in cool, moist conditions.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep soil consistently moist at 60-70°F. Brassicas do not need heat -- they prefer cool germination.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: True leaves developing -- slightly waxy and blue-green in color.
growth_stages.user_action: Watch for damping off -- good airflow and not overwatering prevents it. Thin to one plant per cell.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Sturdy plants with multiple leaf sets, ready to go outside.
growth_stages.user_action: Harden off well before transplanting. Net immediately after planting to protect from cabbage white butterflies -- do not delay on this.

growth_stages.name: Head Forming
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Central head beginning to form. On broccoli, a tight green dome. On cauliflower, a white curd appearing in the center.
growth_stages.user_action: For cauliflower, tie the outer leaves over the developing curd to blanch it and keep it white. Do this as soon as the curd is visible.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Broccoli: tight green head before any yellow flowers open. Cauliflower: firm white curd at full size. Cabbage: firm, dense head that does not give when squeezed.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest broccoli with a long stem cut -- side shoots will continue producing for weeks. Cauliflower and cabbage are once-and-done harvests.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Harvest time -- how did it look?

notifications.title: Time to start your brassicas indoors
notifications.body: Broccoli, cauliflower, and cabbage need 6-8 weeks indoors before transplanting. Start now -- they grow slowly at first but reward the patience. Cool temperatures suit them perfectly.

notifications.title: Brassicas outside -- net them immediately
notifications.body: Cabbage white butterflies lay eggs on brassica leaves within hours of planting. Cover with fine mesh netting immediately after transplanting -- before you do anything else. Caterpillar damage can devastate an unprotected crop.

notifications.title: Cauliflower curd forming -- time to blanch
notifications.body: Tie a few outer leaves loosely over the developing curd now to protect it from light. This keeps the cauliflower white and tender. Check every few days -- once the curd is visible it develops quickly.

notifications.title: Check your broccoli heads
notifications.body: Broccoli heads that are ready to harvest look like tight green domes with no yellow showing. Once you see any flower buds opening it is past its best. Cut with a long stem and watch for side shoots to develop.

notifications.title: Start a fall brassica crop
notifications.body: Brassicas do well as a fall crop and often taste better -- frost sweetens cabbage and broccoli. Start seeds now for a crop that matures in the cooler autumn months.

notifications.title: How are your brassicas getting on?
notifications.body: Check under the netting for caterpillar damage -- they can strip a plant surprisingly fast. Also look at the developing head for any signs of bolting or discoloration.

weather_triggers.title: Heat stress -- brassicas may bolt
weather_triggers.body: Sustained high temperatures cause broccoli and cauliflower to bolt -- heads open into flowers before they are full size. Harvest anything that looks close to ready before the heat peaks.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- watch for clubroot and downy mildew
weather_triggers.body: Humid conditions favor several brassica diseases. Ensure good spacing and airflow. Check leaves for yellowing or powdery patches and remove affected material promptly.

weather_triggers.title: Late frost -- protect young brassicas
weather_triggers.body: Established brassicas handle frost well, but young transplants need protection for the first few weeks. Cover with fleece tonight.

germination.text: Brassicas are reliable germinators in cool conditions -- 60-70F is ideal. They do not need heat mats.
Sow into cells or modules rather than trays -- brassicas develop long tap roots and resent root disturbance.

seedling.text: Grow brassica seedlings in the coolest, brightest spot you have. Warmth makes them soft and leggy.
Feed with a dilute liquid feed once the first true leaves appear. Brassicas are hungry plants from the start.

established.text: Net immediately after transplanting. Cabbage white butterflies find brassicas within hours and lay clusters of yellow eggs on leaf undersides. Check the netting is secure all around -- one gap and caterpillars will find it.

Brussels sprouts are tall plants and the heaviest-laden brassica in the garden. Stake plants once they pass 18 inches; in exposed sites, hill soil up around the base to keep them upright through autumn winds.

head_forming.text: Sprouts form in the leaf axils starting from the bottom of the stalk and progressing upward over weeks. Tiny green knobs appearing where each leaf meets the stem is the cue.

Some growers top the plant -- pinching out the growing tip -- once the lowest sprouts are pea-sized. This redirects the plant's energy into evening up sprout size on a single stalk. It is optional; ungtopped plants produce a longer harvest window.

harvest.text: Harvest sprouts from the bottom of the stalk upward as each one reaches 1 to 1.5 inches across and is firm to the touch. Snap them off with a downward twist or cut with a knife. The plant continues maturing the upper sprouts for weeks.
Wait until after the first hard frost if you can -- frost converts starches to sugars and dramatically improves flavor. This is the single biggest variable in how good homegrown sprouts taste.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 50-100 sprouts per plant over the season
yield_expectations.peak_production: Brussels sprouts are harvested from the bottom up over several months
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Brussels sprouts are a long-season crop that demands patience. The reward is months of harvesting from one plant through autumn and winter.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Established brassicas handle frost well -- it actually sweetens them. But young transplants in their first 2-3 weeks are more vulnerable. A hard freeze can damage or kill recently transplanted seedlings.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Cover new transplants with fleece for the first 2-3 weeks after planting if frost is possible. Once established they are among the hardiest vegetables you can grow.

failure_diagnostics.label: Caterpillars or pests
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cabbage white butterflies lay eggs on brassica leaves and the caterpillars can strip a plant in days. This is by far the most common reason brassicas fail. If you did not net, this is almost certainly what happened.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Net immediately after transplanting -- before you do anything else. Fine mesh netting secured all the way around is the single most important thing you can do for brassicas. Check netting for gaps weekly.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too much water or clubroot
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Brassicas in waterlogged soil develop root problems. Clubroot -- a soil-borne disease -- causes swollen, distorted roots and wilting. Once present in soil it persists for many years.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Improve drainage before planting. If clubroot is suspected, rotate brassicas to a new bed and do not grow them in the affected soil for 4-5 years. Liming to raise soil pH above 7 discourages clubroot.

failure_diagnostics.label: Too little water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Brassicas need consistent moisture to develop good heads. Drought stress causes premature flowering in broccoli and cauliflower, and split heads in cabbage.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently and mulch around plants to retain moisture. A dry spell during head formation is the most damaging period.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor head development
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Cauliflower is the most demanding -- it needs consistent temperatures and care to form a good curd. Broccoli heads opening into yellow flowers usually means the temperature swung too warm. Both benefit from 6+ hours of sun.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Cauliflower in particular needs a consistent, cool growing environment. Autumn sowings often perform better than spring ones in warmer zones. Shade cloth can help in warm spells.

fertilizer.notes: Feed balanced fertilizer monthly. Switch to a lower-nitrogen, higher-potassium feed once plants start flowering for better pod production.
fertilizer.npk_hint: 10-10-10 -- switch to low N once flowering

succession.reason: Continuous-harvest crop that produces from a single planting all season. Succession isn't necessary.

pests.name: Corn earworm
pests.symptoms: Small round holes in pods, often near the tip. Inside the pod, a green, brown, or reddish striped caterpillar up to 1 3/4 inches long with scattered black spots. Frass (dark droppings) visible at entry holes.
pests.cause: Helicoverpa zea moth larvae, the same species also called tomato fruitworm. Multiple generations per season, heaviest pressure in mid to late summer.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick affected pods and destroy. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) to young pods at first sign of damage. Spinosad is effective on later instars.
pests.prevention: Scout pods twice a week during peak bloom. Harvest every 2-3 days so larvae have less time to develop inside pods. Till garden residue in fall to expose overwintering pupae.

pests.name: Stink bugs & leaffooted bugs
pests.symptoms: Pods curl, twist, or develop wart-like protrusions where bugs have fed. Small dimples or dark spots on pod surface. Shield-shaped stink bugs or narrow leaffooted bugs visible on plants, especially in morning.
pests.cause: Several species, including brown and green stink bugs and the leaffooted bug (Leptoglossus spp.). They pierce pods with needle-like mouthparts and suck sap, deforming developing tissue.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick adults and egg masses (look for barrel-shaped eggs in tight clusters on leaf undersides). Insecticidal soap knocks down nymphs but has little effect on hard-shelled adults.
pests.prevention: Clean up weedy borders and overwintering sites near the garden. Encourage predatory wasps and assassin bugs by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of small soft-bodied insects on new growth and undersides of leaves. Leaves may yellow or curl. Sticky honeydew followed by sooty black mold.
pests.cause: Cotton aphid (Aphis gossypii) is the most common species on okra. Populations build quickly in warm weather, especially on plants pushed with excess nitrogen.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with a strong water spray. Insecticidal soap or neem oil applied to the underside of leaves. Ladybugs and lacewings provide effective natural control.
pests.prevention: Avoid over-fertilizing with nitrogen, which produces soft growth that aphids favor. Interplant with flowering herbs to support beneficial insects.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms: Tiny round shot-holes in leaves, worst on seedlings and young plants. Small shiny black beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause: Several flea beetle species feed on okra foliage. Most active in spring on young plants; mature okra tolerates damage well.
pests.organic_treatment: Row covers until plants are established and flowering. Diatomaceous earth applied to dry foliage. Neem oil if damage is heavy on seedlings.
pests.prevention: Set out transplants rather than direct-seeding so plants pass through the vulnerable seedling stage indoors. Keep garden weed-free to reduce overwintering habitat.

diseases.name: Root-knot nematodes
diseases.symptoms: Stunted, yellowing plants that wilt in afternoon heat despite adequate water. Poor pod set. Pulling a plant reveals knotty galls and swellings on the roots -- the signature sign.
diseases.cause: Meloidogyne spp., microscopic soil-dwelling roundworms. UGA lists root-knot nematode as the most serious disease of okra. Sandy soils and warm climates favor the pest.
diseases.organic_treatment: No effective in-season chemical treatment for home gardeners. Remove and destroy infested plants including roots at end of season.
diseases.prevention: Rotate okra with non-host crops (corn, small grains, brassicas) for 2-3 years. Solarize infested beds in summer with clear plastic. Plant French marigolds (Tagetes patula) as a trap crop. Add compost to boost beneficial soil microbes.

diseases.name: Fusarium wilt
diseases.symptoms: Lower leaves yellow, wilt, and drop while upper foliage remains green initially. Vascular tissue inside stem shows brown streaking when cut. Whole plant collapse over 1-2 weeks.
diseases.cause: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. vasinfectum, a soil-borne fungus. UGA reports wilt pressure is much worse where root-knot nematodes are also present, since nematode feeding creates entry wounds.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure once a plant is infected. Remove and destroy affected plants; do not compost.
diseases.prevention: Long rotation (4+ years) out of okra and cotton. Control root-knot nematodes, which open the door for Fusarium. Keep soil pH above 6.0.

diseases.name: Southern stem blight
diseases.symptoms: Sudden wilting of an otherwise healthy plant. White cottony fungal growth at the soil line, often with small tan mustard-seed-shaped sclerotia. Lower stem becomes bleached and shredded.
diseases.cause: Sclerotium rolfsii, a soil fungus most active in hot humid weather. Overwinters as sclerotia in soil and crop debris for several years.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove infected plants with a trowel-deep perimeter of soil. Bag and discard; do not compost. No effective organic rescue treatment.
diseases.prevention: Rotate with grass crops for 3-4 years. Bury crop residue deeply or remove it. Avoid piling mulch against plant stems where the fungus thrives.

diseases.name: Anthracnose
diseases.symptoms: Sunken, water-soaked lesions on pods that turn dark and may show pinkish spore masses in humid weather. Pods become unmarketable. Leaf spots with tan centers and dark borders may also appear.
diseases.cause: Colletotrichum spp. fungus. Spreads by rain splash in warm wet weather. Overwinters on crop debris and seed.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected pods as soon as spots appear. Copper-based fungicide (labeled for okra) applied preventively during wet periods.
diseases.prevention: Use certified disease-free seed. Rotate out of okra for 2-3 years. Space plants for airflow and stake or thin if canopy becomes dense.

crops.harvest_ready: Pick at 3-4 inches, every 2 days. Larger pods become tough and fibrous very quickly. Thumbnail should pierce skin easily.

start_method.notes: Direct sow after last frost when soil is very warm (70°F+). Soak seeds 24 hours first. In zones 3-6, start indoors 3-4 weeks before in biodegradable pots.

storage.fridge: 3-5 days -- okra is sensitive to cold, ideal 45-50°F
storage.freezer: Slice or leave whole, blanch 3 minutes, freeze -- excellent
storage.notes: Okra stored too cold (below 45°F) develops brown spots. Use the warmest part of the fridge.

varieties.note: Clemson Spineless is the standard -- spineless pods are much easier to harvest than spiny types.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Pest-deterrent claim without matching established pattern. Default to traditional pending review.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. This claim's nematode component aligns with the extension-documented mechanism, but the 'concurrent companion' application pattern reflects popular gardening practice rather than extension protocol.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: 'Fennel suppresses neighbors' is a common gardening-book claim. Limited research; allelopathy is real but specific claim pattern is traditional.

container_notes.notes: Can be grown in containers. 5-gallon minimum. Compact varieties like Baby Bubba work best.

rotation.avoid_after: Other malva family plants
rotation.note: Few specific rotation concerns -- general 2-year rotation is sufficient.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Large seed leaves emerging. Okra germinates well in warm soil.
growth_stages.user_action: Nick or soak seeds overnight to speed germination. Soil must be 65°F+ -- okra refuses to germinate in cold soil.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Distinctive lobed leaves developing. Okra grows fast once warm.
growth_stages.user_action: Thin to 18 inches -- okra gets large. Water consistently.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Tall plants 2-3 feet, woody stems. Beautiful hibiscus-like flowers forming.
growth_stages.user_action: Feed with a balanced fertilizer. Okra is a hungry plant that keeps producing if well-fed.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Pods at 2-4 inches -- tender and snap-crisp when broken.
growth_stages.user_action: Pick every 2-3 days. Okra pods left past their prime become tough and woody in days. Wear gloves -- okra irritates skin.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Slowing pod production, woody stalks, nights cooling below 55 degrees F.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest any tender pods before first frost -- larger pods turn fibrous quickly. Cut down the woody stalks and chop or shred before composting; whole stalks can take a long time to break down.
growth_stages.log_prompt: How was your okra season? Worth logging what worked.

notifications.title: Time to plant your okra
notifications.body: Get your okra in the ground now. Prepare the soil well and water in after planting.

notifications.title: Check your okra for harvest
notifications.body: Your okra should be approaching harvest readiness now. Check the crop-specific signals and harvest at the right moment for best flavor.

notifications.title: How is your okra doing?
notifications.body: You have not logged anything in a while -- how is it looking?

germination.text: Okra needs warm soil to germinate -- 70 to 95 degrees, ideally 80+. Direct-sow after soil is reliably 70 degrees and last frost is 2 to 3 weeks past. Okra is one of the most heat-loving common vegetables.
Soak seeds in water for 12 to 24 hours before sowing to soften the hard seed coat. Sow 1/2 to 1 inch deep, 4 to 6 inches apart in rows 3 feet apart. Germination takes 7 to 14 days in warm soil.

seedling.text: Thin seedlings to 12 to 18 inches apart once they have 2 to 3 true leaves. Crowded okra produces fewer pods.
Okra seedlings tolerate heat that would stress most vegetables. They do not, however, tolerate cool weather -- nights below 60 degrees substantially slow growth.

established.text: Okra grows rapidly in heat -- plants reach 4 to 8 feet tall by midsummer in warm climates. The taller varieties may benefit from staking in windy sites.
Water deeply once a week and mulch to retain soil moisture. Side-dress with compost or balanced fertilizer at first flowering. Okra is moderately heavy-feeding but not as demanding as cucurbits.

harvest.text: Pick okra pods at 2 to 4 inches long -- larger pods become woody and tough almost overnight. Daily picking during peak production is essential; pods left to mature signal the plant to stop producing.

Wear long sleeves and gloves -- okra leaves and stems carry fine spines that cause skin irritation in some people. Cut pods cleanly with a knife or pruners; the stems are tough and pulling damages the plant.

end_of_season.text: Okra production drops as nights cool below 60 degrees. Plants are killed by light frost. Harvest all usable pods before first expected frost.
Pull and compost spent plants. Rotate to a new bed each year -- okra has fewer rotation concerns than most crops because it shares few pests with common vegetables.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 30-50 pods per plant over the season
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Okra is easy and prolific in warm climates. In cooler zones, choose the shortest-season varieties.
yield_expectations.peak_production: Mid-to-late summer is the heavy run -- pods size up fast in heat, and a productive plant gives a handful every 1 to 2 days at peak.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost or cool-weather damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Okra is a tropical-origin heat lover -- damaged at any stage by cold and killed by light frost. Cold soil at sowing (below 70 degrees) rots seed before germination. Cool nights below 60 degrees stunt growth severely; okra is a rare crop where cool weather, not frost, is often the limiting factor in marginal zones.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Wait to direct-sow until soil reaches 70 degrees minimum and night temperatures stay above 60. In cooler zones, start transplants indoors 4 to 6 weeks before last frost (use peat pots to minimize root disturbance) and use black plastic mulch outdoors. Choose short-season varieties (Clemson Spineless at 55 days) for cool-summer regions.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Okra has fewer serious pests than most vegetables. Flea beetles, aphids, and stink bugs are the headline pests; corn earworm occasionally bores into pods. Root-knot nematodes damage roots in sandy southern soils. Southern stem blight, anthracnose, and powdery mildew are the main diseases.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Hose off aphids; tolerate moderate flea beetle damage on established plants. For root-knot nematodes, rotate okra with crops that do not host the pest (most legumes, brassicas). Choose disease-resistant varieties for southern gardens. Okra's relatively short pest list is one of its appeals.

failure_diagnostics.label: Root rot or fungal issues
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Persistent waterlogging causes root rot -- rare in established okra because the deep taproot tolerates moderate drought, but young plants in heavy clay can drown. Wet foliage drives powdery mildew and bacterial blight in humid summers.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil. Water at the base, not overhead, and water early in the day so foliage dries before evening. In heavy clay or wet sites, plant in raised beds. Established okra tolerates dry conditions well; do not overwater.

failure_diagnostics.label: Slow growth or small pods
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Okra is more drought-tolerant than most warm-season vegetables but produces smaller, tougher pods under severe drought stress. Yields drop substantially when plants are water-stressed during flowering and pod development.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water deeply once a week -- 1 inch minimum, more in heat. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture and reduce evaporation. Okra's deep taproot makes it more drought-tolerant than shallow-rooted crops, but consistent water still produces best yields.

failure_diagnostics.label: Tall thin plants with few pods
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Okra needs full sun -- 8 hours minimum -- and serious heat to flower and fruit well. In partial shade plants grow tall and leafy but produce few flowers and pods. Okra is a hot-sun, hot-soil, hot-air crop; cool partial-shade conditions are the wrong environment.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in the sunniest, hottest spot available. South-facing exposure or near a heat-reflecting wall is ideal in marginal zones. In cool-summer climates, accept that okra is not the right crop and grow cool-season vegetables instead.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Peachtree borer
pests.symptoms: Gummy, amber-colored sap mixed with sawdust at base of trunk near soil line. Weakened, declining tree.
pests.cause: Synanthedon exitiosa clear-wing moth larvae. Bore into trunk near soil.
pests.organic_treatment: Dig out larvae by hand in autumn. Apply beneficial nematodes around trunk base in autumn.
pests.prevention: Keep base of trunk clear of mulch and debris. Apply pyrethrin spray to trunk base in early September.

diseases.name: Brown rot
diseases.symptoms: Brown soft spots on ripening fruit, rapidly expanding. Fuzzy gray-brown spore masses develop. Fruit mummifies on tree.
diseases.cause: Monilinia fructicola/laxa fungus. Spreads rapidly in warm humid conditions near harvest.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove and destroy all affected fruit immediately -- do not compost. Apply sulfur fungicide preventively near harvest.
diseases.prevention: Remove mummified fruit from tree and ground. Improve air circulation with pruning. Avoid fruit injury.

diseases.name: Black knot
diseases.symptoms: Hard black galls/swellings on branches and twigs. Galls enlarge each year. Severe infection kills branches.
diseases.cause: Apiosporina morbosa fungus. Affects plum, cherry, and related stone fruits.
diseases.organic_treatment: Prune out knots 4 inches below visible growth in winter. Destroy -- do not compost.
diseases.prevention: Remove wild plum/cherry trees nearby. Annual inspection and removal of small knots.

crops.harvest_ready: Background yellow, slight give at stem end, easy detachment. Similar to peach but firmer at pick.

storage.room_temp: Ripen on counter, then use immediately
storage.freezer: Peel, slice, freeze flat then bag -- excellent
storage.notes: Same as peach -- ripen at room temperature, refrigerate only when fully soft.

varieties.note: Mericrest is the most cold-hardy nectarine -- reliable in zones where most nectarines struggle.

start_method.notes: Plant bare-root trees in late winter/early spring while dormant. Container trees can go in spring through early autumn. Stake against wind for the first 2 years.

container_notes.notes: Fruit trees need to be grown in the ground. Dwarf varieties on very dwarfing rootstocks can be tried in very large (30+ gallon) containers but are challenging and rarely as productive.

rotation.avoid_after: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Bare-root or potted tree just planted. Base of the trunk right at soil level, and the graft union -- the knobby joint where the variety was grafted onto the rootstock -- sits 2 to 4 inches above the ground.
growth_stages.user_action: Dig the hole twice as wide as the roots and the same depth. Spread the roots over a small mound in the bottom of the hole. Stake firmly against wind. Don't add fertilizer to the planting hole. Water in deeply.

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: First leaves breaking from the dormant branches. New shoot tips extending. The tree is putting almost everything into root growth.
growth_stages.user_action: Water deeply once a week through the first summer. Pinch off any flowers that form -- year-one fruit costs the tree more strength than it returns. Keep weeds and grass cleared 2 to 3 feet around the trunk.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Strong shoot extension from the trunk. The first major side branches are starting to take shape.
growth_stages.user_action: Stone fruit trees are trained to an open-vase form: 3 to 5 main branches angled outward at roughly 45 degrees, evenly spaced around the trunk, with no central leader. Pick those 3 to 5 main branches and remove everything else cleanly back to the trunk. Use branch spreaders (small props that hold a branch at a wider angle) or hanging weights so the chosen branches stay angled outward as they grow.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Leaves fully dropped, buds tight on the stems. The tree is in true winter dormancy.
growth_stages.user_action: First-year dormancy is a holding period -- the work happens later. Mulch heavily around the base before hard freeze. Wrap the trunk in young-tree wrap to prevent sunscald and rodent damage. Major pruning waits until late winter (the next stage).
growth_stages.log_prompt: Tree wrapped and mulched for winter?

growth_stages.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Tree fully dormant; buds tight; late winter into early spring.
growth_stages.user_action: Maintain an open-center (vase) form: 3 to 5 main scaffold branches angled outward from a short trunk, with no central leader. Stone fruit needs sun and air movement through the canopy. Remove dead, diseased, damaged wood, then anything growing inward.

growth_stages.name: Blossom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Pink or white bloom opening. Apricot is earliest and most frost-exposed.
growth_stages.user_action: Watch overnight temperatures closely -- stone fruit blooms ahead of apple. Cover smaller trees with fleece on frost nights. Avoid sprays while pollinators are active.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Petal fall complete; small green fruitlets visible. A natural drop reduces the load in late spring.
growth_stages.user_action: Thin to one fruit every 4 to 6 inches on the branch (peach and nectarine especially). Stone fruit overload makes the fruit small and breaks branches.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Background color shift complete (yellow on peach/nectarine; full color on plum/cherry); fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure.
growth_stages.user_action: Pick when fruit lifts and twists free with a gentle motion -- forced fruit is not yet ripe. Stone fruit ripens fast and over a short window; check daily during peak.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest Sanitation
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Mummified fruit hanging on tree or fallen below; leaves yellowing.
growth_stages.user_action: Remove every mummified fruit from the tree and the ground -- these are the brown rot spore source for next year. Apply a potassium feed after harvest while leaves are still working.

notifications.title: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text: Set the graft union a few inches above final soil level. Burying it lets the scion root and you lose the dwarfing rootstock effect.
Stake securely for the first two seasons. Drive the stake into the hole before the tree goes in to avoid root damage later.

establishment.text: Water deeply once a week through the first growing season. Roots are still inside the original root ball and dry out quickly.
Mulch a 3-foot circle around the trunk to hold moisture. Keep mulch a few inches clear of the trunk to prevent collar rot.

first_growth.text: Stone fruit trains to an open-center form, not a central leader. Choose 3 to 5 scaffolds angled outward from a short trunk and remove the central leader once the scaffolds are set.
Wide-angled scaffolds are stronger and let light into the interior. Use spreaders or weights to set the angle in the first two seasons.

dormancy.text: First dormancy is when you commit to the open-center form. Stand back and look at the structure before you cut.
Make clean cuts just above an outward-facing bud. Ragged stubs invite disease, especially Cytospora canker on stone fruit.

dormant_prune.text: Maintain the open-center vase: no central leader, 3 to 5 scaffolds, an open interior. Light and air through the canopy is the main brown rot control you have.
Work the three Ds first -- dead, diseased, damaged -- then thin to keep the open form. Stone fruit tolerates and rewards heavier annual pruning than pome fruit.

blossom.text: Stone fruit blooms ahead of apple, so spring frost risk is higher. Watch overnight forecasts and cover small trees with fleece on frost nights. Apricot is the earliest bloomer and the most frost-exposed.
Do not spray during bloom. Pollinators are working and the flower window is short.

fruit_set.text: Thin peach and nectarine to one fruit every 4 to 6 inches along the branch. Unthinned stone fruit stays small and the weight breaks limbs.
Plum and cherry usually self-thin reasonably well, but a heavy set is still worth thinning by hand to improve fruit size.

harvest.text: Stone fruit ripens fast and over a short window -- check daily during peak. Fruit should lift and twist free with a gentle motion; if it resists, leave it another day.
Pick into shallow containers to avoid bruising the fruit underneath. Stone fruit does not finish ripening off the tree the way pears do.

post_harvest.text: Remove every mummified fruit -- those leathery brown remnants on branches and ground are the spore source for next year's brown rot. This is the single most important post-harvest task on stone fruit.
Apply a potassium feed while leaves are still working. The feed goes into next year's flower buds, not this year's growth.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 120-150 lbs from a mature standard tree (peach-equivalent yield -- same species)
yield_expectations.peak_production: Full production hits around year 4 to 6 on standard rootstocks, year 3 to 4 on dwarfing stocks. A well-thinned mature stone-fruit tree produces a heavy crop over a 1 to 2 week harvest window.
yield_expectations.first_year_note: No fruit in year one. The tree puts everything into roots and scaffold structure. Remove any flowers that form -- they cost more in tree vigor than they return in fruit.
factors: open-vase pruning for sun and air
consistent water from pit-hardening through harvest

crops.hardiness_notes: Nectarines are genetically identical to peaches -- the difference is a single recessive gene that produces smooth skin instead of fuzzy skin. Hardiness and chill hour requirements are essentially the same as peach (generally zones 5-9). However, nectarines are notably more disease-prone than peaches because the smooth skin lacks the protective fuzz that deters fungal pathogens and insects. Brown rot, bacterial spot, and peach leaf curl are all more severe on nectarines, which makes reliable fruit production in humid eastern zones harder than for peaches. The same early-spring bloom risks apply -- fruit buds suffer damage at -13F and meaningful loss at -18F. In warm climates (zones 8b+), low-chill varieties (Arctic Star, Desert Delight, Sunraycer) under 300 chill hours are required. Miniature varieties (Stark HoneyGlo, Garden Delight) stay under 6 feet, making nectarines practical for containers or small gardens. Self-fertile; no pollinator required.

varieties_detail.notes: Canadian-bred cold-hardy nectarine from Ontario, hardy to -30F. Disease-resistant to brown rot and bacterial spot -- the top choice for humid eastern zones where other nectarines fail. Medium-sized freestone yellow fruit. Self-pollinating. Ripens August.
Cold-hardy New Hampshire-bred nectarine. Large red-skinned freestone fruit with yellow flesh. Self-pollinating. One of the more reliable nectarines for zones 5-6 growers.

Large freestone with deep red skin and yellow flesh. Crack-resistant with good shelf life. Cold-hardy buds reduce spring frost crop losses. Self-pollinating. Widely available and popular for home orchards.

The flavor benchmark among nectarines -- classic high-acid, high-sugar profile. Large yellow freestone with red blush. Self-pollinating. Adaptable across a wide range of conditions. Best mid-range choice for zones 6-8.

Low-chill white-fleshed nectarine for warm climates. Large fruit with dark red skin and crisp, sweet white flesh. Self-pollinating. Early ripening. Makes nectarines possible in zones 8-9 where standard varieties fail.

crops.chill_hours_note: Low-chill varieties available -- check variety before purchasing for warm zones

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost killed the blossom
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Stone fruit blooms before apple, often when frost is still common. A single hard frost during the brief bloom window can eliminate the year's crop. Apricot is the earliest-blooming and most frost-exposed -- in colder zones it can lose the crop most years.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Watch overnight forecasts through bloom and cover smaller trees with horticultural fleece on frost nights. In frost-prone sites, choose later-blooming varieties on your next planting -- apricot in particular has varieties selected for late bloom that ride out spring frost better.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Brown rot (Monilinia) is the headline disease on stone fruit -- it turns ripening fruit into soft brown lesions, then leathery mummies. Plum curculio leaves crescent-shaped scars on young fruit. Peach leaf curl distorts new leaves in spring. Cherry fruit fly maggots ruin cherries near harvest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Sanitation drives brown rot control: remove every mummified fruit from tree and ground at the end of the season. For peach leaf curl, a single dormant copper spray before bud-swell prevents the season's infection. Open-center pruning helps everything by drying the canopy faster after rain.

failure_diagnostics.label: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Pollination needs vary by stone fruit type. Peach, nectarine, and sour cherry are usually self-fertile and set fruit alone. Sweet cherry and many plums and apricots need a compatible second variety with overlapping bloom. A self-sterile tree alone will bloom heavily and set nothing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Check the pollination requirement of your variety before assuming poor weather. If a partner is needed, plant a compatible second variety within 100 feet -- a neighbor's tree counts if it is close enough. Bloom-time charts from extension publications help match pollinators.

failure_diagnostics.label: Root problems or waterlogging
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Stone fruit is unusually intolerant of wet feet. Trees in saturated soil show yellowing leaves, weak shoots, and gummy bark splits at the base (Phytophthora collar rot). Decline can be rapid -- a stone-fruit tree can fail in a single wet spring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Drainage is set at planting. On a wet site, plant the next tree on a 12-inch raised mound or move sites entirely. Stone fruit on its own roots tolerates wet less than pome fruit -- choose a Phytophthora-resistant rootstock if available.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Stone fruit needs 6 to 8 hours of direct sun to color, sweeten, and ripen evenly. In shade or in a crowded canopy, fruit stays small and pale and brown rot pressure increases because the canopy stays wet longer.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Maintain the open-center form with annual pruning -- this is more important on stone fruit than on any other tree fruit. Light and air through the canopy is both a yield driver and a disease control. Site new trees in full sun, away from buildings or larger trees that will shade them as they mature.

provenance.reason: Pollinator category is mechanistically grounded. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.reason: Soil-category claim has a mechanistic basis. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Allium sulfur-based volatile organic compounds have documented aphid-repellent effects (Durenne and Gosset, 'Companion Plants for Aphid Pest Management,' Insects 2018, 9(4):112). The companion application is described by several extensions at home-gardening rigor: Mississippi State University Extension ('Companion planting improves gardens,' Snyder via Reeves) explicitly states 'Chives tend to repel aphids'; Utah State University Extension ('Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting,' Mohr et al.) lists onions, garlic, and chives as repelling common garden pests; UC Cooperative Extension Master Gardener publications (Butte County 'Best Friends in the Garden' and Fresno County 'Winter companion planting to repel insects') likewise list allium VOCs among aphid-repellent companions. These extension sources describe the pairing at tradition-plus-plausible-mechanism rigor rather than validated protocol -- the Kansas State Extension / Johnson County 'Companion Planting' page caveats that allium sulfur repellency is 'centralized to the garlic itself -- and only with certain pests.' The earlier catalog attribution to 'UC IPM' does not match UC IPM's Pest Notes on aphids (pn7404), which focus on reflective mulches, water sprays, soaps, and natural enemies rather than allium interplanting.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Bad companion claim, no pattern match. Default to traditional pending review.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Peachtree borer
pests.symptoms: Gummy, amber-colored sap mixed with sawdust at base of trunk near soil line. Weakened, declining tree.
pests.cause: Synanthedon exitiosa clear-wing moth larvae. Bore into trunk near soil.
pests.organic_treatment: Dig out larvae by hand in autumn. Apply beneficial nematodes around trunk base in autumn.
pests.prevention: Keep base of trunk clear of mulch and debris. Apply pyrethrin spray to trunk base in early September.

diseases.name: Brown rot
diseases.symptoms: Brown soft spots on ripening fruit, rapidly expanding. Fuzzy gray-brown spore masses develop. Fruit mummifies on tree.
diseases.cause: Monilinia fructicola/laxa fungus. Spreads rapidly in warm humid conditions near harvest.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove and destroy all affected fruit immediately -- do not compost. Apply sulfur fungicide preventively near harvest.
diseases.prevention: Remove mummified fruit from tree and ground. Improve air circulation with pruning. Avoid fruit injury.

diseases.name: Black knot
diseases.symptoms: Hard black galls/swellings on branches and twigs. Galls enlarge each year. Severe infection kills branches.
diseases.cause: Apiosporina morbosa fungus. Affects plum, cherry, and related stone fruits.
diseases.organic_treatment: Prune out knots 4 inches below visible growth in winter. Destroy -- do not compost.
diseases.prevention: Remove wild plum/cherry trees nearby. Annual inspection and removal of small knots.

crops.harvest_ready: Bright red, tart flavor when tasted. Good indicator is color -- leave longer for less acidity.

storage.freezer: Freeze on a tray then bag -- excellent, and essential since crop comes all at once
storage.notes: Sour cherries are almost never eaten fresh -- freeze or process immediately after picking.

varieties.note: Meteor and North Star are genetic dwarfs -- 8-10 feet, fully self-fertile, and very cold-hardy. Perfect for small gardens.

start_method.notes: Plant bare-root trees in late winter/early spring while dormant. Container trees can go in spring through early autumn. Stake against wind for the first 2 years.

container_notes.notes: Fruit trees need to be grown in the ground. Dwarf varieties on very dwarfing rootstocks can be tried in very large (30+ gallon) containers but are challenging and rarely as productive.

rotation.avoid_after: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Bare-root or potted tree just planted. Base of the trunk right at soil level, and the graft union -- the knobby joint where the variety was grafted onto the rootstock -- sits 2 to 4 inches above the ground.
growth_stages.user_action: Dig the hole twice as wide as the roots and the same depth. Spread the roots over a small mound in the bottom of the hole. Stake firmly against wind. Don't add fertilizer to the planting hole. Water in deeply.

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: First leaves breaking from the dormant branches. New shoot tips extending. The tree is putting almost everything into root growth.
growth_stages.user_action: Water deeply once a week through the first summer. Pinch off any flowers that form -- year-one fruit costs the tree more strength than it returns. Keep weeds and grass cleared 2 to 3 feet around the trunk.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Strong shoot extension from the trunk. The first major side branches are starting to take shape.
growth_stages.user_action: Stone fruit trees are trained to an open-vase form: 3 to 5 main branches angled outward at roughly 45 degrees, evenly spaced around the trunk, with no central leader. Pick those 3 to 5 main branches and remove everything else cleanly back to the trunk. Use branch spreaders (small props that hold a branch at a wider angle) or hanging weights so the chosen branches stay angled outward as they grow.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Leaves fully dropped, buds tight on the stems. The tree is in true winter dormancy.
growth_stages.user_action: First-year dormancy is a holding period -- the work happens later. Mulch heavily around the base before hard freeze. Wrap the trunk in young-tree wrap to prevent sunscald and rodent damage. Major pruning waits until late winter (the next stage).
growth_stages.log_prompt: Tree wrapped and mulched for winter?

growth_stages.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Tree fully dormant; buds tight; late winter into early spring.
growth_stages.user_action: Maintain an open-center (vase) form: 3 to 5 main scaffold branches angled outward from a short trunk, with no central leader. Stone fruit needs sun and air movement through the canopy. Remove dead, diseased, damaged wood, then anything growing inward.

growth_stages.name: Blossom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Pink or white bloom opening. Apricot is earliest and most frost-exposed.
growth_stages.user_action: Watch overnight temperatures closely -- stone fruit blooms ahead of apple. Cover smaller trees with fleece on frost nights. Avoid sprays while pollinators are active.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Petal fall complete; small green fruitlets visible. A natural drop reduces the load in late spring.
growth_stages.user_action: Thin to one fruit every 4 to 6 inches on the branch (peach and nectarine especially). Stone fruit overload makes the fruit small and breaks branches.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Background color shift complete (yellow on peach/nectarine; full color on plum/cherry); fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure.
growth_stages.user_action: Pick when fruit lifts and twists free with a gentle motion -- forced fruit is not yet ripe. Stone fruit ripens fast and over a short window; check daily during peak.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest Sanitation
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Mummified fruit hanging on tree or fallen below; leaves yellowing.
growth_stages.user_action: Remove every mummified fruit from the tree and the ground -- these are the brown rot spore source for next year. Apply a potassium feed after harvest while leaves are still working.

notifications.title: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text: Set the graft union a few inches above final soil level. Burying it lets the scion root and you lose the dwarfing rootstock effect.
Stake securely for the first two seasons. Drive the stake into the hole before the tree goes in to avoid root damage later.

establishment.text: Water deeply once a week through the first growing season. Roots are still inside the original root ball and dry out quickly.
Mulch a 3-foot circle around the trunk to hold moisture. Keep mulch a few inches clear of the trunk to prevent collar rot.

first_growth.text: Stone fruit trains to an open-center form, not a central leader. Choose 3 to 5 scaffolds angled outward from a short trunk and remove the central leader once the scaffolds are set.
Wide-angled scaffolds are stronger and let light into the interior. Use spreaders or weights to set the angle in the first two seasons.

dormancy.text: First dormancy is when you commit to the open-center form. Stand back and look at the structure before you cut.
Make clean cuts just above an outward-facing bud. Ragged stubs invite disease, especially Cytospora canker on stone fruit.

dormant_prune.text: Maintain the open-center vase: no central leader, 3 to 5 scaffolds, an open interior. Light and air through the canopy is the main brown rot control you have.
Work the three Ds first -- dead, diseased, damaged -- then thin to keep the open form. Stone fruit tolerates and rewards heavier annual pruning than pome fruit.

blossom.text: Stone fruit blooms ahead of apple, so spring frost risk is higher. Watch overnight forecasts and cover small trees with fleece on frost nights. Apricot is the earliest bloomer and the most frost-exposed.
Do not spray during bloom. Pollinators are working and the flower window is short.

fruit_set.text: Thin peach and nectarine to one fruit every 4 to 6 inches along the branch. Unthinned stone fruit stays small and the weight breaks limbs.
Plum and cherry usually self-thin reasonably well, but a heavy set is still worth thinning by hand to improve fruit size.

harvest.text: Stone fruit ripens fast and over a short window -- check daily during peak. Fruit should lift and twist free with a gentle motion; if it resists, leave it another day.
Pick into shallow containers to avoid bruising the fruit underneath. Stone fruit does not finish ripening off the tree the way pears do.

post_harvest.text: Remove every mummified fruit -- those leathery brown remnants on branches and ground are the spore source for next year's brown rot. This is the single most important post-harvest task on stone fruit.
Apply a potassium feed while leaves are still working. The feed goes into next year's flower buds, not this year's growth.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 20-40 lbs from a mature semi-standard tree -- lower than sweet cherry but reliably self-fertile
yield_expectations.peak_production: Full production hits around year 4 to 6 on standard rootstocks, year 3 to 4 on dwarfing stocks. A well-thinned mature stone-fruit tree produces a heavy crop over a 1 to 2 week harvest window.
yield_expectations.first_year_note: No fruit in year one. The tree puts everything into roots and scaffold structure. Remove any flowers that form -- they cost more in tree vigor than they return in fruit.
factors: open-vase pruning for sun and air
consistent water from pit-hardening through harvest
