crops.hardiness_notes: Sour cherries (also called tart or pie cherries) are dramatically more forgiving than sweet cherries. They are genuinely cold-hardy to zone 4, self-fertile, bloom late enough to escape most spring frosts, and tolerate a wider range of soils. Sour cherries are the practical choice for home growers in challenging climates where sweet cherries struggle. The tradeoff is that the fruit is too acidic for most fresh eating -- sour cherries shine in pies, preserves, juice, and dried applications. In warm climates (zones 8+), sour cherries have the same chill hour limits as sweet cherries (700-1,200 hours) and fail to break dormancy. Dwarf varieties (North Star, Meteor, Romeo, Juliet) stay under 10 feet tall, making sour cherries genuinely practical for small gardens where sweet cherries would overwhelm the space. Trees begin bearing in year 3-4 and can produce 30-50 quarts at maturity.

varieties_detail.notes: The gold standard sour cherry -- accounts for 95% of US commercial tart cherry production. Bright red fruit with yellow flesh and clear juice. Self-fertile. Medium-sized tree (15-20 feet). Named for the Montmorency Valley in France where it originated in the 1600s.
Dwarf sour cherry (8-10 feet) bred by University of Minnesota. Self-fertile, extremely cold-hardy, disease-resistant. Dark red fruit with red flesh. Best choice for small gardens in cold zones.

Dwarf sour cherry (under 10 feet) also from University of Minnesota. Self-fertile. Large bright red fruit. Blooms late, reducing spring frost risk. Similar to North Star but with larger fruit and slightly later harvest.
Hungarian tart cherry, sweeter than Montmorency with darker fruit and juice. Good for fresh eating in addition to pies and preserves. Self-fertile. Ripens slightly later than Montmorency.

Canadian-bred dwarf hybrid (Prunus fruticosa x cerasus) -- extremely cold-hardy, staying under 8 feet. Self-fertile but cross-pollination between Romeo and Juliet increases yield. Fruit is tart-sweet, good for both fresh eating and preserves. The hardiest cherry option for zones 2-3.

crops.chill_hours_note: Highest chill requirement of common fruits. Zones 4-6 ideal

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost killed the blossom
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Stone fruit blooms before apple, often when frost is still common. A single hard frost during the brief bloom window can eliminate the year's crop. Apricot is the earliest-blooming and most frost-exposed -- in colder zones it can lose the crop most years.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Watch overnight forecasts through bloom and cover smaller trees with horticultural fleece on frost nights. In frost-prone sites, choose later-blooming varieties on your next planting -- apricot in particular has varieties selected for late bloom that ride out spring frost better.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Brown rot (Monilinia) is the headline disease on stone fruit -- it turns ripening fruit into soft brown lesions, then leathery mummies. Plum curculio leaves crescent-shaped scars on young fruit. Peach leaf curl distorts new leaves in spring. Cherry fruit fly maggots ruin cherries near harvest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Sanitation drives brown rot control: remove every mummified fruit from tree and ground at the end of the season. For peach leaf curl, a single dormant copper spray before bud-swell prevents the season's infection. Open-center pruning helps everything by drying the canopy faster after rain.

failure_diagnostics.label: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Pollination needs vary by stone fruit type. Peach, nectarine, and sour cherry are usually self-fertile and set fruit alone. Sweet cherry and many plums and apricots need a compatible second variety with overlapping bloom. A self-sterile tree alone will bloom heavily and set nothing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Check the pollination requirement of your variety before assuming poor weather. If a partner is needed, plant a compatible second variety within 100 feet -- a neighbor's tree counts if it is close enough. Bloom-time charts from extension publications help match pollinators.

failure_diagnostics.label: Root problems or waterlogging
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Stone fruit is unusually intolerant of wet feet. Trees in saturated soil show yellowing leaves, weak shoots, and gummy bark splits at the base (Phytophthora collar rot). Decline can be rapid -- a stone-fruit tree can fail in a single wet spring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Drainage is set at planting. On a wet site, plant the next tree on a 12-inch raised mound or move sites entirely. Stone fruit on its own roots tolerates wet less than pome fruit -- choose a Phytophthora-resistant rootstock if available.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Stone fruit needs 6 to 8 hours of direct sun to color, sweeten, and ripen evenly. In shade or in a crowded canopy, fruit stays small and pale and brown rot pressure increases because the canopy stays wet longer.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Maintain the open-center form with annual pruning -- this is more important on stone fruit than on any other tree fruit. Light and air through the canopy is both a yield driver and a disease control. Site new trees in full sun, away from buildings or larger trees that will shade them as they mature.

crops.name: Microgreens Mix
crops.description: The fastest crop to harvest -- full of nutrition and flavor in 7-14 days. Grow on a windowsill year-round. Sunflower, radish, pea, and broccoli are best-performing varieties.

3.notes: Grow indoors on a sunny windowsill or under grow lights year-round.

fertilizer.notes: Microgreens are harvested within 2 weeks of germination -- no fertilizer needed. Good seed-starting mix is sufficient.

succession.tip: Sow a new tray every 1-2 weeks year-round indoors. Microgreens are harvested once -- cut the whole tray at the soil line when the first true leaves appear. This is pure succession growing: sow, harvest in 7-14 days, start the next tray. Keep 2-3 trays at different stages so you're never waiting. Used potting mix can go straight into the compost or outdoor beds.

pests.name: Fungus gnats
pests.symptoms: Small flies around growing trays. Larvae in growing medium.
pests.cause: Bradysia species.
pests.organic_treatment: Yellow sticky traps. Let medium dry between waterings.
pests.prevention: Good airflow. Avoid overwatering.

diseases.name: Damping off
diseases.symptoms: Seedlings collapse at soil level shortly after germination. Stems appear pinched.
diseases.cause: Various Pythium and Fusarium fungi in overly wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected trays. Improve air circulation.
diseases.prevention: Use sterile growing medium. Do not overwater. Good airflow.

watering.frequency: Mist twice daily during germination, once daily after
watering.amount: Keep growing medium moist but not waterlogged
watering.method: Bottom watering preferred -- prevents damping off and mold
watering.signs_overwater: Gray mold, damping off, foul smell

crops.harvest_ready: Harvest when first true leaves appear (cotyledons fully open, first true leaf just emerging) -- typically 7-14 days from seeding depending on variety. Cut at soil level with scissors. Don't wait until leggy.

storage.fridge: 5-7 days in sealed container lined with paper towel -- keep dry
storage.freezer: Not suitable
storage.notes: Harvest and refrigerate immediately. Do not wash until ready to eat. Paper towel absorbs condensation.

varieties.note: Sunflower microgreens are the most satisfying for beginners -- large seeds germinate reliably and the flavor is excellent.

start_method.notes: Sow seeds densely on damp growing medium (coco coir, hemp mat, or potting mix). No soil preparation needed -- use trays specifically for microgreens.

container_notes.notes: Microgreens are always grown in shallow trays indoors -- a 10×20 inch propagation tray is standard. No minimum gallon requirement.

rotation.avoid_after: N/A
rotation.note: Indoor tray crop -- no rotation needed.

growth_stages.name: Sowing
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Seeds evenly distributed on moist growing medium.
growth_stages.user_action: Sow densely and evenly. Mist thoroughly, cover with a blackout lid or second tray, and press down firmly to ensure seed contact with the medium.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Seeds sprouting -- white roots and pale shoots pushing up under the blackout cover.
growth_stages.user_action: Leave covered and check moisture daily. The weight of the tray on top helps seeds develop straight, strong stems.

growth_stages.name: Blackout Phase
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Shoots pushing against the lid -- they should be pale yellow and reaching upward.
growth_stages.user_action: When shoots are pressing against the blackout cover, move to light. The stretch in darkness builds stem length.

growth_stages.name: Growing in Light
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Greening up fast as chlorophyll develops. Cotyledons (seed leaves) opening fully.
growth_stages.user_action: Water from below by setting the tray in water and allowing it to absorb upward -- this avoids mold on the surface. Harvest when seed leaves are fully open.

notifications.title: Move your microgreens to light
notifications.body: Your microgreens should be ready to move from blackout to light -- check that shoots are pressing against the cover. Move to a bright windowsill or under grow lights now. They will green up within hours.

notifications.title: Check your microgreens for harvest
notifications.body: Microgreens are ready when the seed leaves are fully open and the first true leaves are just beginning to show. Harvest with scissors just above the soil line. Rinse and use immediately for the best flavor.

sow.text: Sow densely -- microgreens are one of the few crops where crowding is desirable. Even coverage without gaps gives the best harvest.
Soak large seeds (sunflower, peas) overnight before sowing. They germinate more evenly and quickly.

germination.text: The weight of a tray or board on top helps seeds press into the medium and develop straight, strong stems in the dark.
Check moisture once a day -- the medium should be moist but not waterlogged. If it feels wet on top, wait before misting again.

blackout.text: Darkness forces upward growth and builds stem length. The stretch is intentional and desirable.
If shoots are very pale or yellow after 5+ days, they have been in blackout too long. Move to light immediately.

light.text: Bottom watering prevents mold, which is the main challenge with microgreens. Set the tray in water for 10-15 minutes rather than misting the surface.
Harvest in the morning when the plants are full of water. Cut, rinse immediately, and use within a day or two.

yield_expectations.per_plant: One tray yields 50-200g depending on variety and tray size
yield_expectations.peak_production: Ready in 7-14 days -- the fastest crop you can grow
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Microgreens are instant gratification -- from seed to harvest in under two weeks. Perfect for getting children interested in growing.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: White fuzzy mold on the surface
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Surface mold is caused by overwatering or poor airflow. It is different from the white root hairs that are completely normal and healthy -- root hairs are orderly and attached to stems, mold is fuzzy and appears on the soil surface.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water from below by setting the tray in water -- never mist the surface once seeds have germinated. Ensure good airflow around the tray.

failure_diagnostics.label: Seedlings fell over at the base
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Damping off is a fungal condition that rots the stem at soil level. It is caused by overwet, poorly ventilated conditions -- especially in the blackout phase.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Do not overwater during germination. Ensure the growing medium is moist but not wet before sowing. Improve airflow once seedlings emerge.

failure_diagnostics.label: Seeds did not germinate evenly
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Patchy germination is usually caused by uneven seed contact with the growing medium, or the surface drying out during germination. Larger seeds like sunflower and peas benefit from pre-soaking.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Press seeds firmly into the surface after sowing. Soak larger seeds for 8 hours before sowing. Ensure the medium is thoroughly moist before you start.

failure_diagnostics.label: Seedlings stayed yellow and pale
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Microgreens kept in blackout for too long become etiolated -- pale, stretched, and weak. Once moved to light they should green up within hours. If they do not, they have been in darkness too long.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Move to light as soon as shoots are pressing against the blackout cover -- usually day 3-5. They green up fast once in light. Do not wait until they look fully grown under the dome.

failure_diagnostics.label: Wilted or crispy after moving to light
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Microgreens dry out fast under grow lights or in a sunny window. They need consistent moisture from below during the light phase.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water from below once a day during the light phase -- set the tray in a shallow dish of water for 10-15 minutes and let it absorb upward.

indoor_cycle.tip: Start new trays weekly for continuous harvest. Rinse and drain seeds before sowing for even germination. Harvest at first true leaf stage -- clip above the soil line with clean scissors.

failure_diagnostics.label: Seeds did not germinate evenly
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Patchy germination is usually caused by uneven seed contact with the growing medium, or the surface drying out during germination. Larger seeds like sunflower and peas benefit from pre-soaking.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Press seeds firmly into the surface after sowing. Soak larger seeds for 8 hours before sowing. Ensure the medium is thoroughly moist before you start.

failure_diagnostics.label: Seedlings stayed yellow and pale
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Microgreens kept in blackout for too long become etiolated -- pale, stretched, and weak. Once moved to light they should green up within hours. If they do not, they have been in darkness too long.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Move to light as soon as shoots are pressing against the blackout cover -- usually day 3-5. They green up fast once in light. Do not wait until they look fully grown under the dome.

failure_diagnostics.label: Wilted or crispy after moving to light
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Microgreens dry out fast under grow lights or in a sunny window. They need consistent moisture from below during the light phase.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water from below once a day during the light phase -- set the tray in a shallow dish of water for 10-15 minutes and let it absorb upward.

indoor_cycle.tip: Soak seeds 8-12 hours before sowing. Press firmly into moist growing medium. Harvest before first true leaves emerge for best flavor -- stems become bitter after that.

crops.name: Pea Shoots
crops.description: Sweet, tender pea shoots harvest in 10-14 days. Soak whole dried peas 6-8 hours first. Can cut-and-come-again once or twice before replanting.

3.notes: Indoor year-round. Soak peas 6-8 hours before sowing.

fertilizer.notes: Cut at 4-6 inches -- too fast-growing to need any feeding. Seeds contain all the nutrition needed at this stage.

succession.tip: Sow a new tray every week indoors, or direct-sow short rows in the garden every 2 weeks. Indoors, pea shoots are ready in 10-14 days as microgreens. In the garden, let them grow to 4-6 inches and snip the top 2-3 inches -- the plant will regrow for 2-3 more cuts before declining. Use dried peas from the bulk food aisle rather than expensive seed packets.

pests.name: Fungus gnats
pests.symptoms: Small flies around growing trays. Larvae in growing medium.
pests.cause: Bradysia species.
pests.organic_treatment: Yellow sticky traps. Let medium dry between waterings.
pests.prevention: Good airflow. Avoid overwatering.

diseases.name: Damping off
diseases.symptoms: Seedlings collapse at soil level shortly after germination. Stems appear pinched.
diseases.cause: Various Pythium and Fusarium fungi in overly wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected trays. Improve air circulation.
diseases.prevention: Use sterile growing medium. Do not overwater. Good airflow.

crops.harvest_ready: Harvest when 3-4 inches tall with 2-3 sets of leaves. Cut above the lowest leaf node -- it will regrow for a second cut. Best flavor when young and tender, about 10-14 days from seeding.

storage.fridge: 3-5 days in sealed bag with paper towel
storage.freezer: Not suitable
storage.notes: More robust than other microgreens. Keep cool and dry.

varieties.note: Any sugar or snow pea variety works for shoots -- field peas are cheapest for large-volume growing.

start_method.notes: Sow seeds densely on damp growing medium (coco coir, hemp mat, or potting mix). No soil preparation needed -- use trays specifically for microgreens.

container_notes.notes: Microgreens are always grown in shallow trays indoors -- a 10×20 inch propagation tray is standard. No minimum gallon requirement.

rotation.avoid_after: N/A
rotation.note: Indoor tray crop -- no rotation needed.

growth_stages.name: Sowing
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Seeds evenly distributed on moist growing medium.
growth_stages.user_action: Sow densely and evenly. Mist thoroughly, cover with a blackout lid or second tray, and press down firmly to ensure seed contact with the medium.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Seeds sprouting -- white roots and pale shoots pushing up under the blackout cover.
growth_stages.user_action: Leave covered and check moisture daily. The weight of the tray on top helps seeds develop straight, strong stems.

growth_stages.name: Blackout Phase
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Shoots pushing against the lid -- they should be pale yellow and reaching upward.
growth_stages.user_action: When shoots are pressing against the blackout cover, move to light. The stretch in darkness builds stem length.

growth_stages.name: Growing in Light
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Greening up fast as chlorophyll develops. Cotyledons (seed leaves) opening fully.
growth_stages.user_action: Water from below by setting the tray in water and allowing it to absorb upward -- this avoids mold on the surface. Harvest when seed leaves are fully open.

notifications.title: Move your microgreens to light
notifications.body: Your microgreens should be ready to move from blackout to light -- check that shoots are pressing against the cover. Move to a bright windowsill or under grow lights now. They will green up within hours.

notifications.title: Check your microgreens for harvest
notifications.body: Microgreens are ready when the seed leaves are fully open and the first true leaves are just beginning to show. Harvest with scissors just above the soil line. Rinse and use immediately for the best flavor.

sow.text: Sow densely -- microgreens are one of the few crops where crowding is desirable. Even coverage without gaps gives the best harvest.
Soak large seeds (sunflower, peas) overnight before sowing. They germinate more evenly and quickly.

germination.text: The weight of a tray or board on top helps seeds press into the medium and develop straight, strong stems in the dark.
Check moisture once a day -- the medium should be moist but not waterlogged. If it feels wet on top, wait before misting again.

blackout.text: Darkness forces upward growth and builds stem length. The stretch is intentional and desirable.
If shoots are very pale or yellow after 5+ days, they have been in blackout too long. Move to light immediately.

light.text: Bottom watering prevents mold, which is the main challenge with microgreens. Set the tray in water for 10-15 minutes rather than misting the surface.
Harvest in the morning when the plants are full of water. Cut, rinse immediately, and use within a day or two.

yield_expectations.per_plant: One tray yields 50-200g depending on variety and tray size
yield_expectations.peak_production: Ready in 7-14 days -- the fastest crop you can grow
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Microgreens are instant gratification -- from seed to harvest in under two weeks. Perfect for getting children interested in growing.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: White fuzzy mold on the surface
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Surface mold is caused by overwatering or poor airflow. It is different from the white root hairs that are completely normal and healthy -- root hairs are orderly and attached to stems, mold is fuzzy and appears on the soil surface.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water from below by setting the tray in water -- never mist the surface once seeds have germinated. Ensure good airflow around the tray.

failure_diagnostics.label: Seedlings fell over at the base

failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Press seeds firmly into the surface after sowing. Soak larger seeds for 8 hours before sowing. Ensure the medium is thoroughly moist before you start.

failure_diagnostics.label: Seedlings stayed yellow and pale
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Microgreens kept in blackout for too long become etiolated -- pale, stretched, and weak. Once moved to light they should green up within hours. If they do not, they have been in darkness too long.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Move to light as soon as shoots are pressing against the blackout cover -- usually day 3-5. They green up fast once in light. Do not wait until they look fully grown under the dome.

failure_diagnostics.label: Wilted or crispy after moving to light
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Microgreens dry out fast under grow lights or in a sunny window. They need consistent moisture from below during the light phase.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water from below once a day during the light phase -- set the tray in a shallow dish of water for 10-15 minutes and let it absorb upward.

indoor_cycle.tip: Soak peas 12-24 hours before sowing. Grow dense; the shoots support each other. Cut-and-come-again -- a second harvest is often possible a week after the first.

crops.name: Celery
crops.description: The most demanding crop in this guide -- needs consistent moisture, steady cool temperatures, and a very long season. But homegrown celery has a depth of flavor you'll never find in a supermarket. Start early, be patient.

3.notes: Start 10-12 weeks early. Celery germinates slowly at 65-70°F -- don't rush. Barely feasible in Zone 3 -- choose fast-maturing varieties like Tango.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Celery is very slow-growing; start seeds indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost for best results. (UMN Extension) Press seeds onto soil surface -- celery seed needs light to germinate. Transplant out after last frost; celery tolerates light frost but not hard freeze. Harden off gradually over 10-14 days.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note: Celery is very slow-growing; start seeds indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost for best results. (UMN Extension) Press seeds onto soil surface -- celery seed needs light to germinate. Transplant out after last frost; celery tolerates light frost but not hard freeze. Harden off gradually over 10-14 days.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: Harvest celery 100-130 days from transplant. Stalks can be harvested individually from the outside or the whole head can be cut. Celery tolerates light frost but hard freeze damages stalks. (UMN Extension; Cornell Extension)
harvest_start.design_note: Cold-zone harvest_end: first_frost + 14d (with protection).

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Celery leaf miner
pests.symptoms: Blotchy white or brown tunnels inside leaves. Leaves blister and die.
pests.cause: Euleia heraclei fly larvae mine inside leaf tissue.
pests.organic_treatment: Remove and destroy affected leaves. Use insect mesh.
pests.prevention: Grow under insect mesh. Destroy affected leaves promptly.

diseases.name: Leaf spot
diseases.symptoms: Brown spots with yellow halos on leaves.
diseases.cause: Septoria apiicola fungus. Seed-borne.
diseases.organic_treatment: Copper-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention: Hot water seed treatment. Rotate crops.

watering.frequency: Every 2-3 days -- celery is very thirsty

crops.harvest_ready: Stalks at least 12 inches, firm and crunchy. Harvest outer stalks or entire plant.

start_method.notes: Start 10-12 weeks before last frost -- celery is very slow. Needs light to germinate -- press seeds onto surface, don't cover. Harden off slowly over 10-14 days.

storage.fridge: 1-2 weeks wrapped in foil -- foil (not plastic) keeps celery crisp much longer
storage.freezer: Chop and freeze raw -- good for cooking but goes limp
storage.notes: The foil-wrap method dramatically extends celery life in the fridge.

varieties.note: Conquistador is the best choice for beginner growers -- more forgiving of inconsistent watering than other varieties.

provenance.label: traditional

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Tiny, very slow seedlings. Celery is one of the most challenging crops to germinate.
growth_stages.user_action: Surface sow -- celery needs light to germinate. Do not cover the seeds. Keep soil surface consistently moist. Germination takes 2-3 weeks even in ideal conditions.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Thread-like seedlings -- tiny and slow. Celery is the marathon runner of vegetables.
growth_stages.user_action: Prick out when large enough to handle, into individual cells. Keep consistently moist -- celery does not tolerate drying out.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: A proper celery plant with multiple stalks developing.
growth_stages.user_action: Celery is a heavy feeder and needs consistent moisture. Feed with a balanced fertilizer every 2 weeks. Blanch by wrapping the lower stalks to get the white, tender stems of shop-bought celery.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Stalks at full size, plant well-developed.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest outer stalks first as with leafy greens, or cut the whole plant at the base. Celery keeps in the ground through light frost and in the refrigerator for weeks after harvest.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Outer stalks tough or hollow, plant beginning to bolt if a warm spell arrives, frost damage on outer leaves.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest the whole plant before hard frost -- celery tolerates light frost but not deep cold. Pull and compost spent plants. If you want to save seed, leave one or two plants to overwinter and bolt the following spring.
growth_stages.log_prompt: How was your celery season? Worth logging what worked.

germination.text: Celery seeds are tiny and slow to germinate -- 14 to 21 days is normal. Surface-sow on a warm tray (70 to 75 degrees), keep consistently moist, and provide light (celery needs light to germinate).
Start indoors 10 to 12 weeks before transplant date -- celery is a long-season crop and slow to grow. Pre-soaking seeds for 24 hours before sowing speeds germination.

seedling.text: Pot up seedlings to 4-inch pots once they have 4 true leaves. Do NOT expose seedlings to sustained cold (below 55 degrees for several weeks) -- this triggers vernalization and the plant will bolt to seed in its first year instead of producing usable stalks.

Harden off carefully and slowly. Transplant outdoors only after soil reaches 60 degrees and night temperatures stay above 55. Cold transplant conditions are the leading cause of celery bolting failures.

established.text: Water consistently -- celery has shallow roots and demands more water than most vegetables. The plant evolved in marshy ground; treat it accordingly. Mulch heavily and never let the soil dry out completely.
Side-dress with compost or balanced fertilizer every 3 to 4 weeks. Celery is heavy-feeding; deficiency shows as slow growth and stringy stalks.

harvest.text: Begin harvesting outer stalks once they reach 6 to 8 inches tall -- cut individual stalks at the base and the plant continues producing from the center. A single plant can be harvested over several months in cool climates.

For blanched (paler, more tender) stalks, mound soil around the base of the plant 2 to 3 weeks before final harvest. This is traditional but optional; modern self-blanching varieties produce tender stalks without earthing up.

end_of_season.text: Celery tolerates light frost and improves in flavor with cool fall weather. Sustained hard freezes (below about 25 degrees) damage the plant; harvest before this point or cover with row cover.
Pull spent plants and compost. Rotate celery to a new bed each year; avoid planting after carrot or parsley (same family, same pests).

yield_expectations.per_plant: One full celery plant -- equivalent to a shop bunch
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Celery is one of the most challenging vegetables to grow but completely worth it. The flavor is more intense than anything shop-bought.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Cold damage and bolting trigger
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Celery has a complex cold relationship: mature plants tolerate light frost and improve in flavor with cool fall weather. BUT young plants exposed to sustained cold (below 55 degrees for several weeks) undergo vernalization -- this is a biological switch that tells the plant to bolt to seed during the following warm weather. Cold-vernalized celery flowers and goes to seed prematurely instead of producing usable stalks. This cold-bolting is the opposite of the heat-bolting most leafy greens experience.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: The single most important rule: do NOT transplant celery into cold soil. Wait until soil reaches 60 degrees and night temperatures stay above 55. In cool-spring zones, start celery later rather than earlier -- it is better to risk a slightly shorter season than to lose the crop to bolting. Cover transplants with row cover during cool spells in the first month outdoors.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Celery shares pests with carrot and parsley (Apiaceae family): celery leaftier, carrot rust fly, and parsleyworm. Aphids cluster on stalks. Septoria leaf spot is the headline disease; bacterial blight and pink rot appear in wet conditions or in poorly-rotated beds.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Floating row cover during the carrot rust fly emergence windows blocks both rust fly and leaftier. Hand-pick parsleyworm caterpillars (or relocate them -- they become black swallowtail butterflies). For Septoria, water at the base, space plants for airflow, and rotate to a new bed each year. Avoid planting celery after carrot or parsley.

failure_diagnostics.label: Root rot or hollow stalks
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Despite preferring marshy growing conditions, celery still needs drainage -- persistent waterlogging causes root rot and crown collapse. Inconsistent watering (a wet-dry cycle) produces hollow or split stalks even with adequate total water.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in fertile, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil. Water consistently rather than letting soil dry and re-wetting heavily. Mulch heavily to stabilize soil moisture. Drip irrigation works well for celery by providing consistent water.

failure_diagnostics.label: Stringy or bitter stalks
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress is the leading cause of stringy, bitter, tough celery stalks. Celery has shallow roots and high water demand; even short dry spells cause the stalks to develop tough fibers and concentrated bitter flavor that does not soften with cooking.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water frequently and deeply -- 1.5 to 2 inches per week minimum, more in heat. Never let celery dry out. Mulch heavily. In hot zones, light afternoon shade extends the productive cycle by reducing water demand.

failure_diagnostics.label: Weak thin stalks
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Celery needs 6 hours of sun minimum but tolerates partial shade better than most vegetables. In deep shade, stalks grow thin, weak, and pale. Light afternoon shade is actually beneficial in hot climates because it reduces water stress.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun in cool climates; partial shade is acceptable and even helpful in hot zones. South or east exposure works well. Avoid heavy shade (north-facing or under tree canopy) which produces poor-quality stalks.

crops.name: Asparagus
crops.description: The ultimate long-game crop. Plant once, harvest for 20-30 years. Year 1 and 2 you let it establish -- no harvest. Year 3 onwards you get thick, sweet spears every spring for the rest of your gardening life. Plant crowns, not seeds.

fertilizer.notes: Perennial. Feed in early spring as spears emerge, and again after harvest finishes to build crown strength for next year. Avoid disturbing roots.

succession.reason: Perennial crop that takes 2-3 years to establish. Not a succession crop.

tasks.description: Cut brown ferns to ground level in late fall after they die back. Apply 2 inches of compost over crowns.
Apply balanced fertilizer (10-10-10) in early spring before spears emerge.

crops.year_one_notes: Do not harvest in years 1-2. Allow all spears to grow into ferns to build root energy. Year 3 harvest for 2-3 weeks only.

good.name: Marigolds
good.why: Deter nematodes -- plant at bed edges from year 2

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. This claim's nematode component aligns with the extension-documented mechanism, but the 'concurrent companion' application pattern reflects popular gardening practice rather than extension protocol.

pests.name: Asparagus beetle
pests.symptoms: Blue-black beetles with cream spots eating spears and fern foliage. Orange-red larvae on fronds. Stems stripped of bark.
pests.cause: Crioceris asparagi (common) and C. duodecimpunctata (spotted). Adults and larvae both feed.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick adults and larvae. Apply neem oil. Cut back ferns at end of season to remove overwintering sites.
pests.prevention: Remove all fern debris in autumn. Interplant with tomatoes.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

diseases.name: Asparagus rust
diseases.symptoms: Orange-brown powdery pustules on fern stems and foliage from midsummer. Fronds die back early.
diseases.cause: Puccinia asparagi fungus. Spreads in warm humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove infected fronds. Apply sulfur-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention: Plant resistant varieties (Jersey Knight, Jersey Giant). Maintain good airflow. Remove fern debris in autumn.

diseases.name: Fusarium crown rot
diseases.symptoms: Spears are stunted and fern growth is thin year after year. Roots show brown/red discoloration when dug up.
diseases.cause: Fusarium soil fungus. Persists in soil long-term.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure. Remove affected plants.
diseases.prevention: Never replant asparagus in previously infected soil. Choose resistant varieties. Ensure good drainage.

watering.frequency: Weekly during establishment years, less once mature

crops.harvest_ready: In year 3+: harvest spears at 6-8 inches with tight, compact tips. Snap or cut at ground level. Stop harvesting when spears thin to pencil-width.

start_method.notes: Plant 1- or 2-year crowns in spring -- from seed takes 3 years to harvest. Dig a 12-inch trench, spread roots over a mound of soil, cover 4 inches. No hardening off.

storage.fridge: 3-5 days standing upright in an inch of water, covered with a bag
storage.freezer: Blanch 2-3 minutes, freeze -- very good
storage.notes: Asparagus converts sugar to starch rapidly after cutting. Eat fresh or preserve quickly.

varieties.note: Jersey Knight and Jersey Supreme are male plants only -- no energy wasted on seeds, significantly higher yield than mixed or female plants.

crops.soil_prep: Asparagus is a permanent crop -- prepare the bed thoroughly before planting. Double-dig to 18 inches. Remove every weed root, especially perennial weeds (couch grass, bindweed). Incorporate generous amounts of well-rotted manure or compost. Raised beds are ideal -- asparagus hates wet feet. pH 6.5-7.0.

container_notes.notes: Not suited to containers -- asparagus crowns need deep soil and produce for 20+ years. Permanent raised bed or ground planting only.

rotation.avoid_after: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note: Asparagus is a long-lived perennial -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the site carefully as the crowns can be productive for 15-20 years and don't transplant well.

growth_stages.name: Planting Crowns
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Crowns planted in a trench 8 inches deep, roots spread out like a spider.
growth_stages.user_action: Prepare a permanent bed -- asparagus stays in place for 20+ years. Plant crowns carefully, spread roots over a mound in the trench, cover with 2-3 inches of soil and fill in gradually as growth emerges.

growth_stages.name: Year One -- Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Fernlike foliage emerging and growing tall. Do not harvest any spears this year.
growth_stages.user_action: Let all spears grow into ferns in year one. Every spear you do not harvest goes back into root energy for future years. It requires patience but the payoff is a 20-year productive bed.

growth_stages.name: Year Two -- Light Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Fat spears emerging in spring.
growth_stages.user_action: Take just 2-3 spears per crown in year two. Let the rest go to fern. You are still building the root system.
growth_stages.log_prompt: How many spears are you seeing?

growth_stages.name: Mature Harvest (Year 3+)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: A full flush of spears each spring. At maturity, a bed gives you weeks of cutting.
growth_stages.user_action: Cut all spears until the end of June, then let everything go to fern. The fern rebuilds the crown for next year. Cut the fern back in autumn when it yellows.

notifications.title: Time to plant your asparagus crowns
notifications.body: Asparagus crowns go in 3-4 weeks before last frost. Prepare a permanent bed with excellent drainage and organic matter -- this planting will produce for 20 or more years. Take time to do it right.

notifications.title: Do not harvest your asparagus this year
notifications.body: Every spear you see this year needs to grow into fern. The fern feeds the roots, and the roots are what will feed you for the next two decades. This is the year that determines whether your asparagus bed is good or great.

notifications.title: Stop cutting asparagus at the end of June
notifications.body: Let all remaining spears go to fern from now on. The fern rebuilds the crown for next year. Cut back the yellow fern in autumn and mulch the bed well.

planting.text: Prepare the asparagus bed better than any other bed in your garden. It will be there for 20 years.
Add a generous amount of compost to the trench before planting. Asparagus is a heavy feeder over its long life.

year_one.text: The hardest part of growing asparagus is leaving it alone in year one. Every spear you do not cut is an investment in the next 20 years of harvest.
Let the ferny foliage reach its full height -- do not cut it back until it yellows in autumn.

year_two.text: Take just 2-3 spears per crown in year two. Stop harvesting by the end of June and let the rest fern out.
The foliage feeds the roots. The roots determine how much you harvest next year.

mature_harvest.text: Cut all spears below soil level with a sharp knife until the end of June, then let everything go to fern.
A well-established asparagus bed in full production gives weeks of cutting in spring -- one of the great seasonal garden moments.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 10-20 spears per crown per season at maturity
yield_expectations.peak_production: A mature bed (year 4+) gives several weeks of cutting each spring
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Asparagus demands patience. Year one nothing, year two a little, year three proper harvest. Year ten is extraordinary.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Cold tolerance and dormancy
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: These three perennials handle winter cold differently. Asparagus is fully cold-hardy through zone 3, dies back to the ground each winter, and emerges from the crown each spring. Strawberry is cold-hardy through zone 3 with mulch, sometimes loses leaves but the crown survives. Artichoke is the cold-tender one -- hardy only to zone 7 reliably, often grown as an annual in colder zones. Late spring frost can damage emerging asparagus spears and strawberry blossoms.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: For asparagus, cover emerging spears with row cover during late spring frosts; damaged spears are tough and bitter. For strawberry, mulch heavily over the crowns before winter and uncover in early spring. For artichoke in zones 6 and below, grow as an annual or dig and overwinter the crown indoors. Hardy artichoke varieties (Imperial Star) survive zone 6 with heavy mulching.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Each of these crops has its own primary pest: asparagus beetle (both common and spotted) chews ferns and lays eggs on spears; spotted wing drosophila (SWD), slugs, and gray mold (Botrytis) are the headline strawberry problems; artichoke is generally low-pest but artichoke aphid clusters in the bracts and slugs damage tender new growth. Asparagus rust and Fusarium crown rot affect asparagus over time; strawberry is also vulnerable to verticillium wilt.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: For asparagus beetle, hand-pick adults and crush egg masses; in heavy infestations, neem or pyrethrin sprays in the cool of the day work. For SWD on strawberry, harvest ripe fruit promptly and clean up drops; row cover during fruit ripening helps. For artichoke aphid, hose off with water or use insecticidal soap. Choose disease-resistant strawberry varieties and renovate beds every 3 to 4 years.

failure_diagnostics.label: Crown rot or root rot
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: All three crops fail in waterlogged soil. Asparagus crowns rot in standing water -- a single wet season can kill an established bed. Strawberry crowns rot at the soil-stem interface in persistently wet conditions, and the fruit develops gray mold in damp weather. Artichoke is similarly intolerant of wet feet.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds. For asparagus, the bed is a multi-year commitment -- excellent drainage at planting prevents 20 years of disappointment. For strawberry, raised beds and straw mulch (the source of the name) keep fruit and crowns dry. For artichoke, mound up the planting site if drainage is marginal.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor establishment or poor yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Drought stress in the establishment year is the leading cause of failed asparagus and artichoke plantings. Strawberry tolerates short drought once established but fruit size and number drop substantially with water stress during fruiting. Asparagus that goes dry in summer produces fewer and smaller spears the following spring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water deeply through the establishment season for all three. Asparagus needs consistent moisture in summer (when it is feeding the crown for next year's spears) more than in spring (when it is producing spears from already-stored energy). Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture for all three.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor yield or weak growth
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: All three want full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to produce well. Shaded asparagus produces fewer and thinner spears; shaded strawberry produces small pale fruit with weak flavor; shaded artichoke grows leaves but produces few or no buds. These are not shade-tolerant crops.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun. Asparagus is a long-term commitment (15 to 20 years productive life), so the site choice matters more than for annual crops. For strawberry, full sun is also better for disease management because foliage dries faster after rain or dew.

pests.name: Onion fly
pests.symptoms: Plants wilt and die. White maggots at the base of bulb eating roots and inner leaves.
pests.cause: Delia antiqua fly. Lays eggs near onion seedlings in spring.
pests.organic_treatment: Insect mesh over bed. Remove and destroy affected plants.
pests.prevention: Grow under fine mesh. Rotate alliums every 3 years. Interplant with carrots -- mutual pest confusion.

pests.name: Thrips
pests.symptoms: Silver streaking and speckling on leaves. Stunted growth. Tiny yellow-brown insects visible.
pests.cause: Thrips tabaci. Worse in hot dry summers.
pests.organic_treatment: Neem oil spray. Insecticidal soap.
pests.prevention: Reflective mulch. Adequate watering in dry weather.

diseases.name: White rot
diseases.symptoms: Plants yellow and die. White fluffy growth at base with small black seed-like sclerotia. Roots and base rotted.
diseases.cause: Sclerotium cepivorum soil fungus. Persists in soil for 20+ years.
diseases.organic_treatment: No cure. Remove all plant material. Do not replant alliums in infected soil.
diseases.prevention: Strict crop rotation. Buy allium seed sets from reputable sources.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms: Gray-purple fuzzy growth on leaves. Leaves yellow and collapse. Worst in wet cool springs.
diseases.cause: Peronospora destructor fungus.
diseases.organic_treatment: Remove affected leaves. Copper-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention: Avoid overhead watering. Space plants for airflow. Rotate crops.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Cloves, sets, or seeds in the ground. No visible growth yet.
growth_stages.user_action: Plant garlic and onion sets pointed end up, just below the surface. For leeks, sow seeds in modules and transplant as pencil-thin seedlings.

growth_stages.name: Early Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Green shoots pushing up from sets or cloves. Slow growth initially -- alliums establish roots first.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep weed-free -- alliums are poor competitors with weeds, especially in early growth.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Strong upright leaves, healthy green color. Onions and garlic developing the bulb underground.
growth_stages.user_action: Stop feeding garlic and onions with nitrogen once the bulb starts forming -- it encourages leafy growth at the expense of the bulb.

growth_stages.name: Bulb Forming
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: For garlic: scapes curling upward on hardneck varieties. For onions: leaves beginning to yellow from the tips and fall over.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest garlic scapes when curled -- they are delicious and removing them redirects energy to the bulb. For onions, bending down any remaining upright leaves once half have fallen speeds final ripening.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Seeing scapes on garlic, or leaves beginning to fall?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Garlic: leaves 2/3 brown. Onions: all leaves yellow and fallen. Leeks: any size -- harvest young for mild flavor.
growth_stages.user_action: Lift carefully with a fork to avoid bruising. Cure in a warm, airy spot for 2-4 weeks before storing -- this is essential for long storage life.

growth_stages.name: Curing and Storage
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Skin papery and tight, neck dry and closed.
growth_stages.user_action: Hang or lay in a single layer in good airflow, out of direct rain, for 2-4 weeks. Garlic and onions not properly cured will not store well.

notifications.title: Time to plant your garlic
notifications.body: Garlic is planted in autumn and overwinters in the ground -- it needs a cold period to develop properly. Plant cloves now, pointed end up, 2 inches deep and 6 inches apart. You will not see much happen until spring, and that is exactly right.

notifications.title: Time to plant your onion sets
notifications.body: Onion sets can go in 3-4 weeks before last frost. Plant pointed end up with just the tip showing at the surface. They establish quickly and are more reliable than growing from seed.

notifications.title: Harvest your garlic scapes
notifications.body: Hardneck garlic sends up curled green shoots called scapes in early summer. Cut them off now -- they are delicious in stir fries and pestos, and removing them directs energy back into the bulb for a larger harvest.

notifications.title: Check your garlic for harvest readiness
notifications.body: When two thirds of the leaves have turned brown, your garlic is ready. Do not wait for all leaves to die -- the outer wrapper deteriorates. Lift carefully with a fork, do not pull by the stem, and handle gently to avoid bruising.

notifications.title: Cure your alliums properly -- it is worth it
notifications.body: Garlic and onions not properly cured will not store through winter. Hang or lay them in a single layer in a warm, airy space out of rain for 3-4 weeks. The necks should be completely dry before storage. This step makes the difference between 3-month storage and 6-month storage.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- watch for rust on your alliums
weather_triggers.body: Allium rust appears as orange powder on leaves in humid conditions. It weakens the plant but rarely kills it. Remove badly affected leaves and ensure good airflow. Rotate alliums to a different bed next year.

weather_triggers.title: Keep curing alliums dry
weather_triggers.body: Rain on curing garlic and onions undoes the drying process and encourages rot. Make sure they are under cover -- a shed, garage, or covered porch is ideal.

planting.text: Plant garlic in your best, most fertile bed. It is in the ground for 9 months -- give it good conditions from the start.
Save the largest cloves from each bulb for planting and eat the small ones. Larger cloves produce larger bulbs.

early_growth.text: Keep allium beds completely weed-free. Onions and garlic have poor, shallow root systems and are easily out-competed. Even small weeds reduce yields significantly.
No need to water garlic in autumn and winter -- rainfall is usually sufficient. Begin watering in spring if it is dry.

established.text: Stop feeding with nitrogen once bulbs start to form. High nitrogen at this stage produces soft, poorly-stored bulbs with thick necks.
Leeks can be earthed up as they grow to blanch the lower stem -- this gives you a longer white shaft and milder flavor.

bulb_forming.text: When onion leaves begin to yellow and fall over, stop watering. The plant is telling you it is finishing -- let it dry down naturally.
Do not bend onion tops manually until at least half the leaves have yellowed on their own. Bending them too early exposes the neck to disease.

harvest.text: Lift rather than pull. A garden fork under the bulb loosens the roots and prevents the stem tearing -- which exposes the bulb to rot during curing.
Harvest on a dry day and leave on top of the soil for a few hours before bringing in. The sun begins the drying process.

curing.text: Curing is the most important step most gardeners skip. 3-4 weeks in warm, airy conditions transforms a perishable vegetable into one that stores for 6-9 months.
Braid garlic and onions for storage if you have enough -- it looks beautiful and is functional. Store in a cool, dry, dark place.

yield_expectations.per_plant: Each shallot planted divides into a cluster of 4-8 shallots
yield_expectations.peak_production: Shallots give excellent yields relative to space
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Shallots are one of the best-value crops in the garden -- one bulb becomes eight. Save the best for replanting next year.

failure_diagnostics.label: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Established alliums are among the hardiest vegetables and handle frost well. Garlic overwintering in the ground is designed for frost. Young onion seedlings are more vulnerable to late hard freezes.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Protect young onion sets if a hard freeze threatens in the first few weeks after planting. Established plants need no protection from ordinary frost.

failure_diagnostics.label: Allium rust or white rot
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Allium rust appears as orange powder on leaves in humid summers -- it weakens but rarely kills the plant. White rot is more serious: a soil-borne fungus that causes bulbs to rot at the base. Once white rot is in soil it persists for decades.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Rotate alliums to a new bed every year. White rot cannot be eliminated from infected soil -- grow alliums elsewhere if you see it. Rust is largely cosmetic -- harvest early and the bulbs are usually fine.

failure_diagnostics.label: Rotting bulbs
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Garlic and onion bulbs rot in waterlogged soil, especially during curing. Rain on curing alliums reverses the drying process and causes neck rot -- one of the most common storage failures.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Ensure excellent drainage. Cure garlic and onions under cover -- a shed or garage with good airflow. Even a few hours of rain on curing bulbs can significantly reduce storage life.

failure_diagnostics.label: Small bulbs
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Alliums that experience drought stress during bulb development produce small, tight bulbs. Irregular watering is a common cause of disappointing allium harvests.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently during bulb formation -- from spring until leaves begin to yellow. Stop watering completely once leaves start to die back naturally.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor bulb development
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Alliums need full sun for good bulb development. The bulbing trigger in onions and garlic is day length -- both need long days combined with warmth to form bulbs. In shade or under trees, they often produce only small, undeveloped bulbs.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant alliums in your sunniest, most open bed. Weed competition also significantly reduces yield -- keep allium beds completely weed-free from early spring.

fertilizer.notes: Tropical grass that loves nitrogen. Feed monthly during the growing season. Reduce feeding in autumn.
fertilizer.npk_hint: high N for leafy growth, e.g. 10-5-5

succession.reason: Perennial tropical grass. Single planting divides and multiplies over time.

tasks.description: Cut back to 6 inches in early spring. In zones below 9, dig up and overwinter indoors in a pot before first frost.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms: Fine yellow or white stippling on leaves. Fine webbing along leaf edges and between blades in heavy infestations. Leaves bronze and dry out. Most severe on indoor or potted plants and during hot dry summers.
pests.cause: Two-spotted spider mite (Tetranychus urticae) is the primary species. UF/IFAS notes spider mites are the most common lemongrass problem and are mostly a concern on indoor plants where humidity is low.
pests.organic_treatment: Rinse plants with a forceful water spray, focusing on leaf undersides. Insecticidal soap or horticultural oil applied weekly for 2-3 weeks. Increase humidity around indoor plants.
pests.prevention: Keep plants well-watered during hot weather. Mist indoor plants or run a humidifier. Avoid dusty conditions -- dust on leaves favors mite buildup.

pests.name: Mealybugs
pests.symptoms: White cottony masses in leaf axils and between stalks at the base of the clump. Sticky honeydew and sooty mold on lower leaves. Clump weakens and grows slowly.
pests.cause: Several mealybug species feed on lemongrass, most often on potted or greenhouse plants where natural predators are absent.
pests.organic_treatment: Dab colonies with a cotton swab dipped in rubbing alcohol. Insecticidal soap or horticultural oil sprayed into the base of the clump. Severe infestations on potted plants: cut the clump back hard and repot in fresh soil.
pests.prevention: Inspect new plants before bringing them home or indoors. Keep the base of the clump clear of dead leaf sheaths where mealybugs hide.

pests.name: Leaf-feeding caterpillars
pests.symptoms: Ragged chewed edges on leaf blades. Caterpillar frass visible between blades. Rarely enough damage to affect plant health, since lemongrass regrows quickly.
pests.cause: Various Lepidoptera larvae occasionally feed on lemongrass foliage. UF/IFAS and PlantVillage (summarizing Gilman 1999) list these as a minor, sporadic issue.
pests.organic_treatment: Hand-pick caterpillars. Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) for persistent infestations -- effective on caterpillars, safe for beneficials.
pests.prevention: Generally not needed. Healthy established clumps outgrow caterpillar damage.

diseases.name: Leaf blight
diseases.symptoms: Reddish-brown spots on leaf tips and margins. Affected leaves look prematurely dried. Heavy pressure can reduce harvestable foliage but rarely threatens the clump.
diseases.cause: Several fungal pathogens, including Curvularia and Helminthosporium species, cause leaf blight on Cymbopogon. Favored by prolonged leaf wetness in humid weather.
diseases.organic_treatment: Hand-remove blighted leaves. Copper fungicide only if infection is severe and positively identified -- UF/IFAS notes lemongrass rarely requires disease treatment.
diseases.prevention: Avoid overhead watering. Space clumps for airflow. Remove and compost old dry leaves in spring.

diseases.name: Rust
diseases.symptoms: Orange or reddish-brown pustules on leaf undersides that release powdery spores when rubbed. Leaves yellow and dry back from tips in heavy infections.
diseases.cause: Puccinia nakanishikii and related rust fungi specific to grasses. Favored by warm humid weather and overcrowded clumps.
diseases.organic_treatment: Cut the clump back hard and dispose of rusted foliage. New growth typically comes in clean.
diseases.prevention: Divide crowded clumps every 2-3 years. Water at soil level. Provide full sun and good airflow.

crops.harvest_ready: Harvest outer stalks at ground level when 12+ inches tall. Inner white stalk is used for cooking.

start_method.notes: Divide existing clumps or buy as plants. Can start from seed but very slow.

storage.room_temp: 1-2 weeks in a glass of water
storage.freezer: Freeze whole stalks -- peel outer layers before using frozen
storage.notes: Lemongrass freezes very well. Freeze extra stalks whole -- slice directly from frozen.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Plant settling in after planting or propagation.
growth_stages.user_action: Most perennial herbs prefer poor, well-drained soil -- do not over-fertilize. Good drainage is more important than rich soil.

growth_stages.name: Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: New growth appearing, roots establishing.
growth_stages.user_action: Water regularly in the first season to establish roots. Once established, most perennial herbs are drought-tolerant.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Abundant leafy growth -- harvest anytime the plant has plenty.
growth_stages.user_action: Harvest by cutting stems back by a third. Never cut into old woody growth on rosemary, sage, and thyme -- they do not regenerate from old wood.

growth_stages.name: Winter
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Plant slowing down or going dormant. Hardy perennials stay evergreen; tender ones die back.
growth_stages.user_action: Give a light haircut before winter to tidy up but avoid heavy pruning -- leave it for spring. Mulch around the base in colder zones.

growth_stages.name: Spring Cutback
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: New green growth beginning to push from the base or lower stems.
growth_stages.user_action: Cut back last year's growth by about half once new growth appears. This annual cutback keeps perennial herbs from going woody and keeps them productive.

notifications.title: Bring lemongrass inside before frost
notifications.body: Lemongrass is tropical and cannot survive frost. Pot up and bring inside before first frost. Keep in a bright spot and reduce watering. It will go semi-dormant and come back strongly in spring.

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- protect tender herbs
weather_triggers.body: Basil, cilantro, and lemongrass are extremely frost-tender. Bring containers inside or cover with fleece tonight. Hardy herbs like thyme, rosemary, and mint are much more frost-tolerant.

weather_triggers.title: Heat alert -- herbs may bolt
weather_triggers.body: Heat triggers bolting in cilantro, dill, and parsley. Harvest as much as possible before temperatures peak. Basil, on the other hand, loves heat -- just remove any flowers that appear.

planting.text: Lemongrass is a tropical Cymbopogon grass -- a true grass, not a Mediterranean herb. It is not cold-hardy below USDA zone 8 and is grown as an annual or container plant in cooler zones. Plant outdoors only after night temperatures stay above 50 degrees.
Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Lemongrass prefers rich moist conditions -- the opposite of Mediterranean herbs. A generous compost amendment at planting helps establishment.

establishment.text: Water consistently and deeply through the first season. Lemongrass grows fast in warm weather and needs steady moisture to fuel that growth -- it is a heavy water user despite the dry-prairie appearance.
Mulch with organic matter to retain moisture. Side-dress with compost or a balanced fertilizer mid-season; lemongrass is a heavier feeder than other culinary herbs.

harvest.text: Harvest entire stems at the base by cutting or pulling -- the swollen lower portion (the bulb) is the part used in cooking. Stems are ready when they are pencil-thick or larger, usually 90 days from planting.

Harvest as needed throughout the growing season. The plant continues producing new tillers from the base; regular harvest encourages this. Save the leafy tops for tea -- they have the same lemon flavor in milder form.

winter.text: In USDA zone 8 and warmer, lemongrass overwinters in the ground but the foliage dies back in zone 8 and 9 cold snaps. Cut back to about 6 inches before winter and mulch heavily; new growth comes from the crown in spring.

In zone 7 and below, lemongrass will not survive winter outdoors. Either dig and pot a clump to overwinter indoors near a sunny window (treating it as a houseplant), or accept it as an annual and replant from purchased stems in spring.

spring_cutback.text: In overwintered plants, cut last year's dead foliage to the ground in early spring before new growth emerges. The crown regenerates fast in warm weather.

Spring is also the time to divide established clumps -- lemongrass clumps fatten quickly and benefit from division every 2 to 3 years. Lift, split into chunks with several stems each, and replant or share.

yield_expectations.per_plant: Multiple stalks per plant -- divide every 2-3 years
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Lemongrass is surprisingly easy to grow in a pot. Fresh lemongrass is incomparably better than dried.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Lemongrass is tropical and frost-tender. Light frost kills the foliage; sustained cold below 30 degrees damages or kills the crown. In USDA zone 7 and below, lemongrass will not survive winter outdoors -- it must be dug and overwintered indoors, or treated as an annual and replanted each spring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Confirm your zone before relying on lemongrass to overwinter outdoors. In zone 8 and 9, mulch the crown heavily before winter. In zone 7 and below, lift a clump in fall, pot it, and overwinter indoors as a houseplant. Do not leave outdoors expecting it to survive -- this is the most common way home gardeners lose lemongrass.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Lemongrass has very few pest or disease problems in most home gardens -- the same lemon oils that flavor it deter most insects. Indoor overwintered plants occasionally develop spider mites or scale in dry indoor air. Rust occasionally affects outdoor plants in humid summers.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: For indoor overwintering, keep humidity up and rinse foliage occasionally. For rust, increase airflow with light thinning of clumps. Outdoors, lemongrass essentially takes care of itself.

failure_diagnostics.label: Root rot or weak growth
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Despite being a heavier water user than Mediterranean herbs, lemongrass cannot tolerate waterlogged soil. Symptoms are yellowing of inner leaves, soft rot at the crown, and stunted growth. Containerized plants in pots without drainage holes fail this way fast.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plant in well-drained soil and use pots with drainage holes for container culture. Water deeply but allow the surface to dry between waterings. Reduce watering substantially in winter for indoor-overwintered plants.

failure_diagnostics.label: Stunted or yellowing growth
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Lemongrass needs more consistent water than most herbs -- its rapid summer growth depends on it. Drought stress shows as narrow, pale, slow-growing leaves and minimal new tiller production. The crop survives but produces poorly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water deeply and consistently through the growing season. Mulch heavily to retain moisture. In hot dry climates, drip irrigation outperforms overhead watering for lemongrass.

failure_diagnostics.label: Leggy or sparse growth
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Lemongrass needs full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to produce strong flavorful stems. In partial shade plants grow tall and floppy with thin pale stems and reduced lemon oil content.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun outdoors. For indoor overwintering, place near the brightest available window (south-facing if possible) or supplement with a grow light. A poorly-lit overwintered lemongrass survives but rarely thrives until back outdoors in spring.

crops.name: Oyster Mushroom
crops.soil: Straw, coffee grounds, or hardwood sawdust substrate
crops.description: The most beginner-friendly mushroom. Oysters grow fast on straw or coffee grounds and fruit in waves every few weeks. Grow indoors year-round in any zone.

fertilizer.notes: Mushrooms get all nutrition from their substrate. Use fresh straw, coffee grounds, or hardwood sawdust. No fertilizer -- it can introduce contamination.

succession.tip: Start a new bag or block every 2 weeks to maintain continuous harvests. Each block produces 2-3 flushes of mushrooms over 4-8 weeks, with the first flush being the largest. By starting a new block every 2 weeks, you always have one block in its prime flush while the next is colonizing. Keep completed blocks -- a spent block can often be triggered for one more flush by soaking it in cold water overnight.

3.notes: Grow indoors in any zone. Temperature control matters more than your USDA zone -- aim for 65-75°F during colonization and 60-70°F during fruiting.

pests.symptoms: Small flies hovering around substrate. Larvae damage mycelium and fruit bodies.
pests.cause: Bradysia species. Attracted to damp organic substrate.

watering.frequency: Mist the fruiting block 2-3 times daily during pinning and fruiting
watering.amount: Maintain 80-95% relative humidity -- use a spray bottle or ultrasonic humidifier

watering.signs_overwater: Bacterial blotch (yellow slimy patches on caps)
watering.signs_underwater: Cracked caps, slow pinning, aborted pins

crops.harvest_ready: Harvest just before the caps fully flatten and before edges begin to curl upward or turn wavy. Caps should still be slightly cupped or convex. Twist and pull cleanly -- don't leave stubs.

storage.fridge: 3-7 days in paper bag (not plastic) in fridge
storage.freezer: Sauté first, then freeze -- raw frozen mushrooms become watery and soft
storage.notes: Paper bag in fridge absorbs excess moisture. Never store in plastic -- mushrooms sweat and rot.

varieties.note: Pearl Oyster is the best starting point -- fastest colonization, most forgiving of temperature variation, very productive.

notifications.title: Mushroom kit set up -- now wait
notifications.body: The mycelium is doing its work in the dark. Keep at the right temperature and resist the urge to open or disturb the kit. You should see white fuzzy growth spreading within a week. If you smell anything unpleasant or see colored patches, something has gone wrong.

notifications.title: Introduce fresh air to trigger pinning
notifications.body: Mushrooms pin when they sense high humidity and fresh air together. Open the kit or bag twice daily for fresh air exchange. Mist the surface to keep humidity high. The contrast between CO2 buildup and the fresh air burst triggers pin formation.

notifications.title: Check your mushrooms for harvest readiness
notifications.body: Harvest just before the caps fully flatten -- the edges should still be slightly curled under. Oysters especially go from perfect to overripe fast. Twist and pull, or cut at the base. Do not leave overripe mushrooms -- they signal the substrate to stop producing.

notifications.title: Soak substrate for second flush
notifications.body: After your first harvest, soak the substrate in cold water for 12-24 hours to rehydrate it. Wring out excess moisture, return to fruiting conditions, and watch for a second flush within 1-2 weeks. Most substrates give 2-3 flushes before exhausted.

inoculation.text: Temperature is everything for mushrooms. Check your specific variety -- oysters like 65-75°F, shiitake 60-75°F, lion's mane 65-75°F. Even a few degrees outside the range slows or stops growth.
Contamination prevention starts at setup. Clean hands, clean surfaces, work quickly when the substrate is exposed.

colonization.text: Healthy mycelium is always white and smells of fresh mushrooms. Any other color -- green, black, pink -- is contamination and needs to be addressed immediately.
Patience during colonization is hard but essential. Opening the kit repeatedly introduces contamination risk. Check once a day at most.

pinning.text: Fresh air exchange is what triggers pinning. Twice daily is ideal -- open the kit, fan it briefly with your hand, mist the surface, close it again.
A humidity tent (a plastic bag with holes) over your kit helps maintain the humidity needed for pinning. Mist the inside of the tent rather than the substrate directly.

fruiting.text: Oyster mushrooms especially grow remarkably fast at peak -- check daily and harvest promptly. They go from perfect to overripe in 24-48 hours.
Harvest by twisting at the base rather than cutting where possible -- it removes the stub that would otherwise rot and contaminate the next flush.

second_flush.text: A good substrate gives 2-3 flushes. Second flushes are often smaller than the first but still worth having.
An exhausted substrate that grows no more mushrooms can be broken up and used as excellent garden compost -- it is rich in mycelium and nutrients.

yield_expectations.per_plant: 200-400g per flush, 2-3 flushes per substrate
yield_expectations.peak_production: Oysters fruit fast -- a flush can be ready within days of pinning
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Oyster mushrooms are the most beginner-friendly variety -- fast, forgiving, and delicious.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Green, black, or pink mold appeared
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Contamination -- usually Trichoderma (green mold) or Neurospora (pink) -- means competing fungi got established before the mushroom mycelium could colonize the substrate. This usually happens because of poor sterilization, exposure to air during inoculation, or too high a temperature.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Work cleanly and quickly when the substrate is exposed. Keep temperature in the right range -- too warm invites contamination. Start fresh with a new kit or properly sterilized substrate.

failure_diagnostics.label: Mycelium grew but no mushrooms appeared
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Mushrooms pin in response to high humidity and fresh air. If the substrate was fully colonized but no pins appeared, the fruiting conditions were not right -- usually insufficient fresh air exchange or humidity too low.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Open the kit or bag twice daily for fresh air exchange and mist the surface to maintain 85-95% humidity. The contrast between CO2 buildup and fresh air is what triggers pinning.

failure_diagnostics.label: Substrate was too wet or soggy
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Overwet substrate prevents oxygen reaching the mycelium and creates ideal conditions for bacterial contamination. It can look and smell unpleasant and the mycelium will not grow through it.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Field capacity is the target moisture level -- squeeze a handful of substrate and only a few drops should come out. Wetter than this is too wet.

failure_diagnostics.label: Substrate dried out
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: A dried-out substrate stalls colonization and prevents fruiting. Oyster mushrooms especially need consistent humidity -- if the substrate cracks or feels dry, production stops.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Mist the growing surface 2-3 times daily during fruiting. Between flushes, soak the substrate in cold water for 12-24 hours to rehydrate it.

failure_diagnostics.label: Wrong temperature
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Temperature outside the optimal range for your variety significantly slows or stops growth. Too warm and contamination risk increases dramatically. Too cool and mycelium growth stalls.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Check the specific temperature requirement for your variety and monitor with a thermometer. A consistent environment is more important than the perfect temperature.

indoor_cycle.tip: Easiest mushroom for beginners. Buy a pre-inoculated kit or grow on sterilized straw. Maintain 75-90 percent humidity. Fresh air exchange is critical -- CO2 buildup causes deformed fruits.

crops.name: Shiitake Mushroom
crops.soil: Hardwood logs (oak, maple, beech) or sawdust blocks
crops.description: The classic gourmet mushroom. Grown on hardwood logs or sawdust blocks, shiitake produces for years. Logs take longer to fruit but yield is generous once established.

crops.name: Lion's Mane Mushroom
crops.soil: Hardwood sawdust or supplemented hardwood substrate
crops.description: A striking white pom-pom mushroom prized for its seafood-like flavor and brain health benefits. Grown indoors on hardwood sawdust blocks. More temperature-sensitive than oysters but worth it.

fertilizer.notes: All nutrition comes from the hardwood sawdust substrate. Use a quality grain spawn and supplemented sawdust block for best yields. Cleanliness matters more than feeding.

succession.tip: Start a new block every 3 weeks. Lion's mane typically produces 1-2 flushes per block before being spent. It's one of the more delicate mushrooms in terms of moisture requirements -- it needs high humidity and dislikes direct airflow. Succession blocks keep production going without over-stressing individual blocks. Harvest when the 'teeth' begin to elongate but before they turn yellow, which indicates overmaturity.

3.notes: Grow indoors in any zone. Temperature control matters more than your USDA zone -- aim for 65-75°F during colonization and 60-70°F during fruiting.

watering.method: Fine mist around the block -- never directly on developing teeth

storage.notes: Lion's mane absorbs enormous amounts of moisture. Fully cook out before freezing.
