notifications.title: Last frost passed -- sow your flowers
notifications.body: Most annual flowers go directly in the ground after last frost. Prepare the bed, sow thinly, and water in. They will establish quickly as the weather warms.

notifications.title: Start deadheading to keep flowers coming
notifications.body: Remove spent flowers regularly -- every few days at peak season. This prevents seed setting and keeps the plant producing new blooms. Five minutes of deadheading extends the flowering season by weeks.

notifications.title: Let the last flowers set seed
notifications.body: Stop deadheading now and let the last blooms set seed. Collect seed heads when they are fully dry -- shake into a paper bag or clip the whole head. Label and store in a cool dry place for next year.

notifications.title: Plant flowers near your vegetables for pest control
notifications.body: Marigolds, nasturtiums, and calendula planted among vegetables deter pests and attract beneficial insects. Get them in now alongside your tomatoes, cucumbers, and brassicas before pest season begins.

weather_triggers.title: Frost warning -- protect tender annual flowers
weather_triggers.body: Tender annual flowers like marigolds, nasturtiums, and zinnias are frost-sensitive. Cover with fleece tonight or bring containers inside. Hardy annuals like calendula and sweet peas handle light frost well.

weather_triggers.title: High humidity -- watch for powdery mildew on flowers
weather_triggers.body: Many flowers are prone to powdery mildew in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow between plants and avoid watering the foliage. Remove affected leaves promptly.

germination.text: Most perennial flowers can be started from seed but establish slowly -- expect to plant in year one and bloom in year two. Many gardeners buy young plants instead of starting from seed.

If sowing from seed, several of these crops benefit from cold stratification (4 to 6 weeks of cold moist treatment in the refrigerator) before sowing -- echinacea and lavender especially. Direct-sown seed in late fall accomplishes the same thing naturally.

seedling.text: Thin or transplant seedlings to recommended spacing once they have 4 to 6 true leaves. Perennials need their permanent home from the start -- moving them later disrupts establishment.
Mulch around young transplants to retain moisture and suppress weeds. Hand-weed close to the plant for the first season.

established.text: Year one is mostly about root development -- many perennials produce minimal foliage and few flowers in the first season. This is normal; resist the urge to give up on a slow-establishing perennial.

By year two most of these perennials hit their stride and begin producing the heavy bloom you planted them for. Echinacea and bee-balm especially become more impressive each year for the first 4 to 5 seasons.

budding.text: Most of these perennials have a single annual bloom window -- echinacea midsummer, lavender early-to-mid summer, bee-balm midsummer, viola spring and fall, chamomile early summer. Buds form weeks before bloom.
Watch lavender for spittlebug at bud stage -- the white foam on stems is unsightly but harmless and rarely needs intervention.

flowering.text: Deadheading extends bloom marginally on most perennials but does not transform their cycle the way it does for annuals -- a perennial generally has one main bloom window per year regardless of deadheading. Deadhead for tidiness rather than to chase a second bloom.

Many perennials attract specific pollinators -- echinacea and bee-balm are bumblebee and hummingbird favorites; lavender draws honey bees in numbers; viola attracts solitary bees. Avoid spraying anything during bloom.

seed_saving.text: Most of these perennials self-seed if you leave seed heads to mature. Echinacea seed heads are particularly attractive to goldfinches and other birds -- leaving them standing through fall is good wildlife support.

To save seed deliberately, collect dried seed heads on a dry day, separate seeds from chaff, and store in paper envelopes in a cool dry place. Most perennial flower seeds need cold stratification before they will germinate; a winter outdoors or in the refrigerator does this.

yield_expectations.per_plant: Continuous blooms throughout the season with regular deadheading
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Flowers in the vegetable garden are one of the most worthwhile additions -- beautiful, functional, and good for pollinators.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Cold or frost damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: These perennials are hardy through their respective USDA zones -- echinacea zones 3-8, bee-balm zones 4-9, lavender zones 5-9 (varies by species; English lavender is hardier than Spanish), viola zones 3-8, chamomile (Roman) zones 3-7. Hard winter cold below the variety's range causes crown damage and may kill the plant entirely.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Confirm your variety's hardiness range before relying on it as a perennial -- some plants sold as perennials are actually annuals or short-lived perennials in cold zones. Mulch crowns in the colder end of the variety's range. For lavender in zones 5-6, choose hardy English lavender (L. angustifolia) and plant on the south side of a wall.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Powdery mildew is the most common problem on bee-balm and to a lesser extent echinacea -- both develop white powdery patches on leaves in humid summers or where plants are crowded. Aster yellows is a viral disease that distorts echinacea flowers. Lavender suffers root rot in poorly-drained soil rather than insect pests.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Choose mildew-resistant bee-balm varieties (Marshall's Delight, Jacob Cline) and space generously for airflow. Remove and destroy plants showing aster yellows -- it spreads via leafhoppers and infected plants do not recover. For lavender, drainage prevention is better than disease cure.

failure_diagnostics.label: Stopped flowering
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Most of these perennials have a single bloom window per year and then move on -- this is not a failure but the plant's normal cycle. After the main bloom, leaves stay green for the rest of the season but no new flowers come. Deadheading extends bloom marginally; in some cases (viola) it can produce a second smaller bloom in fall.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Plan plantings with succession in mind so something different is blooming each month rather than expecting any single perennial to bloom continuously. Allow some seed heads to remain for wildlife and self-seeding.

failure_diagnostics.label: Wilting or stunted growth
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Lavender prefers dry conditions and is harmed by frequent watering -- drought is rarely lavender's problem. Bee-balm, echinacea, viola, and chamomile prefer consistent moisture and stress under drought, with leaf wilting and reduced bloom.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water bee-balm, echinacea, viola, and chamomile during dry spells -- 1 inch per week is the rough target. Lavender needs water only during establishment and prolonged drought; once established it actively resents regular watering.

failure_diagnostics.label: Leggy growth or poor bloom
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Most of these perennials prefer full sun. Lavender requires 6 to 8 hours of direct sun and grows poorly in any shade. Echinacea and bee-balm tolerate light afternoon shade. Viola actively prefers part shade in hot summers and may stop blooming in full sun once temperatures climb.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Match the variety to the available light. For shaded perennial-flower spots, viola is the most cooperative; for full sun, lavender, echinacea, and bee-balm all thrive.

crops.name: Sweet Pea
crops.description: Climbing annual with intensely fragrant flowers and nitrogen-fixing roots. Attracts early-season pollinators and improves soil for neighboring vegetables. Requires a trellis. NOTE: flowers and seeds are toxic -- do not eat.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces, stems, and sometimes fruit. Leaves may yellow and die. Worst in warm days with cool nights.
diseases.cause: Fungal disease favored by humid conditions with poor air circulation.
diseases.organic_treatment: Spray with diluted neem oil or a baking soda solution (1 tsp per quart water). Apply potassium bicarbonate spray. Remove and destroy affected leaves.
diseases.prevention: Space plants for good airflow. Water at soil level, not on foliage. Choose resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation.

germination.text: Sweet pea (Lathyrus odoratus) is a cool-season climbing legume, not a true pea. Sow seeds outdoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost, or start indoors in mid-winter and transplant out in early spring. Sweet pea is one of the few flowers that wants cold soil, not warm.
Soak seeds in water overnight before sowing to soften the hard coat -- some growers nick the seed coat with a file as well. Germination takes 10 to 21 days; do not give up early.

seedling.text: Pinch the growing tip when seedlings are 4 inches tall to encourage branching. This is the single most useful technique for boosting sweet pea yield.
Provide trellising before transplanting or as soon as direct-sown seedlings emerge. Sweet pea needs to climb from day one and resents being moved or having a trellis added later.

established.text: Train tendrils onto netting, twine, or wire support as plants climb. Some varieties grow 6 to 8 feet tall and need substantial support; bush varieties top out at 3 feet.
Water consistently and feed every 2 weeks with a balanced fertilizer -- sweet pea is one of the few flowers that responds well to regular feeding. Mulch heavily to keep roots cool.

budding.text: Buds form 8 to 10 weeks after sowing in spring-sown plants. The budding-to-flowering transition is fast in cool weather; faster than for most annual flowers.
Watch for powdery mildew at the bud stage, especially in still humid weather. Spacing and trellising for airflow are the main preventive measures.

flowering.text: Pick flowers regularly -- sweet pea is one of the all-time great cut flowers and the more you cut, the more it produces. A plant that goes to seed stops flowering completely; deadheading is essential here.

Heat ends the sweet pea bloom cycle -- when daytime temperatures consistently exceed 80 degrees, plants stop flowering and decline rapidly. In hot zones, sweet pea is over by early summer; cool zones may extend the bloom into July.

seed_saving.text: If saving seed, allow a few late flowers to set pods. The pods turn from green to brown and dry on the vine; collect when fully dry. Many sweet pea varieties are open-pollinated and come true from saved seed.

Plan to replace plants entirely each year -- sweet pea is a cool-season annual and does not repeat-perform from the same root system the way perennial vines do. Save seed or buy fresh seed each fall for next spring's sowing.

yield_expectations.per_plant: Generous early-season bloom flush; reduces sharply in summer heat
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Sweet peas are a cool-season crop -- early spring through early summer -- not a continuous summer flower. Plan for a flush rather than a season.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Cold tolerance and heat damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Sweet pea is unusual among flowers in tolerating cool weather and dying off in heat. Young plants tolerate light frost; mature plants flower through cool spring weather but stop and decline once daytime temperatures consistently exceed 80 degrees. The end of sweet pea is heat, not cold.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Sow as early as possible -- 4 to 6 weeks before last frost in most zones, or even in fall in mild-winter zones for spring bloom. Choose heat-tolerant varieties (Old Spice series, Cuthbertson types) for warmer zones, and accept that sweet pea is a spring crop only in hot regions.

failure_diagnostics.label: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Powdery mildew is the headline sweet pea disease, especially in still humid conditions or on crowded plantings. Aphids cluster on tender new growth. Slugs damage young seedlings. Sweet pea root rot can take hold in poorly-drained soil.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Space plants for airflow and trellis to keep foliage off the ground. Water at the base rather than overhead to keep foliage dry. For aphids, hose off or wait for predators. For slugs, set traps or use a barrier method around seedlings.

failure_diagnostics.label: Stopped flowering
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Two main causes: heat stress (the most common, when daytime temperatures exceed 80 degrees consistently) and seed set (the plant's signal that its job is done). A sweet pea that has set even a few seed pods stops producing new flowers; consistent deadheading or harvest prevents this.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Deadhead religiously -- check daily during peak bloom. In hot climates, accept that sweet pea has a 6 to 8 week window in spring and plan succession plantings of warm-season flowers to follow.

failure_diagnostics.label: Wilting or poor bloom
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Sweet pea has shallow roots and needs consistent moisture, especially during bloom. Drought stress shortens the bloom cycle and produces small flowers on short stems. Heat amplifies drought damage substantially.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water consistently -- 1 inch per week minimum, more in heat. Mulch heavily to keep roots cool and conserve moisture. Drip irrigation outperforms overhead watering for sweet pea by both providing consistent water and keeping foliage dry.

failure_diagnostics.label: Leggy or sparse growth
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Sweet pea needs full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to flower well. In partial shade plants grow tall and leafy with sparse bloom. In hot climates, light afternoon shade can extend the bloom cycle by reducing heat stress without compromising flower production.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Site in full sun in cool climates, full morning sun with afternoon shade in hot climates. South or southeast exposure is ideal.

crops.name: Radish Microgreens
crops.description: The fastest microgreen -- bold, peppery flavor ready in 5-7 days. One of the easiest crops to grow and a great entry point for microgreen beginners.
crops.tip: Radish microgreens are the best crop to start with -- they germinate in 24 hours and are ready in less than a week. Sow densely and keep the blackout lid on until you see the seed hulls rising.

watering.frequency: Mist 2-3 times daily during germination; once or twice daily once in light
watering.amount: Keep growing medium moist but never waterlogged
watering.method: Bottom watering or fine mist -- top watering can cause damping off
watering.signs_overwater: Gray mold, foul smell, stems rotting at base
watering.signs_underwater: Dry crispy sprouts, slow germination, wilting seedlings

crops.harvest_ready: Harvest at 5-7 days when cotyledons are fully open and bright purple-pink. Don't wait -- radish microgreens turn bitter and tough quickly. Cut at soil level with scissors.

storage.fridge: 5-7 days in a sealed container lined with paper towel
storage.freezer: Not suitable
storage.notes: Harvest and refrigerate immediately. Do not wash until ready to eat. The paper towel absorbs moisture and prevents rapid deterioration.

varieties.note: China Rose is the most widely grown radish microgreen -- reliable germination, consistent pink color, and excellent spicy flavor.

fertilizer.notes: Microgreens draw all their nutrition from the seed and growing medium. No fertilization needed for 5-7 day crops.

pests.name: Fungus gnats
pests.symptoms: Tiny flies around trays; larvae damage roots and stems at soil level
pests.cause: Overwatering creating wet growing medium
pests.organic_treatment: Allow medium to dry slightly between waterings; yellow sticky traps
pests.prevention: Don't overwater; use clean growing medium; bottom-water where possible

diseases.name: Damping off
diseases.symptoms: Seedlings collapse at soil line, stems thin and water-soaked
diseases.cause: Overwatering, poor airflow, contaminated medium
diseases.organic_treatment: Improve airflow; reduce watering; discard affected tray and start fresh
diseases.prevention: Use clean trays; don't overwater; sow at correct density; ensure airflow

start_method.notes: Sow seeds densely (cover tray surface) on damp growing medium. No soaking needed. Cover with second tray for 2-3 day blackout phase, then move to light.

container_notes.notes: Grown in shallow 10×20 inch trays -- standard propagation trays work perfectly. No minimum gallon requirement.

rotation.avoid_after: N/A
rotation.note: Indoor tray crop -- no rotation needed. Clean trays between batches.

3.notes: Indoor year-round. No soaking needed -- sow dry directly on growing medium.

growth_stages.name: Sowing
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Seeds evenly distributed on moist growing medium.
growth_stages.user_action: Sow densely and evenly. Mist thoroughly, cover with a blackout lid or second tray, and press down firmly to ensure seed contact with the medium.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Seeds sprouting -- white roots and pale shoots pushing up under the blackout cover.
growth_stages.user_action: Leave covered and check moisture daily. The weight of the tray on top helps seeds develop straight, strong stems.

growth_stages.name: Blackout Phase
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Shoots pushing against the lid -- they should be pale yellow and reaching upward.
growth_stages.user_action: When shoots are pressing against the blackout cover, move to light. The stretch in darkness builds stem length.

growth_stages.name: Growing in Light
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Greening up fast as chlorophyll develops. Cotyledons (seed leaves) opening fully.
growth_stages.user_action: Water from below by setting the tray in water and allowing it to absorb upward -- this avoids mold on the surface. Harvest when seed leaves are fully open.

notifications.title: Move your microgreens to light
notifications.body: Your microgreens should be ready to move from blackout to light -- check that shoots are pressing against the cover. Move to a bright windowsill or under grow lights now. They will green up within hours.

notifications.title: Check your microgreens for harvest
notifications.body: Microgreens are ready when the seed leaves are fully open and the first true leaves are just beginning to show. Harvest with scissors just above the soil line. Rinse and use immediately for the best flavor.

sow.text: Sow densely -- microgreens are one of the few crops where crowding is desirable. Even coverage without gaps gives the best harvest.
Soak large seeds (sunflower, peas) overnight before sowing. They germinate more evenly and quickly.

germination.text: The weight of a tray or board on top helps seeds press into the medium and develop straight, strong stems in the dark.
Check moisture once a day -- the medium should be moist but not waterlogged. If it feels wet on top, wait before misting again.

blackout.text: Darkness forces upward growth and builds stem length. The stretch is intentional and desirable.
If shoots are very pale or yellow after 5+ days, they have been in blackout too long. Move to light immediately.

light.text: Bottom watering prevents mold, which is the main challenge with microgreens. Set the tray in water for 10-15 minutes rather than misting the surface.
Harvest in the morning when the plants are full of water. Cut, rinse immediately, and use within a day or two.

yield_expectations.per_plant: One tray yields 50-200g depending on variety and tray size
yield_expectations.peak_production: Ready in 7-14 days -- the fastest crop you can grow
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Microgreens are instant gratification -- from seed to harvest in under two weeks. Perfect for getting children interested in growing.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

succession.tip: Sow a new tray every 1-2 weeks year-round indoors. Each tray is a single harvest -- cut at soil level when seed leaves are fully open. Keep 2-3 trays going at different stages so you always have something ready.

failure_diagnostics.label: White fuzzy mold on the surface
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Surface mold is caused by overwatering or poor airflow. It is different from the white root hairs that are completely normal and healthy -- root hairs are orderly and attached to stems, mold is fuzzy and appears on the soil surface.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water from below by setting the tray in water -- never mist the surface once seeds have germinated. Ensure good airflow around the tray.

failure_diagnostics.label: Seedlings fell over at the base
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Damping off is a fungal condition that rots the stem at soil level. It is caused by overwet, poorly ventilated conditions -- especially in the blackout phase.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Do not overwater during germination. Ensure the growing medium is moist but not wet before sowing. Improve airflow once seedlings emerge.

failure_diagnostics.label: Seeds did not germinate evenly
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Patchy germination is usually caused by uneven seed contact with the growing medium, or the surface drying out during germination. Larger seeds like sunflower and peas benefit from pre-soaking.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Press seeds firmly into the surface after sowing. Soak larger seeds for 8 hours before sowing. Ensure the medium is thoroughly moist before you start.

failure_diagnostics.label: Seedlings stayed yellow and pale
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Microgreens kept in blackout for too long become etiolated -- pale, stretched, and weak. Once moved to light they should green up within hours. If they do not, they have been in darkness too long.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Move to light as soon as shoots are pressing against the blackout cover -- usually day 3-5. They green up fast once in light. Do not wait until they look fully grown under the dome.

failure_diagnostics.label: Wilted or crispy after moving to light
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Microgreens dry out fast under grow lights or in a sunny window. They need consistent moisture from below during the light phase.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water from below once a day during the light phase -- set the tray in a shallow dish of water for 10-15 minutes and let it absorb upward.

indoor_cycle.tip: The fastest microgreen. Mild peppery flavor. Sow thickly for a dense mat. No pre-soaking needed.

crops.name: Broccoli Microgreens
crops.description: One of the most nutritionally dense microgreens -- contains up to 100× the sulforaphane of mature broccoli. Mild, slightly earthy flavor with a satisfying crunch.
crops.tip: Broccoli microgreens are worth growing for the nutrition alone -- the sulforaphane content is highest when harvested young (8-10 days). Mist evenly and keep good airflow to prevent mold on the dense canopy.

watering.frequency: Mist twice daily -- morning and evening
watering.amount: Keep medium moist throughout -- broccoli doesn't tolerate drying out
watering.method: Bottom watering after the blackout phase; mist lightly from above to maintain humidity
watering.signs_overwater: White fuzzy mold on stems (different from root hairs -- mold is fuzzy, root hairs are straight)
watering.signs_underwater: Slow growth, wilting despite watered medium, pale yellow leaves

crops.harvest_ready: Harvest at 8-10 days when first true leaves just begin to form but cotyledons are still the main leaf. Cut at soil level. The window is narrow -- harvest on time for maximum sulforaphane.

storage.fridge: 5-7 days in a sealed container with paper towel
storage.freezer: Not suitable
storage.notes: Broccoli microgreens are more perishable than radish. Refrigerate immediately and consume within a week.

recommended: Red Acre Cabbage blend (adds color to mix)
varieties.note: Standard broccoli seed works well -- no special microgreen variety needed. Buy untreated seeds only (fungicide-treated seeds are not safe for eating as microgreens).

fertilizer.notes: Seed nutrients are sufficient for the 8-12 day growing period.

pests.name: Fungus gnats
pests.symptoms: Small flies near trays; larvae in growing medium
pests.cause: Overwatering
pests.organic_treatment: Reduce watering; bottom-water only; yellow sticky traps
pests.prevention: Good airflow; clean growing medium; don't overwater

diseases.name: Mold / damping off
diseases.symptoms: Fuzzy white or gray mold on stems or growing medium surface
diseases.cause: Overwatering, high humidity, poor airflow, sowing too densely
diseases.organic_treatment: Increase airflow with a small fan; reduce watering; harvest immediately if mold appears
diseases.prevention: Good airflow; correct sowing density; don't overwater; clean trays between batches

start_method.notes: Sow densely on damp medium. Blackout for 3 days, then move to light. A small fan for airflow dramatically reduces mold risk on dense brassica canopies.

container_notes.notes: Standard 10×20 propagation trays. Good airflow around the tray is important to prevent mold.

rotation.avoid_after: N/A
rotation.note: Clean and sanitize trays between batches to prevent disease carryover.

crops.name: Arugula Microgreens
crops.description: Intensely peppery -- more flavorful as a microgreen than at any other stage. Small delicate leaves with a big flavor punch. Ready in 7-10 days.
crops.tip: Arugula microgreens are one of the most satisfying to grow -- the flavor is extraordinarily intense, much more so than mature arugula. Mucilaginous seeds will clump when wet -- scatter dry and mist gently.

watering.frequency: Mist twice daily -- arugula is more drought-tolerant than other microgreens
watering.amount: Keep medium lightly moist -- arugula can handle slightly drier conditions than peas or broccoli
watering.method: Fine mist from above or bottom watering. Note: arugula seeds are mucilaginous (gel-coated) -- they will clump if soaked

crops.harvest_ready: Harvest at 7-10 days when cotyledons are fully open. The characteristic peppery bite is strongest at this stage -- don't wait for true leaves or flavor fades.

storage.fridge: 3-5 days -- arugula microgreens are more perishable than radish
storage.freezer: Not suitable
storage.notes: Very perishable. Harvest just before serving for maximum flavor and texture.

varieties.note: Standard arugula seed works well. Avoid treated seeds. Wild arugula varieties produce more intense flavor.

fertilizer.notes: No fertilization needed for the short growing period.

pests.name: Fungus gnats
pests.symptoms: Small flies near trays
pests.cause: Overwatering
pests.organic_treatment: Reduce watering frequency; yellow sticky traps
pests.prevention: Good airflow; clean medium; bottom watering

diseases.name: Damping off
diseases.symptoms: Seedlings collapse at soil line
diseases.cause: Overwatering and poor airflow
diseases.organic_treatment: Discard tray; improve airflow; reduce watering
diseases.prevention: Don't overwater; use clean medium; good airflow

start_method.notes: Scatter seeds dry -- do not pre-soak or wet before sowing, as arugula seeds are mucilaginous and will form a sticky mass. Sow evenly and mist gently after placing. Blackout 2-3 days.

container_notes.notes: Standard 10×20 trays. Arugula microgreens tolerate slightly lower light than other varieties.

rotation.avoid_after: N/A
rotation.note: Clean trays between batches.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Microgreens dry out fast under grow lights or in a sunny window. They need consistent moisture from below during the light phase.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water from below once a day during the light phase -- set the tray in a shallow dish of water for 10-15 minutes and let it absorb upward.

indoor_cycle.tip: Peppery, nutty flavor. Prefers slightly cooler temperatures (60-68 degrees F) than other microgreens. Harvest at first true leaf for best flavor.

crops.name: Wheatgrass
crops.description: The classic juicing green -- rich in chlorophyll, enzymes, and vitamins. Harvest at 7-10 days for juicing or adding to smoothies. One of the most productive crops per tray.
crops.tip: Soak wheat berries for 8-12 hours before sowing -- this is the key difference from other microgreens. Hard red winter wheat is the most reliable variety. Harvest just before the second leaf blade emerges for peak nutrition.

watering.frequency: Water once daily -- wheatgrass needs consistent moisture but tolerates less frequent watering than other microgreens
watering.amount: Keep medium consistently moist -- wheatgrass is thirsty
watering.method: Bottom watering is ideal -- fill the bottom tray and let medium absorb. Avoids wetting the grass blades which can cause mold.
watering.signs_overwater: Mold at base of grass blades, yellowing from the base up
watering.signs_underwater: Tips yellowing, slow growth, dry brittle texture

crops.harvest_ready: Harvest at 7-10 days when grass is 6-8 inches tall and the second blade is just beginning to emerge (the 'joining' stage). Cut just above the growing medium. Can sometimes get a second cut -- juice quality drops significantly.

storage.fridge: Cut wheatgrass: 1 week standing upright in a cup with a small amount of water. Juice: 24 hours maximum.
storage.freezer: Freeze juice in ice cube trays -- good for up to 6 months
storage.notes: Wheatgrass juice oxidizes rapidly -- juice and drink immediately for maximum nutrition. Frozen juice cubes are a practical way to preserve a large harvest.

recommended: Hard Red Winter Wheat (most widely grown, reliable)
varieties.note: Hard Red Winter Wheat is the standard -- widely available as wheat berries from health food stores. Use whole, unhulled berries only.

fertilizer.notes: Wheatgrass draws entirely from the seed and medium. No fertilization needed.

pests.name: Mold at base
pests.symptoms: White or gray fuzzy mold at soil line between grass blades
pests.cause: Overwatering, poor airflow, sowing too densely
pests.organic_treatment: Harvest immediately if mold appears; improve airflow with a small fan
pests.prevention: Bottom-water only; good airflow; correct sowing density; don't let medium stay waterlogged

diseases.name: Root rot
diseases.symptoms: Yellowing from roots up, slimy roots, collapse before harvest
diseases.cause: Waterlogged growing medium
diseases.organic_treatment: Improve drainage; discard tray
diseases.prevention: Never let trays sit in standing water; drain thoroughly after bottom watering

start_method.notes: Soak wheat berries 8-12 hours before sowing. Rinse well. Sow densely in a single even layer -- berries should touch but not pile up. Blackout for 3 days, then move to bright light.

container_notes.notes: Standard 10×20 trays. Wheatgrass needs more light than most microgreens -- place in the brightest spot available or under a grow light.

rotation.avoid_after: N/A
rotation.note: Sanitize trays between batches. Mold can persist in tray crevices.

growth_stages.name: Sowing
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Seeds evenly distributed on moist growing medium.
growth_stages.user_action: Sow densely and evenly. Mist thoroughly, cover with a blackout lid or second tray, and press down firmly to ensure seed contact with the medium.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Seeds sprouting -- white roots and pale shoots pushing up under the blackout cover.
growth_stages.user_action: Leave covered and check moisture daily. The weight of the tray on top helps seeds develop straight, strong stems.

growth_stages.name: Blackout Phase
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Shoots pushing against the lid -- they should be pale yellow and reaching upward.
growth_stages.user_action: When shoots are pressing against the blackout cover, move to light. The stretch in darkness builds stem length.

growth_stages.name: Growing in Light
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Greening up fast as chlorophyll develops. Cotyledons (seed leaves) opening fully.
growth_stages.user_action: Water from below by setting the tray in water and allowing it to absorb upward -- this avoids mold on the surface. Harvest when seed leaves are fully open.

notifications.title: Move your microgreens to light
notifications.body: Your microgreens should be ready to move from blackout to light -- check that shoots are pressing against the cover. Move to a bright windowsill or under grow lights now. They will green up within hours.

notifications.title: Check your microgreens for harvest
notifications.body: Microgreens are ready when the seed leaves are fully open and the first true leaves are just beginning to show. Harvest with scissors just above the soil line. Rinse and use immediately for the best flavor.

sow.text: Sow densely -- microgreens are one of the few crops where crowding is desirable. Even coverage without gaps gives the best harvest.
Soak large seeds (sunflower, peas) overnight before sowing. They germinate more evenly and quickly.

germination.text: The weight of a tray or board on top helps seeds press into the medium and develop straight, strong stems in the dark.
Check moisture once a day -- the medium should be moist but not waterlogged. If it feels wet on top, wait before misting again.

blackout.text: Darkness forces upward growth and builds stem length. The stretch is intentional and desirable.
If shoots are very pale or yellow after 5+ days, they have been in blackout too long. Move to light immediately.

light.text: Bottom watering prevents mold, which is the main challenge with microgreens. Set the tray in water for 10-15 minutes rather than misting the surface.
Harvest in the morning when the plants are full of water. Cut, rinse immediately, and use within a day or two.

yield_expectations.per_plant: One tray yields 50-200g depending on variety and tray size
yield_expectations.peak_production: Ready in 7-14 days -- the fastest crop you can grow
yield_expectations.first_year_note: Microgreens are instant gratification -- from seed to harvest in under two weeks. Perfect for getting children interested in growing.

moon_phase_preference.source_note: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

succession.tip: Sow a new tray every 1-2 weeks year-round indoors. Each tray is a single harvest -- cut at soil level when seed leaves are fully open. Keep 2-3 trays going at different stages so you always have something ready.

failure_diagnostics.label: White fuzzy mold on the surface
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Surface mold is caused by overwatering or poor airflow. It is different from the white root hairs that are completely normal and healthy -- root hairs are orderly and attached to stems, mold is fuzzy and appears on the soil surface.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water from below by setting the tray in water -- never mist the surface once seeds have germinated. Ensure good airflow around the tray.

failure_diagnostics.label: Seedlings fell over at the base
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Damping off is a fungal condition that rots the stem at soil level. It is caused by overwet, poorly ventilated conditions -- especially in the blackout phase.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Do not overwater during germination. Ensure the growing medium is moist but not wet before sowing. Improve airflow once seedlings emerge.

failure_diagnostics.label: Seeds did not germinate evenly
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Patchy germination is usually caused by uneven seed contact with the growing medium, or the surface drying out during germination. Larger seeds like sunflower and peas benefit from pre-soaking.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Press seeds firmly into the surface after sowing. Soak larger seeds for 8 hours before sowing. Ensure the medium is thoroughly moist before you start.

failure_diagnostics.label: Seedlings stayed yellow and pale
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Microgreens kept in blackout for too long become etiolated -- pale, stretched, and weak. Once moved to light they should green up within hours. If they do not, they have been in darkness too long.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Move to light as soon as shoots are pressing against the blackout cover -- usually day 3-5. They green up fast once in light. Do not wait until they look fully grown under the dome.

failure_diagnostics.label: Wilted or crispy after moving to light
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: Microgreens dry out fast under grow lights or in a sunny window. They need consistent moisture from below during the light phase.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Water from below once a day during the light phase -- set the tray in a shallow dish of water for 10-15 minutes and let it absorb upward.

indoor_cycle.tip: Soak wheat berries 8-12 hours before sowing. Very dense planting. Harvest when grass is 6-7 inches tall by clipping just above soil. Juice fresh -- wheatgrass loses potency within hours.

crops.name: Cilantro Microgreens
crops.description: The slowest of the microgreens -- 14-21 days -- but with distinctive, intense cilantro flavor that's highly sought after in Asian and Latin cooking. Worth the patience.
crops.tip: Cilantro microgreens require cracking the seeds before sowing. The 'seed' is actually a fruit containing two seeds -- crush lightly with a rolling pin to split, or soak for 24 hours first. This dramatically improves germination.

watering.frequency: Once daily -- cilantro microgreens are more drought-tolerant and slower growing
watering.amount: Keep medium lightly moist -- less water than pea shoots or broccoli
watering.method: Bottom watering preferred -- top watering can mat and rot the dense canopy
watering.signs_overwater: Mold, collapsed seedlings, very slow germination

crops.harvest_ready: Harvest at 14-21 days when first true leaves begin to emerge alongside cotyledons. The flavor is most intense just as true leaves appear. Cut at soil level.

storage.freezer: Not suitable
storage.notes: More robust than arugula microgreens. Keep dry and refrigerated.

recommended: Calypso (slow bolt -- useful for longer growing window)
varieties.note: Crack or pre-soak all cilantro seeds regardless of variety -- this is the single biggest factor in germination success.

fertilizer.notes: For the longer 14-21 day growing period, a dilute liquid seaweed feed on day 10 can help if growth seems slow.

pests.name: Fungus gnats
pests.symptoms: Small flies near trays; larvae in medium
pests.cause: Overwatering during the longer growing period
pests.organic_treatment: Yellow sticky traps; reduce watering
pests.prevention: Good airflow; don't overwater; clean medium

diseases.name: Damping off / mold
diseases.symptoms: Seedlings collapse, mold at soil line
diseases.cause: Overwatering and poor airflow during the long germination period
diseases.organic_treatment: Discard tray; improve airflow; reduce watering
diseases.prevention: Don't overwater; crack seeds before sowing; good airflow throughout

start_method.notes: Essential step: lightly crush seeds with a rolling pin to split the seed hull, OR soak for 24 hours before sowing. Without this, germination is patchy and slow. Sow on damp medium, blackout 4-5 days.

container_notes.notes: Standard 10×20 trays. The longer growing time means more attention to airflow and watering consistency.

rotation.avoid_after: N/A
rotation.note: Clean trays thoroughly between batches.

uscrn.name: NOAA U.S. Climate Reference Network (USCRN)
uscrn.publisher: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information / Atmospheric Turbulence and Diffusion Division
uscrn.note: Network-level reference: Diamond, H.J., T.R. Karl, M.A. Palecki, C.B. Baker, J.E. Bell, R.D. Leeper, D.R. Easterling, J.H. Lawrimore, T.P. Meyers, M.R. Helfert, G. Goodge, and P.W. Thorne, 2013: U.S. Climate Reference Network after One Decade of Operations: Status and Assessment. Bull. Amer. Meteor. Soc., 94(4), 485-498. DOI: 10.1175/BAMS-D-12-00170.1. Soil moisture and temperature methodology reference: Bell, J.E., M.A. Palecki, C.B. Baker, W.G. Collins, J.H. Lawrimore, R.D. Leeper, M.E. Hall, J. Kochendorfer, T.P. Meyers, T. Wilson, and H.J. Diamond, 2013: U.S. Climate Reference Network Soil Moisture and Temperature Observations. J. Hydrometeor., 14(3), 977-988. DOI: 10.1175/JHM-D-12-0146.1. Triplicate-redundancy variability companion: Palecki, M.A., and J.E. Bell, 2013: U.S. Climate Reference Network Soil Moisture Observations with Triple Redundancy: Measurement Variability. Vadose Zone J., 12(2), vzj2012.0158. DOI: 10.2136/vzj2012.0158. USCRN provides the soil-temperature observations used to validate this dataset's soil-temp planting anchors at zone level. Soil moisture and temperature are measured in triplicate at five depths (5, 10, 20, 50, and 100 cm); anchors in this dataset are validated against the 5 cm depth record.
uscrn.citable_for: NOAA US Climate Reference Network station-level climate data. Citable for soil-temperature, air-temperature, and precipitation observational data feeding the Phase 1.1 anchor pipeline. Not citable for biological-mechanism claims.

weatherkit.name: Apple WeatherKit
weatherkit.note: WeatherKit is the resolution-layer data source for bolt-threshold and heat-pause anchors. Underlying service: Apple Weather. Data products used: current conditions, hourly forecast (10-day, up to 240 hours), and daily forecast (10 days). Coverage: global, with US coordinate-level resolution adequate for gardener microclimate purposes; updates hourly to sub-hourly. WeatherKit is a forecast service, not a historical-validation dataset; its role in this dataset is resolution at notification time, not validation. Known limitation: 10-day forecast horizon constrains sustain-window math for bolt thresholds in cool-season crops where the relevant window can exceed 10 days; the methodology page documents the resolution approach for that case. Per Apple's WeatherKit attribution requirements, apps that display Apple Weather data must include the Apple Weather trademark and a link to additional data sources.
weatherkit.citable_for: Apple WeatherKit API for weather forecast and current-conditions data. Citable for forecast-driven app behavior. Not citable for biological-mechanism claims; not a research source.
